A 502 FROM A MUTATING GITHUB ENDPOINT DOES NOT MEAN THE MUTATION DID NOT HAPPEN — do not retry it (2026-08-06).

WHAT HAPPENED: gh pr merge returned exit 1 with "non-200 OK status code: 502 Bad Gateway" from nginx. The PR still read state=OPEN, mergeable=MERGEABLE, mergeState=CLEAN, 0 fails, 0 pending - every signal saying "retry me". I retried three times. Each subsequent attempt failed with a DIFFERENT error: "GraphQL: Merge already in progress (mergePullRequest)".

SO THE FIRST CALL SUCCEEDED SERVER-SIDE AND ONLY ITS RESPONSE WAS LOST. The 502 was a failure to hear the answer, not a failure to act. Every retry was fighting a merge that was already running, and the PR reading OPEN was just the API not yet reflecting an in-flight operation.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE SECOND ERROR, NOT THE FIRST. A genuine "merge did not happen" retries into the same 502 or into a real refusal (CONFLICTING, failing checks). "Already in progress" is positive evidence the first attempt took. Read the error TEXT on retry rather than the exit code.

AND CHECK WHETHER THE API IS BROADLY UNHEALTHY BEFORE ASSUMING AN OUTAGE: gh api rate_limit, gh pr list and git ls-remote were all fine here, which localised it to one in-flight merge rather than a GitHub incident. That took one command and stopped me diagnosing the wrong thing.

THE ACTION IS TO WAIT ONE TICK. The merge completes on its own; the next survey shows it MERGED. This is the same family as the reaping and merging errors this session - a signal that reads as "nothing happened" when something did - but with the polarity reversed, which is why it fooled me for four attempts.

A 502 ON gh pr merge --rebase CAN LAND THE COMMITS ON TRUNK WHILE THE PR STAYS OPEN FOR GOOD - so neither PR state nor waiting a tick is the effect check (2026-09-13). Extends 502-on-merge-means-it-may-have-happened, whose closing line ("the next survey shows it MERGED") did not hold here.

WHAT HAPPENED: twice in one session (PR #9788 and PR #9786) the rebase-merge returned 502 Bad Gateway, the PR read state=OPEN mergedAt=null, and it never flipped - #9788 was still OPEN over half an hour later and had to be closed by hand. Yet the content WAS on main: #9788 as 50c19ddaec, #9786 as 6f8cd459b2, each a rebased commit whose git patch-id --stable equals the PR head's. Three other 502s the same day (#9780, #9785, #9786's first attempt) genuinely did not land. So a 502 splits three ways: landed-and-MERGED, landed-but-OPEN, not-landed.

THE EFFECT CHECK IS TRUNK CONTENT, NOT PR STATE: git fetch origin main, then git cherry origin/main origin/<branch> ('-' = an equivalent commit is on trunk, '+' = not), or compare git patch-id --stable of the PR head against trunk commits touching the PR's files. Only a '+' licenses a retry. A '-' means fast-forward the checkout, record the landing on the beads, and close the PR with a comment naming the trunk sha.

THE CLOSE ITSELF CAN 502 AND LAND LATE: #9788's close returned 502 and took effect; check state before re-closing, and check for an existing comment by count before re-commenting.

A MERGE GUARD MUST NOT READ gh pr merge's RETURN AS THE VERDICT - have it re-read the PR state and exit distinctly (not 0) when the state is not MERGED, so a chained fast-forward cannot follow an unconfirmed merge.

A BEAD CAN BE WIDENED BY THE AUDIT WHILE A WORKER IS ALREADY HOLDING IT, AND A CORRECT NEWEST-FIRST WALK AT DISPATCH TIME WILL MISS IT (2026-09-03).

MEASURED. A worker on rf2-6me0 did the history walk exactly as prescribed and CORRECTLY reported zero text changes — because at that moment there were none. The audit's expansion landed at 02:11:24, minutes later, while the worker was mid-task. It discovered this only because 'bd close' echoed back a title it had never seen; it re-walked the history, REOPENED the bead, and did the widened work in a second commit.

WHY THE EXISTING RULES DO NOT COVER THIS. Everything written about bead currency is about the read at the START — order by tracker timestamps, walk newest-first, the description is the oldest text. All of that is correct and all of it is a read of a SNAPSHOT. Nothing says the snapshot can move under you, and on this project it routinely can: the merged-PR audit runs continuously and reopens or rewrites beads as it goes, which is the same mechanism that makes 'this cluster is the entire remaining backlog for the lane' a false claim.

THE CHEAP DEFENCE, WHICH COST THIS WORKER NOTHING AND SAVED THE TASK: READ WHAT bd ECHOES BACK. Close and update commands print the bead's CURRENT title. If that title is not the one you have been working from, the bead moved — stop and re-walk before believing your work is complete. That is a free check on every mutation you were going to make anyway.

THE SECOND DEFENCE, for a long task: re-walk the history once more before writing the PR body, not only at dispatch. A bead held for an hour on this project has a real chance of having been rewritten.

AND THE MAYOR-SIDE VERSION OF THE SAME THING: do not treat a brief's account of a bead as durable. Tell workers the bead outranks the brief — which the dispatch template already says — AND that the bead outranks the bead as they first read it.

A BEAD'S DESCRIPTION CAN DESCRIBE WORK THAT BEAD ITSELF ALREADY DID — CHECK THE COMMIT LOG FOR THE BEAD'S OWN ID BEFORE DISPATCHING (2026-08-21, rf2-w01c).

WHAT NEARLY HAPPENED. rf2-w01c's description says 'topo/ has no clock driver at all' and asks a worker to build one. I was about to dispatch that. Measured first: implementation/hicasso/test/re_frame/bench/hicasso/topo/clock_app.cljs exists at 673 lines and clock_witness_dom_cljs_test.cljs at 288, and clock_app.cljs names the 4x4 table 11 times.

THE DECISIVE EVIDENCE WAS THE COMMIT SUBJECT, not the file listing. git log on that path returns 23f3d13064, 2026-08-16: 'feat(hicasso): the topology tournament's clock table gets a driver (rf2-w01c)'. THE BEAD BUILT ITS OWN DELIVERABLE FIVE DAYS EARLIER AND ITS DESCRIPTION WAS NEVER UPDATED. A second commit, 858cf77e9d on 2026-08-18 (rf2-yorfi), refined it further.

WHY THIS SHAPE IS EASY TO MISS. A bead that is 'partly done' usually reads as partly done. This one reads as NOT STARTED, in its most prominent field, while its own id appears in the commit that completed the work. Nothing in the tracker links the two: the commit cites the bead, but the bead does not cite the commit. And a long-lived bead with a build half and a measure half is exactly where it happens, because the build half lands, the bead legitimately stays open for the measurement, and the description keeps describing the world before the build.

THE CHEAP CHECK, one command, before any dispatch that says 'build X': git log --format='%h %cI %s' -- <the path the bead names>, and READ THE SUBJECTS FOR THE BEAD'S OWN ID. If the bead id appears there, the description is describing a world that ended. Do this in addition to grepping for the alleged missing symbol — the grep tells you the file exists, the log tells you WHO built it and under which bead, which is what distinguishes 'someone else overtook this' from 'this bead already did it'.

WHAT REMAINED HERE, and it changes the dispatch entirely: only the WINDOW. The estimand is CLOCK, so it needs a quiet box rather than a free bench slot, and it is not dispatchable while other workers are live. The bead is now bannered at the top of its DESCRIPTION with that correction — see [dispatch-directive-must-live-in-the-description], which is the same remedy for the same class of failure.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: [dispatch-directive-must-live-in-the-description] covers a directive that lives only in NOTES. This is the other half — a DESCRIPTION that is not merely missing a directive but is affirmatively false about the tree, and false in the direction that manufactures work.

A bead whose fix has landed but which stays open for a LIVE WITNESS must say so in its DESCRIPTION's first line, not only in its notes — rf2-amh0 consumed three worker slots because three mayors briefed from its description, which still reads as a current bug report. The general rule: when a bead is reopened by a merged-PR audit for an observation rather than for work, prepend a STOP banner to the description and retitle it, because bd list and bd ready show the title and briefs get written from the description.

A BLOB-HASH "MISMATCH" CAN BE MSYS PATH MANGLING, NOT A REAL MISMATCH — but I TESTED IT and the plain form is safe (2026-07-26).

THE REPORT: the viewer-404 worker hit a blob-hash MISMATCH that was "MSYS mangling : into ;". It re-verified in PowerShell and ALL FOUR BLOBS MATCHED. So the mismatch was in the measuring instrument, not the artefact.

I TESTED IT IMMEDIATELY RATHER THAN PROPAGATE IT, because three of my standing hazards proved false today. IN THE PLAIN FORM IT DOES NOT REPRODUCE: git rev-parse HEAD:scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, the quoted form, --verify, and git ls-tree ALL RETURN THE SAME HASH here. So "MSYS mangles the ref:path colon" is NOT a general truth and must not go into briefs as one.

WHAT IS LIKELY ACTUALLY HAPPENING: MSYS converts arguments that look like Windows paths, and a WORKTREE-ABSOLUTE path such as C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2-worktrees/... carries its own colon. A comparison across worktrees using absolute paths is the shape that gets mangled — not HEAD:relative/path. The worker was comparing two worktrees; I was not.

THE PRACTICAL RULE, narrow and verified: a blob-hash MISMATCH IS NOT AUTOMATICALLY A CONTENT DIFFERENCE. Before acting on one, re-run it a second way. Two colon-free alternatives exist and both work here: git ls-tree <ref> <path> | awk to take the hash, or re-run in PowerShell. AND USE REPO-RELATIVE PATHS, never worktree-absolute ones, in git arguments.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A NORMAL HAZARD: I MANDATE BLOB-HASH VERIFICATION IN EVERY BRIEF as the way to confirm what landed — it is what caught a bead I closed on a merge that did not carry it, an hour ago. AN UNRELIABLE VERIFIER IS WORSE THAN NONE, because it produces false alarms on correct work and would train workers to distrust the one check that has been catching real stale merges all day. Twenty PRs today merged a state older than the worker tip; blob hash is how that is found.

AND THE DISCIPLINE THAT MADE THIS RECORDABLE RATHER THAN CARGO-CULTED: the worker did not report "blob mismatch, something is wrong". It re-measured a second way, found the instrument at fault, and said so. That is the third false signal it caught in one bead — the others being an rc=1 from Node module resolution in a throwaway dir, and a waitForSelector timeout that was a same-document hash-navigation trap.

A BY-NAME LAW IS ONLY AS TOTAL AS ITS NAMING FUNCTION — the D022 defect worth generalising (2026-07-26, PR #7081).

THE DEFECT: the disjoint-plane guard compared RAW CLOJURE KEYS, while the crossing named keyword keys by `name` and everything else by `str`. So :key / "key" / :x/key all collapsed onto ONE React prop name — as did :children / "children" and :onSelect / "onSelect" — AND EVERY SECOND SPELLING WALKED PAST THE CHECK WRITTEN TO STOP IT. The guard was not weak; it was comparing in a different space from the thing it guarded.

THE FIX SHAPE, AND IT IS THE ONE THIS ARTEFACT KEEPS CONVERGING ON: it was closed AT THE NAMING BOUNDARY, NOT PER CHECK. A host prop name is EXACT — an unqualified keyword, which is ALREADY THE LAW the declaration states for :callbacks. That makes host-prop-name TOTAL, and every by-name law total with it, SO NO NEW PER-CHECK MACHINERY APPEARS. Fixing it per-check would have added N guards and left the N+1th wrong.

THE GENERALISATION: WHENEVER A CHECK AND THE THING IT CHECKS DISAGREE ABOUT IDENTITY, FIX THE IDENTITY FUNCTION, NOT THE CHECK. Ask what canonical form the law is stated over, and make one function total for it. This is the same move as making a projector reach by SHAPE rather than by a slot roster (rf2-wd9im), and the same as keying a pairing off the WHOLE operation keyword rather than its name half (rf2-6tags) — three instances this week of "a list of cases is a roster that rots; a total function is not".

TWO PROCESS NOTES FROM THE SAME PR WORTH KEEPING. (1) IT VIOLATED A FENCE I SET, CORRECTLY: react.cljs was fenced to a live optimisation worker, but the defect lives in host-props/host-element — D022 own code. It disclosed the violation, and VERIFIED the just-merged optimisation was untouched by checking line ranges (optimisation at 187-836, host block starts at 930) and confirming none of its six changes was altered. That is how to cross a fence: unavoidable, disclosed, and proven non-conflicting.

(2) ITS NON-VACUITY ARGUMENT IS THE BEST FORM I HAVE SEEN: the browser delta +5 tests / +27 assertions is EXACTLY its file browser-mode count, WHICH PROVES NO MOUNTED ROW TOOK THE skip! PATH. A raw count would not show that. And it REPLAYED THE MOUNTED ASSERTIONS TEN FURTHER TIMES — 11 runs byte-identical — applying the flaky-green rule unprompted.

A CAPPED LISTING USED AS A LOCATOR LICENSES A FALSE **ABSENCE** CLAIM, AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT AND WORSE REGISTER THAN THE COUNT TRAP CLAUDE.md ALREADY RECORDS. Measured 2026-09-20 on this repo, by the mayor, against itself.

CLAUDE.md instrument item (b) says: never pipe a census through `head` when the COUNT is the deliverable, because the cap reports itself as the population. TRUE, AND NOT THE WHOLE SHAPE. The count is often NOT what you are asking for — you are asking WHERE something is, to check a citation. A capped locator hands back real, correct, verifiable hits, so nothing reads as broken; and then the next inference is the damaging one: **"the site is not in this listing, therefore the cited line is stale."** Absence inferred from a truncated listing, asserted about someone else's correct work.

WHAT IT COST. Verifying an item's citations before briefing a worker, I ran `grep -n ":source :store" <file> | head -5` and `grep -n "schemas-by-frame" <file> | head -5`. The true counts are **7** and **19**. Both real call sites sat past the cap — `interceptors/panel.cljs:494` and `schemas/panel.cljs:547-555` — i.e. EXACTLY where the item said they were. I concluded "neither resolves at this trunk", wrote a table headed "THE ITEM'S NUMBERS ARE ALL STALE" into the brief, and offered replacements (`:34`, `:221`) that are DOCSTRING MENTIONS of the call rather than the call. The worker checked, found the item right and the brief wrong, followed the item, and said so.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE COUNT CASE. A wrong count is a wrong number. This attacks the TRACKER'S CREDIBILITY: it tells a worker that a correct item is stale, in a brief the worker is told to trust over its own reading. Had the worker complied, it would have edited around two mentions and never reached the actual reads — and the "evidence" for the item's central claim would have gone missing with a plausible explanation attached.

IT ALSO REPRODUCES A DEFECT THE SAME BRIEF WARNS ABOUT. Citing a docstring MENTION as the call site is the rf2-uwvpi defect, which that brief's own text names — reached here from the opposite direction, by the mayor, while correcting someone else.

THE GUARD, and the first half is not enough on its own:
  * TAKE THE COUNT BESIDE THE LISTING, ALWAYS, FROM THE SAME NEEDLE: run `grep -c` and `grep -n` together. If the count exceeds the lines shown, you are looking at a fragment and you know it.
  * **NEVER CONCLUDE ABSENCE FROM A CAPPED LISTING AT ALL.** No cap, or no absence claim. "Not in the first 5" is not "not in the file", and only the uncapped run can say the second.
  * A LOCATOR WANTS NO CAP. The reason to cap is display volume, and a locator's output is a handful of lines; capping it buys nothing and risks everything.
  * WHERE THE ANSWER CONTRADICTS A WRITTEN CITATION, RE-RUN UNCAPPED BEFORE WRITING THE CONTRADICTION DOWN. The moment you are about to tell someone their reference is wrong is the moment to distrust your own instrument, not theirs.
  * PREFER A CLAIM ABOUT THE CODE OVER A CLAIM ABOUT A LINE. "The only real call is inside `registry-value`" survives a rebase; ":494" does not. A line number is the most perishable thing you can put in a brief.

CONTROL, BOTH WAYS, ON THE SAME FILES: uncapped, `grep -c` reads 7 and 19 against the 5 rows each capped run displayed; the capped rows themselves are all genuine hits, which is precisely why the truncation is invisible.

SEE ALSO [[a-count-and-its-breakdown-must-come-from-one-command]] — same family, a census whose parts and total came from different commands; here the parts and total came from ONE command and the CAP silently separated them.

=== SECOND DOOR, SAME DAY: A HARDCODED RANGE IS A CAP THAT DOES NOT LOOK LIKE ONE, AND IT SLIPS EVERY GUARD ABOVE ===

The guards above all assume the cap is VISIBLE — a `| head -N` you can see and delete. **A range you wrote
yourself is the same truncation wearing the costume of precision, and "a locator wants no cap" is
satisfied in form while the identical failure occurs.**

WHAT HAPPENED (2026-09-20, hours after the entry above, same mayor, same session). Briefing a worker on a
markdown table row, I verified the table's shape with a Python loop over `range(2108, 2117)` and reported
"table `:2108`-`:2116`, 4 pipes on every row". **The table actually runs `:2108`-`:2118` — eleven rows,
not nine.** The worker re-derived it and corrected me.

**I DID NOT MEASURE THE RANGE. I INHERITED IT** from an earlier item's prose ("header `:2108`, separator
`:2109`, and every row `:2110`-`:2116`") and re-reported it as my own measurement — which is the
supporting-detail trap, arriving inside the instrument rather than in the sentence around it.

**WHY IT IS INVISIBLE IN A WAY `head` IS NOT.** My script printed nine rows, every one reading `4`. That
output is indistinguishable from a complete, passing table verification. There is no cap in the command
to notice, no count beside the listing to disagree with it, and no truncation marker — the numbers simply
stop where I told them to, and stopping looks like ending. **Had `:2117` or `:2118` carried a broken pipe
count, my output would have been byte-identical.**

**AND IT LANDED ON THE ONE CHECK WITH NO BACKSTOP.** Nothing in this repository validates markdown table
column counts or rendering; the hand pipe-count IS the gate, which is exactly why the brief asks for it.
So the false clean fell on the check that exists *because* no automated one does — the worst possible
place for a silent truncation, and chosen for that reason by the same brief that then truncated it.

THE GUARD, extending the list above:
  * **DERIVE A RANGE, NEVER DECLARE ONE.** For a table: walk outward from the row you care about until
    the pipe count drops to 0 on each side, and report the boundaries you FOUND. One extra line of code,
    and it is the entire difference between checking a table and checking a guess about a table.
  * **PRINT THE ROWS OUTSIDE YOUR RANGE TOO.** A verification that shows `:2107` at 0 pipes and `:2119`
    at 0 pipes has proved where the table ENDS; one that starts and stops inside it has proved nothing
    about its extent. **Show the zeros on both shoulders** — they are the control, and they cost nothing.
  * **A RANGE COPIED OUT OF PROSE IS A CLAIM, NOT A MEASUREMENT**, and it decays exactly as line numbers
    do. If you did not derive the endpoints in the command that printed the result, say so.
  * **ASK WHAT A FAILURE WOULD HAVE LOOKED LIKE.** If the answer is "identical output", the check is
    ornamental. That question discharges this whole family in one line and would have caught both doors.

SO THE CLASS IS WIDER THAN `head`: **any bound the author supplies rather than measures — `head -N`, a
`range()`, a `sed -n 'A,Bp'`, a `--limit`, a date window, a directory root — truncates silently and
reports its own bound as the population.** The session that produced both of these also produced a THIRD:
a census rooted at `tools/xray/spec/` that missed a site one level up, surviving five PRs. Same shape,
three different bounds — a count cap, a line range, and a path root.

SEE ALSO [[a-brief-supporting-detail-is-a-claim-label-or-measure-it]] — the range came from prose and was
reported as measured, which is that entry's exact failure reached through a tool instead of a sentence.

A CENSUS THAT FLAGS ALMOST EVERYTHING IS NOT A DEFECT CLASS — IT IS A BROKEN COMPARISON SET, AND IT READS AS CORROBORATION (2026-09-03).

WHAT HAPPENED. Three beads independently reported the same shape: a marker in the tree gated on a bead id that does not exist. I tried to census the class by matching every rf2-* token across implementation/, tools/, docs/, spec/ and examples/ against the tracker export. Result: 5,179 distinct cited ids, 4,997 absent. I nearly reported that as a finding.

IT IS MEANINGLESS. The tracker holds ~516 issues; the tree carries thousands of historical citations, and this repo DELIBERATELY keeps them as provenance. CLAUDE.md itself cites rf2-0yp7w as the authoritative ui/freehand retirement disposition, and rf2-0yp7w.4 — its own child — is absent from the tracker too. So 'cited but absent' is the NORMAL state of a citation older than the current tracker, and a scan that flags 96% of its subject has told you about its own scope, not about the tree.

THE SHAPE OF THE MISTAKE, which loops.md already names for the inverse: a search returning ZERO is not a check that passed. THE INVERSION READS EVEN BETTER, because a scan returning EVERYTHING looks like a rich finding rather than like silence. Ask what the instrument COMPARED, not what it answered.

THE REAL CLASS, once scoped correctly, is narrow and worth fixing: not 'a citation to a dead bead' but A LIVE CONDITIONAL GATED ON NOTHING — a PROVISIONAL marker, a pending-on annotation, a 'revisit when X lands' note whose X cannot be found. A historical citation records why something is as it is and ages harmlessly. A pending marker is a promise to revisit that nobody can discharge, and it sits in the tree forever looking like live tracking. Search the MARKER VOCABULARY (PROVISIONAL, pending, 'until rf2-', 'when rf2-', 'blocked on rf2-'), then resolve only the ids those markers gate — and expect THREE outcomes, not two: phantom id, real-and-open (leave alone), real-and-closed (the promise was discharged, so the marker is stale, which is a different fix).

THIS IS THE SECOND INSTRUMENT FAILURE IN TWO BACKLOG-REREAD TICKS AND THEY ARE THE SAME FAMILY — a sweep whose comparison set was wrong. The other was bd-json-piped-to-jq-emits-crlf-and-silently-breaks-id-loops, where the set was right and the KEYS were corrupted. Both produced a confident number. The defence that works for both: exercise the instrument in both directions using data drawn from the SAME pipeline as the real input, never a literal typed on the command line.

A CHAINED GATE REPORTS ONLY ITS FIRST FAILURE — THE && SHORT-CIRCUITS, SO ONE RED CAN HIDE N MORE OF THE SAME DEFECT. Measured 2026-09-07 on PR #9334.

WHAT HAPPENED. An alias-rename sweep reded one CI job. The failure named exactly one broken roster premise, in one file, at one line. I read the log, verified the cause at source, confirmed by reading ALL ELEVEN premises in that file that only one referenced an alias, and briefed the worker that the fix was one line. The worker fixed it — and then found TWO MORE of the identical defect in a DIFFERENT file, check_bundle_isolation.cjs, which CI had never mentioned.

WHY CI NEVER MENTIONED THEM: the npm script chains its phases with &&. The first gate exited non-zero, so the second never ran. The log therefore contains complete, accurate, and radically incomplete information — every word of it true, and it names one third of the problem.

MY DIAGNOSIS WAS THOROUGH IN THE WRONG DIMENSION. I enumerated every premise in the file the error named, which felt like completeness and was in fact a search bounded by the error message. The right question was not "what else is wrong in this file" but "what else does this command run, and would I have heard about it".

THE RULE: when a chained runner fails, READ WHAT ELSE THE CHAIN INVOKES before concluding the failure is the whole of it. Read the npm script, the shell chain or the job's step list; then either run the remaining phases locally or state plainly that they are unmeasured. A green re-run after fixing the first link is the only thing that proves the rest, and until it exists the correct claim is "the first gate now passes", not "the PR is green".

AND CENSUS THE SHAPE, NOT THE INSTANCE. The worker generalised properly: git grep -l -F 'premise:' returns five files repo-wide; only two hold literal source-string rosters that a rename can invalidate. One of the others pins that named FILES EXIST — a path roster no rename can move — and two use the word in prose only. That one command discharged the class repo-wide, where fixing the reported instance would have left two live and a third latent.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT LESSON FROM THE SAME PR, about where a rename sweep is structurally blind: the failing gate is an npm script in ONE WORKFLOW JOB'S STEP LIST, reached by no scripts/ sweep and no artefact test alias. So a worker who runs every gate script and every artefact suite still never invokes it. Before a rename slice, read the STEP LIST of every CI job covering the surface, not only the gate scripts a brief names.

A PYTHON RATCHET THAT GRADES CLOJURE-FAMILY FILES THROUGH A CODE-LINE EXTRACTOR IS VACUOUSLY GREEN ON A COMMENT-ONLY CHANGE, AND IT IS GREEN ON THE ONE FILE IT ARMED FOR (2026-09-12, found by worker storydeps-a while landing rf2-52rj, PR #9715).

THE MECHANISM. `scripts/check_retired_image_keys.py` does cover `tools/story/deps.edn` — `tools/` is in `DEFAULT_SOURCE_DIRS` and `.edn` is in `_CLJ_SUFFIXES` — but it reads those files through `_clj_code_lines`, which strips comments before grading. A retired key PLANTED IN THE COMMENT the PR edited left the gate at exit 0. So the gate is armed, runs, names the file, and inspects nothing the diff touched.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY NARROW. A comment-only or docstring-only change is exactly the shape this repo produces in quantity — every prose-staleness correction under rf2-zaat, rf2-52rj and rf2-i0cj is one — and the coverage question a worker asks is "does this gate read this PATH", which answers YES. The green then reads as coverage. Nothing on screen separates "graded and clean" from "the extractor deleted my diff before grading".

SAME FAMILY, DIFFERENT AXIS, as the doc gates' fenced-code blindness recorded in CLAUDE.md (both `check_doc_slugs.py` and `check_readme_links.py` strip fences before reading a single link). There the extractor drops CODE and keeps prose; here it drops PROSE and keeps code. Neither is a bug — both are deliberate — and both make a path-based coverage answer misleading in the same way.

THE GUARD, and it is the one this repo already prescribes for every other gate: PLANT A FAULT IN THE LINES YOU ACTUALLY CHANGED, not merely in the file. A plant in the file's code region proves nothing about a comment-only diff. If the plant cannot turn the gate red, say so and do not claim the green — storydeps-a did exactly that, reporting the gate as green and explicitly refusing to cite it.

WHAT TO NOMINATE INSTEAD for a comment-only change to a Clojure-family file: the gate that proves the file still PARSES and RESOLVES (a JVM `clojure -M:test` run from the artefact), plus a structural equality check on the parsed form before and after, which establishes that no coordinate, exclusion or alias moved. That is a real claim; "the retired-spelling ratchet is green" is not.

A JVM LANE READS THE UNSELECTED :cljs READER-CONDITIONAL BRANCH BUT NEVER COMPILES IT. SO IT CATCHES
EVERY FAULT THAT BREAKS READING AND IS BLIND TO EVERY FAULT THAT READS AS WELL-FORMED DATA -- WHICH IS
NEARLY EVERY REAL DEFECT.

**THIS CORRECTS THE EARLIER HEADLINE UNDER THIS KEY, WHICH READ "invisible ... even for an outright syntax
error". THAT IS FALSE AS A UNIVERSAL AND IT FAILS IN A NEW DIRECTION -- see THE TRAP below, which is now
the most valuable part of this memory.**

MEASURED 2026-09-18 by the mayor, directly, with clojure.core/read at {:read-cond :allow :features #{:clj}}
-- the JVM feature set -- over eight fixtures whose damage was asserted before each read (a quote count
checked against an expectation, so a READ OK cannot come from a fixture that was never broken; round one
of this probe was mis-built, every "broken" fixture carrying an EVEN quote count, and read OK for that
reason alone).

FAULT CONFINED TO THE UNSELECTED :cljs BRANCH -- the JVM reader's verdict:
  * unterminated string (odd quote count)      -> READ FAILS "EOF while reading string"   VISIBLE
  * unbalanced delimiter                       -> READ FAILS "EOF while reading"          VISIBLE
  * invalid token :::x                         -> READ FAILS "Invalid token: :::x"        VISIBLE
  * invalid number 1abc                        -> READ FAILS "Invalid number: 1abc"       VISIBLE
  * EVEN stray quotes -- string closes early,
    leftover re-tokenises as symbol + string,
    producing a MALFORMED defn arglist         -> READ OK                                 INVISIBLE
  * unknown reader tag #no.such/tag            -> READ OK                                 INVISIBLE
  * bare unquote ~x outside a syntax quote     -> READ OK                                 INVISIBLE

CONTROLS BOTH WAYS, so a READ OK means something: the same even-quote damage in a :clj branch -- one the
feature set KEEPS -- read OK at 2 forms and handed back the malformed (defn f "doc " extra " tail" [] 1)
verbatim, which is READING succeeding on text that COMPILATION would refuse; :::x in a :clj branch failed
identically to :::x in the :cljs branch, showing reading is branch-BLIND for lexical faults; and plain
nonsense outside any conditional failed.

THE MECHANISM, AND IT IS THE WHOLE RULE: the reader must READ the unselected branch to know where it ENDS.
It cannot skip lexically. What it discards is the branch's VALUE, after reading it. So the boundary is not
:clj versus :cljs at all -- **it is READ-time versus COMPILE-time**, and the conditional only moves
compilation.

WHY THE OLD HEADLINE LOOKED TRUE. It came from ONE measurement (rf2-kk986, PR #9976): a stray double quote
in a new docstring, invisible to implementation/core's 2313 JVM tests, to the full 21-artefact sweep, to
all 46 Python ratchets, and to clj-kondo -- whose finding counts were BYTE-IDENTICAL either side, which is
the sharpest half, since comparing counts is the correct discipline under item (w). All of that is still
true and still worth knowing. It was a stray quote leaving an EVEN count, i.e. case B above. It was
REFUTED as a universal by rf2-ic8lz's worker the same day, which planted a stray quote at config.cljc:900
inside a #?(:cljs ...) and took the tools/xray JVM suite to exit 1 ("Invalid token") and clj-kondo to
exit 3 with 18 errors -- case C/E above. **Two workers, the same plant described the same way, opposite
results, and the difference was entirely whether the wreckage still lexed.**

**THE TRAP, WHICH IS NEW AND WORSE THAN THE THING IT REPLACES: THE OBVIOUS POSITIVE CONTROL CAN PASS WHILE
THE BLINDNESS STANDS.** A worker checking whether its JVM lane grades a :cljs branch plants a syntax error,
watches the lane go RED, and concludes the lane sees the branch. It does not. It saw a READ error. The
lane remains blind to wrong arity, wrong argument shape, a misspelled var, a dangling reference after a
deletion -- **the entire class of defect anybody actually ships** -- because every one of those reads as
well-formed data. So the plant fails in the REASSURING direction for the exact question it was written to
answer, and the reassurance is strongest for the most careful worker.

THE GUARD, UNCHANGED IN FORCE AND SHARPER IN REASON: for any change touching a .cljc, ask which branch the
changed forms sit in; if the answer is :cljs, a JVM green is not evidence about them and must be declared
as such -- nominate the CLJS lane, or state plainly that you are relying on CI. **And do not let a red
syntax plant stand in for that.** If you want a positive control that actually exercises the blindness,
plant a SEMANTIC fault -- a call to a var that does not exist, or a wrong arity -- and show the JVM lane
staying green on it. That green is the finding.

THE CLASS, past this repo: a dialect-conditional region is COMPILED only by the dialect that selects it,
while being READ by both. Any staged pipeline has this shape -- the early stage sees everything, the late
stage sees only its own branch, and a gate belonging to the late stage of the other dialect is blind to
precisely the faults the late stage would catch. Ask what a gate COMPILES, not what it opens and not what
it parses.

Related here: CLAUDE.md's rf2-uwa9r / rf2-d3l8g paragraph records CLJS publication pins graded by the node
lane alone, routed by NAMESPACE SUFFIX. Same class, different door -- routed by reader conditional inside a
single file. Do not fold the two together. Item (w)'s clj-kondo entry is the adjacent instrument note.

A CLJS TEST DOUBLE MUST MIRROR THE ARITY *SHAPE* OF WHAT IT REPLACES, NOT MERELY THE ARITY ITS CALLER HAPPENS TO USE — and getting this wrong fails on ClojureScript while passing on the JVM from the same `.cljc` source. Measured 2026-09-05 on `tools/story` (PR #9214).

THE MECHANISM, read in the emitted JavaScript rather than inferred:
  * `prepare-variant` is a two-arity `defn` — `([variant-id] [variant-id opts])`.
  * ClojureScript compiles a one-argument call site to the ARITY-SPECIALISED entry point:
        re_frame.story.runtime.prepare_variant.cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$1(variant_id)
  * The test's `with-redefs` double was `(fn [v] …)` — a SINGLE-arity fn, which compiles to a plain JS function carrying NO `cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$1` property.
  * `with-redefs` assigns that plain function straight over the fn object, so the call site reaches for a property that does not exist:
        TypeError: …prepare_variant.cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$1 is not a function

WHY THE JVM LANE PASSES ON THE SAME SOURCE: Clojure dispatches through the VAR on argument count at run time and has no static arity specialisation, so a single-arity double standing in for a multi-arity fn is invoked perfectly happily. **A green JVM suite is therefore no evidence at all about double shape.** This is a second member of the family with "test:cljs does not report :infer-warnings": a whole class of defect that only the ClojureScript compilation path can see.

THE RULE: when you `with-redefs` a multi-arity fn in a `.cljc` test, give the double EVERY arity the real fn has — not just the one the code under test calls today. A caller added later, or a code path you did not trace, reaches an arity your double lacks and fails with a TypeError that names a mangled JS property, which reads as a build or cache problem rather than a test bug.

AND FIX THE SIBLING DOUBLES EVEN WHEN CI HAS NOT NAMED THEM — this is NOT gold-plating, and the worker proved why. It also repaired the `reset-variant` double, which nothing had yet called. With the old single-arity double in place, the CLJS negative control (reverting the fix to check the witness still catches the original defect) would have ERRORED before reaching either assertion — so the control could not have reported at all. A malformed double does not merely hide one bug; it disables the instrument that proves the test is honest.

THE DIAGNOSTIC ROUTE WORTH COPYING: when a CLJS-only failure names a mangled property like `cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$N`, READ THE EMITTED JS. The worker found `stepper_state.js:80` and `stepper_state_cljs_test.js:910` and settled the question in two reads, rather than theorising about caches or stale builds. The mangled name IS the evidence.

A HEALTHY SIGN TO LOOK FOR AFTER SUCH A FIX: the assertion TALLY RISES. Here 35 -> 37, because three assertions sitting behind the exception ran for the first time. An arity repair that leaves the count unchanged did not actually unblock anything.

RELATED: [[test-cljs-does-not-catch-infer-warnings-that-break-under-advanced]], [[harness-reported-exit-code-disagrees-with-the-captured-one]].

TRACKER INTEGRITY: where beads close on PR-OPEN rather than on merge, a CLOSED bead can describe work that never landed — and no loop will ever re-read it.

Normally benign: changes merge within the hour and the window is invisible. It becomes real when a PR cannot merge — measured 2026-09-01, two drafts held by agents that went dormant, both beads CLOSED, git cherry reporting one unmerged patch each against main.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A REVERTED CLOSURE: a reverted closure reappears in the open list, where the backlog loop reads it. This one does not reappear anywhere. The backlog reread reads OPEN items by design, so a closure that was never TRUE is read by nothing, ever. The next person to touch that surface finds the defect still present with a closed item asserting it was fixed.

THE CHEAP DETECTION, worth running whenever a change sits unmerged for an unusual length of time: for each branch with an open PR, git cherry origin/main <branch> and grep for a leading +. Any non-zero count on a branch whose bead is closed is a tracker claim the trunk cannot back.

THE SYMMETRY WORTH REMEMBERING: this is the exact inverse of an OPEN item that is already DONE. Both are the tracker disagreeing with the tree. The open-and-done direction is caught by reading the tree during the backlog loop; the closed-and-undone direction is caught by nothing, because no loop reads closed items.

A committed run.cjs / shadow-cljs bench transcript trips the portability gate. Every hicasso lane driver prints 'shadow-cljs - config: <ABSOLUTE PATH>\implementation\shadow-cljs.edn', so committing a raw transcript as a dataset makes scripts/check-no-hardcoded-paths.sh (portability.yml, no || true, no continue-on-error) exit 1 with two violations per file (literal 'miket' + personal-named path). REDACT that one line to '<worktree>\implementation\shadow-cljs.edn' with an inline marker, and state the redaction in a README beside the data and on any page calling the transcript 'unedited' — the banner is load-bearing evidence that the run read the worker's worktree and not the mayor checkout, so deleting it costs real provenance. GREP TRAP that cost a round trip: a pattern written 'C:\Users\miket' in SINGLE quotes returns a FALSE ZERO on this setup — the backslashes are eaten before grep sees them. Use grep -F, or 'Users.miket' with a dot wildcard. Verified 2026-08-16 on PR #8329 (rf2-07rnj): gate exit 1 -> 0.

CONTROL DESIGN: "a green sabotage run is a reason to stop, not to proceed" has a specific mechanism worth naming — the control SETUP can make the defect unreachable, so the control passes against the very bug it exists to detect and reads as proof.

Measured 2026-09-01, rf2-mocn3 / PR #8883, caught by the worker itself. The defect: SSR Form-2 arity detection used try (apply inner args) / catch ArityException / retry (inner), so an ArityException thrown INSIDE a correctly-invoked inner is mistaken for an arity mismatch and the inner runs a SECOND time. The control counted invocations. Its first shape used a ZERO-arity inner under a ONE-arg component — so (apply inner args) threw on the invocation itself, before ever entering the body, and the retry path was never reached. Counter finished at 1. Green against exactly the defect it was built to detect, and it would have shipped as evidence.

THE PROPERTY THAT MATTERS: for that retry to bite, the arity must MATCH on the first call, so the exception has to come from the body rather than from the invocation. The control has to put the code into the state where the bug is reachable — being merely "a test of the right function" is not enough.

GENERALISE IT AS A QUESTION TO ASK OF EVERY CONTROL, before running it and again if it comes back green: does my setup actually reach the code path the defect lives on, or does it fail earlier for an unrelated reason that looks like the same red? A control that fails EARLY is indistinguishable from one that fails RIGHT, because both are red — and one that passes early is indistinguishable from a fixed bug.

The rule that saved it is the doc rule already written: a green sabotage is a STOP. The worker took the green as a reason to investigate rather than to proceed, found the setup defect, reshaped the row, and added a companion same-arity row discriminating on the argument count in the exception message (which a counter cannot express). Both then went red under sabotage on both consumers.

A RULING THE COORDINATOR MAKES TO UNBLOCK A WORKER IS A LEAN, AND LABELLING IT "RULED" TELLS THE
WORKER THE PREMISES-ARE-CLAIMS SENTENCE DOES NOT APPLY TO IT.

The dispatch method already treats a stated preference and an asserted number as claims. A ruling is
the case it does not reach. When a worker hands back a convention question and the coordinator
answers it SO THE WORK IS NOT BLOCKED, the natural wording is a heading like "RULED, SO YOU ARE NOT
BLOCKED ON IT" -- which says in terms that this content is settled and therefore NOT among the claims
the preamble told the worker to check.

MEASURED 2026-09-11. A coordinator ruled which of two shapes should repair a class of test rows that
execute in no lane, citing a sibling PR as the shipped precedent. Both halves were wrong and both
were one config file away:

  * shadow-cljs.edn states that :node-test's `cljs-test$` ns-regexp matches BOTH suffixes
    (`-cljs-test` AND `-dom-cljs-test`), so DOM-tagged files run on BOTH targets. The prescribed
    move therefore ADDED a lane rather than removing one.
  * the cited precedent (PR #9681) was RED IN CI at the moment it was cited, for exactly that
    reason -- it had moved two localStorage rows into a -dom-cljs-test file unguarded, and the node
    lane ran them where localStorage does not exist.

THE REMEDY: attach to a ruling what the method already demands of a lean -- the measurement that
decides it, named in the same breath. A convention question is "which of these two shapes is right",
and what decides it is nearly always a mechanism you can READ: a selector, a config key, a build
target. Read it, quote it, cite the line. And where the ruling cites a precedent, CHECK THAT THE
PRECEDENT IS GREEN -- a shape is not demonstrated by a change that has not passed.

WHERE YOU CANNOT DECIDE IT CHEAPLY, SAY THAT INSTEAD OF RULING. "Both shapes exist here; I have not
established which is right; establish it and tell me" costs the worker the same tick a ruling was
meant to save, and cannot be wrong. A ruling's whole value is removing a question, so a ruling that
has not answered the question is worse than the hold it replaced.

Note the mechanism claim -- that the LABEL is what stops the checking -- is reasoning rather than a
measurement. What was measured is only that the ruling was wrong and cheap to check. The remedy does
not rest on the mechanism.

A CORRECTED HISTORICAL MEASUREMENT IS WITHDRAWN TO A FLOOR AND RE-BASELINED AT TIP - IT IS NOT RE-MEASURED. This memory was ASKED FOR by rf2-y1jkm's own closing ruling note ("a one-line bead memory for the general rule this ruling applies would be worth having ... three refusals and a mayor overwrite were spent on this bead before the rule was written down anywhere") and never written. Withdraw the wrong figure to a FLOOR, re-baseline at the current tip, and record the correction. File a new, explicitly LABELLED synthetic-attribution measurement bead only if the historical attribution later becomes DECISION-BEARING. Do not authorise a spliced-tree or reconstructed-history measurement to rescue a number nothing consumes - the reconstruction is uncertifiable on any tree that could produce it, and the cost lands on a quiet-box window that real work wants.
