THE API-MANIFEST LANE IS SEVEN CO-EDITED FILES, NOT FIVE — and the two extra are NON-VACUITY ANCHORS that spell the surface as a LITERAL NAME SET. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.121 worker (PR #6772) while adding t/with-render.

THE FIVE EVERYONE KNOWS: the facade block; spec/api-manifest.edn (REGENERATED); spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (classification row); spec/API.md (roster row); docs/api/<ns>.md (member heading).

THE TWO THAT BITE:
  6. implementation/scripts/api-manifest/probe/test/.../cljs_manifest_probe_cljs_test.cljs
  7. implementation/scripts/api-manifest/test/.../freehand_test_enrolment_test.clj
Both hard-code the surface as a literal list of names, so adding a public var makes them WRONG.

⚠️ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE DANGEROUS PART: only the JVM one (7) FAILS LOUDLY. The CLJS one (6) was caught only by READING — the worker spotted it before it ran. So a worker that adds a verb, sees the JVM anchor red, fixes it, and goes green has NOT necessarily fixed both. CHECK BOTH BY READING, do not rely on a red to find them.

The JVM anchor also asserted a SINGLE :kind for all rows, which breaks the moment the surface gains a member of a different kind. The fix made it stricter rather than looser: pin each NAME against its DERIVED :kind (here five :fn and one :macro) instead of asserting one kind for the set.

GENERAL FORM, and this is why it is worth remembering beyond this lane: A NON-VACUITY ANCHOR THAT ENUMERATES A SURFACE IS A MAINTENANCE COUPLING. It exists to stop the gate passing on an empty set, which is right — but it converts every addition to that surface into an edit of the test. When you write one, prefer deriving the expected set from the same source the gate reads, or at minimum make it fail LOUDLY on both hosts. An anchor that silently tolerates drift on one host is worse than none, because it teaches you the surface is covered when it is half-covered.

ALSO CONFIRMED ON THIS LANE (unchanged, still true): the rebase trap. git AUTO-MERGES the generated spec/api-manifest.edn with no conflict markers and leaves a STALE :var-count, and the resulting drift error reads like a formatting or toolchain problem. Cure is plain gen, then --check exit 0, AND an EMPTY git diff on that file. The empty-diff step is the one people skip and the only one that proves the committed file equals the generator output.

spec/API.md AND spec/api-manifest*.edn ARE ONE FENCED HOLDING — FILTERING ON THE FIRST ALONE SENDS A WORKER INTO A HELD FILE (measured 2026-09-06, cost one worker cycle).

WHAT I DID. Six workers were being dispatched at once. To find beads that could run in parallel with the single spec/API.md holder, I filtered the ready list for beads whose text does NOT mention spec/API.md, and dispatched two of them (rf2-kuky.82, rf2-kuky.86) as an API-free cluster. The worker came back with no PR: BOTH beads name spec/api-manifest.edn and spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn as their CENTRAL DELIVERABLE, and those files were held by the API.md holder. In its words: 'the brief said neither bead names spec/API.md — true, but both name spec/api-manifest*.edn, which is the same fenced holding.'

WHY THEY ARE ONE HOLDING AND NOT THREE FILES: the manifest is GENERATED from the tree by implementation/scripts/api-manifest/gen.clj, and the lint job grades API.md and both sidecars together as one drift-check. A worker that moves a public name must regenerate, which rewrites both EDN files and usually API.md's rows too. So any bead touching one of the three touches all three in practice, and two workers on any of them conflict every time.

THE FILTER THAT IS ACTUALLY RIGHT: match /spec\/API[.]md|api-manifest/ — one alternation, both halves. Matching only the first read 8 of 32 kuky beads as API-free when the true figure was smaller.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, and this is the sixth fence error in one session: a fence is not a filename, it is the SET OF FILES ONE CHANGE MOVES TOGETHER. Generated files travel with their source; a spec row travels with the manifest row it pins; a catalogue row travels with the emitter that raises it (spec/009 + spec/Conventions.md, recorded separately on rf2-kuky.43). Before dispatching a bead as parallel-safe, read its own 'Spec, docs, examples, skills, tests' section and take the UNION of what it names — do not pattern-match one representative filename out of a long description.

AND THE CHEAPER CHECK THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT: both beads were also BLOCKED by open beads (.82 by rf2-kuky.20, whose own STOP rule fired; .86 by .31/.84/.85). bd ready listed them because bd does not model those as blocks edges, so the ready view was not the authority I treated it as. Read a candidate's dependency list AND its own stated blockers before briefing it, not just its surface.

TO ANSWER "WHICH TOOLS READ THIS FILE?", RUN THE TOOLS UNDER AN AUDIT HOOK THAT RECORDS REAL `open` CALLS.
DO NOT SEARCH THEIR SOURCE FOR READ VERBS. The search answers a different question and is wrong in BOTH
directions at once.

WHY THE SEARCH FAILS, both ways, measured on re-frame2 over several weeks:
  * TOO NARROW -- a verb list (`slurp`, `io/reader`, `io/resource`) MISSES a reader that opens through a
    helper spelling none of them. `implementation/scripts/api-manifest/.../xray_spec_check.clj` reads its
    chapter through a `repo-file` helper and is invisible to every one of those verbs.
  * TOO WIDE -- widening the verb list then ADMITS files that merely MENTION a chapter in a comment or a
    docstring while slurping something else entirely. One chapter was NAMED by 48 files and OPENED by none.
  * AND THE SCOPE IS USUALLY WRONG TOO -- a sweep confined to the directories you expect readers to live in
    cannot find the one that lives somewhere else.

THE COST WAS REAL AND MINE. I published "exactly four Xray spec chapters are read by code" off such a
sweep; it was FIVE. That count was quoted in four dispatch briefs and two bead notes before a worker found
the fifth by accident. A three-sided trap -- scope, verb list, and the widened verb list -- each side
plausible, each failing quietly.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT WORKS (a worker's, 2026-09-18, and it is strictly better than what I had prescribed):
run every candidate tool under a hook that records the actual `open` calls it makes, then read the
recording. It is a DYNAMIC measurement of what the process touched rather than a STATIC guess at what its
text implies. On this repo it found `check_view_lifetime_residue.py` reading a file that reasoning about
the script's purpose would never have suggested.

WHY IT IS BETTER IN KIND, not merely more thorough: helpers, indirection, computed paths, config-driven
roots and inherited base classes all defeat a source search by construction, and none of them defeats a
recording of syscalls. The recording also gives you the FULL PATH, which the next paragraph shows you need.

THE SECOND HALF, MET IN THE SAME ACT: A BASENAME MATCH INFLATES WHEN THE TREE REPEATS FILENAMES. The same
worker's first probe keyed on the basename `000-Vision.md` and over-counted, because SEVEN tracked files
carry that name. Re-run on full paths, the count was right. Spec trees numbered per tool
(`tools/<x>/spec/000-Vision.md`) repeat basenames by convention, so this is structural here rather than
bad luck. **Key on the full path; a basename is not an identity.** Same family as selecting a bead record
by a bare id grep instead of on the identity field.

THE LIMITS, so this is not over-sold: a dynamic recording sees only the paths the run actually took, so a
conditional branch not exercised reads as absent -- it is complete about THIS run and not about the
program. Drive the tool the way CI drives it, and where a branch matters, exercise it deliberately. The
static search remains useful for generating CANDIDATES to run; it is unfit as the answer.

THE CLASS: prefer measuring what a program DID to inferring what its source implies, whenever the question
is "what does it touch". Reach for the same move for network calls, env vars, spawned processes and files
written, not only files read.

ADDED 2026-09-18 — THE REFINEMENT THAT COST A FALSE CLAIM IN TWO DISPATCH BRIEFS: RUN THE HOOK OVER THE
WHOLE CANDIDATE POPULATION, NEVER OVER A NAME-FILTERED SHORTLIST. A tool that GLOBS THE TREE names no
file, so it cannot appear in a name census, and pre-filtering by name removes exactly the readers the
hook exists to find.

The sentence above says the static search "remains useful for generating CANDIDATES to run". **True, and
insufficient — because the candidate set it generates is itself name-shaped, and that is where the
population gets silently truncated.** The hook then runs faithfully over a shortlist that could never
have contained the answer, and returns a confident, well-measured, wrong number.

MEASURED, and the claim in question was one I had propagated myself. A worker established that
`tools/xray/spec/019-Cross-Cutting-Insight.md` "has exactly ONE reader and it is a JVM test", deriving it
from a NAME census plus a verb search: 8 non-markdown files name the chapter, 7 carry zero read verbs. I
repeated that in a later dispatch brief — **while telling that same worker to re-derive it with an audit
hook rather than a verb search.** It did, and refuted me. I then re-measured it myself with my own hook
over ALL 46 `scripts/check_*.py`, keyed on the FULL PATH:

    real open() calls recorded            31,990
    scripts that opened NOTHING                0     <- the hook was live for all 46
    scripts that OPEN 019                      5     <- check_doc_slugs, check_retired_composition_vocab,
                                                       check_retired_image_keys, check_retired_spellings,
                                                       check_view_lifetime_residue
    CONTROL, open 007-UX-IA.md                 6
    CONTROL, open a NONEXISTENT chapter        0

**FOUR OF THE FIVE ARE REPO-WIDE RATCHETS THAT GLOB THE TREE AND NAME NO CHAPTER ANYWHERE.** So the name
census was not merely incomplete — it was structurally incapable of finding them, and its answer of ONE
was not a near miss but a different question answered accurately: *how many files that NAME this chapter
also read it?*

**IT FAILS IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION FOR THE ONLY QUESTION IT IS ASKED.** "Exactly one reader, and it is
lane-free" authorises skipping every other gate and reporting a cheap, confident green. The true answer
put four more ratchets on the surface.

**AND THE WRONG ANSWER READS AS THE RIGOROUS ONE**, which is what makes it expensive: it arrives carrying
a control (7 of 8 files carry zero read verbs) and a named instrument, so it looks exactly like the
careful derivation this memory prescribes. The control was live and correct about its own population.

THE GUARD, in one line: **define the population by what could POSSIBLY read the file — every script in the
directory, every suite in the lane — and run the hook over all of it.** 46 scripts is a few minutes; the
shortlist that feels efficient is the thing that breaks it. **And take a control that a name census could
not have produced**: a nonexistent path must read 0, and some file you know is read must read non-zero.

**THE SECOND LESSON IS ABOUT PROPAGATION RATHER THAN MEASUREMENT, and it is the one I keep relearning:
a finding that arrives through a report is a CLAIM, and repeating it into a brief makes me its author.**
This is the second time in one session — the first was a source cite I repeated without re-reading, also
refuted by the worker I handed it to. **Re-derive, or attribute it explicitly as unverified and tell the
worker to settle it.** A brief is the worst place for an inherited claim, because the worker reads it as
established and spends its scepticism elsewhere.

BEFORE FENCING AN ITEM AS "BLOCKED ON A DECISION", ASK WHAT WOULD DIFFER IN THE DELIVERABLE UNDER
EACH OPTION. If nothing would, it is not decision-blocked and it is dispatchable now.

The failure has a specific shape and it is not laziness: the item's prose genuinely names an unmade
decision, so the fence LOOKS derived rather than assumed. What goes wrong is assuming the deliverable
must state the FINAL state of the system, when it only has to state the CURRENT one — and the current
one is usually measured and settled.

MEASURED 2026-09-12. A bead asked for one stale sentence in `tools/story/deps.edn` to be corrected:
it claimed, unqualified, that Xray renders through the installed adapter. Half had gone false when
Xray's shell moved onto its own React root. I fenced it on an open architecture decision — whether
the embedded panel door would ALSO move — closed its parent, and pointed the work at that decision's
bead. The merged-PR audit refuted it in one line: "No runtime migration, new API or decision about
future element-shaped panel embedding is required to describe today's split accurately." Right: the
sentence had to describe today (mount verbs on owned roots, embed door still on the adapter), which
was measured and true regardless of the ruling. Describing today's behaviour is not deciding
tomorrow's.

THE COST DIRECTION IS WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A MEMORY. The error moves an item from "dispatchable
now" into the operator's queue, where it is invisible as work and waits on a human who was never
needed. It reads as diligence at the moment it is made, and the fence is then re-derived and
re-confirmed by every later pass, because each pass reads the same true sentence about an unmade
decision.

THE TEST, and it is the same discriminating question the method prescribes for corrections: name what
the deliverable would LOOK LIKE under option A and under option B. Two different artefacts means the
fence is real. The same artefact either way means you are fencing on a decision the work does not
consume. A third answer — "the artefact is the same but would need updating later if B is ruled" —
is NOT a fence either; it is a coordination note on the deciding item.

RELATED: the dispatch template's "separate needs-a-decision from needs-work-under-a-decision; the
second is dispatchable now and tends to sit in the first pile." The rule was already written and I
had read it twice that day. What was missing was a test that fires at the moment of fencing.

CROSS-MODE SNAPSHOT TESTS ON outerHTML ARE A FALSE NEGATIVE — the two emitters write attributes in DIFFERENT ORDER. Found 2026-07-24 by the F5h virtual-table pilot, whose first browser parity row failed on this and nothing else.

THE OBSERVATION: [:span.acme-cell {:role ... :data-col ...}] renders its attributes as `class role data-col` INTERPRETED and `role data-col class` COMPILED — the sugar class is written FIRST by one emitter and LAST by the other. Nothing in a browser observes this; the structural trees are identical because attrs are a map; and no user-visible behaviour differs.

⚠️ BUT IT MAKES outerHTML STRING EQUALITY USELESS FOR CROSS-MODE PARITY. A snapshot test comparing rendered HTML strings across interpreted and compiled will fail for a reason that means nothing, and — worse — the obvious "fix" is to loosen the comparison, which throws away the real coverage.

THE RIGHT ORACLE, which the pilot adopted: compare a DOM SHAPE — tag, SORTED attribute map, text, and children in document order. That is STRICTER than string equality in every way that matters and blind only to write order. Do not normalise by sorting the HTML string; extract the structure and compare it.

GENERALISES: whenever two independent code paths produce the same semantic artefact, the serialised form may differ in ways the semantics do not. Before asserting equality on a SERIALISATION, ask whether the serialiser guarantees a canonical order. If it does not, compare the STRUCTURE, not its rendering. Same family as the earlier finding that a per-line census cannot see a claim that wraps — the representation carries incidental detail the assertion should not depend on.

AN AUDIT NOTE DISCRIMINATES A LEGITIMATE REOPEN FROM A CLOSE THAT DID NOT STICK — 7 for 7 today (2026-08-01).

THE PROBLEM: beads kept appearing OPEN whose PRs had merged, so the ready list overstated the board and I was at risk of dispatching workers at finished work.

THE TEST, which is cheap and has not failed yet: grep the bead for an AUDIT note.
  - HAS an audit note (e.g. 'MERGED-PR AUDIT #NNNN ... REOPENED') -> LEGITIMATELY OPEN. The audit loop reopened this exact owner with a bounded new charge. The newest note is the live scope; the description is history. Dispatch it — but brief from the NOTE, not the title or description.
  - NO audit note, yet its PR merged -> THE CLOSE DID NOT STICK. Verify the work is on main (git log origin/main --grep=<bead-id>) and CLOSE it with the evidence.

CONFIRMED BOTH WAYS TODAY. Lost closes, verified on main and closed: rf2-023vi, rf2-qwydk, rf2-2rtt6.29, rf2-lrtwj, rf2-x5dvk, rf2-dtpfv. Legitimate reopens with real charges, dispatched: rf2-5prok (though ITS charge turned out already discharged by a later PR — check the note's PR number against what has since merged), rf2-6i0i2, rf2-rxkht, rf2-m6if4, rf2-eane2, rf2-2rtt6.32, rf2-2rtt6.44.

TWO REFINEMENTS WORTH KEEPING:
  1. An audit note can itself be STALE. rf2-5prok's note audited the ORIGINAL PR and a later PR had already fixed the charge. So: read the note's PR number, then check whether anything merged after it addressed the same thing.
  2. THIS IS WHY THE BOARD GROWS WHILE MERGES LAND. The audit loop files against every merge, so a high merge rate produces a high file rate. 'Drive to 0 open' is not reachable by dispatching harder; the reachable goal is that every open bead is either genuinely open, waiting on an operator ruling, or waiting on a quiet box. Verification closes more beads per minute than dispatch does.

A TWO-SECOND STATUS FLIP IN bd history DOES NOT DISTINGUISH AN AUDIT REOPEN FROM A TRACKER REVERT — ONLY THE COMMENTS DO (2026-08-21, rf2-onozm).

WHAT HAPPENED. worker/ladder-onozm closed rf2-onozm. Minutes later it read open. bd history showed CLOSED at 04:33:02 and OPEN at 04:33:04 — two seconds apart, author root, no reason attached and the close text gone. That is exactly the signature CLAUDE.md describes for the JSONL-revert artefact, so I called it a revert and re-closed with a reason asserting 'No AUDIT-REOPEN marker, no unmet obligation'. It reverted again. I re-closed a SECOND time. Both re-closes were wrong: the merged-PR audit of #8591 had deliberately reopened the bead with a specific, evidenced, unmet obligation, and by the second attempt it had also posted a correction naming my error and saying not to close.

WHY THE SIGNATURE FAILS. The audit writes through the same tracker mechanism as everything else, so it produces the same shape: a status flip seconds apart, author root, no visible reason on the history line. The history listing prints commit, time, author, title and status and NAMES NO CHANGED FIELD, so it cannot tell you WHY the status moved. There is no signature in the timing, the author or the gap.

WHY MY MARKER CHECK MISSED IT — this is the operative half. The audit left its finding as a COMMENT. I grepped the NOTES, via a truncated bd show. bd show renders notes and comments in separate blocks; a grep over one is blind to the other, and the single hit mine did return was a description string about a different bead, which I dismissed. So 'no AUDIT-REOPEN marker' was a fact about where I looked, never about the bead.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT WORKS, and mayor-backlog-reread.md already prescribes it: bd comments <id> --json ordered by created_at descending. Run it BEFORE any re-close, without exception. bd show | grep is not a substitute and neither is reading notes.

A CORROBORATING TEST THAT COSTS NOTHING: check whether the reopen is TARGETED. A revert sweeps whatever the stale export held, so sibling beads closed in the same batch revert together. An audit reopens exactly the bead whose obligation is unmet. Here worker/ladder-onozm closed TWO beads on one PR — rf2-onozm and rf2-2rtt6.140 — and only rf2-onozm came back, twice, while rf2-2rtt6.140 stayed closed through the same checkpoints. One returning and its sibling not is strong evidence of an audit; both returning together is evidence of a revert. Corroboration, not proof — still read the comments.

AND CORRELATE THE COMMIT LOG: git log --oneline on main showed 'chore(beads): audit PR #8591' landing inside each flip window. That commit subject is the audit announcing itself, and it is visible from outside the tracker entirely.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT SETTLES HOW TO ACT WHEN UNSURE: re-closing an audit reopen DESTROYS a real finding and looks like tidiness; leaving a reverted close open costs one tick and is caught by the next backlog reread. So when the evidence is ambiguous, LEAVE IT OPEN and investigate. Never re-close on the history shape alone.

AN AUDIT REOPEN IS WORK, NOT A REVERT — AND THE STATUS FIELD CANNOT TELL YOU WHICH (2026-08-09).

WHAT I DID WRONG. This session had SIX genuine silent tracker reverts (beads closed, later reading open, nothing owed). I built a field-read audit for them and it worked. Then the merged-PR audit hook began REOPENING beads with real findings, and my audit could not distinguish the two: both present as "a bead I recorded closed now reads open". I re-closed SIX beads with the phrase "NOTHING IS OWED" -- rf2-hic-000 three times -- while their notes carried named, unmet obligations with file and line.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE NOTES, NOT THE FIELD.
  - GENUINE REVERT: reads open, carries NO new note. Re-close with evidence that the work is on main.
  - AUDIT REOPEN: reads open AND carries a new "MERGED-PR AUDIT #NNNN" note naming a defect. That is the hook deliberately reopening THE EXACT OWNER instead of filing a new bead. It is a statement that acceptance is not met. Re-closing it destroys the finding.

WHAT THE HOOK ACTUALLY FOUND, to show these are not nitpicks: invariants.md missing the core controlled-field contract (#7712); the K1 record's lapse terms not executable as written (#7713); the correction ledger specifying an impossible post-merge write (#7714); dispositions.md section 1.2 reproducing a stale review snapshot and calling nine rows Gap when the tracker now owns every cited proof (#7717); a pre-registration amendment that must re-freeze the file at a new commit because the cited hash is now stale (#7718); and product/README.md pointing a clean worker checkout at a GITIGNORED file for its refresh contract (#7711).

THE RULE: before re-closing anything that reads open, read its NOTES bottom-up. Grep for "MERGED-PR AUDIT", "reopened exact owner", "remains outstanding". Only a reopen with no new note is churn. This is the same trap recorded in reference_gcchurn_reclose_misses_audit_obligations -- I had that memory and still checked the wrong thing, because the loop instruction says "read the status FIELD" and I followed it literally.

AND NOTE THE SECOND-ORDER EFFECT: my re-closes made the session's closed-count overstate real progress, in exactly the direction the revert audit exists to prevent. A verification tool that misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch.

"A BEAD I CLOSED NOW READS OPEN" HAS A THIRD CAUSE, AND IT PRESENTS EXACTLY LIKE THE FIRST (2026-08-13, rf2-maiw).

MY TAXONOMY HAD TWO ENTRIES AND THEY ARE BOTH STILL RIGHT:
  (A) SILENT REVERT -- reads open, NO new note, nothing owed. Re-close with evidence from the tree.
  (B) AUDIT REOPEN -- reads open AND carries a "MERGED-PR AUDIT #NNNN" note naming a defect. Real work. Re-closing destroys the finding.

THE THIRD: (C) A WORKER DELIBERATELY REOPENED IT, because the bead's own notes reserve part of it for the operator. rf2-maiw's worker closed it, then reopened it, reporting: "its own notes say it is deliberately open for remedies (b) and (c), which are the operator's call -- the bead governs over my instinct to close." It was right.

WHY IT DEFEATS THE (A)/(B) DISCRIMINATOR: (C) carries NO audit note, because it is not an audit. And the close reason VANISHES, because the reopen removed it. Those are exactly the two tells I use to identify (A). So I grepped for MERGED-PR AUDIT, found only a pre-existing one, concluded "silent revert", and RE-CLOSED IT TWICE with a reason asserting "Nothing is owed" -- which was false, since two operator-owned remedies were owed and named on the bead.

THE CORRECTED CHECK, and it subsumes all three: BEFORE RE-CLOSING ANYTHING THAT READS OPEN, READ THE BEAD'S OWN NOTES FOR A RESERVATION -- do not merely grep for an audit marker. Look for "deliberately open", "remedies (b)/(c)", "operator's call", "awaiting", "NOT closing". A bead that says it should be open outranks my recollection that I closed it. "Verified CLOSED, then OPEN" is evidence of a revert ONLY when the bead itself does not say otherwise.

AND NOTE THE ASYMMETRY OF COST, which is why the default must be to leave it open: re-closing a (B) destroys an audit finding; re-closing a (C) destroys an operator-reserved decision and stamps a false "nothing is owed" on the record. Failing to re-close an (A) costs one bead looking open for a tick. The cheap error and the expensive error are not the same size.

THE SESSION-CLOSURE AUDIT STILL EARNS ITS PLACE -- a genuine (A) fired in the same hour, on rf2-maiw's own sibling rf2-qzm8, which reverted and needed re-closing. So the audit is right and its DISCRIMINATOR was too narrow, which is the same defect class this repo hunts everywhere else: a check that verifies the absence of one marker rather than the presence of the real signal.

BEFORE DISPATCHING AN AUDIT-REOPENED BEAD, CHECK WHETHER A LATER COMMIT ALREADY CLOSED THE FINDING. Cost a full dispatch cycle on 2026-07-24 (rf2-wh5to).

THE MECHANISM: a three-lens audit reads PR #N, finds a residual, and REOPENS the bead with a rider. But the audit is written against the tree AS OF #N. If a commit AFTER #N already fixed the residual, the rider is stale on arrival and the bead is reopened for work that is done. The worker then verifies, finds everything satisfied, and writes no code.

WHY IT IS HARD TO SPOT: the fixing commit is often BUNDLED WITH UNRELATED WORK and its subject line says nothing about the finding. In this case the status-honesty repair landed in e7636a59ff (PR #6663) bundled with a goog.DEBUG override-provider fix — so grepping the log for the symptom, the bead id, or anything topical finds NOTHING. Only reading the actual current source settles it.

THE CHECK, cheap, before dispatching any audit-reopened bead: read the CURRENT source at the named site and confirm the defect is still present. Do not grep the log for the bead id (fixes get bundled and rarely cite the reopen), and do not trust the rider prose — it was true once. One file read.

⚠️ THE DISPATCH WAS STILL NOT WASTED, and this is worth keeping in proportion: the worker VERIFIED rather than assumed, ran a non-vacuity probe on the SHIPPED test (inverted an assertion, gate redded EXIT=1 naming the test, restored byte-identical), swept for sibling tests pinning the same falsehood, and confirmed the .cljc proof tests are actually reachable by the CLJS runner rather than orphaned by reader conditionals. That produced real evidence the fix is live and load-bearing. A "no code written" outcome that is VERIFIED is a legitimate and valuable result — the failure mode to avoid is a worker that assumes the bead is stale and closes it without looking.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: always grep origin/main for the bead id before dispatch (three already-shipped dispatches in one earlier session). This adds the harder case — the fix exists but is NOT discoverable by id, because it shipped inside someone else commit.

THE AUDIT-REOPEN SCAN MUST BE TIME-KEYED, NOT PR-KEYED (2026-08-11, supersedes the method in audit-reopen-scan-over-jsonl).

I built the scan to look for MERGED-PR AUDIT notes naming THIS SESSION'S merged PR numbers. That is wrong, and it missed two live reopens: rf2-hic-092 (P2, audit #7788) and rf2-hic-046 (P3, audit #7756), both stamped 21:08 mid-session, both for PRs merged long before my session started.

WHY: the merged-PR audit hook works a BACKLOG. It reviews PRs on its own schedule, so a reopen arriving during my session can name a PR from hours or days earlier. Keying on the numbers I merged makes the scan blind to exactly the reopens I did not already know about - which is the entire population it exists to find.

Worse, it fails QUIETLY and looks rigorous: I had a positive control on it (asking for a known hic-007 reopen and getting `true`), and the control PASSED while the scan was still blind, because the control tested the jq mechanics rather than the SELECTION PREDICATE. A control has to exercise the thing that can be wrong.

THE CORRECTED SCAN - every open bead carrying any audit note, newest-updated first, no PR numbers anywhere:

  jq -r 'select((.status//"")=="open") | select(((.notes//"")|tostring)|test("MERGED-PR AUDIT")) | "\(.updated_at)  \(.id)  [P\(.priority)]  \(.title[0:56])"' .beads/issues.jsonl | sort -r | head -12

Read down until updated_at predates the session; anything above that line is a reopen to triage. Guard every field with `//""` - `.id`, `.status` and `.notes` are all null on some rows, and an unguarded `test()` aborts jq mid-file with "null cannot be matched", which prints errors but still exits having skipped rows.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the repo's own house rule turned on my own instrument: a filter that can only find what you already knew is not a detector. Ask what population the check is supposed to cover, then ask what a member of that population looks like when you have never heard of it.

HOW TO FIND AUDIT REOPENS ON BEADS YOU DID NOT CLOSE (2026-08-11).

The closure audit ("re-check everything closed this session") only covers ids I closed. The merged-PR audit hook also reopens beads I never touched, and those are invisible to it AND to a `bd list --status open` recount taken before the hook lands. rf2-hic-007 was reopened by MERGED-PR AUDIT #7842 and I found it only by accident - `bd close rf2-hic-024` refused with "blocked by open issues [rf2-hic-007]".

THE DELIBERATE SCAN, over the export:

  jq -r 'select(.status=="open") | select(((.notes//"")|tostring)|test("MERGED-PR AUDIT #(7839|7842|7843)")) | "\(.id) [P\(.priority)] \(.title[0:70])"' .beads/issues.jsonl

TWO GOTCHAS THAT MADE EARLIER ATTEMPTS SILENTLY RETURN NOTHING:
1. `.notes` is a STRING, not an array. `(.notes//[])|map(...)` throws "Cannot iterate over string" on every bead that has notes - i.e. exactly the ones you want.
2. A plain grep with `[^}]{0,4000}` between the id and the audit string CANNOT WORK: note bodies contain braces, so the character class stops early. It returned a clean empty for five PR numbers while hic-007 demonstrably carried the note.

ALWAYS RUN A POSITIVE CONTROL. Ask the scan a question you already know the answer to:

  jq -r 'select(.id=="rf2-hic-007") | ((.notes//"")|tostring|test("MERGED-PR AUDIT #7842"))' .beads/issues.jsonl   # must print true

An empty result from an unvalidated filter is indistinguishable from a broken filter, and this is the same fail-open class the merge criterion exists to close. The control is what turns "found nothing" into evidence.

ALSO: bd REFUSES to close a bead blocked by an open dependency. That guard is load-bearing - it caught this - but when the blocker was reopened for an UNRELATED later defect, the right move is `bd close --force` with a reason naming why the edge does not bear on this deliverable.

THE MERGED-PR AUDIT REOPENS A PARENT BEAD WHEN ONE OF ITS DISCOVERED-FROM DESCENDANTS LANDS (2026-08-14, established on rf2-hic-055 after three reopens; supersedes my first, wrong diagnosis).

WHAT I FIRST THOUGHT, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG. rf2-hic-055 reopened twice with no new comment, so I concluded the audit could not see my discharge evidence because it sat in a close REASON, which a reopen discards. I moved the evidence into a COMMENT. It reopened a third time anyway, with the comment present. Hypothesis refuted by its own remedy.

THE ACTUAL PATTERN, from four consecutive audit commits with no exceptions:
  audit of PR #8151 (the bead own repair)                 -> REOPENED
  audit of PR #8154 (rf2-xc11, a DISCOVERED child)        -> REOPENED
  audit of PR #8156 (rf2-yfz7, unrelated)                 -> stayed closed
  audit of PR #8157 (rf2-0xd6, a GRANDCHILD via rf2-xc11) -> REOPENED
Descendants trigger it; unrelated merges do not. It follows the DISCOVERED edge transitively, at least to grandchildren.

READ IT AS DESIGN, NOT AS A BUG. When a child of an audit finding lands, re-examining whether the parent is still discharged is a reasonable thing for an audit to do. It only LOOKS like churn because the answer keeps being yes. So do not "fix" it and do not fight it.

THE OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE. A bead with open discovered-from descendants will reopen once per descendant merge, however well you close it. Do not spend a cycle diagnosing each one. Instead: check whether the trigger PR belongs to a descendant, and if so re-close citing the existing discharge. When the LAST descendant has landed there is no further trigger, and that is the point at which a further reopen becomes real information.

HOW TO IDENTIFY THE TRIGGER CHEAPLY. Walk the recent tracker-export commits and print the bead status at each: for c in $(git log --format=%h -8 origin/main -- .beads/issues.jsonl); do git show $c:.beads/issues.jsonl | filter for the id, print status and comment count; done. The commit subject names the audited PR, and the DISCOVERED section of the bead names the descendants. Two facts, one command.

SUPERSEDES the mechanism half of close-reason-does-not-survive-a-reopen-put-the-discharge-in-a-comment. That memory RULE still stands on its own merits — a close reason genuinely does not survive a reopen, so putting the discharge in a comment is still right, and it is what makes the re-close cheap. But it is not why this bead kept reopening.

THE MERGED-PR AUDIT RECORDS ITS FINDING AS A COMMENT, NOT IN THE NOTES FIELD. Grepping notes for AUDIT-REOPEN and concluding from its silence is a FALSE NEGATIVE, and it cost a wrong re-close on 2026-08-21.

MEASURED. rf2-csca8 was closed, then reopened by the post-merge hook. The notes carried no marker, so it was re-closed as a lost write. The marker was a COMMENT created 2026-08-21T00:41:23Z headed 'MERGED-PR AUDIT #8619 — REOPENED THIS EXACT OWNER; NO DUPLICATE BEAD', carrying a substantive statistical defect (an independent Fisher test pinned where the data are paired). The re-close buried it for six minutes.

THE CHECK THAT WORKS, in order:
1. bd comments <id> --json, sorted by created_at descending. This is where the audit writes.
2. comment_count across the reopening commit. It went 15 to 16, which is by itself proof a finding was attached.
3. Only then the notes field.

AND TO IDENTIFY THE WRITER, trace the bead's status through the .beads commits: git log --format=%H --since=... -- .beads/issues.jsonl, then read the bead out of each commit. The flip is attributable to an exact commit — here chore(beads): audit PR #8619 — which distinguishes a deliberate audit reopen from a lost write in one pass. Do this BEFORE re-closing, not after.

A SINGLE BEAD REVERTING WHILE THE REST OF THE BATCH HOLDS is a signal it was reopened deliberately, not that the export time-travelled. 7 of 8 closures held here.

THE AUDIT-REOPEN SCAN MUST READ THE DATABASE, NOT THE EXPORT (2026-08-11; second correction to audit-reopen-scan-over-jsonl and audit-reopen-scan-must-be-time-keyed).

My jq scan reads .beads/issues.jsonl. That file is an EXPORT, refreshed only when a checkpoint runs - so it lags the Dolt database by however long since the last `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh`. Any reopen the audit hook writes AFTER the last checkpoint is invisible to the scan, because the export still carries the pre-reopen row.

CAUGHT LIVE: rf2-hic-076 read OPEN via `bd show` while `jq 'select(.id=="rf2-hic-076")'` on the export reported `status=closed`, complete with a closed_at timestamp. Same bead, two instruments, opposite answers. The audit note (MERGED-PR AUDIT #7852) existed in the database and not in the file.

WHICH INSTRUMENT WINS: `bd show` reads the database and is AUTHORITATIVE. The export is a snapshot. This is the same property CLAUDE.md warns about for a different reason (committing a stale export time-travels the tracker) - the file is downstream of the truth, in both directions.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR THE LOOP: the CLOSURE AUDIT is the reliable detector, because it loops `bd show <id>` per id and reads the status FIELD from the database. The jq scan over the export is a convenience for spotting reopens on beads I never touched, and it is only as fresh as the last checkpoint. So: run the closure audit first and trust it; if the jq scan is used, CHECKPOINT IMMEDIATELY BEFORE IT so the export is current, and treat a disagreement between the two as the export being stale rather than the database being wrong.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, third time this session: an instrument that answers from a cached artefact rather than from the source will be confidently wrong exactly when the source has just changed - which is exactly when you are asking. The other two instances were `git branch -r` (a cache, not remote state) and `gh run list --json status` returning lowercase while `gh pr checks --json state` returns uppercase.

A MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN REOPEN A BEAD BY WRITING TO ITS *NOTES* FIELD, WHERE 'bd comments' RETURNS NOTHING (measured 2026-08-17).

THE INSTANCE. rf2-k9rzr was verified CLOSED immediately after PR #8429 merged. On the next full backlog reread it read OPEN with 'bd comments rf2-k9rzr --json' returning an EMPTY LIST. The reopening audit was real and substantial — 'MERGED-PR AUDIT PR #8429 - completeness and implementation-quality correction', arguing that the PR's own replacement prose supplies the decisive counter-evidence to closing its item 5, and that 'the orphan is a two-host cluster, not one diagnostic string'. It was in the NOTES field.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. A mayor sweeping the backlog with 'bd comments <id> --json' sorted by created_at — the obvious and otherwise correct method — sees NO COMMENTS on that bead and reads it as an unremarkable open item with only its original description. The finding is invisible. The bead was reopened for a reason and the reason cannot be seen by the sweep.

THIS IS THE EXACT CASE THE REPAIRED RULE NAMES. PR #8432 removed the false slogan 'a bead's description is a historical document and its comments are the current state' and replaced it with: establish which text is newest by tracker timestamp, never by position, AND NEVER BY WHICH FIELD IT SITS IN. rf2-hic-047 was the counterexample cited when that landed (newest comment 2026-08-12, newer notes mutation 2026-08-15). rf2-k9rzr is the second measured instance inside twelve hours, and the sharper one, because there were zero comments at all rather than merely older ones.

THE PRACTICAL FIX FOR A BACKLOG SWEEP. A comments-only sweep is incomplete by construction. Either walk 'bd history <id> --json' newest-first to the first change in ANY text-bearing field (description, notes, acceptance, design), or — cheaper for a bulk pass — read the rendered 'bd show' and look for a NOTES block, then order what you find by the history's timestamps. Treat 'NO COMMENTS' in a sweep as 'no comments', never as 'nothing new'.

Autonomous-decision mode (Mike, 2026-05-29 overnight): when Mike EXPLICITLY delegates decisions + says keep-moving (e.g. going to bed, 'done by morning'), the mayor DECIDES in-scope design/technical forks itself — per its own recommendations + the job's goals + the pre-alpha-masterpiece stance (ELEGANCE+CORRECTNESS primary) — and proceeds WITHOUT stopping to ask. This supersedes the usual surface-and-await-go / 'don't action floated ideas' posture FOR THE DELEGATED JOB ONLY. Non-negotiable guardrails stay intact: record EVERY decision in the bead notes + merging PR body (so Mike can review/reverse each in the morning); merge only on green CI (--admin = review-bypass only, never past a failing touched-surface gate); worktree-boundary blocks + stance in every dispatch; recover worker deaths (discard degraded partial work, re-dispatch); commit+push bead structure on each signal; keep ai/dashboard.md as the morning hand-off with a running decisions-log. Quality bar does NOT drop to 'keep moving' — the masterpiece stance governs.

Background workers can end with a garbled final message (e.g. 'I will wait for the background task completion notifications') after doing substantial work but BEFORE committing/pushing/opening the PR. Distrust the completion report; verify ground truth: gh pr list --head, git rev-list origin/main..branch (commits), git status --porcelain (uncommitted). piwhsw (2026-06-09) did the full EP-0002 resolver across 8 files but left them all UNCOMMITTED. Salvage: commit the WIP in the worktree (NO beads, NO AI attribution), push, open the PR yourself, bd close --force (epic-blocked), and let CI be the authoritative completeness gate since the garbled ending means the work may be mid-edit.

A BACKGROUNDED GATE CAN RUN IN ANOTHER WORKER'S WORKTREE AND GRADE THEIR DIFF (rf2-g2mxd, 2026-08-03).

THE MECHANISM, and it is the most dangerous false-green found this week. A worker backgrounded its spine as:

    cd <its own worktree> && sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh

THE `cd` DID NOT SURVIVE BACKGROUNDING. scripts/test-fast-pr.sh derives spine_root/diff_root from BASH_SOURCE[0], so a RELATIVE invocation adopts whatever cwd the shell actually has. The run executed entirely inside a DIFFERENT live worker's worktree (slimresid-e7zxb), classified THAT worker's diff, and produced the two-concurrent-spines signature — 13 phantom test_quiet_shadow_node_cljs_test failures — inside someone else's checkout.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE OTHER FALSE GREENS: the result is a REAL colour attached to SOMEONE ELSE'S DIFF. Not a truncated log, not a stale exit code — a complete, internally consistent run that graded the wrong work. The only visible symptom was a foreign path in an mkdocs INFO line NINETY LINES DOWN.

THE RULES:
• INVOKE BACKGROUNDED GATES BY ABSOLUTE PATH: sh /abs/path/to/worktree/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh — never 'cd X && sh scripts/...' for anything backgrounded.
• BEFORE BELIEVING A GATE, CHECK THE ROOT IT RESOLVED, not just its exit code. If the log names a path that is not your worktree, the run is not yours.
• Cross-check its SURFACE CLASSIFICATION against your own diff — a run reporting jvm=false node=false when your diff is full of .cljs is grading something else. (That is how a sibling caught a different collision the same hour.)

PROPOSED REPO FIX, on rf2-g2mxd: have the spine echo its RESOLVED ROOT as line 1 of its output, so the mismatch is visible immediately instead of ninety lines down.

FAMILY: this joins the pipe's exit status, the SIGTERM'd wrapper's exit 0, the shared-scratchpad clobber, the two-valued probe, and the ungated bench lane. The general form is THE INSTRUMENT REPORTED ON SOMETHING OTHER THAN YOUR SUBJECT — and the defence is always the same: verify the instrument was pointed at you before believing its verdict.

BACKGROUNDED IS NOT KILLED — a harness that moves a long gate to the background at the 600s cap does NOT invalidate its exit code (2026-08-05).

MY STANDING RULE, in every brief: "a killed or timed-out run's exit code is MEANINGLESS - read the runner's own terminal marker." That is correct and stays. But a worker today hit the adjacent case and flagged that my rule reads as covering it: the harness moved scripts/test-fast-pr.sh to the background at the 600s foreground cap, THE RUN CONTINUED TO COMPLETION, and it reported exit 0 with PASS fast PR spine. Nothing was killed. The exit code is meaningful.

THE DISTINCTION TO WRITE: a run that is TERMINATED mid-flight has a meaningless code. A run that is DETACHED and later completes has a real one. The discriminator is whether the runner printed its own terminal marker - which is what the rule already tells workers to read, so the fix is to stop implying that backgrounding alone is the hazard.

WHY IT MATTERS: two workers today reported exit codes with an apology attached because they had been backgrounded, and one nearly re-ran a completed 30-minute spine to get a "clean" foreground result. That is wasted wall-clock produced by my own wording.

ALSO WORTH SEPARATING, from the same report: "Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js" in a FRESH worktree with no node_modules is NOT the reap signature. The reap signature is a gate reporting files that PLAINLY EXIST as missing. A worker that has not run npm ci and hits a genuinely absent module has an ordinary environment gap, and the documented junction is the answer. Confusing the two sends a worker looking for a mayor error that did not happen.

BACKLOG COUNTING — `bd list --status=open` EXCLUDES EPIC CHILDREN; `bd ready` includes them. On 2026-07-19 I reported "backlog 49" for many hours while `bd ready --limit 0` held 70. The 23-bead gap was entirely dotted epic-child ids (rf2-vxgfnd.141, .143, .164, .166, .167, .176, .188, .195, .196, .249, .271, .292, .295, .296, .97, .97.1, rf2-6ajm6z.1) plus five (TRIGGER-GATED) P4s. About 16 were genuinely dispatchable and sat undispatched while I ran 2-4 workers and reported the pool as nearly drained.

THIS IS THE SECOND OCCURRENCE of the same failure — the existing memory recount-ready-backlog-each-tick records under-saturating at 1-3 workers while 108 beads were ready. Same cause both times: a count that silently omits a whole class.

THE COUNT TO USE: `bd ready --limit 0 | awk $1=="○"{print $2} | sort -u | wc -l` — field-based, on the ready list, which is the pool that matters for dispatch. Do NOT count `bd list --status=open`, and do NOT grep -c on a bare glyph.

TWO GREP TRAPS HIT WHILE DIAGNOSING THIS, both of which produced silently wrong numbers rather than errors: (1) an unanchored `grep -oE rf2-[a-z0-9]+` over list output counts ids appearing inside DESCRIPTIONS too — that gave 94 against a true 61 earlier in the session; (2) a `^\s*[○◐●]?\s*rf2-` regex matched NOTHING and returned 0 ids, which reads as "empty pool" rather than as a broken pattern. Always sanity-check that ready ⊆ open ⊆ total; if ready > open, the counter is wrong, not the tracker.

SILENT DAMAGE: backticks inside a DOUBLE-quoted shell string are command substitution, so `bd update --append-notes "...`x`..."` silently deletes the backticked terms before bd ever sees them. bd prints its normal success line. Measured 2026-09-01 (rf2-6c12m.33 worker): six terms vanished from a load-bearing sentence and the remaining text STILL SCANNED as English — it read "in plain backticks (, , )" — so nothing on screen looked wrong. Caught only by re-reading the note afterwards.

THIS IS A SIBLING OF THE --notes-REPLACES TRAP, with the same silence and a different mechanism: there the tool destroys content, here the SHELL does, before the tool is reached. Both are invisible until somebody re-reads the bead, which on a held bead may be never.

THE FIX IS THE QUOTING, not the content: use a SINGLE-quoted string (backticks are literal inside single quotes), or a heredoc, or drop the backticks. Single quotes are the cheap default and cost nothing.

WHY IT BITES EXACTLY WHERE IT HURTS: the notes most likely to carry backticks are the TECHNICAL ones — file paths, symbols, commands, keyword spellings — which are also the notes whose precision is the whole point. A prose note about a decision survives; a note recording an exact symbol spelling gets gutted.

ALWAYS PROBE AFTER WRITING a note that mattered: re-read it and check for known content from the start, middle and end. That probe already guards the --notes trap and the >27000-character truncation; it catches this one too, and it is the only thing that does.

A FALSE REFUTATION I ALMOST RECORDED, AND HOW IT RESOLVED — this is the durable half. THE AGGREGATOR IS NOT CREATED UNTIL ITS needs: RESOLVE, so any PR still in flight reads band-minus-one no matter what its matrix is. #8266 had one check non-green at the time.

SO THERE ARE NOW THREE DISTINCT CAUSES OF A BAND-MINUS-ONE READING, and their remedies differ:
  1. STALE BASE — computed against a superseded matrix. Remedy: gh pr update-branch, then re-read.
  2. GENUINELY ONE CHECK SHORT — a real gap. Remedy: investigate the missing job.
  3. STILL IN FLIGHT — the aggregator has not been created yet. Remedy: WAIT. update-branch is the wrong move and re-triggers everything.
Cause 3 was documented by rf2-nfgib's worker in PR #8254 and is what made this resolvable in one command instead of a misdiagnosis. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS ALWAYS THE SAME: diff the check NAMES, never reason from the count.

'Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again.' USUALLY MEANS THE PR BRANCH IS OUT OF DATE WITH BASE — THE REMEDY IS 'gh pr update-branch <n>', NOT RETRYING (established 2026-08-07 after seven failed retries).

CORRECTING AN EARLIER MEMORY OF MINE. I first blamed a beads audit hook that pushes 'chore(beads): audit merged PR NNNN' to main after each merge. That hook IS real — I watched main move abb49f1ad4 -> aeadb93841 in eight seconds with no merge of mine — and during a burst it can genuinely race a merge. But it was NOT the cause here: I later confirmed main sat stable at one sha across 21 seconds and three fetches while the merge still refused, seven attempts in, with and without --admin.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE: the PR branch was 83 commits behind main. For a rebase-merge GitHub replays the branch onto base, and a sufficiently stale branch is refused with this message even when the PR reads mergeable=MERGEABLE and mergeState=CLEAN. The message names the base, so it reads like a transient race; it is a staleness condition.

THE REMEDY: 'gh pr update-branch <n>'. It moves the head (here f060635c30) and the PR goes MERGEABLE/BLOCKED pending fresh CI on the new head — which is the honest outcome anyway, since the branch is now tested against the main it will land on.

THE DISCRIMINATOR between the two causes, cheap: fetch origin/main, wait ~10s, fetch again. Moving with no merge of yours = hook queue draining, wait it out. Stable but still refusing = the BRANCH is stale, run update-branch. Check how far behind with 'git rev-list --count origin/<branch>..origin/main' — tens of commits is the tell.

DO NOT confuse either with a 502 from a mutating endpoint, where the mutation may HAVE happened and blind retry is wrong. 'Base branch was modified' is an explicit refusal: nothing happened, and retrying is safe but useless until you fix the staleness.

WHEN A NEW TEST CAUSES WIDESPREAD FAILURES IN UNRELATED SUITES, BASELINE MAIN BEFORE DIAGNOSING. Learned 2026-07-24 by the bench-evidence worker, which caught it on itself.

THE INCIDENT: its first B1 draft used Promise.all over two act() mounts and LEAKED A LIVE ROOT on rejection. That cascaded into 98 FAILURES ACROSS UNRELATED SUITES plus a suite-wide timeout — failures in pilot_field and pilot_overlay, which its change had nothing to do with. It ran the suite with its own new file REMOVED, proved main was green (642 tests, 0 failures), and only then knew the fault was entirely its own.

⚠️ WITHOUT THAT BASELINE IT WOULD HAVE CHASED PHANTOM REGRESSIONS in other people work — and in a repo with several workers in flight, the natural (wrong) conclusion is "someone else broke main".

THE RULE: a broad, cross-suite failure after a LOCAL change is almost always YOUR change leaking shared state, not a real regression elsewhere. Before diagnosing anything: remove your new file (or stash-free equivalent: check out the pre-change tree) and re-run. If main is green, the fault is yours and the blast radius is a CONTAMINATION signal, not a map of what is broken.

THE SPECIFIC HAZARD, worth knowing on its own: in a shared-process test bundle, a LEAKED REACT ROOT contaminates every later suite. Promise.all over concurrent mounts is the classic way to leak one — on rejection the other mount is never released. Fix shape: await each mount IN TURN, disambiguate them, and release in a `finally`. This is the same family as the process-global tables that must be reset between suites; anything holding a live handle across a test boundary poisons alphabetical successors.

RELATED FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER: THE BROWSER LANE DISCARDS CONSOLE OUTPUT ON SUCCESS. Published evidence records are only captured under RF2_VERBOSE_TESTS=1. So a test that intends to inspect emitted evidence sees nothing on a passing run unless that flag is set — another way an assertion can be measuring an empty stream.

THE BASH TOOL HALVES BACKSLASH RUNS ON A PLAIN COMMAND LINE TOO, NOT ONLY INSIDE A HEREDOC (2026-09-13; reported by worker storytest-a, measured by the mayor).

CLAUDE.md instrument item (o) scopes the defect to a QUOTED heredoc. The defect is wider than that. Measured on an ordinary Bash-tool command line, inside SINGLE quotes, where bash itself preserves every character:

| command | bytes | intact would be |
|---|---|---|
| `printf '%s' 'x\\)y' \| wc -c` | 4 | 5 (one backslash arrived, not two) |
| `printf '%s' 'x\\\\)y' \| wc -c` | 5 | 7 (two arrived, not four) |
| `printf '%s' 'x\\dy' \| wc -c` | 4 | 5 (halved before a letter too) |
| `printf '%s' 'x\)y' \| wc -c` | 4 | 4 (control: a lone backslash is untouched) |

Single quotes give bash no chance to interpret anything, so the halving happens in the tool before the shell runs. That is the mechanism (o) already names.

WHERE IT BITES: a jq regex like "^rf2-fzbj\\." or a filter containing \\) typed on the command line arrives with half its backslashes, so it matches something else or dies. There were two instances in one session: the mayor's jq test("^rf2-fzbj\\.") and a worker's jq filter.

GUARD: the same as (o).
- Put any backslash-bearing text in a file written with the Write tool, and read it from there: jq -f, a Python script file, or "$(cat file)".
- Or avoid the backslash entirely: in jq, [.] instead of \., and startswith() instead of an anchored regex.
- Verify by effect, e.g. count bytes, since every exit code is 0.

Related: jq-backslash-dot-collapses-use-character-class (the jq concretion), the-bash-tool-silently-strips-backslashes-from-heredoc and heredoc-strips-backslashes-false-zero (the heredoc form). This note does not edit CLAUDE.md (o).

`bd update --claim` AUTO-STAGES .beads/issues.jsonl, AND `git commit` TAKES THE WHOLE INDEX — so a worker that claims its bead and then commits carries the tracker onto its branch WITHOUT EVER TYPING `git add .beads`. Found by the rf2-ejb9h worker, 2026-08-08, which caught it in its own commit and stripped it before pushing.

WHY THIS IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE. CLAUDE.md's beads-durability rule is "worker branches carry code, spec, docs and tests — never .beads/issues.jsonl", and every worker brief repeats it. But the rule reads as an instruction about what to `git add`, and the leak does not come through `git add` at all. It comes through the tracker tool staging on the worker's behalf during a step the brief REQUIRES (claim the bead), followed by an ordinary `git commit -m`. A worker can follow every written instruction and still push a tracker snapshot.

WHAT THAT SNAPSHOT DOES IF IT LANDS: .beads/issues.jsonl is a full-database export, so committing a worker's stale copy TIME-TRAVELS THE TRACKER — beads closed since the worktree was cut reopen, beads filed since vanish. PR #6677 landed exactly that: 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral.

THE FIX, worker-side, and it is index-only so the working file is untouched:
  git restore --staged .beads/issues.jsonl
then commit. Do it BEFORE the commit, not after — an amend rewrites a pushed sha.

THE FIX, brief-side: say "your claim auto-stages the tracker; run `git restore --staged .beads/issues.jsonl` before your first commit" rather than only "do not add .beads". The existing wording tells a worker not to do something it was never going to do deliberately.

THE BACKSTOP HELD AND SHOULD KEEP BEING RUN: `sh scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh origin/main` (pass the base ref — bare invocation exits 1 by design) reports "No beads-database paths in this PR diff" and is the gate that catches this if the worker does not. The pre-commit hook in linked worktrees is the other arm, once installed via `sh scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: a worker reporting "I left the staged .beads for your heartbeat" is doing the right thing, not being lazy — the tracker database is the mayor's to commit. Absorb it with the ordinary `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` cycle, which re-exports from Dolt rather than trusting whatever file is sitting there.

SECOND AND THIRD OCCURRENCES IN ONE SESSION, WITH A TIMELINE THIS TIME — a bd close can evaporate MINUTES after bd show confirms it, and the close REASON is destroyed with it.

WHAT THE DOCUMENTED RULE ALREADY SAYS (CLAUDE.md, rf2-51uz1): clearing .beads after a close reverts the export to its pre-close state and the next checkpoint writes that revert back over the database. The stated remedy is the fixed order — checkpoint FIRST (re-export from Dolt), THEN git checkout HEAD -- .beads, THEN fetch/rebase.

WHAT IS NEW, AND WHY THE ORDER ALONE IS NOT SUFFICIENT PROTECTION: I followed that order every time this session and still lost two closes.

Occurrence 1 (2026-09-06, mid-session): rf2-kuky.78 and rf2-kuky.79 were closed together with rf2-88f1 in ONE command. All three printed the success line. Later the same session .78 and .79 read OPEN while 88f1 — same command, same second — was still CLOSED. So the reversion is not per-command and not deterministic across a single invocation.

Occurrence 2 (2026-09-06 23:xx), measured from bd history rather than inferred:
  23:44:47  bd close rf2-qqn9         -> history shows [P1 - closed]
  23:47:33  still closed
  23:48:30  still closed
  23:49:01  still closed
  23:53:39  [P1 - open]   <- REVERTED, and close_reason went to length 0
It survived FOUR history entries and roughly nine minutes before reverting. A verify-immediately-after-close would have passed, and did.

THE THREE CONSEQUENCES THAT MATTER:
1. VERIFYING RIGHT AFTER THE CLOSE IS NOT ENOUGH. bd show returned CLOSED at 23:44 and the close was gone by 23:53. The only reliable detection is re-verifying every close of the session at the NEXT backlog reread, which is exactly where both occurrences were caught. Treat "verify after close" as necessary and not sufficient.
2. THE CLOSE REASON IS LOST, NOT JUST THE STATUS. close_reason read length 0 afterwards. On this project a close reason is a normative record carrying the five-clause merge evidence, so losing it is worse than losing the status — the status is one command to restore, the reasoning is not. KEEP THE CLOSE REASON IN A FILE. Both re-closes this session were cheap only because the text was still sitting in the scratchpad; writing it inline would have meant reconstructing it from memory.
3. NOTES ARE NOT AFFECTED THE SAME WAY. On rf2-qqn9 the notes field survived intact at 62,154 characters across the reversion while close_reason went to zero. So an --append-notes record is more durable than a close reason, which is an argument for putting anything load-bearing in the notes as well as the reason.

DETECTION RECIPE, cheap and reliable: at every backlog reread, list every bead this session closed and run bd show on each, reading the DATABASE rather than the export. Two of thirteen had reverted at the reread that found this one; eleven were fine. Do not sample — check them all.

NOT YET ESTABLISHED, and I am not asserting it: the exact trigger. The order was correct on every cycle, so "clearing .beads after a close" does not explain these. Candidate mechanisms worth measuring by whoever picks this up — a git worktree add checking out .beads/issues.jsonl into a new linked worktree, and bd auto-importing an export it considers newer than the database. Both ran within the nine-minute window. Neither is proven.

bd close on an ALREADY-CLOSED bead silently leaves close_reason UNCHANGED, while printing its full
success line and ECHOING THE NEW REASON BACK, so the output is indistinguishable from a real amend.
Measured 2026-09-17 on rf2-4nkf4: a corrected 6261-character reason file was passed as
--reason-file; bd exited 0, wrote 6459 bytes to stdout beginning "OK Closed rf2-4nkf4 - ..." followed
by the NEW text, and 0 bytes to stderr, while bd show --json still read the OLD 6263-character
reason carrying the exact defect being corrected. Re-run twice with the same result.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE: this project treats close reasons as NORMATIVE RECORDS (a ruling is often the
close reason of a closed dependency, which is why bd gc's decay phase is banned), so "amend a close
reason" is an act people genuinely attempt - and the obvious spelling for it reports success.

IT FAILS IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION and defeats the obvious verification: the echoed stdout IS the
new text, so reading the command's own output confirms the amend that did not happen. Only
re-reading the FIELD refutes it - bd show <id> --json | jq -r '.[0].close_reason' - which is the same
rule CLAUDE.md item (k) gives for probing the field rather than the rendering.

THE AMEND PATH is reopen-then-close, and the reopen ERASES close_reason and closed_at first (already
documented under CLAUDE.md Beads durability), so write the replacement to a FILE before reopening -
the file is then the only copy of the reason during the window. For a cosmetic blemish, weigh that
erase window against the defect; leaving it recorded is often right.

SAME FAMILY as bd remember silently storing nothing when content begins with --- : a bd write that
no-ops while echoing your own content back as proof of success.

TWO bd close hazards, both hit for real on 2026-08-07/08. Pass close reasons and notes via --reason-file / a quoted heredoc, never an inline double-quoted shell string.

HAZARD 1 — RE-CLOSING DOES NOT REPLACE THE STORED REASON. `bd close` on an ALREADY-CLOSED issue prints success and leaves the previous reason in place. The rf2-0fixc worker discovered this the hard way: its first close reason was damaged, it re-closed with --reason-file, bd reported success, and the OLD damaged text was still stored. It had to append a correction note instead. So a botched close is not fixable by closing again — verify with `bd show` and append a correction if the text is wrong.

HAZARD 2 — INLINE DOUBLE-QUOTED STRINGS GET SHELL-MANGLED. Backticks inside a double-quoted argument are COMMAND SUBSTITUTION. The mayor hit this on a `bd remember` call whose body quoted `gate root: <path>` in backticks: bash executed the contents, printed a `gh pr create` usage dump into the middle of the memory, and stored the mangled result — exit 0, no warning. The rf2-0fixc worker hit the same class on a close reason ("shell backtick substitution ate one fragment"). Markdown-ish prose about a codebase is FULL of backticks, so this is not an edge case, it is the normal case.

THE SAFE FORMS:
  bd close <id> --reason-file <file>
  bd update <id> --append-notes "$(cat <<'EOF'
  ...text with `backticks` and $vars, safe because the heredoc marker is QUOTED...
  EOF
  )"
The quoted heredoc marker ('EOF', not EOF) is what disables substitution. An unquoted marker re-opens the hole.

AND SEPARATELY, THE ONE THAT COST REAL DATA: `bd update --notes` REPLACES notes; use --append-notes. See [bd-update-notes-replaces-existing-notes-it-does] — the same session destroyed 57,413 characters of the EP-0038 epic's note history that way.

BD CONFIG UNSET LIES ABOUT CUSTOM STATUSES (found 2026-07-25, rf2-gtynf). 'bd config unset status.custom' reports SUCCESS and a following 'bd config get status.custom' then reads '(not set)' — but the status is NOT retired: 'bd statuses' still lists it, and a bead can still be moved into it (exit 0). The only thing that actually retires a custom status is 'bd config set status.custom ""' (explicit empty string). DETECTION: 'bd statuses' disagreeing with 'bd config get' is the tell — trust 'bd statuses' and an actual move attempt, never the config read. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS BEAD: status.custom lives ONLY in the Dolt DB, never in tracked config, which is the same shape as the issue-prefix trap (rf2-cchlf). A fresh clone has no custom statuses, so 'bd bootstrap' REJECTS any exported row carrying one — proved end-to-end: a DB with the custom status accepted a bead into it, exported, and a fresh 'bd bootstrap --yes' of that export failed exit 1. So a custom status is a fresh-clone bootstrap landmine, not a cosmetic preference. GENERAL RULE: after any bd config mutation, verify with the command that READS THE BEHAVIOUR (bd statuses, an actual state transition) rather than the command that reads the setting — this tool has at least two settings where the config read and the effective behaviour disagree.

bd create --deps blocks:X makes the NEW issue BLOCK X (X gains a dependency on the new issue), the opposite of reading blocks:X as blocked-by-X. Measured 2026-09-14: rf2-0ae7o.2 was created with --deps discovered-from:rf2-3vd8u,blocks:rf2-3vd8u meaning to wait on rf2-3vd8u; the new bead showed only the discovered-from edge, while rf2-3vd8u gained rf2-0ae7o.2:blocks, and bd close rf2-3vd8u later refused with blocked by open issues [rf2-0ae7o.2]. Nothing errors at create time, so the wrong edge surfaces only when a close or ready listing disagrees. By contrast bd dep add A B --type blocks makes A depend on B (A is blocked by B): rf2-0ae7o.3 got rf2-0ae7o.1:blocks and rf2-0ae7o.2:blocks as intended. Guard: to make a new bead WAIT on X, create it without the blocks dep and then run bd dep add <new> X --type blocks; verify by reading the dependencies array of BOTH beads. Repair: bd dep remove <X> <new>.

bd -C <worktree-path> show|update <id> answers no issue found and exits nonzero, printing a JSON error object on stdout, while the same id resolves through a plain bd show from the mayor checkout and from a cwd inside the worktree. Measured by the mayor 2026-09-15 15:5x AUSEST: control bd show rf2-yemtm --json from the mayor checkout returned the bead (in_progress); bd -C C:/Users/miket/code/re-frame2-worktrees/storyj1frictions-a show rf2-yemtm --json returned Error fetching rf2-yemtm: no issue found plus {"error": "no issues found matching the provided IDs"} and a nonzero exit. Guard: run bd with the cwd inside the worktree, never through -C, and verify every write through bd show <id> --json.

bd DB is effectively SHARED across worktrees, not per-worktree. Observed 2026-05-23: the panel-audit worker (running in its own worktree, NO PR) ran 'bd create rf2-ad7zx.5-.11' + 'bd close .4', and those changes appeared in the MAYOR checkout's bd — while the audit worktree's own .beads/issues.jsonl did NOT contain them. GOOD PRACTICE for no-PR workers (audits especially): after the worker finishes, VERIFY the mayor's bd reflects its bead changes (bd show), then commit+push the mayor's .beads/issues.jsonl mirror so origin matches — the beads will NOT arrive via a PR. Also: still push NEW beads to origin BEFORE dispatching workers that must claim them (a fresh worktree seeds from the committed mirror).

THE BEAD DEFER FIELD IS `defer_until`, NOT `deferred_until` — AND THE WRONG NAME RETURNS A WELL-FORMED NULL FOR EVERY ROW (2026-09-08).

MEASURED: `bd list --json | jq '.[] | select((.deferred_until//"")!="" ...)'` reported `deferred_until=NULL` for all four deferred beads, which reads as "these beads carry no defer date" — a clean, plausible, wrong answer that contradicted the prose notes on those same beads. The real field is `defer_until`, and it holds 2026-09-16 for rf2-fo4ng / rf2-8urba / rf2-8o66x and 2026-10-06 for rf2-elrh.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN ANNOYING: jq's `//` and `.missing` return null silently for a key that does not exist, so a misspelled field is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty one. The failure lands in the REASSURING direction for the question a defer query is usually asked — whether a hold is real — and it invites exactly the wrong conclusion, that prose warnings about lapsing dates describe a mechanism the tracker is not running.

THE GUARD: get the field names from the record itself before selecting on them — `bd show <id> --json | jq -r '.[0] | keys | join(", ")'` — or probe for the VALUE you expect (`to_entries[] | select(.value|tostring|test("2026-"))`) which finds the key by its content and names it. The second form is what caught this.

SAME CLASS as CLAUDE.md's instrument list: an instrument that hands back a clean-looking answer with nothing on screen to betray it. Here the wrong key, elsewhere the wrong pathspec or the hyphen-spanning `\b`.

`bd export` SILENTLY DROPS EVERY MEMORY UNLESS YOU PASS `--include-memories` (bd 1.1.2, measured 2026-09-08).

WHAT HAPPENED: during a beads GC, the checkpoint script refused the post-GC commit by design and printed its sanctioned escape — a hand-rolled `bd export` plus an explicit-path commit. A plain `bd export` writes ONLY issues. On this database that would have dropped all 926 `bd remember` memories from `.beads/issues.jsonl` in one commit, and the export would have looked entirely healthy: valid JSONL, every issue present, no error, normal success line.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN ANNOYING: the export mixes two populations — issues and memories — and every count anybody reads is a TOTAL. A memories-only loss changes the row count by an amount that reads like ordinary churn, and `bd stats` reports ISSUES ONLY, so it stays completely healthy across exactly this event. The pre-commit hook's 90%-of-HEAD floor is the only thing that might catch it, and on a database where memories are a minority it would not fire.

THE GUARD: any hand-rolled export must be `bd export --include-memories`. `scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` does the right thing on its own — this bites only when you follow the script's own escape hatch and roll the export by hand, which is precisely when nobody is watching for it.

THE RECONCILIATION THAT CATCHES IT: count the two populations separately and check they sum to the row count. `grep -c '"_type":"memory"'` (or `bd memories`' header count) plus `bd stats`' Total Issues should equal the export's line count. If the total moved and the issue count did not, the delta is memories.

RELATED: [[checkpoint-row-drop-can-be-memory-consolidation]] — the same two-population confusion read from the other direction, where a legitimate memory cull looks like tracker data loss.

bd EXPORT FROM THE WRONG WORKING DIRECTORY SILENTLY RETURNS A DIFFERENT DATABASE (2026-08-14, hit by the rf2-3lrb worker; more dangerous than the encoding trap beside it).

WHAT HAPPENED: a bd export run with cwd in the session scratchpad auto-discovered a DIFFERENT beads database and returned a plausible-looking snapshot — 789 issues where the real tracker has 1130, and 79 "open" carriers of a text block where the true count was 18. Nothing errored. The output had the right shape, the right field names and internally consistent counts. A scripted pass keyed on those numbers would have rewritten the wrong population, or reported a false census, with no signal at all.

THE RULE: run bd export from the REPO ROOT, and CROSS-CHECK the total against bd stats before believing any number derived from it. Two commands, and the second is what makes the first trustworthy. Also note plain bd export drops infra and memory rows — use --all when the count matters.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE ENCODING TRAP: mangled em dashes at least corrupt something visible. A wrong-database export is a complete, coherent, wrong answer — the same failure class as a gate that runs in a sibling worktree and reports its verdict as yours. Both are "internally consistent run about the wrong subject", which is far harder to catch than a broken one.

THE COMPANION ENCODING RULE, now stated correctly and wider than I first wrote it: the damage is the WINDOWS CONSOLE ENCODING, not bd. python -c ... > file mangles U+2014 the same way. The working rule is NO TEXT CROSSES A CONSOLE PIPE OR STDOUT REDIRECT: read with bd show --json redirected to a file and parsed as UTF-8, write with bd update --body-file from a UTF-8 file, and do intermediate reporting from inside Python with an explicit encoding. Verified across two consecutive scripted passes over 19 bead descriptions each: zero U+FFFD.

RUNNING ANY bd COMMAND FROM A WORKER WORKTREE AUTO-STAGES .beads/issues.jsonl AND DIRTIES A BRANCH THAT MUST NEVER CARRY IT (2026-08-10).

FOUND BY the rf2-xlsh worker, which deliberately SKIPPED writing a bd note for exactly this reason and said so in its report. CLAUDE.md already records that bd auto-stages and never commits, but the consequence for a WORKER has not been written down: a worker told to "claim the bead" or "add a note" stages a full-database export onto its own branch, and the PR-boundary rule says worker branches must never carry .beads/issues.jsonl or .beads/metadata.json.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. Every dispatch brief tells the worker to run `bd update <id> --claim` and most tell it to close on PR-open. Each of those stages the export. A worker that then runs `git add -A`, or that commits without checking `git status`, carries the tracker snapshot into its PR. That is the time-travel hazard: the snapshot is whatever the worktree held when it was created, so merging it reopens beads closed since and deletes beads filed since. PR #6677 landed exactly that, 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral.

THE WORKER'S OWN MITIGATION, which is the right one: it did not run bd at all, and cited the bead in the PR title and body instead so the merged-PR audit hook still has its trail. The hook keys on the bead id in the PR text, not on a bd write.

WHAT TO PUT IN BRIEFS: tell the worker to stage explicit paths, never `git add -A`, and to check `git status --short .beads` is empty before every commit. If a brief asks for a bd claim or close, add that those commands stage the export and the worker must unstage it (`git restore --staged .beads`) before committing. A worker that would rather skip the bd write entirely and rely on the PR text is making a defensible choice, not a lazy one.

THE MAYOR OWNS .beads COMMITS. Only the mayor checkout checkpoints the tracker, via sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh, which re-exports from Dolt rather than trusting whatever file is on disk.

`bd gc` HAS A DECAY PHASE THAT SILENTLY DELETES CLOSED BEADS — pass `--skip-decay` unless you positively intend it (found 2026-09-08 by the rf2-gwxj dossier, while investigating the 1.3 GB store).

WHY IT IS A FOOT-GUN RATHER THAN A DOCUMENTED FEATURE: the obvious reason to reach for `bd gc` is disk reclamation, and in that frame DECAY is not what you are asking for. It removes closed beads, whose close reasons are treated as NORMATIVE RECORDS in this repo — CLAUDE.md's nightly-red rule says in terms 'Never reopen the closed bead: its close reason is a normative record', and the retained-record ruling for worker/receipts-hic081 lives on a CLOSED bead (rf2-lafmr) and is the only thing standing between a hygiene sweep and deleting a spike branch. Losing closed beads would delete rulings, not clutter.

ALSO: `bd gc` DOES NOT RECLAIM THE STORE ANYWAY. Only `bd flatten` reclaims Dolt's noms directory, so reaching for gc to shrink the store gets you the destructive half with none of the benefit.

RELATED, from the same investigation: Dolt runs EMBEDDED here, so `bd flatten`'s GC phase is a corruption path unless run at fleet-zero (no live mayor loop, no worker worktrees holding the DB). Never run flatten or gc while anything else is writing beads.

The full analysis is rf2-gwxj and its dossier ai/decisions/rf2-gwxj.beads-store-size-flatten.md (local-only).

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE STANDING BEADS-GC INSTRUCTION, BOTH DATA-LOSS-ADJACENT, MEASURED 2026-09-06 FROM --help AND DRY RUNS.

(1) `bd gc` PHASE 1 'DECAY' *IS* A PRUNE (default 90 days). The recurring GC instruction describes gc as 'decay old issues, compact Dolt commits, run Dolt GC' and describes prune separately as the deleting one — which reads as though gc is the safe verb and prune the dangerous one. They are not disjoint: running `bd gc` without `--skip-decay` DELETES closed beads. **`--skip-decay` is mandatory on this project**, where close reasons are normative records and bead ids are cross-file citations. With --skip-decay, gc's phase 2 is informational only (it prints 'use bd flatten to squash') and phase 3 is DOLT_GC(), neither of which deletes a bead.

(2) `bd restore` DOES NOT RECOVER FROM `bd compact`. The instruction says 'note bd restore exists to recover a compacted issue's pre-compaction content', which invites treating `bd compact` as reversible. It is not. `bd restore` pairs with `bd admin compact` (semantic summarisation that discards original bead text). Plain `bd compact` is a Dolt COMMIT squash — it cherry-picks survivors and SWAPS MAIN — and is irreversible; anything landing in the swap window is discarded.

THIRD FACT THAT DECIDES THE WHOLE TASK ON THIS INSTALL: Dolt runs EMBEDDED (in-process), not as a server — every `bd` invocation is its own OS process sharing .beads/embeddeddolt/.dolt/noms. Dolt's GC safepoint protocol is per-SERVER, and there is no server, so DOLT_GC() rewriting the chunk store while another process writes is a CORRUPTION path rather than mere lock contention. **Every compaction/GC verb is therefore fleet-zero work**, not something to run while workers hold beads.

AND THE PAYOFF IS SMALL, IN THE SAME SHAPE AS THE PRUNE PREMISE: `bd compact --dry-run` reads 16,441 Dolt commits of which only 1,785 are older than 30 days — an 11% reduction. At 150-200 tracker commits a day, recent history dominates, exactly as recent closures dominate the closed-bead population.

WHERE THE SPACE ACTUALLY IS (.beads = 6.2 GB): the live database is 472 MB of noms, i.e. 7.6%. 5.0 GB is .beads/backup/ — of which ~2.5 GB is an ORPHANED quarantine directory local-diverged-remnant-20260803-095318/ left by a 2026-08-03 divergence recovery. **No bd verb reaches it**; it is a filesystem delete and the single biggest safe win. Another 685 MB is a regenerable git-remote-cache.

TWO INSTRUMENTS THAT MISREPORT HERE, both exit 0 with a reassuring answer: `bd admin compact --dolt` probes .beads\dolt, which does not exist on this install (the real directory is .beads\embeddeddolt, per `bd dolt show`), and prints 'No local Dolt directory found; nothing to collect' — reading as 'already tidy' having never looked. And `bd doctor --check artifacts`, the only bd-native cruft cleaner, prints 'not yet supported in embedded mode'. So there is no working isolated Dolt-GC verb on this install.

bd history <id>'s NEWEST ENTRY IS A DATABASE-COMMIT TIME, NOT A BEAD-MUTATION TIME — ON A BUSY TRACKER EVERY BEAD SHARES THE SAME NEWEST TIMESTAMP (measured 2026-08-23 10:03 AUSEST, tip c951fe8ef3).

WHAT I DID AND WHAT IT RETURNED. Asking 'when did each held bead last really change?', I took the max timestamp out of 'bd history <id>' for all 21 open+deferred beads. Every one came back 2026-08-23 09:50:19 — identical to the second, across beads I had not touched in days. That is the reassuring, useless answer: it says everything changed a minute ago.

THE MECHANISM. bd history lists Dolt commits, and every bd write commits the database, so a commit appears in a bead's history whether or not that bead moved. rf2-3t2nq shows 9728 entries; its four newest snapshots (09:50:19, 09:50:18, 09:34:21, 09:06:03) diff to NO FIELDS DIFFERING against their predecessors.
