THE PATTERN IN MY OWN BEHAVIOUR, third instance today: I relayed a bead's malli attribution trail whose own dates disproved it; I relayed "the guide overpromises" for a paragraph already corrected on main; and I relayed this. IN ALL THREE THE WORKER MEASURED AND THE MEASUREMENT INVERTED THE STORY. A report from a worker is evidence about what that worker saw, not a fact about the tree - and when I pass one on as a premise it acquires an authority it has not earned.

WHAT scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py ACTUALLY ANSWERS — corrected 2026-08-14 after the audit of PR #8161 refuted my first version of this memory.

CITE IT, BUT DESCRIBE IT CORRECTLY. It derives the gap between scripts/test-fast-pr.sh and the REQUIRED CI SET — which required steps the fast SPINE does not run. Derived from the three aggregators needs:, each job gate steps from its run: bodies, and the spine own invocations, so a new required job or a new step inside an existing job is reported by construction. Modes: --list full report, --brief digest, --check drift ratchet.

IT DOES NOT INSPECT WHAT A GIVEN WORKER RAN, and my earlier wording — "which required CI checks your local gates do not cover" — is wrong in BOTH directions. If the worker did not run the spine, the checks the spine would have covered are missing from its coverage yet absent from the report. If the worker ran one of the reported checks directly, the report still lists it. I wrote that wording into a bead, into a merged sentence in mayor-dispatch.md, and into several briefs before the audit caught it.

THE CORRECT BRIEF INSTRUCTION IS TWO FACTS, NOT ONE: cite the script as the canonical fast-spine-versus-required-CI gap, AND require the worker to state whether the spine ran plus any targeted gates it ran directly. Only the pair lets a reader compute real coverage.

THE ORIGINAL POINT STILL STANDS: do not send a worker to read .github/workflows/* by hand, and do not enumerate required checks in a brief — the required set moves. The citation target was right; my description of what it answers was not.

CITE THE HARNESS-DISAGREEMENT CENSUS AS DERIVED, AND DO NOT APPEND MY OWN SIGHTINGS TO IT (2026-08-14, found by the method-reread loop grading my own briefs).

THE NUMBER: at least 44 instances across 29 distinct workers in three days, at least 23 of them runs the worker already knew should be red, every one surfacing as exit 0. It was re-derived from 600 merged PRs whose bodies preserve the first-hand pairs, and it replaced a figure of "fifteen across five" that had been understated by two thirds.

THE DOC ADDS AN INSTRUCTION I HAD BEEN HALF-BREAKING: "Recount that census when you cite it; do not carry it forward by adding the instances you have just seen, which is how it came to be understated by two thirds."

WHAT I WAS DOING: pasting the 44/29/23 figures correctly, then appending phrases like "including twice in this session". That is inaccurate on its face — the 44 was derived from merged PRs BEFORE this session, so this session sightings are not among them — and it is the exact shape the warning names. A future mayor reading my brief could reasonably write "46" and the drift restarts.

THE RULE: paste the census figures verbatim as a DERIVED result with its derivation named, and if a fresh sighting is worth mentioning, mention it as a SEPARATE sentence that does not imply it extends the count. Better still, mention it without a number at all: "it happened again on a control run this session whose captured code was 1" carries the warning without touching the census.

WHO THE RECOUNT INSTRUCTION IS FOR: whoever UPDATES the document, not every brief that pastes the block. Recounting 600 PRs per dispatch is not feasible and is not what it asks.

NAMING THE "AUTHORITY" FOR A CONTRACT BY GREPPING ITS EPIC OR DOC-ID FINDS THE FILE THAT DISCUSSES IT,
NOT THE FILE THAT HOLDS IT -- AND A BRIEF THAT SHIPS THAT CITE SENDS A WORKER TO READ THE WRONG FILE.

MEASURED 2026-09-18. Writing a fence note for rf2-m2ye2 I needed the authority for the framework's closed
effect-key set. I grepped `EP-0025` across `implementation/`, took the top hit --
`implementation/core/src/re_frame/classification.cljc`, which carries EP-0025 in its first ten lines --
and wrote into the brief that it "is the authority for the closed set ... READ IT". The worker checked and
refuted it: the real holder is **`implementation/core/src/re_frame/events.cljc`, `closed-effect-map-keys`
at :278**. Controls: `clear-sensitive` reads **0** in classification.cljc and **5** in events.cljc.
`projection.cljc`'s own comment had cited it correctly all along; only my brief was wrong.

WHY THE GREP PICKS THE WRONG FILE, AND IT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN BAD LUCK. An epic id, a spec number or
a ticket id is written where the change is EXPLAINED -- a namespace docstring, a rationale comment, a
migration note. The data structure that actually defines the contract is often a small `def ^:private`
with no id near it at all, because its author had nothing to justify. **So the id-shaped search ranks
commentary above definition by construction**, and the top hit reads like an authority precisely because
it is the most discursive file on the subject.

IT FAILS IN THE DIRECTION THAT LOOKS RIGOROUS. A brief citing a specific file and calling it the authority
reads as better sourced than one that says "find the closed set". The worker either burns a cycle
discovering the cite is wrong, or -- worse -- reads the named file, finds nothing resembling a closed set,
and doubts its own search rather than the brief. That is the same shape CLAUDE.md prices for dangling
`ai/findings/` paths and for the reopened-bead dispatch clause: an unsatisfiable instruction is read by
the worker as its own failure.

THE GUARD: **cite the SYMBOL, and let the symbol locate the file.** Search for the thing that holds the
data -- the def name, the key set, the var -- not the id that explains it, and confirm the file you name
actually contains it before writing the cite. A one-line check does it: grep a member of the set (here
`clear-sensitive`) across the candidate files and require a non-zero count in the file you are about to
name, with a control showing another file reads zero. **Where you cannot resolve the holder cheaply, say
"find X and say where you read it from" rather than naming a file** -- an honest instruction to search
beats a confident wrong pointer, and the worker was going to verify anyway.

THIS IS A MAYOR-SIDE DEFECT IN BRIEF CONSTRUCTION, WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH A MEMORY AT ALL. It is the
fifth premise of mine a worker corrected in one session; the others were a gate's roots, a relayed
"one reader" claim, a bead's notes wrongly described as empty, and a ruled-against promise that had in
fact already fired. **The common thread in all five is a claim I took from one instrument's top answer and
did not cross-check before it left my hands** -- and the fix in every case was one cheap control taken
from the target. The workers caught all five, which is the system working; the cost is a cycle each time,
and the cycle is avoidable.

Related: [[a-jvm-test-lane-never-loads-a-non-test-clj-namespace]] is the same session's other
brief-construction correction -- there I nominated a gate that could not fail on the file in question.
Both are the mayor asserting something about WHERE a property lives without asking the artefact.

scripts/check_skill_migration_cites.py's TYPE-DRIFT check computes migration_type_b MINUS skill_type_b, so it only catches the corpus calling something Type B that the SKILL omits — never the reverse. Measured 2026-09-02 (rf2-131wu): the corpus Type-tag summary listed M-5 and M-16 as wholly Type A against their own per-rule bodies, and the gate was green throughout because the drift ran in the unchecked direction. A control that can only fail one way is worth knowing about before you cite its green as evidence about a classification table.

Claim is not dispatch (learned 2026-06-23, the d3pku1 incident): claiming a bead (bd update --status=in_progress) does NOT dispatch a worker. The mayor claimed rf2-d3pku1, then got interrupted by incoming operator rulings (vw5h1r/mtzv5m/xmnlvc) and never launched the Agent — but reported d3pku1 as a 'running worker' for ~20 loop ticks based solely on the bead being in_progress. The error surfaced only on a liveness check (no worktree, no remote branch, no PR for the bead). RULE: an in_progress bead is NOT proof a worker is running. Before reporting a bead's worker as in-flight, verify the artifact exists — a worktree (git worktree list), a remote branch, OR an agent-launch confirmation. When claiming-then-dispatching across multiple tool calls and an interruption lands between them, re-confirm the dispatch actually happened. THE .claude/commands/*.md ARM BELONGS TO check_readme_links.py, NOT check_doc_slugs.py — I HAVE NOW NOMINATED THE WRONG ONE REPEATEDLY (2026-08-19).

THE FACT, established three ways by a worker and reproduced: check_doc_slugs.py DEFAULT_ROOTS is ("docs", "spec", "skills", "migration") — no .claude. CLAUDE.md under Build and Test says the command-file arm is check_readme_links.py --ci. mayor-dispatch.md own two-link-gates paragraph says the same. And the discriminating test: on a tree with a planted fault in .claude/commands/mayor-dispatch.md, check_readme_links.py --ci went EXIT 1 naming the file and line, while check_doc_slugs.py returned EXIT 0 and never mentioned the fault.

WHY I KEEP GETTING IT WRONG. The two gates split by PATH and the split does not follow the intuition. check_doc_slugs sounds like the general documentation gate, so a file full of prose feels like its territory. It is not: it owns docs/, spec/, skills/, migration/ and tools/*/spec. Everything else — repo-root markdown, every README beside source, and .claude/commands/ — is check_readme_links.py --ci. And the job that runs BOTH is named verify-readme-links, so the job name misleads in the opposite direction.

THE RULE: NOMINATE BY PATH, NEVER BY JOB NAME AND NEVER BY WHAT THE GATE SOUNDS LIKE. Before naming a gate in a brief, check the gate own roots. If a brief nominates the wrong gate, the worker either wastes a cycle discovering it or — worse — runs the wrong gate, gets a green that proves nothing, and reports coverage it does not have.

THIS IS THE SAME CLASS rf2-hrrvk WAS FILED FOR and the fix that landed for it did not stop me repeating it, because the fix documented the split rather than changing how I choose. The behavioural change is: read DEFAULT_ROOTS (or the equivalent) at source when writing the brief, and say in the brief WHY that gate covers that path.

ONE MORE THING WORTH KEEPING, from the same worker: the command-file resolver matches only .md-suffixed references, so path-shaped tokens like .beads/ or p0_run.cjs in command-file prose are outside what it resolves. A green there is real but narrow — it means the markdown references resolve, not that every path mentioned exists.

THE .claude/commands/ TREE IS COVERED BY NO GATE AT ALL (found 2026-08-07, PR #7641).

THE GAP, verified rather than assumed: 'mkdocs build --strict' builds only docs/, and check_doc_slugs.py's roots are docs, spec, skills, migration and tools/*/spec. So .claude/commands/mayor-*.md — the codified mayor loop bodies, the single source of truth the method tells you to keep in sync with docs/the-mayor-method/ — is validated by nothing. A broken link, a dangling anchor or a malformed front-matter block there ships silently.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN ITS SIZE. bootstrap.md says 'when a method rule changes in this tree, re-read the matching mayor-*.md command files — the link gate catches renamed files, not semantic drift.' That sentence assumes a link gate covers them. It does not. The stated backstop is absent, so the drift the sentence warns about is completely unpoliced.

WHAT TO DO MEANWHILE: any worker editing .claude/commands/** hand-verifies front matter, links and headings, and says so in the PR body — the same discipline docs/design/** already requires because mkdocs excludes it. Do not nominate mkdocs or check_doc_slugs for that tree; both exit 0 having read nothing, which is the fail-open this project keeps finding in its own instruments.

NOT FILED AS A BEAD deliberately: nothing is broken today, and adding a root to the slug checker is a speculative fix nobody has asked for. Recorded so the next person editing those files knows the gate they would reach for is empty. If a real breakage ever ships from that tree, file it then with the evidence.

TWO GATE-COVERAGE CORRECTIONS, both found by probing rather than reading (2026-08-07).

CORRECTION 1 — the claim that .claude/commands/ is covered by NO gate is WRONG, though nearly right. scripts/check_readme_links.py (rf2-1yy75) DOES resolve markdown path references inside .claude/commands/*.md and runs --ci in the docs tier. Probed: it exits 1 with BROKEN COMMAND-FILE REFERENCE naming the file and line. It covers ONLY those path references — not front matter, not headings, not structure. The honest statement: path references are gated; everything else in that tree is not, and must be hand-verified.

CORRECTION 2 — check_doc_slugs.py MASKS FENCED CODE BLOCKS, so it does not link-validate anything inside them. This matters enormously for docs/the-mayor-method/bootstrap.md, where the ENTIRE prompt body lives inside a fenced text block. A deliberate broken anchor INSIDE the fence gave exit 0; the same anchor OUTSIDE the fence gave exit 1 naming file and line. So "check_doc_slugs.py passed on bootstrap.md" says nothing about the prompt text itself — which is the part anyone actually reads.

WHY BOTH MATTER TOGETHER: same failure shape this project keeps meeting — a gate that runs, exits 0, and verified less than you assumed. Same remedy: prove selection by injecting a deliberate break AT THE EXACT SITE you are editing, not merely somewhere in the file. A probe outside the fence would have proved coverage that does not exist inside it.

FOR BRIEFS: when a dispatch touches .claude/commands/ or a fenced prompt body, require the worker to hand-verify and state what it checked — and never let "the slug checker passed" stand as evidence for fenced content.

- Command-file front matter is ONE key, not two: --- / description: / ---. A brief saying 'confirm it parses as two keys' is asking for something false.

MEASURED 2026-08-21: `gh run list --branch
--commit ` returned an EMPTY array for two PRs whose runs demonstrably existed, then returned 4 runs each on a retry moments later with the identical command. The emptiness was TRANSIENT, not a query defect. WHY THIS IS DANGEROUS: it fails OPEN in the merge criterion. An empty result reads as 'no live runs', which SATISFIES clause 4 vacuously - the same shape the criterion already warns about for an abbreviated sha, reached by a different route. A mayor who treats empty as terminal merges a PR whose runs it never checked. THE DISCRIMINATION, and it costs one extra command: an empty clause-4 result is NOT EVIDENCE. Corroborate before believing it, by BOTH of: 1. Retry the identical combined query. 2. Run the BRANCH-ONLY form and compare headSha yourself: `gh run list --branch
--limit 10 --json status,headSha,name`. Clause 4's substance is 'no run on THIS head is nonterminal', and comparing headSha in the output is what the clause actually asks for - the --commit flag is only one mechanism for it. THE BRANCH-ONLY FORM ALSO SHOWS WHY THE COMPARISON MATTERS RATHER THAN THE FLAG: PR #8604's branch listing carried runs on TWO shas - four on the current head and four on an older 25c285fe4ebd - and only the headSha comparison excludes the stale ones. A stale-sha run is not evidence about this head. ALWAYS PRINT THE RUN COUNT, never just the nonterminal count. A test written as 'nonterminal==0' cannot distinguish 'all runs finished' from 'there are no runs', and those are opposite facts. Print `runs=\(length)` beside it.

CLAUSE 5's JOB-KEY COUNT IS A PROXY; THE PR'S OWN TOTAL IS THE DIRECT MEASUREMENT — when the total already equals the current band, a non-zero job-key count is MOOT (2026-08-15 16:34 AUSEST).

MEASURED WHILE MERGING PR #8302. My fuller clause-5 check read jobs=1 risk=2 against its merge base, which by the procedure I adopted this morning demands gh pr update-branch and a re-check. I merged without it and then went back to see whether that was safe. IT WAS, and the reason generalises:

  #8302 total = 100  =  the current band
  and its rollup CONTAINED 'JVM epoch under the production gate' — the very job added since its base

So its checks were computed against the CURRENT matrix, not its base's. GitHub Actions evaluates a PR on the MERGE REF, which already includes main's current workflows — so a PR whose base predates a new job can still run that job.

THEREFORE THE TEST ORDER SHOULD BE:
  1. Does the PR's OWN total equal the current band? If YES, its check set is current — the stale-base concern cannot apply, and the job-key/risk counts are moot. Merge on the other clauses.
  2. Only if the total is BELOW the band do the job-key and step-only counts do any work: they discriminate 'behind by a real job' from 'in flight' from 'genuinely one short'.

WHY I HAD IT BACKWARDS: I adopted the job-key count as a PRE-FILTER and ran it first, because that is the order clause 5 describes. But clause 1's band comparison is the DIRECT measurement of the same property, and a direct measurement outranks a proxy for it. The proxy exists for the case where the direct measurement is ambiguous, not the reverse.

WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE, and the distinction matters: the job-key count is still the right instrument when the total is short, and the step-only qualification is still necessary there — a widened classifier glob flips a row SKIPPED->executed under an unchanged name, which the band cannot see because clause 1 counts skipped rows. That reasoning stands untouched.

THE COST OF THE OLD ORDER WAS NEVER A BAD MERGE — it was needless CI restarts on PRs that were already current, which is the cheap direction. So this is an efficiency correction, not a safety one. Say so when writing it up rather than dressing it as a near miss.

CLAUSE 5's JOB-KEY ZERO IS NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT — on zero, READ the intervening workflow diff and confirm it is STEP-ONLY (2026-08-15 13:53 AUSEST).

THE MAYOR'S OWN PROCEDURE, in the order to run it. Both commands, every time, never one:

  # 1. did a JOB KEY appear?  (two leading spaces; git, never gh pr diff)

Non-zero on (1) = new job, re-check properly. Zero on (1) AND zero on (2) = step-only, skip update-branch. Zero on (1) with a hit on (2) = STILL A MATRIX CHANGE.

No job key is added. And clause 1 counts a skipped row like any other, so THE BAND DOES NOT MOVE TO BETRAY IT EITHER. A strategy.matrix arm adds rows to an existing job; a name: change relabels one. CLEANUP MUST PARSE `git worktree list`, NEVER CONSTRUCT NAMES (2026-07-19, second instance of this root cause in one session).

BUG: my hygiene loop derived a worktree branch as "worker/<dirname>" and derived the worktree from a branch by the same rule. WORKTREE DIRECTORY NAMES AND BRANCH NAMES ARE INDEPENDENT. Concrete case in this repo: the directory re-frame2-worktrees/core-handbook-html has branch worker/codex-audit-live checked out. Consequences of the wrong derivation, both live:
  (a) core-handbook-html resolved against a NONEXISTENT branch worker/core-handbook-html -> no PR found -> any decision keyed on that lookup is meaningless, and had a same-named PR existed it would have acted on the WRONG branch.
  (b) worker/codex-audit-live appeared to have NO worktree -> nominated for deletion WHILE CHECKED OUT. A belt-and-braces re-check (git worktree list | grep -c <branch>) aborted it; the primary scan was simply wrong.
Also missed: a detached-HEAD worktree (fix-6365-consumers) has NO branch at all, so any name-derived lookup silently returns nothing rather than erroring.

CORRECT SOURCE: `git worktree list` prints "<path> <sha> [<branch>]" or "(detached HEAD)". PARSE THAT. Path and branch are BOTH given — never construct either from the other, and handle the detached case explicitly.

SAME ROOT CAUSE AS THE WORKTREE I DESTROYED EARLIER TONIGHT (see memory: i-destroyed-a-live-worker-worktree): there I keyed a destructive action on a BRANCH NAME that collided with a historical merged PR. Both bugs are one mistake — DERIVING IDENTITY FROM A NAME INSTEAD OF READING IT. Names are not unique across time (bead ids repeat across sessions) and not unique across dimensions (dirname != branch). Key destructive operations on read identity: the SHA, the parsed branch, the PR headRefOid.

STANDING CHECKLIST for any destructive worktree/branch operation:
  1. Live-worker skip list first, unconditionally.
  2. Parse identity from `git worktree list`; never construct.
  3. Require merged-PR headRefOid == worktree HEAD before removal (name match proves nothing).
  4. Require 0 commits ahead of origin/main OR state==MERGED before branch deletion.
  5. Canary `ls implementation/node_modules | wc -l` (baseline 101) before and after every batch.
  6. Re-verify immediately before the destructive call; if the re-check disagrees with the scan, ABORT and investigate — the scan is the thing that is wrong.

CLEANUP GAP: "0 commits ahead + clean + no PR" MATCHES BOTH A DEAD-STALE WORKTREE AND A FRESHLY-STARTED LIVE ONE. Found 2026-07-24 before it caused damage.

THE SITUATION: my hygiene pass reaps worktrees that are 0 commits ahead of main, clean, and have no PR — the profile of a worker that never started. That is correct for STALE ones. But a worker that started SECONDS AGO has exactly the same profile: it has created its worktree and not yet committed anything. A worktree named pr-audit-6756, belonging to a DIFFERENT session audit loop, sat at 0-ahead/clean/no-PR while actively running.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS FRESHNESS, NOT SHAPE. A dead-stale worktree is parked on an OLD main commit and its files have not been touched in hours. A live one sits at or near CURRENT origin/main and has filesystem activity within minutes.

ADD TO THE STANDING CHECKLIST, as a rule that fires BEFORE any 0-commit removal:
  (a) Is HEAD at or very near current origin/main? Stale ones are behind by many commits — check `git -C <wt> rev-list --count HEAD..origin/main`. A large number means genuinely abandoned; ~0 means it just branched.
  (b) Any filesystem activity in the last ~30 minutes (excluding node_modules and .git)? `find <wt> -maxdepth 2 -newermt "-30 minutes"`. If yes, IT IS LIVE — skip unconditionally.
  (c) Is the worktree one I dispatched this session? If I cannot account for it, assume ANOTHER SESSION owns it and skip. Concurrent sessions independently create worker/* worktrees and branches in this repo; my dispatch list is not the full roster.

⚠️ THIS IS THE THIRD TIME THE SAME ROOT CAUSE HAS THREATENED LIVE WORK: I destroyed a live worktree by matching a HISTORICAL merged PR on a branch NAME, and separately nominated a checked-out branch for deletion by deriving the worktree from the branch name. All three are the same mistake — INFERRING LIVENESS OR IDENTITY FROM A PROPERTY THAT DOES NOT CARRY IT. A name is not identity; a commit count is not liveness.

STANDING RULE, unchanged and reinforced: reaping is only ever safe on (1) a merged PR whose headRefOid EQUALS the worktree HEAD, or (2) a worktree that is BOTH zero-commit AND demonstrably cold AND accounted for. When in doubt, leave it — an unreaped worktree costs disk; a reaped live one costs a worker its work.

AFTER A /clear, TaskList RETURNS NOTHING WHILE PRE-CLEAR BACKGROUND WORKERS ARE STILL ALIVE AND WILL STILL NOTIFY (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED. A fresh mayor session started with /clear. Two worker worktrees stood under the worktree parent: residue4-o9yo4 and workcount-n1b9h. TaskList returned 'No tasks found'. I checked both trees and each read: zero commits ahead of origin/main, clean git status --porcelain, and NO remote branch. I concluded both workers were dead, that there was nothing to salvage, and redispatched BOTH beads to new workers.

BOTH WERE ALIVE. residue4-o9yo4 reported done 25 minutes later with PR #8496 and two beads' worth of work including a refusal. workcount-n1b9h had 5,036 files touched in the last 30 minutes — a worker mid-gate. I had two duplicate executors out, and one of the pairs was BENCH-CLASS, where two concurrent runs WEDGE rather than fail.

EVERY SIGNAL I READ WAS TRUE AND NONE OF THEM MEANT WHAT I TOOK IT TO MEAN.
- TaskList empty: the harness's task registry does not survive /clear, but the AGENTS do. An empty TaskList after /clear is a statement about the registry, not about the fleet.
- Zero commits / clean tree: this is the EXPECTED reading for the commonest healthy state. A worker inside a long gate commits nothing by design. loops.md says exactly this and I read it an hour earlier.
- No remote branch: a worker pushes at milestones, not continuously. Absence of a remote ref is not absence of a worker.

THE ONE SIGNAL THAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT, AND IT COSTS ONE COMMAND:
  find <worktree> -newermt '30 minutes ago' -type f | grep -v '/\.git/' | wc -l
Near-zero is a strand. Thousands is a live gate. Run it on EVERY worktree before concluding anything about EVERY worker, and run it FIRST — before the commit count, before the remote check, before TaskList.

RULE FOR A POST-/clear MAYOR: enumerate git worktree list, sweep each tree for recent file activity, and treat any tree with activity as HELD by a live worker you cannot see. Do not redispatch its bead. TaskList is blind to it, SendMessage cannot reach it by a name you no longer have, and its completion notification WILL arrive — the agent id survives even though your listing does not.

COST HERE: two duplicate dispatches, both caught and stopped before they made any edit, so zero lost work. The catch was the pre-clear worker's own completion notification arriving and naming a bead I had just redispatched. That is luck, not a control.

CLJ-KONDO LOCAL/CI VERSION SKEW — the local binary reports NINE PHANTOM ERRORS that CI does not. Quantified 2026-07-24 by two workers independently.

LOCAL on this machine: clj-kondo v2025.10.23. CI PINS: 2026.04.15.

The older local version reports 9 errors of the form `Expected: throwable, received: boolean/nil` in `implementation/ui/test/**` — DONOR TEST CODE — which CI version does not report at all. A worker reproducing a lint failure locally will chase nine non-existent failures in code it did not touch.

THE RULE: when a lint or gate verdict must be AUTHORITATIVE, read CI OWN JOB LOG rather than trusting a local run.
  gh pr checks <PR> --json name,state,link      # find the job id
  gh run view --job=<id> --log-failed           # what CI actually said
If you must reproduce locally, pin the CI version first. And run CI exact invocation from .github/workflows/lint.yml — same flags, same lint paths — not a convenient approximation of it.

⚠️ THIS COMPOUNDS WITH THE PIPED-EXIT-CODE TRAP (see piping-a-gate-into-tail-discards-its-exit-code). Together they produce the worst case: a local run that reports failures CI does not have, through a pipe that hides the exit code, so a worker can conclude either "I broke something" or "I am green" with equal confidence and be wrong both times. Capture to a file, echo the exit code, and when it matters read CI log.

MAYOR NOTE — A SEQUENCING ERROR I MADE ON THE SAME INCIDENT, worth not repeating: several PRs were red on clj-kondo. One worker reported that a specific open PR carried the fix, so I instructed another worker to STAND DOWN and wait for that PR to merge. Wrong on two counts: (a) the fix had ALREADY landed on main as a separate direct commit, and (b) the PR I named was a different change. The correct remedy was simply A REBASE ONTO CURRENT MAIN. Had the worker obeyed, its gate would have stayed red and we would have lost a cycle; it had already rebased and told me so.
GENERALISATION: when a gate is red because of something INHERITED, the fix is almost always "rebase onto a main that has the remedy", NOT "wait for a specific PR". Verify WHERE the remedy actually is (git branch -r --contains <sha>) before telling anyone to wait on anything.

scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py READS THE clj-kondo VERSION PIN OFF lint.yml's INSTALL STEP BY ITS LITERAL COMMAND SHAPE (2026-08-11, rf2-rkl9 / PR #7888).

WHY THIS BIT. The rf2-rkl9 worker replaced lint.yml's two-hop clj-kondo install with a direct fetch of the pinned release archive. That is a one-file change by every obvious reading — and it broke a REQUIRED gate in a second file. check_fast_pr_gap.py knew only the `install-clj-kondo --version <pin>` shape, so with the installer gone `--check` exited 1 with "the clj-kondo version pin could not be read". Separately, the new lines stopped matching SETUP_PATTERNS, which misreported the installer as an unrun CI gate and moved the undecided-check count from 96 to 97.

BOTH FIXES WENT AT THE PARSER, not at the workflow: the pin now anchors on `clj-kondo/releases/download/v<pin>/`, which is a TIGHTER anchor than the old one, and the self-test fixture moved to match.

THE GENERAL RULE: a workflow edit can break a checker that parses that workflow, and nothing in the diff shows it. `.github/workflows/**` is already hot-zone for CONFLICT reasons; this is a second, independent reason to treat it carefully — the blast radius reaches scripts that read it. Before editing a workflow step, grep `scripts/` for the literal command strings in that step.

THE OTHER HALF OF THAT BEAD, worth keeping because it refutes a plausible remedy at source. The obvious fix was "pre-fetch the release zip with the same retry flags, then let the installer use it". IT CANNOT WORK. `script/install-clj-kondo` does `rm -rf "$filename"` immediately before its own `curl -o "$filename" -sL "$download_url"`, so a pre-fetched copy is deleted unread. Its curl carries no `-f` and no retry and is not configurable. **Any remedy that keeps that installer keeps the bug** — which is why the fix had to perform the download itself. I had written the pre-fetch option into the bead as the preferred, smaller remedy; only reading the installer showed it was unimplementable.

ADJACENT AND NOT A DEFECT, so nobody re-files it: test.yml's Babashka setup has the same two-hop shape, but wraps the WHOLE install in a 3-attempt outer loop, so its archive download is already covered.

A CLJS COMPILE GATE CAN FAIL OPEN ON EXIT CODE: shadow-cljs grades a reference to a REMOVED VAR as a WARNING and still exits 0. For a deletion, the discriminating signal is the WARNING COUNT against a zero baseline, not the exit status.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 by worker/vest-a while removing three superseded vestiges (PR #9162). It ran the panel-gallery compile as a check that nothing still referenced what it deleted. A planted reference to a removed var produced a warning and exit 0. Anyone gating a CLJS deletion on exit status alone gets a green over a broken tree.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN AN ORDINARY GATE QUIRK: the standing rule everywhere else is "quote the captured exit code, never the harness's". That rule is right, and it is NOT SUFFICIENT HERE — the captured code is a truthful 0 about a compile that emitted a real defect. The gate is not lying about its status; the status simply does not carry the finding.

THE RULE FOR A CLJS DELETION:
1. Record the warning count on a CLEAN baseline first (vest-a's was 0 across 710 files, and 0 across 1892 for the main build).
2. Re-run after the deletion and compare COUNTS, not exit codes.
3. The reintroduced-call check remains the strongest single probe, and there it DID bite properly: a 3-arity call gave an ArityException, a removed var gave "No such var", a removed private gave "Unable to resolve var". Those are the checks to lean on.

GENERALISE CAREFULLY RATHER THAN BROADLY: this is a property of how shadow-cljs grades undeclared/removed vars in that build, not a claim that every compile gate fails open. Check the tool's own grading before assuming either way — and note the same repository has a gate that grades a missing markdown ANCHOR at INFO while --strict promotes only WARNING, so exit 0 over a real finding has now been measured twice here through two unrelated tools.

cljs.core/pr-str has exactly TWO branches that descend into a foreign JS value and NEITHER carries a seen-set: object? (prints #js {..} by walking js-keys) and array? (prints #js [..] by walking elements). Every other branch a foreign value can take -- #inst, regex, symbol, the terminal #object[Ctor] -- is bounded and recurses into nothing.

React 19's createContext returns an object whose Provider key points back AT THE CONTEXT ITSELF ((identical? ctx (.-Provider ctx)) is TRUE, asserted in re-frame.ssr.foreign-value-hash-cljs-test). So ANY code that pr-strs a value reachable from a hiccup form carrying a context provider dies with 'RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded'. The cycle is a property of the object graph, not of React: (let [o #js {}] (unchecked-set o "self" o) o) reproduces it.

Two consequences worth carrying:

1. When a walk/serialiser must handle foreign values, stopping at object?/array? stops the descent PRECISELY where pr-str would have started it. That is the cheap, provable fix -- no seen-set threading through the walker. rf2-56iys fixed re-frame.ssr.hash/canonical-edn-into exactly that way, in two CLJS-only cond branches.

2. pr-str of a foreign object ALSO leaks JS function .name into the output (#js {:component #object[f]}), and :advanced renames those. So descending is not merely a crash risk: it silently makes any hash/digest built on it differ between dev and release builds. Same class as rf2-jsa2ml's #fn[] token.

DIAGNOSTIC/ERROR PATHS ARE THE UNDER-COUNTED SITE. (pr-str el) inside a thrown error MESSAGE explodes the same way, and the value also rides out in ex-data :extra, so a downstream logger explodes at ITS boundary instead of the emitter's. re-frame.ssr.emit + re-frame.ssr.ui-tree have ten such sites (rf2-9s68n).

MEASURING A HASH CHANGE HONESTLY: dump canonical form + hash for a corpus to a file before and after, then diff byte-for-byte. rf2-56iys's probe covered 75 entries (parity fixtures + nil-prune pairs + the Hicasso SSR corpus + 41 hand-built branch-coverage values); 61 were byte-identical and every changed entry provably contained a foreign JS value.

REMOVING A CLJS VAR THAT STILL HAS CALLERS DOES NOT FAIL THE BUILD — IT WARNS AND RETURNS undefined (observed 2026-08-07, rf2-ani6y).

WHAT HAPPENED: prop-name was moved out of front/codec.cljs into a shared .cljc. Three call sites elsewhere still asked codec/prop-name (walk_profile_app twice, walk_vs_reagent_app, plus a clock_views docstring). ClojureScript answered a removed var with an :undeclared-var WARNING and the value undefined. The compile stayed EXIT 0. The breakage surfaced only downstream, as 7 ERRORS in walk_profile_baseline_cljs_test — a test failure that looks like a test problem, at a distance from the actual cause.

WHY IT MATTERS: a refactor that moves or renames a var can leave the build green and the code broken. "npm run test:hicasso-compile exits 0" is NOT evidence that every caller resolved. The signal is the WARNING COUNT, not the exit code — four separate builds reporting "0 warnings" is what actually proves the move was complete.

THE RULE: after moving or renaming any CLJS var, grep the whole tree for the OLD fully-qualified name (including docstrings, which will not warn at all), and require the compile to report ZERO warnings rather than merely exit 0. Quote the warning count in the PR body.

SAME SESSION, SAME CLASS, WORTH PAIRING: the three cache seeds in that codec were hand-typed TWICE — once in the def and once in reset-caches! — with an :each fixture making the SECOND copy the live one. A drift introduced in the first was therefore measurably invisible: nothing read it. Duplicated constants where only one copy is live are a silent-divergence trap of exactly the kind the .cljc extraction existed to delete.

CLJS EMITS NO ARITY CHECK FOR A SINGLE-FIXED-ARITY defn — a wrong-arity call does NOT throw, it silently BINDS THE WRONG THING. Measured 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.128 worker while building the regression test for a shipped arity bug.

THE CASE: `note-failing-view!` is `[thrown view-id]`. A caller passed ONE argument. On the JVM that is an ArityException. IN CLJS IT IS NOT AN ERROR AT ALL — `view-id` landed in the `thrown` position and `thrown` became the only bound arg.

⚠️ WHAT MADE IT INVISIBLE, and this is the generalisable part: the value was then used as a WEAKMAP KEY. A CLJS Keyword IS an object, so the guard `attributable?` ACCEPTED it. The write succeeded against the wrong key. The real exception therefore carried no note, and the error report shipped `unknown-view` with `:loss {:reason :failing-view-unobserved}` — in the worker phrase, "A CONFIDENT nobody-saw-the-thrower FOR A PLAINLY OBSERVED FAILURE."

That is worse than a crash: the system emits a DEFINITE NEGATIVE about something it plainly witnessed, and every downstream consumer believes it.

THREE RULES THAT FALL OUT:
1. In .cljc, do NOT rely on arity errors to catch a wrong-arity call — the JVM raises, CLJS does not. A cross-host fix green on the JVM has NOT been exercised on CLJS (see also identical-on-a-keyword-literal, the same asymmetry in a different guise).
2. A TYPE/SHAPE GUARD THAT ACCEPTS TOO MUCH TURNS A WRONG-ARITY BUG INTO A WRONG-DATA BUG. `attributable?` was doing its job — a Keyword genuinely is a valid WeakMap key. When a guard exists to reject non-objects, it will not notice the object is the WRONG object. Prefer a guard that asserts the value IS WHAT IT SHOULD BE, not merely that it CAN be used.
3. ⚠️ WHEN TESTING SUCH A BUG, "SOMETHING WENT WRONG" IS NOT AN ASSERTION. The defect produces a well-formed report with the wrong content. A test asserting a throw, or an error, or a non-empty report, PASSES AGAINST THE DEFECT. Assert the ATTRIBUTED IDENTITY.

MAYOR NOTE: my brief asserted the runtime consequence was "the seam itself throws while a render throw is unwinding". That was JVM-shaped and WRONG on the host where the bug lived. The worker verified past me and said so. This is the standing symptoms-not-causes lesson again — I described a CAUSE I had not measured, and the correct brief would have said only "this path is untested; determine what the defect actually does on each host."

IN CLJS, CALLING A MACRO BY ITS BARE NAME WHEN IT IS ONLY `:refer`-ED INTO ITS OWN NAMESPACE IS A **WARNING**, NOT AN ERROR — the build succeeds, and the emitted call SWALLOWS THE ENTIRE MACRO BODY INTO THE UNDEFINED FUNCTION'S ARGUMENT LIST. Measured 2026-09-05 on `re-frame.core/with-new-frame`, both directions, on a minimal consumer.

THE MEASUREMENT:
    rf/with-new-frame   -> compile exit 0, 0 warnings   |  run exit 0, 4/4 assertions
    bare with-new-frame -> compile exit 0, "Use of undeclared Var" WARNING  |  run exit 1, TypeError, NOTHING ASSERTED

SO THE FAILURE IS NOT "IT WON'T COMPILE". It compiles, ships, and at run time the binding never binds and the body never executes as a body — it is passed as arguments to something undefined. A test written that way reports zero assertions and can read as a pass to anyone checking only the exit code of the compile step.

THE MECHANISM, and it is the part worth carrying: `with-new-frame` is `#?(:clj (defmacro …))`, and the CLJS branch of `re-frame.core` carries a **self-`:require-macros` with an explicit `:refer` list**. That `:refer` lands the name in `re-frame.core` ITSELF, never in a consumer's namespace. So the macro is reachable as `rf/with-new-frame` and never bare — the namespace's own comment says so. **Whether a CLJS macro resolves depends on HOW its namespace is required, not on whether the macro exists**, and a `git grep` that finds the `defmacro` proves nothing about a consumer's reach.

THIS JOINS THE CLJS-ONLY FAMILY, all measured in one session:
  * `test:cljs` does not report `:infer-warning`s, so `:advanced` property renaming is invisible in dev.
  * A `with-redefs` double must mirror the ARITY SHAPE of a multi-arity fn, because CLJS compiles the call site to `cljs$core$IFn$_invoke$arity$N`; a green JVM suite is no evidence about it.
  * And this: an undeclared Var is a warning that silently eats the form.
**A green JVM read is never evidence about CLJS resolution.** Where a sample targets CLJS, compile AND RUN it on CLJS, and read the assertion count.

AND THE DISCIPLINE THAT CAUGHT IT: the worker's own first witness reported "exit 0, zero assertions" because `-main` never fired. It noticed and fixed it with `*main-cli-fn*` rather than banking the green. **Read the assertion count, not only the exit code** — that rule has now caught a vacuous witness four times in one session.

RELATED: [[a-cljs-test-double-must-mirror-the-arity-shape-not-just-the-arity-used]], [[test-cljs-does-not-catch-infer-warnings-that-break-under-advanced]].

A CLOSE REASON DOES NOT SURVIVE A REOPEN, SO AN AUDIT NEVER SEES IT — PUT THE DISCHARGE IN A COMMENT (2026-08-14, diagnosed on rf2-hic-055 after it reopened TWICE with no new finding).

THE LOOP. rf2-hic-055 carried merged-PR audit #8140 obligation as a COMMENT. PR #8151 discharged it. The worker closed the bead; the audit of #8151 (commit d0a19bafce) reopened it. I re-closed with a long evidence-bearing close reason (commit 172dd317bd); the audit of #8154 (commit 69e02c9b40) reopened it AGAIN. Both reopens changed only status and closed_at — comment count stayed 2 both times, and the newest comment was still #8140 from 2026-08-13.

THE MECHANISM, and it is my record-keeping rather than the audit judgement. The audit reads NOTES and COMMENTS, where the unresolved-audit text sits describing a live defect. A close REASON is a different field and a reopen discards it. So every discharge I wrote was invisible to the thing that kept reopening the bead, and the audit went on doing the correct thing with an obligation that read as unanswered. It would have recurred on every future merge touching that bead family.

THE RULE. When closing a bead that carries an audit obligation in its notes, write the discharge as a COMMENT first — naming the obligation, the PR that discharged it, and the source-verified evidence — and only then close, with the close reason POINTING AT that comment. The comment is the durable record; the close reason is a pointer.

HOW TO TELL A CHURN REOPEN FROM A REAL ONE, cheaply. Diff the tracker export at the audit commit -- git show THE_SHA -- .beads/issues.jsonl -- piped through a JSON filter for the bead id, printing status and comment COUNT. A real reopen adds a comment. A churn reopen changes status and closed_at only. That distinction takes one command and is the whole discriminator: loops.md is right that most reappearances are the audit working, and this is how you find the minority that are not.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: gcchurn-reclose-misses-audit-obligations warns against re-closing a reopened bead without reading its notes. This is the opposite failure — the notes WERE read and the obligation WAS discharged, but the answer was recorded where nothing could read it. Both rules apply; neither replaces the other.

A CLOSE REASON'S 'pushed' CLAUSE IS A CLAIM, NOT EVIDENCE — TEST IT AGAINST THE REMOTE (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: rf2-hic-081's close reason ended 'Spike commits are pushed on worker/receipts-hic081 and retained as the experiment's record.' It was false when written and stayed false for seven days. git ls-remote --heads origin returned empty for that branch while the local ref carried all three spike commits. The worktree had already been reaped on the worker's FINISHED report, so the experiment's only copy was a local branch in the mayor checkout — one disk, no backup, and a bead publicly recording it as safe.

WHY IT PASSED INSPECTION: the sentence sat among clauses that genuinely were verified — 530 tests, 2465 assertions, an allocation control with a negative arm, a named erasure failure. Specificity reads as verification. It is not: every other clause described work the worker DID, where this one described a state of a remote the worker only asserted.

THE TEST IS ONE COMMAND, so there is no excuse for inferring it: git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/<branch>. Empty means not pushed. Run it on any close reason claiming a branch is retained, and on any spike or refusal bead in particular — those are exactly the beads with no PR to prove the push, because a spike that graduates nothing never opens one.

THE STRANDED SWEEP IS WHERE THIS BELONGS. A branch with commits, no remote, no PR and no worktree is indistinguishable from a strand at first read, and the remedy is the same either way: push it. Salvage costs nothing and is never wrong. Do it before deciding what the branch MEANS.

CLOSING A BEAD MAKES EVERY DOCUMENT THAT CITES IT STALE — and I proved it on myself within the hour (2026-08-14).

WHAT HAPPENED. I ruled on rf2-5q8o and closed it as a DECLINE. Ninety minutes later a worker sweeping dispositions.md for pointers to closed beads found TWO cells calling rf2-5q8o open. I had created a fresh instance of the exact defect class I had that worker cleaning up.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS. A bead close is a tracker operation and feels self-contained. But this repository's records CITE BEAD IDS AS OWNERS — 'open correction rf2-xxxx', 'awaiting rf2-yyyy', 'scheduled by rf2-zzzz'. Every one of those is a claim about a bead's STATE, and closing the bead falsifies it silently. Nothing in the tracker knows the document exists.

THE CHECK, and it costs one command before any close or ruling: grep the tracked tree for the bead id. If a record cites it, either fix the citation in the same breath or file the correction with the close. `git grep -l <bead-id>` is the whole thing.

AND NOTE WHAT MADE THIS INSTANCE SUBTLER THAN THE OTHERS: the SUBSTANCE was right — the decline is correct and the reasoning stands. Only the LIVENESS was wrong. So a reader checking the claim finds it accurate and moves on, while the pointer quietly promises that something is scheduled to happen. A half-true cell survives review better than a false one.

THIS APPLIES TO THE MAYOR MOST, because the mayor closes the most beads and writes the fewest documents — so the blast radius of a close is invisible from where the close is made.

I closed rf2-kqxe6.10 (R6 integrated proof) on its merged SHA once its dependencies cleared. Before closing a bead, grep its notes for residual language — AUDIT-REOPEN, unmet, still owes, not discharged, RESIDUAL — and either discharge it in the close reason with evidence, or file it as its own bead BEFORE closing. `cmd /c` INVOKED FROM GIT BASH SILENTLY DOES NOTHING AND RETURNS EXIT 0 — it drops into an interactive shell instead of running the command. From PowerShell the identical command works. RESOLVES an earlier memory that recorded this as unresolved with conflicting evidence.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 on a scratch directory, three invocations of the same junction:
  Bash:        cmd /c mklink /J <link> <target>   -> printed only the Windows banner, EXIT 0, NO LINK CREATED
  PowerShell:  cmd /c mklink /J <link> <target>   -> "Junction created for <link> <<===>> <target>", link present
  PowerShell:  New-Item -ItemType Junction        -> link present, readable through
The tell in the Bash case is the output: the Windows version banner followed by a prompt string (`C:\...>`), which is an interactive shell waiting, not a command that ran.

THIS RESOLVES THE CONFLICT that made the earlier memory unresolved. One worker reported cmd /c mklink silently failing; others created junctions the same day with what looked like the same recipe. Both were right — the difference was never the command, it was WHICH SHELL invoked it. Workers using PowerShell succeeded; workers using Bash got a silent no-op and exit 0.

CONSEQUENCE FOR DISPATCH BRIEFS, and it is not only the create: EVERY `cmd /c rmdir "<junction>"` cleanup line in a brief has the same defect when a worker runs it from Bash. It reports success and removes nothing. That is the more dangerous half, because a surviving junction is what later cleanup follows into the mayor's real node_modules — the failure mode that emptied it twice historically.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF:
  create:  powershell -NoProfile -Command "New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path '<worktree>\implementation\node_modules' -Target '<mayor>\implementation\node_modules'"
  remove:  powershell -NoProfile -Command "(Get-Item '<worktree>\implementation\node_modules').Delete()"
AND VERIFY BOTH, because exit 0 proves nothing here: after creating, list the linked path; after removing, confirm the link is gone AND that the mayor's node_modules still counts what it did before (the canary reads 103 with `ls -A`).

THE GENERAL RULE THIS BELONGS TO: on this machine, a Windows-native tool invoked through Git Bash can no-op with exit 0. Do not trust an exit code from a cross-shell invocation — verify the EFFECT.

comm ON TWO jq-PRODUCED ID LISTS REPORTS NO DIFFERENCE EVEN WHEN THE SETS DIFFER — CRLF AGAIN, THROUGH A NEW DOOR, AND IT FAKED AN 'ALL CLOSURES HELD' RESULT (measured 2026-09-06).

WHAT HAPPENED. The §3 closure-revert check compares the previous tick's non-closed bead ids against this tick's:
  jq -r '.[].id' prev.json | sort > a ; jq -r '.[].id' now.json | sort > b ; comm -13 a b
It printed NOTHING for appeared and NOTHING for disappeared — the reassuring answer — while wc -l read 99 and 100. A bead had reopened (rf2-88f1, an audit finding a real defect in merged code) and the check said everything was fine.

THE CAUSE is the already-recorded one reached through a different tool: jq writes CRLF on this box, so every line in both files ends \r. comm then compares 'rf2-88f1\r' against 'rf2-88f1\r' — which should match — but the CR also rides into sort's collation, and the two files' orderings disagreed enough that comm, which requires both inputs sorted in the SAME collation, walked off and emitted nothing for both directions. Two empty answers, no error, exit 0.

THE TELL, AND IT IS THE ONLY ONE: the COUNTS. 99 vs 100 with an empty comm output is arithmetically impossible. Always print both line counts beside a set difference, and treat 'no difference' plus 'different totals' as an instrument failure rather than a finding. A set-difference check whose EMPTINESS is the reassuring outcome needs a control that must be non-empty — here, the shared set, which must equal the smaller count (it read exactly 99 after the fix).

THE FIX: strip CR and pin the collation before any set operation.
  tr -d '\r' < a | LC_ALL=C sort > a2   (same for b)   then comm -13 a2 b2
Verified: after stripping, comm correctly reported one appeared id and zero disappeared, and the shared set read 99.

GENERALISE IT: this now bites grep -f (recorded), pattern joins (recorded), and set operations (this). Anywhere jq output is COMPARED rather than merely displayed, strip CR first. And note the failure shape is always the same — not an error, but a clean, plausible, empty answer.

A COMMIT'S SUBJECT IS NOT ITS CONTENTS, AND THE DANGEROUS MISMATCH REVERTS RATHER THAN ADDS (2026-08-19).

Commit 799334f970 on worker/armconf-c4hhk read 'bench(p0): amend the level-assignment rule at run 3 of 70'. It carried 24 files — one studio record and 23 under implementation/core/src/ — at 611 insertions and 910 deletions, and the 23 were a REVERSION to pre-retirement content: core.cljc's + side re-introduced 're-frame.ui.frames/mint-frame-ops', a string absent from origin/main and belonging to a tree deleted weeks earlier.

MECHANISM: a worktree whose implementation/ content predated sweeps that had since landed on main, plus a git add -A or commit -a. The worker meant to commit one record file.

WHY NOTHING CATCHES IT. A revert of merged work is well-formed, compiles, and passes every gate the tree has. The five merge clauses measure whether CI is GREEN, and CI is green. The commit message is accurate about the part its author knew about. 'Scope did not sprawl' does not describe it either — sprawl is EXTRA work, which announces itself; this is files the author never edited, at content OLDER than the trunk.

THE CHEAP DETECTOR, one command: git diff --name-only <merge-base> <branch>. Read the file LIST against what the bead asked for. A path the bead does not explain is a finding whichever direction it runs. Then for any surprising file, test the DIRECTION rather than the size — a string present on the branch and absent from origin/main means the branch is older, not newer.

CHECK THE WHOLE FLEET WHEN YOU FIND ONE, and expect it to be one worker rather than a pattern: the other six live branches carried zero implementation/core/src/ paths, which is what made the finding specific enough to act on.

AND WHEN YOU CANNOT MESSAGE THE WORKER — it predates a /clear, so TaskList is empty while it provably runs — do not repair its branch under it. Record the finding and the exact fix-forward on the bead, and bind the merge loop instead: no PR from that branch merges while the offending paths are in its diff.

The CLJS lane split into two foreground phases is: (1) node scripts/compile-node-test.cjs node-test out/node-test.js (2) node out/node-test.js, both from implementation/ (this is exactly package.json's test:cljs, unsplit). COMPRESSING A PRECISE STATEMENT INTO A SHORTER ONE CHANGES ITS MEANING — a distinct failure from relaying an unverified fact (2026-08-06).

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker reported an id shipped "in the catalogued family (Conventions.md section Reserved namespaces)". Precise and true - Conventions.md reserves the :rf.warning/* NAMESPACE, and the id sits inside it. I wrote into the next brief that the id was "catalogued in Conventions.md section Reserved namespaces". FALSE: git grep hicasso -- spec/ is completely EMPTY, and the source PR said so itself in its own "Not in this PR" section.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE SAME AS MY OTHER SEVEN ERRORS. Those were facts I passed on without reading the source. THIS one I read correctly and then SHORTENED, and the shortening moved the claim from "the namespace is reserved" to "the id is catalogued". Nothing was misread; a qualifier was dropped because it looked like padding.

THE SHAPE TO WATCH: a worker's careful phrasing is often carrying a distinction on purpose. "in the catalogued family" versus "catalogued". "the adoption tier deliberately carries no such hash" versus "there is no hash". "measured 154-171s" versus "about 160s". When I compress, I should ask whether the words I am dropping are doing work - and the tell is that a careful worker chose a longer phrase where a shorter one existed.

PRACTICAL RULE: when quoting a worker's finding into a brief, QUOTE IT rather than paraphrase it. It costs a few characters. Eight of my briefs today carried a claim a worker then had to correct, and this is the only one where the original was in front of me and correct.

CONCURRENCY COST: SATURATING WORKERS TIMES OUT A HARNESS SELF-TEST (2026-07-25). With 6-7 concurrent workers each running shadow-cljs compiles, 'npm run test:cljs' can fail rc 1 with 2 failures that are BOTH spawnSync ETIMEDOUT in re-frame.test-quiet-shadow-node-cljs-test — the harness's own subprocess self-test, which re-spawns the built runner under a 60s ceiling whose own comment says it 'returns in well under a second'. It is machine load, not behaviour, and a diff that cannot reach that surface (e.g. a single freehand test file) still trips it.

HOW TO HANDLE IT, in this order: (1) confirm the failing tests are exactly that namespace and exactly ETIMEDOUT — anything else is a real failure; (2) confirm the diff structurally cannot touch the harness self-test; (3) RE-RUN rather than declaring it green. Do NOT wave it through on the first red, and do NOT --admin past it: an ETIMEDOUT that is really contention looks identical to an ETIMEDOUT that is really a hang, and only the re-run distinguishes them. The rf2-z0blg worker handled this correctly — it flagged the rc 1 honestly, explained why it believed it was load, and re-ran rather than reporting green.

MAYOR-SIDE IMPLICATION FOR DISPATCH POLICY: the operator's saturate-at-6 target has a measurable cost — it makes local worker gates flakier, which in turn makes workers spend turns re-running and makes a genuine failure harder to see against the noise. When several workers are simultaneously in a CLJS-heavy phase, expect this and prefer sequencing the CLJS-heavy ones over adding a seventh. Related known pattern: under 40+ concurrent PRs the skill-MCP-drift and JVM-epoch CI gates flake the same way.

CONCURRENT WORKERS SHARE ONE SESSION SCRATCHPAD DIRECTORY, AND THEY SILENTLY OVERWRITE EACH
OTHER'S FILES. Give every dispatched worker its OWN subdirectory in the brief.

MEASURED 2026-09-10 by TWO INDEPENDENT WORKERS in one saturated session, neither aware of the
other:
  * `speccont-a` found its `contprobe.py` replaced mid-session by `methodcont-a`'s version -- it
    identified the intruder by its docstring, which read "Rebuilt for rf2-fwlj group 1".
  * `disclose-a` found its `pr-body.md` and `bead-note.txt` overwritten by `storykey-a`.

Both happened to survive it: speccont-a noticed and moved to a private subdirectory, and
disclose-a's two files had already been submitted. NEITHER WAS DETECTED BY ANYTHING; both workers
noticed by accident while re-reading a file they had written.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY UNTIDY. The colliding names are exactly the ones every
worker independently invents -- `pr-body.md`, `bead-note.txt`, and a probe named after the class
being measured -- so collision is likeliest precisely when several workers are on the SAME bead or
the same class of work, which is when the mayor deliberately saturates. The failure is silent in
both directions: the writer's write succeeds, the reader's read succeeds, and the content is
simply someone else's. A worker that reads back a probe it did not write can measure the wrong
thing and report a confident number.

WORST CASE, not yet observed: a worker passes a note to `bd update --append-notes` via
`"$(cat <file>)"` -- the form CLAUDE.md prescribes to dodge the backtick-substitution trap -- and
appends ANOTHER worker's note to its bead. Both the shell and `bd` report success.

THE GUARD, and it belongs in the DISPATCH BRIEF because the worker cannot know it is sharing:
name a per-worker subdirectory explicitly, `<scratchpad>/<worker-name>/`, and tell the worker to
create it as its first act and keep everything inside it. Do not rely on distinctive filenames --
the whole point is that independently-chosen names converge.

NOT the same as the `/tmp` handoff hazard CLAUDE.md item (n) records. That one is ONE agent whose
Python and shell steps disagree about a path. This is TWO agents agreeing about a path perfectly.

GATE A WORKER GATES ON AN OBSERVABLE, NOT ON MY GUESS — this is how to overlap a dispatch with a live measurement window (2026-08-14, invented for rf2-34yg and confirmed working).

THE PROBLEM: a clock measurement window needs a quiet box and refuses if the box is loud, so a heavy dispatch alongside it wastes a real measurement. But holding every dispatch until the window reports costs hours of throughput, and I had been doing exactly that all session.

WHAT I DID WRONG FIRST: inferred from a worker commit ("docs: fix a misnumbered arm reference") that its measurement rounds were finished and it had moved to write-up. That inference was WRONG — checking properly, it had opened no PR and its recent writes were .cpcache entries and out/node-test.js, i.e. a build running a gate. The doc commit was made BETWEEN runs.

THE TECHNIQUE THAT WORKED, and it survives my inference being wrong: brief the new worker to do all reading, editing and reasoning FIRST, then — before running anything heavy — check whether the measurement worker has opened a PULL REQUEST for its branch. An open PR is an observable that means the measurement finished. Tell it to poll in a bounded loop WITHIN ITS TURN, and give it an explicit escape: if the PR has not appeared after a reasonable wait, say so in the report and run anyway. Never end a turn waiting for an event.

MEASURED RESULT: the worker polled about 4.5 minutes, saw the PR appear on poll 10, and ran only then. It also sampled processor queue length on every poll and reported 0 throughout. No measurement was disturbed and no throughput was lost to my being wrong about the window state.

WHY THE ESCAPE CLAUSE IS NOT OPTIONAL: a conditional wait is exactly the shape that strands a worker — seven strandings in one day all came from waiting for an event that never arrived. The escape converts a possible strand into a reported delay.

GENERALISES: any time a fence depends on another worker s state, gate on something the new worker can OBSERVE (a PR, a merged commit, a file on main) rather than on my reading of tea leaves. My inference was wrong and the dispatch was still safe, which is the whole point.

WHAT I DID. I clustered rf2-ipx7h and rf2-r5iy7 as "two hicasso gates that exist but no CI lane runs", and dispatched a worker to arm them. Neither gate's subject was on main.

THE RULE I ALREADY HAD, in my own words: a bead describing another PR's code dispatches only after that source PR MERGES, because beads close on PR-open, so CLOSED IS NOT ON MAIN. rf2-qgbu5 read closed. I took that as "landed". It meant "PR opened".

WHAT MADE IT LOOK SAFE, and why that reasoning was wrong: two workers had independently reported the same finding hours apart, which I treated as strong corroboration. It was — of the FINDING. Two true reports about a branch are still reports about a branch. Corroboration of a claim says nothing about whether the claim's subject has landed.

THE CHECK THAT COSTS ONE COMMAND: before dispatching any bead that names a file, gate, script or path, confirm THAT PATH EXISTS ON MAIN. Not that the bead is closed, not that a worker reported it, not that two did. `git ls-tree origin/main -- <path>` or a grep at trunk tip. If the path is absent, the bead is fenced behind its source PR and the fence goes on the bead.

THE WORKER REFUSED CORRECTLY AND COST NOTHING BUT ITS OWN HOUR: no branch, no PR, no edits, both trees clean, and it deliberately did not claim either bead, since claiming without working leaves a phantom in_progress. It also wrote full audit notes onto both so the follow-on does not repeat the hour. That is the licence to refuse doing exactly what it exists for.

A CONFLICTING PR RUNS ZERO CHECKS — so an empty rollup can mean DIRTY, not merely early (2026-08-15 19:12 AUSEST).

MEASURED on PR #8314. It read 'no checks reported on the branch' for about thirteen minutes and gh run list --branch worker/release-gra70 returned NOTHING AT ALL. I first read that as workflows still starting. It was not: gh pr view gave mergeable=CONFLICTING, mergeStateStatus=DIRTY. GITHUB DOES NOT START WORKFLOWS ON A PR THAT CANNOT MERGE, so a seventeen-file change had never been tested by CI at all.

THE DISCRIMINATION IS ONE COMMAND AND I SHOULD RUN IT WHENEVER A ROLLUP IS EMPTY:
  gh pr view <n> --json state,mergeable,mergeStateStatus
  mergeable=UNKNOWN  -> genuinely still computing; wait
  mergeable=CONFLICTING / mergeState=DIRTY -> it will NEVER go green; it needs a rebase
Corroborate with gh run list --branch <branch>: zero runs on a branch whose PR has been open for minutes is the dirty signature, because an early PR still shows queued runs.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE PR: clause 5 already says an EMPTY ROLLUP IS NOT GREEN because it reports no failures too. This adds the other half — an empty rollup is not necessarily PENDING either. Left alone, a conflicting PR sits at 'no checks' indefinitely and every sweep reads it as in-flight. It is the quietest way for work to stall: nothing red, nothing to chase, nothing happening.

THE REMEDY IS RESUME, NOT REDISPATCH. Its author holds the reasoning; a fresh worker would re-derive the whole change. And rebasing is not mechanical here: NEVER resolve a .beads or generated-file conflict with --theirs/--ours, and on a hot-zone file like implementation/shadow-cljs.edn read BOTH intents before merging, because main may have refactored under it.

A CONTRIBUTING CAUSE WORTH NAMING: that worker had DELIBERATELY not rebased, reasoning that main's changed paths were disjoint from its own and test.yml had not moved. That reasoning was sound WHEN MADE. Four PRs then landed under it. So the lesson is not 'always rebase' but 'a not-rebasing decision has a shelf life, and the PR going CONFLICTING is when it expires'.

A CONSOLE SHIM IN THE BROWSER LANE PASSES VACUOUSLY — replacing js/console.warn does NOT intercept what the runner sees. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.114/.115 worker, in its own harness, before shipping.

THE MECHANISM: the worker wrote an `advisories` helper that replaced `js/console.warn` and counted the sentences it captured, to assert that N advisories were published. THE WARNINGS STILL REACHED PLAYWRIGHT CDP CAPTURE AND THE COUNTER STAYED AT 0. So the assertion "exactly N advisories were published" was TRUE-BY-EMPTINESS: it would pass whether the code published N, zero, or a thousand.

WHY: in `npm run test:browser`, console output is captured by Playwright over the Chrome DevTools Protocol AT THE BROWSER LEVEL, not by whatever the page has bound to `js/console.warn` at that moment. Rebinding the JS symbol changes what PAGE code calls; it does not change what the RUNNER observes, and it does not stop the real emission.

THE FIX THE WORKER CHOSE, and it is the right one: DO NOT ASSERT ON CONSOLE OUTPUT IN THE BROWSER LANE. Assert on the TRACE RECORDS instead — which was the bead actual contract anyway. The console sentence is a human-facing rendering of the event; the record is the thing with a schema.

⚠️ THIS JOINS THE ROSTER OF WAYS "GREEN" HAS MEANT "NOTHING WAS MEASURED" IN THIS REPO, now at seven:
  1. a bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` from the wrong dir (0 tests, exit 0)
  2. a CLJS runner selecting nothing after a namespace rename
  3. a clojure.test MAP fixture swallowing the body (cljs.test is fine)
  4. multi-var `-v ns/a ns/b ns/c` running only the first var
  5. an ns outside the runner regexp holding reader-conditional tests neither host runs
  6. a non-zero exit masked by a pipe into tail/grep, with a green summary above it
  7. NEW: a console shim in the browser lane counting zero while the output flows past it

THE DEFENCE IS THE SAME ONE EVERY TIME AND IT IS CHEAP: make the assertion FAIL ON PURPOSE before trusting it. Publish a known number and confirm the counter sees it; if the counter reads 0 when something plainly happened, the harness is broken, not the code. A counter that has never counted anything has not been tested.

GENERAL FORM: when a test asserts on OBSERVED OUTPUT rather than on a RETURNED VALUE, ask WHO IS DOING THE OBSERVING. If the observer sits outside your process or below your language runtime — a CDP capture, a subprocess pipe, a native logger — then rebinding a symbol inside the runtime does not intercept it.

A PATCH-ID CONTAINMENT TEST IS VACUOUSLY TRUE ON A BRANCH WITH ZERO COMMITS, SO A FRESHLY DISPATCHED WORKER SORTS INTO THE 'SAFE TO DELETE' BUCKET.

Measured 2026-09-11 on the mayor's own branch sweep. The script classified 23 worker branches by 'git cherry origin/main <branch>' and printed everything with no '+' lines under the heading 'CONTAINED (all commits patch-equivalent at tip - safe to delete)'. Five branches dispatched roughly fifteen minutes earlier landed in that bucket, each carrying a worker in flight.

THE MECHANISM: a branch with no commits satisfies 'every commit is present at trunk' trivially - there are no commits to fail the test. So the proof is perfectly valid AND completely uninformative, and the branch is indistinguishable from a fully merged one. Nothing on screen betrays it: the cherry output is simply empty.

IT FAILS OPEN, AGAINST LIVE WORK. This is rf2-2yp5's finding (the branch sweep's ownership zero cannot see a live worker) arriving through a different door and in a stronger form - not an ownership record that does not exist yet, but a containment PROOF that is sound and says nothing.

THE REPAIR IS THREE INPUTS, NOT TWO:
  1. 'git cherry' for containment, never 'git rev-list', which reports every REBASE-merged branch as unmerged because a rebase replays commits under new identities. '-' is proof of containment; '+' is only the absence of proof.
  2. AN EMPTY BRANCH GETS ITS OWN BUCKET and is never a deletion candidate on containment evidence.
  3. THE LIVE SET, from the worktree list AND the dispatch ledger read BY FIELD. Note the non-obvious half: a worktree's PRESENCE does not separate live from spent, because spent-but-unreaped worktrees have one too. The ledger's dispatch timestamp is what actually distinguishes them.

GENERALISES BEYOND BRANCHES: any test of the form 'every X satisfies P' is TRUE when there are no X. A census, a ratchet, a conformance sweep and a containment check all return their most reassuring answer on an empty input. Ask how many X there were before reading what the test said about them.

Related: [[bd-json-shapes-differ-list-show-history]].

CONTENT-VERIFICATION AFTER REBASE — token presence is NOT sufficient for ORDERING/TIMING fixes. My standing rule (grep the rebased artefact for a token unique to your change) is necessary but incomplete. rf2-zo5n9's worker (2026-07-18) identified the gap precisely: its fix was about WHEN a :type-ref-fn thunk is forced, so a rebase could preserve every token while relocating the force point and silently reinstating the race the fix cured. It re-verified the ORDERING in the rebased file instead: system-id-collision trace (L463) -> (continue?) fence (L495) -> force (type-ref-fn) (L523) -> stamp :rf/machine-type (L529) -> swap (L530). RULE FOR BRIEFS: after a rebase, ask what KIND of fact the fix asserts. Presence/absence of a behaviour -> grep a unique token differentially (branch N, main 0). Ordering, timing, or placement -> re-verify the sequence itself; tokens can all survive while the semantics revert. Same principle as rf2-59car's cross-host tag: verify the property the fix actually claims, not a proxy that correlates with it.

CORE HOSTS CROSS-ARTEFACT SOURCE-SCANNING RATCHETS, SO A DIFF TOUCHING NO CORE FILE CAN STILL RED THE CORE LANE. `implementation/core/test/re_frame/egress_chokepoint_conformance_test.clj` (rf2-mrtis6) scans EVERY artefact's src/ tree AS TEXT — so it sees artefacts that are not even on core's test classpath — for callers of the always-on union-record fan-out chokepoints (`dispatch-error-record!` / `dispatch-frame-teardown-report!`). Every caller must either route untrusted slots through `project-egress` OR sit on `structural-only-allow-list`.
PROVEN LIVE: PR #7168 made `re-frame.routing.url-change` a new caller (the ruled SSR-404 promotion), did neither, and reddened BOTH core jobs on one identical assertion while touching no core file. The worker had gated ssr and routing thoroughly and never ran core.
THE DISPATCH RULE THIS GIVES: when a brief promotes an emit to an always-on axis, adds a late-bind hook consumer, or changes a facade export, PUT THE CORE LANE IN THE GATE LIST even when the diff has no core file. Fences (what you may not edit) and gate scope (what your change can reach) are DIFFERENT questions and I had been conflating them.
AND THE ARM CHOICE IS ON THE MERITS, NOT COST: `project-egress` projects tree slots against the frame's CLASSIFICATION REGISTRY, so for a route MISS — which by definition matched no route and therefore has no :params/:query schema to path-target — it rides the URL through untouched under a live frame, or blanket-redacts the structured path under a frameless one. Routing's own `redact-url-carriers` policy exists precisely for that gap. Reaching for project-egress there would have been strictly WEAKER and would have traded away ruled behaviour.

CORPUS SCANS RUN AFTER `mkdocs build` DOUBLE-COUNT (2026-07-26, rf2-txe8o worker). `mkdocs build` generates a GITIGNORED docs/spec/ mirror of the spec tree. Any grep/census run afterwards silently counts those mirrored files as additional rows -- observed +3 phantom rows on a reg-route site census. The mirror is gitignored, so `git status` shows nothing and there is no visible cue that the tree just grew. PRACTICAL RULE, and it is the same one already recorded for generated docs/site: scan TRACKED FILES ONLY -- use `git grep` (or `git ls-files | xargs grep`), never a bare recursive `grep -r`, for any count you intend to quote. And be aware the hazard is TIME-DEPENDENT: the same command gives different answers before and after a docs build in the same worktree, so a count taken early and re-checked late will appear to have moved for no reason. This is the fourteenth measurement error of the same family this session (a cheap proxy standing in for the real population), and the only one whose value changes underneath you rather than being wrong from the start.

CORRECTION, SECOND REVISION: THE EMPTY --log-failed HAD A CAUSE, AND IT WAS NOT THE COMMAND (2026-07-26). I twice recorded conclusions about gh run view --log-failed being unreliable — first blaming in_progress status, then declaring it simply flaky on this repo. Both were wrong, and the worker whose PR I was diagnosing supplied the real answer.

ITS FIRST COMMIT CONTAINED A MACROEXPANSION ERROR: it wrote (v/defview name {:compiled true} "doc" ...) when the grammar is name docstring? opts?. A macroexpansion failure kills BOTH CLJS lanes at COMPILE time — so no test ever ran, no deftest failed, and there was NO FAILING TEST OUTPUT FOR --log-failed TO SHOW. The command was working correctly; the job had produced no test failures to report, only a compile abort.

SO THE REAL DIAGNOSTIC RULE IS: an empty --log-failed on a CLJS lane is EVIDENCE, not a tool failure. It suggests the lane died before running tests — a macroexpansion error, a compile abort, or a par-compile failure — rather than a failing assertion. That is a different class of defect from a red test and points at different code. When it happens, ask the worker whether the lane COMPILED, not which test failed.

WHY I GOT IT WRONG TWICE: I treated an absent signal as a broken instrument instead of asking what would produce an absent signal. The two runs where --log-failed DID work (the broken-anchor cascade, the Google Fonts 503) both had real step failures with output; the two where it returned nothing were both compile-time deaths. The pattern was there and I invented a tool-reliability story over it.

SUPERSEDES both earlier notes on this command. Keep the practical half of them — one retrieval attempt, then hand the worker the check names — but the reasoning was wrong and the empty result is informative.
