    echo "exit=$?"
That $? is SED'S status, not the script's. It printed 0 and told me nothing. The guard happened to be armed, so the wrong instrument agreed with the truth -- which is the worst outcome, because nothing on screen disputes it.

WHY IT SLIPPED PAST A RULE I HAD JUST WRITTEN DOWN. The method tree says "Never pipe a gate through a filter. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, so a red runner reads green", and I had put the same discipline into two PR bodies hours earlier. But I did not read this as piping a gate: the pipe was there to INDENT output for readability, not to filter anything, and it was a guard-check rather than a test runner. Neither distinction matters to the shell. Any pipe -- sed, head, tr, cat, tee -- replaces the status you wanted with the formatter's, and formatters essentially always succeed, so the answer is a reassuring 0 whatever happened upstream.

THE CORRECT FORM, one command line, one shell:
    out=$(cmd 2>&1); rc=$?
    printf '%s\n' "$out" | sed 's/^/  /'   # format AFTER capturing rc
Capture first, decorate second. And when a --check style probe returns 0 with ZERO BYTES of output, corroborate independently rather than trusting it -- here, ls -l on .git/hooks/pre-commit (present, executable, 4585 bytes) plus the script's own header line "--check  # exit 0 if installed & current, 1 otherwise", which establishes that silence-on-success is the designed contract.

GENERALISE: I add "| sed 's/^/  /'" to almost every command for readable output. Every one of those pipes silently voids $? for the command I actually care about. If the line's purpose is to learn an exit code, it must not end in a pipe -- no exceptions for formatting.

COUNT A JOB'S STEPS BY THE STEP KEYWORD, NEVER BY THE COMMAND FORM YOU EXPECT — measured three times on one job in one night, wrong twice. 2026-09-07.

THE JOB: lint.yml's `api-manifest`, lines 609-738. It has NINE `run:` steps: an installer, SEVEN `clojure -M -m re-frame.api-manifest.<check>` invocations, and `clojure -M:test`.

MY THREE ANSWERS, IN ORDER:
  "three"  — built from a CI failure log plus two greps. The failure named one step; I inferred the neighbours.
  "seven"  — after a worker corrected me, built from `grep -oE 'clojure -M -m [a-z.-]+'`.
  "eight"  — a second worker's, correct for gate steps: my seven plus `clojure -M:test`.

WHY THE SECOND ANSWER WAS WRONG, AND IT IS THE INSTRUCTIVE ONE. `clojure -M -m` CANNOT MATCH `clojure -M:test`. The pattern presupposed the invocation form — main-namespace dispatch — and the eighth step uses an alias instead. So the count was a measurement of "steps shaped like the ones I already knew about", which is exactly the shape of answer that feels like a survey and is a tautology. It returned a clean, plausible, non-zero number, so nothing on screen betrayed it.

THE RULE: to count what a job runs, anchor on the STEP KEYWORD (`run:`, or `uses:` for actions) inside the job's line range, and read the commands out of that. Find the range with the job key and the next sibling key rather than by eye. Never grep for a command pattern and call the result the step count.

AND A SECOND FAILURE IN THE SAME BREATH, worth recording because it is the more embarrassing one: my first attempt at the correct method used `awk '/^  api-manifest:/,/^  [a-z-]+:$/'` and returned ZERO, because the range end pattern also matches the start line. A zero from a broken range reads exactly like "this job has no run steps". The working form takes the start line with grep -n, finds the next sibling with an awk NR>start guard, and slices with sed.

THE GENERAL FORM OF ALL THREE MISTAKES IS ONE MISTAKE: I kept asking an instrument a question shaped like the answer I expected. A failure log names the step that failed, not the job's contents. A command-form grep finds commands of that form, not steps. A range whose terminator matches its start finds nothing. Each returned something plausible, and only the third was obviously broken.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ARITHMETIC: this project's rule is that a JOB'S STEP LIST IS THE OBLIGATION, not the subset a brief names. A brief that undercounts the steps under-specifies the obligation, and the eighth step here is a full test suite. Two PRs in one session went red on steps a brief had not named.

A COVERAGE PLANT MUST NOT OVERLAP A GATE RUN (2026-08-11, rf2-eo9n / PR #7870).

Nearly every brief I write demands the same drill for silent-on-success gates: plant a bogus anchor, quote the exit 1, restore, confirm green. A worker's first fast-PR spine run went RED purely because the plant was still in the tree while the spine ran. Not a finding - the plant racing the gate.

WHY IT IS EASY TO HIT: the spine takes ~25 minutes and is therefore BACKGROUNDED (the harness kills a foreground command at 10). The plant-and-restore cycle takes seconds. So a worker naturally starts the long gate, then does the quick coverage proof while waiting - and the two overlap invisibly. The resulting red looks like a real failure in CI history.

THE RULE FOR BRIEFS: sequence them explicitly. Do the plant/restore drill FIRST, verify the restore by hash, and only THEN start the spine. Or wait for the spine's .exit file before planting. Never interleave.

AND IF IT HAPPENS: restore, hash-verify, RE-RUN, and say in the PR body that the first red was a plant race - otherwise a reviewer reading CI history is misled by a red that means nothing. The rf2-eo9n worker did exactly that, which is why it was diagnosable.

RELATED, same worker, worth keeping: plant with PYTHON rather than `sed -i`. On Windows sed -i rewrites CRLF->LF, so `git diff` and `git status` both read clean while the bytes differ - see crlf-defeats-byte-identical-restore. Restore with `git checkout --` and verify by sha256.

CRASH RECOVERY RECIPE — PROVEN 2026-07-23 when the Claude Code host process exited with 6 workers mid-run. Follow in this order; the order is the whole point.

THE ONE FACT THAT DECIDES EVERYTHING: workers have died two entirely different ways in one session — a stream watchdog killing them after a long silent stretch, and the host process exiting. In BOTH cases the line between "fully recovered" and "lost" was exactly: WAS IT PUSHED? Commits on a worker branch survive anything. Uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.

STEP 1 — GROUND TRUTH, before touching anything. For each worktree, git-only (never a filesystem walk):
  git -C <wt> rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD     # unpushed commits
  git -C <wt> status --porcelain | grep -v .beads    # uncommitted WIP
  git ls-remote --heads origin <branch> | wc -l      # is the branch on origin at all
Classify: branch-on-origin = safe. Commits-but-no-remote = AT RISK. Zero-commits-plus-dirty-plus-no-remote = MOST at risk.

STEP 2 — MERGE ANY GREEN PR FIRST. A PR that was green when the process died is free progress and it unblocks whatever was sequenced behind it.

STEP 3 — PUSH THE COMMITTED-BUT-UNPUSHED WORK YOURSELF. This is pure durability and carries no judgement risk: the commits already exist, you are only making them survivable. Do NOT open a PR from them.

⚠️ STEP 4 — DO NOT COMMIT A WORKER UNCOMMITTED WIP YOURSELF. Tell the worker to do it. There is a recorded incident in this project where a mayor committed a worker partial work as a recovery PR and merged an incomplete state that broke main. Uncommitted files are mid-edit by definition; only the worker knows whether they form a coherent commit. The mayor pushes COMMITS, never creates them from someone else WIP.

STEP 5 — RESUME EVERY WORKER, with a message tailored to ITS state, leading with durability:
  - Say plainly it was not stopped for cause and its work is safe — a worker that thinks it failed behaves worse.
  - For the most-at-risk one, make the FIRST instruction "commit what you have (even as a WIP commit) and push, BEFORE rebasing, BEFORE gates, BEFORE anything."
  - Tell it exactly what landed on main while it was gone, and whether its rebase is EXPECTED (sequenced deliberately) rather than a surprise to investigate.
  - Re-state only the must-survive laws and traps specific to that worker — not the whole original brief.
THIS WORKED, MEASURED: the worst-off worker went from 0 commits / 12 uncommitted files / no remote branch to 3 commits pushed on its first resumed turn.

STEP 6 — clear any stale .git/index.lock left by the abrupt exit, then re-export beads FROM DOLT (never git checkout over them) and checkpoint.

PREVENTION, now standard in every dispatch brief and worth more than the recipe: "COMMIT AND PUSH AS YOU GO — not at the end", stated WITH the reason (two mechanisms have killed workers; incremental pushing is the only defence against both). Also: a bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface — saturation is right, but keep it within what one recovery pass can handle.

AFTER A CRASH, CHECK LANDED-NESS WITH A 600-COMMIT WINDOW BEFORE SALVAGING ANYTHING (2026-08-03).

Recovering from a host crash that killed ~18 workers, I found 14 worker worktrees with commits and NO remote branch — the classic 'stranded work' shape. I pushed 13 of them for durability, which the method explicitly sanctions.

Then I compared their commit SUBJECTS against main. Against 'git log --oneline -60 origin/main' only 2 of 13 looked landed. Against -600, ALL 13 had landed. The branches were pure residue: workers that had already shipped via PRs that already merged, leaving behind unreaped worktrees whose local branch ref simply predated the squash-merge onto main.

THE COST OF THE NARROW WINDOW: I nearly dispatched ~11 salvage workers to 'finalise' work that was already on main, and I did push+delete 13 redundant branches. On a repo merging this fast, 60 commits is a few HOURS of main. A 2-day-old worker branch needs hundreds.

THE RULE: before treating an unpushed worker branch as stranded, diff its commit subjects against at least 600 commits of origin/main (use 'git log --format=%s -600 origin/main' + 'grep -Fxq' per subject). A worktree with commits and no remote is USUALLY residue, not loss. Real loss looks different: UNCOMMITTED modified files (that worktree genuinely died mid-edit), or commits whose subjects appear nowhere on main.

ALSO: 'gh pr list --state open' returning 0 is a strong corroborating signal — if no PRs are open, no worker is mid-flight, so every branch is either landed or abandoned.

THIS CHECKOUT IS CRLF, SO A MULTI-LINE PATCH ANCHOR SILENTLY MATCHES NOTHING (2026-08-11, rf2-czlb / rf2-3f11).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker planting a sabotage edit found its first multi-line patch attempt matched nothing and reported no error — the edit simply did not apply. Cause: the working tree carries CRLF line endings, so any anchor spanning a newline fails to match a pattern written with LF. It found it only because it verified the restore by SHA-256 rather than by reading `git diff`.

TWO PRACTICES THAT FOLLOW, both cheap:
  - USE SINGLE-LINE ANCHORS when patching by string match. A pattern that crosses a line boundary is a coin flip on this checkout.
  - VERIFY EVERY RESTORE BY HASHING THE BYTES, never by `git diff`. This is already the standing rule for sabotage restores, and here is the reason it exists: a CRLF-flipping rewrite reads CLEAN in `git diff` while having changed every line, and the inverse — an edit that never applied — also reads clean. `git diff` cannot distinguish "unchanged" from "not attempted".

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND SABOTAGE. The plant-and-restore discipline is how this project proves a guard is exact rather than merely present. If the plant silently does not apply, the sabotage run comes back GREEN and the worker concludes the guard fired when nothing was ever broken — a false proof of a real guard, which is worse than no proof at all. The same failure would make a "restored" tree quietly different from the committed one.

Brief it as: "verify the restore by hashing the bytes, not by reading `git diff` — this checkout is CRLF, and both a failed patch and a line-ending rewrite read clean there."

ON WINDOWS, `git diff` CANNOT VERIFY A BYTE-IDENTICAL RESTORE - VERIFY BY HASH (2026-08-11, found by the rf2-dly1 worker, PR #7859).

Every dispatch brief I write demands the same coverage drill for silent-on-success gates: plant a bogus anchor, quote the exit 1, RESTORE BYTE-IDENTICALLY, confirm green. A worker doing exactly that used `sed -i` to plant and restore, and `git diff` came back EMPTY while the sha256 DIFFERED. `sed -i` had rewritten the working copy CRLF -> LF. The content was identical; the bytes were not.

WHY git diff LIES HERE: with autocrlf normalisation, git compares the normalised form, so a pure line-ending change is invisible to `git diff` and to `git status`. Both report clean. The file on disk has changed for every tool that reads bytes rather than lines - and on this repo that includes the digest-pinned sample blocks under docs/core/, which hash exact block text.

THE FIX, two parts:
1. VERIFY BY HASH, not by `git diff`: record sha256 before planting and compare after restoring. The worker caught it precisely because it hashed.
2. RESTORE WITH `git checkout -- <path>`, which writes the exact checked-out bytes, rather than a second `sed -i` that re-applies the same normalisation.

PUT THIS IN THE DISPATCH BRIEF. I ask for this drill in nearly every dispatch, and until now the brief said "restore byte-identically" and let the worker choose how to check - which on Windows means most of them check with `git diff` and get a false pass. The claim "restored byte-identically, git status clean" is NOT evidence on this platform.

GENERAL SHAPE, and it is the same one that keeps recurring: an instrument answering from a NORMALISED view rather than the raw artefact is confidently wrong exactly about the difference you are checking for. Same family as `git branch -r` being a cache, `gh run list` returning lowercase status, and the beads export lagging the database.

A MULTI-LINE PATCH ANCHOR SILENTLY NO-OPS ON THIS REPO CRLF CHECKOUTS, AND THE SABOTAGE RUN THEN COMES BACK GREEN (2026-08-18).

Measured by rf2-0yp7w.9 slice 2 (PR #8502): "Two plants silently no-opped first and both runs came back green — a multi-line anchor does not match a CRLF working tree, and unchanged and not-attempted are the same diff. Only the hash caught it."

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN ANNOYING. The planted-fault route exists to prove a gate READ YOUR WORKTREE. The worker plants a fault, expects red, and reads green. The green does not say "the plant failed to apply" — it says, to a tired reader, "this gate does not cover my surface" or worse "the control does not bite". Both conclusions are false and both are actionable in the wrong direction: one abandons a gate that works, the other reports a hollow control that is not hollow. The evidence in the report is internally consistent either way.

THE DIFF CANNOT CATCH IT. "Unchanged" and "not attempted" produce the identical diff, so a worker verifying its restore by reading a diff sees exactly what a correct plant-and-restore looks like.

TWO RULES, AND BOTH ARE NEEDED:
1. ANCHOR A PLANT TO A SINGLE LINE WITH NO NEWLINE IN IT. Multi-line anchors are the failure; on a checkout whose line endings are translated they match nothing, with no error.
2. HASH BEFORE THE PLANT AND AFTER THE RESTORE, using version control content hashing against the COMMITTED OBJECT (git hash-object), never a plain byte digest of the working file — a checkout during a rebase rewrites the working file after you hashed it, so a plain digest reports a CORRECT restore as failed. Three hashes tell the whole story: pre-plant, planted, post-restore. If pre-plant equals planted, the patch never applied and the green means nothing.

This is the Windows/CRLF half of a rule the dispatch template already carries in general terms. It is worth its own record because the general rule reads as a caution while this is a reproducible property of every checkout in this repository, and it has now bitten twice in one run.

MY CRLF REMEDY IN BRIEFS IS THE WRONG REFLEX FOR MOST TRACKED FILES (2026-08-06).

WHAT I HAVE BEEN WRITING: "spec/** files are stored CRLF here; if the diff explodes, rebuild byte-exactly from the base blob and `git -c core.autocrlf=false add`."

WHAT THE rf2-ix9tk WORKER MEASURED on spec/004-Views.md: the override staged 2906 changed lines out of 2906 - it forced CRLF INTO AN LF INDEX. The plain `git add` gave 2/2, exactly the intended change.

THE REASON, and it is the discriminator to use: the file is `i/lf w/crlf` - LF in the INDEX, CRLF in the WORKING TREE, which is what `core.autocrlf=true` is FOR. The normalisation on add is CORRECT and is what keeps the index clean. Disabling it makes the working-tree CRLF the thing that gets stored, which is a whole-file diff.

THE CORRECTED RULE: use PLAIN `git add`. Then check `git diff --numstat`. Only if a plain add blows the diff up does the override become a candidate - and check `git ls-files --eol <path>` first to see which way the file is actually stored. The numstat check is the load-bearing half and always was; the remedy I attached to it was cargo.

WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG: it came from a real incident (a worker DID produce a ~4,200-line diff on spec/011-SSR.md for a +45-line change) and I generalised the CURE from one file to a whole tree without re-testing. Same shape as the git-grep-ref hazard I propagated for a session and the node_modules canary I quoted for weeks: BOILERPLATE IS THE LEAST-AUDITED TEXT I PRODUCE, because it is copied rather than composed. Re-test one boilerplate claim per retrospective.

ALSO CORRECTED IN THE SAME REPORT: my `.beads` hygiene check told workers to run `git diff --numstat origin/main..HEAD`. That is TWO-DOT, so it shows my own checkpoint commits as though they were the worker`s, and three workers in a row reported a false `.beads` positive. Use the MERGE BASE (or `sh scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh origin/main`, remembering it exits 0 with no base ref so the ref must always be passed).

EDITING A CRLF-STORED FILE UNDER core.autocrlf=true SILENTLY NORMALISES THE WHOLE FILE TO LF — a multi-thousand-line whitespace diff that reads as real content. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.103 worker, which caught it before committing.

THE CASE: spec/011-SSR.md is stored on main with CRLF. A normal edit produced a ~4,200-line diff on a HOT-ZONE file for a change that should have been +45 lines. Nothing warned; the diff simply looked enormous.

THE CURE the worker used: rebuild the file BYTE-EXACTLY from its base blob plus the intended change, then re-add with `git -c core.autocrlf=false add <file>`. Committed diff came out at +45 insertions and nothing else.

THE CHECK, and it is cheap: after ANY edit to a tracked file, run `git diff --numstat` and confirm the line counts match what you intended. A diff far larger than your change is a line-ending normalisation, not your edit.

⚠️ THIS COMPOUNDS WITH THE HOT-ZONE RULE. spec/ files are sequential-never-parallel precisely because they collide; a whole-file normalisation guarantees a conflict with every other branch touching that file, and buries the real change so a reviewer cannot see it. On a hot-zone file the damage is not cosmetic.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: `sed -i` on a tracked file does the same thing for the same reason on this Windows checkout — which is why briefs forbid it and require the Edit tool. This is the SAME hazard reached through an ordinary edit rather than through sed, so the sed ban alone does not cover it. Put the numstat check in briefs that touch spec/ files, not just the sed ban.

MAYOR NOTE: my briefs already say "no sed -i" and "check git diff --numstat shows only the lines you intended" — the second half turned out to be the load-bearing one, and I had been treating it as a footnote to the first.

DECAYED (GC-DELETED) BEADS ARE RECOVERED WITH bd import FROM A PRE-GC EXPORT, NOT bd restore — AND bd import --dry-run DOES NOT VALIDATE STATUS (2026-09-14, rf2-1g115, bd 1.2.2). (1) bd restore only restores the pre-compaction CONTENT of an issue that still EXISTS in compacted form; on a bead removed by gc decay it exits 1 "issue not found", even though the GC commit message (d7d7b61dcc) says "restorable via bd restore". (2) The working route: take the record from the export in the commit BEFORE the GC (MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git show "<gc>^:.beads/issues.jsonl", jq select on ._type=="issue" and .id, strip carriage returns), write one JSONL line per bead, and bd import <file>. Upsert semantics, never deletes, keeps the ORIGINAL id, status, close_reason, created_at and closed_at, so cross-file citations resolve with no edits. Verify by FIELD against the recovered record (close_reason length and an interior phrase beside a nonsense control). (3) TRAP: bd import --dry-run reported "created 4" but does not validate status; the real import then refused the WHOLE batch atomically with "invalid status: in_review" (nothing written). bd 1.2.2 no longer accepts in_review. Import the valid rows, and map a retired status deliberately (rf2-m6tu was restored as deferred with a note naming its original status).

DELETING A DECORATIVE ROW LEAVES THE CLAIM UNWITNESSED — the discriminating-row rule has a second half (2026-08-11, AUDIT #7835 on rf2-wjag).

WHAT I HAD BEEN TEACHING: for every negative row, ask what single narrowing of the implementation would let it pass while the property is broken. If such a narrowing exists, the row is decorative. That is right, and it has caught real defects all session.

WHAT I PRAISED, AND WHY IT WAS ONLY HALF RIGHT: a worker wrote a cold-probe row, found its mutation red nothing, DELETED the row and recorded the finding in the namespace docstring. Its words: "Claim real, witness not." I called that the rule applied by a worker to its own work, unprompted — and it was, as far as it went.

THE AUDIT COMPLETED IT: the row was decorative AS WRITTEN because the frame it used (a make-frame frame) had no stale projection to flush. The CLAIM was real and became UNWITNESSED by the deletion. The only thing still exercising it was a prototype-tree row — exercising the prototype runtime, not the package implementation, which is exactly the dependence the bead existed to end.

THE COMPLETED RULE: "this row cannot fail" is a finding about THE ROW'S CONDITIONS, not about whether the claim deserves a witness. The three outcomes, in order of preference:
  1. REWRITE the row with the conditions that make the mechanism load-bearing (here: an image-loaded frame rather than a fresh one). This is almost always the answer.
  2. DELETE it only if the claim is already covered elsewhere IN THE SAME ARTEFACT — and name the coverer. Coverage in a donor, prototype or sibling tree does not count when the bead's purpose is to stop relying on that tree.
  3. If the claim genuinely cannot be witnessed here, say so and say WHY, in the artefact — as the erasure worker did for defview coordinates, where a filename sentinel would be red on a correct build.

MAYOR APPLICATION: when a worker reports deleting a row, ask what still witnesses the claim. The report will usually not volunteer it, because the deletion feels like the finding — and it is a finding, just not a complete one.

TWO BRANCHES CAN DELETE DIFFERENT NAMES FROM ONE NAMESPACE AND EACH SILENTLY DESTROY THE OTHER'S
TEST CONTROL — a merge hazard that produces a COMPILING, PASSING test whose control is false, with
no textual conflict to warn you. Measured 2026-09-07 in the rebase of PR #9358 over PR #9356.

WHAT HAPPENED. rf2-kuky.80 (PR #9356) deleted `re-frame.routing/clear-route`. PR #9358 deleted
`current-url` and `route-sub-fn` from the SAME namespace. Each side's deletion test needed a
positive control to prove its nil meant "deleted" rather than "namespace never loaded" — and each
side reached for a name the OTHER side was deleting:
  * main asserted `(some? current-url)` to prove the `clear-route` nil was a real deletion
  * the branch asserted `(some? clear-route)` for the mirror reason
Taking EITHER side wholesale yields a test that compiles, runs and passes — while its control now
asserts the presence of a name that no longer exists, so the control is dead and the assertion
proves nothing. The worker retargeted both controls at `match-url`/`route-url` (names neither side
touched) and removed `clear-route` from the `kept` vector.

WHY NOTHING WARNS YOU. The clash is SEMANTIC, not textual. The two deletions are in different
regions of the file, so git reports no conflict; the merge is clean; the suite is green. The only
signal is knowing what the control was FOR. A reviewer reading the diff sees two unrelated
deletions land tidily.

THE GENERAL SHAPE, worth more than the instance: A DELETION TEST'S CONTROL IS A DEPENDENCY ON A
NAME SURVIVING, and that dependency is invisible to every tool. Any two concurrent branches
pruning the same namespace are candidates. The same session recorded a sibling case with the same
signature — rf2-kuky.60's new test landed written against the positional grammar rf2-kuky.80
retires, no conflict, caught only by clj-kondo.

THE GUARD, in order of cost:
  1. CHOOSE CONTROLS THAT NOTHING IS RETIRING. Prefer a name central to the namespace's purpose
     over a neighbouring name that happens to be handy — the handy one is exactly what a
     concurrent pruning bead is most likely to be deleting.
  2. When rebasing a deletion change over another deletion change in the same namespace, READ
     BOTH SIDES' TEST CONTROLS SPECIFICALLY. Not the assertions — the controls.
  3. The revert check (`git diff origin/main...HEAD`, three-dot, read for what you would UNDO)
     catches the textual half but NOT this: both sides' lines can survive while the meaning does
     not. This one needs a human-shaped read.

VERIFYING A DELIVERABLE IS NOT THE SAME AS CHECKING FOR UNMET OBLIGATIONS — I conflated them and stranded work (2026-08-14).

WHAT I DID. rf2-d6ai8 flipped open three times with no comment attached. I applied the churn discriminator, verified its DELIVERABLE at source each time — requirements-mine.md carried the re-taken pass-1 entry, PR #8178 merged — and re-closed it. On the third pass I called it "churn (third status-only flip)".

WHAT I MISSED. The bead's NOTES carried an explicit unmet obligation added after the deliverable landed: "Keep this exact requirements-mine owner open until those false premises are corrected there." rf2-gvysu had also been closed as a duplicate OF d6ai8. So both owners were closed while all three false rows were still on main. The work was stranded, and it took a worker reading both beads to find it.

THE DISTINCTION I COLLAPSED. My own backlog-reread rule says: READ THE BEAD NOTES BEFORE RE-CLOSING ANYTHING, and grep them for AUDIT-REOPEN, unmet, obligation. I substituted a different and easier check — does the thing the bead was filed to produce exist on main? Both are necessary. A bead can have its original deliverable landed AND carry a later obligation that keeps it open, and the second is invisible to a source check on the first.

THE TELL I SHOULD HAVE NOTICED: a bead that reopens THREE TIMES is not behaving like churn. Churn is a flag flipping; three flips with a duplicate closed alongside it is a signal that something is actively holding the bead open. The repetition itself was evidence and I read it as noise.

THE RULE, GOING FORWARD. Before re-closing any reopened bead, do BOTH: (a) verify the deliverable at source, and (b) grep the full notes for an obligation added after that deliverable landed. If a sibling or duplicate bead exists, read it too — a duplicate closed against an owner that is itself closed leaves nobody holding the work.

ALSO WRONG IN THE SAME DISPATCH, and worth the same care: I told that worker the L6 machinery "landed today". It had not — PR #8187 was still OPEN at dispatch time and merged mid-pass. Stating an in-flight PR as landed is the same class of error as quoting an unverified constant: check the state at dispatch time, not from memory of a report.

The badge does not merely differ, it fails in the direction that costs a worker, and it does so on the two beads with the tracker's hardest operator gates in front of them. rf2-hic-090 is the bead that has already consumed FOUR dispatches (PRs #8312, #8395, #8445, #8560), each running its evidence families correctly and each declining to close for the same unruled reason. Dependency-chain gating gotcha: workers close their bead on PR CREATION (not merge), so a 'bd dep add A B' where B closes-at-PR-creation makes 'bd ready' surface A as soon as B's PR is OPENED — BEFORE B's code is on main. If A and B touch the same files (surface-conflict sequencing), dispatching A off origin/main then conflicts when B merges. WHAT I HAD BEEN DOING WRONG: fencing the WHOLE measurement lane behind one-window-at-a-time. That is right for clock work and wasteful for counter work. It cost throughput repeatedly in one session — I held a doc cluster, an audit and a tracker pass off a box that a counter census did not need quiet.

WORKTREES ACCUMULATE BECAUSE THEY ARE DIRTY, NOT BECAUSE NOBODY TRIED TO REAP THEM (2026-08-18).

A hygiene pass reaped 9 of 11 leftover worktrees whose PRs had MERGED. The two refusals were both REMOVE_REFUSED_DIRTY - git will not remove a worktree holding modified or untracked files, and the removal script surfaces each offending path prefixed [KEEP] with the message that RETRYING WILL NEVER CLEAR THIS. That is the whole mechanism behind a pile of stale worktrees: every pass reaps the clean ones and leaves the dirty ones, so the dirty ones are all that is left.

DO NOT REACH FOR --force. The script says --force DELETES the [KEEP] paths, and its own text distinguishes them from build output: an uncommitted edit, a note, a draft. On this pass one refusing worktree held a modified deps.edn plus an untracked test and an untracked script; another held a MODIFIED .github/workflows/test.yml (hot zone), a modified .claude/commands file, and a DELETED studio record.

THE CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR BEFORE DECIDING ANYTHING: check whether the [KEEP] paths already exist at origin/main. For the first worktree both untracked files were PRESENT on main - the branch's PR had merged and the worktree was simply sitting on a pre-merge commit, so its 'untracked' files were a stale local copy of landed work, at risk of nothing. That check is two git cat-file calls and it converts an alarming refusal into a nothing.

STILL LEAVE THEM. Even when the content is provably safe, force-deleting buys one worktree and risks a draft nobody has read. Leaving two dirty worktreees costs disk and a line in git worktree list.

A MERGED PR IS STRONGER EVIDENCE THAN A COMPLETION REPORT, and it is what makes an old worktree reapable at all. The hygiene rule says reap only on the agent's own completion report - correct for a worker dispatched THIS session, where a report is obtainable. For a leftover from a prior session no report exists and never will, so the rule as literally written would freeze them forever. A verifiably MERGED PR says the work is on main, which is what the report was evidence FOR. Match on exact head-ref, and re-derive the ahead-count in the same command as the delete.

TWO READINGS OF A MUTABLE REMOTE STATE, TAKEN AT DIFFERENT TIMES AND DISAGREEING, ARE NOT EVIDENCE THAT EITHER INSTRUMENT IS STALE — THE STATE CHANGED. Attributing the disagreement to the instrument invents a defect that does not exist and sends the next reader hunting a caching bug. Found 2026-09-20 by the mayor, about the mayor, during a `loops.md` §5 method reread.

WHAT HAPPENED. Verifying a PR, `gh pr list --json isDraft` reported `isDraft: true` and, in a later call, `gh pr view <n> --json isDraft` reported `draft: false` for that same PR. I wrote down **"the list's draft flag was stale"** and repeated it across three subsequent ticks as a standing caution.

**IT IS FALSE.** Re-measured back-to-back in one shell on a live PR: `gh pr list` and `gh pr view` **both** read `draft=false`. The instruments agree when read at the same instant. What actually happened is in my own transcript: the worker **marked the PR ready between my two calls**, and its completion notification — saying in terms "PR #10113 is ready for review" — arrived in the gap. **Both readings were correct about the moment each was taken.**

WHY THE WRONG DIAGNOSIS IS ATTRACTIVE. "My tool lied to me" is a complete, self-contained story that needs no further evidence and flatters the reader's carefulness. "The world moved between my two questions" requires noticing that the two questions were asked at different times — and in an agent transcript those calls look adjacent, sitting in consecutive blocks with nothing between them but, in this case, a notification that was the whole explanation. **The gap is invisible in the record precisely where it matters.**

THE COST IS NOT THE PRACTICE, IT IS THE REASON. The practice I adopted — read the state with `gh pr view` immediately before acting — is CORRECT and I kept it. But it is correct for a different reason than the one I gave: not because a listing lies, but because **a merge criterion must be evaluated against the state at the moment of merging**, which is exactly why the method prescribes verify → merge → fast-forward → verify. A right practice resting on a wrong mechanism is fragile: drop the mechanism and the practice looks like superstition; keep it and someone eventually files a bug against `gh`.

THE GUARD:
  * **BEFORE BLAMING AN INSTRUMENT, ASK WHETHER THE SUBJECT IS MUTABLE AND WHETHER THE TWO READS WERE SIMULTANEOUS.** A PR's draft flag, a rollup, a process census, a branch tip and a worker's status are all mutable on the scale of seconds.
  * **REPRODUCE BACK-TO-BACK IN ONE CALL BEFORE WRITING DOWN THAT AN INSTRUMENT IS WRONG.** Two commands in one shell invocation is the whole test, and it takes one line. It is what refuted this.
  * **LOOK FOR AN EVENT IN THE GAP.** A task notification, a worker's last act, a merge landing — the explanation is usually sitting in the record between the two calls, and it reads as unrelated context rather than as the cause.
  * **SAY WHICH INSTANT A READING DESCRIBES**, not just what it said. "Draft at 20:14" and "ready at 20:22" do not conflict; "the list says draft, the view says ready" invents a conflict out of two true statements.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS WORTH RECORDING: a genuine instrument defect belongs in the catalogue and protects everyone; an invented one costs a future reader a hunt through `gh`'s cache behaviour for something that was never there. **This project's CLAUDE.md carries a long, hard-won catalogue of instruments that really do misreport on this machine, and its value depends on not being diluted with entries that are really races.**

CONTROL, BOTH WAYS, SAME SESSION: on the same day the mayor recorded TWO genuine instrument findings that survived exactly this test — a capped locator returning a false absence, and an unsourced denominator — so this is not "never blame the instrument", it is "reproduce simultaneously first, because one of the three will be a race."

SEE ALSO [[an-unsourced-denominator-asserts-headroom-nobody-measured]] and [[a-capped-listing-licenses-a-false-absence-claim]] — same session, same discipline: a claim repeated across ticks that nobody had re-run.

TO TELL AN AUDIT REOPEN FROM A BARE STATUS REVERT, ASK WHETHER TEXT GREW WHILE THE BEAD WAS CLOSED — compare the notes length AT THE LAST CLOSE against the NEWEST notes length. Growth means an audit wrote its reason; no growth means only the status moved. Established 2026-09-05 after two WRONG re-closes destroyed real audit findings.

THE CORRECT PROBE:
  bd history <id> --json  ->  walk newest-first, find the first snapshot whose status is "closed",
  compare (.Issue.notes | length) THERE against the same field in the NEWEST snapshot.
  grew > 0  ->  AUDIT REOPEN. Leave it open. Read the added text; it is the specification.
  grew == 0 ->  candidate revert, but see the null-field caveat below.

TWO PROBES I USED BEFORE THIS, BOTH WRONG, BOTH FAILING TOWARD "TIDY UP":

1. A MARKER GREP over a fixed pattern set — AUDIT-REOPEN, "REOPENED THIS EXACT", REOPENED, "still owed", "residual". A real audit note opened "AUDIT 2026-09-04 — MERGED PR #9187: reopened because ..." — LOWERCASE "reopened", header matching nothing in the set. I ran a control on unrelated text known to be present, saw 1 hit, and concluded the instrument was live. IT WAS. A CONTROL PROVES THE INSTRUMENT EXECUTES; IT DOES NOT PROVE THE PATTERN SET IS COMPLETE. To validate a pattern set, control against a POSITIVE INSTANCE OF THE TARGET — a bead you already know carries an audit note — not against arbitrary present text. This is the sharpest form of the standing "a search returning zero is not a check that passed" rule.

2. AN ADJACENT-PAIR LENGTH COMPARISON at the reopen boundary. This assumes the status change and the note are ONE mutation. THEY OFTEN ARE NOT: an audit commonly flips status and appends its note in a SEPARATE, LATER mutation, so the adjacent pair reads unchanged on a genuine audit. Anchoring to the boundary was an improvement over comparing the newest N — which reads unchanged on BOTH classes once a bead has settled — but it is still wrong.

THE NULL-FIELD CAVEAT: if notes is EMPTY on both sides, "unchanged" proves nothing — an absent field hashes constant and reports a clean walk in the same words a genuinely unchanged one does. Fall back to a field that DOES vary on that item (description, acceptance_criteria), and confirm the deliverable is on main in the TREE before closing.

WHAT ACTUALLY EXPOSED THE ERROR, and it is the transferable part: I ran the new probe against a CONTROL BEAD I was already confident was a genuine audit reopen. It answered "revert". That contradiction — not any new evidence about the beads under test — falsified the method. RUN A NEW DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST A CASE WHOSE ANSWER YOU ALREADY KNOW, AND BELIEVE THE CONTRADICTION OVER THE PROBE.

THE COST: two beads carrying substantive second-carrier work were closed with a confident, well-argued, wrong reason — rf2-hic-064 (four accuracy repairs against captured CI gate numbers) and rf2-2hpxo (six named epoch exports whose durable facade rationale contradicts the code). Both are now reopened with the correction recorded on them. Two others re-closed the same session were re-checked and confirmed genuine reverts; those stand.

AND THE STANDING RULE THIS VIOLATED, from docs/the-mayor-method/README.md: "read the item's notes before re-closing anything. The instinct to re-close a 'reverted' item destroys a real finding and looks like tidiness." Reading the NOTES means reading the text, not measuring it. When in doubt, print the text added since the last close and read it.

DISPATCH BRIEF FIX (mayor, 2026-07-25): three workers in one session ended their turn with work committed-but-unpushed and NO PR, each waiting for a long local gate (scripts/test-fast-pr.sh spine) to finish first. The instruction 'do not end your turn with uncommitted work' is NOT sufficient — workers read it as satisfied by a local commit. Every editing brief must instead say, in this order and with the reasons: (1) PUSH as you go, not at the end, because pushed commits are the only durable worker state and a worker that dies mid-run takes local commits with it; (2) OPEN THE PR as soon as commits exist, because a PR is how work becomes visible to the merge gate and is NOT a claim of green — state any still-running gate in the '## Quality gates' section as reliance-on-CI, which is acceptable, whereas a silent omission is not; (3) the merge decision is CI's, not the worker's local run, so if a gate later reds it is a fix-worker on the existing branch and needed no waiting. Recovery when it happens: SendMessage-resume the SAME worker (it holds the branch and worktree; never dispatch a second worker onto one branch). Pair this with the two log hygiene rules workers also miss: capture gate output to a WORKTREE-LOCAL path (the machine temp dir is shared, so two concurrent workers writing one log path read each other's green), and echo the exit code explicitly (piping a gate into tail/grep returns the PIPE's status, not the runner's, so a failed run reads as '0 failures').

A DISPATCH DIRECTIVE THAT LIVES ONLY IN NOTES DOES NOT STOP DISPATCHES — put it at the TOP of the DESCRIPTION (2026-08-21, rf2-63t1i).

WHAT HAPPENED. rf2-63t1i went out THREE times to three workers at the same settled (a)/(b) fork, on 2026-08-20 10:07, 2026-08-20 11:46 and 2026-08-21 04:20. All three correctly returned a source-located NO EDIT. The bead's NOTES field had said DO NOT DISPATCH THIS AS A PROSE FIX since 2026-08-18 and had named the earlier workers. Each dispatch cost a full worker cycle.

THE MECHANISM, and it is structural rather than careless. A mayor writing a brief reads the bead to find out what the work IS, and the work is described in the DESCRIPTION. That field is the OLDEST text on a bead by construction — corrections accrete into NOTES and comments below it. So the field a brief is naturally drawn from is precisely the field least likely to carry the current disposition. A head-truncated show makes it worse by returning the description and stopping before NOTES, but the trap survives reading the whole bead, because the description is what answers the question the mayor is actually asking.

mayor-dispatch.md ALREADY carries the rule that catches this — establish which text is newest by TRACKER TIMESTAMP, never by position and never by which FIELD it sits in — and the rule did not prevent three dispatches. A rule that has failed three times against the same bead is not enforced by restating it.

THE FIX THAT WORKS: when a bead becomes non-dispatchable, PREPEND the disposition to the DESCRIPTION as a banner, in the form *** DISPOSITION ... DO NOT DISPATCH ... *** followed by why, what is established, what is actually owed and who owns it, then a --- ORIGINAL DESCRIPTION FOLLOWS --- fold. The banner is in the field the brief is drawn from, so it cannot be missed by the reading pattern that causes the failure. Applied 2026-08-21 to rf2-63t1i, rf2-egdaq, rf2-hic-090 and rf2-ps7ia — the four ready-list beads whose directive lived only in NOTES.

HOW TO FIND THE REST: list every open, in_progress, blocked and deferred bead as JSON and flag any whose NOTES match a directive pattern (DO NOT DISPATCH, DO NOT RE-DISPATCH, REMOVED FROM THE DISPATCH POOL, NOT DISPATCHABLE, DO NOT TAKE, HELD FOR MIKE, OPERATOR CALL, DISPOSITION) while the DESCRIPTION does not. dispatch-id uniqueness: the portable trace contract (re_frame/trace/projection.cljc:182 + pair-mcp spec 003:2486) only guarantees a :rf.trace/dispatch-id is unique WITHIN a frame -- cascades group by [frame dispatch-id], not dispatch-id alone. BUT the current runtime over-delivers: router.cljc allocates ids from a process-GLOBAL monotonic counter (defonce dispatch-counter, swap! inc), so cross-frame same-id collisions essentially never happen today. This makes any consumer that keys cascade events / trace-events by dispatch-id ALONE (rf2-1we9fa: the pair preload cascade-bundle-events did exactly this) a LATENT bug -- correct against the global-counter accident, broken against the contract. It flips latent->LIVE the moment id allocation honors the per-frame contract, which EP-0010 (deterministic replay ids) and EP-0013 (N realms in one page, per-realm/per-frame counters) will introduce. Rule for trace/cascade consumers: always key by (frame, dispatch-id); reuse the framework projection (group-cascades) rather than re-deriving the grouping with a weaker key. Do not rely on global-counter uniqueness.

THE DISPATCH LEDGER IS APPEND-ONLY AND WORKTREE DIRECTORY NAMES ARE REUSED, so keying a lookup on
the path alone and taking the LAST match can hand you a row from a different worktree entirely.
Measured 2026-09-07 17:02 AUSEST during a §4 stranded sweep.

WHAT HAPPENED. The sweep mapped live worktrees to beads with
`grep -F "/$w<TAB>" ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv | tail -1`. For `xray-a` it returned four beads
(rf2-jy64, rf2-j0yk6, rf2-l1hh, rf2-wdckf) and an agentId — for a worktree I had created minutes
earlier and NEVER DISPATCHED. The row was dated 2026-09-03, four days old, belonging to a PRIOR
xray-a worktree that had been reaped; all four of its beads were closed. `tail -1` picked it
because it was the only match, and the sweep reported a live worker holding four beads that no
agent was working.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY WRONG: it fails in BOTH directions from one row.
  * It manufactures a phantom worker — a tree that looks dispatched and busy, so the mayor does
    not dispatch into it, and a free slot is silently withheld.
  * Read the other way, it would attribute a LIVE worker's tree to somebody else's finished beads,
    and the §4 sweep's remedy for an unowned tree is to reap it. Reaping a live worker's worktree
    on a four-day-old row is the destructive version of this.
Neither presents as an error. The row is well-formed, the fields parse, the beads exist.

THE MECHANISM, which generalises past this file: an APPEND-ONLY log keyed by a REUSABLE name has
no unique key at all. Directory names here are short and thematic (xray-a, views-c, core-a) and get
recreated tick after tick as surfaces come back into scope, so the same path names many distinct
worktrees over a session's life. CLAUDE.md's ledger contract already warns against addressing rows
BY INDEX; this is the same lesson one level up — the row is also not addressable by PATH.

THE GUARD: disambiguate by TIME as well as path. Compare the row's `dispatched` timestamp against
the worktree's own creation or first-commit time and reject a row that predates the tree. Or, more
simply and what the mayor now does: WRITE A ROW WHEN THE WORKTREE IS CREATED, even when no dispatch
follows, with `(not-dispatched)` in the agentId field and `--` for beads. A tree with no row is
indistinguishable from a tree whose row is stale; a tree with a fresh row saying "nothing was
dispatched here" is unambiguous.

AND THE SWEEP SHOULD SAY WHICH IT FOUND. "No row" and "a row I could not trust" are different
findings with different remedies, and collapsing them is how the destructive reading gets reached.

STOP ADDING THE LINE-BREAK SEARCH WARNING TO BRIEFS UNLESS I HAVE MEASURED IT ON THAT TARGET — twice in one day it was false, and a false hazard is not free. 2026-09-07.

WHAT I KEEP DOING. The three-pass census rule (line-oriented / whitespace-collapsed / comment-markers-stripped-then-collapsed) exists because a target broken across two lines is invisible to any line-oriented search. It is a real and well-evidenced hazard. So I have been adding a target-specific warning to briefs — "a line-oriented grep for X returns ZERO because the clause wraps" — as a helpful concretion of it.

TWICE TODAY THAT WARNING WAS FALSE, and both times a worker measured and refuted it:
- rf2-gwoz: I claimed a line-oriented grep for "install-* is not in the closed roster" returns 0. It returns 1; the clause sits on one line. I had run only the flattened pass and asserted what the other would say. What I had actually seen wrapped was bd show's RENDERING of my own note.
- rf2-2zl9 (the views-a rider): I warned the id might be written across a line break and told the worker to run the flattened pass. All three passes agree at 5 hits; it is not line-broken.

WHY THIS IS WORTH A RULE RATHER THAN A SHRUG. A false hazard costs a worker real effort confirming a trap that is not there, and it can be worse than that: when the worker's own measurement disagrees with the brief, the natural first hypothesis is that the FILE changed shape, not that the mayor guessed. That sends the worker looking for a phantom edit. And it debases the warning — a worker who has seen two false ones reads the third, real one as boilerplate.

THE DISTINCTION TO HOLD. The three-pass RULE is generic and belongs in every census brief: run all three passes, because the passes disagree unpredictably. A target-specific CLAIM — "this particular string wraps" — is a measurement, and I must not state it unless I have run the line-oriented pass myself on that file. Predicting one pass from another is precisely what the rule forbids.

THE CHEAP FORM THAT IS ALWAYS SAFE: "run all three passes; I have not measured which of them sees this target." That carries the whole benefit and asserts nothing. Where I HAVE measured, state the numbers and the file, so the worker can tell a measurement from a guess.

AND CREDIT WHERE THE PROCESS WORKED: on the second occasion I did write into the brief that I had over-warned about this exact hazard earlier the same day and that the worker should measure rather than believe either of us. It measured, refuted me, and said so plainly. Telling a worker that a specific warning of mine has a track record of being wrong is worth doing when I cannot be bothered to measure — but measuring is cheaper than either.

If you catch yourself typing a figure into a template, ask what re-measures it -- and if the answer is "nothing", delete the figure rather than checking it once more.

DO NOT REAP A WORKTREE WHEN ITS PR MERGES — REAP WHEN ITS AGENT REPORTS DONE (2026-08-01, my error, caught by the worker).

WHAT I DID. After merging PR #7337 I ran scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh against worker/heapaxis-2rtt6-34. The removal FAILED on a Windows file lock — but the script had already done its first job and DISARMED THE node_modules JUNCTION. The agent was still alive. Its next shadow-cljs invocation failed with 'shadow-cljs not found', and it spent a tool round diagnosing before reporting 'my worktree's junction has vanished... Recreating it'. It recovered on its own and the mayor's real node_modules was verified intact at 101 throughout, so nothing was damaged — but I cost a live worker a diagnostic detour for no reason.

THE MISTAKE IS THE TRIGGER, NOT THE SCRIPT. A merged PR means the WORK landed; it does NOT mean the AGENT finished. Agents legitimately continue after opening a PR — updating the PR body, re-running a gate, hardening a mutation proof, answering a resume message. The safe trigger is the agent's own completion notification, or an explicit confirmation from it that it is done with the tree.

THE RULE: reap a worker worktree only when BOTH are true — (1) its PR is merged, AND (2) its agent has reported done (or has been confirmed dead). If a reap fails on a file lock, that is often a SIGNAL the tree is still in use; do not retry in a loop, and check whether the agent is alive before trying again.

RELATED, ALREADY KNOWN AND STILL TRUE: the guard script is correct to disarm the link before removing (that is what stops git worktree remove following it into the mayor's real node_modules), and it correctly refuses rather than forcing when the removal cannot complete. The failure mode here is entirely in WHEN I invoked it.

SECOND MECHANISM FOR THE SAME RULE, demonstrated 2026-09-07 and worth stating because it bites in the OTHER direction — the agent HAS reported done and the tree is still needed. A worker finished the require-alias walk, reported done in full, and opened PR #9334. CI then went red on one job: a gate's self-test premise pinned a spelling the sweep had legitimately changed. The cheapest repair was to RESUME that same agent — it held the whole context, and the file was already inside its fence — and a resume runs in the agent's ORIGINAL WORKTREE. Had I reaped on the completion report alone, the resume would have had nothing to run in and the fix would have cost a fresh worker a full brief and a cold read of a 355-file rename.

SO CONDITION (1) IS NOT CEREMONY. Between "the agent reported done" and "the PR merged" there is a window in which CI can still fail, and the standard repair in that window is a resume, which requires the tree. Both conditions guard real hazards: (2) protects a live agent from having its tooling pulled out; (1) protects a finished agent's ability to come back. Neither substitutes for the other.

A PRACTICAL COROLLARY: when several workers report done at once and their PRs are still building, the correct hygiene outcome is often NOTHING REAPED. That is not a skipped loop — a hygiene pass that removes nothing because every tree is either live or awaiting a mergeable PR has done its job. Enumerate, test, record why each was spared, and stop.

DO NOT WARN A WORKER ABOUT A HAZARD YOU HAVE NOT MEASURED ON THE TARGET IN FRONT OF YOU — three instances in two days, each costing a worker real effort confirming a trap that was not there. 2026-09-07.

THE THREE:
  1. "this error id may be broken across a line, run the flattened pass" — all three passes agreed at 5 hits; it was not line-broken.
  2. the same warning again, a day later, on a different target — also false.
  3. "the bead cites lines 3115/3117/3120/3121; RE-DERIVE, citations across this epic have drifted on six beads" — the citations were EXACT at tip. The worker checked, found them correct, and said so.

THE THIRD IS THE INSTRUCTIVE ONE BECAUSE THE PREMISE WAS TRUE. Citations on that epic HAD drifted on six beads in one session, one of them by 133 lines. So the base rate was real and the warning felt like diligence. But a base rate is not a measurement of the instance, and I had the instance in front of me: `sed -n '3117p' <file>` is one command and would have shown the line intact.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS: a GENERIC RULE is free to state and belongs in every brief — "cite the construct, not the line", "run the census three ways", "a zero is not a check that passed". These cost the worker nothing because they describe a method. A SPECIFIC CLAIM about the target — "this line has moved", "this string wraps", "this file is stale" — is a MEASUREMENT, and stating it unmeasured spends the worker's context on a hunt that may have no quarry, and worse, teaches them to distrust citations that are fine.

THE RULE: state the generic rule; measure before adding the specific warning. If measuring is not worth it, say "unverified" in the brief so the worker prices it correctly — do not launder a base rate into an assertion about this target.

AND NOTE THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS EASY TO REPEAT: when the warning is right, the worker fixes something and nobody notices the warning did work; when it is wrong, the refutation lands in the report and looks like the worker being thorough rather than the mayor being sloppy. A `$`-ANCHORED REGEX RETURNS A FALSE ZERO ON A CRLF FILE — the line ends `\r\n`, so `$` sits after the `\r` and a pattern like `'^### Foo$'` matches nothing on a heading that plainly exists. Measured 2026-09-05 by a worker whose `rg '^### …$'` came back empty for a heading it could see in the file; a control exposed the zero immediately.

WHY IT BELONGS WITH THE OTHERS: this repo is `core.autocrlf=true`, so many files are CRLF in the worktree and LF in the index. Every `$`-anchored search over working-tree markdown is therefore suspect, and the failure mode is the worst kind — a clean exit 0 and an empty result set, indistinguishable from an honest "not present". A worker concluding "that heading does not exist" from such a zero would then ADD a duplicate heading, or report a missing anchor that is not missing.

THE FIXES, in order of preference:
  * Drop the `$` when you only need the prefix — `'^### Foo'` matches regardless of line ending.
  * Or match the ending explicitly: `'^### Foo\r?$'`.
  * Or search the INDEX rather than the worktree (`git grep`), where the blob is LF.
  * And always control it: run the same pattern against something you KNOW is there. A control caught this one in a single command.

THIS IS THE SAME CRLF FAMILY AS TWO OTHER MEASURED FAULTS: a `\n`-anchored PLANT that silently matched nothing on a CRLF-checked-out file (the gate then returned a clean exit 0), and `sed -i` silently converting a whole CRLF file to LF while "succeeding" (4637 CRs to 0). **On this box, assume line endings are CRLF in the worktree until you have checked, and never let a line-ending-sensitive pattern produce a conclusion without a control.**

RELATED: [[sed-i-silently-rewrites-a-crlf-file-to-lf]], [[gh-pr-edit-reports-exit-0-having-patched-nothing]].

AN INTERRUPTED DOLT GENERATIONAL GC CAN ROLL THE BEADS TRACKER BACK MID-SESSION, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE CORRUPTION (2026-08-03).

SYMPTOM SEQUENCE, in one 10-minute window: 'bd export' failed with 'error opening table file: table file not found: .dolt/noms/<hash>'. Then EVERY bd command — ready, list, show — exited 1. THE MISSING TABLE NAME DIFFERED BETWEEN CONSECUTIVE CALLS (18uc3mpc..., then 5l677oov...), noms/oldgen existed but was EMPTY, and the noms/ file count went 7 -> 91 across a couple of minutes. That is a generational GC rewriting table files, not disk damage.

IT RECOVERS ON ITS OWN. Roughly two minutes later bd returned exit 0 with no intervention. DO NOT rebuild the database from JSONL while this is happening — 'bd export' failing is NOT proof of data loss, and a rebuild from a checkpoint would discard everything since it.

THE REAL DAMAGE IS A PARTIAL ROLLBACK, AND IT IS SILENT. After recovery the tracker had time-travelled: a bead closed ~20 minutes earlier was back to IN_PROGRESS with its ORIGINAL 'Updated' date, and 5 note-appends were gone. But it was PARTIAL — a second close from the same pass SURVIVED. So you cannot assume all-or-nothing; verify each write individually with 'bd show'.

WHAT SAVED IT: the worker that made the writes still had them in its transcript. When bd broke I immediately messaged it to STOP all bd use and report every close/update verbatim WITH its verification evidence, then re-applied the 7 writes by hand and checkpointed at once. WITHOUT THAT REPLY THE WORK WAS UNRECOVERABLE — the JSONL checkpoint predated the writes.

RULES: (1) a tracker-mutating worker's report is a durable artefact — make its brief require verbatim reasons + evidence, not a summary; (2) checkpoint IMMEDIATELY after re-applying, do not batch; (3) row counts move under you because an automated merged-PR-audit process also commits .beads — 'HEAD had N' changing between your own checkpoints is NOT necessarily corruption; (4) beads-checkpoint.sh's shrinkage guard is the right instrument to ask 'did I lose bulk data?' — a clean round-trip at the same row count means the answer is no.

Beads Dolt off-box remote (configured 2026-08-10, rf2-4l67v): origin = private https://github.com/day8/re-frame2-beads.git (git-backed dolt remote; data under refs/dolt/data). Recovery drill lessons: (1) dolt's git-backed fetch/pull FAILS with 'fatal: $GIT_DIR too big' when the checkout sits under a long Windows path (e.g. deep Temp/scratchpad nesting) — always clone to a SHORT path (C:/Users/miket/code/<name>) for recovery drills; (2) on the SAME machine, bd bootstrap prefers a locally-registered database/remote over the tracked sync.remote, so a same-box round-trip is NOT a true second-machine test — repoint the clone's dolt origin explicitly to test the off-box copy; (3) bd can exit 0 while printing a push/pull ERROR — always read the output text, never trust the exit code alone; (4) an empty GitHub repo must be initialized with one commit/branch before the first dolt push.

THE DONE-IN-TREE SWEEP KEYS ON THE BEAD ID, SO WORK THAT LANDED UNDER A SIBLING'S ID IS INVISIBLE TO IT.

The backlog-reread sweep is 'for each open id, git log origin/main --grep=<id>'. Measured 2026-09-04: rf2-o80n asked for a route-link row in chapter 20's translation table. The row ALREADY EXISTED at tip, added by PR #9131 in commit c05871bf0b — a PR filed against DIFFERENT beads, which merged after rf2-o80n was filed. The sweep returned NOTHING for rf2-o80n, because #9131's message never names it. A worker was dispatched and its whole deliverable was the refutation.

SO THE SWEEP HAS A KNOWN BLIND SPOT AND IT IS NOT THE FALSE-POSITIVE KIND. It cannot see work that landed under a neighbour's id, which is the common case whenever one PR fixes a surface several beads describe. The complement is the loop's own rule, one level up: CHECK THE TREE, NOT THE ITEM. For a bead that asks for a specific artefact — a table row, a section, a symbol — grep the ARTEFACT at tip, not the id in the log. That check costs a line and would have saved a worker cycle.

THE SWEEP ALSO HAS A FALSE-POSITIVE MODE, which is the safe direction: with the anchored form (dots escaped, trailing boundary class), rf2-6r9j.35 and rf2-2vpm each returned a commit whose message a literal grep -F shows does NOT contain the id. Treat every hit as a POINTER and confirm with grep -F on the commit message before believing it.

AND THE ANCHOR IS STILL MANDATORY IN THE OTHER DIRECTION: unanchored, 'rf2-6r9j.1' matched five commits naming .161, .101, .17, .104 and .121. Anchored it matched none. Escape the dots and append a trailing boundary class: --grep="<escaped>([^0-9A-Za-z.]|$)" with -E.

STRIP CR FIRST. 'jq -r .[].id' emits trailing \r on Windows and every grep in the loop then misses. A control built from hardcoded literal ids tests the grep and never the pipeline — it passed while the real sweep read a false clean over 48 ids. Pipe through tr -d '\r' and build the control from the SAME pipeline.

Donor-sweep metric mismatch: the narrow grep is NOT the ledger's signal. When de-donoring a surface for EP-0036 F6, 'git grep -E "re-frame\.ui|re_frame/ui|re-frame2-ui" returns zero' does NOT mean scripts/check_donor_inventory.py agrees. Its DONOR_EVIDENCE_RE (check 4, DONOR-LEDGER-DRIFTED) is deliberately LOOSER and also matches re_frame.ui, re_frame2_ui, implementation/ui, node-test-ui, check-ui-, run-ui-, test:ui. Consequences both ways: (a) a sweep that satisfies the narrow grep can leave a still-pending ledger row silently green, so 'zero donor references' is not proof the row is disposable; (b) finishing the job (rewriting that path) FLIPS the gate to rc=1 naming the exact ledger line, so any complete de-donoring MUST be paired with the row's status change in spec/conformance/freehand/donor-inventory.md in the SAME PR. Also note the census (checks 2/3) is narrower still — CENSUS_REQUIRE_RE needs a libspec bracket and CENSUS_COORD_RE needs 'day8/re-frame2-ui {' — so three different donor definitions are in play. Always run 'python scripts/check_donor_inventory.py --ci' and read the rc; never infer disposition from a text grep.

MIKE: DRIVE THE OPEN COUNT TO ZERO, AND MEASUREMENT BEADS RUN WHEN THE BOX IS QUIET (2026-08-14).

His words: 'Drive that number to 0. If you run out of beads to do, then do the measurement ones because the box will be quiet.'

THIS RESOLVES A CONSTRAINT I HAD BEEN TREATING AS A BLOCKER. Several hicasso beads are TIMING MEASUREMENTS — tau, the interpreter-walk mount cost, allocation constants, a reader-array cost, a profile re-take, three budget gates. They cannot run honestly while five workers compile, so I had parked them as 'needs a quiet machine' with no rule for when that arrives.

THE RULE IS NOW: THE BOX IS QUIET EXACTLY WHEN NOTHING ELSE IS DISPATCHABLE. So measurement beads are the TAIL of the queue, not a separate track. Dispatch everything else first; when the dispatchable pool empties, the fleet drains, and the machine becomes the quiet box those beads need. The scheduling constraint and the priority order agree.

PRACTICAL FORM:
  While non-measurement beads remain dispatchable, saturate with those.
  When the pool empties, STOP dispatching and let the fleet drain to zero workers.
  Then dispatch measurement beads — ideally ONE AT A TIME, because two concurrent measurement workers reintroduce exactly the contention that makes the numbers worthless.

AND THAT LAST POINT IS THE ONE TO BRIEF: a measurement bead's whole value is a trustworthy number. Running two at once, or running one beside a compile, silently corrupts the deliverable in a way no gate detects. A measurement worker should say what else was running while it measured.

THIS SITS UNDER THE PHASE ORDER RATHER THAN BESIDE IT: measurement beads are stage 1-3 work (complete / correct / good quality code), so they lead the queue by stage — but they execute last by scheduling. Both are true and they do not conflict.

WHEN COLLAPSING DUPLICATE BEADS, THE SURVIVOR IS THE EARLIER OWNER WITH MORE CONTENT — not the one with the sharper framing (2026-08-15 16:54 AUSEST).

MEASURED ON MYSELF. rf2-15bqc and rf2-4ncab were the same finding: same four -h-fn recovery keywords, same emitters (impl/intent.cljs, impl/controlled.cljs), same Spec 009 lines. At 15:47 I closed 15bqc AS A DUPLICATE OF 4ncab. An audit then closed 4ncab AS A DUPLICATE OF 15bqc — the opposite direction.

THE AUDIT WAS RIGHT AND I LEFT IT STANDING. My reason was that 4ncab 'carries the sharper framing' — it states the CONSTRAINT ('the ids move with their emitters, or not at all') rather than only the symptom. The audit's reasons were stronger:
  - 15bqc is the EARLIER exact owner
  - it already carried the authoritative complaints.md ruling, the full emitter list, the one-pass repair AND the troubleshooting-doc tail
So it had both provenance and more content. Framing is cheap to copy forward; accumulated content and history are not.

THE RULE: prefer the earlier owner, and prefer the bead carrying more verified content. If the loser has a better framing sentence, COPY THE SENTENCE ONTO THE SURVIVOR — that costs one note. Do not close the richer bead to keep the better-worded one.

WHY NO DAMAGE WAS DONE, and this is the part that made it safe: BOTH closes carried the loser's unique evidence forward. Mine moved 15bqc's two extra surfaces (troubleshooting.md, hicasso.cljc) onto 4ncab; the audit's moved 4ncab's bench-mirror evidence onto 15bqc. Net result is one bead holding everything. THE CARRY-FORWARD IS WHAT MAKES A COLLAPSE REVERSIBLE — a close that merely says 'duplicate of X' is not.

DO NOT RE-CLOSE THE SURVIVOR. The method's own rule applies directly: the instinct to re-close a 'reverted' bead destroys a real finding and looks like tidiness. Read the notes first. Here the reopen was an audit converging on the better survivor, and the correct action was to leave it alone and record why.

CONTEXT ON WHY DUPLICATES ARISE AT ALL HERE: these two were filed HOURS APART by DIFFERENT workers approaching the same residue from opposite directions, neither visible to the other because both were mid-flight. That is rf2-a30v2's blind window one level up.

DUPLICATE deftest — CLJS WARNS, THE JVM IS SILENT. rf2-9e4lf (#6349, 2026-07-18) verified this with a standalone probe rather than assuming: a Clojure namespace defining the same deftest twice, with the FIRST body deliberately failing, reports 'Ran 1 tests... 0 failures' and emits ZERO diagnostic output. Clojure's 'already refers to' warning only fires ACROSS namespaces, so there is no JVM equivalent of shadow-cljs's :redef-in-file. CONSEQUENCE: a duplicate deftest in a .cljs/.cljc file is detectable (shadow-cljs warns on every build — rf2-qo5xk's went unread for months); the same defect in a .clj file is COMPLETELY INVISIBLE. Only the test count reveals it. PROOF TECHNIQUE (use this, not a green suite): to show a resurrected test body actually executes, temporarily INVERT one of its assertions and confirm the suite reds AT THE NEW SYMBOL NAME — that is impossible while the body is being replaced. Then revert and gate on the reverted tree. A green suite plus a +1 count is weaker: the count can rise for unrelated reasons and green proves only that nothing failed. Both instances found so far (qo5xk, 9e4lf) were genuinely DISTINCT tests collapsed onto one symbol by different causes — a rename sweep and a copy-pasted parallel test block — so archaeology first, never assume the cause from a sibling case.

WHEN DUPLICATION KEEPS RECURRING, THE DEFECT IS DISCOVERY — not the duplication (2026-08-14, rf2-040s1 worker).

THE SITUATION. A bead said two scripts independently parse the same build-summary line and asked whether to unify them. THE WORKER FOUND THREE. The third had been doing it for eleven days BEFORE the bead was filed, reached the identical verdict, and recorded the SAME reason for not reusing the others. So the bead's own trigger — 'unify when a third lane wants the line' — HAD ALREADY FIRED, unnoticed by its author.

IT REFUSED THE UNIFICATION, ON A REASON NEITHER AUTHOR HAD RECORDED: one gate's pattern is a FILTER, not merely an id capture — it deliberately FAILS on any summary whose id was not requested. An id-agnostic shared pattern would hand that gate every id the compiler prints and reopen a settled question across 54 builds. And what actually differs between the three is the SELECTION POLICY, not the regex: reconcile a requested set / every row must read zero / take the last row so a dependency's summary is not mistaken for the lane's. A shared module would remove three regexes and leave three policies.

IT ALSO ESTABLISHED THE DUPLICATION CANNOT FAIL QUIETLY: all three refuse an unreadable summary, so a compiler reformat yields three RED gates rather than a silent pass. Duplication that fails loudly is far cheaper than an abstraction that hides a policy.

THE REAL FIX WAS DISCOVERY. Two authors solved one problem against one wall and neither found the other. So the roster of readers is now stated IN ALL THREE FILES, with the full argument in one and short pointers in the others — one owner for the prose, so it cannot drift.

AND IT REPLACED THE COUNT WITH A POLICY TEST. The bead said 'unify when a third wants it'; three had arrived and the count was still wrong, so the count was never checkable. The new rule: a lane whose selection policy one of the three already implements CALLS that reader's export; a lane with a genuinely new policy writes its own and adds itself to the roster.

GENERALISE: before proposing to unify duplicates, ask what they share and what they DIFFER on. If the difference is policy rather than mechanism, unification hides the policy. And if the same duplication keeps appearing, the thing to fix is how the next author FINDS the existing one.

A '; echo "EXIT=$?"' WRAPPER MASKS THE REAL EXIT CODE OF A GATE (2026-08-01, reported by the rf2-6jqa8 worker as a process note).

Wrapping a gate invocation as 'cmd ; echo "EXIT=$?"' reports the exit status of the LAST command in the list, and in some shells/pipelines the wrapper itself perturbs what $? holds — the worker found it masked scripts/test-fast-pr.sh's real exit code. A worker doing this can report a FALSE GREEN in perfect good faith.

BRIEFS ALREADY SAY 'echo every exit code' and 'never pipe a gate through tail/grep'. ADD: capture the status of the gate ITSELF (run it, then read $? immediately, or use the tool's own reported status), and never let a convenience wrapper sit between the gate and the number reported. If a gate's exit code and its printed output disagree, believe the gate and investigate the wrapper.

RELATED, SAME WORKER, WORTH KEEPING: a FRESH worktree has no implementation/node_modules, so the CLJS tier of the fast-PR spine dies with 'shadow-cljs is not recognized' before running anything. That is an environment gap, not a regression — junction it (and unlink the LINK, never the target, before reporting done).

Editing .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh ALSO requires editing implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs — the classifier carries a large JS self-test suite that pins every arm by exact path, and it runs in test.yml's 'JS harness self-tests (quiet reporters + path policy)' job via 'npm run test:script-policy'. It is NOT reachable from the fast-PR spine on a machine without implementation/node_modules (a worker worktree has none unless it junctions one), so a classifier change can look locally clean and red in CI. Reproduce with: cd implementation && npm run test:script-policy (pure Node, needs no node_modules). Measured on rf2-r4j91/PR #8200: moving migration_hicasso_codemod from the implementation/freehand arm to implementation/hicasso reddened it immediately. The suite's house style is worth matching when you touch it — each lane asserts the positive arm, the outputs the shared arm must NOT narrow, a dark-surfaces negative, and a NON-VACUITY row that lifts the real dependency (an io/file form, a deps.edn :paths entry) out of the artefact and requires the classifier to arm on exactly that path.

EIGHTH FALSE-GREEN CLASS: A CANNED STUB IS DOCUMENTATION WITH A TEST'S AUTHORITY (2026-07-25, found by the F6c worker against its own shipped work).

WHAT HAPPENED: in PR #6978 it wrote a canned MCP response envelope containing :classification :callback. THERE IS NO SUCH MEMBER — the vocabulary is closed at seven (:vector :options :ui-event :handler :fn :dynamic :spread). It had read the tool docstring's prose 'on any other classification it is a callback' as naming a VALUE, when it names the COMPLEMENT of :vector/:options. The site was unreachable twice over: it paired the fabricated value with :sync? true, but synchronous-outcomes is #{:event-vector :event-options :event}, so :sync? true rides only :vector/:options/:ui-event — :handler and :fn are excluded DELIBERATELY because what they dispatch is unknowable when the door would open. A callback site with :sync? true cannot exist.

WHY EVERY SUITE STAYED GREEN, which is the whole lesson: a canned stub asserts the CONSUMER's wire handling. Nothing checks the stub against the PRODUCER's closed vocabularies. So a fixture can depict output the producer cannot emit, and the tests that read it will pass forever — while the stub sits in the one place an agent reads to learn the shape. Its own words: 'a canned stub is documentation with a test's authority.'

HOW THIS DIFFERS FROM THE OTHER SEVEN: (1)-(6) are misreading a verdict; (7) is a stale compile cache computing a verdict from stale input; (8) is a verdict computed correctly over INVENTED INPUT. No exit-code discipline catches it, and no cache-clearing catches it either.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when a diff adds or edits a canned envelope, fixture, sample response or documented example payload, check every VALUE in it against the producing source's vocabulary — not against the consumer's prose, and not against a docstring sentence. Closed vocabularies are the specific hazard: if a keyword is drawn from a fixed set, find the set. And check the combination, not just the members: two individually-valid values can name a state the producer cannot reach.

ELISION ORACLE REFINEMENT: THE TWO-BUNDLE CONTROL IS INSUFFICIENT — YOU NEED A THIRD BUNDLE WITH THE TIER ABSENT (2026-07-26, rf2-etqma, and it caught its own trap).

I had recorded that the correct elision oracle is a CONTROL BUILD: same entry, same :advanced level, goog.DEBUG the only variable, asserting string-literal sentinels PRESENT in the DEBUG=true control and ABSENT in production. That is right as far as it goes and it is NOT sufficient.

WHAT THE WORKER FOUND: five keywords it first reached for as sentinels (possible-sites, static-proof, no-static-analysis, connected-occurrences, uncorrelated) are PRESENT in bundle A — the untouched release with NO tool tier required at all. They belong to a SIBLING namespace closed vocabularies (evidence). THE ELISION RULE IS ABOUT CONSEQUENCE, NOT OWNERSHIP — and I propagated the wrong axis in briefs all day (2026-08-02, corrected by the rf2-bl8k7 worker, PR #7361).

WHAT I KEPT WRITING: 'a check that catches the programmer's own mistake may be elided; a path that receives untrusted input guards itself unconditionally.' That is DIRECTIONALLY right but the axis the docs stated — and that I repeated — was 'what may be elided is settled by OWNERSHIP, not by subject matter', i.e. framework-declared survives and programmer-declared elides.

THAT AXIS MISPREDICTS FOUR OF THE FIVE SURVIVORS. Verified from source by the worker:
  :rf.schema/at-boundary (spec.cljc:165)          — schema declared by the PROGRAMMER (the handler's own reg-event :schema)
  managed HTTP :decode (http/decode.cljc:227-233) — PROGRAMMER
  validate-route-shape (routing/registry.cljc:1190-1214) — PROGRAMMER (reg-route)
  recordable cofx :schema (cofx.cljc)             — PROGRAMMER (reg-cofx)
  reserved :rf.server/* args (ssr/response.cljc)  — framework, THE ONLY ONE
Elided side, confirmed dev-gated: validate-app-schema! (validate.cljc:643), step-1 validate-event! (router.cljc:784), flow-output (flows.cljc:204).

SO AUTHORSHIP DOES NOT SEPARATE THE TWO SIDES. CONSEQUENCE DOES.

THE CORRECT STATEMENT, now on main: elision is settled by WHAT THE CHECK IS FOR, not by who declared the schema it reads.
