Event-handling pipeline atomicity (Mike CONFIRMED 2026-05-24). Architecture: interceptors (incl. the path std-interceptor) mutate the :db/:fx EFFECTS in interceptor context; app-db gets a SINGLE deferred install only after the ENTIRE chain (all :after interceptors + the flow transform) is done. Flows run at the OUTERMOST :after (framework-prepended :rf/flows, fires last) because flows read full-app-db :inputs and path's :after reshapes :db. CONTRACT: ANY throw BEFORE install (cofx, handler, interceptor :after, flow) => the deferred install simply does NOT happen => app-db UNCHANGED, NO :rf.event/db-changed, NO :fx. No partial commit (a flow throw must NOT commit prior flows' writes). The :db install is the atomic commit boundary. The ONLY post-commit stage is :fx: an fx throw surfaces an error but does NOT wind back app-db (fx side-effects http/nav/dispatch may already have fired and are irreversible). Uniform: flow-throw behaves like every other pre-install throw.

TO ASK WHETHER A BRANCH HAS A PR, USE THE API'S EXACT head= FILTER RATHER THAN SCANNING PR PAGES (2026-08-23).

THE COMMAND: gh api -X GET repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls -f state=all -f 'head=<owner>:<branch>' 
It queries the WHOLE pull-request set by exact head ref and returns [] when there is none. No paging, no substring matching, no window to be wrong about.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. The hygiene loop's rule is 'never delete a branch whose PR is not verifiably MERGED, keyed on exact headRefName equality'. I had been answering it by pulling gh pr list --state all --limit 400 and equality-filtering in Python. That is correct as far as it goes and it has TWO failure modes the head filter does not:

1. THE WINDOW. 400 PRs covered #8326-#8726. Both orphan branches' tips date from 2026-08-11 and 2026-08-15, whose PRs would sit BELOW that window -- the scan's zero was a zero over the wrong range, and it read exactly like a zero over the right one. Widening to pages 5-6 reached #8126 and still could not prove absence, only extend it.

2. THE COST. Each widening is another API round trip and another chance to mis-set the range. The head filter answers in one call and its answer is total.

MEASURED: head=day8:worker/receipts-hic081 and head=day8:worker/retire-delete each return 'NO PR of any state', confirming what the paged scan could only suggest. Both branches therefore carry genuinely-new work (git cherry '+' counts 3 and 1) that has never been proposed for merge, and under the rule they can never be deleted on evidence -- only on the operator's explicit word.

THE GENERAL SHAPE: when a rule says 'compare for equality yourself', prefer an instrument that takes equality as INPUT over one that returns a page you then filter. The filter is right; the page is the risk.

AN EXAMPLE HOST CAN BE AHEAD OF THE SHIPPED ADAPTER — READ EXAMPLES AS A CONFORMANCE ORACLE FOR ADAPTER GAPS (observed 2026-09-07 by worker/ssr-b delivering rf2-8v89, PR #9377).

WHAT WAS OBSERVED. examples/capabilities/ssr/ssr_streaming/core.cljc already accumulated :failed-boundaries correctly, while the SHIPPED Ring adapter (implementation/ssr-ring/src/re_frame/ssr/ring/streaming.clj) did not — its FIFO drain loop read each continuation's :failed? to choose the failed wire template but never accumulated the ids, and never passed :failed-boundaries to build-final-payload. So for as long as rf2-8v89 existed, the example demonstrated the contract the adapter failed to honour.

WHY THIS IS A REUSABLE PROBE RATHER THAN AN ANECDOTE. Spec 011 §Streaming SSR ALREADY STATED the contract — the repair was conformance, not a spec change. An example host is written against the spec by someone reading the spec, while an adapter is written against the runtime by someone reading the runtime; where the two disagree, the example is often the one that read the normative text. That makes a diff between what an example DOES and what an adapter SUPPLIES a cheap, high-yield probe for adapter gaps that no gate catches — the example compiles, the adapter compiles, and nothing compares them.

HOW TO USE IT: when auditing an adapter surface, read the corresponding examples/ host for state it maintains or fields it populates that the adapter never supplies, and check the spec to see which side is right. Do not assume the adapter is authoritative because it ships.

BOUNDED BY the repo rule that examples are TEST-FREE (locked 2026-05-19, rf2-8cevm): no *.spec.cjs may live under examples/, so this probe is a READING exercise for an auditor, never a licence to add a test under examples/ to pin the gap. Pin it in the adapter's own suite instead — which is what rf2-8v89's fix did.

A NON-CODE EXCLUSION THAT STOPS AT COMMENTS LEAVES STRING BODIES SEARCHABLE — AND THE FIX IS TWO PROJECTIONS, NOT ONE (2026-08-06, rf2-t4j7c, PR #7620).

THE DEFECT: a gate blanked COMMENTS so prose could not stand in for a call. It deliberately KEPT string literals, and it had to — the scans own targets include the strings release, --config-merge and the require path. So the same `resetLaneBuildCache(IMPL, BUILD)` text SITTING IN A LOG LINE stood in for the call exactly as comment text had. Reproduced on unmodified main: a rider with no executable reset, carrying that text in a const string and repeated in a template, returned null from requires, clearsFirst, noLiteralId AND sameBuildId — 40 tests, 40 pass, exit 0.

THE FIX SHAPE, and it generalises: ONE SOURCE, TWO BLANKED VIEWS, both the ORIGINAL LENGTH so offset comparisons still hold across them. `code` (comments blanked, strings kept) feeds discovery, the require check and the spawn-side reads that legitimately need string text. `exec` (comments AND string bodies blanked) feeds the clear call and its build-id argument, which must be executable to count. The question is never "what is not code" in general — it is WHAT MUST THIS PARTICULAR SCAN NOT SEE, and different scans in one gate can have different answers.

THE REVERSE MUTATION IS WHAT PROVED BOTH HALVES LOAD-BEARING, and it is the better half of the proof: pointing sameBuildId back at `code` makes it FALSELY report a correctly-wired probe carrying a decoy log line as "clears DECOY but releases BUILD". So the split does not only close a false GREEN, it prevents a false RED. A projection change that only ever tightens is suspicious; check whether the looser view was also inventing findings.

AND IT WROTE THE UNCOVERED EDGE INTO THE HEADER rather than leaving it for the next audit: spawn-side reads must still see string text, so that half is deliberately unprotected. It also re-argued the failure-direction claim for the SECOND view rather than assuming it carried over, and bounded it honestly as "a direction, not a proof". When you add a projection, the safety argument does not inherit — restate it per view.

THIS IS THE THIRD ROUND ON THIS ONE GATE (comment text, then regex-in-substitution, now string bodies), each found by an audit of the previous fix. The pattern is not incompetence: each repair narrowed the aperture and revealed the next-widest way a token could masquerade as a call. Expect a masking gate to take several rounds, and expect each rounds audit to find the shape the last one made visible.

AN EXCLUSION-LIST TEST ROSTER ENROLS NEW NAMESPACES SILENTLY — a namespace you add today joins every
lane whose roster is an exclusion list, with no warning and no opt-in. Measured 2026-09-07 on
`scripts/test-ssr-prod-gate.sh` (the `jvm-ssr-prod-gate` CI job).

WHAT HAPPENED: worker ssr-a added `re-frame.ssr-frame-resolution-test`, gated `clojure -M:test`
green in the NORMAL profile, and CI failed at the exact head on the production-gate lane
(`-Dre-frame.debug=false`). The new namespace had joined that lane BY DEFAULT because the roster is
an EXCLUSION list — per rf2-lwtlk the known-red roster reached zero and the `-n` selector went with
it, so the script now runs every `.*-test$` namespace in the artefact.

THE ACTUAL DEFECT WAS THE TEST, NOT THE CODE, and the discrimination matters because the two need
different fixes: two assertions discriminated one image's registration from another by reading the
descriptor's `:doc`, and `:doc` is a pure-documentation key that `registrar/strip-pure-documentation`
DROPS before metadata is stored when `debug-enabled?` is false (Spec 001 §Production elision
contract). So the code was correct under elision; the assertion was reading something that legitimately
does not exist there.

THE REPAIR SHAPE WORTH COPYING: the worker did not weaken the assertions to buy a green. It resolved
each frame's `:handler-fn` through its own generation and CALLED it — the handler is executable and is
never stripped, and running it is what the test was always about; the `:doc` was a label standing in
for it. **The ordinary-lane assertion count stayed identical at 4194**, two `:doc` assertions becoming
two handler-fn assertions, one for one. That unchanged count is the evidence that nothing was dropped
to buy the green, and it is the number to quote when repairing an elision failure.

TWO THINGS TO CARRY FORWARD:
  1. WHEN YOU ADD A TEST NAMESPACE, ask which lanes just enrolled it. An exclusion-list roster gives
     no signal at all. Read the runner script rather than the CI job's comment — on this one the
     comment claimed 28 namespaces / 247 tests / 1379 assertions while the script ran 646 / 4028, an
     understatement of ~2.4x (filed as rf2-0zsm).
  2. THE PROFILE GAP IS NOT A COVERAGE GAP. The same artefact reads 4194 assertions in the normal
     profile and 4028 under the production gate; the difference is dev-only instrumentation compiling
     out, not tests going missing. Do not read the lower number as lost coverage.

FAN-OUTS DEFEAT PRE-LOOP GUARDS — a check taken BEFORE a loop does not fence the loops later iterations. Found by rf2-sdeae (P1, #6361, 2026-07-18). rf2-qfrh4 had fenced every epoch-restore SEAM on the exact-ownership token, but three of those seams are fan-outs: the guard ran once, then the loop kept invoking callbacks that could seat a successor mid-flight. Three interleavings were constructed on the same thread, inside the callback, between the read and the write. Sharpest: the quiesce chain first hook (:machines/on-frame-restored!) destroys frame A and seats B; A second hook (:http/abort-in-flight-for-frame!) then aborts B in-flight requests — a dead frames tail mutating a live successor. RULE: when auditing an ownership or liveness guard, ask whether the guarded region contains ITERATION or CALLBACK RE-ENTRY. If it does, the guard must travel INTO the region (widen the token through the loop) rather than gate its entry. FIX SHAPE that worked: an ORDER fix, not a new gate — detach-slots! removes slots in one swap-vals!, THEN aborts the detached values, so no host side effect runs inside the retriable swap. The sibling timers/release-frame! already did this; the work-ledger table was the odd one out, so the fix converged on established local discipline instead of inventing a mechanism. BONUS SIGNAL WORTH COPYING: the adversarial re-entrancy case exposed unbounded amplification — a callback re-entering release-frame! re-read the not-yet-dropped slot and re-aborted it 1101 times in the red run. If a re-entrancy test produces a COUNT rather than a boolean, the count is the evidence. Related: rf2-uhouu (#6339) collapsed two reads into one atomic decision; this is the same discipline in the opposite direction — the decision existed and had to travel.

A DISPATCH FENCE IS NOT ALWAYS SPELLED "DO NOT DISPATCH" — the pre-dispatch grep needs the POSITIVE forms too. Measured 2026-09-04, the third gap found in this instrument in one session.

THE CHECK. Before dispatching any bead, grep its notes for a hold, because `bd ready` reads dependency EDGES and can never see a PROSE fence. The pattern I had been using was: FENCED | DO NOT DISPATCH | SEQUENCED | RELEASE CONDITION | HOLD UNTIL | Mike rules | STILL MIKE | DOSSIER | RECOMMENDATION | operator call.

WHAT IT MISSED. rf2-i6kh carries, in capitals: "DISPATCH ONLY AFTER rf2-2hpxo's PR HAS MERGED, never merely opened." The old pattern returns ZERO on that bead. I dispatched it; the worker read the bead, found the line, and correctly STOPPED without a PR, having first measured the surface and banked the results. One worker cycle spent, nothing damaged.

WHY THE GAP IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT. Every term in my pattern was a PROHIBITION ("do not", "hold", "fenced"). A precondition can equally be written as a PERMISSION with a condition attached — "dispatch only after X", "once Y merges", "after Z lands" — and those share no substring with the prohibitions. A keyword list built from the prohibitions will therefore keep missing the permissions, and adding one more term does not fix the class.

THE WIDENED PATTERN, verified to fire on rf2-i6kh where the old one was silent (it returns "DISPATCH ONLY", "AFTER rf2-2hpxo's PR HAS MERGED", "precondition"):

A FENCE HAS TWO RELEASE CONDITIONS AND THEY FIRE ON DIFFERENT EVENTS. A fence note that states one release line silently answers only one of them, and the half it leaves unanswered is the half that governs the next DISPATCH decision.

  * RE-DISPATCH ("do not send a second worker at this bead or branch") releases on A COMPLETION REPORT, or a recorded death. This is the reaping rule's condition, and a report really does discharge it.
  * SURFACE ("this worker holds these files") releases on THE PR MERGING. Not on the report.

WHY THEY DIFFER: a worker that has reported still has an OPEN PR editing those files. A second worker branched off trunk does not carry that PR's changes, so the two diffs collide at merge -- which is precisely what the fence existed to prevent, reached by way of the fence's own release line. The project rule is explicit that two items touching one hot file are sequenced until the first PR MERGES, not until its author reports.

MEASURED 2026-09-16 on the re-frame2 mayor session. The standing fence text read "Release: a completion report, or a recorded death" and, one line below, "The worker holds <surfaces> for the duration" -- with "the duration" undefined. At the moment this was found, THREE workers had reported while their PRs remained open on the surfaces they had held. Under a literal reading all three surfaces read as released, and all three were one dispatch away from a guaranteed merge conflict.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY IMPRECISE: it fails in the PERMISSIVE direction for the only question a fence is asked. "Is this surface free?" answers YES on the strength of a report, and the answer looks well-founded because a real completion report really was quoted -- the operational test ("can you quote the sentence where this agent says it is done?") passes honestly while answering the wrong question. Nothing on screen says a second question was needed.

THE GUARD: state BOTH conditions in the fence, name the EVENT for each, and use two tests rather than one --
  "Can you quote the sentence where this agent says it is done?"  -> reaping.
  "Has the PR that edits this surface MERGED?"                    -> dispatching.
A yes to the first and a no to the second means: reap the worktree if you like, but do not dispatch onto that surface.

AND GENERATE THE FENCE FROM ONE PLACE. This drifted because the text was retyped inline per tick; the repair was a script that emits it, with the same "two copies of a rule disagree within days" reasoning that applies to any extracted block.

A FENCE NEEDS BOTH SIGNALS, AND I DROPPED THE OLD ONE BECAUSE THE NEW ONE HAD JUST BITTEN (2026-08-15 14:15 AUSEST). WHAT I GOT WRONG. I briefed worker/stale-uvazt that 'skills/reagent-migration/** is FREE — verified at dispatch against every open PR and every live worktree.' IT WAS NOT. origin/worker/mount-7mtcf held SEVEN of the twelve files, including evals/evals.json. The worker found it, tested liveness properly (merge-base --is-ancestor says NOT merged, so not a rebase leftover; tip 1d576c2a8b at 13:29; bead still open; no PR yet) and correctly REFUSED half the cluster as blocked. HOW I MISSED IT, AND THIS IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. I ran inside each live worktree and read mount-7mtcf as CLEAN. It WAS clean — because it had COMMITTED its work. The committed three-dot diff (git diff --name-only origin/main...worker/) is the signal that would have shown those seven files, and I did not run it for that path. SO I INVERTED THE VERY TRAP I HAD JUST LEARNED. Earlier today rf2-42bj2 established that a worker at ZERO COMMITS looks empty by three-dot diff while holding real working-tree edits — so I started checking porcelain. Then I quietly stopped checking the diff, because porcelain was the signal that had recently caught something. The two signals answer DIFFERENT questions and neither subsumes the other: git diff --name-only origin/main...worker/
-> what the worker has COMMITTED git status --porcelain (inside the worktree) -> what it has NOT yet committed A worker mid-task flips between them: uncommitted early, committed at milestones, and CLEAN-BUT-COMMITTED for the whole stretch between a commit and its PR. That last state is invisible to porcelain and is exactly where mount-7mtcf sat. THE RULE IS THEREFORE: RUN BOTH, ALWAYS, AND UNION THE RESULTS. Adding a third check (PR state) separates a live holder from a rebase-merged ghost, but it does not replace either of the first two. WHY IT COSTS: an omitted holder is a stale-NARROW fence, which mayor-dispatch.md itself names as the expensive direction — two workers on one file merge-conflict and can silently revert each other. Here it cost half a cluster instead, only because the worker re-derived rather than trusting me. GENERAL FORM, since this is the second time today I have done this shape: WHEN A NEW CHECK IS ADDED BECAUSE THE OLD ONE FAILED, THE OLD ONE IS STILL REQUIRED. The new check exists because the old one was insufficient, not because it was wrong. Same error as clause 5's job-key count, where zero turned out to be necessary and not sufficient.

WHAT MY BRIEFS SAY: "Your surface is X. You are fenced out of spec/*, .github/workflows/*, package.json, shadow-cljs.edn. Worker A holds Y, worker B holds Z." That is a NAMED SURFACE plus a LIST OF FORBIDDEN PATHS. A file that is in neither is UNDEFINED, and the worker has to guess.

THE TWO FAILURES THE ENUMERATION ALLOWS: a worker crosses silently into a contended file (a real collision nobody sees until the merge), or a worker DOESN'T make a correct small change because it was not obviously permitted.

THE FIX, one clause added to the fence paragraph in every brief:

I already write the stop-and-report form for ANTICIPATED crossings (a new build id, an npm script, a new :rf.error/* id); this generalises it to the unanticipated ones, which are the only ones that surprise me.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a diff shows a file outside the brief's surface, READ THE FILE LIST OF EVERY OTHER LIVE WORKER BEFORE REACTING. Directory-level overlap is not collision. I check this now; I nearly did not.

A POLLING PROCESS IS INVISIBLE TO THE STRANDED SWEEP'S WRITE CLOCK — IT MOVES EXACTLY ONE FILE, $GIT_DIR/FETCH_HEAD (measured 2026-08-23 10:28 AUSEST).

WHAT SIX SWEEPS GOT WRONG. The worktree pr-audit-8445 was read on seven consecutive stranded sweeps and reported each time as silent for hours: file-tree newest write 03:13:10, git index 03:38:20, both static. Each sweep correctly declined to reap it, but on the reasoning 'cannot tell from spacing alone'. It was in fact alive the whole time. Reading .git/worktrees/pr-audit-8445/FETCH_HEAD three times gave 10:26:44, 10:27:26, 10:28:08 — 42 seconds apart, twice. Something in there runs git fetch on a 42-second cadence.

THE MECHANISM. A process that only polls neither edits a file nor touches the index, so the two clocks a sweep naturally reaches for never move. But a fetch is a write, and it lands in exactly one place: FETCH_HEAD, which is PER-WORKTREE ($GIT_DIR for a linked worktree is .git/worktrees/<name>, so a fetch run from the mayor checkout writes .git/FETCH_HEAD and never the worktree's). That per-worktree property is what makes it usable as a liveness probe.

THE CONTROLS MAKE IT A DISCRIMINATOR RATHER THAN AN OBSERVATION. Every worker worktree HAS a FETCH_HEAD — hotzone 08-21 09:37:38, repoint 08-21 09:15:58, specsize 08-22 00:29:33 — each frozen at the moment that worker died. Only the live one moves. Worktrees created by a different harness had none at all. So the file's PRESENCE says nothing; two reads a minute apart say everything.

WHY IT MATTERS AND IN WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILS. The blind spot makes a LIVE process look STOPPED, which is the direction that authorises reaping. The existing guidance gets you to the right suspicion and then stops one step short: it says a worker that is only READING touches nothing. A poller is not merely reading — it writes, once per interval, to a file the sweep was not looking at.

HOW TO RUN IT: stat .git/worktrees/<name>/FETCH_HEAD twice, 30-60 seconds apart. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration. Absence of movement is still not proof of death — it only restores the situation the older clocks described.

FOOTNOTE ON THE TWO OLDER CLOCKS, since they disagree and both are real: .git/worktrees/<n>/index moves when the worker stages or commits; the file tree moves when it edits or checks out. Neither is wrong, they answer different questions, and the earlier sweeps' recorded numbers were the index clock.

THE HEAD==origin/main VERIFICATION CAN READ A STALE origin/main FOR SEVERAL COMMANDS RUNNING, AND IT LOOKS EXACTLY LIKE DIVERGENCE (2026-08-16 01:44).

WHAT I SAW. The merge sweep's closing check printed 'local==origin: NO' with local=e56fc00ccb and origin/main=401bd15991. I then ran, in order: rev-parse both refs (same mismatch), 'git fetch origin main -q', rev-parse both again (SAME mismatch), 'git pull --ff-only origin main' which printed 'Already up to date' and exited 0, and rev-parse a third time (STILL the same mismatch). Three consecutive reads agreed that the refs differed.

THEY DID NOT DIFFER. A fourth check resolved it: git rev-parse HEAD and git rev-parse origin/main both returned e56fc00ccb75a3f4f8098a5b62a515a6d1f9832d, merge-base --is-ancestor answered YES in BOTH directions, and rev-list --count was 0 both ways. The refs were identical the whole time and the SHORT read was showing a stale remote-tracking ref.

THE MECHANISM: 'git fetch origin main' and 'git pull origin main' NAME A BRANCH, so git writes FETCH_HEAD and does not necessarily update refs/remotes/origin/main. The pull can therefore be genuinely up to date while the tracking ref a later rev-parse reads still holds the previous tick's value. CLAUDE.md's rule to NAME THE REMOTE AND BRANCH on the pull is right for the pull itself — it stops the bare form no-opping against a racing audit push — but it is exactly what leaves the tracking ref behind for the verification that follows.

WHY IT MATTERS: the mayor's post-merge verification IS 'git rev-parse HEAD must equal git rev-parse origin/main'. If that comparison can read a stale ref for several commands in a row, a clean tree reports as divergence, and the remedies for real divergence — pull --rebase, force-with-lease, resetting — are all destructive against a tree that was never wrong.

WHAT SAVED IT is already written in CLAUDE.md and I nearly did not apply it: 'one mismatch is not yet evidence either ... read both refs again before believing it.' I read them a fourth time with the FULL SHAs and ancestry rather than the short form, and the phantom vanished. Note the rule says read AGAIN, not read TWICE — here it took four.

THE RELIABLE CHECK, and use this rather than repeating reads: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor HEAD origin/main' AND the reverse, or 'git rev-list --count' both ways. Ancestry resolves the objects rather than trusting a possibly-stale ref label, and it answers the question the mayor actually has — is the checkout the same tree as the remote — instead of the question the short SHAs answer, which is whether two ref labels happen to print the same characters right now.

TO FORCE THE TRACKING REF FORWARD when you do want it current: 'git fetch origin' with NO branch name, or an explicit refspec ('git fetch origin refs/heads/main:refs/remotes/origin/main'), which is the form already used in this session for worker branches and which does update the ref.

TO FIND WHO OWNS A CAMPAIGN OF UNOWNED BEADS, THERE ARE TWO AGENT POPULATIONS ON THIS BOX, NOT ONE — AND A TRANSCRIPT FILE'S MTIME IS NOT AN EVENT TIME. Measured 2026-09-12/13 attributing rf2-fzbj, a 44-slice review campaign whose parent and children carried created_by Mike Thompson and no claimant.

WHAT WENT WRONG, and it nearly routed a 44-worker campaign to the wrong owner. A peer Claude mayor searched the Claude transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/<project>/ and found a third one, 7d3d54f3, "last written 23:43:29" — one minute after the parent bead appeared — carrying 13 Workflow launches and 95 bd-create lines. It concluded that session owned the campaign. Every part was plausible and the conclusion was wrong:
  * 7d3d54f3 was the mayor's OWN pre-continuation transcript. Its INTERNAL events ended 2026-09-11T10:51:29Z and the mayor's current transcript began three seconds later. The 23:43 figure was the file's mtime; something touched the file without recording an event.
  * Its Workflow launches and bd creates were days old, and it mentioned the bead id ZERO times.

THE ACTUAL OWNER WAS NOT A CLAUDE SESSION AT ALL. Codex keeps its own rollouts under ~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<timestamp>-<id>.jsonl. There, sub-agent rollouts started at 23:43:08, :17, :23, :29, :35, :40 — a fan-out beginning 43 seconds after the parent was created — and they named rf2-fzbj; the root was a long-running Codex rollout from two days earlier, written that night. The children's own phrasing had said so all along: "Root owns the durable tracker checkpoint and push", "Reviewer: review_tools_pair_mcp", "WORKTREE_ROOT=(none)". That is Codex root/sub-agent vocabulary, and the same harness family runs the merged-PR audit.

THE METHOD, in order:
  1. Read a transcript's INTERNAL timestamps (first and last "timestamp" field), never its mtime. A continued session leaves its predecessor transcript behind, ending seconds before the successor begins — that adjacency identifies it as the same lineage, not a peer.
  2. Count mentions of the bead id in each candidate. Zero is disqualifying.
  3. Search BOTH populations: ~/.claude/projects/<project>/*.jsonl AND ~/.codex/sessions/. A campaign whose children have no ledger rows and no worktrees is the signature of an agent that does not use this repo's dispatch contract — look in Codex first.
  4. Take a positive control on the search instrument over the same files (a string any recent session there must carry), so a zero means absence.
  5. Check the harness's own claim about itself: "zero real Workflow tool_use calls" means parse the JSON for type=tool_use with name=Workflow; a raw string grep also matches the tool's SCHEMA text (6 false hits in the mayor's own transcript, 0 real).

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE LOOPS. Beads created_by the git user carry no agent identity, the dispatch ledger only sees agents that honour its contract, and the stranded sweep starts from worktrees — so an out-of-repo campaign is invisible to all three at once. Its children read as open, P1/P2, unblocked, dispatchable. The correct move is to hold them and route remediation ownership to the operator, and to know that a THIRD writer will be checkpointing the tracker in the same checkout.

MERGE-LOOP HAZARD: the draft interlock does NOT protect a fix worker. The method has workers publish as a draft and mark ready as their last act, so the merge loop cannot merge out from under a live author. A FIX worker dispatched onto an EXISTING branch inherits a PR that is already marked ready — by its original author, who has finished — so nothing in the rollup or the PR state says a second worker is currently inside that branch. The merge criterion tests the change, the change goes green, and the merge lands while the fix worker is still running.

Observed 2026-09-01: PR #8873 was merged on a clean five-clause pass while its fix worker (dispatched ~34 min earlier onto worker/routing-encoding-j3tud) was still live and had not reported done. Nothing was lost — its commits were what went green and they landed — but that was luck about timing, not a guarantee: had it been mid-way through a second commit, the merge would have taken a partial change.

THE ASYMMETRY TO REMEMBER: for an ordinary dispatch, draft/ready is a reliable liveness signal. For a fix dispatch, it is stale by construction and says nothing. The mayor holds the only live-worker knowledge (the dispatch ledger and the agent listing), so on a PR that has a fix worker assigned, check the agent is finished before merging rather than trusting the PR state. Candidate method-doc gap; raise at the next method-reread rather than acting on it here.

A FIX WORKER CANNOT 'git worktree add <path> <branch>' WHEN ANOTHER WORKTREE STILL HOLDS THAT BRANCH — git refuses two checkouts of one branch, and the fix is --detach, never --force.

MEASURED 2026-09-04 on PR #9147. I dispatched a fix worker onto the existing branch worker/census-a while the original census-a worktree was still registered (deferred from reaping because its PR was open). The recipe in my brief — 'git worktree add <newpath> worker/census-a' — FAILED for that reason.

THE CORRECT RECIPE, which the worker found and which should go in every fix-worker brief:
  git -C <mayor> fetch origin
  git -C <mayor> worktree add --detach <newpath> origin/<branch>
then commit on the detached HEAD and publish with an explicit refspec:
  git push origin HEAD:<branch>
When the branch has not diverged that is a plain FAST-FORWARD — no --force and not even --force-with-lease. And --detach avoids the alternative of forcing a second live checkout onto one branch, which is the thing the ban on concurrent same-branch workers exists to prevent.

TAKE THE TIP FROM THE REMOTE, NOT THE LOCAL REF, AND THIS IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL. Measured twice in one session. On #9147 the local worker/census-a was 940ea6c299 — the same three commit subjects on an OLDER base — while origin/worker/census-a was 09e72fa9eb. On #9142 the local ref was 5f05dd6698 while the remote had already been rebased to a3cd526469. A worker branching from the stale local ref silently drops remote-only work, and the diff afterwards looks entirely reasonable.

RELATED HYGIENE INTERACTION: this only arises because the loop DEFERS reaping a reported worktree whose PR is still open (free insurance). That deferral is correct and should stay; the recipe is what has to change.

FLAKE PROOF — a run count is not always the right evidence; sometimes a MARGIN is. I briefed rf2-ybqse to prove stability with 20+ consecutive runs. Its worker (2026-07-18) correctly pushed back: focused runs could not exercise that flake at all (the bug lived in the gap between namespace LOAD and render, which a focused run collapses), and full-suite runs cost ~4 min each. It ran 20 focused + 3 full and supplied the better proof — the measured margin between the fixture's :stale-at and the render-time clock: +30461ms pre-fix (29.5s of a 60s horizon already burned), -13700ms when deliberately shrunk to falsify (reproducing the reported failure string verbatim), +60000ms post-fix. At a constant 60000ms the failure is UNREACHABLE rather than merely unobserved. RULE FOR BRIEFS: ask for proof the failure is unreachable, and let the worker choose the instrument. Repeated green runs prove absence-of-observation; a margin, an invariant, or a falsification run can prove absence-of-possibility. Demanding N runs can also mislead — N greens on a test that structurally cannot fail in that mode is a false-green about a false-green. ALSO: this class of flake (wall-clock captured in a top-level def, compared against a render-time clock) is invisible in isolation and only appears when a bundle loads all namespaces before executing any.

FLATTENING WHITESPACE DOES NOT UNDO A RENDERER'S MID-TOKEN LINE BREAK — and the break is not only a FALSE ZERO, it MANUFACTURES IDENTIFIERS THAT DO NOT EXIST. Measured 2026-09-04, three times in one session, the third time inside a dispatch brief.

THE MECHANISM. `bd show` hard-wraps its output. It breaks lines at spaces AND inside tokens, at hyphens and at underscores. Flattening with `tr -s ' \n' ' '` turns that break into a SPACE, so the token is now two words and neither is the original.

INSTANCE 1 — THE FALSE ZERO. Probing a freshly appended note for `ls-files` returned 0 after flattening. The text was intact; the renderer had split `git ls-` / `files`, so the flattened form read `git ls- files` and the token genuinely did not occur. This is the dangerous variant precisely BECAUSE flattening is the documented remedy for wrapped text: a zero that SURVIVES the fix reads as strong evidence of real damage, and the next move after that is a recovery from git history that was never needed.

INSTANCE 2 and 3 — THE FABRICATED IDENTIFIER, which is worse and which the earlier version of this memory did not cover. Extracting file paths from `bd show` output with a flattened regex produced `oke_dom_cljs_test.cljs` — a fragment of `per_keystroke_dom_cljs_test.cljs` split at an underscore. I PUT IT IN A DISPATCH BRIEF as a real file. The worker had to spend effort establishing that it "does not exist and never did"; the bead had never named it. The same extraction later yielded `mine.md` and `keystroke.md` from `requirements-mine.md` and `per-keystroke.md`. Verified: all three fragments return 0 from `git ls-files`, both real names return 1.

SO THE FAILURE IS BIDIRECTIONAL. A mid-token break can make a present token invisible (false negative) OR mint a plausible token that was never there (false positive). The false positive is the expensive one, because it propagates into work instructions where a person or agent will try to act on it, and a well-formed filename carries no signal that it was assembled by a line wrap.

THE RULES.
1. NEVER extract identifiers — file paths, symbols, ids — from RENDERED output. Take them from the source of truth: `git ls-files`, `git grep -l`, `bd show --json`. Rendered text is for reading, not for harvesting.
2. If you do harvest from rendered text, VALIDATE EVERY EXTRACTED PATH before it reaches a brief, a bead or a report: `git ls-files <path>` returning 0 means you invented it.
3. A zero that survives flattening is NOT proof of absence. Probe a substring with no hyphen, underscore or dot, or print the neighbouring text with `grep -o -E '.{0,80}<anchor>.{0,120}'` and read it. That costs one command and settles it outright.
4. A positive control proves the INSTRUMENT works, not that the TARGET can be spelled the way you spelled it. Both instances passed their controls.

FREEHAND API-MANIFEST IS A SERIAL LANE for public-verb beads — the biggest merge-friction in the Freehand build wave (2026-07-23). re-frame.freehand is a FULLY-ROWED manifest surface: adding ANY public verb requires FIVE co-edited files in ONE PR — implementation/freehand/src/re_frame/freehand.cljc (facade block), spec/api-manifest.edn (REGENERATE, never hand-edit), spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (classification row), spec/API.md (roster row + remove the declared-vacancy prose), docs/api/re-frame.freehand.md (member heading + remove vacancy prose). FOUR gates enforce it: the api-manifest gen --check entry point, api-md-check, doc-api-check, and the CLJS manifest probe under npm run test:cljs.

THE TRAP THAT COST THREE REBASES (presence PR 6713, measured — the most important part): git rebase AUTO-MERGES the generated spec/api-manifest.edn with NO conflict markers, merging the var ROWS correctly while leaving a STALE :var-count HEADER (observed 517 against a set of 519). The file looks cleanly merged and is SELF-INCONSISTENT. The drift gate then reds with "var set identical; :meta or formatting differs — regenerate", which READS LIKE a formatting or toolchain problem and sends you hunting the wrong cause. IT IS NOT A TOOLCHAIN TRAP. Cure: run the plain generator (no --check flag) to overwrite byte-exact, then --check must exit 0 AND git diff spec/api-manifest.edn must be EMPTY after that fresh run — the empty diff is the proof the committed file equals the generator output.

RULE: for a GENERATED file, a clean auto-merge is NOT evidence of correctness. Treat every rebase touching api-manifest.edn as resolve-by-REGENERATE whether or not git reported a conflict.

OTHER OPERATIONAL FACTS: (a) verb-adders are a SERIAL LANE — merge one, rebase the next onto it, and HOLD the lane still for the worker you are waiting on or it rebases forever against a moving main. (b) doc-api-check requires a member heading in docs/api for every new advanced or front-porch var. (c) the CLJS manifest probe CACHES the metadata namespace across a metadata-only edit — clear .shadow-cljs to re-verify locally. (d) INTERNAL-only beads (manifests/elision, the checker, the test surface, cell/shell correctness fixes) do NOT touch this surface and parallelize freely — dispatch those alongside verb work to keep saturation without lane contention.

MAYOR PLAYBOOK: brief every verb-adding bead with "add your metadata row, REGENERATE the manifest, add the API.md row and the docs/api member IN THE SAME PR or the gate reds", treat it as a serial-lane occupant, and hold the lane still while it rebases. This tax is real ceremony, flagged to Mike as a candidate is-this-over-engineering review — do NOT weaken the gates unilaterally, it is his call.

RESOLVED 2026-07-23 by PR #6700 — the fixture-cache warning is NO LONGER needed in Freehand worker briefs. Freehand conformance fixtures are now a shadow-cljs build dependency, so a fixture-only edit invalidates the cache and the compiled test sees the new expectations.

WHAT THE BUG WAS, kept because the shape recurs: re-frame.freehand.conformance/fixture inlined its .edn at MACRO-EXPANSION time, and shadow-cljs had no dependency edge from a test namespace to the fixture it inlined. A fixture-only edit therefore did not invalidate the build cache, and the compiled test kept asserting the PREVIOUS expectations. A green CLJS or browser conformance run after a fixture change was worthless. The JVM side was never affected.

MEASURED TWICE, INDEPENDENTLY, by two workers with no stake in each other's finding — which is why it was believed rather than argued about. The route-link slice mutated a fixture and got 484 tests / 2746 assertions / 0 failures, green on a fixture that MUST fail; its probe passed TWICE before it cleared the cache. The CI-classifier slice separately flipped FH-CALL-001 :predicates :view? true->false and saw a warm cache recompile 1 file and report 0 failures, versus 124 files and 1 failure after clearing.

⚠️ THE GENERAL LESSON, WHICH OUTLIVES THIS FIX AND IS WHY THIS MEMORY SURVIVES: a table-driven gate whose expectations are INLINED AT COMPILE TIME can silently decouple from its data. Whenever test expectations live in a separate file that a macro reads, ASK WHETHER THE BUILD SYSTEM KNOWS ABOUT THAT EDGE — and prove it the only way that counts: mutate the data WITHOUT clearing any cache and require RED. A fix verified only after a cache clear proves nothing, because that is the broken state's own behaviour.

TWO SEPARATE HOLES EXISTED ON THIS PATH; both are now closed and neither alone sufficed. rf2-drpa3.66 (#6699) made the CI jobs RUN on a fixture change — the classifier had no route for spec/conformance/freehand/fixtures/** so both newly-required host jobs skipped. rf2-drpa3.65 (#6700) made the compiled test SEE the change. Scheduling and compilation are independent failure modes; check both when a data-driven gate looks green.

Fresh worker worktrees revert bead claims: a new worktree checks out a stale-content/new-mtime .beads/issues.jsonl, and the FIRST bd invocation inside it re-imports that stale JSONL into the shared dolt DB, clobbering any claims/closes made between 'git worktree add' and the worker's first bd call. Rule: claim beads AND commit .beads/issues.jsonl BEFORE creating worker worktrees; re-verify claims/closes after a wave of new worktrees comes online.

From Git Bash on this box, MSYS rewrites a leading-slash WINDOWS FLAG into a path: schtasks /query becomes schtasks 'C:/Program Files/Git/query', which the tool refuses with exit 1 and no stdout. Piped into grep with 2>/dev/null that is indistinguishable from an honest empty result — measured 2026-09-08 while verifying git maintenance tasks, where it read as 'no tasks registered' when all three existed. Fix: prefix MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1, or use PowerShell's structured cmdlet (Get-ScheduledTask). Same class as CLAUDE.md instrument item (d) but reached through a /FLAG rather than a ref:path. Always read the runner's own exit status (PIPESTATUS for a pipeline), never the pipeline's.

A FROZEN MEMORY STORE CAN RESURFACE AS AN APPARENTLY-LIVE INSTRUCTION — and I relayed one as Mike's current word (2026-08-14, rf2-e5xag worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched a bead to fix a "stale" voice instruction, telling the worker that the operator's directly-stated preference in the loop body governs over the command file. THE WORKER REFUSED AND REFUTED THE PREMISE.

The command file says ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English for chat. That is accurate against TWO LIVE bd records dated 2026-08-09 and 2026-08-10, the second recording "ASKED THREE TIMES". The competing "human voice, tight not terse" statement is real but dated 2026-07-13 and lives in the ~/.claude store that CLAUDE.md FROZE on 2026-07-25.

AND THE PART THAT MATTERS FOR EVERY FUTURE DISPATCH: the wording I quoted as the operator's live preference — "matching the page's register", "full sentences over dash-chained fragments" — TRACES PHRASE BY PHRASE to that frozen July record. The frozen store is injected into agent system prompts as a one-line bullet, INCLUDING MINE. So the frozen memory generated both the bead AND the brief that dispatched it a second time.

THE GENERAL TRAP: a frozen or deprecated memory store does not stop being READ. It stops being MAINTAINED. Its content keeps arriving in system prompts and keeps sounding like current instruction, and nothing marks it as superseded at the point of use.

THE CHECK: when an instruction and a repository record disagree, DATE BOTH AND FIND THEIR STORES. `bd memories <topic>` returns the live ones with dates; the frozen store is the one CLAUDE.md names as retired. Recency plus store authority settles it — and if the apparently-live text traces phrase-by-phrase to the frozen store, it is an echo rather than a statement.

I HAVE NOT CHANGED MY CHAT REGISTER ON THIS ALONE. The question of what Mike wants TODAY is his to settle, and the worker correctly set the bead to blocked and awaiting him rather than closing it.

check_fast_pr_gap.py's EXIT CODE IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT A CI GATE AND ITS SPINE LANE ARE IN STEP. I told a worker to quote it as exactly that, and it measured me wrong (2026-09-03, ciarm-a, rf2-bn5f).

MEASURED IN THREE TREE STATES: merge base -> exit 0, 97 unrun; workflow steps alone (CI half landed, spine half missing) -> exit 0, 99 unrun; both halves -> exit 0, 97 unrun. Read at source, run_check returns 1 only on gap.problems, i.e. STRUCTURAL defects. An uncovered required checker moves the REPORT, not the exit code.

SO THE INSTRUMENT IS THE UNRUN COUNT RETURNING TO BASELINE, NOT THE EXIT CODE. A green exit says the gap checker itself is structurally sound; it says nothing about whether your two halves landed together. Quote the unrun count before and after, against the merge base's count as the control.

THE GENERAL FORM, because this is the third instrument this session that answered a question it was not asked: BEFORE CITING A GATE AS EVIDENCE FOR A CLAIM, READ WHAT ITS NON-ZERO EXIT ACTUALLY MEANS. A gate that exits 0 on the condition you care about is not a gate for that condition, however apt its name. Siblings: check_doc_slugs.py exits 0 on a broken link inside a fence; the skills-structural suite passes with an unresolvable var planted in a fixture it never reads; mkdocs --strict exits 0 on an unnavigated page because omitted_files is graded INFO.

ALSO FROM THE SAME WORKER, AND IT IS A PLACEMENT RULE WORTH KEEPING: verify-skill-mcp-drift INSTALLS NO PIP PACKAGES and being dependency-free is its STATED DEFINING PROPERTY - every check_skill_*.py armed there is pure stdlib. A local green for such a checker can be an artefact of the dev machine having the dependency - reproduce the import failure in both directions before trusting placement.

GATE BASELINES: TEST COUNTS ARE STABLE, ASSERTION TOTALS ARE NOT. Established by the rf2-vxgfnd.298 worker (#6395) on 2026-07-19, which chased a baseline discrepancy instead of waving it through. Controlled same-tree comparison (swap the file to main version and back): 929 TESTS both ways, but full-suite ASSERTION totals drifted run-to-run on an IDENTICAL tree — 16136 / 16141 / 16143 observed in implementation/ui — because generative suites vary their assertion counts per run. I had been quoting assertion baselines to workers (~16119, ~16132, ~16149, ~16154) as if they were stable, which invites two failures: a worker treats normal drift as a regression it caused and hunts a phantom, or treats a real small regression as drift. USE INSTEAD: the TEST COUNT as the primary signal, plus a DETERMINISTIC pin namespace (e.g. the guide-truth pins at 19 tests / 663 assertions) where one exists. Quote assertion totals only as an order-of-magnitude sanity check, and say so when briefing. The one thing that still matters absolutely: a non-zero count, because a bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` from implementation/ silently runs 0 tests and prints "Ran 0 tests" which READS AS GREEN.

THE PASTE-IT-WHOLE RULE ASSUMES THE SCARCE RESOURCE IS WORKER SLOTS. LATE IN A LONG SESSION IT IS THE MAYOR'S REMAINING CONTEXT (measured 2026-08-13, third instance).

mayor-dispatch.md line 23 says paste the gate-mechanics block whole. My earlier fix for compressing it was 'dispatch fewer workers at once' - the block costs 156 lines plus 43 for the boundary block, so three parallel briefs cost over 550 lines of boilerplate.

I THEN DISPATCHED EXACTLY ONE WORKER AND STILL COMPRESSED. The measurement-window brief dropped the wedge paragraph, the read-the-clock paragraph, the artefact-naming rationale, and the hash-proves-source-not-runtime caution. Worker count was one. The remedy I had recorded did not apply.

THE ACTUAL CONSTRAINT IS THE MAYOR'S CONTEXT BUDGET, and it tightens monotonically across a session while the block stays the same size. Early ticks can afford the whole block; late ticks cannot afford it at all. So the compression is not a discipline failure that willpower fixes - it is a resource curve, and it will recur in every long session at roughly the same point.

TWO THINGS FOLLOW.

1. WHAT I DROPPED WAS NOT RANDOM, AND THAT IS THE ONE MITIGATION AVAILABLE. Each time, the load-bearing ordering survived - the arithmetic, 'detaching is CORRECT', 'do not apologise'. What went were mechanism paragraphs. If a brief must be trimmed, trim toward what the WORKER'S SITUATION cannot reach: a solo measurement window genuinely cannot hit the two-workers-wedge case, so dropping that paragraph there costs less than dropping it from a brief sent while three workers run. Say in the brief that it was trimmed and why.

2. THIS IS WORTH TELLING THE OPERATOR, because it bounds how long a mayor session runs at full fidelity. It is not a bug in the rule; the rule is right about what a worker needs. It is a limit on the mayor, and the honest response is to name it rather than to keep promising the whole block and delivering most of it.

DO NOT 'FIX' THIS BY PROPOSING READ-BY-REFERENCE. mayor-dispatch.md already ruled that question and gave its reason: a worker told to read a file may not, and the block's ordering is what a summary destroys.

GATE EXIT-CODE TRAP, SECOND VARIANT (2026-07-25, found by the rf2-kqxe6.20 worker): a BACKGROUNDED or compound gate invocation can report 'exit code 0' while its log says FAIL. The worker's first scripts/test-fast-pr.sh run was reported exit 0 while the log read 'FAIL CLJS node integration' — the 0 belonged to a TRAILING ECHO in the compound command, not to the runner. This is distinct from the known pipe variant (piping a gate through tail/grep returns the PIPE's status). So the rule needs both halves in briefs: (a) never pipe a gate through tail/grep; (b) never read the exit status of a compound or backgrounded command as the runner's — capture the runner's own status immediately into a variable (rc=$?) on the line after the runner, echo THAT, and cross-check it against the log's own PASS/FAIL lines before believing either. A gate that reports success while its log says FAIL is the single most dangerous failure mode available to a worker, because it produces a confident false green.

RELATED ROOT CAUSE worth briefing alongside it: a FRESH worker worktree has no node_modules, so shadow-cljs is not on PATH and any CLJS/node arm dies for environmental reasons that look like test failures. Fix is 'npm ci' under implementation/ inside the worktree (NOT a junction into the mayor tree — a junction makes git worktree remove destroy the mayor's real node_modules). Multiple workers hit this today. Also observed: rewrite-local-root-coord and 'implementation JS harness helpers' flake on Git-Bash fork exhaustion (0xC0000142, 'fork: Resource temporarily unavailable') when several JVMs are live, then pass uncontended — load-sensitive, not a real failure.

BEFORE NOMINATING A GATE, READ TESTING.md's LANE TABLE. I HAVE NOMINATED THE WRONG LANE THREE TIMES AND THE TREE DOCUMENTED THE RIGHT ANSWER EACH TIME.

CLAUDE.md says in terms: 'The canonical matrix and PR/nightly/release split lives in TESTING.md; workflow gates live in .github/workflows/.' I was not reading it. All three of my wrong nominations were answerable from that file in one lookup.

THE THIRD AND WORST, 2026-09-11: I nominated 'npm run test:cljs' and the Xray feature gate for a worker whose entire deliverable was a boundary DOM witness. NEITHER RUNS A DOM SUITE. TESTING.md line 28 states it outright - 'Browser unit - test:browser | DOM-dependent tests only (*_dom_cljs_test.cljs)' - and line 196 documents the exact failure I walked into, in a repair of the same mistake made at the classifier level: ':browser-test selects .*-dom-cljs-test$, so the package's three DOM suites were already IN this lane - the lane just never ran on a diff that touched them, while the consolidated :node-test build compiled the same namespaces and reported each DOM row as a STATED GREEN SKIP. The surface passed having executed none of its DOM assertions, which is worse than an unclassified surface: that at least fails loudly the first time somebody looks.'

THE LANE IS CHOSEN BY THE NAMESPACE SUFFIX: '-dom-cljs-test' goes to :browser-test (npm run test:browser, CI job cljs-browser); everything else to :node-test (npm run test:cljs). Read the suffix, then the table, then name the lane.

THE REPAIR IS PROCEDURAL, NOT TEXTUAL, AND THAT DISTINCTION IS THE POINT. The reflex on finding a repeated failure is to write more documentation. There is nothing to add here - the document is correct, specific, and names this very failure mode. Adding a fourth statement of a rule that is already stated twice would be the overshoot the method warns about. What was missing was the LOOKUP.

SO THE CHECK AT MERGE TIME, which does not depend on my remembering: for any PR touching a '*_dom_cljs_test.cljs', confirm the worker's report quotes a captured 'npm run test:browser' exit code. If it does not, its DOM-suite evidence is not evidence, whatever test:cljs reported - and CI's cljs-browser job WILL run the suite, so the PR reds for reasons the report does not predict.

A GATE THAT DERIVES REACHABILITY FROM RAW YAML COUNTS COMMENTS AS EXECUTION — and 92% of the workflow corpus is comments (2026-08-06, rf2-6ckzl).

THE DEFECT. scripts/check_gate_scheduling.py answers "is this gate scheduled to run in CI?" by searching the workflow YAML. It searched the RAW file. test.yml carries paragraph-long job comments that NAME the commands they explain, so A COMMENT MENTIONING A COMMAND MARKED THAT GATE AS SCHEDULED. Measured: only 39,567 of 511,152 chars of the workflow corpus is executable — 8%. The gate was reading its answer out of the other 92%.

THE SHARPEST INSTANCE, and it is the reason this is worth a memory rather than a bug report: the test:mcp-conformance disposition pinned its ci-runs-it-directly probe on the JOB ID mcp-conformance-re-frame2-pair, which appears 8 TIMES IN RAW YAML AND ZERO TIMES IN ANY run: VALUE. Its premise had never once been confirmed by anything CI executes. A scheduling claim resting entirely on prose, in the checker whose whole job is to verify scheduling claims.

THE FIX SHAPE: derive reachability from run: VALUES ONLY - inline, block/folded scalars, and the "- run:" first-key form - excluding name:, if:, with:, the defaults: run: mapping, and comments at every level. Transitive closure preserved, no new dependency, still pure-static.

THE LOAD-BEARING VERIFICATION: identical counts before and after on the live tree (40 gates / 34 scheduled / 6 declared). That is what proves nothing real was leaning on prose, so the tightening cannot red main. A tightening that CHANGES the live counts is telling you something was depending on the loophole - read it before shipping.

WHY THIS GENERALISES. This project has found the "a comment justifying an omission is an unverified assertion" pattern five times. THIS IS THAT PATTERN ONE LEVEL UP: not a human trusting a comment, but a MACHINE CHECK trusting one. Any checker that greps a file containing both executable content and prose has this defect available to it. Ask of every static checker: WHAT SUBSET OF THE FILE IS IT ENTITLED TO READ, and is it reading only that?

TWO PROBE TRAPS CONFIRMED IN THE SAME RUN: (1) a SUBSTRING probe was satisfied by a sibling step whose name merely extended it (...-live-overflow matching ...-live) - require complete-token match; (2) a mutation that FAILED TO APPLY (Python rejected a POSIX path form) produced two "green" verdicts the worker nearly read as results. The confirm-the-mutation-applied assert is what caught it. A mutation that did not take is indistinguishable from a gate that did not fire.

LOCAL GATE RE-RUNS ARE WORTH AVOIDING, BUT THEY ARE NOT WHY A WORKER TAKES TWO HOURS. This memory is a CORRECTION of its own first version, which over-claimed; the retraction is the useful part.

WHAT I FIRST WROTE, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG. I measured 1,419 gate runs across 1,009 distinct gate names in the shared session scratch, called it a 1.41x re-run multiplier, and presented it as the cause of two-hour workers. THAT NUMBER IS A HISTORICAL AVERAGE ACROSS THE WHOLE SCRATCH DIRECTORY — many days and many sessions of workers — not a measurement of the session in front of me. If two-hour workers are new, a figure that was equally true on the good days cannot explain them. I quoted an accumulated total as if it were a rate.

EVERY HYPOTHESIS FOR 'WHAT CHANGED' WAS REFUTED, and recording the refutations is worth more than the guesses. (1) That briefs nominated more gates: refuted by reading the PR bodies of #9356, #9364, #9368 and #9371, all merged the SAME DAY under previous mayors, every one running the full test-fast-pr.sh spine, with #9368 stating it re-ran the whole set after each rebase. (2) That the spine grew: refuted — 1687 lines at HEAD, HEAD~50 and HEAD~150, unchanged since 2026-09-04. (3) That orphaned gate JVMs accumulate: refuted as a standing condition — a classification of every java/node process by owning worktree found ZERO orphans; the 15 node processes were idle MCP servers at ~5-16 MB each. (4) That I over-saturated: refuted — the ledger shows previous hours dispatching 10 and 7, against my 3.

WHAT THE EVIDENCE ACTUALLY SHOWS: duration tracks BEAD SIZE, not process. Measured across one day — #9372 api(http) 36 files 2h20m; #9375 api(views) 48 files 2h07m; #9376 routing/resources/machines 7 files 1h31m; #9377 four SSR bugs 15 files 1h16m. Both two-hour workers are api(*) beads from the rf2-kuky API-review epic, whose deliverable is a public-name change that must move spec/API.md, BOTH api-manifest sidecars, docs, the migration guide and tests TOGETHER. And large PRs are not new either: #9356 was 100 files the same day and merged fine.

SO THE CONCLUSION IS 'NO CHANGE FOUND', and the lever is bead SPLITTING rather than gate policy: an api(*) bead touching 36-48 files should be two or three beads, split by surface group (code, then spec+manifest, then docs/migration). That also makes them mergeable one at a time in the serial API lane instead of conflicting there.

THE TWO GATE RULES STILL STAND ON THEIR OWN MERITS, as efficiencies rather than as the cause: do not re-run a heavy gate after a rebase (push, and let CI's automatic re-run be the evidence about the new base), and do not iterate red-to-green on a heavy gate locally (that is CI's loop; iterate only on the focused failing-first test). CI runs the entire 87-check matrix in 22 minutes in parallel; the local spine is FULLY SEQUENTIAL — no xargs -P, no parallel, no background jobs — so it uses about one core of twenty-four.

THE METHODOLOGICAL LESSON, which is why this memory kept its key instead of being deleted: an accumulated total answers 'how much has ever happened here', never 'what is happening now'. Before blaming a measurement for a NEW behaviour, check that the measurement is scoped to the window the behaviour appeared in.

TWO GATE FACTS THAT CORRECT MY OWN BRIEFS (2026-08-11, rf2-5i4e worker, PR #7833).

1. check_doc_slugs.py DOES NOT OPEN REPO-ROOT MARKDOWN — INCLUDING CLAUDE.md. Its own docstring (rf2-znup0) says repo-root markdown is out of scope and it "exits 0 on a broken link in any of them". The worker's words: "several briefs have nominated it for root-markdown edits and got a green that verified nothing." scripts/check_readme_links.py is the gate that owns repo-root files; it probed that one too (exit 1 on CLAUDE.md:128, restored, hash equal both sides).

But a plant in an OUT-OF-SCOPE file also produces silence — the proof technique and the failure mode look identical. Planting only proves coverage if you plant in a file the gate actually reads.

NOMINATE NARROW GATES: LOCAL GATING IS ~3x CI'S WALL CLOCK FOR LESS COVERAGE (measured 2026-09-07 21:50 AUSEST, Mike's instruction 'we can't have background tasks running for hours').

THE MEASUREMENT, on ONE commit (PR #9372, head ae0bed90ce): CI ran the ENTIRE 87-check matrix — four workflows in parallel — in 22 minutes (tests 22, docs 7, lint 4, portability 0). The worker's LOCAL fast-PR spine took 62 minutes for a SUBSET, and ran it twice after a rebase: ~112 minutes of gate to reach a verdict CI had already produced in 22.

WHY. scripts/test-fast-pr.sh is 1687 lines and runs FULLY SEQUENTIALLY — grep for xargs -P, parallel, background jobs and trailing & returns nothing — so it uses about ONE core of twenty-four. CI fans the same coverage across parallel runners. Local gating is not a cheaper CI; it is a far more expensive one.

MEMORY PRESSURE COMPOUNDS IT BUT IS NOT THE CAUSE. At six workers the box read 4.5 GB free of 63.4 GB (93% used) with 2.4 GB in Windows Memory Compression, i.e. thrashing. But the largest consumer was the OPERATOR'S OWN CHROME at 95 processes / 27 GB — checked, not assumed: zero carried automation flags, all ran from Program Files against the real user profile. Five worker JVMs held ~10 GB. And scripts/reap-stale-test-processes.ps1 (dry-run) found NO stale lock-holders, so orphaned test processes were not it either.

TESTING.md ALREADY SAID ALL OF THIS AND THE BRIEFS IGNORED IT — this is a briefing defect, not a discovery. Three lines govern: 'scripts/test-fast-pr.sh is a SPINE, NOT A MIRROR. PASS fast PR spine is entirely compatible with a red required check'; 'Do not read the list from here; DERIVE it' (python scripts/check_fast_pr_gap.py --brief names every required check the spine does not run, with the local command for each); and the Windows-local policy, 'CI (Linux) is AUTHORITATIVE for the full JVM suite … then push and let CI run the authoritative suite'.

THE POLICY, and it is what a brief must nominate: (1) failing-first tests per bead, red then green — the deliverable, not a gate; (2) the ONE artefact suite the diff touches, cd implementation/<artefact> && clojure -M:test, never test-jvm-implementation.sh unless the refactor is broad; (3) check_fast_pr_gap.py --brief as a REPORT to learn what CI owns, not a suite to run; (4) anything whose SUBJECT is the diff — a ratchet over a touched path, a prod-gate lane when the production posture moved, gen --check when a public name moved. DO NOT nominate the full spine by default: it already tiers itself on the changed-surface classifier, so naming it beside per-artefact suites double-runs the work.

TIME-BOX EVERY BRIEF AT ~40 MINUTES OF GATE. Past that: push, open or update the PR, mark it ready, and report which gates ran and which were left to CI. The five merge clauses are read against CI, never against a local run, so an hour of local gating delays the merge decision without improving it. The trade is that a worker occasionally pushes something CI catches — that costs a re-run, never a bad merge.

GH'S `-q '.[0]|"..."'` EMITS THE LITERAL FOUR-CHARACTER STRING `null` ON AN EMPTY RESULT SET, NOT AN EMPTY STRING — so the universal shell guard `[ -n "$x" ]` is SATISFIED and the not-found branch never runs. Measured 2026-09-20 on a stranded sweep.

THE SHAPE. `gh pr list --head <branch> --state all --limit 1 --json number,state,headRefOid -q '.[0]|"\(.number) \(.state) \(.headRefOid)"'` on a branch with NO pull request prints `null` and exits 0. It does not print nothing. So:

    pr=$(gh pr list --head "$br" ... -q '.[0]|"..."')
    if [ -n "$pr" ]; then   # <-- TRUE. "null" is four characters.
      prnum=$(echo "$pr" | cut -d' ' -f1)   # "null"
      ...compare "$head" to "$proid"...     # "null" never equals a sha

...and every branch with no PR is reported as HAVING a PR whose head disagrees with the worktree's. In the instance measured, a worktree sweep painted `PR#null/null/draft=null PIN-DIFFERS` across the mayor checkout and five audit worktrees — six healthy, clean, in-trunk checkouts reported as carrying divergent work.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN THE TYPO IT LOOKS LIKE. It fails toward MANUFACTURING WORK: `PIN-DIFFERS` is the exact string a stranded sweep is scanning for, so the sweep invents stranded work on precisely the checkouts that have none, and the next move is to go hunting for commits that do not exist. That is the (p) register — an instrument that spawns effort against something with nothing wrong with it — reached through an EMPTY RESULT rather than a field's type or case.

IT IS jq's `.[0]` ON AN EMPTY ARRAY, NOT A gh BUG, which is why it generalises: any `gh ... --json ... -q '.[0]|...'` over a set that can legitimately be empty does this, and so does any other `jq -r` indexing past the end. `null` is also what a MISSING FIELD yields, so the same four characters mean two different things.

THE CONTROL THAT SEES IT, AND THE ONE THAT DOES NOT. A sweep whose entities all have PRs passes forever — the bug only appears on the empty case, which is the case a sweep is usually run to find. Take the control from an entity KNOWN to have none.

THE GUARD, any of three:
  * test for the literal too: `[ -n "$pr" ] && [ "$pr" != "null" ]`
  * make jq answer in-band: `-q '.[0].number // "NONE"'`, or `-q 'if length==0 then "NONE" else ... end'`
  * check the ARRAY first: `--json number -q 'length'` and branch on 0 before projecting.

Prefer the second — it puts the not-found case in the tool's own output instead of relying on every caller to remember a sentinel.

SAME FAMILY as CLAUDE.md items (p) and (q) — the obvious `gh` JSON filter is silently wrong — but about the ABSENCE of a record rather than the VALUE of a field, so neither of their guards (gate on `.status` first; case-fold both sides) reaches it. Candidate for a lettered CLAUDE.md instrument item under a ruling; recorded here meanwhile.

`gh pr view --json ... > file` CAN FAIL ITS **WRITE** AND LEAVE AN EMPTY FILE, AND THE DOWNSTREAM jq THEN REPORTS BLANK FIELDS THAT READ LIKE 'THIS PR HAS NO CHECKS' (measured twice, 2026-09-06).

WHAT HAPPENED. In two consecutive merge ticks, a loop of `gh pr view <n> --json number,headRefOid,isDraft,headRefName,statusCheckRollup > /tmp/k<n>.json` failed for the SAME two PRs (#9306, #9316) while succeeding for a third (#9317) in the same loop. The shell reported `jq: error: Could not open file ...: Invalid argument` on stderr, and the formatted row printed with every field EMPTY:
  #9306 draft=      total=    ok=    skip=    FAIL=   PEND=
An immediate manual retry of the identical command exited 0 and wrote 27,145 bytes, and `gh api rate_limit` read 5000 remaining — so gh was healthy and this is transient, not an outage or a throttle.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN ANNOYING. The merge criterion's clause 1 is 'a NON-EMPTY rollup in the band measured this tick'. A blank read is not a rollup at all, but formatted into a table beside real rows it looks like a PR that simply has no checks yet — i.e. 'not a candidate, skip it'. That fails SAFE for merging (you skip a PR you could have merged) but fails OPEN for reporting: I would have told Mike a green PR was still building. And the failure is INTERMITTENT and correlated with the LARGER payloads, so the PRs most likely to be affected are the ones with the fullest rollups — exactly the merge candidates.

THE TELL, AND IT IS THE ONLY RELIABLE ONE: blank is not zero. A PR with genuinely no checks yet returns total=0, not total=<empty>. Print the write's EXIT STATUS beside each row (`> file; w=$?`) and treat any non-zero as 'unmeasured', never as 'nothing there'. A count of 0 and an empty string must never format identically.

THE FIX: skip the intermediate file. Read the fields directly with gh's own jq:
  gh pr view <n> --repo <o/r> --json statusCheckRollup -q '[.statusCheckRollup[]] | "total=\(length) ok=\([.[]|select(.conclusion=="SUCCESS")]|length) fail=\([.[]|select(.conclusion=="FAILURE" or .conclusion=="CANCELLED")]|length) pend=\([.[]|select(.status!="COMPLETED")]|length)"'
That removed the failure entirely on the same two PRs in the same shell. If a file IS needed (e.g. to query the same payload several ways), write it under the session scratchpad rather than /tmp, check the exit status, and re-read on non-zero.

SAME FAMILY AS THE REST: an instrument whose FAILURE is indistinguishable from a legitimate answer. jq's CRLF joins, `grep -iF` aborting to an empty stdout, `grep -P` refusing in this locale, `bd` swallowing a while-loop's stdin, a skipped CI step inside a green job — every one hands back something that reads like data.

gh pr diff <n> -- <path> IS A LOUD FAILURE THAT A PIPELINE TURNS SILENT — use git diff for any path-scoped PR diff (2026-08-15 13:02 AUSEST; CORRECTED from an earlier wrong version of this record).

WHAT I FIRST RECORDED, AND WHY IT WAS WRONG. I wrote that gh 'accepts the pathspec, exits 0, and prints nothing. NO ERROR, NO WARNING.' A worker (rf2-g76j3, PR #8280) checked that premise and refuted it. I RE-VERIFIED MYSELF:
  gh pr diff 8279 -- .github/workflows/test.yml   -> EXIT 1, stdout 0 lines,
                                                     stderr 'accepts at most 1 arg(s), received 2'
gh does NOT accept a pathspec at all. It rejects the command loudly.

THE REAL FAILURE MODE IS THE PIPELINE, NOT THE TOOL. What I actually ran was
  gh pr diff <n> -- <path> 2>/dev/null | grep -cE '...'
and that construction destroys both halves of the evidence: 2>/dev/null discards the error message, and the pipe makes the exit status GREP's rather than gh's. grep succeeds on empty input and prints 0. So a loud, correct refusal is laundered into a confident, wrong zero.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT THE GATE RULES ALREADY NAME — 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its last command's.' I have that rule in every worker brief and broke it in my own merge check. The rule is not about test runners specifically; it is about any command whose exit code carries the answer.

THE CORRECT FORM for a path-scoped diff of somebody's branch:
  git diff origin/main...worker/<branch> -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'
Two leading spaces, because job keys nest under jobs: — see job-key-test-needs-two-space-indent.

MEASURED ON THE KNOWN-NONZERO CASE, which is what made the disagreement visible: PR #8279 adds job key hicasso-naming-census. git returns 1; gh-with-pathspec returns 0; gh without a pathspec returns 238 lines and exit 1... no, exit 0 for the plain form. The plain form works; only the pathspec form is rejected.

THE DURABLE LESSONS, in order of value:
 1. A COMMAND THAT FAILS LOUDLY BECOMES SILENT THE MOMENT YOU PIPE IT AND REDIRECT ITS STDERR. Check exit codes on the producing command, not on the pipeline.
 2. A DISCRIMINATOR ONLY EVER TESTED ON ZERO-ANSWERS IS UNTESTED. Both defects in this one-line test — the unindented regex and this — survived because every case they had been asked genuinely had the answer zero.
 3. MY OWN DURABLE RECORDS ARE CLAIMS TOO. This one asserted a mechanism I had not isolated, and a worker refuted it in one command. Record what was MEASURED, and say which part is inference.

`gh pr edit` CAN REPORT EXIT 0 WHILE HAVING PATCHED NOTHING — measured 2026-09-05 by a worker correcting its own PR body: the first `gh pr edit` returned `EDIT_EXIT=0` and the body was unchanged. It re-ran and VERIFIED BY EFFECT, reading the body back rather than trusting the status.

THIS EXTENDS A FAMILY THAT IS NOW LARGE ENOUGH TO BE THE DEFAULT ASSUMPTION ON THIS BOX: A REPORTED SUCCESS IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT SOMETHING HAPPENED.
  * `cmd /c mklink` / `rmdir` from Git Bash: exit 0, no junction created or removed.
  * `pkill` anchored on a bare verb: exit 0, nothing killed (Git-bash command lines carry full Windows paths).
  * `grep -c $'\0'`: returns the file's LINE COUNT from an empty pattern.
  * `grep -iF`: SIGABRT, exit 134, empty stdout — reads as a clean zero.
  * The task harness: reported exit 0 where the runner's own `.exit` file read 1, observed by SEVEN workers in one session, one of them three times in a single run, ALWAYS in the green direction.
  * `check_provenance_pins.py`: printed a fabricated pin as `unresolvable` and still exited 0.
  * `sed -i`: silently rewrote a CRLF file to LF (4637 CRs to 0) while "succeeding".
  * A `\n`-anchored plant on a CRLF-checked-out file: matched nothing, the gate then returned a clean exit 0, which reads as "the gate cannot see my worktree".
  * And now `gh pr edit`.

THE RULE: CHECK THE WORLD, NOT THE STATUS. After a mutating command, read back the thing you mutated — the PR body, the junction listing, the process list, the file's bytes, the exit FILE you wrote yourself. On this machine the exit code is a hint; the effect is the evidence.
