TWO SEPARATE gh HAZARDS, OFTEN CONFLATED — keep them distinct (2026-09-03, corrected same day).

=== HAZARD 1: the 100-file cap is REAL, and it truncates a PR's FILE LIST ===
'gh pr view N --json files' and 'gh pr list --json files' return at most 100 filenames, silently — well-formed JSON, no marker. MEASURED on day8/re-frame2 PR #9103: 'gh pr view 9103 --json files --jq .files|length' = 100; 'gh api --paginate repos/day8/re-frame2/pulls/9103/files --jq .[].filename | wc -l' = 401.

It matters because the mayor's overlap check is
  comm -12 <(git diff --name-only <merge-base> origin/main | sort) <(gh pr view N --json files ...)
so on a PR over 100 files the right side is a truncated sample and a real overlap in files 101..N reads as NO OVERLAP. Fails OPEN.
FIX: gh api --paginate repos/<owner>/<repo>/pulls/<N>/files --jq '.[].filename'
DETECTOR: 'gh pr view --json changedFiles' reports the TRUE total even when files[] is capped. changedFiles != (files|length), or a length of exactly 100, means truncated.

=== HAZARD 2: gh/git LISTINGS CAN RETURN A STALE VIEW — this is NOT the cap ===
DO NOT attribute a missing PR to the 100-file cap. A worker A/B'd it: 'gh pr list --state open --json number,headRefName' and the same call WITH files both returned the same 3 PRs. The cap truncates a PR's file list; it does NOT drop PRs from a listing. Its 'git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/worker/<prefix>*' pattern form was also control-tested and works.

What actually happened: at one instant, THREE independent probes — two different 'gh pr list' shapes and one 'git ls-remote' — all returned a view stale by 3-9 MINUTES, missing a PR created 9 minutes earlier and a branch that existed on the remote. The worker read their agreement as corroboration when it was CORRELATED STALENESS. Root cause not reproduced; do not invent one.

THE DEFENCE FOR BOTH: a NEGATIVE from any listing needs a POSITIVE CONTROL THROUGH THE SAME COMMAND SHAPE — 'does this return something I know exists RIGHT NOW?' Independent probes agreeing is not corroboration when they share a stale cache. This is the census-control discipline applied to listings, and the listing is usually the load-bearing negative.

=== AND: PR-vs-TRUNK OVERLAP IS NOT PR-vs-PR OVERLAP ===
The mayor's tick checks each PR against the trunk. That never sees TWO OPEN PRs editing the same file. Measured: #9108 and #9105 both edited tools/template/spec/005-Repo-Split.md and neither worker nor the tick knew, because no one compared the two PRs to each other. When several PRs are open, cross-check them pairwise with the paginated file lists before choosing a merge order.

gh pr merge CAN FAIL SILENTLY WITH "Base branch was modified" (2026-07-26). The command returned, my script read state and got OPEN, and nothing in the summary line said why. Running the merge again WITHOUT redirecting stderr showed it: GraphQL: Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again. (mergePullRequest).

CAUSE: main moved between the check-reading and the merge call — in this case by my own preceding merge in the same sweep. The PR was MERGEABLE / mergeStateStatus CLEAN with 72 pass / 0 fail / 0 pending, so it was genuinely green; only the base had advanced.

FIX: retry. It succeeded immediately on the second attempt. This is NOT an --admin candidate and not a gate problem.

TWO LOOP LESSONS: (1) my sweep already verifies state == MERGED after every merge, which is what caught this — keep that, and never delete a branch on the assumption a merge succeeded (a memory already records that deleting a branch pre-merge auto-closes the PR). (2) I was discarding stderr with >/dev/null 2>&1 on the merge call, which hid the reason. Send merge output somewhere readable, or re-run the merge verbatim when the state check says OPEN — the error message is the diagnosis and it costs one call.

EXPECT THIS MORE when merging several PRs in one sweep: each merge invalidates the base for the ones after it, so later merges in a batch are the likely victims. Retrying in the same pass is fine.

gh pr merge can fail with 'Pull Request has merge conflicts' AFTER the monitor reports GREEN (checks green ≠ mergeable — a sibling merge can conflict it in the gap). NEVER chain merge+cleanup in one command: verify state==MERGED before any branch/worktree deletion. Recovery if violated: the deletion output prints the tip sha — git branch <name> <sha>, push, gh pr reopen, rebase, resolve, force-with-lease.

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION FAILS CLOSED ON A CASE MISMATCH BETWEEN TWO gh COMMANDS (2026-08-13).

gh pr checks --json state returns UPPERCASE: SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS.
gh run list --json status returns lowercase: completed, queued, in_progress.

mayor-merge.md clause 4 said 'runs whose status is all COMPLETED'. A literal test of .status != "COMPLETED" therefore counts every FINISHED run as nonterminal. It reported all six open PRs as blocked (runs@sha=5 nonterminal=5, identically) when all five runs on each were completed/success. Caught only by dumping the raw JSON.

USE (.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED".

TWO THINGS WORTH KEEPING. First, the direction: unlike every other trap in the merge criterion this one fails CLOSED, so it never ships a bad merge and never announces itself either - it presents as a CI queue that will not drain, which is entirely believable and can burn ticks indefinitely. The identical reading across all six PRs was the tell; real CI does not stall six branches in lockstep.

Second, the neighbouring fail-OPEN version of the same clause: --commit takes the FULL 40-char headRefOid. An abbreviated sha matches nothing and returns [], which reads as 'no live runs' and passes clause 4 vacuously. Same clause, one argument away, opposite direction.

`gh run view --log-failed` RETURNS ~81 BYTES WHILE A RUN IS STILL IN PROGRESS — that is "not finished yet", NOT "this machine cannot fetch logs". Measured 2026-09-04, and I misdiagnosed it in a dispatch brief.

WHAT HAPPENED. PR #9188 had one failing check. `gh run view <id> --log-failed` returned nothing; `gh run view --job <id> --log` returned 81 bytes. I concluded the log fetch was broken on this box, wrote that into the fix worker's brief as a machine quirk, and told it to obtain the text some other way. The worker ran `gh api repos/day8/re-frame2/actions/jobs/<job-id>/logs` and got the full log immediately. The run had simply still been in progress when I asked; GitHub does not serve a complete job log until the job finishes.

WHY THE MISREADING WAS TEMPTING. This box genuinely does have several instrument faults that return empty (grep -iF aborting, jq CRLF, sed range collapse), so "the tool is broken here" was a live hypothesis with precedent. But it was the WRONG hypothesis, and the cost was that the brief told a worker something false about its own environment.

THE RULE: BEFORE CALLING A FETCH BROKEN, CHECK WHETHER THE THING BEING FETCHED EXISTS YET. For a CI log that means reading the run's own status first — `gh run view <id> --json status,conclusion`. An in-progress run has no complete log to serve.

AND THE WORKING FORM IS WORTH KEEPING: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/jobs/<job-id>/logs` returns a finished job's full log directly, including per-step boundaries, which is what made the real cause visible — the failure was in step 7 (a generated-artefact drift check), not step 6 (the test suite), and only the step breakdown showed that.

RELATED: [[never-put-an-uncontrolled-extraction-in-a-brief]].

gh run rerun CANNOT clear a trunk-inherited red on a PR. A re-run replays the workflow against the FROZEN EVENT PAYLOAD and the same refs/pull/N/merge sha the original run graded, so it re-grades the identical tree and fails identically — it does not pick up a repaired main. Measured 2026-09-08: after PR #9467 fixed trunk's api-manifest drift, I re-ran the failed lint workflow on PRs #9468 and #9469 expecting the inherited Public-API manifest drift-check red to clear; attempt=2 failed exactly as attempt=1 on both. ONLY A NEW PUSH creates a new merge ref, so the remedy for a trunk-inherited red is a REBASE, never a re-run. The re-run is not merely useless here, it is misleading: a second identical failure reads as 'the failure is real and mine' when it is still the old base. Corollary for the merge criterion: a PR's rollup describes the tree its CI actually graded, which after trunk moves is NOT main+PR as it stands now — which is the same ungraded-merge-product gap that lets a broken tree onto trunk in the first place.

THE TWO gh COMMANDS IN THE MERGE CRITERION USE OPPOSITE CASE VOCABULARIES, AND A FILTER WRITTEN FOR ONE SILENTLY MISCLASSIFIES THE OTHER (2026-08-10).

  gh pr checks <pr> --json state    -> UPPERCASE:  SUCCESS, SKIPPED, IN_PROGRESS
  gh run list --commit <sha> --json status -> lowercase: completed, in_progress

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION USES THE SECOND ONE. I wrote its check as
`select(.status != "COMPLETED") | length` — copying the case from clause 2's vocabulary —
so it matched NOTHING and counted EVERY run as nonterminal. On PR #7774 it reported
"clause4 not-COMPLETED: 5" for a PR whose five runs were all `completed/success`.

THIS ONE FAILED CLOSED, WHICH IS WHY IT COST ONLY A MINUTE. An over-blocking clause 4
refuses a green PR; the method already names that failure ("a guard that blocks forever is
not safe, it is differently wrong") but it is far cheaper than the fail-open direction.
Had I written the inverse test — count runs EQUAL to "COMPLETED" and require the count to
match the total — the same typo would have passed a branch with live runs on it.

WHAT SAVED THE EARLIER MERGES. I printed the run list and read the statuses BY EYE for
every merge before this one, and lowercase `completed` reads correctly to a human. The
defect only bit when I switched from printing to counting. So: a filter you cannot eyeball
is exactly where a vocabulary mismatch hides.

THE FIX: compare case-insensitively — `select((.status|ascii_upcase) != "COMPLETED")` — or
print the values alongside the verdict so the two can never silently disagree. Prefer
printing: the criterion is read by a human every tick anyway.

THE GENERAL RULE, which this repo keeps rediscovering in its own instruments: when one
check joins two data sources, the join is where the vocabularies must be proved equal. Do
not assume a tool speaks one language because two of its subcommands describe the same
domain.

A BRANCH WITH NO *OPEN* PR IS NOT A STRAND — query --state all before calling it one (2026-08-15 14:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED TODAY. worker/settled-10lyy reported worker/rung3-hic033 as 'a stranded branch (merge-base 2026-08-12, no PR, clean worktree) carrying an unmerged budgets.md diff — live hygiene for the mayor'. Every observable it listed was true. The conclusion was wrong.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..worker/rung3-hic033   -> 5   (looks unmerged)
  gh pr list --head worker/rung3-hic033 --state all       -> #7953 MERGED
  its commit subject located in origin/main               -> present

IT IS A REBASE-MERGED GHOST. The five 'unmerged' commits are the PRE-REBASE versions of work that IS on main under different hashes. A rebase-merge rewrites commits, so the original objects stay reachable from the branch ref forever and every count-based test reports them as outstanding.

THE TWO TESTS THAT SEPARATE GHOST FROM STRAND, and both are cheap:
  1. gh pr list --head <branch> --state ALL  — the default is open-only, which is exactly how a merged PR reads as 'no PR'.
  2. locate the branch tip's commit SUBJECT in origin/main — survives the hash rewrite that defeats every sha comparison.

WHY THE ERROR IS ASYMMETRIC AND WHICH WAY IT COSTS: calling a ghost a strand wastes a dispatch re-doing landed work, or worse, revives a diff main has since moved past — the conflict-resolution-reverts-a-refactor failure. Calling a strand a ghost loses real work. So run BOTH tests rather than picking one.

THIS IS THE PR-STATE HALF OF THE FENCE RULE DOING ITS JOB — mayor-dispatch.md already says the diff alone cannot separate a live unpushed worker from a merged leftover whose fork point predates its own merge. Multiple workers have now hit it from the other side: one found FOUR branches holding a file it wanted and every one was a merged leftover; another found five, same answer; a third found three of nine. GHOSTS ARE THE COMMON CASE ON THIS REPO — roughly 70 worktrees exist and almost all are dead.

DISPOSITION FOR rung3-hic033 SPECIFICALLY: reapable branch, hygiene-loop work, nothing to salvage.

'git branch -d' IS NOT A GUARD AGAINST DELETING UNMERGED WORK — IT COUNTS 'MERGED TO ITS UPSTREAM' AS MERGED, SO A PUSHED BRANCH DELETES AS READILY UNDER -d AS UNDER -D (measured this session, 2026-08-23).

WHAT HAPPENED. Reaching for -d as the safe form, I deleted worker/receipts-hic081. It carried THREE commits that exist nowhere else — 'git cherry origin/main' reads +3 new — and -d deleted it without a murmur, because the branch was fully merged to its OWN upstream, which is all that refusal tests. Nothing was lost only because the commits were on origin; the branch was restored at ae14841ab3 and its upstream re-set, verified equal.

THE REAL LESSON IS NOT ABOUT THE FLAG. Ten minutes earlier I had declined to test a removal script's dry-run against a live worktree, on exactly the reasoning that an experiment on live state is not free. Then I ran an experiment on a branch because a branch felt cheap. The category was the same and only the object differed.

THE GUARD THAT ACTUALLY WORKS is patch-equivalence against the TRUNK, computed yourself before deleting anything: 'git cherry origin/main <branch>', where a leading + is a commit genuinely not in main and a leading - is one already contained. This repo merges by REBASE, which is why ancestry and ahead-count are both wrong here, in opposite directions — and why -d's own notion of merged is wrong a third way.

A RELATED TRAP LIVES IN THE SAME CONFIG. A local branch keeps its branch.<name>.merge upstream setting after the remote branch is gone and the remote-tracking ref has been pruned. Three worker branches are in that state right now. A dangling upstream silently changes what -d compares against, so the flag's behaviour depends on repository state you cannot see from the command line.

AND NOTE WHICH TEST APPLIES TO WHAT: merge state is the test for a BRANCH, never for a worktree. A worktree is reaped only on its worker's own quotable completion report.

THIS REPO MERGES BY REBASE, SO ANCESTRY SAYS "UNMERGED" ABOUT WORK THAT DEMONSTRABLY LANDED — AND `git branch -d` IS AN ANCESTRY TEST. Measured 2026-09-12 on a real merged branch, both directions in one sitting.

THE MEASUREMENT. `worker/opendoc-a` tip `d7be1e3c1c` was merged as PR #9716 by `gh pr merge --rebase`, landing on trunk as the rewritten commit `4a89200805`.
  * `git cherry origin/main d7be1e3c1c` reads `- d7be1e3c1c` — the MINUS means the patch is already upstream. Containment PROVEN.
  * `git merge-base --is-ancestor d7be1e3c1c origin/main` reads NOT AN ANCESTOR.
Same branch, same instant, opposite answers. The rebase rewrote the sha, so no ancestry relation survives even though every line of the work is on trunk.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING A CURIOSITY. `git branch -d` refuses on ancestry unless the branch equals its UPSTREAM ref, and it says so in its warning: "merged to refs/remotes/origin/<branch>, but not yet merged to HEAD". So it succeeds for the wrong reason while the remote-tracking ref survives, and REFUSES a fully-merged branch the moment that ref is pruned — at which point the only door left is `git branch -D`, which deletes without any containment test at all. The convenient path degrades from "right by accident" straight to "no check", with no stage in between where it is right on purpose.

THE ANSWERS ARE NOT SYMMETRIC, and this is the half that stops it becoming a licence. `-` (contained) is PROOF and is the only thing that authorises deletion. `+` (not contained) is the ABSENCE of proof, never evidence of unmerged work: patch identity covers the diff's CONTEXT lines, so a sibling landing in neighbouring lines leaves fully-merged work reading as `+`. A branch list read as a backlog is a list of phantoms.

CONTROL TAKEN, and take one every time, because a test that only ever returns `+` looks identical to a broken one. Run it against a tip you KNOW landed — the `-` above is that control. Both spike branches kept under rf2-p0hx read `+` on every commit, which agrees with their retention ruling by an independent route.

`docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md` §4 Branches already states the rule in OS-neutral form ("Where the project merges by REBASE, both obvious containment tests are wrong... The test is patch-equivalence"). This memory is the CLI concretion and the measured control, not a new finding — the drift was reaching for the convenient default instead of the prescribed test.

THE BRANCH-DELETION TEST "git cherry origin/main <ref> IS ALL MINUS" IS VACUOUSLY TRUE ON A FRESH BRANCH THAT HAS NO COMMITS AT ALL, SO IT PASSES ON A BRANCH A LIVE WORKER IS USING (2026-09-20, mayor, found during §4 hygiene).

Measured on this tree. A branch created at `origin/main` whose worker has not yet committed:
`git cherry origin/main worker/xrnav2-v2435` prints **0 lines — 0 plus, 0 minus**. The rule reads "delete
only when every line is `-`", and a set with no lines satisfies that universally-quantified test trivially.
A genuinely merged branch reads **>= 1 minus** (its landed commits, patch-equivalent to trunk); the retained
spike `worker/receipts-hic081` reads 3 plus / 0 minus, the unmerged shape.

So the three cases are NOT two:
- **>= 1 plus** — unmerged work. Refuse. (This is the case the rule was written for.)
- **0 plus, >= 1 minus** — genuinely merged. Safe to delete.
- **0 plus, 0 minus** — NOTHING HAS BEEN COMMITTED YET. Indistinguishable from "merged" under the rule as
  worded, and it is the state of every freshly dispatched worker's branch.

**IT FAILS IN THE DESTRUCTIVE DIRECTION**, which is what earns it a memory: the third case is not an
untidy-tracker problem, it is deleting the branch out from under a running worker mid-dispatch. And it is
most likely exactly when hygiene runs — a §4 sweep in the same tick as a §2 dispatch sees brand-new
branches at their most vulnerable.

**TWO THINGS MASKED IT and neither is the rule working.** (1) `git branch -d` AND `-D` both refuse a branch
that is checked out in any worktree, so git's own guard catches it — that is git's design, not the
coordinator's test. (2) The sweep read its classifier's output rather than piping it into a delete. Note the
first guard evaporates the moment the worktree is reaped before the branch pass, which is the ordinary
ordering.

**THE GUARD, two conjuncts, both cheap:**
1. **Require at least one `-` line**, not merely zero `+` lines — positive evidence that the branch's commits
   actually landed, rather than the absence of evidence that they did not.
2. **Require that NO worktree holds the branch** — `git worktree list` is the check, and it is the one that
   speaks to liveness rather than to history.

**GENERALISES: a universally-quantified test over a possibly-empty set is a vacuous pass waiting to
happen**, and this project has met the shape before in a different register — CLAUDE.md records a gate that
cannot fail on a file containing none of what it inspects, and a CR == CRLF check that reads `0 == 0` on a
file whose carriage returns the instrument could not see. **Whenever a rule says "every X is Y", ask what it
answers when there are no X at all**, and make the non-emptiness an explicit conjunct rather than an
assumption.

that looked like it was working; there the constant was wrong, here the predicate is right and its domain

TO ASK 'DOES THIS BRANCH CARRY ANYTHING MAIN DOES NOT HAVE?', USE git cherry — NOT git rev-list --count (2026-08-13, third rev-list miss in one session).

I escalated to Mike that two guide-rewrite branches were COMPETING WHOLESALE REWRITES that conflicted and needed him to pick one. They were not competing. They had landed as a deliberate SEQUENCE, and every branch tip was PATCH-EQUIVALENT to main.

  git rev-list --count origin/main..BRANCH   read 1     <- misleading
  git cherry main BRANCH                     prints '-' <- already landed

A rebase-merge leaves the ORIGINAL commit object unreachable from main while its PATCH is fully present. rev-list counts OBJECTS; the question is about CONTENT. git cherry marks '-' for patch-equivalent and '+' for genuinely unlanded.

THE PATTERN IS BIGGER THAN THIS ONE COMMAND. A rev-list count misled three separate times in one session:
  1. liveness  - the ahead count is INVARIANT UNDER REBASE, so a working worker read as stalled (rf2-0vvw)
  2. the check band - a mid-run rollup total is a FLOOR, not a count; 92 became 93 when it settled
  3. unlanded work - object reachability is not patch equivalence (this one)

Each time the number was real and the QUESTION IT ANSWERED was not the question I was asking. Before quoting a count, say out loud what set it counts and whether that is the set you care about.

COST HERE: a false P2 escalation to the operator, a bead held at 'needs Mike' for several ticks, and three further beads fenced behind it that were never actually blocked.

GIT CHERRY'S '+' IS NOT PROOF THAT WORK IS ABSENT FROM THE TRUNK. Its '-' IS reliable; its '+' is not.

MEASURED 2026-09-04, and I got this wrong in a stranded sweep. `git cherry origin/main worker/retro-b` reported one commit '+', so I concluded six files of skill-layout work had never reached the trunk, pushed the branch to make it 'durable', and REOPENED a closed bead on it. All of that was wrong: the deliverable was already on origin/main at commit 0093c1858c — same author date, same message, same stat. The worker sent to re-land it found the truth in one directory read.

WHY CHERRY SAID '+'. It compares PATCH-IDS, and a patch-id is computed over the hunk INCLUDING ITS CONTEXT LINES. The trunk's copy and the branch's copy differed in the blob index line and TWO CONTEXT LINES — a neighbouring sentence that had since gained a fourth skill in a list. Same change, different patch-id, so '+'.

SO THE ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE POINT, and it is the safe direction that is trustworthy:
  '-' means an identical patch is on the trunk. Reliable. Use it to authorise a branch delete.
  '+' means NO IDENTICAL PATCH was found. It does NOT mean the content is absent — the trunk may carry the same change with one line of drift around it.

THIS DOES NOT RESTORE --is-ancestor OR git branch -d. Under `gh pr merge --rebase` every merged branch is rewritten, so ancestry reports merged work as unmerged and the ahead count agrees with it. Cherry remains the better instrument for containment; it is simply not a proof of ABSENCE.

THE DECISIVE TEST IS THE SOURCE AT TIP, and it is the loop's own rule one level up — CHECK THE TREE, NOT THE RECORD. Before declaring anything stranded, `git show origin/main:<path>` and look for the content. One command. I skipped it because cherry felt authoritative, which is exactly how a well-formed wrong answer gets believed.

AND THE COST OF BEING WRONG HERE IS NOT ZERO: re-landing a stale copy of a region silently REVERTS whatever landed in it since. The cherry-pick the worker attempted conflicted on exactly that sentence — the trunk named four skills, the stranded hunk three — so the 'salvage' would have deleted a sibling's work while passing every gate.

RELATED: a branch whose cherry reads all '-' is still safe to delete, so the hygiene loop's branch rule is unaffected.

A `$` ANCHOR PLACED DIRECTLY AFTER LITERAL TEXT RETURNS A FALSE ZERO IN `git grep` ON THIS CHECKOUT, AND EVERY MAYOR GOVERNING FILE IS CRLF (measured 2026-08-20).

MECHANISM. The files are stored and checked out with CRLF terminators, so a `\r` sits between the last literal character and end-of-line. `git grep` matches against that `\r`; `^` is unaffected, and `.*$` is unaffected because `.` matches the `\r`. Only literal-text-then-`$` fails, and it fails SILENTLY as "no matches".

MEASURED, on `.claude/commands/mayor-posture.md`:
  leading `^` only ........................ 1 hit
  `.*$` .................................... 1 hit
  full literal line + `$` .................. 0 hits  <-- FALSE
  same literal line, no `$` ................ 1 hit

SPREAD, and this is why it matters rather than being a curiosity: `file -b` reports CRLF for ALL of `docs/the-mayor-method/{dispatch-prompt-template,loops,bootstrap}.md`, ALL of `.claude/commands/mayor-{merge,dispatch,posture,hygiene,method-reread}.md`, and `CLAUDE.md`. `dispatch-prompt-template.md` is 900 of 900 lines CRLF. The entire surface the method-reread loop audits is affected.

HOW IT BIT. The method-reread loop's duplicate-block check ran `git grep -l "^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$"` and returned EMPTY — for a heading that demonstrably exists at `dispatch-prompt-template.md:478`. Unanchored, it returns exactly 1 file, which is the correct answer. Had a second copy of that block existed, the check would have reported clean.

WHY NO DISPATCH WAS EVER HARMED. The block extraction uses `sed`, not `git grep`, and `sed` on this Git Bash STRIPS the `\r` on read — `sed -n '/^WORKTREE BOUNDARY — MANDATORY$/,/^```$/p'` still returns its 51 lines, and the extracted text is clean LF. So the paste path is sound and only the VERIFICATION path was blind. Do not "fix" the extraction.

THE RULE: never end a `git grep` pattern with a `$` straight after literal text on this repo. Drop the `$`, or use `.*$`. And this is the standing "a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed" rule biting the mayor's own audit — run a positive control on any census whose zero you are about to believe.

GIT GREP SILENTLY MISSES HITS THAT RIPGREP RETURNS ON THIS CHECKOUT — measured 2026-08-14 23:35 AUSEST by worker/arch-hic087 during rf2-hic-087's mechanism census (PR #8258).

WHAT WAS MEASURED. An anchored hook-call-site census over implementation/hicasso/src read 14 with 'git grep -E' and 16 with rg, against a tree that was BYTE-IDENTICAL across the rebase (verified). Two hits, roughly 12% of the population, were invisible to git grep. The worker recorded the correction on its published page rather than absorbing it silently, which is the only reason it is knowable.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A TOOL PREFERENCE. Every census on this programme is a published NUMBER that later work cites — native-share, retained-tooling, mutable-globals, public-surface, allocation. A census run with git grep can be low and internally consistent, and nothing downstream can tell. A census is not reproducible unless it records the tool as well as the pattern.

THE RULE: use rg for any census whose number gets published, and RECORD THE TOOL alongside the pattern and the count. If a census must use git grep (for example to restrict to tracked files), cross-check the total with rg and say both numbers.

A SECOND TRAP FROM THE SAME BEAD, and it is Clojure-specific: A PREDICATE NAME ENDS IN '?', WHICH IS ALSO A REGEX QUANTIFIER. The worker's grep '\bscope?\b' matched 'scop' followed by an optional 'e', so it reported two LIVE evidence vars as dead code. Escape the '?' or use a fixed-string search whenever a Clojure symbol ends in '?' or '*' or '+'. In a dead-code census this fails in the dangerous direction: it deletes live code.

BOTH TRAPS SHARE ONE SHAPE — a census that is wrong reads exactly like a census that is right, because the only evidence is the number itself. That is why a positive control (seed something the census must catch, confirm it is named, remove it) is now standard on this programme's censuses.

`git grep` with a pattern that STARTS WITH `/` is MSYS path-mangled on this Windows host and silently returns ZERO for everything — including patterns that certainly match. Found by a worker on 2026-09-04 and reproduced by the mayor on the same tree:

  git grep -c "/client-root" -- 'examples/real-apps/realworld_http/*'   -> no output, exit 0
  git grep -c "client-root"  -- 'examples/real-apps/realworld_http/*'   -> core.cljs:1
  grep -rn "client-root" examples/real-apps/realworld_http/             -> 1 hit

MSYS sees a leading `/` as a Unix path and rewrites it to a Windows path before git ever sees it, so the pattern searched for is not the pattern written.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG: it fails OPEN and it defeats the standard control. A census over qualified names — `/render!`, `/mount!`, `"/client-root"` — is a normal thing to write when looking for a var by its unqualified tail. The zero looks exactly like "this symbol is not used", which is usually the conclusion the census exists to support. And a control that SHARES THE SHAPE of the target (the advice that catches most census bugs) is mangled identically, so the control reads zero too and confirms the wrong answer. Only a SECOND, DIFFERENT instrument catches it — `grep -rn` is not MSYS-mangled the same way.

WHAT TO DO:
- Never start a `git grep` pattern with `/`. Anchor on the namespace side instead (`census.clj` not `/census`), or match the bare tail and filter, or escape as `[/]client-root`.
- Keep the two-instrument rule for every census, and make the second instrument a DIFFERENT TOOL rather than a different pattern in the same tool. This is the case that proves why "two independent instruments" means independent in mechanism, not just in wording.
- The already-recorded sibling trap is the pathspec one: `git grep -- 'implementation/*/src'` matches NOTHING because a git wildcard pathspec matches the whole path — use `implementation/*/src/*`. That is a PATHSPEC bug; this one is a PATTERN bug. They are different and both fail open.

RELATED, from the same worker: every file in `migration/reagent-to-hicasso/codemod/` is pure CRLF and carries non-ASCII, so edits there need byte verification (crlf==lf count, UTF-8 decode) and emitted EDN is worth hex-checking for U+FFFD. Console `?` glyphs on this host are terminal rendering, NOT corruption — do not chase them.

`git log --grep=<bead-id>` IS A PREFIX MATCH, AND THE BACKLOG REREAD'S CHECK 5 RUNS ON IT — measured 2026-09-04.

CHECK 5 of the backlog reread asks, for every open bead, "is this already DONE in the tree?" and the prescribed instrument is `git log origin/main --oneline --grep=<id>`. That instrument OVER-REPORTS on any hierarchical id, because the pattern is an unanchored regex and `.` matches any character.

MEASURED: `--grep=rf2-6r9j.24` returned THREE commits, none of which mention rf2-6r9j.24. Two were siblings whose ids merely START with it — rf2-6r9j.244 and rf2-6r9j.249 — and the third carried its id in the commit BODY where `--oneline` does not show it. Anchored as `--grep='rf2-6r9j\.24[^0-9]'` the same query returns ZERO. This repo's ids are dotted and hierarchical (rf2-6r9j.24 / .53 / .161 / .244 / .249), so every short-numbered child of a large epic is exposed.

THE DIRECTION OF THE FAILURE IS THE PROBLEM. Check 5's action on a hit is to consider CLOSING the bead. So a false positive pushes toward closing an open item on the strength of a commit that was about a different bead entirely — and the commit will look plausible, because a sibling of the same epic is usually adjacent work in the same files. It fails toward "looks done".

THE FIX IS THE ANCHOR, and it costs nothing: `--grep='<id>[^0-9]'`, or `--grep='<id>\b'` where the id does not end in a digit. Escape the dots too — `rf2-6r9j.24` as a regex also matches `rf2-6r9jX24`, which is harmless here but free to rule out.

THE RULE THE LOOP ALREADY CARRIES SAVED IT ANYWAY, and this is why that rule is written the way it is: "a hit is a POINTER, confirm in source before closing". On the same sweep, rf2-6r9j.53's single hit was GENUINE — Mike's own commit 866e452d37 naming the bead in its subject — and confirming it meant reading the corrected docstring at tip, not trusting the grep. One instrument found both a false positive and a true one in the same run; only the source read told them apart.

AND NOTE WHAT THE TRUE HIT WAS: an operator ruling that landed as a COMMIT rather than as a note on the bead. No other loop would ever have found it — dispatch reads `bd ready`, merge reads PRs. That is the whole reason check 5 exists, so keep running it; just anchor the pattern.

git rm --cached DOES NOT PROTECT FILES FROM A LATER CHECKOUT — and this will bite rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 at 85 files. Found by the ai/decisions untracking worker (#6424) on 2026-07-19, in its own worktree.

THE HAZARD: `git rm --cached` leaves the file on disk IN THE BRANCH WHERE IT RUNS — but the COMMIT RECORDS A DELETION. Any later rebase, checkout, or `git reset --hard` ACROSS that commit removes the working-tree copies too, silently and with no warning. The worker rebased onto post-#6422 main and its four dossiers vanished from disk; it caught this only on a final on-disk verification and restored them.
⚠️ THE SAME THING HAPPENS IN EVERY OTHER CHECKOUT WHEN THE COMMIT MERGES. The mayor loop `git reset --hard origin/main` after a merge will delete the operator working copies. On 2026-07-19 I backed the four dossiers up to the scratchpad BEFORE merging #6424 and restored them after, so they end up UNTRACKED BUT PRESENT — which is what "should not be tracked" means. "Untrack" is not "delete".

⚠️ rf2-vxgfnd.99.1 WILL HIT THIS AT 85 FILES (ai/findings/new-substrate-synthesis + new-substrate-codex). Its brief MUST carry:
  1. Back up the full tracked ai/ set to a location OUTSIDE the repo before the untracking commit.
  2. A POST-REBASE ON-DISK RE-VERIFICATION step — after any rebase or checkout, confirm the files are still present, not just that the index is right.
  3. The same restore step in the mayor merge sequence, or the operator local working material disappears from every checkout that pulls.
  4. State explicitly whether the operator wants them KEPT on disk or genuinely DELETED — do not infer. Mike instruction was "this path should NOT be tracked", which is about the index, not the filesystem.

GENERAL FORM: an index-only operation still produces a tree-changing commit. Whenever you `git rm --cached` anything a human is still using as working material, the deletion propagates to every working tree that later checks out that commit. Back it up first; verify on disk afterwards; and say plainly to the operator that the files will vanish from their checkout unless restored.

GITHUB MODELS BRANCH PROTECTION TWICE - A CLASSIC-PROTECTION 404 IS TRUE AND NOT DISPOSITIVE. Measured 2026-09-07 on this repo, recorded against the mayor on rf2-mfzw, and preserved here because that bead is decay-eligible and the only other written copy is in the GITIGNORED ai/dispatch-blocks.md, which is regenerated from a template that does not carry it.

WHAT HAPPENED. Asked "is main protected?", the coordinator ran `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/branches/main/protection`, got HTTP 404 with "Branch not protected", TOOK A CONTROL (checked the exit code and stderr, to tell a real 404 from an unreadable endpoint - the false-zero shape this project guards everywhere), and concluded main was unprotected and that the five-clause merge criterion was the only thing gating trunk. That statement reached the operator before a worker refuted it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE: an active REPOSITORY RULESET (id 16120663) requires three status checks - "All required checks passed", "Lint required" and "Docs required" - and enforces `deletion`, `non_fast_forward` and `required_linear_history`. `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/rulesets` returns exit 0 and lists it. Classic branch protection and rulesets are two independent systems modelling the same fact; the 404 was a true answer about one of them.

WHY THE CONTROL DID NOT SAVE IT, and this is the transferable half. The control was well built and aimed at the WRONG AXIS. It answered "is this endpoint readable?" when the open question was "is this endpoint the whole answer?". Almost every instrument rule in this project guards the first question. This one guards the second: BEFORE CONCLUDING ANYTHING FROM AN ABSENCE, ASK WHAT ELSE COULD CARRY THE SAME FACT. A second system modelling the same thing is invisible to any amount of rigour applied to the first.

PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR A COORDINATOR: the three required contexts above are enforced by the platform, so a check outside that set (the renamed "PR guards ..." check, for one) is graded but not platform-required - which is why the rf2-mfzw rename was safe. Check both endpoints before asserting anything about what gates trunk, and re-read the ruleset rather than quoting the id above, which can change.

GitHub's REBASE-MERGE can put a tree on trunk that NO CI RUN EVER GRADED, and the merge criterion does not ask about it. Measured 2026-09-08: PR #9459 was self-consistent at its own head and fully green at 87/87; the rebase-merge replayed it onto a moved main where a sibling had made the IDENTICAL edit to spec/api-manifest.edn's :var-count line for a DIFFERENT removal. Git merges two identical edits without a conflict, the row deletions sat far apart, and the product declared 496 vars while carrying 495 — gen --check exit 1 on trunk. Clause 5 asks whether the check set was computed against the current matrix; it never asks whether the MERGE PRODUCT was graded at all, and on a generated file that gap is reachable. The cheap guard for a mayor: after merging anything that touches a generated file, run that file's own check on the fast-forwarded trunk before moving on. The cheap guard for a worker: count rows independently of any declared count field, on main as well as on your branch — a peer derived 'expected' from main's DECLARED count on this very tree and would have been wrong by one, and the natural reaction to that mismatch is to doubt your own removal count rather than suspect trunk.

GitHub splits a markdown TABLE ROW on every `|`, INCLUDING pipes inside a backticked code span. So writing a gate name, a shell alternation or any `||` inside a code span in a table cell silently adds columns to that row and breaks the table's rendering. Nothing in this repo catches it: no gate validates prose, tables or rendering at all, and the two link gates strip fences before extracting.

Caught 2026-09-04 by a worker's own hand check before it landed — its first draft of a TESTING.md row wrote the gate as a code span containing `||`, which took that row to 5 pipes against the table's 3. Reworded as prose. This is the concrete case for the standing rule that table column counts are verified BY HAND and said so in the PR body: the check is not ceremony, it has caught a real defect.

If a pipe is genuinely needed inside a table cell, escape it as `\|`. Prefer rewording to prose.

RELATED, same worker, same run — the harness's reported exit code disagreed with the captured one on TWO of three sabotage runs: the harness said "exit code 0" while the file the runner wrote read 1. Both were deliberately sabotaged runs, so believing the harness would have read as "the control does not bite" and inverted the conclusion. Quote the number the runner itself wrote to a file; never the harness's report about the same run.

A GLOB OVER THE SHARED SCRATCH DIRECTORY MATCHES A PEER WORKER'S GATE ARTEFACT AND HANDS BACK THEIR EXIT CODE FOR YOUR OWN UNFINISHED RUN — it fails OPEN, printing a 0 that was never about your tree.

Measured 2026-09-20 by the rf2-a28eo worker (PR #10093): a read of `gate-xrayjvm-*.exit` matched artefacts written by a DIFFERENT live worker and printed their `0` for a run of its own that had not finished.

WHY IT GENERALISES rather than being one worker's slip: several workers run concurrently against ONE session scratchpad directory, and gate-artefact names are CONVENTIONAL (`gate-<lane>-<something>.exit`, `<lane>.log`), so the namespace is shared by construction. A glob cannot tell whose file it found. Nothing on screen distinguishes a peer's success from your own — the file exists, it parses, it contains `0`.

IT FAILS IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION for the only question a gate artefact is ever asked ("did my run pass?"), and it is MOST likely to fire exactly when your own run is slow or wedged — i.e. when the artefact is missing precisely because something is wrong. The lane's silent-wedge failure mode makes that the common case, not the rare one.

THE GUARD, three parts:
1. Read a gate result by a LITERAL, RUN-UNIQUE path — embed your worktree name or the branch in the filename and read that exact string. Never a `*`.
2. Capture the exit code on the SAME command line as the run (`cmd; echo "EXIT=$?"`), so the code and the run cannot be separated by anything.
3. Delete your own artefacts by literal path when done, so the next worker's glob — if they write one — has less to find.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT MISREPORT WAS MEASURED IN THE SAME SESSION AND IS THE REASON (2) IS NOT OPTIONAL: the harness reported exit 0 for a RED run whose captured code was 1. So neither the harness's report nor a globbed artefact is trustworthy on its own; only a code captured beside its own command is.

Related: this is the same family as CLAUDE.md instrument item (b) — a pipeline's status being its LAST command's — reached through the FILESYSTEM rather than through a pipe.

A GREEN ROLLUP WHOSE RELEVANT GATE WAS *SKIPPED* IS NOT EVIDENCE THE GATE WOULD PASS — and clause 2 of the merge criterion cannot see the difference (measured 2026-09-05 on PR #9306).

THE SITUATION. PR #9306 (rf2-kuky.18) removed a Story-shell page-wide no-op :errors listener that had been MASKING 8 real Xray errors. Its own worker measured `npm run test:story-feature-load` RED on the change and told me to sequence the PR behind the fix (rf2-avi7). Then the rollup came in at 87/87: 10 skipped, 77 success, zero failures, zero non-terminal. All FIVE clauses of the merge criterion were satisfied. The obvious read — 'the worker was wrong, CI is the authority, merge it' — is the trap.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY TRUE. The job named 'Story/Xray browser gates (PR-smoke)' RAN and SUCCEEDED, which is what makes this convincing: it is not an absent job, it is a GREEN job. But its step 'Run the FULL Story feature-load gate (direct-runner change, rf2-65ajl)' was SKIPPED inside it. Read from the API rather than inferred:
  gh api repos/<o>/<r>/actions/jobs/<job_id> -q '.steps[] | "\(.conclusion // .status)\t\(.name)"'
gave 'skipped  Run the FULL Story feature-load gate'. The step is gated on the classifier output `story_full_gate`, which by design arms ONLY on the feature-load gate's own spec modules and its run/serve orchestration — NOT on ordinary Story/Xray runtime changes (test.yml ~4100-4127 explains the reasoning at length; it exists so a normal Story PR does not pay for an extra testbed compile). #9306 changed observability runtime code, so it did not arm.

AND THE NIGHTLY RUNS IT UNCONDITIONALLY. expensive-tests.yml has 'Gate — Story feature-load' under `if: ${{ !cancelled() }}`. So merging #9306 on its green rollup would not have produced a red PR anywhere — it would have produced a RED NIGHTLY, discovered by the nightly-red channel that CLAUDE.md itself records taking SEVEN DAYS to reach a human on the last occasion (rf2-4a0c, issue #8423).

THE GENERAL RULE. Clause 2 accepts 'skipped' as passed, and it is right to — path-filtered jobs are the normal case and a skipped job usually means 'your diff cannot affect this'. But SKIPPED IS THE ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE, NOT EVIDENCE OF ABSENCE. The five clauses are a FLOOR: they establish that nothing CI ran objected. They are not a licence to merge in the face of positive, measured evidence of a defect that CI did not run. When a worker reports a gate red and the rollup is green, the discriminator is NOT 'who do I believe' — it is 'did that gate actually execute on this head?', answered at the STEP level, because a skipped step hides inside a green job and the rollup shows only the job.

HOW TO CHECK IT CHEAPLY. Probe the rollup for the gate by name (`jq '.statusCheckRollup[] | select((.name|ascii_downcase)|test("<gate>"))'`), and TAKE A CONTROL from another PR — here #9298 showed the same check SKIPPED where #9306 showed it SUCCESS, which is what first proved the two PRs were being graded differently. Then descend to the step list via the jobs API. A job-level green with a step-level skip is invisible at every level above the last one.

SO: HOLD THE PR, and say plainly that the hold is not a clause failure. The bead's own worker was right and the rollup was also right; they were answering different questions.

GREPPING A GATE LOG FOR 'FAIL' HITS ITS OWN SELF-TEST CONTROL LINES — count them against a known-good run before believing a failure (2026-08-15 20:02 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/release-gra70 (rf2-gra70, PR #8314). Its fast-PR spine log contained 35 matches for FAIL while the run exited 0. Those 35 are CONTROL LINES of the form 'PASS ... FAILS' — a self-test asserting that a deliberately-broken input fails. The worker's discriminator was simple and right: THE SAME COUNT APPEARED IN A RUN THAT EXITED 0, so 35 is the baseline rather than a signal.

WHY THIS MATTERS: the standing rule is already 'never pipe a gate through a filter, because a pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's'. This is the mirror failure — reading the LOG instead of the exit code, and being misled in the opposite direction. One makes a failure look like a pass; the other makes a pass look like a failure. THE EXIT CODE FROM THE RUNNER'S OWN LINE IS THE VERDICT. A log grep is at best corroboration, and only against a known baseline.

GREP -F COMBINED WITH -i SILENTLY RETURNS ZERO ON THIS PROJECT'S GREP BUILD (measured 2026-09-03 by the xray-b worker, and its CONTROL is the only reason it was caught).

MEASURED, same needle, same tree, same invocation shape:
  grep -ri  <needle> -> 43 hits
  grep -rFi <needle> ->  0 hits

No error, no warning, exit status of an ordinary no-match. So a census written with -F for literal safety AND -i for case-insensitivity reports ZERO and looks exactly like a clean tree.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG: -F is the flag careful people add. It is the correct instinct — a needle containing regex metacharacters (a dot, a question mark, brackets, and this repo is full of names like machine-has-tag? and :rf.error/...) must be matched literally. So the census that combines -F and -i is the one written BY the person being careful, and it is the one that lies. The reward for care is a false zero.

THE DEFENCE IS A CONTROL THAT BITES, AND NOTHING ELSE. A search returning zero is not a check that passed. Every census in this project must be run alongside a needle KNOWN to be present, drawn from the same pipeline with the same flags; if the control also reads zero, the instrument is broken, not the tree. The xray-b worker had exactly that control at 43 and caught its own broken census on the first read. A worker without one would have reported 'premise does not hold, zero carriers' with complete confidence.

RELATED FAILURES OF THE SAME FAMILY ALREADY RECORDED HERE: bd --json emitting CRLF so grep -F matches nothing (fixed with tr -d '\r'); a whitespace-collapsed pass and a line-oriented pass disagreeing 97 vs 117 with neither a superset; a punctuation-final needle missed by a word-boundary pattern. The generalisation is one sentence: A CENSUS IS AN INSTRUMENT, AND AN INSTRUMENT IS NOT TRUSTED UNTIL IT HAS BEEN SEEN TO MOVE.

BEFORE DISPATCHING ANY BEAD, GREP ITS NOTES FOR A FENCE — `bd ready` IS A DEPENDENCY VIEW AND CAN NEVER BE A HOLD VIEW. Measured 2026-09-04, having made this exact mistake while knowing the rule.

THE TWO QUESTIONS ARE DIFFERENT AND ONLY ONE HAS AN INSTRUMENT. "Is this bead unblocked?" is answered by `bd ready`, which reads dependency EDGES. "Is this bead held?" is answered only by reading the bead's NOTES, where sequencing fences, operator holds and release conditions are written as PROSE. A fenced bead therefore appears on the raw ready list looking perfectly dispatchable, and nothing in the dispatch path contradicts it.

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched rf2-hic-064 after confirming its dependency edges were clear and seeing it on `bd ready`. Its newest note reads, in capitals, "FENCED — DO NOT DISPATCH UNTIL: rf2-hic-063 closes". I never opened the notes.

THE AGGRAVATING DETAIL, and the reason this is a PROCESS defect rather than a lapse: I HONOURED THE SAME KIND OF FENCE ON A DIFFERENT BEAD IN THE SAME TICK. rf2-xtqs carried a prose fence; I waited for its PR to merge, and I wrote in my own dispatch notes that "bd ready CANNOT SHOW THIS — it filters dependency blockers only; a prose hold is invisible to the scheduler". Forty minutes later I dispatched a fenced bead without applying the sentence I had just written. KNOWING A RULE IS NOT THE SAME AS HAVING A STEP THAT EXECUTES IT.

AND THE FENCE'S AUTHOR HAD ANTICIPATED EXACTLY THIS. The note's own rationale reads: this fence exists "because this bead APPEARS ON THE RAW READY LIST WITH NO ACTIVE BLOCKERS and is not dispatchable". A previous mayor saw the failure coming, wrote the warning on the only surface that could carry it, and it still did not fire — because the dispatch path reads a list, not a bead.

THE FIX IS ONE COMMAND PER DISPATCH CANDIDATE, not a resolution to be careful: grep the bead's notes for FENCED / DO NOT DISPATCH / SEQUENCED / HOLD / release condition, and read what it says. Do it for every candidate, including the ones that look obviously clear — the fenced one looks identical to the rest, which is the whole problem.

WHAT SAVED IT was the preamble clause "THIS BRIEF'S PREMISES ARE CLAIMS, NOT FINDINGS — check each at source". The worker applied it to my assertion that its dependencies were clear, found the fence, reasoned about whether it should hold, ran anyway on the bead's own Green definition, and reported the tension instead of hiding it. That clause has caught a mayor error in three separate dispatches in one session; it is the highest-yield sentence in the dispatch template.

POSTSCRIPT ON THE RULING: the fence should not in fact have held — its stated concern (unclosed PROSE dependencies) was discharged, and its release condition sat behind a deferred operator decision, so read literally it fenced the audit indefinitely. Getting the right answer by not looking is still not looking.

For hang-vs-slow discrimination, compare a running job against a high PERCENTILE of its own recent cost, never against its MAX. The max is an order statistic that grows monotonically with sample size by construction, so a threshold phrased as 'past its own max' silently TIGHTENS when you sample fewer runs and loosens when you sample more - it is not a property of the job. Measured 2026-09-17 on this repo's docs workflow, truncating ONE dataset at three sample sizes: first 12 runs -> max 8.1 min, first 24 -> max 9.5, first 39 -> max 11.2. Over those same 39 runs the median read 8.9 and p95 read 10.8. The median is the stable statistic: an earlier n=24 sample also read median 8.9, while its max of 10.8 was really about the p95 of the larger sample. So the earlier practice of quoting 'median 8.9, max 10.8' was quoting a percentile and calling it a maximum, and re-sampling moved the threshold without anything about the job changing. Use the median as the expectation and a p90/p95 as the ceiling, state n, and re-take both rather than carrying them forward. Related failure shape: a measured constant that goes stale exactly where it has to be right, which the mayor-method reread loop names the check-count band as its standing example. Note the cost of being wrong here is small and fails safe if the discriminator REPORTS rather than concludes - 'past its own ceiling' should raise a question about a run, never a verdict that it is hung.

THE HARNESS'S OWN COMPLETION NOTICE CAN REPORT "exit code 0" FOR A COMMAND THAT FAILED (2026-08-10).

WHAT HAPPENED. The rf2-2rtt6.143 worker ran sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh as part of a compound command ending in a grep. The spine FAILED - its own $? was 1, on "CLJS node integration: Cannot find module shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js". The harness's completion notice for that run reported EXIT CODE 0, because the status it surfaced was the trailing grep's, not the script's. The worker caught it only because it read $? directly, as briefed.

THIS IS THE PIPELINE-EXIT-CODE TRAP ONE LEVEL UP. Every brief in this repo says "never pipe a gate through tail/head/grep - a pipeline's exit status is its last command's, so a red run reads green". That rule is usually explained as a risk to the WORKER. It is also a risk to the MAYOR: the tool result I read can carry the same lie. A green-looking completion notice is not evidence a gate passed.

THE ONLY TRUSTWORTHY FORM: run the gate alone, redirect to a worktree-local log, and echo $? into its own file on the very next command.
    sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > gate-spine.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > gate-spine.exit
Then read gate-spine.exit. Never append a filter to the same command line as the gate, not even to shorten output for a report.

THE HARNESS EXIT-CODE DISCREPANCY HAS A MECHANISM, AND IT IS NOT A BUG (2026-08-14, rf2-5gka worker).

ALL DAY workers reported the harness saying exit 0 while their captured value said 1 — five consecutive runs for one worker, all three red runs for another, a spine run for a third. I recorded it as a harness defect and briefed workers to distrust the harness number. The mechanism is simpler and it is our own doing:

  THE TRAILING `echo "EXIT=$?"` OWNS THE SHELL'S STATUS.

Every brief in this repository tells workers to redirect a gate to a log and echo the runner's exit code on ONE command line. That trailing echo succeeds, so the SHELL exits 0 — and the harness reports the shell's status, correctly. The gate's own status was captured into the log by `$?` a microsecond earlier.

So the harness is not lying. It is reporting the last command in the pipeline, which is the echo we asked for. Both numbers are true about different things.

THE RULE IS UNCHANGED BUT ITS REASON IS NOW CORRECT: for any redirected gate, the harness number is MEANINGLESS — not wrong, just answering a different question. Quote the captured one. And do not go looking for a harness bug: there isn't one to find, and workers have spent time wondering.

WORTH SAYING IN BRIEFS AS THE REASON RATHER THAN THE RULE, because a worker who understands why will apply it correctly to shapes we have not anticipated — a pipeline ending in `tee`, a compound command ending in a cleanup, anything where the last command is not the gate.

THE HARNESS HARD-KILLS A FOREGROUND COMMAND AT 10 MINUTES — so 'run the gate in the foreground to completion' is UNSATISFIABLE for the fast-PR spine (2026-08-11, measured by the catalogrows-vkle worker).

ITS WORDS: 'a foreground run is not achievable here — the harness hard-kills foreground commands at 10 minutes, and my first foreground attempt died exactly there (exit 143, mid-JVM tier).' Exit 143 is SIGTERM. I hit the same class myself at the mayor's own 2-minute tool ceiling when chaining bd export behind other measurements under six concurrent workers.

CONSEQUENCE FOR BRIEFS, and this supersedes the bare 'foreground only' line: the spine must be DETACHED to finish. That is not a violation and must not be briefed as one. What matters is not foreground-ness — it is (a) unpiped output, (b) the exit code captured on the SAME command line into a file, (c) the gate root line checked against the worker's own worktree, and (d) THE WORKER STAYING IN ITS TURN, polling the log and .exit file until it exits, rather than ending the turn to wait for a notification that may never arrive.

The catalogrows worker did exactly this and said so plainly: 'The run is detached only so it can finish; the output is unpiped and the exit code is captured the way you specified, and I am waiting on it rather than reporting around it.' That is the correct shape.

THE HARNESS'S REPORTED EXIT CODE DISAGREES WITH THE RUNNER'S OWN, AND IT ERRS TOWARD GREEN — measured directly 2026-09-05, TWICE IN ONE WORKER, both times the harness reporting 0 where the worker's own `.exit` file read 1.

This is no longer inference. Every worker brief in this project carries the instruction "quote the number you captured, never one the harness reports about the same run", and until now that rested on scattered observations that every disagreement surfaced as exit 0. One worker on rf2-xpd8 hit it twice in a single session and said so plainly: "The harness disagreed with my captured exit code twice, both times reporting 0 where my .exit file read 1. I quoted mine."

WHY THE DIRECTION MATTERS. A disagreement that errs toward RED is self-correcting — the worker investigates and finds nothing wrong. A disagreement that errs toward GREEN is silent: a failing gate reads as passing, the worker reports success, and the merge decision fails open. Both observed instances were the green direction.

THE PROCEDURE, unchanged but now evidenced:
  * Redirect the gate to a log and echo the runner's own `$?` to a `.exit` file, ON ONE COMMAND LINE IN ONE SHELL — never piped, because a pipeline's status is its LAST command's.
  * Quote the number from that file. An ABSENT exit file is NO VERDICT, not a pass.
  * Name the artefacts for the worktree AND the attempt, and confirm the file you read is your own current attempt's — a peer's run can overwrite a generic name, and a killed shell's orphan keeps writing to the file a restarted run is using.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE BOX'S OTHER SILENT-SUCCESS FAULTS, and the family is now large enough to state as a rule: ON THIS MACHINE, A REPORTED SUCCESS IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT SOMETHING HAPPENED. `cmd /c` junction create/remove exits 0 having done nothing; `pkill` anchored on a bare verb exits 0 having killed nothing; `grep -c $'\0'` returns a plausible count from an empty pattern; `grep -iF` aborts with empty stdout that reads as a clean zero; `gh run view --log-failed` returns 81 bytes while a run is in progress. CHECK THE WORLD, NOT THE STATUS.

AND A SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, the mirror image — A TEST CAN PASS WITH ZERO ASSERTIONS. Its first witness reported "2 tests, 0 assertions, exit 0" because `re-frame.schemas` is optional and late-bound, so the ns never loaded and the deftest bodies never ran. It caught this itself and fixed it by putting the require in the ns form. READ THE ASSERTION COUNT, NOT ONLY THE EXIT CODE: a green with an implausibly low assertion count is a vacuous run, and this repo's suites report both numbers.

A COMMITTED FILE WHOSE CONTENT HASH IS CITED MUST BE PINNED `text eol=lf` IN .gitattributes, OR THE RETENTION VERIFIES WRONG ON WINDOWS. Found by the rf2-rguy1 worker, 2026-08-08, and the audit that commissioned the work did not name it.

THE MECHANISM. This box runs core.autocrlf=true. An unpinned .json is CRLF-rewritten ON CHECKOUT, so the bytes in a Windows working tree are not the bytes that were committed. A reader who recomputes the digest to check the page's claim gets a DIFFERENT hash and concludes the evidence is corrupt — or, worse, a later pass "corrects" the published digest to the CRLF one and the Linux/CI reader then disagrees instead. Either way the retention looks done and verifies wrong.

WHY IT IS THE NASTY CLASS. The whole point of retaining evidence and citing its hash is that a fresh clone can verify a claim WITHOUT trusting the page. A silently platform-dependent digest defeats exactly that property while leaving every visible sign of success: file present, size right, page cites a hash, gates green. It is the same shape as a gate that exits 0 having verified nothing.

THE FIX, and it must be tested rather than assumed:
  1. Pin the path in .gitattributes: `path/to/*.json text eol=lf`
  2. Round-trip it: delete the file, `git checkout -- <path>`, re-hash, confirm the digest is unchanged and the file carries zero CR bytes.
Copying with `cp` and comparing with `cmp` is NOT sufficient — that tests the copy, not the checkout. Re-verify out of the git index: `git cat-file blob <rev>:<path> | sha256sum`.

WHERE IT APPLIES BEYOND THIS CASE: any committed artefact whose bytes are load-bearing — retained benchmark datasets, golden files, fixtures a test hashes, provenance sidecars. If a doc anywhere cites its sha256, it needs the pin.

RELATED, from the same worker: bind evidence to its inputs at BOTH ends. Forward, the producer should hash what it actually feeds the browser (the dist bundle the server hands out) before launching Chromium, and refuse a stale or absent dist rather than measuring it. Backward, a retained run gets a provenance sidecar whose digests are RE-HASHED FROM THE SURVIVING ARTEFACTS, never copied from the prose they are meant to corroborate.

I HAVE NOW TWICE READ A TRUNCATED OUTPUT AND REPORTED THE TRUNCATION AS THE ANSWER (2026-08-18/19). Same defect, two different tools, and the second time was WHILE CORRECTING SOMEONE ELSE FOR THE SAME KIND OF ERROR.

INSTANCE 1 — the tracker. Reading beads with "bd show <id> | head -N" gave me the DESCRIPTION, which is the oldest text, and I briefed two workers from it. Both beads newest comments said the work had already landed. Recorded as never-read-a-bead-with-head.

INSTANCE 2 — a census. Slice 2 of a retirement sweep reported two donor hits in implementation/shadow-cljs.edn. I re-derived and announced a CORRECTION to five, writing it onto the bead as a mayor count-correction so the worker would not brief from the smaller number. My command was:
    grep -nF "freehand" implementation/shadow-cljs.edn | head -5
The real count is ELEVEN. Lines 923-934 are an entire second block. I did not miss them through a bad pattern - the pattern was right and I truncated its output to five lines, then published "FIVE" as a measurement. The worker found eleven with the same command minus the head.

THE SHAPE, AND IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY MISCOUNT. head -N returns exactly N lines whenever there are at least N matches, so the output LOOKS complete at precisely the moment it is not. A truncated census is indistinguishable from a full one by inspection, and the number N is one you chose rather than one the tree gave you. It fails silently and it fails toward under-counting, which is the direction that sends a worker to fix part of a problem and report it closed.

THE RULE: NEVER PIPE A COUNT OR A CENSUS THROUGH head. If the output is long, that is information - use grep -c for the number, or read all of it. head is for glancing at a file, never for measuring anything you will assert. Where the number underwrites a brief or a bead comment, take it with -c and quote the command.

THE SECOND-ORDER LESSON, which is the one I keep having to learn: a MAYOR CORRECTING A WORKER IS STILL MAKING A CLAIM. Announcing "the count is five, not two" reads as authority and gets believed - the worker had to spend effort disproving my correction as well as the original. A correction deserves MORE verification than the thing it corrects, not less, precisely because it arrives with the weight of a second opinion.

Incident 2026-06-10 (commit 7aea52459): a mayor-loop heartbeat 'git add .beads/issues.jsonl; commit' caught the file MID dolt-re-export (transiently EMPTY/truncated) and committed+pushed a 0-line issues.jsonl to main (numstat tell: 'N deletions(-), 0 insertions' where N=full file size + working-tree still shows full content = staged blob is empty). Dolt DB was intact (bd reads fine); only the git-tracked jsonl export was truncated. RECOVERY: bd re-exports the full jsonl into the working tree; re-add + commit it. GUARD (now mandatory in the heartbeat): before committing .beads, (1) wc -l .beads/issues.jsonl must be > a sane floor (e.g. >1000), AND (2) after 'git add', verify the STAGED blob non-empty via 'git show :.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -l' BEFORE 'git commit' — abort the commit if either is empty. Authoritative integrity check = git cat-file -p <commit>:.beads/issues.jsonl | wc -lc (NOT 'git show origin/main:path' which can mis-resolve transiently).

A BASH HEREDOC ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP STRIPS BACKSLASHES, SO A REGEX INSIDE `python - <<'PY'` SILENTLY BECOMES A DIFFERENT REGEX AND RETURNS A FALSE ANSWER (2026-08-10).

REPORTED BY THE rf2-re0m WORKER after it nearly published a wrong number. It ran a
throwaway `python - <<'PY' ... PY` script to count Markdown links inside fenced regions.
The heredoc ate the backslashes in its patterns, so the pattern that should have matched
`](` matched nothing, and the script reported ZERO fenced links — on a tree that had seven.
It caught the discrepancy, re-ran everything from WRITTEN SCRIPT FILES, and got the true
counts.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE BACKSLASH BUG ALREADY ON RECORD. The known form is
`git worktree add` and `cmd /c mklink` losing path separators — those FAIL, loudly and
immediately, and you go fix the quoting. This form SUCCEEDS. Python compiles the mangled
pattern happily, the script exits 0, and you get a plausible number that is wrong in the
safe-looking direction: zero findings, nothing to do, ship it. A verification tool that
misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch.

THE RULE: never put a regex, or any backslash-bearing text, through a heredoc in the Bash
tool on this setup. Write the script to a file and run the file. If a throwaway script
reports a suspiciously clean result — zero findings where you expected some — re-run it from
a file BEFORE believing it.

AND THE GENERAL SHAPE, which is the reason to remember it: an ad-hoc verification script is
itself unverified. When its answer is the evidence for a claim, the script needs the same
red-first discipline as a test — prove it can report a non-zero count on known-bad input
before trusting its zero.

5. Then ensure the XRAY INTEGRATION is complete, correct, and quality.
6. Then ensure the COMMENTS are complete, correct, and quality.

SHARED-BUILD-ID CACHE TRAPS SELF-HEAL — every trial must start COLD (rf2-2rtt6.20).

The hicasso P0 lane runs N different programs under ONE shadow-cljs build id
(:hicasso-bench via --config-merge), so they share one build cache entry. Shadow
derives the cache dir from the build id alone, fixed in `new-build` BEFORE
--config-merge is applied, so --config-merge can NEVER reach :cache-root.

CARRIER is `shadow-js/` (npm-conversion cache), NOT the Closure name-stability
maps. `convert-sources-simple` invalidates its index on SHADOW-CACHE-KEY /
cache-affecting-options and never on the set of npm modules the build needs.
Reagent arms cache 14 modules with no react/jsx-runtime; a UIx arm built over
that index compiles clean and dies at first execution with "Cannot read
properties of undefined (reading 'd')".

TWO METHODOLOGY TRAPS worth remembering:
1. THE TRAP SELF-HEALS. Once the shadow-js index has accumulated every arm's
   modules, replaying the poisoning builds cannot take them back out. A control
   run from a WARM cache came back ALIVE and was meaningless. Every trial must
   rm -rf .shadow-cljs/builds/<id> first. A positive result without a DEAD
   control proves nothing.
2. DON'T BLOCK A/B COMPARISONS. Running all of main's reps then all of the
   branch's confounds the variable with box load drift — the same
   block-vs-interleave fault order_guard exists to catch. REFLECT the order.
   Blocked it looked like the branch caused an M2 guard refusal (main 0,0,0 /
   branch 2,0,0); reflected, MAIN refused and BRANCH passed in the same round.

When the harness clears the cache before every rep, a "clear the cache" fix is a
literal NO-OP in that comparison: both sides emit a byte-identical bundle
(sha256-verified), so any difference is variance BY CONSTRUCTION. That logical
argument beats statistics.

COST: clearing the whole per-build cache entry is ~free — warm 34s/26s vs
cleared 33s/37s. Time is JVM start + classpath + the Closure :advanced pass, not
the CLJS compile the cache holds. "It costs a full recompile" does not survive
measurement. Bonus: always-cleared builds are byte-DETERMINISTIC.

A MERGED-BUT-UNREAPED WORKTREE STILL REPORTS AS A HOT-FILE HOLDER UNDER A THREE-DOT DIFF — TEST MERGED-NESS WITH `git cherry` AND EXCLUDE IT (measured 2026-09-05). This is the THIRD correction to the holder check and it fails CLOSED, so it silently costs throughput rather than correctness.

THE SITUATION. resources-a's PR #9305 had MERGED and its changes were on main. Its worktree still existed at the old branch head, never rebased. `git -C <wt> diff origin/main...HEAD --name-only` therefore still listed spec/016-Resources.md, spec/API.md, both api-manifest sidecars and implementation/core/src/re_frame/core.cljc — because three-dot compares against the MERGE BASE, and a merged-then-unrebased branch still differs from its old base by exactly the commits that already landed. Every one of those files read HELD. All of them were free. I had been carrying spec/API.md as locked across three ticks partly on this reading, and it had been open the whole time.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS `git cherry`, WHICH ANSWERS 'ARE THESE COMMITS ALREADY UPSTREAM' RATHER THAN 'DO THESE TREES DIFFER':
    git cherry origin/main worker/<name>
Lines beginning `-` are already on main (matched by patch-id, so a REBASE MERGE still matches — which is exactly why the diff cannot see it and this can). Lines beginning `+` are genuinely unmerged. A branch whose output is all `-`, or empty, holds NOTHING: skip it entirely in the holder census, and reap it.

MEASURED, WITH A CONTROL THAT DISCRIMINATES — the point being that a rule which calls every worktree free is as useless as one that calls them all held:
    resources-a  merged(-)=1  unmerged(+)=0   <- PR merged; holds nothing
    ssrnode-d    merged(-)=1  unmerged(+)=0   <- PR merged; holds nothing
    uixdoc-a     merged(-)=1  unmerged(+)=0   <- PR merged; holds nothing
    devcon-a     merged(-)=0  unmerged(+)=1   <- PR #9306 OPEN; genuinely holds spec/009
    testfix-a    merged(-)=0  unmerged(+)=2   <- PR #9298 OPEN; genuinely holds its files
The two with open PRs separated cleanly from the three without.

SO THE HOLDER CHECK NOW HAS THREE CORRECTIONS, AND THEY FAIL IN DIFFERENT DIRECTIONS — which is why each had to be found separately:
  (1) Enumerate from `git worktree list`, NOT from open PRs. A worker with no PR yet holds files invisibly. Fails OPEN.
  (2) Use THREE-dot, not two-dot. Two-dot reports what MAIN changed on a stale branch. Fails CLOSED.
  (3) Skip worktrees whose branch `git cherry` says is already upstream. Fails CLOSED.
Plus `git status --porcelain` for uncommitted work, since a worker mid-edit may not have committed.

THE STANDING LESSON UNDERNEATH ALL THREE: reaping is not merely tidiness. An unreaped worktree actively corrupts the dispatch fence and throttles the fleet, and the symptom — 'nothing is dispatchable this tick' — looks exactly like a genuinely busy backlog. When saturation is blocked by locks, RE-VERIFY THE LOCKS before believing them; do not carry a lock forward across ticks on a previous tick's reading.

ASKING WHICH WORKER HOLDS A HOT FILE HAS TWO WRONG INSTRUMENTS, AND THEY FAIL IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS (measured 2026-09-05, five live worktrees).

THE DELIVERABLE is the fence question from loops.md S3: which of the hot-zone files (spec/009, spec/API.md, spec/Conventions.md, spec/Spec-Schemas.md, spec/006, spec/Tool-Pair.md ...) is currently held by a live worker, so a bead touching it stays sequenced rather than dispatched.

WRONG INSTRUMENT 1 - ASKING THE OPEN PRS. 'gh pr list --json files' enumerates only workers that have OPENED a PR. A worker mid-task has a worktree and commits but no PR, so it holds nothing visible. Measured: spec/009-Instrumentation.md read FREE by the PR sweep while devcon-a was actively editing it on worker/devcon-a. This UNDER-reports, and it fails OPEN - the reassuring answer is the wrong one, and dispatching on it manufactures the conflict the fence exists to prevent. ENUMERATE FROM 'git worktree list', not from PRs. (Same shape as the loops.md S4 instruction to start the stranded sweep from the WORKTREE list rather than the in_progress list - one door, two loops.)

WRONG INSTRUMENT 2 - TWO-DOT DIFF AGAINST origin/main. Having switched to worktrees, the natural query is 'git -C $w diff origin/main --name-only'. Two-dot reports files differing in EITHER direction, so for a branch whose base is stale it lists everything MAIN changed since the fork as well as what the WORKER changed. Measured on testfix-a: two-dot named 6 spec files, three-dot named 1. Four of the five extras (spec/006, spec/API.md, spec/Conventions.md, spec/Spec-Schemas.md) were trunk movement, not worker edits. This OVER-reports, holding four hot slots against nobody - it fails CLOSED, so it costs throughput rather than correctness, but it is the harder one to notice because a fence that is merely too tight never produces a symptom.

THE CORRECT READ combines both fixes and adds uncommitted work, since a worker mid-edit may not have committed yet:

  git worktree list | grep re-frame2-worktrees | awk '{print $1}' | while read -r w; do
    { git -C "$w" status --porcelain | awk '{print $2}'
      git -C "$w" diff origin/main...HEAD --name-only; } | tr -d '\r' | sort -u
  done

The 'tr -d $'\r'' is not decoration - see the jq/CRLF family; git is clean here but the pipeline is often joined with jq output.

CONTROL THAT DISCRIMINATES: run two-dot and three-dot on the same worktree and compare counts. Equal counts mean the branch is current and the two instruments agree by luck; differing counts localise the staleness to that worktree and tell you the two-dot answer was inflated. A single instrument agreeing with itself proves nothing.
