I CALLED THREE ORDINARY STALE WORKTREES "HUSKS" ALL SESSION, AND HUSK IS A TERM WITH AN OPERATIONAL CONSEQUENCE (2026-08-24).

THE METHOD DEFINES A HUSK PRECISELY: a partial removal, where the tool deregistered the worktree and deleted its metadata, then hit a lock and stopped. Its signature is four things -- it no longer appears in the worktree listing, pruning has nothing to clear, a status check inside it FAILS AND PRINTS NOTHING, and because of that a clean/dirty test reads it as CLEAN.

MY THREE FAIL ALL FOUR, and on the decisive axis they are the exact inverse: they are LISTED, their metadata directory is PRESENT, status works fine, and it reports them DIRTY (one staged file each). They are ordinary registered stale worktrees.

WHY THE WORD MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING LOOSE VOCABULARY: "husk" ROUTES TO A DIFFERENT REMEDY. The method says the ordinary removal path refuses a husk forever and that you must reach for the tool's acknowledged-husk path, which disarms links before deleting. Someone reading my sweep reports -- me, after a context roll -- would reach for that special path for trees where the ordinary path is the correct one, and would skip the ordinary path on the belief it cannot work.

THE OUTCOME HAPPENS NOT TO CHANGE, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED SO LONG. They stay either way. But the REASON differs, and the reason is what a later decision keys on: they stay because they are DIRTY and carry no completion report, not because they are unremovable-by-construction. Dirty is a state waiting never clears; husk is a state retrying never clears. Different remedies, different escalations.

NO DOCUMENT DEFECT. The definition is precise, testable in one command per criterion, and I never tested it -- I inherited the word from an earlier report and repeated it perhaps twenty times. THE CHECK IS CHEAP: does the worktree listing show it, and does a status check inside it return output? Two commands separate the two states completely.

GENERAL SHAPE: a term of art in the method carries its remedy with it. Using one loosely does not stay loose -- it silently prescribes.

CONSIDERED AND DELIBERATELY NOT FILED (2026-08-11): the theoretical clock-hold leak in hm/hydrate!. Recorded so a future auditor does not rediscover it, file it, and re-litigate a decision already taken.

THE OBSERVATION, from the rf2-4mvd / rf2-w2e6 worker (PR #7883), which reported it explicitly as "not a bead": hm/hydrate! installs the page-wide virtual clock (around mounted.cljs:798) immediately before handle-for, inside a setTimeout callback with nothing between them. IF handle-for ever threw there, the clock hold would leak — and because it sits in a timer callback, the throw would not reach the promise, so nothing would surface it.

THAT IS STRUCTURALLY THE SAME SHAPE AS rf2-4mvd, which was real and is now fixed: mount! installed the clock before mint-frame! and a throw escaped before any handle existed, leaving the page-wide clock installed for the rest of the run.

WHY IT IS STILL NOT WORK:
- Both beads scope their repair to mount! in terms. Widening a bounded repair on a hunch is the exact anti-pattern this project keeps paying for.
- handle-for is map-building. It does not realistically throw, whereas mint-frame!'s :initial-events path raises :rf.error/initial-events-step-failed BY DESIGN — a deliberate, reachable throw. That asymmetry is the whole difference between the two sites: one had a documented escape, this one has a hypothetical.
- The stance rejects speculative hardening. Filing it would be gold-plating, and the worker said so itself rather than quietly widening its diff, which was the right call twice over.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THE ANSWER — and this is the useful part of the record. File it if any of these becomes true:
- handle-for gains a genuine failure mode (validation, a lookup that can miss, anything that raises).
- Anything else is inserted between install-clock! and handle-for in that callback, widening the window.
- A hydrate! path is observed leaving a clock installed in practice. A reproduced symptom outranks this reasoning immediately; do not argue a live symptom away with this note.

DO NOT treat this entry as authority that the site is CORRECT. It is authority that the site was LOOKED AT, by someone who had just fixed the sibling defect, and judged not worth work under the current stance. Those are different claims, and the second is the only one anybody verified.

A BRANCH WITH UNLANDED COMMITS AND NO PR MAY BE A DELIBERATELY RETAINED RECORD, NOT A STRAND — check the owning bead's close reason before calling it stranded (2026-08-15 16:05 AUSEST).

MY HYGIENE PASS FILED rf2-fuuqd naming two branches as stranded work. Triage found ONE was superseded and the OTHER was never stranded at all. My heuristic — pushed commits, no PR, subject not on main — is necessary but not sufficient, and it misclassified a record the project had deliberately kept.

  worker/receipts-hic081  KEEP. rf2-hic-081 closed with, verbatim: 'Spike commits are pushed on worker/receipts-hic081 and RETAINED AS THE EXPERIMENT'S RECORD; nothing from them lands on main.' All four follow-ons closed and landed (#7898, #7878, #7879); the design is on main in specification.md, decision-brief.md and lanes/left-field-ideas.md; impl/receipt.cljs is correctly absent. No rebase, no PR, no bead owed. A future hygiene pass that 'rescues' it would re-litigate a closed decision.

  worker/fontlic-trei     DELETED by the mayor after verifying every claim independently. Its font-licensing problem DOES NOT EXIST on main: zero font binaries are tracked (git ls-tree matching .otf/.ttf/.woff/.eot returns nothing). Mike's own PR #8113 deleted the font outright at 17:05:00, TWO MINUTES AFTER the branch tip at 17:03:17 — and git merge-base --is-ancestor confirms they are SIBLINGS, not ancestor/descendant. Two answers to one question; the repo took the stronger one. rf2-trei is closed on exactly that and preserves the branch's durable finding verbatim, including the OFL text in the .ttf name table and both sha256s. Landing the branch would have RE-ADDED 123KB of binaries main deliberately dropped.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE OWNING BEAD'S CLOSE REASON, and it is cheap: search the tracker for the branch name before calling anything stranded. A retained record says so in the bead that closed it. A genuine strand has no such sentence.

A SECOND TEST THAT PAID HERE: git merge-base --is-ancestor <branch> origin/main. It separates 'superseded by a sibling' from 'never landed'. A sibling commit answering the same question the other way is invisible to a subject-match against main — the subjects differ, so the branch reads stranded while the question is settled.

THE ASYMMETRY STILL GOVERNS: calling a strand a ghost loses work; calling a record a strand merely wastes a dispatch. So the hygiene rule 'delete only branches whose PR is verifiably MERGED' remains right as the DEFAULT, and both these branches correctly survived it. Deletion here was a considered exception with the evidence written down, not a rule change.

CORRECTION 2026-09-07 (rf2-94l1). THE DISCRIMINATOR ABOVE IS RIGHT AND ITS COMMAND WAS BROKEN, in the reassuring direction. "Search the tracker for the branch name", run as `bd search '<branch>'`, DEFAULTS TO OPEN ISSUES -- and a retained-record ruling lives on a CLOSED bead by definition, so the prescribed check could never find one. It returns nothing, or it returns a previous sweep's own filing, and "nobody owns this branch" is exactly the answer that authorises deleting it. That false zero is what re-filed this settled question a third time (rf2-fuuqd -> rf2-7ngc -> rf2-jojz). Measured on worker/receipts-hic081: default 1 hit, --status closed 3, --status all 4.

USE --status all, NOT --status closed. Filtering to closed alone swaps one blind spot for another: it drops rf2-xcqk, the OPEN bead that carries the standing KEEP and its release condition. All-statuses is the superset and the only safe form.

AND NO STATUS FLAG IS ENOUGH, because bd search MATCHES TITLES AND IDS ONLY. A retention recorded in a CLOSE REASON -- which is where retentions are written -- is invisible to it at every status. Measured: `bd search "retained as the experiment" --status all` returns 0 while the export carries that phrase in 4 records; control `bd search "stranded sweep" --status all`, same two-word shape but present in a TITLE, returns 1. So the four hits above are luck: they are beads whose TITLES happen to name the branch. Grep .beads/issues.jsonl instead -- it carries titles, descriptions, notes and close reasons -- where "receipts-hic081" matches 7 records against bd search's 4. See [[bd-search-matches-titles-only-and-excludes-closed]].

THE CHECK, in full, before filing ANY branch as orphaned or stranded: `bd search '<branch>' --status all`, a grep of .beads/issues.jsonl for the branch name, and `bd memories`. The tracked normative copy is docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md section 5, "Branches", which carried no tracker check at all until rf2-94l1 added one. [[absent-remote-branch-is-the-signature-of-a-merge]] carried a second copy of the same broken instruction and is corrected alongside this one.

Hygiene reaped a live worker's worktree mid-gate (rf2-azopg, 2026-08-07): PR #7660 was merged while the worker's 'sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' was still running, and the hygiene loop then removed the worktree underneath it. node_modules vanished mid-run and the CLJS :node-test tier reported 5 failures in re-frame.test-quiet-shadow-node-cljs-test, ALL of them a spawned-subprocess 'Cannot find module react'. The failure looks like a real regression and is not one. HYGIENE RULE THE MAYOR BROKE (2026-07-25): do NOT prune a worker's worktree on 'its PR merged'. Prune only when BOTH hold: the PR is verifiably MERGED from that exact branch, AND the worker agent has actually reported completion. I pruned re-frame2-worktrees/fh-tfind-004d on the merge signal while its agent was STILL RUNNING; the deletion pulled the tree out from under its running gate, whose only output was 'bash: line 1: gate-logs/fastpr.log: No such file or directory' — a redirect failing because its cwd had been deleted. That notification LOOKED like a gate red and was not, which is the second harm: a phantom failure that could have triggered a pointless fix-worker. Nothing was lost only because the push-first instruction had already put both commits on origin; had the worker been holding its PR for the local spine (the old behaviour), the prune would have destroyed the only copy. docs/the-mayor-method/README.md already says it: 'leave local cleanup until the worker is closed and the worktree is verifiably clean' — I honoured the merge half and skipped the worker-closed half. Practical check before any prune: no live agent for that worktree, worktree git status clean, PR head == worktree branch read from 'git worktree list --porcelain'. Also note the partial-removal failure mode on Windows: file locks leave orphaned untracked trees (implementation/, spec/, tools/, site/, __pycache__) with no .git, already off the worktree registry so 'git worktree prune' is a no-op; deleting them is safe ONLY after confirming the tree's node_modules was a real npm ci directory and not a junction, and re-checking the mayor's own implementation/node_modules canary (~101 entries, must not be a reparse point).

I CREATED A DUPLICATE EXECUTOR BY INFERRING A WORKER'S DEATH FROM SHAPE (2026-07-25). A dispatched worker showed zero commits, no remote branch, and HEAD identical to origin/main after ~30 minutes, during a period when the operator had reported an internet outage. I concluded it had been killed at launch and re-dispatched a fresh agent onto ITS EXISTING worktree and branch. It was alive and mid-flight with ~203 insertions / 76 deletions plus a 147-line untracked namespace — all uncommitted.

THE METHOD ALREADY WARNS ABOUT EXACTLY THIS: 'zero commits, clean tree, no PR describes both an abandoned worker and one that started a minute ago; the discriminator is FRESHNESS, not shape.' I used shape.

WHAT SAVED IT: the second agent detected the collision from advancing file mtimes, deleted ONLY its own untracked near-duplicate file after verifying nothing referenced it, touched none of the peer's files, did not commit/push/PR, and reported. That is the behaviour to reward. The correct recovery was to SendMessage-resume the live peer and tell it to commit and push immediately — never a third executor.

MECHANICAL RULE, since 'check freshness' as a policy is what I failed to apply: BEFORE re-dispatching onto an existing worktree, require ALL THREE — (a) a recorded terminal notification for that agent (completed/failed/killed), (b) file mtimes under the worktree older than several minutes (check the newest source file, not just git state), and (c) git state showing no uncommitted work. Absent (a), assume ALIVE regardless of (b) and (c) and message it instead. An idle-looking worker costs a slot; a duplicate executor on one branch risks corrupting real work and wastes two agents.

COROLLARY: a worker that has been running a long time with zero commits is a PUSH-DISCIPLINE problem, not a liveness signal. The right intervention is 'commit and push now', not re-dispatch.

I DELETED THE MAYOR'S node_modules WITH THE DOCUMENTED RECIPE, BECAUSE `cmd /c rmdir` DID NOT EXECUTE FROM THE BASH TOOL. 2026-07-28, removing worktree composing-18216 (PR #7201) after its worker warned me it had junctioned `implementation/node_modules` into the mayor checkout.
WHAT HAPPENED, EXACTLY. I ran `cmd /c rmdir "<path>"` via the Bash tool. It printed the Windows banner and a fresh prompt — i.e. it launched an INTERACTIVE cmd shell and never ran the rmdir. The canary right after still read 101, which I misread as 'junction cleared' when it actually meant 'nothing happened yet'. `git worktree remove --force` then followed the live junction and emptied the real directory: canary 101 -> 0. Recovered with `npm ci` at `implementation/` (exit 0, ~4 min).
THE TWO CORRECTIONS. (1) `cmd /c rmdir` IS NOT RELIABLE FROM THE BASH TOOL ON THIS SETUP — use PowerShell instead: `[IO.Directory]::Delete(path, $false)` removes a junction without following it, and REFUSES a real populated directory, so it is self-verifying in both directions. (2) THE CANARY MUST BE READ AS A DELTA WITH A KNOWN EXPECTED VALUE, NOT AS A NUMBER THAT LOOKS FINE. After clearing a junction the correct assertion is `Test-Path <junction>` == False, not 'the mayor still has 101 entries' — the mayor ALWAYS has 101 entries until the moment it doesn't.
WHY THE SAFEGUARDS DID NOT FIRE. My hygiene sweep detects junctions correctly and has done so all session. This removal skipped it because the worker had already TOLD me there was a junction, so I went straight to the fix — and the fix was the untested half of the recipe. Knowing about the hazard is what let me skip the check that would have caught the failed remediation.

I DESTROYED A LIVE WORKER WORKTREE (2026-07-19) — deterministic branch names collide with HISTORICAL merged PRs.

WHAT HAPPENED: my deferred-cleanup loop removes a worktree when `gh pr list --head worker/<name> --state all` reports MERGED. I derive branch names deterministically from the bead id, so I dispatched rf2-vxgfnd.195 onto `worker/shadow-host-gates-195` — the SAME name a previous session had used for the same bead, whose PR #6030 merged on 2026-07-16. The cleanup matched that historical PR, and removed the live worktree plus the branch (local AND origin) while the worker was mid-run. Work lost, worker orphaned.

WHY THE OBVIOUS GUARDS DID NOT CATCH IT: the worktree was clean (worker had not committed yet) so the dirty-check passed; the PR state was genuinely MERGED so the state-check passed; `--state all` is what made a long-closed PR visible. Every individual condition was satisfied. This is the SECOND time I have removed a running worker worktree (the first was k8l1m), and the deferred-cleanup pattern I adopted after that incident did not prevent this one, because it addressed timing rather than identity.

TWO FIXES, USE BOTH:
1. MAINTAIN AN EXPLICIT LIVE-WORKER SKIP LIST. I dispatch the workers, so I know their worktree names — skip every one still running, unconditionally, before any state check. This is the reliable guard; the PR-state heuristic is the unreliable one.
2. REQUIRE THE MERGED PR TO BE *THIS* WORKTREE WORK, not merely same-named: compare `git -C <worktree> rev-parse HEAD` against the PR `headRefOid` (`gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid`), or require `mergedAt` to be LATER than the worktree creation. A name match alone proves nothing — bead ids are stable across sessions, so a re-dispatch of any partially-delivered bead reproduces the collision exactly.

GENERAL LESSON: a deterministic naming scheme makes names non-unique ACROSS TIME. Any cleanup keyed on a name will eventually match a historical artefact. Key destructive operations on identity (a SHA, a creation time), never on a name.

ALSO NOTE: a bead can stay legitimately OPEN after a PR citing it merges — #6030 delivered part of rf2-vxgfnd.195 (the final_schedule probe harness) while its four synthetic arms remained. So "a merged PR names this bead" does NOT mean the bead is done, and must never be used to infer cleanup safety either.

WHY THE BOARD MAKES THIS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN CARELESS: a merged-PR audit reopens a bead by APPENDING a note and leaving title and description untouched. `bd show` prints DESCRIPTION FIRST and notes last, so THE OLDEST TEXT IS THE MOST PROMINENT. On a board where roughly one bead is reopened per merged PR, most reopened beads are therefore misdescribed by their own most-visible field. `bd ready` compounds it by showing only the TITLE, which is older still.

THE ONLY THING THAT HAS ACTUALLY WORKED, and it worked all six times: every brief carries "THE BEAD OUTRANKS THIS BRIEF — read it bottom-up, newest note first, description LAST. Tell me where I am wrong." Six workers refused six wrong premises. That sentence is a MECHANISM, not a courtesy, and must never be trimmed for brevity.

AND THE SECOND-ORDER COST, which is worse than the wasted dispatch: a brief asserting a false premise with the mayors authority invites a worker to IMPLEMENT it. ROOT CAUSE: I compose a brief from context and reach for the id from recall, or I run bd create, do not capture the id it printed, and then refer to the bead later as though I know its id. bd create output ends with Priority/Status lines and I have repeatedly not scrolled to the id.

And after every bd create, immediately echo the created id (or grep it back by title) BEFORE referring to the bead again.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a wrong id in a brief sends a worker to bd show on a nonexistent bead. Three audit workers hit that and had to be corrected mid-flight. Worse, a plausible-but-wrong id could resolve to a REAL DIFFERENT bead and silently redirect work — that has not happened yet and is the failure I am actually guarding against.

I OVERRODE A RECORDED DEFERRAL WITHOUT ACKNOWLEDGING IT — SECOND TIME TODAY — AND THE WORK TURNED OUT JUSTIFIED FOR A REASON NEITHER I NOR THE DEFERRAL KNEW (2026-07-26).

rf2-jl7gz carried a note from the #7051 audit: "STAYS DEFERRED — measured zero corpus exposure". I dispatched it anyway, in a brief that never mentioned the deferral. The worker built it and FLAGGED the override rather than silently complying — same shape as rf2-n4by4 earlier the same day, where the bead said "ENFORCEMENT NEEDS A RULING, do not pick one silently" and my brief silently picked one. Two instances in one session of the same defect: I read beads for FACTS and miss their RECORDED DISPOSITIONS. A deferral, a reserved ruling and a held decision are all instructions addressed TO ME, and a brief that overrides one without saying so leaves the tracker unable to distinguish a considered reversal from an oversight.

BUT THE DISPATCH WAS RIGHT, AND THE REASON IS THE GENERALISABLE PART: THE DEFERRAL WAS MEASURED ON ONE DIRECTION OF A BIDIRECTIONAL GATE. "Zero corpus exposure" meant no FALSE GREEN was reachable today — no bad row passing. The worker found the same miscount was ALSO COSTING EVIDENCE: the `~#js [fx]` unquote island and the reader-conditional arm pairing were ALREADY DROPPING REAL EDGES, so the FALSE-RED direction was live and had never been measured. In its words, the miscount "was costing evidence as well as inventing it".

SO THE RULE: A DEFERRAL MEASURED ON ONE DIRECTION OF A TWO-DIRECTION CHECK IS NOT A DEFERRAL. Before honouring "zero exposure" on any gate that can be wrong in both directions — a census, a redaction, a refusal, a roster — ask which direction was measured. Under-matching and over-matching have different corpora and only one of them is usually counted.

THE OTHER THING WORTH KEEPING, because it is the cleanest instance yet of a probe that cannot discriminate: the bead own axis-2 case (`#_#?(:clj (def fx …))`) REDS UNDER THE OLD READER TOO, measured not assumed. Read short it does leave `(:clj (def fx …))` standing exactly as the bead describes — but `_DEFINER_RE` is anchored to a top-level form HEAD and the survivor head is `:clj`, not `def`, so no binding registers and the row reds either way. The wrapper the miscount leaves is INERT. A TAG target discriminates because there the survivor IS the form: `#_#js (def fx …)` leaves the `def` at top level to bind the fixture, giving a silent green. The worker kept the `#?` case but RELABELLED it as a regression guard on the anchoring rather than as evidence. That is the right disposal for a case that cannot fail for the reason it was written.

AND A SELF-CAUGHT REGRESSION WORTH THE SWEEP: `##NaN` is written straight into the adapter suites, and the first draft read the second `#` as a tag over `NaN`, turning `##Inf` into `##Inf 3`. Its own extent table caught it. When extending a reader rule, enumerate the OTHER `#`-prefixed forms — `#(`, `#{`, `#"`, `#=`, `#!`, `##`, and namespaced maps `#:ns{…}` — and say which need the rule and which do not.

I BROKE THE PIPELINE-EXIT-CODE RULE I BRIEF WORKERS ABOUT, IN MY OWN MERGE LOOP (2026-08-11).

WHAT I WROTE, trying to be defensive about the known post-merge pull abort:

  git pull --ff-only origin main 2>&1 | tail -1 || git pull --rebase origin main 2>&1 | tail -2

THE `||` NEVER FIRED. A pipeline's exit status is its LAST command's, and `tail` succeeds whatever it is fed. So the fallback was unreachable, and both merges left the checkout diverged (1/2 then 2/9) with the reassuring line "fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting." printed and ignored. No damage — I noticed on the ref comparison and rebased cleanly — but the guard I wrote was decorative.

WHY IT IS WORTH RECORDING RATHER THAN JUST FIXING: this is the SAME defect class the method documents for gate runners, and I have put it in every worker brief tonight — "never pipe a gate through tail/head/grep, a pipeline's exit status is its last command's". I then wrote exactly that pattern into my own control flow, because I was thinking about the OUTPUT (I only wanted the last line) and not about the EXIT CODE. The trap is that piping for brevity and branching on success look independent and are not.

THE CORRECTED SHAPE, for any command I want to both trim and branch on:

  git pull --ff-only origin main > /tmp/pull.log 2>&1; rc=$?; tail -1 /tmp/pull.log
  [ "$rc" -eq 0 ] || git pull --rebase origin main > /tmp/pull.log 2>&1

Redirect to a file, capture the code, THEN trim for display. Never let a display filter sit between a command and a branch that reads its result.

MAYOR-SPECIFIC: the post-merge pull now aborts routinely, because the audit hook pushes to main asynchronously and my own beads checkpoint commits locally. So the fallback is the COMMON path, not the exception — which makes an unreachable fallback exactly as bad as no fallback. Verify the outcome by comparing HEAD to origin/main rather than trusting either the printed line or a branch that may not have run.

I PRESCRIBED AN UNSOUND FIX AND A WORKER CAUGHT IT BY MEASURING (2026-08-01, rf2-8vvdo / PR #7336). Record the lesson, not the incident.

WHAT HAPPENED. A core test reddened under load because it asserted a PROCESS-WIDE weak-map count for strict equality; the diagnosing worker filed rf2-8vvdo proposing (<= (.size m) baseline) as a STRONGER replacement, and I briefed that fix as-is while telling the implementing worker 'the fix must be stronger, never weaker' and 'prove it still catches the original defect'.

THE IMPLEMENTING WORKER REFUSED IT AND WAS RIGHT. (<= (.size m) baseline) cures the false RED by buying a false GREEN under the same load: a SIBLING entry expunging in our entry's place satisfies it while OUR entry is still leaked. It did not argue this — it MEASURED it, with a probe of (and (<= (.size m) baseline) (.containsKey m our-key)) that PASSED, i.e. the proposed assertion held with the leaked entry still in the map, before the throwable was even released. That is precisely the fail-open class my own brief forbade.

THE CORRECT SHAPE, which the bead itself had offered as an alternative: assert THE ENTRY'S OWN ABSENCE, not a population count. (= (inc baseline) (.size m)) -> (= 1 (count our-keys)); (= baseline (.size m)) -> (not (.containsKey m our-key)). It also found the bead had diagnosed only ONE of the two assertions — the sibling assertion carried the identical defect and would have left the test load-sensitive.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is mine: WHEN A BEAD PROPOSES A SPECIFIC FIX, THE BRIEF MUST TREAT IT AS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT A SPECIFICATION. I passed a diagnosing worker's proposed patch through to an implementing worker with my authority attached, which converts a suggestion into an instruction and invites compliance over judgement. Correct form: state the DEFECT and the ACCEPTANCE CRITERION (here: 'the assertion must fail when this entry leaks, whatever else the process is doing'), cite the bead's proposal as one candidate, and say explicitly that a better shape is welcome and a refusal with evidence is a complete answer.

SECOND-ORDER POINT WORTH KEEPING: an assertion about a SHARED, PROCESS-WIDE quantity can almost never state a claim about ONE participant. Prefer identity over population whenever the property is about a specific object — count-based proxies fail open under concurrency in both directions.

I REPEATED THE gh --jq --arg BUG AFTER RECORDING IT (2026-07-26). gh accepts the jq PROGRAM as the argument to --jq, so writing "gh pr list --json ... --jq --arg B \"$b\" \x27<program>\x27" makes --arg the program and the real program a stray argument. The query returns EMPTY, not an error. I hit this once on a hygiene sweep where every PR read as pr=none, recorded it, and then wrote the identical construction again on the next hygiene sweep.

THE FIX: fetch once to a file with gh --json, then pipe/read that file with the jq BINARY, where --arg is valid: gh pr list --json number,state,headRefName > /tmp/prs.json, then jq -r --arg B "$b" \x27...\x27 /tmp/prs.json.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE TYPO: both times, the broken query fed a DESTRUCTIVE decision — branch deletion gated on "is this PR merged?". Both times the gate FAILED SAFE and refused, because an empty result does not match *MERGED. That is the only reason a broken query did not delete a live branch. Design destructive gates so the empty/unknown case refuses; do not rely on the query being right.

TWELFTH WRONG MEASUREMENT THIS SESSION, and the first outright repeat. The others were varied (loose greps matching comments, row-count as a proxy for content, diffing a worktree against moved main, reading a file before the pull landed, --is-ancestor after a rebase-merge). This one I had already written down. Recording a trap is not the same as building the habit that avoids it — for shell constructions specifically, the habit that works is: never put --arg on a gh command line.

MY RECURRING BRIEF DEFECT IS OVERSTATING A GATE'S OR A FENCE'S SCOPE — TWICE IN ONE SESSION, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS (2026-08-21, found by the method-reread loop grading its own briefs).

INSTANCE 1 — THE HOT ZONE. I wrote 'spec/ is HOT ZONE and single-toucher' into a brief and carried it generally. CLAUDE.md's hot-zone bullet is an ENUMERATION of 8 named spec pages, and git ls-files 'spec/*.md' returns 52. A blanket fence covers 44 pages the tree never asked to serialise. Cost direction: COVERAGE — a worker warned off a file nobody holds declines work it was free to take, and nothing on screen says so. See [hot-zone-names-eight-spec-pages-not-the-spec-tree].

INSTANCE 2 — THE FENCED-LINK RULE. I pasted into EVERY brief this session: 'Both gates strip fenced code blocks before they read a single link... if your edit lands inside a fence, neither gate is your gate.' That is FALSE for docs/design/hicasso/ and docs/the-mayor-method/, which is where nearly every worker this session was editing. scripts/check_doc_slugs.py:1708 sets FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES = ('docs/design/hicasso', 'docs/the-mayor-method'), and its own header says: 'In the trees listed in FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES a markdown doc link inside a fence is itself reported. Everywhere else it is SILENTLY skipped.' CLAUDE.md states the exception correctly; my boilerplate dropped it.

THE SHARED SHAPE, and it is what makes this one lesson rather than two: BOTH ERRORS TOOK A GENERAL RULE AND DROPPED ITS CARVE-OUT. The hot-zone rule has a list; I used a glob. The fence rule has an exception roster; I used the general case. In each the general half is memorable and the carve-out is not, which is the same failure mode the PROJECT STANCE paraphrase has — the lenses survive a summary and the when-to-stop clauses do not.

WHICH DIRECTION EACH RUNS, because they differ and both are quiet. Instance 1 understates what a worker MAY TOUCH. Instance 2 understates what a gate COVERS, so the worker hand-checks (harmless) and then MISREPORTS coverage in its PR body — the same both-directions misreporting the fast-spine-gap clause already warns about. Neither produces an error message.

THE FIX THAT GENERALISES: when a brief states a gate's or a fence's scope, NAME THE CONSTANT OR THE LIST IN THE TREE rather than paraphrasing it — FENCED_DOC_LINK_TREES, DEFAULT_ROOTS, CLAUDE.md's hot-zone bullet. A prose list drifts and this repository has been bitten by exactly that before (rf2-yxuta, rf2-8pb5k). Naming today's value alongside the constant is useful; presenting it AS the definition is the defect.

WHERE THE FIX LANDED: .claude/commands/mayor-dispatch.md, which governs how a dispatch brief is written and may name repository paths and script names freely. NOT docs/the-mayor-method/**, which is generic by design and carries no repo specifics — putting it there would be the layering error the method-reread loop exists to catch.

ANY BEAD THAT ADDS AN `:rf.error/*` ID IS A FORCED spec/009 TOUCH, SO IT IS NEVER HOT-ZONE-FREE (2026-08-10, found by the rf2-hic-007 worker).

WHAT HAPPENED. I dispatched rf2-hic-007 with the surface fenced to "the macro and error
files only" and treated it as parallel-safe against five other live workers. The worker
decided, correctly by my fence, to REPORT spec-drift rather than edit a hot-zone file — and
then the fast-PR spine failed it. `check_keyword_catalogue_drift` CHECK A reds on a new
`:rf.error/*` id unless spec/009-Instrumentation.md is edited IN THE SAME PR. It is an
explicit same-PR co-edit invariant, not a nightly reconciliation.

So the edit was mandatory, and the bead was hot-zone work that neither the bead nor my
brief had classified as such.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR DISPATCH, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. spec/* is on the fixed hot-zone
list: sequential, never parallel. If two beads that each mint a diagnostic id run
concurrently, both are forced into spec/009 and they collide — and neither one's stated
surface says "spec/". The collision is invisible at dispatch time unless you ask the extra
question.

THE RULE: before dispatching, ask whether the bead can plausibly MINT A NEW DIAGNOSTIC ID.
If yes, treat it as touching spec/009 and sequence it against every other id-minting bead,
regardless of what its Surface line says. Beads that obviously qualify: a new refusal, a new
error shape, a complaint-catalogue entry, anything the guide teaches as "refuses with ...".
rf2-hic-021 (the complaint catalogue) is the clearest future instance — it mints ids by
definition.

AND THE GENERAL SHAPE: a bead's stated Surface line is what its AUTHOR expected to touch,
not what the gates will force. A repo-wide co-edit invariant can drag any bead into a hot
file. Where a gate enforces "change X and Y together", X's owners inherit Y's contention.

AN ID-SET COMPARISON BETWEEN THE BEADS DATABASE AND THE COMMITTED EXPORT CANNOT SEE AN EDIT. It answers
"has a bead appeared or vanished?", never "has a bead CHANGED?" -- so a peer that edits an existing
bead's notes or description moves the database without moving any count, and the guard reports IN SYNC.

MEASURED 2026-09-17. The every-tick check adopted for the Xray review wave compared non-terminal bead
IDs in `bd list --limit 0 --json` against the same set in `git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl`. It caught
six peer-filed beads that existed only in Dolt. It would NOT have caught the peer appending a resume
plan to the epic's notes, which is the single most load-bearing edit of that wave -- a 3 KB block whose
loss would strand three review slices with no record of when or whether they were coming back.

THE FIX IS ONE FIELD: compare `updated_at` per bead as well as the id set.

    DB       -> {id: updated_at}
    export   -> {id: updated_at}
    drift     = ids present in both whose updated_at differs

Measured working on the epic in both directions: with notes identical it read 0 drift, and the bead's
own updated_at agreed to the second (2026-09-17T06:20:54Z) across DB and export.

THE SHAPE WORTH CARRYING: a guard written against "things appear and vanish" is blind to "things change",
and the blindness is invisible because the guard keeps passing. It is the same reassuring-direction
failure the guard itself was written to catch, one level in -- which is the tell that a guard deserves
its own control, not just the thing it guards. Take the control from the target: edit something, confirm
the guard notices.

exists at all) and [[ready-is-not-dispatchable-report-beads-list-as-ready]] (the other way bd's honest

identical? ON A KEYWORD LITERAL IS JVM-SOUND AND CLJS-UNSOUND — it silently makes a sentinel check unreachable on CLJS. Found by the rf2-6t6qk/rf2-uoy6m worker (#6452), 2026-07-19, while making the trace deferral seam cross-platform.

THE BUG: deferred-continue marked "baseline unread" with a ::unread KEYWORD and compared it with identical?. On the JVM keywords are interned so identical? works. ON CLJS KEYWORD LITERALS ARE NOT GUARANTEED REFERENCE-EQUAL, so the check never matched — every call fell through to level-testing the LIVE predicate instead. Consequence: a cascaded :rf.event/dispatched envelope whose target-live? was unbound post-drain read FALSE and THE EVENT WAS SILENTLY DROPPED. Not an exception — a dropped event.

THE META-LESSON, the important half: this was the CLJS-ONLY FACE of rf2-eaxnai REGRESSION 1. The JVM cure shipped in PR #6365 and looked complete; the CLJS half of the same defect survived undetected because no CLJS test exercised the path. A cross-host .cljc fix is NOT done when the JVM suite is green. It surfaced here only because making the seam cross-platform FORCED the CLJS gate to run it (4 cofx_cljs_test failures), and the worker instrumented the flush to diagnose rather than working around it. Fix was a dedicated OBJECT sentinel, not a keyword.

RULE: in .cljc, never use identical? against a keyword/string/number literal as a sentinel — use a dedicated object value. And when a .cljc correctness fix ships green on ONE host, ASK EXPLICITLY whether the other host exercises the same path; if no test does, that is a GAP, not a pass. Cross-ref rf2-eaxnai REGRESSION 1, PR #6365 (JVM-only cure), PR #6452 (cross-host fix).

ALSO FROM #6452 — JVM GATE TIMEOUTS ON THIS BOX ARE RESOURCE CONTENTION, NOT HANGS. Repeated 10-minute harness timeouts on implementation/core clojure -M:test were environmental: jstack showed the JVMs actively inside clojure.test with NO Java-level deadlock and no "waiting to lock". Cause: multiple agents running JVMs concurrently, AND each timed-out run ORPHANS a ~1.8 GB JVM that compounds contention. Worker guidance: if a JVM gate times out, jstack before concluding hang, kill YOUR OWN orphaned JVMs only, re-run. Mayor guidance: saturating 6 workers that each run a full JVM suite is a real resource ceiling on this machine — a timing-out gate is a signal to check concurrency, not to assume a stuck worker.

A CLJS GUARD WRITTEN WITH identical? ON KEYWORD LITERALS IS ALWAYS FALSE IN A DEV BUILD, AND AN ABSENCE-ASSERTING SUITE STAYS GREEN OVER IT (2026-08-19).

Measured by rf2-oaksj (PR #8508). The first implementation of the client-only adoption trace used identical? to compare keyword literals. identical? is reference equality, and a DEV build emits no shared constants table, so the two literals are distinct objects and the guard never fired. Nothing was ever emitted.

WHY IT SURVIVED ITS OWN TEST SUITE, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING. Every row of the first suite asserted an ABSENCE — no event here, no event there, at most once. A mechanism that emits NOTHING AT ALL satisfies every absence assertion perfectly. So the suite was GREEN OVER DEAD CODE, and it would have stayed green forever. This is the hollow-gate shape exactly: the control could not catch its own case, and the proof of coverage was the blind spot.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: a sabotage run that came back GREEN. The worker interrogated the control instead of believing it. That is the method rule "a green sabotage run is a reason to stop, not to proceed" paying for itself on a real defect rather than a hypothetical.

TWO RULES:
1. In CLJS, compare keywords with = , not identical?. Under :advanced a shared constants table can make identical? appear to work, so this defect PASSES IN PRODUCTION AND FAILS IN DEV — the opposite of the usual direction, and it will not reproduce in a release-build check.
2. A test suite for an emitter must prove the POSITIVE case. If every assertion is an absence, the suite cannot distinguish "correctly silent" from "structurally incapable of speaking". Add at least one row that fails when nothing is emitted.

The fix taken was to switch to booleans, which REMOVES the failure mode rather than repairing the comparison — the right shape, per the rule that a hollow control is replaced rather than patched.

TO PROVE A REPRODUCED BEHAVIOUR IS CORRECT RATHER THAN DEFECTIVE, IMPLEMENT THE FIX AND MEASURE WHAT IT BREAKS. Established 2026-09-05 on rf2-f3yl, and it is the strongest form of a "not a defect" verdict this project has produced.

THE SHAPE. A bead claimed `reg-flow`, called cold outside a drain, does not materialise a new flow's initial output until some later unrelated drain — the same shape as a sibling defect (rf2-g1zb) that HAD been fixed the day before. The premise held: reproduced three ways with the db seeded first, each with an empty `:rf.event` trace proving nothing drained, including two arms the bead never predicted (a re-registration returns the PREVIOUS derive's value).

THE WORKER THEN BUILT THE SYMMETRIC FIX ANYWAY — the one the bead's own "if it reproduces" plan called for — and ran the suite: **30 failures and 69 errors**, from a green 253/6119. And the errors gave the reason rather than merely the count: `reg-flow` adds a flow that has NEVER RUN, so settling forces a first evaluation at a moment the caller did not choose; the direct form is documented for boot code that registers BEFORE it seeds; so that evaluation throws `:rf.error/flow-eval-exception` out of `reg-flow` itself. A `:derive` is not required to be total on nil.

THAT IS QUALITATIVELY BETTER EVIDENCE THAN AN ARGUMENT. "This is intended behaviour" is an opinion; "the fix produces 69 errors and here is the mechanism" is a measurement. It also protects against the opposite failure — a worker who reasons its way to "not a defect" and is simply wrong ships nothing and no one finds out.

WHEN TO REACH FOR IT: any bead whose verdict is heading toward "reproduced but correct", "works as designed", or "the premise holds but should not change". The cost is one implementation the worker then reverts; the return is a close reason a third carrier cannot reopen on reasoning alone.

TWO COROLLARIES THE SAME WORKER ESTABLISHED:
  * **A SIBLING DEFECT IS NOT A TEMPLATE.** The clear-flow case WAS a defect and this one is not, and the distinction is precise: `clear-flow` leaves a value no live flow OWNS (orphaned, incoherent), while a re-registration's stale value IS owned and is refreshed unconditionally on the next drain (merely late). "Same shape as the one we just fixed" is a hypothesis, not an inheritance.
  * **A SPEC THAT EXCLUDES SOMETHING WITHOUT SAYING WHY INVITES THE QUESTION BACK.** `spec/013-Flows.md` explicitly excluded `reg-flow` from the settle guarantee — it was not silent — but gave NO REASON, which is exactly why the question was reopened one day after the sibling landed. Recording the REASON alongside an exclusion is what stops the same bead being refiled. The worker closed that gap as its deliverable.

AND A CAUTION ABOUT FRESH CARVE-OUTS: the exclusion sentence this bead asked to revisit was ONE DAY OLD, added by the sibling's own PR as a scope fence rather than as a considered ruling. Check the age and provenance of a carve-out before treating it as settled doctrine — a fence someone erected yesterday to bound their own PR is not a decision.

RELATED: [[a-cljs-test-double-must-mirror-the-arity-shape-not-just-the-arity-used]].

IN_PROGRESS IS A BLIND SPOT IN THE DISPATCH LOOP — audit it every few ticks, not just bd ready. On 2026-07-19 I found rf2-kxkag (P2) and rf2-lgeron (P3) sitting IN_PROGRESS with every stated blocker long since cleared: kxkag waited on rf2-74vlo (CLOSED), lgeron on rf2-sy7zr (CLOSED), rf2-vxgfnd.96.3 (CLOSED) and four surfaces that were all free. Both were fully dispatchable and INVISIBLE, because `bd ready` does not list in-progress beads and every saturation check I run reads from `bd ready`. They would have sat indefinitely.
SAME SHAPE AS the epic-child undercount (see backlog-counting-bd-list-status-open-excludes-epic): a whole CLASS invisible to the count in use. Different mechanism, identical consequence — I under-dispatched while believing the pool was drained.
THE CHECK: `bd list --status=in_progress --limit 0`, then for each, confirm a worker is ACTUALLY live. If none is, read the NOTES: it is either (a) a stale claim for shipped work -> close with evidence, (b) a PARTIAL delivery whose blockers may have cleared -> re-verify each blocker and DISPATCH, or (c) genuinely held on an operator ruling -> leave.

⚠️ AND THE TRAP THAT ALMOST BIT: my first instinct was to close all three as delivered, because their commits ARE in main. TWO CARRIED EXPLICIT "PARTIAL" MARKERS — one written by me: "PARTIAL in #6310 — DO NOT CLOSE ON THAT MERGE." A merged PR citing a bead does NOT mean the bead is done. Precedents this session: #6030 merged a FIFTH arm of rf2-vxgfnd.195 while all four DESCRIPTION arms remained; rf2-84173 shipped its second arm while AC1 and AC3-arm-1 stayed undelivered. CLOSING WOULD HAVE BURIED THE REMAINDER PERMANENTLY — a closed bead never resurfaces in any count.
RULE: before closing any bead on a merged PR, grep its NOTES for PARTIAL / remain / not delivered / arm N / AC-N. If the marker is there, the bead stays open and the remainder gets dispatched.

INLINING A PLAIN-`defn` HELPER INTO A FRESCO BOUNDARY IS THE RULED REPAIR; HEADING IT IS THE FOOTGUN.
THE DIRECTION IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT `render-panel!`'s DOCSTRING IMPLIES, AND THAT DOCSTRING IS
WRONG TWICE.

Measured 2026-09-11 by a zero-edit research dispatch against the sixteen already-migrated Xray files,
after I had spent several briefs asserting the opposite from one docstring.

THE RULING: HD-016, `docs/design/fresco/decisions.md:1031`. A head-position view var is a boundary
child; a plain function CALL inlines into the enclosing boundary, and any `sub` it performs DONATES
its read upward. The codec's own error text names both remedies -- "call it, or make it a view"
(`implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco/impl/codec.cljs:1786`) -- and `sub`'s public docstring
(`implementation/fresco/src/re_frame/fresco.cljc:433`) says reads work "inside an inlined helper".

THE MECHANISM, WHICH IS WHY HEADING IS WORSE RATHER THAN MERELY DIFFERENT. `current-frame` reads the
React context off the IN-FLIGHT component. A `reg-view` carries a `:contextType`; a plain `defn` does
not. So a helper CALLED inside a boundary body sees the boundary as the in-flight component and
resolves the frame correctly, while the SAME helper HEADED makes Reagent mint a component for the
plain fn, which has no `:contextType`, resolves nil, and raises. `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md`
calls this the "Plain-fn footgun".

AND THERE IS NO `:rf/default` FALLBACK. `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:1996` states the ambient
read "resolves to nil and RAISES `:rf.error/no-frame-context` -- the operation fails fast rather
than silently routing to a conventional default. There is no silent fall-through to `:rf/default`."
Confirmed at `implementation/core/src/re_frame/views/provider.cljs:247`, where `current-frame`
bottoms out at nil and the docstring says the runtime never synthesises `:rf/default`.

WHY THE DOCSTRING READS AS IF IT GENERALISES, AND WHY IT DOES NOT. `render-panel!` builds its
provider-wrapped panel INSIDE A PLAIN FUNCTION, so calling the panel view at that point would
evaluate outside any React render at all -- no in-flight component, nil, raise. Its conclusion is
right FOR THE MOUNT SEAM and says nothing about an arbitrary helper deep inside an
already-provided tree. Those are different positions with opposite answers.

WHAT INLINING GENUINELY COSTS, so the trade is made on mechanism rather than impression:
  NOTHING LOST  frame routing (improved), substrate reads (they donate upward).
  REAL          reconciliation identity -- no component of its own, so no memo bail-out.
  REAL          re-render granularity -- a donated read invalidates the WHOLE enclosing boundary.
                This is a live design input: Xray keeps `tab-bar` and `detail-panel` as SEPARATE
                boundaries reading the same slot precisely so a tab click does not re-render the
                panel below.
  REAL          keys -- an inlined item in a `for` has no element of its own to key; the remedy is a
                keyed fragment around the call.
  NOT AT ISSUE  per-instance state would be fatal, but a Fresco boundary body has no per-instance
                storage either, so no capability is surrendered.

THE TWO QUESTIONS THAT DECIDE A SITE, both answerable by reading it:
  Q1 Does the helper answer hiccup, and is that hiccup head-free ALL THE WAY DOWN?
     Yes -> inline. No -> island it behind `as-child`, or promote the offending descendant.
     THE SECOND HALF IS THE ONE THAT BITES: a call site is not evidence of a head-free subtree --
     only reading what the callee returns is. Use a TRANSITIVE instrument that crosses namespaces.
  Q2 Does it read the substrate, or hold form-2 state? Read-only is still fine to inline.

AND THE CENSUS TRAP THAT COMES WITH IT: a `reg-view` head grades `:invalid` down the IDENTICAL codec
arm as a plain `defn`, because `boundary-head?` reads one own property that only `defview` sets. Any
head census that counts only plain `defn`s understates the work by roughly two-thirds.

INSTRUMENT NOTE, MEASURED: a pattern matcher over-counts head sites by about a quarter. Parameter
vectors, `:keys` destructuring, `:refer` vectors and `get-in` PATH vectors whose first element
happens to share a name with a top-level `defn` all present as heads. Use a real s-expression reader
that tracks lexical scope, and control it against a subtree with a hand-written census.

Related: [[reagent-as-element-hollow-for-meta-vs-attrs-keys]].

ENUMERATING THE BLOCKING STATUSES IS FAIL-OPEN. INVERT IT (2026-08-10).

FOUND BY THE rf2-vfsrd WORKER against the live CLI, not by reading docs. The merge criterion said "zero QUEUED and zero IN_PROGRESS". The GitHub CLI also returns REQUESTED, WAITING and PENDING. A check in any of those three is neither QUEUED nor IN_PROGRESS, so a blocklist of two names reads it as absent and the PR looks settled.

THE CORRECT FORM IS POSITIVE: every run at the CURRENT HEAD SHA must be COMPLETED. Then an unanticipated status blocks instead of vanishing - the same inversion the provenance-pins gate needed when its trailing-character blacklist accepted %3F, : and & (rf2-styo). Twice in one day, the same defect shape: enumerate what is bad and the unimagined case defaults to accepted.

MY OWN SWEEP SURVIVED ONLY BY ACCIDENT. I count total, ok, skip, canc, fail, q, inprog and I check that ok+skip == total. That sum catches a REQUESTED check, because it would be inside total and outside every named bucket. But the arithmetic was doing work I had not consciously assigned it. State the rule as: ok+skip must EQUAL total, and separately every run must be COMPLETED. Do not rely on q==0 and inprog==0 alone.

THE COMMAND MUST ALSO BE ABLE TO PERFORM ITS OWN JOIN, and the prescribed one could not. `gh run list`'s table has NO headSha column and `gh pr checks` has NO conclusion field, so the documented spelling could not key runs to the head SHA at all. The worker verified both against the live CLI and wrote an executable form: gh pr view --json headRefName,headRefOid, then gh pr checks --json name,state,bucket, then gh run list --branch <head> --commit <oid> --json status,headSha,name.

LESSON BEYOND THE CRITERION: a documented command is not a verified command. If a rule prescribes a check, run the check once and confirm the fields it names actually exist.

"IS THROWN?" IS NOT A WITNESS. A SABOTAGE PROVED IT GREEN (2026-08-10).

WHAT HAPPENED. The rf2-hic-011 worker built the I7 ambient-read legality matrix and ran the bead's own named sabotage: remove read-key!'s nil-frame guard. It expected the escaped-read rows to red. THE READS STILL THREW - from subscribe-once, with :rf.error/no-frame-context instead of :rf.error/hicasso-sub-outside-render. So a row written as (is (thrown? ...)) would have stayed GREEN under the exact perturbation the bead named as its acceptance sabotage.

THE POINT GENERALISES BEYOND THIS SUITE. A throw assertion proves that SOMETHING failed, not that the guard under test failed, and not that it failed for the reason claimed. Any second defence downstream keeps the test green while the mechanism it names is gone. In a layered runtime there is almost always a second defence.

WHAT TO DEMAND IN A BRIEF INSTEAD: assert the exact error identity - the id and the payload as an exact map - not merely that an exception occurred. That worker asserted :rf.error/hicasso-sub-outside-render, the emitting function, the phase and the query as one map, so a different throw from a different layer reds.

THE SAME REPORT CARRIED A SECOND INSTANCE OF THE FAMILY. Its P2 control caught a defect in its own suite: a timer row's follow-up body re-read a key the enclosing body had also read, so accumulation was swallowed by the row's own expected set. Only the perturbation exposed it. Three other workers tonight found defects in their own tests the same way - a StrictMode row that could not see additivity, a passive-effect race where four rows passed by luck, a coverage floor that survived deleting the sections it guarded.

SO THE RULE FOR EVERY WITNESS BEAD: perturb, confirm red, restore, confirm green - and when it does NOT red, that is the finding. Do not adjust the control until the witness is understood. Half of tonight's most valuable results came from a control refusing to red.

THE 'DID THIS WORKFLOW CHANGE MOVE THE CHECK SET?' TEST NEEDS TWO LEADING SPACES, AND THE UNINDENTED FORM FAILS OPEN (2026-08-15 02:07 AUSEST).

THE TEST'S PURPOSE. Merge clause 5 asks whether a PR's check set was computed against the CURRENT workflow matrix. The operational question is whether the check SET moved, not whether the FILE moved: a STEP added to an existing job changes .github/workflows/* without adding any row to any PR's rollup, so nothing behind it needs gh pr update-branch. The discriminator is whether a new top-level JOB KEY appeared.

THE BROKEN FORM I USED ALL SESSION:
  git diff <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:$'
It requires a lowercase letter IMMEDIATELY after the '+'. But job keys are nested TWO-SPACE INDENTED under 'jobs:', so this pattern matches NO job key in this repository at all. It is a constant zero, not a discriminator.

THE CORRECT FORM:
  git diff <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/ | grep -cE '^\+  [a-z][a-z0-9_-]*:[[:space:]]*$'
THE TWO LEADING SPACES ARE THE TEST.

MEASURED BY worker/clause5-byoxk over the last 20 .github/workflows commits, parsing job-key sets inside the jobs: block at rev^ and rev: the broken form read 0 on ALL TWENTY and MISSED ALL FIVE commits that genuinely added a job. The indented form matched ground truth 20/20 with zero false positives. All 129 job keys across 13 workflow files are lowercase-start and bare, so the pattern is exact for this repo.

I VERIFIED IT MYSELF before recording: on 366e4fca79 — the commit that added provenance-pins-corpus and moved the band 97 -> 98 — the unindented form reads 0 and the indented form reads 1.

WHY NO HARM CAME OF IT, AND WHY THAT IS NOT REASSURING. I used the broken form before merging #8256, #8258, #8270, #8271, #8272 and #8274. Every one was a step addition, so ZERO WAS THE RIGHT ANSWER — reached for the wrong reason. The one real job addition this session (#8264) was caught by a DIFFERENT signal entirely: its total read 98 while its sibling #8265 read 97 on the same tree. So the count discriminated and the regex contributed nothing. A test that has only ever been asked questions whose answer is zero cannot be distinguished from a working one by its results.

IT FAILS IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION. Reading a real job addition as 'no matrix change' skips update-branch on PRs computed against a superseded matrix — precisely the bad merge clause 5 exists to prevent. Over-counting would cost one needless CI restart; under-counting reaches the merge.

THE CORRECTION LANDED in .claude/commands/mayor-merge.md via PR #8276 (rf2-byoxk), WITH a sentence recording that the unindented form fails open — because the broken form survives in rf2-byoxk's own bead text and in PR #8273's body, where a future reader will meet it.

GENERAL LESSON, worth more than the regex: A GATE THAT HAS ONLY EVER RETURNED THE EXPECTED ANSWER IS UNTESTED. This is the same defect class as the architecture census matching mutable globals by bare name, whose positive control passed because it seeded a UNIQUE name; and as a sentinel that is green on a real leak. Before trusting a discriminator, run it against a case whose answer you know is NON-zero.

IN A jq REGEX ON THIS BOX, WRITE `[.]` NOT `\.` — THE BACKSLASH IS COLLAPSED BEFORE jq SEES IT AND THE FILTER DIES AS A COMPILE ERROR (measured 2026-09-05, twice in one session).

WHAT HAPPENS. A jq filter containing test("spellings\.1") reaches jq as test("spellings\.1") minus one backslash, i.e. the JSON string contains a bare backslash-dot, which is not a valid JSON escape. jq refuses to compile:
  jq: error: Invalid escape at line 1, column 4 (while parsing '"\."')
Doubling the backslash inside single quotes did NOT survive either — the error message shows jq receiving the single-backslash form both ways, so this is not the ordinary shell-quoting rule people expect.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A SYNTAX NIGGLE. A jq COMPILE error exits non-zero and prints to STDERR. Inside a pipeline whose stdout is being counted, or with `2>/dev/null` anywhere in the chain, it looks exactly like an honest empty result. The first time this bit me today the filter was `test("kuky\.(33|18|51|28)")` in a merged-PR cross-check, and my `|| echo "(none above = clean)"` fallback printed a REASSURING answer for a query that had never run. The second time it silently returned nothing for a bead-sequencing lookup where an empty result would have meant 'no blocker' and would have authorised a dispatch.

THE FIX, and it needs no escaping at all: use a CHARACTER CLASS.
  test("ref spellings[.]")            not  test("ref spellings\.")
  capture("spellings[.](?<n>[0-9]+)")  not  capture("spellings\.(?<n>[0-9]+)")
A one-character class is exactly a literal dot in every regex dialect, is immune to every layer of quoting between here and jq, and reads fine.

THE DISCIPLINE THAT CATCHES IT REGARDLESS. Any jq filter whose EMPTINESS would be read as a finding needs a CONTROL THAT MUST MATCH. I now pair every such query with a probe I know must return a row — e.g. after searching all beads for 'ref spellings.N', re-run the same capture against rf2-kuky.24 alone, which declares spellings.2, and assert it prints 2. If the control comes back empty the filter is broken, not the data. Take the control from the DATA, not spliced in as a shell literal, for the same reason as the CRLF case: a literal never travels the pipeline the data travelled.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY: jq writes CRLF here, so a pattern JOINED from jq output matches only its last alternative, and a jq-produced list compared with comm/join/diff reports everything as different. `tr -d '\r'` after any jq that feeds a join or a set operation.

JQ: INSIDE contains(f), THE DOT REBINDS TO CONTAINS' OWN INPUT — so map(select($t | contains(.))) asks "does $t contain $t" and is TRUE for every element. Measured 2026-09-07.

THE BROKEN FORM, which reads perfectly:
  ($held | map(select($t | contains(.)))) as $hits
Intent: keep the held-path strings that appear in $t. Actual: for each element, contains(.) evaluates its argument against the SAME input contains received — which is $t, not the element. So it tests $t against itself, returns true, and $hits comes back as the WHOLE list every time.

THE FIX — bind the element before crossing into contains:
  ($held | map(. as $k | select($t | contains($k)))) as $hits

WHAT IT LOOKED LIKE IN PRACTICE, and why it is worth a memory rather than a shrug. I was scanning 42 ready beads for which held surfaces each one touches, to decide what was safe to dispatch. The broken query reported that ALL 42 beads touched ALL 17 held surfaces — a uniform, confident, completely wrong answer. A grep-based scan of the same data had already reported the opposite for one of those beads. Two instruments disagreeing is what forced the check; without the disagreement the jq answer would have stood, and it would have said "nothing is dispatchable" for a reason that was pure artefact.

THE DISCRIMINATING TEST TOOK ONE COMMAND: take a single bead's text to a file, grep it for five of the terms (all 0), then run jq's contains on the same file for the same five terms (all true). Same bytes, same needles, opposite answers — so the fault is in the instrument, not the data. That is the cheapest possible resolution of an instrument disagreement and it should be the reflex.

RELATED AND ALREADY RECORDED, this is a new mechanism for an old class: see a-census-returning-everything-means-the-comparison-set-is-wrong. That memory names the SHAPE — a scan that flags everything has told you about itself, not about the tree, and it reads as a rich finding rather than as silence. This is the same shape reached through jq scoping rather than through a wrong comparison set. Its closing advice is what caught this one: exercise the instrument in both directions with data drawn from the SAME pipeline as the real input.

GENERALISE ONE STEP, because contains is not the only offender: ANY jq builtin taking a FILTER argument re-evaluates that filter against its own input — has, inside, index, test, endswith. The same bug appears as select(.field | test(.)) or map(select($x | inside(.))). The rule: whenever a filter argument should refer to the ENCLOSING iteration variable, bind it with `. as $k` first. If a jq predicate returns the same answer for every element, suspect this before suspecting the data.

THE jq CRLF DEFECT HAS A THIRD DOOR: A SET COMPARISON BETWEEN A jq-PRODUCED FILE AND A NON-jq-PRODUCED ONE. Measured 2026-09-05 18:0x AUSEST by the mayor, on its own §3 backlog reread.

WHAT IS ALREADY RECORDED (CLAUDE.md, instruments item (e)): jq-1.8.1 on this box writes CRLF, so a pattern JOINED from `jq -r` output matches nothing but its last alternative, and a grep pattern file built that way misbehaves. Both recorded doors are about PATTERNS.

THE THIRD DOOR IS `comm`, `join`, `diff`, or any line-keyed set operation. I built the in_progress bead list with `jq -r ... | sort` and the held-by-worktree list with `git worktree list | ... | awk | sort`, then ran `comm -23`. It reported ALL SEVEN in_progress beads as orphans with no live worktree — which, if believed, is the stranded-worker signature whose remedy is to reopen and redispatch every one of them.

The two lists were VISUALLY IDENTICAL on screen. The difference was invisible: `od -c` showed the jq side ending `\r \n` and the awk side ending `\n`, so every key differed by one byte and comm correctly reported two disjoint sets.

WHY THIS DOOR IS WORTH ITS OWN NOTE. The recorded doors fail toward a FALSE ALL-CLEAR (a search reads zero). This one failed toward a FALSE ALARM, which is the more visible direction and is how it got caught. BUT THE MIRROR CASE IS SILENT: `comm -13` or an intersection keyed the same way would report "nothing in common" or drop a real member, and a set comparison that returns a plausible-looking subset raises nothing. The direction of failure depends on which side of the comparison jq is on, so neither direction can be trusted.

THE TELL AND THE FIX. The tell is a set operation reporting NO OVERLAP AT ALL between two lists that visibly share members — total disjointness is almost never the real answer. The fix is one of:
  - `tr -d '\r'` between jq and any file destined for a line-keyed operation;
  - keep BOTH sides in jq (a jq-to-jq comparison is self-consistent and gets the right answer, which is why this hides);
  - or do the comparison inside jq itself.
And CONTROL IT: append a needle you know is unique to one side and confirm the operation reports it. My control was `rf2-FAKE` spliced into one list, which comm correctly returned — proving the instrument works once the line endings agree, and that the seven-orphan reading was an artefact.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS BELONGS TO, which is already in the gate-mechanics block and keeps earning its place: ANY instrument that can answer "nothing here" gives the same answer when misused, and a misused one raises no error. Exercise it once against an input it should flag. That applies to set operations exactly as it applies to searches.

`jq -r` EMITS CRLF ON THIS BOX, SO EVERY ID LOOPED FROM IT CARRIES A TRAILING CARRIAGE RETURN — and the resulting failure reads as a clean "nothing found". Measured 2026-09-04.

WHAT HAPPENED. I built a fence check — for each ready bead, read its notes and grep for FENCED / DO NOT DISPATCH / SEQUENCED — precisely to stop myself dispatching a fenced bead again. It reported fourteen of fifteen beads CLEAR. It had read none of them.

`bd ready --limit 0 --json | jq -r '.[].id'` emits `rf2-aunp\r\n`. Looping over that gives `bd show "rf2-aunp\r"`, which answers:

    Error fetching rf2-aunp: no issue found matching "rf2-aunp\r"

62 bytes, printed to STDOUT. The grep then searched that error message for fence markers, found none, and the check printed "(clear)". A confident, uniform, entirely fabricated all-clear.

WHY IT SURVIVED THREE ROUNDS OF DEBUGGING. The single-bead form works perfectly — `bd show rf2-aunp` alone returns 4932 bytes — and so does a loop over a LITERAL list (`for id in rf2-aunp rf2-60jv`). Only the jq-fed loop fails, so every isolated test of the pieces passes. I first blamed tracker lock contention, then blamed command substitution, and materialising the ids to a file made it WORSE (all fifteen failed instead of fourteen) — which looked like evidence for the contention theory and was actually the CR surviving the round trip. The mechanism only became visible when I stopped theorising and printed the failing output.

TWO FIXES, USE BOTH. Strip it at the source — `jq -r ... | tr -d '\r'` — and GUARD THAT THE READ SUCCEEDED before believing what it did not find: check the response is plausibly large (`[ "$bytes" -lt 400 ] && echo "READ FAILED"`) rather than treating an empty grep as a clean bill of health. The byte count is what turned a silent false-clear into a visible `*** READ FAILED (63 bytes)`.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS IS AN INSTANCE OF: A NEGATIVE RESULT FROM A COMPOSED PIPELINE PROVES NOTHING UNLESS THE READ ITSELF IS SHOWN TO HAVE SUCCEEDED. Grep on an error message is indistinguishable from grep on a clean document — both print nothing and exit 1. Any check whose ACTION on "found nothing" is to PROCEED must first prove it looked at something.

AND THE IRONY IS THE POINT: this was the instrument I adopted THAT SAME TICK to prevent a dispatch error, and it failed in exactly the direction the original error failed — toward "clear, go ahead". A safeguard that fails open is worse than none, because it converts a known unknown into a false certainty.

RELATED: [[grep-notes-for-a-fence-before-every-dispatch]], [[git-log-grep-id-is-a-prefix-match]], [[flattening-does-not-undo-a-mid-token-line-break]].

jq lexes `?//` as ONE token (the alternative-destructuring operator), so the natural
spelling `.Field?//empty` is a SYNTAX ERROR, not "optional-field, else empty".

Measured 2026-09-09 on jq-1.8.1, both directions, on one 4.3 MB file already on disk:
  jq '[.[]|(.Issue?//empty)|select(.status=="closed")]|length'   -> rc=3, compile error,
      "syntax error, unexpected ?//" with a caret under the ?//, NOTHING on stdout
  jq '[.[]|(.Issue? // empty)|select(.status=="closed")]|length' -> rc=0, prints 15
The ONLY difference is the spaces around //.

WHY IT COST THREE SWEEP GENERATIONS: it fails LOUDLY on stderr and SILENTLY on stdout.
Every census idiom in this repo pipes with `2>/dev/null`, which throws away the entire
error, and `$(jq ...)` then captures the empty string. A guard written as
`[ -z "$n" ] && echo UNREAD` reports "unread" for every record; a guard written as
`${n:-0}` reports ZERO CLOSED SNAPSHOTS FOR EVERY BEAD — a clean, plausible,
completely false "no reverted closures found".

It is the CLAUDE.md instrument-(a) rule (READ STDERR) arriving through a door where the
error text is the only evidence that exists: the exit status is swallowed by the pipeline
or the substitution, and the empty stdout is indistinguishable from an honest zero.

GUARD: capture jq's stderr to a file and PRINT IT in the failure branch, and give the
sweep an explicit UNREAD state distinct from zero — never let a failed filter collapse
into the same answer as a successful one that found nothing. A sweep that cannot tell
"found nothing" from "found nothing because it did not run" has no result at all.

A CONTENT PROBE RUN IMMEDIATELY AFTER 'bd update --append-notes' READS THE PRE-APPEND EXPORT AND LOOKS LIKE A FAILED WRITE (observed twice, 2026-08-23).

WHAT HAPPENS: bd update returns success, but .beads/issues.jsonl has not been rewritten yet. A python/grep probe against the file in the SAME command block reports the old notes length and zero hits for the new text. Both times this read as 'the append did not land'. Both times it had landed.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: re-read the export in a LATER command block. Both times the second read showed the full append (rf2-hic-090 5496->7529, rf2-hic-064 9642->11452) and the subsequent checkpoint had committed the post-append export.

DO NOT 'FIX' IT BY RE-RUNNING THE UPDATE. A second --append-notes on a write that already landed duplicates the note silently; nothing errors and the damage is only visible on a later read.

ALSO: 'bd show' is NOT a substitute probe. It wraps long lines, so a grep for a phrase that spans a wrap returns 0 on text that is present. The export is the authority on notes content; bd show is for status and headers.

RETRACTED 2026-09-21 — SUPERSEDED BY [[windows-junction-detection-two-wrong-answers-before-the]],
which says "Supersedes" this memory in terms. READ THAT FIRST.
The replacement detector prescribed below, `fsutil file queryfileid`, DOES NOT WORK: a deliberately
created control junction reported a DIFFERENT file id from its target, so this test calls a real
junction "not a junction" — the same fail-open answer as the `cmd /c dir /AL` form it was meant to
replace, on the one path that has already emptied the mayor's real node_modules. THE WORKING
DETECTOR, validated against a control junction, is the `ReparsePoint` attribute plus `LinkType` /
`Target` via PowerShell `Get-Item -Force`.
WHAT STANDS: the opening claim that `cmd /c dir /AL <path>` prints only the cmd banner from the Bash
tool, which the corrector carries forward as its own wrong-answer (1); and the belt-and-braces
non-following `[IO.Directory]::Delete(path, $false)` before `git worktree remove`.
The original text is preserved below unchanged.

Junction detection via `cmd /c dir /AL <path>` DOES NOT WORK from the Bash tool on this Windows setup - it prints only the cmd banner and no listing, so every directory reports 'no junction'. A hygiene brief that keys 'rmdir the junction first' on that command silently degrades to 'treat everything as a real directory' (or, with a fail-closed rule, 'treat everything as a junction'). Working replacement: compare file identity with `fsutil file queryfileid` - a junction shares the target's id, a real directory has its own - validated against a deliberately-created control junction. Belt-and-braces: a NON-FOLLOWING `Directory.Delete(path, recursive:false)` before `git worktree remove` unlinks a junction and fails harmlessly on a populated real directory. Related: [[junction-safe-worktree-cleanup]].

Junction-rmdir trap (RECURRED 2x, 2026-06-10): a worktree's implementation/node_modules is often a JUNCTION to the mayor checkout's real node_modules (workers npm-install/junction it to run node gates). 'git worktree remove --force' on such a worktree DELETES THROUGH the junction into the mayor's REAL node_modules (emptying it to 0) UNLESS the junction link is removed FIRST. THE BREAKING BUG (hit twice): building the rmdir path via bash sed inside a nested powershell double-quoted string — e.g. cmd /c rmdir '$(echo $p|sed 's#/#\#g')' — the sed errors 'unterminated s command' (nested-quote mangling), rmdir gets a broken path + fails ('syntax of the command is incorrect'), the junction survives, and worktree-remove nukes the target. CORRECT junction removal (PowerShell-native, NO bash sed, NO backslash conversion): powershell -NoProfile -Command "$p='<FORWARD-slash path>'; $i=Get-Item $p -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue; if($i -and $i.LinkType){ [System.IO.Directory]::Delete($p,$false) }; Test-Path $p"  — [System.IO.Directory]::Delete(path,$false) removes the reparse point WITHOUT recursing into the target; forward-slashes work fine in .NET; VERIFY Test-Path returns False BEFORE git worktree remove. RECOVERY when nuked: npm ci --prefix <mayor>/implementation. Supersedes the prior trap note.

A JUNCTION INTO SHARED node_modules IS WRITABLE THROUGH THE LINK, so any installer a gate runs in the worktree rewrites the MAYOR's real tree (2026-08-29). What happened: a worker junctioned tools/mcp-conformance/node_modules at the mayor's real one (as its brief said, for a gate that needed it); the mcp-conformance runner invokes 'npm ci', which deletes node_modules and reinstalls INTO the junction target - the mayor's tree read 0 entries afterwards, while the worker's tree (post-unlink, real install) read 92. implementation/node_modules and pair-mcp were untouched because no gate ran an installer there. The existing rule (unlink before removal so cleanup does not delete THROUGH the link) covers deletion, not write-through. RULE: junction shared dependencies only for trees no nominated gate reinstalls; where a gate runs npm ci/npm install, the worker installs its OWN node_modules in the worktree (npm ci from the lockfile) and never links. Remedy when it happens: 'npm ci' in the mayor checkout's own directory from its lockfile - no data is lost, only time. Check every tools/*/node_modules count after a worker that ran an MCP/conformance gate.

JVM alloc bench: escape analysis makes a retired arm bimodal by arm order. In read_attribution.clj (rf2-a8bw0, PR #7157) the eager-payload arm S1-EAGER read 136.0 B/call in every FORWARD round and 72.0 in every REVERSED round — a clean 64 B step, not noise. 64 B is the two-entry PersistentArrayMap; the JIT scalar-replaces it when the arm runs earlier in the plan and require-current-frame! inlines into it. So on the JVM an arm that ALLOCATES-THEN-DISCARDS can read its own cost or zero depending on position, while an arm that never evaluates the expression reads flat. Two consequences: (1) always run both arm orders and quote the RANGE for any arm whose object does not escape — a mean hides a JIT decision; (2) the SHIPPED (deferred) arm being flat across all rounds is the stronger evidence, because it has nothing for EA to remove. Separately: a thread-bound dynamic Var deref costs 32 B/read on the JVM (Var.getThreadBinding -> PersistentHashMap.entryAt allocates a MapEntry) — this is the floor under every *current-frame* read and it does NOT exist in CLJS.

JVM ALLOCATION PROFILES CAN MIS-RANK A CLJS TARGET, AND THIS PROJECT'S BROWSER SUBSTRATE IS A CLJS TARGET. Measuring `subscribe` on a cache hit (rf2-j8ls2), the LARGEST single term — ~760 B of ~1,800, 41% — was the JVM's dynamic `binding`. It DOES NOT EXIST IN CLOJURESCRIPT: CLJS `binding` expands through `with-redefs` to `let` + `set!` + `try`/`finally` restore (confirmed in cljs/core.cljc, clojurescript-1.12.145), allocating ZERO. Proof in the same run: the same fn with a nil target, binding nothing, measured 16-40 B against 752-808 B bound.
CONSEQUENCE: any bead RANKED off a JVM allocation profile may be ranked wrong for the browser. Three were, and needed re-ranking (rf2-x0fe2, P1). `ThreadMXBean/getThreadAllocatedBytes` is JVM-only and there is no equivalent CLJS instrument, so this is not a gap you can close by re-running.
WHAT SURVIVES: a RATIO between two arms that BOTH pay the JVM-only term (e.g. Freehand's port vs a Reagent view body, both bound) is much more robust than either absolute — removing the term moved that comparison only 97.4% -> 94.9%. WHAT DOES NOT: absolute B/call, and any ordering of terms.
RULE: state the runtime beside every allocation figure, and before ranking work off one, ask which terms are runtime-specific.

clojure -M:test IN tools/xray CANNOT LOAD A .cljs FILE — it passes a CLJS sabotage GREEN with byte-identical counts (2026-08-15 17:18 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/xrayroster-wtznc (rf2-wtznc, PR #8310). I nominated 'clojure -M:test in tools/xray' as the gate for a change to tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/mount.cljs. The worker planted a real fault — removing :rf.adapter/uix, the exact entry its PR documents — and that runner came back GREEN with test and assertion counts identical to the control. THE LANE THAT ACTUALLY REACHES mount.cljs IS npm run test:cljs. Under it the same plant failed at exactly one test — mount-cljs-test/open!-on-react-element-substrate-refuses-cleanly — which is what makes the claim test-pinned rather than prose.

SO: FOR A tools/* ARTEFACT, MATCH THE RUNNER TO THE FILE EXTENSION. A .clj/.cljc change is the JVM runner's; a .cljs change needs the CLJS lane. A .cljc file is reachable by both and each sees a different half. Nominating the JVM runner for a CLJS file produces a confident green over a file it never opened.

THIS IS THE FIFTH GATE TODAY FOUND REPORTING SUCCESS WHILE VERIFYING LESS THAN THE READER ASSUMED, and the pattern is now the finding rather than any single instance:
  mkdocs --strict            does not cover docs/design/**
  the warnings-fatal compile does not police cross-namespace private-var access
