THE JVM WEAK-REFERENCE GC TEST IS THIS REPOSITORY LOAD-FLAKE SIGNATURE — confirmed end to end on 2026-08-14.

THE INSTANCE. PR #8183 (operator-authored, arming the classifier gates) went red on "JVM core under the production gate (-Dre-frame.debug=false)" with ONE failure in 1986: jvm-weak-node-record-does-not-strong-pin-its-abandoned-reaction. The rollup check "All required checks passed" also read FAILURE, which is that job blocking the merge rather than a second defect — do not count it as two.

THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT RESOLVED IT, and it is the general one. (a) CAN THE DIFF REACH THE SURFACE? That PR touched .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh and implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs — CI classifier files that cannot influence whether a garbage collector reclaims a weakly-held record. (b) IS TRUNK GREEN? The last four test.yml runs on main were success. Both true means flake; re-run the job.

CONFIRMED BY OUTCOME: the job came back green with no change to the branch, and the PR merged on the full 93-check band.

WHY THIS TEST SPECIFICALLY. A weak-reference assertion depends on the GC actually collecting inside the test window. Under six concurrent workers, three browser engines and a shadow-cljs compile, it sometimes does not. The test is not wrong; it is timing-coupled to machine load in a way the rest of the JVM suite is not.

DO NOT FIX IT BY LOOSENING THE ASSERTION. It guards against an abandoned reaction being strong-pinned, which is a real memory-leak guard. The flake is environmental. If it becomes frequent enough to cost real time, the repair is to force collection deterministically or isolate the test from the loaded lane — file that rather than weakening the guard.

RELATED AND ALREADY RECORDED: skill-versus-MCP-drift and JVM-epoch gates flake under heavy concurrency by the same mechanism. The classifier arming that #8183 landed makes MORE PRs run the JVM tier, so expect this flake more often rather than less.

THE rf2-kuky EPIC IS 42/47 ONE SERIAL LANE, AND THAT — NOT THE BEAD COUNT — IS WHAT GATES THE DRIVE TO ZERO (measured 2026-09-07 20:50 AUSEST).

MEASUREMENT. Classifying every OPEN rf2-kuky.* child by whether its own text names spec/API.md or spec/api-manifest*: 42 HOTZONE, 5 free. The five free ones are rf2-kuky.81 and .83 (resources :scope policy), .41 (schema doc drift), .94 and .95 (the clear-* doc follow-ups from rf2-kuky.80). Everything else is a public-name change, and a public-name change moves spec/API.md, spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn and spec/api-manifest.edn TOGETHER — lint.yml's api-manifest job grades all three on one surface.

WHY THE COUNT MISLEADS. 47 open children reads as 47 dispatchable units and it is nothing like that. At one hot-zone dispatch at a time, 42 beads is ~28 hours of wall clock however many worker slots are free. Saturating six workers does NOT speed this epic up; it only speeds up everything that is not this epic.

THE LEVER IS CLUSTER SIZE, NOT FLEET SIZE. Four same-family beads per dispatch turns 42 into ~11 units. The epic is already shaped for it — several children are explicitly numbered series (boot 1/4-4/4 = .74/.75/.76/.77; egress 1/4-4/4 = .88/.90/.92/.93) and the rest fall into families that share their spec section: observability .19/.20/.65/.67/.69, trace .52/.53/.72, resources .34/.81/.83/.85, views .57/.59/.62, routing .66/.68, registry .31/.84, ssr .87/.89, http .12/.13, machines .63/.70, epoch .73/.82.

DO NOT READ THE PR FILE LIST AS EVIDENCE THE LANE IS FREE. On 2026-09-07 two hot-zone children were in flight at once (kuky.11 on PR #9372, kuky.58 on PR #9375) and NEITHER PR's file list showed spec/API.md — both were drafts still mid-work, and the manifest edit is the LAST thing such a worker does. A file list read mid-draft says nothing about which lane the change will land in; classify from the BEAD, not from the in-progress diff.

THE CONFLICT IS CHEAP WHEN IT HAPPENS. loops.md contemplates this exact case: several green changes sharing one serial-lane file, each merge flipping the rest to conflicting, resolved by messaging the author rather than by a fix worker. So one or two concurrent hot-zone dispatches is a deliberate throughput trade, not a mistake. Three or more is.

THE rf2-kuky API-REVIEW FAMILY IS ONE SERIALISED SURFACE, NOT ~30 PARALLELISABLE BEADS — dispatch it as CLUSTERS OF FOUR THROUGH A SINGLE WORKER, never as parallel workers (measured 2026-09-05).

WHAT I MEASURED. Of the 60 ready beads this tick, 23 were rf2-kuky.* and I mapped the spec surfaces each one names. Nearly every one names spec/API.md, and the ones that do not are mostly beads that ADD or DELETE public names — which moves spec/API.md and BOTH manifest sidecars (spec/api-manifest.edn, spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn) whether the bead text mentions them or not. rf2-kuky.58 is the clean example: its text names only spec/002, spec/006 and docs/, but its target API adds h/frame-root and h/frame-provider as public Hicasso heads, so it necessarily moves the manifest.

WHY THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. spec/API.md is a hot-zone file, so the fence permits exactly ONE holder at a time. A backlog that reads as 23 independent P2/P3 items is therefore a QUEUE OF DEPTH 23 behind a single lock. Saturating six workers on it is not merely inadvisable, it is impossible — five of the six would be fenced off the file they need, and any that were not would conflict on merge.

I LEARNED THIS THE EXPENSIVE WAY IN MINIATURE: I fenced spec/api-manifest*.edn OUT of rf2-kuky.27's scope on the reasoning that the bead was about test vars. Wrong — deleting four public v1 vars necessarily moves manifest rows, and PR #9298 went red on 'Public-API manifest drift-check' as a direct result. THE RULE: if a bead adds, deletes or renames a PUBLIC name, it touches spec/API.md and both manifest sidecars. Do not reason from the bead's prose about which files it names; reason from whether the public surface moves.

THE DISPATCH PATTERN THAT FOLLOWS. The loop body already licenses it — 'for P2, P3 and P4, if possible, cluster up to 4 beads with the same surface area into a single dispatch'. For this family that is not an optimisation, it is the ONLY way to get throughput: one worker holding the API.md lock, carrying four kuky beads, making one coherent edit to the shared files and one manifest regeneration. Four beads per lock-acquisition instead of one. Cluster by sub-domain so the four cohere — observability (.17/.19/.20/.21), views (.56/.58/.60/.61), machines (.14/.15/.16/.26), ssr (.42/.43/.44), registry (.24/.25/.30/.32), boot (.1/.2/.3/.4), schema (.39/.40), routing (.36/.37/.38).

TWO SEPARATORS WHEN BUILDING A CLUSTER. (1) Exclude the RULING/DECISION beads — they need Mike, and bundling one into an implementation cluster stalls the whole cluster behind a hold. (2) Check the sub-domain against what is CURRENTLY held: the observability cluster was unbuildable this tick because .17/.19/.20 all name spec/009-Instrumentation.md, which devcon-a held via PR #9306.

SO THE STEADY STATE IS ONE KUKY WORKER AT A TIME, and the rest of the fleet's saturation has to come from OUTSIDE the family — tools/xray, tools/mcp-conformance, skills/, implementation/ internals. Plan the tick that way rather than discovering it at dispatch time.

LABELLING A SEARCH RESULT WITH A PATTERN YOU DID NOT RUN — and then CONFABULATING a reconciliation for the discrepancy it creates. Measured on the mayor TWICE in one session, 2026-09-04, which is what makes it a habit rather than a slip.

INSTANCE 1 — THE WRONG PATTERN, CORRECTLY TOTALLED. rf2-6r9j.35's acceptance criterion is a repository-wide zero for the fixed string `js/require "react-dom/test-utils"`. I searched the BARE TOKEN `react-dom/test-utils`, got 13 occurrences across 10 files, and wrote that into a brief labelled as the criterion's string. Facing a prior worker's report of 7, I explained the gap: "its 7 is FILES and mine is OCCURRENCES". Measured side by side on one tree: bare token 13/10, criterion string 7/7. The prior worker had been exactly right on both axes, and my "correction" was noise about a different question.

INSTANCE 2 — A PARTIAL PROBE, A TOTAL CONCLUSION. Filing rf2-wcps I asserted that six measured hazards were absent from CLAUDE.md, "verified" by searching five tokens: ripgrep, mklink, New-Item -ItemType Junction, head -N, token axes. NONE of those characterises the fifth hazard (a gate GRADING a finding below its failure threshold). The worker found that hazard's mkdocs half ALREADY IN CLAUDE.md, written out in full at line 128, and correctly declined to add it again. I ran a probe covering five of six and reported a conclusion covering six of six.

THE COMMON SHAPE: the search I ran and the claim I made were about different things, and nothing in the output says so. A count does not carry its own pattern, and a probe set does not carry its own coverage. Both times the number was real and the sentence around it was false.

THE RULE:
1. QUOTE THE EXACT PATTERN NEXT TO THE NUMBER, always — the literal argument you passed.
2. WHEN A CRITERION NAMES A STRING, SEARCH THAT STRING. Not a token from it, not a paraphrase. A criterion specifies the instrument as much as the target.
3. WHEN YOU CLAIM SOMETHING ABOUT A SET OF N ITEMS, RUN N PROBES AND SHOW N RESULTS. A per-item table makes a missing row obvious; a summary sentence hides it. If one item has no distinctive token, that is the finding — say you could not probe it.
4. A DISCREPANCY WITH A PRIOR MEASUREMENT IS A REASON TO RUN BOTH INSTRUMENTS, NOT TO EXPLAIN THE GAP. Print both. One command.
5. BE MOST SUSPICIOUS OF A UNITS EXPLANATION — "files versus occurrences", "before versus after", "including versus excluding" are the first reconciliations to mind and therefore the likeliest to be reached for without evidence.

WHY THE CONFABULATION IS WORSE THAN THE WRONG NUMBER. A bare wrong count invites checking. A wrong count WITH A PLAUSIBLE RECONCILIATION closes the question — it reads as diligence, survives review, and propagates into tracker notes where the next reader inherits it.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT from census-piped-through-head-reports-the-cap: that is a real count of the right pattern, truncated. These two are a real count of the WRONG pattern, and a real probe of a PARTIAL set, both wearing the full claim's name.

LARGE-BEAD WORKER PATIENCE: a big facade/refactor bead touching ~100 files (e.g. csbbwu, m90brg) legitimately runs 40+ min at '99 modified / 0 commits' — it commits ONCE at the very end after a long tail of call-site fixes + a heavy gate suite (test:cljs 8000+ tests, JVM core, bundle-isolation, adapter-smokes, mkdocs, manifest, skills-check, drift). Do NOT mistake 'no commits across several ticks' for a STALL on a large bead. Observed 2026-07-08: I prematurely TaskStop'd m90brg — the kill-reveal showed its last action was 'rerun core JVM tests to confirm this fixes all 3 errors' (actively debugging, not hung). DISTINGUISH stall-vs-working by the worker's LAST ACTION (a SendMessage status-ping, or the kill-reveal line), NOT by commit count. For a large-bead worker: send a status-ping first; only stop if it (a) confirms stuck, (b) doesn't respond across 2 pings, or (c) its last-action shows a tight retry loop on one gate (the mkdocs-stall pattern). WIP survives a stop (uncommitted files remain), so recovery = re-dispatch a finish-worker to the SAME worktree to continue from the WIP.

npm run lint:js LIVES IN A SEPARATE ROOT npm PROJECT, SO A WORKER WITH ONLY implementation/node_modules CANNOT RUN IT — AND THE FAILURE DOES NOT LOOK LIKE A LINT FAILURE (2026-08-06, rf2-t4j7c).

THE MECHANISM: lint:js belongs to the root package (re-frame2-lint), not to implementation/. A worker that runs `npm ci` inside implementation/ — which is the standard advice for a fresh worktree, because that is where the CLJS/node tiers need it — does NOT get eslint. Invoking the gate then fails with "eslint is not recognized", which reads as a broken environment rather than as a gate that never ran. The gate is SILENTLY UNRUNNABLE, and a worker can honestly report every other gate green while lint has never executed once.

THAT IS EXACTLY HOW PR #7609 REACHED CI RED. The worker ran test:script-helpers and node --check ×4 and reported them all 0; lint was the one gate it could not run and did not notice it could not run.

THE BRIEF LINE TO ADD FOR ANY JS-TOUCHING BEAD: run `npm ci` at the REPO ROOT as well as under implementation/, and report lint:jss own exit code. An "is not recognized" error from a gate is NOT an environment excuse — it is the gate telling you it did not run, which is the same class as the mkdocs soft-skip and the killed-wrapper exit 0.

AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN BRIEF, in the repos favour: I told the worker the tree was at ONE live ESLint suppression with rf2-kvsm1 open to retire it. It is at ZERO — kvsm1 already retired the last directive, and eslint.config.mjs records it ("the suppression went with the code it guarded"). So a disable there would have been the ONLY one in the tree, not the second. My constraint was stale in the direction that made the wrong answer look cheaper.

THE FIX IT CHOSE, AND THE REASONING THAT MAKES IT MORE THAN A LINT SILENCER: the negative fixture requires the module and never calls it, which trips no-unused-vars. It dropped the BINDING (`require(./lane_cache.cjs);` with nothing bound) rather than suppressing. That is not quieter, it is STRONGER — a refactor that deletes the clear leaves one of two shapes, and they are not equally dangerous. If the binding SURVIVES, no-unused-vars reports the orphan and lint catches that driver a gate earlier. If the binding GOES TOO, nothing in the lint path can see anything wrong: the file parses, every name is used, and only the missing CALL separates it from a correct driver. THE SECOND VARIANT IS THE ONE NO OTHER GATE OWNS, so it is the one worth modelling. Proved rather than asserted: with a comment-only rider in the discovery directory, lint:js exits 0 while the gate exits 1 on the same file.

IT ALSO DECLINED AN IGNORES ENTRY on the configs own stated terms — that list is for trees that are GENERATED and can carry JS, "not when a file in it happens to have complained". These fixtures are hand-authored, and keeping them in the lint path is what stops them drifting into shapes no real driver could take.

LINTER DIAGNOSTIC CODES GET RENUMBERED — pin the fix against the runner version AND a newer one. On 2026-07-19 the rf2-lsp1i CI fix found shellcheck reports the same finding under two codes: 0.9.0 (what ubuntu-24.04 ships) emits SC2317 on the rm line; 0.10+ emits SC2329 on the function line. Disabling only SC2317 passes TODAY and goes red silently the moment the runner image updates; disabling only SC2329 leaves CI red now. The fix names BOTH, verified that 0.9.0 tolerates the unknown SC2329 silently. RULE: when suppressing a linter diagnostic, install the EXACT version CI runs (reproduce the failure byte-for-byte first) AND at least one newer version, then satisfy both. A suppression validated only against the current runner is a time bomb. DIAGNOSIS TECHNIQUE WORTH COPYING: the worker established the cause by BISECTION, not assertion — a minimal trap-cleanup script lints clean; truncating the real script at one line is clean and at another reproduces; deleting only the trailing `exit 0` makes the diagnostic vanish. That isolated the real trigger ("shellcheck models the EXIT trap as the fall-through ending, and every path here exits explicitly") rather than accepting the message at face value. SCOPE RULE: the disable was FUNCTION-scoped with a comment stating why the code is reachable — never file-level, never blanket. Removing the trap handler instead would have leaked three temp files per run.

A LOCAL GATE RUN CAN PASS FOR AN ENVIRONMENT REASON AND TELL YOU NOTHING ABOUT CI — measured 2026-08-18, PR #8477.

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker added scripts/check_workflow_job_timeouts.py, wired it into the verify-skill-mcp-drift job, and verified it by running it locally: captured exit 0, self-test exit 0, live run exit 0 over 117 jobs. Every rule about capturing your own exit code was followed correctly. The PR still went red in CI, both steps exiting 3:

    NOT CHECKED: workflow job timeouts. PyYAML is not importable on this
    interpreter, so nothing here examined .github/workflows/. This is NOT a pass.

THE CHECKER WAS RIGHT AND THE VERIFICATION METHOD WAS WRONG. This machine carries PyYAML 6.0.2; the CI job installs no pip packages by deliberate design. So the local green was an artefact of the developer environment, and it was indistinguishable from a real pass by every test the worker applied.

THE GENERAL RULE, which is NOT covered by 'quote the number you captured': that rule protects against a number that is present and wrong, and against one that was never written. THIS is a third case — a number that is present, correct, and ABOUT A DIFFERENT ENVIRONMENT. When a gate's behaviour depends on the interpreter, the installed packages, the OS or the shell, a local run is evidence about YOUR box and not about the runner. Ask explicitly: WHAT DOES THIS CHECK DEPEND ON THAT THE RUNNER MIGHT NOT HAVE? An import, a binary on PATH, a locale, a line ending, a case-insensitive filesystem.

THE CHEAP DISCRIMINATOR: read the JOB the check will run in, not just the check. Does it install anything? Does it check out with fetch-depth 0? The dependency question is answered in the workflow file, and reading it costs one look.

WHAT MADE THIS RECOVERABLE IN ONE RUN rather than several: the checker REFUSED loudly instead of failing open. It could have caught ImportError and skipped, and then it would have vouched for 117 jobs it never opened, forever, on every PR. A checker that cannot do its job must say so and exit non-zero. That is the same principle as 'a search that returns zero is not a check that passed', applied to the tool's own preconditions.

AND THE MAYOR'S HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG, which is worth keeping: I briefed the fix worker that a step-counting meta-gate had probably been armed by the new steps. It had not — every sibling meta-gate was green throughout. I labelled it a hypothesis rather than a finding and told the worker to believe the log over me, and it did. Label speculation as speculation and the cost of being wrong is nearly zero.

RETRACTED AND CORRECTED 2026-09-07 12:55 AUSEST. The original entry here claimed
`git ls-remote --heads origin 'refs/heads/<prefix>/*'` returns a silent, intermittent empty result
on this machine. THAT WAS WRONG. The command is fine; the fault was in my own pipeline, and the
retraction matters more than the original claim because a false instrument-warning makes a future
reader abandon a working form for a slower one.

RE-MEASURED, in both directions, with a control, three consecutive runs in one shell:
  * control, unfiltered: `git ls-remote --heads origin` then counting refs/heads/worker/ -> 9
  * the accused form: `git ls-remote --heads origin 'refs/heads/worker/*'` -> runner exit 0,
    9 lines, EMPTY STDERR, on run 1, run 2 and run 3
  * every pattern variant works too: 'refs/heads/worker/*', 'worker/*', '*worker*',
    'refs/heads/worker/**' each return 9
There is no intermittency and no defect in ls-remote.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED — a FIELD-COLLAPSE false zero, manufactured downstream of a runner that
succeeded. My pipeline was:
    git ls-remote --heads origin 'refs/heads/worker/*' | sed 's|.*refs/heads/||' | awk '{print $2}'
`ls-remote` emits `<sha>\trefs/heads/worker/<name>`. The `.*` in that sed is GREEDY, so it matches
the sha AND the tab as well as the prefix, leaving ONE field — `worker/<name>` — where the writer
assumed two. `awk '{print $2}'` on a one-field line prints the empty string, so nine refs came out
as nine empty strings. Verified: after that sed, `awk '{print NF}' | sort -u` reads exactly `1`.

AND THE 'INTERMITTENCY' WAS AN ARTEFACT OF COMPARING TWO DIFFERENT PIPELINES, not two runs of one.
The earlier invocation that "worked" printed a different field. Same runner, different downstream.
That is worth more than the mechanism: I diagnosed a tool from two non-identical commands and
called the difference intermittency, which is the least falsifiable shape a wrong diagnosis can
take and the one hardest to argue with later.

THE GENERAL LESSON, which is the part to keep: READ THE RUNNER'S OWN EXIT STATUS AND ITS RAW OUTPUT
BEFORE BLAMING THE RUNNER. Capture to a file, check the exit code of the command itself rather than
a pipeline's, and count the RAW lines. Every field-splitting step between a runner and a count is
somewhere a zero can be manufactured, and a manufactured zero is indistinguishable from an honest
one. CLAUDE.md's instrument-misreport item (f) makes exactly this point for a different command
(`… | wc -l` printing 0 and exiting 0 over a pathspec that legitimately matched nothing), and that
item was ITSELF corrected on 2026-09-07 (commit c5e4e17e1a) for the same species of over-diagnosis:
it originally blamed a machine-specific mid-path glob, and the truth was documented pathspec
semantics plus a downstream zero. Two entries in one day diagnosing a downstream artefact as a tool
defect. Suspect the pipeline first.

A MACHINE-WIDE EXCLUSIVE NEEDS AN ARBITER, NOT AN ANNOUNCE-AND-TAKE PROTOCOL. Where the resource wedges silently when two holders overlap, every worker obeying the protocol perfectly is still not enough, because the protocol has no step at which anyone checks whether the resource is actually free.

MEASURED 2026-09-16 on the re-frame2 mayor session, a genuine near-miss caught only by luck of message ordering. The standing protocol was: "announce to the mayor when you take it and when you release it." Two workers and the coordinator each did exactly what it required, and the resource still ended up doubly held:
  1. Worker A announced it was RELEASING, and said it would announce again before re-taking.
  2. The mayor, on the strength of that, told Worker B "the exclusive is FREE - take it now."
  3. Worker B announced TAKING.
  4. Worker A announced RE-TAKING, as it had promised.
Nobody broke the rule. The failure is that ANNOUNCE-AND-TAKE IS NOT A LOCK: an announcement is a notification, and a notification does not ask permission, so two correct announcements compose into a collision.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY UNTIDY: the resource in question wedges SILENTLY -- no error, no exit file, no output - so neither run fails in a way its worker can see. Each worker would have waited on a build that never completes and eventually reported a hang or a timeout, and the coordinator would have had two "infrastructure" reports and no reason to connect them. The cost lands as two destroyed runs plus a false diagnosis.

THE FIX, AND IT IS A COORDINATOR RULE NOT A WORKER RULE:
  * FIRST ACQUIRER HOLDS. An announcement is not an acquisition when someone else is already in the window.
  * The coordinator NEVER tells a worker the resource is free on the strength of a release message alone. A release is evidence about the past. Before granting, check that nobody has announced a take since.
  * Grant explicitly, to ONE worker, and keep a queue. Tell the next worker it is queued and that its place is held, so it does not have to ask again -- an asking worker is a worker tempted to assume.
  * When told to yield, the yielding worker KILLS any run already started rather than letting it finish; a half-overlapped run is as wedged as a fully overlapped one.

AND TELL THE YIELDING WORKER WHOSE FAULT IT WAS. Here the worker that had to yield had followed the protocol exactly; saying so plainly costs nothing and stops it treating a coordination failure as a mark against its own run. It had also kept its idle window deliberately short - the good behaviour that made the gap.

THE DEEPER SHAPE: a rule phrased as "announce X" tells you what to SAY and not what to CHECK. Where the cost of two holders is silent destruction, the protocol needs a step that can REFUSE, and only something that sees all holders can refuse. If no such arbiter exists, the exclusive is not actually exclusive.

ADDED 2026-09-18, THE SAME COORDINATOR CAUGHT BY ITS OWN METHOD-REREAD LOOP: A GRANT AND A USE ARE
DIFFERENT FACTS, AND THE COORDINATOR'S RESTATEMENT OF "HELD" IS THE THING THAT GOES STALE.

I granted the lane to one worker, and over the next forty minutes wrote "the exclusive is held by <that
worker> this tick" into FOUR dispatch briefs and TWO fence notes. Then the method-reread loop asked its
discharging question -- can you state the check you made THIS pass? -- and the honest answer was no: what
I could quote was my own earlier sentence. Re-verified BY EFFECT, filtering on process NAME (node.exe /
java.exe) plus worktree path against a live control of 9 such processes running: **ZERO shadow-cljs
processes.** The only worktree-bearing process was a different worker's plain `clojure -M:test` JVM run
with no shadow-cljs anywhere on its classpath.

**THE READING THAT LOOKS OBVIOUS AND IS WRONG: "the lane is idle, therefore it is free."** It is not. A
GRANT is state about PERMISSION and it is live until the holder releases; process absence is state about
USE at one instant. Neither implies the other. A holder between runs, or one that has not started yet,
shows exactly the same process table as a holder that has finished. **So process absence is NOT a
release** -- which is the mirror of this memory's existing rule that a release MESSAGE is not a release
either. Both are evidence about a moment; only the holder can end the grant.

**WHAT THE COORDINATOR SHOULD SAY, AND IT IS A PRECISION FIX RATHER THAN A PROTOCOL CHANGE**: "the lane
is GRANTED to X" -- never "held", which implies an active run and manufactures a contradiction the moment
anyone looks at the process table. The instruction to other workers is identical under either wording
(start no build), so nothing was harmed; what was wrong was that I could not have defended the sentence.

**AND THE ACT THE FINDING CALLS FOR IS A QUESTION, NOT A RECLAIM.** An announcement notifies and does not
ask -- that is this memory's whole thesis -- so a coordinator that discovers an idle lane ASKS the holder
whether it still needs it, says in terms that the grant stands until answered, and offers three answers
(still need it / done with it / not started yet). Reclaiming on an idle process table would be the
coordinator committing the exact error the protocol forbids in workers.

**WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING TIDINESS: the filter has a cost that accrues silently.** Two ready
items were excluded from dispatch for this lane alone, on a grant I had not re-checked in forty minutes.
An exclusive-resource filter is the only dispatch exclusion with a release condition, so it is the only
one that can quietly stop protecting the fleet and start refusing the backlog -- and a coordinator reading
back its own confident sentence will never notice.

**THE GENERAL SHAPE, past this lane: any coordinator-held piece of state that is ASSERTED into outgoing
messages becomes self-corroborating, because the next tick reads its own output.** The discharging test is
not "do I believe it" but "can I state the measurement I took this pass". Re-run the check; do not re-read
your own report.

THE MICROTASK/MACROTASK DISCRIMINATOR IS `invalidate-cell!` SPECIFICALLY, NOT "THE COLLECTOR" — my brief's rule was too broad (2026-08-11, rf2-2l17).

WHAT I BRIEFED. Chasing the fourth carrier of "the repair arrives a macrotask later", I told the worker the discriminator was WHO SCHEDULES THE DEFERRAL: "where the runtime schedules it in its own collector, the ruling repaired the scheduling and microtask is correct; where React or a timer owns it, macrotask stands."

WHY THAT IS WRONG, established at source by that worker: the ruling moved `invalidate-cell!` ONLY. Other deferrals in the SAME FILE are still real macrotasks and their prose is correct:
  - `collector.cljs:332` and `:972` describe `flush!`'s render-phase deferral, and `flush!` STILL USES `js/setTimeout … 0` at `:1017`.
  - `arm-cell-reaper!` at `:623`/`:627` is a genuine `setTimeout 0` — "one macrotask of grace" for a keyed reorder.
  - `arm1/runtime.cljs` is a separate FROZEN DONOR COPY that still calls `js/setTimeout … 0` at `:807`, so its prose at `:798` and both `ratom_activation_cljs_test` rows are accurate for the code they describe.
  - `spec/006-ReactiveSubstrate.md:1091` makes the core escrow reaper's macrotask class NORMATIVE — "It MUST be a macrotask" — which is what the `spine.cljs` and `react_shared_suite.cljs` hits are describing.

Had the worker applied my rule mechanically it would have "corrected" at least seven accurate statements and broken a normative spec line.

THE CORRECT DISCRIMINATOR: does the sentence describe `invalidate-cell!`'s deferred repair? Then microtask. Anything else — `flush!`, the cell reaper, the escrow reaper, a timer callback, React's own passive-effect scheduling, or the frozen arm1 donor — is still a macrotask and its prose is right.

THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is the same one three times over now: A DISCRIMINATOR STATED AT THE LEVEL OF A COMPONENT ("the collector") IS ALMOST ALWAYS TOO BROAD; STATE IT AT THE LEVEL OF THE FUNCTION THE RULING ACTUALLY TOUCHED. The worker's line is the one to keep: "source is the authority."

WORTH RECORDING TOO: the sweep was 362 hits across 123 files, every one read, and exactly ONE needed changing. That ratio is why "read every hit" is the work and the grep is only the index — and it is the evidence that the sweep-in-one-pass rule pays for itself. NO FIFTH CARRIER EXISTS; that hunt is closed.

"MAIN IS GREEN" IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT A BRANCH CAUSED A FAILURE — the failing job may be SURFACE-GATED AND SKIPPED ON MAIN (2026-08-12, PR #7945).

WHAT I DID. A node-test row reddened on a branch. I checked `gh run list --branch main` for the `tests` workflow, saw `success`, and concluded the branch caused it. I dispatched a fix-worker on that basis and told it so in the brief.

WHY IT WAS WRONG. `tests` reported success on main, but THE NODE-TEST JOB INSIDE IT WAS SKIPPED — surface-gated on paths the main commit did not touch. Run 31540419223 at the merge-base 5ac9d4aa17 never ran the job that was failing. A green workflow whose relevant JOB never executed is the same fail-open class this repo hunts everywhere else: it verifies the absence of bad news rather than the presence of good news.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT SETTLES THIS CLASS IN ONE STEP, from the worker:
  gh run list --workflow tests --limit 40 --json databaseId,headBranch,conclusion
then diff the FAIL line across branches. If an UNRELATED branch fails the identical assertion, the defect is pre-existing and no fix-worker should be pointed at the branch. Here a DOCS-ONLY branch (worker/cbident-hic029, two markdown files) had failed the same row four hours earlier with `actual: (not (= 4 1))`.

THREE MORE OF MY PREMISES FAILED IN THE SAME CALL, all from reading the rollup rather than the runs:
  - "Two CI failures" was ONE RUN, TWO ATTEMPTS. `gh pr checks` cannot show that; `gh run view` can.
  - "Identical numbers, so not a flake" holds PER RUNNER only. The same assertion gave 4→2 on one runner and 4→1 on another. FAILURE COUNTS WERE A STEP FUNCTION OF RUNNER SPEED, which is the signature of a wall-clock race, not of determinism.
  - So "deterministic numbers ⇒ not a flake" is a bad rule. The right question is whether the numbers are stable ACROSS RUNNERS.

THE ACTUAL MECHANISM, for the record: `arm-entry-reaper!` armed `setTimeout(…, 4)` at each entry's own minting inside `render-body`, while `lane/settle!` is `setTimeout(…, 0)` armed after ALL renders. Node drains one duration's timer list per pass, so the row turned on `settle-armed − first-mint < 3 ms` — and the harvest itself takes 1.2-2.0 ms. The test's own setup wall-clock was being charged against React's commit margin. Pre-existing on main; it only stops hitting other PRs once the fix merges.

THE RULE: before dispatching a fix-worker for a red on a branch, establish that the failing JOB actually RAN and PASSED somewhere the branch is not. A workflow-level "success" is not that. And sweep other branches for the same FAIL line first — it costs one command and it is the difference between fixing a defect and sending a worker to hunt one that is not there.

MY MATRIX COLUMN IS A PROXY FOR CLAUSE 5, AND IT OVER-BLOCKS (2026-08-11, PR #7835).

WHAT I COMPUTE: `git merge-base --is-ancestor <latest .github/workflows commit> <pr base>` — "does this PR's base contain the newest workflow commit?" When it says NO I have been treating clause 5 as failed.

WHAT CLAUSE 5 ACTUALLY SAYS: when a merge CHANGES THE WORKFLOW MATRIX — a new required job, a changed classifier, a re-scoped path filter — the PRs behind it WHOSE SURFACE THAT CHANGE COVERS do not inherit its verdict. The trigger is a changed MATRIX, not a moved FILE.

THE CASE: #7835 showed matrix=NO because two workflow commits landed after its base — a comment reword in lint.yml (rf2-93u6) and the GATE_PREFIXES widening plus prose corrections (rf2-rbdc). NEITHER ADDS, REMOVES OR RE-SCOPES A JOB. I measured it instead of assuming: diffing the check-name sets between #7835 and the last PR that reached 91/91 showed exactly ONE difference — "All required checks passed", the AGGREGATOR, which attaches only once the jobs it waits on finish. The job set is otherwise identical, so the matrix is unchanged and clause 5 is satisfied.

THE 90-vs-91 BAND DIFFERENCE WAS ALSO THE AGGREGATOR, not a missing job. Reading a short total as "a job never ran" is the same over-blocking error one field over.

THE REFINEMENT: when matrix=NO, do not stop — DIFF THE CHECK-NAME SETS against a recently-merged PR. If they match (modulo the pending aggregator), the matrix did not change and the PR is not stale in the sense clause 5 means. If they differ, name the job that appeared or vanished and THEN require the update-branch.

WHY THIS MATTERS BOTH WAYS: the method already warns that this guard fails in both directions — keyed too loosely it lets a PR through against a superseded matrix; keyed too tightly it blocks forever on a base that is merely older. A guard that blocks forever is not safe, it is differently wrong. My proxy is the second failure, and update-branching on it costs a full CI cycle and can introduce a conflict for nothing.

SISTER LESSON: my-sweep-conflates-failure-and-cancelled. Same root — a cheap summary reused as if it were the criterion.

MAYOR CI-merge gotcha: gh's statusCheckRollup includes STALE entries from superseded commits — when a worker force-pushes a fix, the prior commit's in-progress checks become conclusion=CANCELLED and its aggregates (e.g. 'Lint required','All required checks passed') linger as FAILURE in the rollup. A naive 'any conclusion!=SUCCESS' filter reads these as failures. For the merge decision use the DEDUPED latest-per-check view: 'gh pr checks <PR>' (pass/pending/fail/skipping per check). Merge only on 0 fail AND 0 pending there. Confirm ambiguity by checking a specific check has both a CANCELLED and a SUCCESS entry (latest wins).

Stop updating ai/dashboard.md. Surface operator-facing state in chat; keep decision gates in ai/decisions.md only. Do not spend tick cycles on the dashboard.

MAYOR dispatch anti-strand: do NOT tell workers to run 'scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' in a brief. On Windows it takes >10 min (slow shadow-cljs compile) and times out the worker's tool cap, so workers background it (or pipe through tail) and then STRAND with work uncommitted/unpushed — observed 4x this session (2dmtyl/.19/.21/.26). MAYOR DISPATCH DRIFT, caught 2026-07-24 on a reread of the method dispatch-prompt-template. Three things I had been omitting from briefs, in descending order of how much they matter.

1. ⚠️ THE WORKTREE BOUNDARY BLOCK MUST GO IN VERBATIM, AND THE GUARD SCRIPT IS NOT IT. I had been writing "run the worktree guard and report WORKTREE_ROOT" and stopping there. The method says plainly that a start-of-session guard CAN BE FOOLED: some edit-tool path resolution resolves a relative path against the SESSION ROOT rather than the git root, so a write lands in the mayor checkout even after the guard passed — the leak happens mid-session, in one tool call. The real backstop is two things I was not asking for:
   (a) re-verify the git root BEFORE EVERY EDIT — `git -C <worktree> rev-parse --show-toplevel` must print the worktree — and use ABSOLUTE paths under it for every write;
   (b) AFTER WRITING ANY NEW FILE, check BOTH TREES. A new GITIGNORED file leaking into the mayor checkout is INVISIBLE in the worker own git status, so it fails silently. This is the worst case and the one a guard cannot catch.
   On a leak the worker must STOP and report both paths — not repair, commit or push.

2. THE PR BODY NEEDS A SECTION HEADED EXACTLY `## Quality gates`. The verbatim heading is a CONTRACT for automated PR audits, not a style preference. List what ran with counts and exit codes; a skipped gate needs a one-line reason there, because a silent skip fails review. Some workers were doing this spontaneously; it should not depend on their initiative.

3. P1 IS ALWAYS SOLO — one bead, one PR — so it merges on its own green and is never blocked by a cluster-sibling. I bundled TWO P1s (rf2-berc2 + rf2-51d4q) into one dispatch because they were the same defect class in the same files. The surface reasoning was right and one agent SHOULD own that surface; the error was in the SHIPPING shape. The method already covers this case: a tightly-coupled surface is its own SERIAL LANE — one agent, but SEQUENCED PRs, later ones rebasing on the earlier merge. Corrected mid-flight by telling the worker to open a PR per bead.

THE GENERAL LESSON: I re-derived my brief boilerplate from memory each wave and it drifted from the written template. The template exists precisely because these are hard-won and non-obvious. Reread the SIBLING files on the cadence, not just the README — the boundary block and the shape-selection rules live in dispatch-prompt-template.md, which I had not opened this session while writing a dozen briefs.

MAYOR dispatch — grep for in-flight work FIRST (bitten 2x): before dispatching any bead/follow-up, run 'git ls-remote origin worker/*' AND 'gh pr list' and grep for a branch/PR already targeting that bead-id or its surface/error-id. A CONCURRENT monitor-loop session independently creates worker/* branches for the same beads I file — e.g. ahjbsi (my spec/009 route-keyword row) duplicated worker/qot6ii-009-row doing the identical row; both merged-collided, needed a cherry-pick rebase to drop the dup. The worker spent effort establishing that my axis was not the axis before it could answer the real question.

INSTANCE 2 — rf2-qbnv4. I wrote 'machine-reservation clause' throughout the bead and the brief. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN FAILURE MODE, distinct from a wrong fact. A wrong fact gets refuted and the worker moves on. AN INVENTED TERM LOOKS LIKE DOMAIN KNOWLEDGE. It reads as though the mayor knows a distinction the worker does not, so a worker either adopts it — propagating a second vocabulary into the tree — or spends real effort proving it is not a thing. THE RULE: BEFORE USING A TERM AS LOAD-BEARING IN A BRIEF, FIND WHERE THE CORPUS DEFINES IT. If it is not there, either use the words the corpus does use, or say plainly 'the corpus has no name for this; I am calling it X for this brief only'. Both are honest. Silently minting one is not.

AND THE TELL IS CHEAP TO CHECK: grep the term across the governing docs before writing the sentence. Two greps would have caught both instances. It is the same discipline as the constants — do not paste a value forward without re-measuring it — applied to words instead of numbers.

WHAT WENT RIGHT AND MUST BE KEPT: both workers were told the bead governs over the brief, and both exercised it. The rf2-qbnv4 worker reported the divergence explicitly as 'one divergence from the brief, deliberate' with its reasoning. That is exactly the behaviour the instruction buys, and it is why a bad frame cost a paragraph rather than a wrong document.

I INCREMENTED A CLOCK IN MY HEAD ACROSS A WHOLE SESSION AND MIS-DATED EVERY RULING BY OVER TWO HOURS, ROLLING THE DATE (2026-08-18).

A worker caught it: my ruling comment on rf2-6zc2q self-stated "2026-08-19 00:45 AUSEST" while its actual created_at was "2026-08-18 22:32 AUSEST". Every mayor comment that night carrying a 00:xx or 01:xx stamp is wrong by roughly the same amount, and several claim the WRONG DAY.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT CATCH IT. There is already a rule saying never type a timestamp from memory, fetch it with date(1). I FOLLOWED IT — once, early in the session — and then advanced that value by hand for hours, because each comment felt like "a bit after the last one". So I never experienced myself as typing a timestamp from memory; I experienced myself as doing arithmetic on a fetched one. The rule as worded does not forbid that, and the drift is invisible from inside: nothing in a long session tells you how much wall-clock has passed, and my estimates ran fast.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. These stamps go into RULINGS, which are the durable record of why a decision was taken. A ruling dated a day ahead of its evidence reads as having been made AFTER material it actually preceded, which inverts the reasoning chain for anyone reconstructing it later. It also silently disagrees with the tracker created_at sitting next to it, and a reader who notices will trust neither.

THE RULE, TIGHTENED: fetch the time for EVERY comment that carries one — one date(1) call per comment, not per session. Never do arithmetic on a previously fetched time. If a stamp is not worth one command, it is not worth writing.

AND THE TRACKER ALREADY KNOWS. created_at is authoritative, correct, and free. Prefer it: where a comment needs a time, the reader can see it without me stating it at all. State a time only where it adds something created_at does not — the time an EVENT happened, as against the time the note was written.

MY GATE BOILERPLATE INVITED A LOST EXIT CODE, AND A WORKER CAUGHT IT (2026-08-11).

MY WORDING, in every dispatch brief for this whole session: 'Redirect to a worktree-local log and echo the runner's own exit code into its own file on the VERY NEXT COMMAND.'

THE FLAW: 'next command' invites splitting it across two Bash tool calls. EACH BASH CALL IS A FRESH SHELL, so $? in the second call reads whatever the new shell last did — typically the 'cd' — NOT the gate. The rf2-hic-092 worker hit exactly this, noticed the captured code was meaningless, and re-ran with both parts on ONE command line. Its words: 'the brief's next command pattern silently fails here — each Bash call is a fresh shell, so $? reads the cd, not the gate.'

WHY IT IS THE NASTY SHAPE: the failure is SILENT and it produces a plausible ZERO. This is the same fail-open class the whole exit-code discipline exists to prevent — the rule meant to stop a pipeline swallowing a red instead swallowed it a different way, because I described the mechanism loosely.

CORRECTED WORDING, use this from now on: 'Run the gate and capture its exit code ON THE SAME COMMAND LINE, in one shell — never split across two tool calls, because each call is a fresh shell and $? will read the wrong thing:

  sh <ABS>/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > gate.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > gate.exit'

The literal example I already give is correct; only the prose around it was wrong, and the prose is what a worker follows when it deviates from the example.

GENERAL LESSON, and it is the third time this session my own boilerplate was the defect: BOILERPLATE IS THE LEAST-AUDITED TEXT I PRODUCE, because it is copied rather than composed. The others were nominating a gate whose exclusion list omits the surface, and hand-listing required checks instead of citing the derived path. Re-test one boilerplate claim per retrospective.

MAYOR SELF-MEASUREMENT: MY JUDGEMENT ABOUT WHAT MATTERS IS GOOD AND MY COUNTS ARE NOT. MEASURED 2026-09-10, the five and what was wrong: rf2-n5as filed 8 sites; 5 were real, and 2 of the 5 I never found. rf2-v44k both findings refuted; the file needed no change at all. rf2-hqti claimed 2 sites; there is 1. rf2-lbs9 census covered commits and not uncommitted state — half a check. rf2-5d85 gave a worker a count (5/5) without stating its scope; it is 7/7 whole-directory. THE COMMON FAILURE IS NOT CARELESSNESS, IT IS ASKING THE WRONG QUESTION. Each time I reached for a probe that could plausibly answer, rather than the question that would FALSIFY the claim: * n5as/v44k — asked "does the marker's text land in an
  • or a

    ?", a reading that reports healthy LOOSE list items as broken. I never asked whether the source was rendered at all; v44k's markers sat inside an HTML comment. * hqti — read two `or` forms as the same shape because they shared their first two alternatives and their purpose, without diffing the alternative LISTS. The whole scoping argument turned on which alternatives were present. * lbs9 — asked "are the commits upstream?" when the question was "is there anything here I would destroy?", which uncommitted work also answers. AND A CONTROL CAN PASS ON THE WRONG AXIS, WHICH IS WORSE THAN NO CONTROL. Suspecting my marker probe matched the wrong occurrence, I verified every probe STRING was unique in the HTML, got occ=1 across the board, and recorded "RELIABLE". Sound control, wrong axis: the defect was in what I asked ABOUT the match, never in which match I found. It converted a hunch into confidence. THE REMEDY IS CHEAP AND IS ALREADY PROVEN IN THE SAME SESSION — LABEL THE UNVERIFIED NUMBER. rf2-v44k carried two findings. Finding 1 I labelled "RELAYED, not reproduced" and told the worker to rebuild the probe; when it was refuted the label had already made it free. Finding 2 I asserted as measured; it sent a worker at a file that needed no editing. Same bead, same session, opposite costs, and the only difference was the label. SO: when filing on your own measurement, either state the FALSIFYING QUESTION you asked and the control that could have fired, or mark the number UNVERIFIED. A bare count in a bead is read downstream as measured fact and travels into dispatch briefs, where it becomes an error the worker has to spend attention undoing. DO NOT ANSWER THIS WITH MORE PROCESS. No checklist, no verification gate, no second probe by default — the project stance forbids exactly that, and the failure is a habit of question-framing rather than a missing step. One label costs a phrase. THE WORKERS ARE THE WORKING BACKSTOP AND SHOULD BE TOLD SO. Every brief that ended "correct me where I am wrong — I would rather be corrected than obeyed" produced a correction, five workers running, five real errors found in my briefs. Keep that sentence in every dispatch; it is earning its place.

A HARD SERIALISATION RULE DELEGATED TO A WORKER AS A CONDITIONAL CHECK BECOMES A SOFT ONE (2026-08-18).

WHAT I DID. The command file says "never dispatch two bench-class workers concurrently EVEN WITH NO WINDOW IN FLIGHT ... it is contention for the MACHINE". I dispatched an adapter-build worker that needed a shadow-cljs release build to measure a bundle delta, while a bench-class worker was live, and wrote into its brief: "if you need a release build, check first whether a bench window is live and say what you found". I turned a prohibition into an instruction to look.

WHY THAT FAILS, and it is not about the worker being careless. A WORKER CANNOT EVALUATE THAT CONDITION. It sees its own worktree and whatever it can derive from open PRs and branches; it cannot see what I am about to dispatch in the next minute, and it has no way to know that a peer whose branch looks idle is thirty seconds from starting a heavyweight run. The fleet-wide view is the mayor s and only the mayor s. Handing the worker the decision hands it to the party with the least information.

IT ALSO FAILS SILENTLY IN THE WORST WAY. Two heavyweight runs WEDGE rather than fail — no progress, no exit file, no error, several gigabytes each. So a worker that checks, sees nothing, and proceeds does not get a clean error; it gets a hang that looks like its own change misbehaving, and it will spend its context debugging the wrong thing.

THE RULE: WHERE A CONSTRAINT IS ABOUT A SHARED RESOURCE, THE MAYOR HOLDS IT ABSOLUTELY AND STATES IT AS A PROHIBITION. Never "check whether X is live", always "do not run X". If the work genuinely needs the resource, either sequence it behind the current holder or dispatch it as its own bead once the resource is free — and say in the brief that reporting the measurement as NOT TAKEN is a correct deliverable, so the worker does not substitute an estimate to fill the hole.

THE TELL that I am about to make this mistake: I find myself writing a conditional into a brief about something outside that worker s worktree. Anything outside its worktree is mine to decide.

A failing PR check goes to a Shape-5 fix-worker on the EXISTING branch (run the actual failing gate, push to that branch). A graduation/status-sync/anchor-fix goes to a worker bead. Doing it inline feels fast but burns the mayor context window the method exists to protect. THE METHOD ALREADY COVERS THE WORKER SIDE. dispatch-prompt-template.md makes "READ THE BEAD BOTTOM-UP; the bead governs over the brief" mandatory in the common preamble, precisely so a stale brief is caught on arrival. Mike 2026-09-15: approval prompts stall his throughput. Permission mode is auto with no allow rules, so a classifier escalates any Bash call it cannot read statically. TRIGGERS, never use: (1) running script files, e.g. sh scratchpad/mayor-merge-pr.sh or python assemble2.py; (2) inline interpreter programs: python -c with a program body, or python fed by a heredoc; (3) creating or writing files from the shell: heredocs, > or >> redirection, tee; (4) command substitution or variables in arguments: $(cat file), NEW=$(...), $SP, $wt; (5) control flow, and long semicolon chains that mix reads with merges, pushes and tracker writes: for, if, [ -e ]; (6) issuing a deletion command yourself. A documented repo test or build command that cleans its own output internally is fine; see mayor-workers-no-rm-deletions. INSTEAD: create files with the Write tool and append ledger rows with the Edit tool. Close with bd close ID --reason-file LITERALPATH. Create with bd create --body-file LITERALPATH --silent, then bd dep add NEWID BLOCKERID so the new bead depends on its blocker. Never use bd create --deps blocks:X: it makes the NEW bead block X, the inverse, and it inverted an edge in this session (see bd-create-deps-blocks-direction). Never put an ASCII apostrophe inside: write it as the typographic ’ or reword. An ASCII apostrophe ends the quote, so the call fails to parse (exit 2, nothing written). A MAYOR NOTE BECOMES THE NEWEST TEXT ON A BEAD, SO A WRONG ONE OVERRIDES A CORRECT DESCRIPTION FOR EVERYONE WHO READS IT NEXT (measured 2026-09-06, rf2-kuky.43).

WHAT HAPPENED. An audit reopened a bead listing four residuals. Three I verified. The fourth — skills/.../ssr-authoring.md:158, described as conflating head and body hashes — my grep could not find, so I read the line myself and concluded it was DELIBERATE v1 documentation of a known limitation rather than stale text. I appended that reading to the bead and instructed the next worker: if it is accurate at tip, record no change needed; do not reword a correct paragraph. The worker checked at source and refuted me. Head has its OWN :rf/head-hash channel (11 occurrences in spec/011; render-head-hash 5 and data-rf-head-hash 6 in implementation/ssr-ring/src, against a control of 0 for the deleted head-snapshot). spec/011 even says folding head and body into one hash WAS REVERTED.

AND IT WAS WRONG IN THE HARMFUL DIRECTION: the stale line said head drift at least SURFACES, misattributed as a body mismatch. It does not — the body channel never sees it and the client never reads :rf/head-hash — so head drift is SILENT. The reader got the opposite of the truth.

WHY THE WRONG READING WAS PLAUSIBLE, AND THIS IS THE REUSABLE PART: the line used the vocabulary that SURVIVED the recent change (:rf/render-hash) and never used the vocabulary the change DELETED (head-snapshot). So it looked untouched by the diff I was auditing. It was — its staleness PREDATED that PR and belonged to a different bead. My grep for the deleted names found nothing, and I read that null as evidence the line was CORRECT rather than as evidence I WAS SEARCHING FOR THE WRONG THING. A null from the wrong query is not a finding.

THE STRUCTURAL HAZARD: bd notes are ordered, and the loop instruction says order a bead's material by the tracker's own timestamps and treat the newest as current. That makes a mayor note MORE authoritative than the description it contradicts, by position alone. Here the DESCRIPTION was right the whole time and the newest text was wrong.

TWO RULES OUT OF IT. (1) When a bead's description and a later note disagree, break the tie by GOING TO SOURCE — never by recency, never by authorship. (2) A mayor note that CONTRADICTS a bead's own description must carry the measurement that justifies it, with a control that discriminates. Mine carried a null result from a query that could not have found the thing either way. Writing 'I could not confirm this' would have been correct and safe; writing 'therefore it is fine, leave it' was neither.

MAYOR OPS: timeout-guard every test-heavy worker dispatch. A worker can ship a NON-TERMINATING fix (rf2-um6d9: a stranded flows fix had (recur (inc i)) lexically inside the inner loop [j ...], rebinding j not i → infinite oscillation) that makes the JVM/CLJS test suite never complete and silently burns the box (~9 cores, 5+ CPU-hours), masquerading as 'slow CI' for an entire session. DETECTION: a hung-but-IN_PROGRESS worker = check the worktree (uncommitted work + 0 commits + no PR across many ticks) AND per-process CPU: CPU-seconds >> wall-minutes (CPU-HOURS in wall-MINUTES, cores pegged) = runaway, not slow. RECOVERY: TaskStop the agent (kills its child JVM), verify children died (an orphaned node-test process may survive → Stop-Process it), then re-dispatch a FRESH worker that (a) distrusts the stranded fix, (b) hard-caps EVERY test run with 'timeout 180 clojure -M:test' / 'timeout 540 npm run test:cljs' so a runaway is caught in <3min not 5 CPU-hours, (c) is authorized to return a root-cause writeup instead of forcing a fix. Make timeout-guards STANDARD in test-heavy dispatch briefs.

THE MAYOR CHECKOUT'S PATH IS A PREFIX OF EVERY WORKER WORKTREE PATH, so a substring grep of the dispatch ledger keyed on the mayor's own path MATCHES EVERY WORKER ROW and maps the mayor to some worker's item. Measured 2026-09-21 during a stranded sweep.

THE LAYOUT GUARANTEES IT, which is why this is structural rather than a typo: the checkout is `<...>/re-frame2` and the worktrees are `<...>/re-frame2-worktrees/<name>`, so the checkout path is a literal prefix of every worktree path. `grep -F "$wt" ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv` with `$wt` = the mayor checkout returns every dispatched row; a `| tail -1` then picks the most recent one and the sweep reports the MAYOR as holding that worker's bead.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE. Entirely plausible. In the instance measured, the mayor checkout was reported as mapped to `rf2-et4l0` — a real, live, correctly-dispatched item that genuinely had a worker. Nothing in the output is malformed; the row exists, the item exists, the worker exists. Only the attribution is wrong.

WHY IT MATTERS. A stranded sweep starts from the worktrees and maps trees to items, and this fabricates a mapping for the ONE tree that must never have one. Downstream that reads as the mayor holding a bead, which invites either a false strand ("the mayor's item has no live agent") or, worse, a reap or redispatch decision taken against the mayor checkout. It also silently suppresses the true answer, which is that the mayor checkout has NO ledger row by design.

IT IS THE INVERSE OF THE HAZARD ALREADY WRITTEN DOWN. CLAUDE.md's ledger bullet records the failure of keying column 1 by BARE NAME, which returned 0 rows for 28 worktrees that had rows — under-matching. This over-matches, from the same field, for the opposite reason, so a reader who fixed the documented one by switching to full paths lands directly on this.

THE GUARD: match the field EXACTLY, never by substring — `awk -F'\t' -v p="$wt" '$1==p{print $5}'` — and expect the mayor checkout and the audit-harness worktrees to return NOTHING. A sweep in which every worktree resolves to an item is the tell: some legitimately have no row.

AND THE SAME PREFIX RELATION BITES ANY path-keyed grep over any file listing both, not the ledger alone.

THE MAYOR'S CHARACTERISTIC ERROR IS REPORTING A CLASSIFICATION IT INFERRED RATHER THAN VERIFIED. Because a mayor repeats its summary every tick, one inference becomes a standing false claim to the operator. THREE instances measured 2026-08-21/22 — and the third came AFTER this memory was first written, so writing it down did not prevent it.

CASE 1, rf2-9wmqd. Reported for hours as 'quiet-box measurement lane'. The bead's OWN FIRST
PARAGRAPH says 'EDIT-SHAPED, LOUD-BOX-SAFE ... needs NO window'. Grouped by TOPIC and the group's
label reported.

CASE 2, rf2-lau0u. Same label, same way. Its fence never asserted it — it said 'Establish FIRST
WHETHER ...; IF IT DOES, it joins the quiet-box lane.' An unresolved CONDITIONAL reported as its
consequent.

CASE 3, rf2-lau0u again, and this one is the sharpest because it wore the clothes of a source
check. I ran the 'does X already exist at tip' guard, grepped for files mentioning h/hydrate! and
files mentioning useId, read the two lists, and reported 'no such witness exists' in a brief.
A witness had existed since 2026-08-14 — server_render_ssr_dom_cljs_test.cljs, added by the SAME
COMMIT as the door, carrying 9 hydrate! and 13 useId references, selected by :browser-test every
PR. TWO LISTS THAT OVERLAP ARE NOT A PAIRING. I never opened a file.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, one question: does the bead SAY this, or did I conclude it? A label like
'measurement lane' or 'awaiting a ruling' — or a finding like 'no witness exists' — is a CLAIM and
needs the same source check as any other. Quote the source in the note that records it; if you
cannot quote it, you inferred it.

THREE SHAPES TO WATCH, one per case:
  - A GROUP LABEL applied by topic rather than read off the item.
  - AN UNRESOLVED CONDITIONAL read as its consequent. 'Establish whether X; if X, hold' is not
    'hold', and it reads naturally as a fence to anyone skimming.
  - A NEGATIVE EXISTENCE CLAIM built from set membership instead of from opening the candidate.
    'No X exists' needs a file opened, not two greps intersected in your head.

AND NOTE THE FAILURE MODE OF THE FIX: the guard 'check whether X exists at tip' was itself added
to the method that same evening, and case 3 is that guard being RUN AND MISREAD. A guard executed
carelessly returns the same reassuring answer as no guard at all.

THE MAYOR MUST VERIFY A PREMISE AT SOURCE BEFORE FILING A BEAD, NOT ONLY BEFORE DISPATCHING ONE (2026-08-11).

WHAT HAPPENED. In one session I filed four beads from workers' incidental asides — findings reported out-of-fence, which is exactly the right thing for a worker to do. I wrote each finding into the bead description at filing time, as the routing rule demands. But I wrote them as FACTS, in the reporting worker's confident register, without opening the files. Two of the four premises were false, and both were caught only because the receiving worker checked:

1. rf2-w8pz. I asserted hd8_rows.cljs was "in the FROZEN BENCH TREE, kept verbatim by a hash manifest", and built the whole brief around the question "is this file editable at all", offering a recorded cannot-fix as the likely outcome. TWO separate workers independently read implementation/hicasso/frozen-sources.edn and found it pins exactly ONE file, front/slot.cljc, after three recorded retirements. The escape hatch I offered did not exist. The bead closed correctly anyway, but on an entirely different reason I had not supplied: git log -S proved denominator-resolution never existed as a binding at all.
2. rf2-dzus. I asserted "no committed dataset records a :clock-resolution, so the 100us clamp is an uncited constant". TWO-THIRDS FALSE. The figure is cited twice with primary sources in docs/design/hicasso/studio/the-candidates-clock.md and named as the Chromium constant kCoarseResolutionMicroseconds in the-clock-behind-the-published-rows.md; and 16 of 38 committed dataset files already serialise granularity. The one-third that held was a real two-line serialisation defect in two sibling runners.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT CATCH IT. The method already says "grep for the alleged broken symbol before DISPATCHING" and "an audit finding is a CLAIM, not automatically work". Both are aimed at the dispatch decision. Neither fires at the FILING decision, and filing is where the claim becomes durable: a bead description outlives the worker, the chat and the mayor, and the next reader has no way to tell a verified premise from a relayed one. A false premise in a bead is worse than a false premise in a message, because it looks like a finding.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS CHEAP TO FIX. Verifying costs one grep or one file read at filing time. Not verifying costs a worker's whole investigation — and it is a worker who is under a fence, on someone else's evidence, spending its context proving the mayor wrong before it can start.

THE PRACTICE:
- Before filing a bead from someone else's report, open the file at the named path and line. If the claim is about absence ("X does not exist", "nothing records Y"), run the search yourself — absence claims are the ones that fail, because the reporter searched for what they expected rather than what is there.
- If you cannot verify it in the moment, FILE IT AS A CLAIM IN THOSE WORDS: "reported by <worker>, NOT verified at source — verify before acting". That is honest and costs nothing.
- The two claim shapes that failed here are both worth naming in any brief you build on them: a FREEZE or manifest constraint (read the manifest; they shrink as things retire), and a NEVER-RECORDED / UNCITED claim (search the docs tree, not just the code).
- Tell the receiving worker explicitly that the bead text is yours and may be wrong. The line "my bead text is a claim, not a fact — verify every path, line number and structural claim before acting on it, and report anything that did not hold" turned both of these into corrections instead of wasted work.

THE SYSTEM WORKED, WHICH IS THE POINT. Both workers read the source, contradicted the bead, recorded the correction, and reached a better disposition than the one I framed. That is the bead-governs-over-brief rule running in the direction nobody designs for: protecting the worker from the mayor.

OPERATOR AUTHORISATION (2026-08-10 ~20:55 AUSEST, Mike, in session) — RUN THIS WHEN THE MACHINE IS QUIET.

Mike's words: "if you get to no dispatchable background agents, then the machine is quiet
and you can run measurement beads."

SO THE GATE IS NO LONGER 'ask the operator'. It is a measurable condition:
  when the dispatchable queue is exhausted and NO background worker is live,
  the machine is quiet and this measurement bead may be dispatched.

WHY THE CONDITION MATTERS, and it is the whole reason this bead was held all session: a
measurement window run against concurrent workers measures the CONTENTION, not the code.
Five or six shadow-cljs spines and a Chromium/Firefox/WebKit browser lane share this one
machine. Shape 6 says it in terms — "one run at a time, never concurrent" — and concurrency
is precisely the interference the window exists to exclude.

DISPATCH IT AS SHAPE 6, NOT SHAPE 1. The inversion is the whole shape:
  - THE CONTROLS ARBITRATE, NOT THE WORKER'S JUDGEMENT ABOUT THE BOX. A worker asked whether
    its machine was quiet enough will always find a reason it was. If a control fails, or the
    arm-order guard exits 2 (a refusal, deliberately not a plain failure), the run REFUSES and
    the worker reports the refusal without weighing it against how the box felt.
  - A REFUSAL IS A DELIVERABLE. Two of three window beads in one day came back as refusals and
    both were correct. If everything refuses, the window succeeded: you now know the rig cannot
    see what you hoped, which is what it was dispatched to find out. Say this in the brief or
    the worker reads its own refusal as failure and hunts for a way to turn it green.
  - NEVER 'fix' a refusal by loosening a gate. Widening a threshold to admit today's run
    retro-admits the failure the gate was built for.
  - DO NOT IMPROVE THE RIG MID-WINDOW. No new instrument, no extra rungs, no third estimator,
    however obvious. File the improvement and run it as its own window.
  - DO NOT RESTATE A PUBLISHED FIGURE ON THIN EVIDENCE. A worker holding four runs all reading
    below both published figures recorded them WITHOUT publishing. That was right.
  - VERIFY THE BOX WITH REAL COUNTERS. `Win32_Processor.LoadPercentage` read 93% while the true
    value was 11%. Use `Get-Counter '\Processor(_Total)\% Processor Time'` and
    `'\System\Processor Queue Length'` — QUEUE LENGTH IS THE DECISIVE NUMBER, because it says
    whether anything is actually waiting for a core, which is the only thing the window cares
    about.
  - ONE RUN AT A TIME. Two runs the worker believes independent still are not.

AND THE MAYOR'S OWN PRECONDITION: verify quiet before dispatching, do not infer it. `git
worktree list` under the re-frame2-worktrees sibling must show no live worker, and the ready
queue must be exhausted of everything else. If a worker reports mid-window, do NOT dispatch
another — the window owns the machine until it finishes or refuses.

The two measurement beads are rf2-hic-006 (named reference profiles + pinned baselines) and
rf2-hic-029 (retaining-host callback identity: the experiment and the verdict). They are a
SERIAL LANE OF TWO: they must not run concurrently with each other either. rf2-hic-006 first —
it pins the baselines every later gate anchors to.

THE COMMON SHAPE, AND IT IS NOT CARELESSNESS. Each worker did the hard part right — controls arbitrated, refusals were delivered, non-zero queue readings were quoted rather than rounded away, one worker disqualified its own designated arbiter mid-analysis and fell back to a floor derived from arithmetic impossibility. What slipped every time was the PROSE ONE LAYER ABOVE THE NUMBER: the summarising sentence, the name of the estimator, the attribution of a spread to a cause. A worker that has just spent an hour being rigorous about a measurement writes its summary in ordinary confident English, and ordinary confident English overclaims.

*** SO PUT THIS IN EVERY SHAPE-6 BRIEF FROM NOW ON. *** The window discipline covers the RUN. Add a clause covering the WRITE-UP:

  "Your published sentences are claims too, and they are audited. For every summarising
   statement you write, name the exact evidence that licenses it and check the arithmetic
   of any comparison in it. Do not attribute an observed spread to a single cause unless
   your own data excludes the others — if your queue samples include a non-zero inside a
   measurement phase, you may not call the dispersion the instrument's alone. Name the
   estimator you actually computed, not the one the surrounding prose habitually says.
   A hedged sentence that survives audit is worth more than a confident one that does not."

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: the numbers all survived. Not one audit overturned a measurement or a refusal. What they corrected was the sentence a future reader would quote — and a future reader quotes the sentence, not the log. An overclaimed summary on a page is how a measured result becomes a false premise in someone else's brief three weeks later, which is precisely the failure the premises-are-claims sentence exists to catch on the input side. This is the same defect on the OUTPUT side, and nothing was checking it until the merged-PR audit did.

CLAUSE 4 OF THE MERGE CRITERION MUST BE QUERIED PER-BRANCH. A GLOBAL 'gh run list --limit N' TRUNCATES AND REPORTS 'NO LIVE RUNS' FOR A BRANCH THAT HAS FOUR (observed 2026-08-07, PR #7626).

WHAT HAPPENED: I evaluated 'are there queued/in-progress runs on this PR's branch' with a single 'gh run list --limit 40' grouped by headBranch. worker/shellbytes-2rtt6-82 did not appear, so I reported it had no live runs. Querying it directly — 'gh run list --branch worker/shellbytes-2rtt6-82' — showed FOUR runs queued on the PR's head sha (tests, portability, docs, lint). They fell outside the 40-item window because other branches' runs filled it.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT AGAIN: clause 4 exists because statusCheckRollup can report pending==0 while runs are queued. I added a second source of truth and then read it through a truncating window, so the second source acquired the same failure mode as the first — it reported the absence of evidence as evidence of absence. Five variants of one bug in a single session: empty rollup passes '0 fail and 0 pending'; status==COMPLETED counts CANCELLED as passed; pending==0 while runs are queued; a rollup total that shrinks after a re-run still looks plausible; and now a truncated run list that omits a branch entirely.

THE RULE: for a MERGE DECISION, query the head branch DIRECTLY — 'gh run list --branch <headRefName> --limit 25' — and confirm no run is queued or in_progress, AND that the runs present are on the PR's current head sha (compare against 'gh pr view --json headRefOid'; stale-sha runs are not evidence about this head). Never use a global limited listing to decide a merge. A grouped overview is fine for a dashboard; it is not fine for a gate.

COROLLARY worth remembering: a rollup can show ONE check while four workflows sit queued on the same sha, because a queued run's checks are not yet attached to the commit. total==1 with 'no live runs' is therefore not 'this PR has one check' — it is 'look again, properly'.

GITHUB'S CHECK ROLLUP USES conclusion:"" FOR AN IN-PROGRESS CHECK, NOT null — a FAIL counter written as select(.conclusion!=null and .conclusion!="SUCCESS" and .conclusion!="SKIPPED") COUNTS EVERY STILL-RUNNING CHECK AS A FAILURE (2026-09-03).

MEASURED: PRs #9085, #9088 and #9089 each read FAIL=1 with the failing name printed as a real gate ('CLJS (shadow-cljs :node-test)', 'CLJS (compile every standalone example build, coverage gate)'). Three PRs on disjoint surfaces failing the same gate looked like a shared breakage on main. It was not: main was green at 13d8f0c2c0 and 4ead138e04, and the runs' own jobs API returned ZERO jobs with conclusion==failure. Reading the offending rollup entries directly showed status=IN_PROGRESS with an EMPTY conclusion and completedAt 0001-01-01T00:00:00Z.

THE FIX IS ONE CLAUSE: add .conclusion!="" — select(.conclusion!=null and .conclusion!="" and .conclusion!="SUCCESS" and .conclusion!="SKIPPED").

THIS FAILS CLOSED, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED UNNOTICED: it invents failures rather than hiding them, so no bad merge was ever admitted — the criterion demands FAIL=0 AND nonterm=0, and an in-progress check trips nonterm anyway. The cost is misdiagnosis: it reads a mid-build PR as broken and invites a fix worker onto a PR that has nothing wrong with it.

A live control is unreliable because recent PRs may genuinely have no failures — mine returned nothing across 20 closed PRs, which proves nothing. MERGING ON GREEN CAN LAND A BRANCH STATE OLDER THAN ITS TIP (2026-07-25). Twice today a PR merged while its worker was still pushing, so the merge captured an EARLIER commit than the branch's tip: #6975 landed one commit short (the worker opened #6982 to carry the remainder), and #6973 landed the v/html code half while its worker was still writing the acceptance suites (which then landed as #6980).

MECHANISM: the merge sweep reads 'fail=0 pend=0' and merges. Between that read and the merge, a live worker can push. GitHub merges the ref as it stood, so the delta silently becomes a follow-up PR — or worse, is briefly absent from main while the bead reads closed.

NEITHER CASE LOST WORK, and the reason is worth keeping: both workers were pushing as they went and both noticed, so each opened a follow-up rather than assuming its work had landed. Push-as-you-go plus a worker that verifies its own merge is what made this benign.

WHAT IT IS NOT: a reason to stop merging on green. Waiting for workers to declare done would idle the pipeline, and a green partial genuinely is worth more than a perfect whole later — that policy is correct and stays.

WHAT TO DO INSTEAD: (1) when merging a PR whose worker has NOT reported terminal, expect a follow-up PR and do not treat the bead as discharged on that merge alone — read the worker's eventual report; (2) tell workers in the brief that a merge may land a state older than their tip, so if their last push is not in the merge commit they should open a follow-up rather than assume it landed (both workers did this unprompted — make it explicit so it is not luck); (3) when a merged PR's beads stay open or in_progress, that is often this, not a partial delivery — ask before inferring.

RELATED, SAME ROOT: three times today I pruned a worktree from under a live worker because the merge sweep had 'PR merged' in hand while terminality lived in task notifications. The pattern across all four incidents is the same — the merge sweep is where mayor actions and live worker state collide, so every destructive or finalising step inside it needs a liveness signal read rather than inferred.

WHY IT KEEPS HAPPENING: the merge sweep reads fail=0 pend=0 and merges. Between that read and the merge call, a live worker can push. GitHub merges the ref as it stood. THE MITIGATION, cheap enough that there is no excuse: before merging a PR whose worker has NOT sent a terminal report, compare the PR head against the remote branch tip --
  gh pr view <n> --json headRefOid   vs   git ls-remote --heads origin <branch>
If they differ, the PR object is stale: re-read it and merge the current head. This is the same identity-not-name discipline that governs worktree pruning -- read the tip, do not assume the PR object is current.

WHAT MADE ALL THREE BENIGN, and it is the thing to keep briefing: every worker was pushing as it went AND checked whether its own work was in the merge commit. Each opened a follow-up PR rather than assuming it had landed. So the brief line "a merge may land a state older than your tip; if your last push is not in the merge commit, open a follow-up rather than assume it landed" is doing real work -- keep it, and note that all three workers did it UNPROMPTED before it was in the brief.

MAYOR-SIDE COROLLARY: when a merged PR beads stay open or in_progress, suspect THIS before inferring a partial delivery or a worker error. And do not close a bead on a merge whose worker has not reported -- read the file list, not the title.

A WILDCARD-BEARING GIT PATHSPEC MUST MATCH THE WHOLE PATH - SO `implementation/*/src` MATCHES NOTHING, AND THE ZERO IS MANUFACTURED DOWNSTREAM.

CORRECTED 2026-09-07 UNDER rf2-uwvv (PR #9350, merged c5e4e17e1a). THIS KEY PREVIOUSLY DIAGNOSED THE SAME MEASUREMENT AS A MACHINE-SPECIFIC DEFECT - "a mid-path `*/` segment dies ON THIS BOX", exiting 0 - AND IT WAS NEITHER. The key name is left in place deliberately so a search for it lands here rather than on the false version. CLAUDE.md's instrument item (f) carries the corrected wording.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, and it is DOCUMENTED GIT PATHSPEC SEMANTICS rather than a property of any machine (identical from Git Bash and from native PowerShell argv):
  * A pathspec CONTAINING A WILDCARD must match the WHOLE path. `implementation/*/src` therefore matches nothing, because every real path continues past `src`.
  * A pathspec with NO wildcard is a leading-DIRECTORY prefix, which is why the plain-directory form works.
  * Default magic `*` SPANS `/`, so naming a descendant works: `implementation/*/src/*` and `.../src/**` both match.
  * A wildcard that really does end where the path ends is fine - `-- 'spec/*/README.md'` matches.

AND GIT REPORTS IT HONESTLY: EXIT 1, EMPTY STDERR. Re-measured 2026-09-09 on a worker worktree: `git grep -c -F 'defn' -- 'implementation/*/src'` returned no output, exit 1, ZERO bytes on stderr; `-- 'implementation/*/src/*'` returned 304 files; `-- implementation` returned 1286 files. THE FALSE ZERO IS MANUFACTURED DOWNSTREAM, where `... | wc -l` prints `0` AND EXITS 0 - a pipeline's status is its last command's. So the instrument is not lying; the counting pipeline is swallowing the refusal.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY WRONG, and this part of the original entry was right and survives: zero is the answer a census WANTS when it is checking that a retired spelling is gone, a symbol is unused, or a surface is clean. And the wildcard pathspec looks MORE careful than the plain-directory form that works, so it reads as the rigorous choice. This repo propagated exactly that: rf2-kuky.8's own text carried `-- tools/*/test` (the working form `tools/*/test/**` reads 1933), and a brief quoting such a pathspec passes the false zero to every worker that follows it.

THE GUARD, in two parts: run the search once against something it SHOULD find, and READ THE RUNNER'S OWN EXIT STATUS rather than a pipeline's. Here both are cheap - the same needle with a plain directory pathspec, and `echo $?` on the bare `git grep`.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT, and worth keeping apart: this repo's memory `the-git-grep-ref-dir-returns-a-false-empty` records `git grep <ref> -- dir/` returning a false empty when a REF is involved. This one has no ref at all. Two different failures, one silent-zero signature.

SO THE RULE HAS TWO HALVES, AND BOTH ARE ABOUT MATCHING THE PROBE TO THE SEARCH:
  1. MATCH THE MEDIUM. Filesystem gate -> move the files. Git-reading gate -> stage the deletion. Marker-discovering gate -> the marker must leave the search space.
