AN ORACLE CROSS-CHECK MUST TEST WHAT THE ORACLE ACCEPTS, NOT ONLY WHAT IT REFUSES — otherwise it confirms your intent rather than the truth. Found by the rf2-drpa3.90/.97/.98 worker (PR #6733, 2026-07-23), and it is the sharpest refinement of the verify-the-verifier discipline this project has.

THE SETUP: the Freehand compile checker hand-rolls reader-conditional branch selection, so the established technique is to cross-check that selection against `clojure.tools.reader` at `:features #{:clj}` and `#{:cljs}` — an oracle independent of the code under test.

THE INSIGHT, in the worker own words: "the oracle only caught it because I cross-checked the ACCEPTING cases, not just the refusing ones... that is what separated the reader refuses this from MY RULE refuses this."

THE CONCRETE CASE IT SAVED: `{#?(:clj :a) #?(:clj 1)}` reads as `{}` for `:cljs` under tools.reader — perfectly legal. A naive "refuse any entry with an elided side" rule would have REFUSED it. That is a FALSE-RED, and false-reds are HARDER to notice than false-greens because the tool looks like it is working — it is confidently rejecting something, and nobody investigates a refusal that matches their expectation. The fix was to DROP an entry whose key AND value both elide, matching the real reader. Neither that case nor the companion `{#?(:clj :a) 1 :b #?(:clj 2)}` (which re-pairs to `{1 :b}` for the real reader) appeared anywhere in the bead.

THE RULE FOR ANY ORACLE-BACKED WORK: enumerate BOTH directions before trusting the cross-check —
  (a) cases the oracle REFUSES that your rule must also refuse (guards against false-green), AND
  (b) cases the oracle ACCEPTS that your rule must NOT refuse (guards against false-red / over-refusal).
Only (a) is the instinctive half, and only (a) is what a bead usually enumerates. A cross-check limited to (a) is not an independent oracle at all — it is a restatement of the intent you already had.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY, ALREADY RECORDED HERE: a probe that has never flagged anything has not been tested; run it against a KNOWN-PRESENT and a KNOWN-ABSENT instance. A blanket mutation that reds three fixtures while leaving two green certifies falsifiability it has not established. A guard proven on cases can still fail on SEQUENCES. This adds the missing axis: a guard proven on refusals can still fail on ACCEPTANCES.

BRIEF LANGUAGE THAT WORKS: "cross-check against <independent oracle>, and enumerate what it ACCEPTS as well as what it refuses — a rule that only reproduces your intended refusals has not been checked against anything."

examples/scripts/run-examples-tests.cjs --filter is path-substring-matched. The worktree name 'shop-testbed' is a substring of every spec path, so a bare 'shop' filter matches everything. When narrowing to a specific testbed, use the path-separator-aware form: 'testbeds\shop' or 'testbeds/shop'. Discovered in PR #1479 rf2-yhxk3 shop build.

A WORKER'S UNBOUNDED POLL LOOPS KEEP FIRING COMPLETION NOTIFICATIONS AFTER IT IS DONE, AND EACH ONE COSTS THE MAYOR A TURN (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: the rf2-9jrhi worker armed several 'until [ -f <exit-file> ]' waiter loops while a detached spine ran - which is the SANCTIONED pattern and it used it correctly. But it reported done without reaping them. Each surviving loop then satisfied its condition independently and fired its own task-notification. Roughly a dozen arrived after the work was complete and merged, all saying the same thing. The worker itself diagnosed them accurately and said it would stop responding; the loops did not care.

COST: each notification is a mayor turn. That is the same currency as a dispatch, spent on nothing.

THE FIX HAS TWO HALVES, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT WAS MISSING:
  1. Bound the poll loop - already in the brief, and it worked.
  2. KILL THE WAITERS BEFORE REPORTING DONE, and say you did. Same class as the node_modules link and the gate artefacts: a worker cleans up what it created. Add it to the same sentence in the gate-mechanics block that already covers the link.

THE MAYOR'S REMEDY WHEN IT IS ALREADY HAPPENING: TaskStop on the finished agent's task id. Do not keep acknowledging them one at a time - that is the cost, not the cure. One TaskStop ends the storm.

DISCRIMINATOR, so a real completion is not mistaken for this: a drained waiter repeats a report you have ALREADY ACTED ON, verbatim or near-verbatim, with the task status already 'completed' and no new PR, bead or head revision. A genuine second completion carries something new. If the content is identical to the last one and the tree has not moved, it is a waiter.

os.loadavg() RETURNS [0,0,0] ON WINDOWS, SO A LOAD RIDER BUILT ON IT SILENTLY RECORDS NOTHING (2026-08-21, rf2-24o2z, PR #8596).

WHY THIS BITES HERE SPECIFICALLY. Windows is the box every measurement window in this repo is taken on. rf2-24o2z asked for 'the box's load at window open' to be recorded in the allocation datasets, so that the mode-rate's mechanism — thermal state against V8 tier accumulation against heap fragmentation — could eventually be separated. The obvious implementation is os.loadavg(). On Windows Node returns [0, 0, 0] unconditionally: not an error, not a throw, just three zeros. Every window would have recorded a perfectly well-formed load field of zero, and the census built on it would have concluded the box was idle for every run ever taken.

THE FAILURE SHAPE IS THE ONE THIS REPO HUNTS EVERYWHERE ELSE: a reading that is PRESENT and WRONG, indistinguishable from a real one, underwriting a conclusion nobody would re-check. It is the sibling of 'a search that returns ZERO is not a check that passed'.

WHAT WAS BUILT INSTEAD: a CPU-times snapshot PAIR — os.cpus() times at window OPEN and again at CLOSE — whose delta gives the busy fraction the run actually saw. That is better than a loadavg on two counts beyond portability: it costs no sleep, and it measures the window's own interval rather than a trailing 1/5/15-minute average that mostly describes what happened BEFORE the window started.

THE GENERAL RULE: before recording any environment fact into a dataset, check what the API returns ON THIS PLATFORM, with a positive control. Cross-platform is a standing constraint here — Mike is on Windows, maintainers are on Mac and Linux — so a value that is merely well-formed on one of the three is not evidence.

TWO SIBLING FINDINGS FROM THE SAME DISPATCH, both worth carrying:
- P0_ALLOC_LEG* IS A BANNED ENV PREFIX in p0_run.cjs, guarding tau from acquiring a dial. A new switch named P0_ALLOC_LEG_ORDER collided with it and the pin fired TWICE — once on the switch, once on the comment explaining the ban. The working name is P0_ALLOC_PASS_ORDER, which is also rf2-fk6pj's own word for the term. Check the banned-prefix pin before naming any new P0 env switch.
- A SEEDED PASS-ORDER DRAW MUST BE BALANCED, and a schedule that happens to reproduce parity must be REDRAWN. An unbalanced draw trades the round-parity tie for the write/position confound the alternation existed to remove — which would have quietly reintroduced the exact defect rf2-fk6pj was filed about. The seed travels in the record as passSeed, because nothing else recovers the schedule afterwards.

OUTAGE PLAYBOOK — CORRECTION TO MY OWN NOTE FROM AN HOUR EARLIER (2026-07-26). I recorded that during a sustained 529 window the right move was to STOP resuming because resumes die on contact. Then I observed resumes DOING REAL WORK (two branches advanced, one worker reported a full Freehand JVM suite green at 1206 tests / 8042 assertions immediately before being killed), concluded the earlier note was too pessimistic, and resumed six workers plus dispatched two.

BOTH READINGS WERE RIGHT FOR THEIR MOMENT, AND THAT IS THE ACTUAL LESSON. The outage had PHASES. Between roughly 19:38 and 19:44 workers were killed AFTER producing work — resuming was clearly correct. From roughly 19:50 onward they died BEFORE THEIR FIRST TOOL CALL: measured, four consecutive resumes of the same worker left its branch tip, local HEAD and uncommitted count all byte-identical, and three freshly dispatched workers never even created their worktrees.

SO THE RULE IS NOT "resume" OR "do not resume" — IT IS: MEASURE WHETHER THE LAST ATTEMPT PRODUCED ANYTHING, AND LET THAT DECIDE THE NEXT ONE. The discriminator is cheap and objective: after a resume, did the remote branch tip move, did the local HEAD move, did the uncommitted count change, or (for a fresh dispatch) does the worktree exist? If none of those moved, the window is in its dead phase and further attempts are pure loss. If any moved, keep resuming — each turn buys real progress even though it ends in a kill.

WHAT DOES NOT WORK AS A SIGNAL: the SendMessage response. It returns "resumed from transcript in the background" identically whether the agent then does ten minutes of work or dies immediately. It confirms delivery, not viability.

AND WHAT STAYS TRUE IN EVERY PHASE, because it is the only thing that made two hours of this survivable: the mayor job is DURABILITY, not throughput. No unpushed commits anywhere (verified per worktree by comparing local HEAD against git ls-remote). Every at-risk uncommitted diff copied OUT of its worktree to a location outside the repo — seven patches by the end, including a 387-insertion core-walker change and a 32-file docs restructure. Never commit them: only that worker knows whether its files form a coherent change. And mark those worktrees EXEMPT from the hygiene reap on their beads, because the reap gate (zero commits, clean, no PR) matches an interrupted worker exactly.

The pair-MCP suite's npm test is 'shadow-cljs compile server-test && node out/server-test.js', and THE COMPILE PHASE EXITS 0 EVEN WITH A FAILING ASSERTION — measured 2026-09-02 on a deliberate sabotage run that printed '1 failures' and still exited 0 from the compile step. The overall npm test is sound because && still reaches the node phase, but a worker that captures and quotes the COMPILE step's exit code reports a false green while the run is red. Quote the NODE phase's captured exit code. Generalises: in any two-phase npm script, quote the phase whose verdict you are claiming.

UNDER FLEET LOAD, `npm run test:cljs` CAN ABORT WITH `aborted par-compile … still waiting for` — the documented rf2-6t03c symptom: shadow-cljs' 60-second `:par-timeout` expiring because several workers are compiling on one box. **IT IS NOT A COMPILE ERROR.** Measured 2026-09-05 by a worker whose reverted-source run aborted FOUR TIMES before giving a verdict.

THE DISCRIMINATOR: the aborted namespace set DIFFERS ON EVERY RUN, and never involves the namespace you changed. A real compile error names the same namespace every time. If the set moves, it is load, not your code.

**AND THE OBVIOUS FIX MAKES IT WORSE IN A WAY THAT LOOKS LIKE A DIFFERENT BUG.** Raising the timeout with `--config-merge` also CLEARS THE BUILD CACHE **after** compiling — so the compile succeeds, and then `node out/node-test.js` dies with `ENOENT` on `goog.debug.error.js`. A worker who reaches for `--config-merge` therefore trades a legible abort for an inscrutable missing-file error, and will spend context chasing a phantom.

**THE REMEDY IS TO RETRY THE PLAIN COMMAND.** Nothing else. The abort is transient and load-dependent; a re-run when the box is quieter succeeds.

WHY THIS MATTERS TO THE MAYOR AS WELL AS THE WORKER: the fleet ceiling is 6, and the heavy CLJS/browser gates are exactly what several workers run at once. **This is a cost of saturation, and it is worth paying** — but a brief should name the symptom so a worker recognises it in one read instead of diagnosing it. It also compounds the harness-vs-captured exit-code disagreement: the same worker measured the harness reporting exit 0 for FIVE background runs whose own `.exit` file read 1. **A run that aborted and a run that failed and a run that passed can all present as "exit 0" through the harness — only the `.exit` file and the log's own summary line discriminate.**

RELATED: [[harness-reported-exit-code-disagrees-with-the-captured-one]], [[worker-gate-browser-compile-sink]].

"I MADE NO TRACKER MUTATIONS, SO NO CHECKPOINT IS NEEDED" IS FALSE WHENEVER A PEER SESSION SHARES THE
BEADS DATABASE. The Dolt database moves without the mayor touching it, the committed export goes stale
silently, and because `.beads/issues.jsonl` is THE MAYOR'S TO COMMIT (CLAUDE.md, Beads durability) nobody
else can carry that work into git. So a peer's filed bead lives ONLY in the local database until the
mayor happens to checkpoint for some unrelated reason.

MEASURED 2026-09-17 during a §5 method reread, and found only because the reread compared two instruments
rather than trusting one. A peer session (rf2-fable-worker) running a review wave from Mike's session
filed an epic, rf2-y8doi, at 05:38:05Z. The mayor had reported "no tracker mutations, so no checkpoint"
for several consecutive ticks and was correct about ITS OWN writes each time.

  bd list --limit 0 --json          -> 12 non-terminal   (the DATABASE)
  git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl -> 11 non-terminal   (the COMMITTED EXPORT)

One bead, present in the database, ABSENT ENTIRELY from git. A checkpoint captured it (the checkpoint
re-exports FROM Dolt rather than trusting the working file, which is exactly why it works here), and the
committed export then read 12.

THE TRAP IS THAT THE OBVIOUS HEALTH CHECK PASSES. `scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh --pre-pull` exited 0,
`git status .beads` showed 0 lines, and the working export was byte-identical to HEAD -- all correct, and
all blind to this. Those instruments compare the WORKING FILE to the COMMIT; they say nothing about
whether either matches the DATABASE. Read in isolation they are a clean bill of health on a tracker with
unsaved work in it.

THE CHECK THAT SEES IT: compare a count taken from `bd` against the same count taken from
`git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl`. A disagreement means the database has moved since the last
checkpoint. Cheap, and it needs no knowledge of who wrote what.

THE GUARD: when any peer session may be writing beads, checkpoint on a SCHEDULE rather than on "did I
mutate anything" -- the mayor is the only party who can commit the tracker, so skipping is a durability
decision taken on someone else's behalf. It fails in the reassuring direction: everything on screen says
clean.

Distinct from the empty-export case CLAUDE.md already covers, which is a REGENERATION event with the
database intact. Here the database is ahead and git is behind.

MY PHRASE PROBES FAIL ON SENTENCE-INITIAL CAPITALS AND NARROW WINDOWS, AND EVERY FAILURE MANUFACTURES A FINDING (four instances 2026-08-23, one method-reread pass).

WHAT HAPPENED. Checking quotes I had been attributing to the method tree, a case-sensitive single-line grep returned NOT FOUND on four of five. Three of the four were VERBATIM PRESENT and my probe missed them:

* "cite the check you made" — the tree begins the sentence "Cite the check you made, or say plainly that you are summarising and from what."
* "where a reader-side rule has failed repeatedly" — the tree has "Where a reader-side rule has failed repeatedly, more text is usually not the repair."
* "Merge state is the test for a BRANCH" — the tree has lowercase "branch"; I had uppercased it myself and then searched for my own alteration.

The fourth, a principle I attributed to the tree in a merged PR body, read as INVENTED under a 180-character context window and turned out to be stated THREE TIMES once I widened the window and varied the phrasing.

THREE COMPOUNDING CAUSES, all mine. (1) Case: re-typing a phrase from memory drops the sentence-initial capital, and grep is case-sensitive by default. (2) Window: a fixed -oE context window centred on a short term misses the statement that sits just outside it. (3) Wrapping: these files wrap near 95 characters, so ANY quoted sentence longer than a clause spans a line break and a single-line grep cannot see it — flatten with tr '\n' ' ' first.

DIRECTION OF THE ERROR IS ALWAYS THE SAME AND ALWAYS THE EXPENSIVE ONE: absent-when-present. It reads as discovering drift, and acting on it means "fixing" a document that is already correct, or filing a correction against a merged PR that needs none. I was one step from both.

THE CONTROL THAT CAUGHT IT, and it is cheap: run a POSITIVE CONTROL through the same instrument before believing a zero — a phrase you have already confirmed present must come back. Mine returned the right two files, which is what licensed trusting the remaining zeros, and then widening and case-folding dissolved three of them anyway.

RELATED: the tree's own rule already governs the underlying slip — cite the check you made, or say plainly that you are summarising and from what. Reap is "Reap only on the worker's own report", not my paraphrase "a quotable completion report". When quoting the method to the operator, copy the string out of the file rather than retyping it.

PIPING A GATE INTO tail OR grep DISCARDS ITS EXIT CODE — a false-green generator affecting EVERY worker. Found 2026-07-24 by the worker whose PR it burned, and refined by that same worker afterwards.

THE MECHANISM: `npm run test:browser | tail -20` exits with the status of `tail`, not the runner. A worker reads "0 failures, 0 errors", sees a zero exit, reports green. The runner had exited NON-ZERO the whole time.

THE BRIEFED FORM — REQUIRE THIS IN EVERY DISPATCH:
  npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate.log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -20 /tmp/gate.log
Capture to a file, ECHO THE EXIT CODE, then read. A worker reporting a gate green must include the EXIT CODE, not just the counts.

⚠️ GREP IS WORSE THAN TAIL, not equivalent. Tail masks the exit code; grep masks the exit code AND hides the explanatory line — because a pattern chosen BEFORE you know what the failure looks like cannot match it. The real message here was "cljs.test summary was green, but the browser emitted 1 uncaught pageerror(s)" and it matched none of the workers `FAIL|failures` patterns. Capture-then-read fixes both: the file keeps everything and you can grep it as many times as the diagnosis needs.

⚠️ SCOPE THE COMPANION RULE CORRECTLY — do NOT over-generalise it. implementation/scripts/run-browser-tests.cjs fails a run on ANY uncaught pageerror even when every assertion passes (rf2-mwx08). That is BROWSER-LANE-SPECIFIC; the JVM and node lanes have no equivalent, and there the summary IS the verdict. State that distinction in briefs, or workers will start distrusting counts everywhere and re-derive exit codes from scratch each time. THE EXIT CODE IS THE UNIVERSAL ANSWER; the pageerror rule is merely why a green summary was never sufficient in that one lane.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY FALSE GREEN: the test summary is GENUINELY green. cljs.test reported 0F 0E inside a job that failed. Every human-readable signal says pass; the failure lives only in the discarded exit code.

A DISCIPLINE THAT PROVABLY WORKED, worth keeping: my brief for the fix DELIBERATELY REFUSED TO NAME A CAUSE (per the standing symptoms-not-causes rule, adopted after three of my asserted causes were wrong). The worker reported afterwards that its first instinct WAS to reason straight to the stale-cache explanation from my candidate list — and what stopped it shipping that was that reproducing gave it A NUMBER IT COULD CHECK (assertion count 3189 vs 3198, explained by main having moved 15 commits) rather than a story it could tell. Had the brief named a cause, it would have had a plausible one to confirm and no reason to look at the count. Symptoms-not-causes is not politeness; it is what forces reproduction over narrative.

RELATED FAMILY — the roster of ways "green" has meant "nothing ran" here: a bare `clojure -M:test -n <ns>` from the wrong dir (0 tests, exit 0); a CLJS runner selecting nothing after a rename; a clojure.test MAP fixture swallowing the body; multi-var `-v` running only the first var; an ns outside the runner regexp holding reader-conditional tests neither host runs. THIS IS THE SIXTH: a non-zero exit masked by a pipe, with a green summary above it.

PIPING DATA INTO `python - <<'EOF'` SILENTLY DISCARDS THE PIPE, because the HEREDOC IS STDIN. The
form `producer | python - <<'PY' ... PY` looks like it feeds the producer's output to the script, and
it does not: the heredoc is attached to fd 0, so `sys.stdin.read()` returns the empty string once the
script itself has been consumed by the interpreter. Exit 0, nothing on stderr, and the script runs to
completion against no data.

MEASURED 2026-09-17 on a stranded sweep: `git worktree list --porcelain | python - <<'PY'` printed a
bare table header and NOTHING ELSE, while `git worktree list` had listed six worktrees seconds earlier
and the same porcelain output redirected to a file read 931 bytes across 28 lines and parsed to 7
blocks.

IT FAILS IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION FOR EVERY SWEEP, which is what makes it worth recording rather
than shrugging at: an empty result reads as "nothing found" — no stranded workers, no matches, no rows
— and that is the answer a sweep usually WANTS. Here it would have reported an empty fleet while a live
worker was mid-run, which is the exact failure the stranded sweep exists to prevent, arriving through
the instrument built to run it.

THE GUARD: never pipe into a heredoc-fed interpreter. Redirect the producer to a FILE and have the
script open that file by an absolute path, or put the script in a file and pipe into that
(`producer | python script.py`). Where the data crosses a Python/shell seam, use the session
scratchpad's absolute Windows path, because Python-on-Windows and MSYS disagree about POSIX-looking
paths (already recorded as CLAUDE.md instrument item (n); a shell-written `/c/Users/...` file is
invisible to Python, which is the SECOND failure this same sweep hit, one command later).

AND TAKE A CONTROL ON THE PRODUCER, not only on the parse. The tell that separated the two failures
here was measuring the intermediate: `wc -c` on the redirected porcelain read 931, so the producer was
known good and the fault had to be in the handoff. A parse that reports 0 blocks is indistinguishable
from an honest empty until something upstream of it is known to be non-empty.

SAME FAMILY as the pipeline-status hazard this project already catalogues (a pipeline's exit status is
its LAST command's, so a failure upstream is invisible): there the exit code lies about a step, here
fd 0 is quietly taken over by a construct written on the same line. Both leave every command reporting
success.

`pkill -f "^find /"` DOES NOT MATCH A GIT-BASH `find` ON THIS BOX — the process's real command line starts with the full Windows path, `"C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\find.exe"`, so a pattern anchored on the bare verb matches NOTHING and exits SUCCESS. Measured 2026-09-04; it cost 63 minutes of an unnoticed whole-filesystem scan competing with peers' gates for disk I/O.

WHY IT IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE: a cleanup command that reports success and removes nothing. Identical in class to the `cmd /c` junction no-op already recorded in CLAUDE.md — exit 0, no output, no effect — and to `grep -c $'\0'` reporting a line count as a NUL count. The worker believes the runaway is dead, stops watching, and the process keeps running.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THIS PROJECT SPECIFICALLY: workers here are told to kill orphaned processes they can prove are theirs, and a heavy gate that two workers cannot coexist on WEDGES rather than fails. An orphan that survives a "successful" kill is exactly the contention source that makes the next worker's gate hang with no exit file and no error — and it is invisible, because the kill reported success.

WHAT TO DO:
  * Allow the full path in the pattern, or drop the `^` anchor: `pkill -f 'find\.exe'` or `pkill -f '/usr/bin/find'`.
  * BETTER — VERIFY BY EFFECT, NOT BY EXIT CODE. List the process afterwards and confirm it is gone. This is the same rule already recorded for junctions: verify the EFFECT, not the exit code.
  * And keep the standing constraint: never kill a process you cannot show is yours. The right proof is walking the parent chain to a DEAD root — the shell your run started and the harness killed. A peer used exactly that to kill only its own orphan while correctly leaving six foreign `node` processes alone.

THE GENERAL RULE THIS BELONGS TO: on this box, a command that reports success is not evidence it acted. Junction creation, junction removal, process kills, NUL probes and log fetches have all returned exit 0 while doing nothing. Check the world, not the status.

The repetition feels like diligence and is actually a symptom. When you notice yourself typing the same paragraph into a fourth dispatch, grep the method for it before typing it a fifth time — the answer is often zero hits.

AND: DO NOT ASSERT WHAT THE METHOD CONTAINS FROM MEMORY WHEN FILING A BEAD ABOUT THE METHOD. Grep first. This is the same rule as "never state a surface's gate coverage from memory", one level up, and I have now broken both versions of it.

A BYTE-DELTA ASSERTION CANNOT PROVE A PLANT LANDED — hash the line, do not measure it (2026-08-15 15:35 AUSEST).

WHAT I HAVE BEEN BRIEFING, and it is incomplete: 'these files are CRLF, so a patch matching \n writes nothing and the gate comes back green on unmodified bytes — assert the match count before and after the write, AND ASSERT THE BYTE-LENGTH DELTA.' The byte-delta half is the weak one.

MEASURED by worker/records-mha1r (rf2-mha1r cluster, PR #8297). It planted '#7-planted-bogus-anchor-mha1r' on dispositions.md:66, replacing an anchor of EQUAL LENGTH. THE BYTE DELTA WAS EXACTLY 0. A worker following my advice literally would have read delta==0 as 'the write did not land', aborted a plant that had in fact landed perfectly, and either retried pointlessly or concluded the gate was untestable. What proved the write was a sha256 of the single line, which changed.

SO THE DELTA CHECK IS NECESSARY-BUT-NOT-SUFFICIENT IN ONE DIRECTION AND OUTRIGHT WRONG IN THE OTHER:
  - a NON-ZERO delta does prove bytes changed;
  - a ZERO delta proves NOTHING — it is equally consistent with a no-op patch and with an equal-length substitution.
Equal-length substitutions are not exotic here. Swapping one anchor slug for another of the same width, flipping a digit, or exchanging two same-length identifiers all produce delta 0.

THE CORRECT ASSERTION, in order of strength:
  1. HASH THE SINGLE LINE before and after (git hash-object on the file, or sha256 of the line). A changed hash proves the write; an unchanged hash proves the no-op. This works for every case including equal-length.
  2. Assert the match count moved 1 -> 0 for the pattern you replaced.
  3. Use the byte delta only as a cheap corroboration when you EXPECT it to be non-zero, and never as the primary test.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE PLANT: the whole point of the plant is to prove the gate reads YOUR tree. If the plant silently no-ops, the gate comes back green and that green is meaningless — the 'a patch that never applied reads clean too' trap. An assertion that itself gives a false negative on a legitimate write pushes a worker toward abandoning the only proof it has.

FOUR WORKERS HIT THE CRLF NO-OP TRAP TODAY AND THE ASSERTION CAUGHT IT EVERY TIME — the mechanism is right; only my choice of measurement was sloppy. Brief the HASH, mention the delta as corroboration.

A BEAD ID IN A PR BODY IS A MENTION, NOT A DELIVERY — never close a bead on the presence of its id
in a merged PR. Measured 2026-09-07: cost one P2 defect left live on main under a CLOSED bead.

WHAT HAPPENED. PR #9361 was dispatched with three beads (rf2-1frc, rf2-oyrj, rf2-ytyq) and merged
carrying fixes for two of them. The mayor mapped the PR to its beads by extracting bead ids from
the PR BODY and closed all three. rf2-1frc appeared in that body because the worker had written a
careful explanation of why it did NOT attempt it — wrong surface (the defect is in
implementation/core/src/re_frame/substrate/spine.cljs, not the UIx adapter), a held spec document,
and a browser suite it would have had to build. So the extraction could not distinguish "delivered"
from "deliberately declined", and it failed in the REASSURING direction: the bead read closed while
the defect stayed on the trunk. The worker's own report caught it and marked the bead
"!! CLOSED IN ERROR"; the mayor reopened it.

THIS IS THE SAME DISTINCTION AS THE TRUNK DONE-CHECK SWEEP, reached through a different door, which
is why it got past me: I had applied it correctly to COMMIT MESSAGES that morning — an id in a
commit body can be a pointer rather than a closure — recorded that lesson, fixed loops.md for it,
and then three hours later read PR BODIES the same wrong way. A rule learned about one text field
does not transfer itself to another.

WHAT TO CLOSE ON INSTEAD, in order of preference:
  1. THE WORKER'S OWN COMPLETION REPORT, saying per bead what it delivered. This is the only source
     that can say "I declined this one, and here is why".
  2. THE MERGED DIFF, checked against the bead's actual deliverable at source with a control that
     bites. A title is better evidence than a body mention, because a title names what the change
     IS; but a title also under-reports — PR #9359's title named only rf2-kuky.60 while the change
     might have carried .58, and the only way to know was to grep the tree (it had not).
  3. Never the presence of an id anywhere.

AND THE FAILURE IS ASYMMETRIC, which is why it deserves a rule rather than care. Closing a bead
whose work did not land buries a live defect under a CLOSED record that no sweep will revisit —
the done-check sweep only reads OPEN ids, so a wrongly-closed bead is invisible to the very
instrument that would otherwise catch it. Leaving a delivered bead open costs one cheap re-check
next tick. When in doubt, leave it open and say why.

CONTEXT THAT MADE IT LIKELIER, worth recognising as a precondition rather than an excuse: this
happened while ten workers were I/O-starved on one box, none had filed a completion report, and
the mayor was closing beads from merge evidence alone because the reports it would normally read
did not exist. A fleet too large to report is a fleet whose beads cannot be closed safely.

THE PR'S OWN CHECK RUN CAN FALSIFY THE PROSE IN ITS DIFF, AND THAT CONTRADICTION IS VISIBLE AT MERGE TIME. Measured 2026-08-22, on a clause I merged and the audit reopened an hour later.

THE EVIDENCE WAS ON MY OWN SCREEN AT MERGE TIME AND I DID NOT CONNECT IT. The rollup I read to clear clause 2 showed "docs: success" -- that job is docs.yml's, and its running at all is a live demonstration that the path arms a gated surface. The diff said the opposite four lines away.

THE GENERAL FORM, which is what makes this worth keeping. The merge criterion says to read the FILE LIST against the item, and I extend it: when the diff makes a factual claim about GATING, the PR's own check run is a free control on that claim, and it is already open in front of you. A claim that a path arms nothing, beside a rollup showing a surface-gated job that ran, is a contradiction you can see without running anything.

THE NARROWER TRAP UNDERNEATH IT. "0 of 28" is one classifier's answer, not a census of gates. This repo has at least three independent gating paths -- test.yml's report-changed-surfaces.sh, docs.yml's own Detect docs surface step (which report-changed-surfaces.sh:44 NAMES in its own comment as a path it does not cover), and lint.yml's. "PR OPENED" IS NOT "WORKER FINISHED" — I BROKE THE SAME ASSUMPTION TWICE IN ONE SESSION, IN TWO DIFFERENT WAYS (2026-08-04).

INSTANCE 1, THE REAP RACE. I folded worktree-reaping into the merge loop so I could not forget it. A worker was still running the fast-PR spine in the tree I deleted: PR merged 02:24:42, worktree removed, spine finished 02:24:53 and reported FAIL implementation JS harness helpers with 11 "Cannot find module" failures naming files that are tracked and present. It looked like a real policy regression.

INSTANCE 2, THE DISPATCH RACE, and this one is worse. PR #7474 could not merge because main had moved, so I dispatched a rebase worker onto the SAME BRANCH. The original worker had not exited -- it was still resolving that very conflict. Its worktree's .git file was deleted underneath it and a new worktree appeared holding its branch at its own rebased SHA. It handled this better than I did: it verified the branch tip carried its complete resolution and pushed a ref-only update from the mayor checkout rather than racing, then flagged the orphaned directory. Nothing was lost, but only because the worker was careful.

THE COMMON ERROR: I treated the PR opening as the worker's last act. It is its last REPORTED act. After opening a PR a worker may still be running gates, updating the PR body, answering a message, or -- as here -- resolving a conflict I asked about.

THE RULES:
1. BEFORE REAPING A WORKTREE: require the worker to be finished, not the PR to be merged. The cheap approximation is to reap on the NEXT tick, once the tree is quiescent.
2. BEFORE DISPATCHING ONTO AN EXISTING BRANCH: confirm no live worker holds it. If a PR needs a rebase or a fix and its worker may still be alive, SEND THAT WORKER A MESSAGE instead of dispatching a second one. Resuming an existing worker is cheaper and cannot race.
3. A branch with a live worktree is CLAIMED. Treat a worktree the way you would treat an IN_PROGRESS bead.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE WASTED RUN: both failure modes produce evidence that looks real. A deleted worktree yields a gate failure naming real files that are present; a hijacked branch yields two agents with divergent views of the same tip. Neither announces itself as an infrastructure fault, and both invite a "fix" for a defect that does not exist.

PR visibility + merge SLA (Mike, 2026-07-13): remote PR head is authoritative. After a coherent checkpoint passes fast deterministic checks, commit/push before any test expected over 10 minutes; active PR must not lag a clean local worktree by more than 15 minutes. Draft may be incomplete but never stale/local-only. Run long CI and independent review in parallel on the pushed SHA. Mayor reconciles local HEAD vs PR HEAD every 5 minutes. Exact-head green + independently cleared merges within 5 minutes, followed immediately by mayor pull. If blocked, report named blocker + exact SHA. This prevents stale green GitHub ticks hiding hours of local work.

A PR CAN BE PERMANENTLY UNMERGEABLE BY A MAYOR WHOSE OWN LOOP MOVES main (2026-08-07, PR #7637, 28 attempts).

THE SYMPTOM: 'Base branch was modified. Review and try the merge again.' on every attempt, with the PR reading 86/86 SUCCESS, all five workflows completed/success at the head sha, mergeable=MERGEABLE, and behind=1.

BOTH TRANSPORTS AGREE, so it is not a client quirk: GraphQL mergePullRequest gives the message, and REST 'PUT /repos/{o}/{r}/pulls/{n}/merge' with an explicit sha gives HTTP 405 with the identical message. Do not spend attempts hunting a different call.

THE MECHANISM, and it is self-inflicted: the beads audit hook and the mayor's own checkpoint pushes each add a commit to main. So the cycle is — gh pr update-branch takes the branch to behind=0, CI restarts (~10 min) on the new head, a checkpoint push lands during that window, the branch is behind=1 again, and the merge refuses. The mayor is the thing staling it.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKS: clear the whole queue first, THEN update-branch, THEN merge NOTHING and PUSH NOTHING until its CI completes. A nominal 'this PR has priority' makes it worse, because priority without an empty window just means more attempts against a moving base. That inversion — merge everything else FIRST so the straggler gets a genuinely empty window — is the counterintuitive part.

WHEN TO STOP: this cost far more attention than the PR was worth (a docs/bench change). If a PR refuses more than about three times and nothing else is blocked on it, shelve it and merge it opportunistically when the tree is quiet for other reasons. Persistence on a blocked item is its own kind of gold-plating.

A PRECEDENT IS A CONCLUSION, NOT A SENTENCE TO COPY — and copying one writes a new falsehood (2026-08-05, learned on rf2-j4bg3).

WHAT I BRIEFED: rf2-e28wl had fixed the ambient-refusal row by STATING THE RULE rather than enumerating operations - "the category is defined by the DOOR, because every ambient resolution goes through require-current-frame!". I told the next worker to follow that precedent on the sibling row.

WHY THAT WAS WRONG, and it is not a near miss: THE REFUSAL ROW CAN SAY "ONE DOOR" BECAUSE THERE IS EXACTLY ONE. Absence has FIVE EMIT PATHS ACROSS THREE NAMESPACES AND 56 CALL SITES - require-current-frame! (21), require-frame-stamp! (27, the carried-stamp seam covering framework fx, timers, HTTP replies, history listeners, SSR hydration and machine lifecycle, WHICH CAN NEVER BE REFUSED because it never consults the resolver), require-frame-provider-target! (8), plus re-frame.ui.frames/resolve-frame which builds the payload and calls the emitter DIRECTLY, bypassing all three, and re-frame.resources' flat throw-error! guards. The worker contracted the CONDITION instead, with primitives as illustration.

SO THE PRECEDENT WAS "DO NOT ENUMERATE WHAT IS OPEN - STATE WHAT IS INVARIANT". The SENTENCE that expressed it was true only of the sibling. Had the worker copied it, the row would have asserted a single door where five exist, which is a WORSE error than the enumeration it replaced, because it reads as authoritative.

THE RULE FOR MY BRIEFS: cite a precedent by its REASONING and the problem it solved, never by its wording, and say explicitly that the wording may not transfer. "Do the same here IF the defect is the same" was in the brief and is what saved it - the worker checked. Without that clause I would have shipped a falsehood through a worker doing exactly as told.

A VERIFICATION PROBE AGAINST A bd FIELD NEEDS THREE NORMALISATIONS, NOT ONE, AND EVERY ZERO I HAVE READ THIS WAY WAS MY PROBE RATHER THAN THE CONTENT (mayor, 2026-09-17/18).

CLAUDE.md item (k) says probe the FIELD, not bd show's rendering. That is right and necessary and NOT sufficient. Probing the field, I read a false 0 five separate times in one session, on text that had landed perfectly every time:

  1. CASE. The field said "SECOND TOKEN AXIS"; the probe was lowercase.
  2. LINE WRAP. The phrase "nil reads as\na value" straddled a newline in the stored text; a flat probe cannot match it. Same mechanism as item (k)'s word-wrap half, which is a fact about hard-wrapped TEXT and not about the renderer, so it survives reading the field.
  3. CARRIAGE RETURNS, when one side came through a jq pipeline and the other did not (item (e)).
  4. MARKDOWN MARKUP. The field carried "computes `at-head?` off the FILTERED vector" with backticks, and "**BUILT**" with asterisks; my probe had neither. TWICE in one tick.
  5. UNICODE PUNCTUATION. The field carried U+2212 MINUS SIGN in "-20"; my probe had an ASCII hyphen. The console then refused to PRINT the character, which is itself the tell.
  6. QUOTE MARKS. The field carried a quoted phrase -- THREE "two lints" sites -- and my probe spelled the same words unquoted. Measured: 0 without a quote strip, 1 with it, control 0. This was the SIXTH instance and it happened AFTER I wrote this memory, using the guard below, because the strip set was '`*_' and did not include quotes.

THE GUARD, and it is one function used everywhere rather than a rule to remember:

    def norm(t):
        t = t.replace('\r','')
        for ch in '`*_' + '"' + '“”':   # quotes included -- see instance 6
            t = t.replace(ch,'')
        return ' '.join(t.split()).lower()
    def probe(text, p): return norm(text).count(norm(p))

Normalise BOTH sides identically: strip CR, strip backticks/asterisks/underscores AND straight and curly double quotes, collapse ALL whitespace including newlines, case-fold. THE STRIP SET IS THE PART THAT GOES STALE -- it has been extended once already, so when a probe reads 0, suspect a character class the set does not cover before suspecting the content. Then ALWAYS run a nonsense negative control in the same batch, because every one of these failures returns a well-formed 0 from a live instrument.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING TIDINESS: the act being verified is "did my close reason / rider land?", and a false 0 there says the write FAILED. The next move is to re-append — which is how rf2-kuky.58 got the same block three times across three sessions, twice LABELLED as a duplicate rather than excised. A false negative on a duplication probe is the reassuring direction, and it manufactures the duplicate it was run to prevent.

AND THE PATTERN IS ADAPTED TO THE DATA, NEVER NORMALISED ALONGSIDE IT (item (e)'s fifth door): stripping bytes cannot repair a regex whose escaped \r is part of its own semantics, because that is a backslash and an r, two ordinary characters. Decide which side is authoritative before reaching for a strip.

Prefer an INTERIOR phrase over a payload's first line — the first line is the likeliest thing to have been re-wrapped, re-indented or given a heading.

PROBE A BEAD'S NOTES FIELD WITH bd show --json, AND NEVER LET THE PROBE STRING CROSS A NEWLINE (2026-09-01, mayor session 9a; refined twice that session, and again 2026-09-08 with a THIRD mechanism from rf2-g2br).

CLAUDE.md says to confirm an --append-notes landed by probing for known content at start, middle and end. There are THREE ways to get that probe wrong, and all of them report data loss that did not happen -- the alarming direction, whose documented remedy is to reconstruct from a git checkpoint, which would DUPLICATE an intact note.

TRAP ONE, THE RENDERER'S WORD WRAP. bd show renders notes into a fixed-width column and LINE-WRAPS. Any probe longer than the wrap width straddles an inserted newline and cannot match however intact the data is. Measured: two of three probes returned 0 through bd show; the raw field via bd show --json measured 10858 chars with all five probes returning 1. Measured again on rf2-g2br: "and recovery brief prescribes" reads 0 through bd show and 1 through `bd show <id> --json | jq -r '.[0].description'`, where it sits unbroken on one line. It hit three independent agents in one session.

TRAP TWO, YOUR OWN SOURCE, and it SURVIVES the fix for trap one. Reading the raw field does not help if the probe string spans a newline you typed yourself. Prose written with hard line wrapping contains real newlines, so a probe copied from a rendered version of your own sentence crosses one. Measured on a note appended minutes after trap one was recorded: probe "only ever decided the fate of dead code" returned 0, while the raw field held "0dcoa only\never decided the fate of dead code." -- present, correct, and unmatchable. Two other probes on the same note returned 1, which is what makes the single zero read as partial truncation.

TRAP THREE, MARKUP STRIPPING -- recorded 2026-09-08 under rf2-g2br (PR #9503, commit 3a366b4072) and now in CLAUDE.md's instrument catalogue as item (k). THE RENDERING DELETES BACKTICKS AND ANGLE-BRACKETED PLACEHOLDERS OUTRIGHT. Measured on rf2-g2br: the field carries 12 backticks and the rendering 0; the probe for a backticked `bd show` reads 0 against 3 in the field; and the field's own guard line `bd show <id> --json` renders as "bd show  --json", which is BROKEN IF COPIED OUT OF THE RENDERING. This one is nastier than the wrap, because a note about this repo is exactly where backticks cluster -- every path, var and flag wants a code span -- and because it fires while you are auditing a note for the SEPARATE `--notes` backtick-substitution damage CLAUDE.md warns about. That is how it was met: a field byte-identical to its source, `cmp` clean, carrying 168 literal backticks, reading 0 through the rendering. An agent just warned about silent note damage reads that 0 and concludes the damage happened -- or, worse, probes for content it DID write, reads 0, and re-appends a duplicate.

THE RULE: read the RAW FIELD, never the rendering -- `bd show <id> --json | jq -r '.[0].notes'` (it returns a LIST; index [0]) -- and choose probe strings that cannot contain a newline and carry no markup. A distinctive fragment of a SINGLE line is the right unit, roughly three to six words, not a whole clause. If a probe returns 0, find the fragment with a substring search and print its neighbourhood before concluding anything: str.find plus a slice settles it in one command.

AND KEEP THE CONTROL BOTH WAYS, because a short markup-free probe reads 1 through the rendering and so looks like a working instrument -- measured on rf2-g2br beside the two zeros: "WORD WRAP" read 1, a nonsense probe read 0. So the rendering appears healthy on exactly the probes that cannot detect the defect.

WHY ALL THREE TRAPS ARE THE SAME ERROR: a probe is an instrument that can answer "nothing here", and any such instrument gives that answer when misused, with no error raised. Trap one measures the renderer's WRAPPING instead of the data; trap two measures YOUR line breaks; trap three measures the renderer's MARKUP STRIPPING. None is a fact about bd. And a length comparison is not the fallback -- chunked appends shift lengths by a byte or two, which CLAUDE.md already warns about.

PRODUCTION BYTES — a var whose :doc is REIFIED by a #' read ships its docstring into the :advanced bundle. Found by the rf2-k9yuy worker (#6350, 2026-07-18): the causal oracle reifies #'re-frame.ui.rules/ledger-state, so that defonce var's docstring survives advanced compilation as production bytes. Confirmed also for tool.evidence/state*. Ordinary defn docstrings strip normally — this is specific to vars reified via #'. TWO CONSEQUENCES. (1) Bundle-size/secrecy: prose you write in such a docstring ships to every consumer. (2) THE TRAP THAT ALMOST SHIPPED A DEAD GATE: the worker's first elision sentinel spelled its fully-qualified grep strings INSIDE that same docstring, so the grep found its own prose (2 hits) and would have false-failed forever — a check whose own text is the thing it detects. Fix: have the docstring delegate the strings to the scanner rather than spelling them. RULE FOR ELISION WORK: (a) grep the REAL release bundle (implementation/out/browser-test-prod-elision/js/test.js, ~2.26MB), never out/node-test.js which is a ~145KB loader; (b) prove the control direction — same build with goog.DEBUG=true must show the symbols; (c) prove the namespace is still COMPILED IN (e.g. re-frame.ui.rules/default present) or 'absent' may just mean 'never there'; (d) make sure your sentinel's own text cannot satisfy its own grep.

THE PRODUCTION-GATE JVM LANES (`-Dre-frame.debug=false`) ARE A SEPARATE CI JOB PER ARTEFACT AND ARE
INVISIBLE TO A NORMAL-PROFILE LOCAL RUN — name them in any brief whose change could behave differently
under debug elision. Measured 2026-09-07: worker ssr-a gated `clojure -M:test` in `implementation/ssr`
to exit 0 with 644 tests / 4194 assertions, honest and complete, and CI then failed at the EXACT head
it had gated on `JVM ssr under the production gate (-Dre-frame.debug=false)`.

WHY THE LOCAL GREEN WAS HONEST: `clojure -M:test` runs the NORMAL profile. The production-gate lane
re-runs the same artefact with debug compiled out. It is its own job in `test.yml`, outside the
fast-PR spine — one of the 99 required checks the spine does not decide — so nothing in a worker's
ordinary gate set reaches it, and `check_fast_pr_gap.py --brief` reports the gap as a COUNT rather
than by name.

THE COST WAS A FULL CI CYCLE AND IT WAS A BRIEFING ERROR, not a worker oversight. The worker ran every
gate its brief named and one it thought of itself; the lane simply was not in the brief.

WHEN IT BITES — any change that could differ between dev and release builds:
  * anything near a `debug-enabled?` guard, a trace emit, or an assertion that is elided in release;
  * a test that ASSERTS on something elided (the test fails, not the code — different fix, same red);
  * a new canonicalisation, hashing or error-enrichment path, because debug-only enrichment tends to
    live exactly there.
This is the same family as the DCE trap recorded for `subs.cache/emit-dispose!`: a seam that exists in
development and is compiled out of release. The browser analogue is `npm run test:browser-prod-elision`.

WHAT TO PUT IN THE BRIEF: tell the worker to read `.github/workflows/test.yml` for the job's exact
invocation and copy it rather than reconstructing the flag placement, and to run the lane covering its
own artefact. Do not paste a command from memory into a brief — the flag placement matters and a
mayor-invented form is another unverified premise.

GENERAL LESSON: `check_fast_pr_gap.py --brief` returning "99 required checks the spine does not decide"
is a number, not a list. A worker quoting it has demonstrated awareness of a gap, NOT coverage of it.
When a change plausibly lands inside that 99, the brief must name the specific lane.

WHAT I TURNED IT INTO, which is false: "that route does not exist". THE DATASETS ON DISK CARRY eventTiming, census, kbShape AND A FULLY-RECONCILED kbWitness.perArm. THIS IS THE COMPRESSION ERROR AGAIN, second instance, same shape as "in the catalogued family" becoming "catalogued in". A careful statement about ONE artefact - a program, a namespace, a roster - became a statement about the WHOLE ROUTE. The qualifier that made it true looked like padding.

THE DISCRIMINATOR TO KEEP: when a report says a PROGRAM does not read something, ask separately whether the DATA carries it. Code and corpus are different artefacts and a claim about one is silent about the other. The same split applies to "the gate does not check X" (the fixture may still contain it) and "the spec does not say X" (the implementation may still do it) - both of which bit today in the opposite direction.

NET EFFECT: a change intended to give the consumer MORE information gives them none. RULE: before promoting any internal map onto a wire/MCP surface, audit every value for EDN round-trippability; prefer `(pr-str x)` for anything that is not plainly data, and drop keys that tell the reader nothing. 2026-09-07, while finishing rf2-kuky.80's documentation migration.

THE MECHANISM: `doc_guide_check.clj` and `skills_check.clj` extract CALL-POSITION references, i.e.
the shape `(rf/<var>`. A stale mention written as backticked prose, or as a cell in a table, is never
in call position — so it sits outside BOTH checks while both run green. Five active documents were
instructing readers to use `clear-*` names that PR #9356 had deleted, and every gate was green over
all five.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS: these are ACTIVE GUIDES and SKILL FILES — the things an agent or
a newcomer reads to learn the API. A deleted name in a code sample fails loudly at compile; a deleted
name in prose is followed. The failure is silent, durable, and lands on exactly the readers least
able to detect it.

AND THE CENSUS THAT FOUND FOUR OF THE FIVE HAD THE SAME BLIND SPOT ONE LEVEL UP. Both merged-PR

CLAUDE.md's item (c) exactly: a census needs two TOKEN AXES, not merely two instruments.

  * When a public name is deleted, sweep prose and tables as a SEPARATE pass from the call-position
    gates, and sweep BOTH the bare and namespace-qualified spellings.
  * Do not read a green `doc_guide_check` / `skills_check` as evidence that documentation is
    consistent with the API. They check something narrower than their names suggest.
  * The discrimination that makes this tractable: does the text say a deleted V2 var still works

PROVE A COMMITTED TEST WOULD HAVE CAUGHT THE ORIGINAL BUG — build a mutant of the broken version. Established by the rf2-fr5yx worker (#6414) closing out my own failure.

BACKGROUND: I commissioned the ai/ ratchet (rf2-lsp1i #6380), accepted a three-teeth proof, merged it, and told the operator his end-state ruling was enforced. It was a STATIC CEILING: 89->61 passed, then 61->62 ALSO passed. All three teeth were genuine; each tested a SINGLE TRANSITION from a pristine baseline. The defect lived only in the composition, and the proof lived only in a chat report, so nothing re-ran it.

WHAT #6414 DID, and what to copy: it did not merely commit the seven arms. It BUILT A FAITHFUL MUTANT OF THE ORIGINAL BROKEN GATE (stale root-commit ceiling + count comparison) and ran the new suite against it. Result: arms 3+4, 5, 6b and 7 FAILED while arms 1 and 2 still passed — and arm 3+4 failed on exactly the right assertion (decrease passed, then the increase also passed, 0 !== 1). That demonstrates the committed test CATCHES THE SHIPPED BUG, rather than merely passing on the fixed code. It also kept a second, lighter control: the old decision rule reproduced in-test and asserted to pass the arms it should pass.

THE RULE: when committing a regression test for a bug that already shipped, do not stop at "green on the fix". Reconstruct the broken behaviour and show the suite REDS against it, arm by arm. A suite that only ever ran against correct code has never been shown to discriminate. This is the same scepticism as the mutation-proof rule, applied to the proof itself — and it is how you find that a tooth is a passenger (rf2-kxork found a suffix rename still contained its sentinel; rf2-vxgfnd.195 arm 4 built a function-name oracle, measured that it could never go red, and DELETED it).

SAFE-FIXTURE TECHNIQUE for gates that inspect the repo: build a throwaway repo under os.tmpdir() and ASSERT IT IS NOT THIS REPOSITORY before writing any guarded path. #6414 used the temp-repo + script-on-stdin form (sh -s) from _changed-surfaces.test.cjs so it runs the REAL script bytes and sidesteps Windows path translation. Never `git add -f` under a guarded tree to test its guard — the fixed ratchet has no in-band escape hatch, so a test that actually tracked a file could not clean up without an operator policy exception.

PROVE "NOTHING CHANGED ON THE TRACKER SINCE MY LAST PASS" FROM THE EXPORT DIFF, NOT FROM MEMORY OR A RE-READ (2026-08-23).

THE PROBLEM. The backlog-reread loop fires hourly and says do NOT rely on memory. On a static board that reads as an instruction to re-read fourteen long beads every hour, which is exactly what the method's own reread loop calls spending context for nothing. But "I remember it was the same" is not evidence either.

THE INSTRUMENT, two halves that together cover the whole window:

1. COMMITTED MUTATIONS: git log --since=<last pass> -- .beads/issues.jsonl gives the checkpoint commits spanning the window; git diff <first>..<last> -- .beads/issues.jsonl shows exactly which records changed. Parse the +/- lines as JSON and collect the id field to get the changed BEAD IDS.
2. UNCOMMITTED MUTATIONS: git status --porcelain -- .beads/. bd AUTO-STAGES on every mutation but never commits, so a clean export proves no tracker write since the last checkpoint.

MEASURED THIS PASS: the window carried exactly ONE changed line, and parsing it returned id=None. That None was not a null to wave through -- inspecting it showed {"_type":"memory", ...}, my own bd remember record. So: ZERO bead mutations in the window, proven, and the deep re-read of all fourteen was genuinely null.

THE TRAP INSIDE THE INSTRUMENT: the export holds more than issues. Memory records share the file and carry no id, so an id-keyed parse reports None rather than nothing. Read what the None was before calling the diff empty -- a records-changed count of 1 with zero bead ids is a DIFFERENT fact from a diff of zero lines, and only one of them is "nothing happened".

WHAT THIS DOES NOT COVER. Two of the loop's four things depend on the WORLD changing rather than the bead: a fence clears when a PR merges or a worker dies, and neither touches the tracker. So pair the export diff with: HEAD == origin/main unchanged (no merges), and the worktree sweep. If the trunk has not moved and no bead has mutated, all four things are provably null.

PROVE WHAT THE GATE READS, NOT THE TEXT IT READS FROM (2026-08-14, rf2-46tt9 worker).

MY INSTRUCTION WAS WRONG FOR ITS CASE. I told three workers to prove a required gate's input was unaffected by extracting the gate-read sections from origin/main and from the branch and diffing them byte-for-byte. That worked for the first two, because they LEFT the fenced section alone. The third worker's edit was INSIDE that section, so the raw text NECESSARILY differed by one line. Its words: "Claiming byte-identity would have been false."

IT PROVED THE RIGHT THING INSTEAD: the DERIVED ROSTER — what the required job actually consumes. 43 ids, 21 surface spans, 0 problems, diff EXIT=0, and the gate's own stdout byte-identical at 15 names and 43 rows. AND IT BUILT THE EXTRACTOR BY IMPORTING THE GATE'S OWN SECTION PARSER, so the proof cannot drift from what CI runs.

THE GENERAL RULE: a gate consumes a DERIVED value, not a file. Prove the derived value is unchanged. Byte-identity of the SOURCE is a sufficient proof only when you did not touch the source — and in that case it is also the easy case. The interesting case is exactly the one where it cannot hold.

AND BUILD THE PROOF FROM THE GATE'S OWN CODE. An independently written extractor can drift from the gate and then prove something CI does not check.

A FORENSIC BONUS WORTH KEEPING. My quoted 42,767-byte figure and its measured 42,663 differ by EXACTLY 104 over 104 lines — one byte per line. The earlier extractor emitted CRLF, this one LF. THIS REPOSITORY'S DOCS ARE CRLF, which also silently no-ops newline-spanning regexes. A byte-count discrepancy that equals the line count is a line-ending difference, not a content difference.

check_provenance_pins.py --changed-since IS BLIND TO AN UNTRACKED FILE, so running it before committing a NEW page is a green over a file it never opened (2026-08-15 13:10 AUSEST).

MEASURED by worker/releasepol-hic061 while adding a new page under docs/design/hicasso/: the gate reported '1 page inspected' while its new file was untracked, and '2 pages inspected' after committing. Same command, same tree, one commit apart.

WHY IT HAPPENS AND WHY IT IS NOT A BUG: --changed-since derives its corpus from git's change detection against a ref. An untracked file is not a change against that ref; git has never heard of it. The gate is behaving correctly and reporting honestly -- it says how many pages it inspected. Nobody reads that number.

WHY IT MATTERS ANYWAY: the failure mode is a CONFIDENT GREEN over unexamined content, which is the same class as three other traps measured today -- a job-key regex that matched no job key, a gh pathspec whose loud refusal a pipeline laundered into zero, and an architecture census whose positive control seeded a name nothing else owned. In every case a check returned the expected answer having verified nothing. The pattern is now firm enough to state as a rule: A GATE THAT CANNOT SEE ITS SUBJECT RETURNS THE REASSURING ANSWER.

THE REMEDY IS PROCEDURAL AND COSTS NOTHING: COMMIT FIRST, THEN RUN THE SCOPED GATE. Or read the 'N pages inspected' line and check N covers what you changed -- the gate already prints the evidence that it examined nothing.

NOT FILED AS A BEAD, deliberately. The gate is correct by construction, the remedy is one habit rather than a code change, and the stance rejects nag-diagnostics and says to close minutiae rather than action it. This record is the durable form. If a worker ever ships a page whose provenance was never checked BECAUSE of this, that is the moment it earns a bead.

GENERALISES TO EVERY --changed-since / --since / diff-scoped gate in this repo, not just this one. A new file is invisible to all of them until it is tracked.

check_provenance_pins.py REFUSES SHA-LIKE AND DATE-LIKE TOKENS IN NEW docs/design/** PAGES, AND IT IS NOT IN THE DOC-BEAD GATE MENU (2026-08-09).

WHAT HAPPENED. Six hic-* Wave A doc beads shipped new pages under docs/design/hicasso/product/. TWO of the six went red on the same gate, for two DIFFERENT token shapes:
  - rf2-hic-003 / PR #7713: the token 20260807 at k1-price-acceptance.md line 23 -- the fixed bootstrap RNG SEED (verified in clock_readjudicate.cjs and asserted in clock_exit_path.test.cjs), NOT a date -- on a line whose nearest commit-word to the left was "PR #". Reported as "(commit word 'PR #' nearest on the left, uncoded)".
  - rf2-hic-073 / PR #7714: the token abc1234 at correction-ledger.md line 55 -- an ILLUSTRATIVE PLACEHOLDER SHA inside a worked dry-run example row. Reported as "(unclassified -- read as a pin (fail toward refusal))".
Both are false positives about tokens never meant as provenance citations. The checker fails toward refusal by design, which is correct behaviour.

THE SECOND RED CHECK IS A SHADOW, NOT A SECOND FAULT. "Docs required" is a docs.yml roll-up; its log reads "needs results: success, success, failure". It goes green the moment the pins job does. Read the LOGS, not the check names, or you dispatch two fix-workers for one bug.

WHY THE BRIEFS MISSED IT. CLAUDE.md names scripts/check_doc_slugs.py as the gate for docs/design/** (mkdocs --strict excludes that tree), so that is what went into the briefs and what every worker ran, green. check_provenance_pins.py ALSO gates that tree on changed pages, and nobody ran it locally. Every worker was honestly green on the gate it was told about. This is the "never nominate a gate that does not cover the surface" failure in its mirror form: the nominated gate was right but INCOMPLETE.

THE FIX FOR FUTURE DOC BRIEFS. Name BOTH gates:
  python scripts/check_doc_slugs.py
  git fetch --no-tags origin main; python scripts/check_provenance_pins.py --changed-since origin/main --verbose
And warn the worker: write dates in ISO form 2026-08-07, never 20260807; never use a hex-looking placeholder such as abc1234 for an example commit -- use a clearly non-hex placeholder instead. The tool does NOT re-pin and states that a human decides each finding, so one false positive costs a full fix-worker round trip.

THE MAYOR'S OWN DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG, AND THE WORKER CAUGHT IT. The fix brief asserted 20260807 was "almost certainly a DATE written without separators" and proposed rewriting it as ISO 2026-08-07. It is not a date. It is the fixed bootstrap RNG seed: literal "seed: 20260807" in implementation/freehand/test/re_frame/bench/hicasso/clock_readjudicate.cjs:383, asserted by assert.strictEqual(EFFECT.seed, 20260807) in clock_exit_path.test.cjs:4058, and written as "the fixed bootstrap seed 20260807" in the source studio page. Rewriting it as a date would have FALSIFIED A REPRODUCER VALUE while turning the gate green. The worker verified the token against the harness source instead of complying, and regrouped it to 20,260,807 -- value preserved, longest hex run now 3 characters, and robust against any future rewording of the line.

THE LESSON FOR BRIEFS: when handing a worker a diagnosis, mark it as a hypothesis to verify, never as a finding to implement. This brief did say "CONFIRM that by reading line 23 before you touch it", and that sentence is the only reason the record survived. Keep it in every CI-fix brief.

THE PROVENANCE-PIN PLANT HAS A TRAP THAT PRODUCES A FALSE NEGATIVE — found by the rf2-hic-048 worker on 2026-08-14.

WHAT HAPPENS. check_provenance_pins.py treats a stranded pin as PASSING when its own block carries a landed pin alongside it. So a worker who plants a stranded SHA in the natural place — beside an existing citation, where SHAs already live — gets exit 0 and concludes THE GATE DOES NOT REACH THIS FILE. It does. The plant was simply neutralised by its neighbour.

THE CORRECT PLANT: put the stranded SHA in a paragraph or block that carries NO landed pin. The same SHA then gives exit 1 naming the line and [STRANDED]. That worker measured both arms — beside a landed pin, exit 0; alone, exit 1 at line 264.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE ONE GATE. The whole plant discipline rests on "if the gate does not redden, it does not reach your edit." That inference is sound only when the plant is genuinely fatal to the property under test. A gate with a block-scoped or set-scoped rule can absorb a plant without absorbing a real defect, and the worker then draws exactly the wrong conclusion — that a covering gate is not covering. Whenever a gate is known to have a scoping rule, the plant must be placed where that rule cannot rescue it.

THE SAME BEAD ALSO CONFIRMED rf2-qfrrp AT SOURCE: run before committing, the same gate inspected 0 files and returned exit 0 — the vacuous green. Run after committing on the same tree it reported 3 files, 34 pins, 32 landed, 2 stranded. Two distinct fail-open modes in one gate: nothing-to-check, and plant-absorbed-by-a-neighbour.

BRIEFS SHOULD SAY: run the provenance gate AFTER committing, quote the pin count rather than only the exit code, and plant a stranded SHA in a block with no landed pin.

So hand-written beads guidance belongs in CLAUDE.md outside the marker block, and mirroring it into AGENTS.md would put prose inside a region a tool rewrites.

PROVING A TOOL DID NOT WRITE NEEDS THREE INSTRUMENTS, AND THE TWO EVERYBODY REACHES FOR BOTH MISS A
REAL WRITE. Measured 2026-09-17 under rf2-oitjw, establishing that a `bd` READ does not dirty a worker
worktree.

The obvious check is `git status --porcelain` plus a content hash of the file. Both can read "unchanged"
while the tool genuinely wrote:

  * A CONTENT HASH CANNOT SEPARATE "did not write" FROM "rewrote the identical bytes". An idempotent
    rewrite is still the tool touching the checkout, and it is invisible to the hash. Take the MTIME
    alongside the hash: unchanged mtime is what rules out a rewrite, and no hash comparison can.
  * `git status --porcelain` IS BLIND TO GITIGNORED SIBLINGS. The write you are looking for may not be
    to the tracked file at all. `.beads/.gitignore` provides for a per-worktree `redirect` file, locks,
    daemon files and export state -- all gitignored, therefore invisible to porcelain, and all genuinely
    tracker state accumulating in a checkout. LIST THE DIRECTORY (`ls -A`) before and after and compare
    the entries. This is the falsifier the other two miss, and on this measurement it was the one
    expected to fire.

So the triple is: porcelain, blob hash AND mtime, and a full directory listing. Measured both the
FRESH-checkout case (`git worktree add --detach`, confirmed 0 porcelain before anything ran) and the
already-in-use case, five read commands each, all ten exit 0, every reading unchanged and the `.beads/`
listing identical at 7 entries both times.

AND TAKE A POSITIVE CONTROL ON THE INSTRUMENT ITSELF, or the zeros mean nothing: an 18-byte append moved
EVERY reading at once -- porcelain 0->1, blob changed, size +18, mtime advanced -- and `git checkout --`
returned all three. That is what makes the unchanged readings evidence rather than a silent instrument.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND `bd`: this is the shape of every "did X touch Y?" question, and it fails in the
REASSURING direction -- the answer you get is "no, nothing happened", which is what you were hoping for.
It is the same family as [[a-file-basename-is-not-a-dispatch-fence]] and the vacuity rule: an instrument
that CANNOT see the thing returns the same answer as one that looked and found nothing.

RELATED, AND THE REASON THIS WAS MEASURED AT ALL: the claim under test came to me as a worker's report,
which I propagated into three live dispatch briefs within the hour WITHOUT testing it, and it was false.
Re-running the test rather than re-reading the report is what caught it. See
[[a-disposition-reported-twice-is-a-rule-you-are-enforcing]].

It reported the row from the earlier base rather than claiming it twice, which is why nothing was lost.

THE DISTINCTION TO ENCODE: a terminal report SUMMARISES AND STOPS. An interim report NAMES SOMETHING IT IS STILL WAITING FOR — a monitor, an in-flight suite, a retry, a rebase it has not done yet. Phrases like 'waiting on', 'in flight', 'I will report its actual exit code', 'the retry is running' mean ALIVE, no matter how complete the rest of the report reads. The harness's completed status is also NOT terminality: a background agent notifies each time it stops with no live children, so the same task-id notifies repeatedly across one job.

SO THE GATE IS NOW FOUR CONDITIONS: (1) PR MERGED, head == the branch read from git worktree list --porcelain; (2) the agent's LAST report contains no outstanding-wait language; (3) no tracked uncommitted work (gitignored residue like .probe/ or .gate-logs/ is fine); (4) its beads closed or explicitly stated as deliberately open. If (2) is ambiguous, DO NOT PRUNE — message the worker and ask. A worktree costs disk; an early prune corrupts a gate run and emits log noise that reads as a real failure.

WHY THIS KEPT HAPPENING: the prune step lives in the merge sweep, so 'PR merged' is the signal in hand and terminality is a fact living in task notifications. Three times I let the available signal stand in for the required one. The fix is not more care — it is refusing to prune whenever terminality is inferred rather than read.

The rule I had already recorded — prune a worktree only when BOTH the PR is verifiably MERGED from that exact branch AND the worker agent has actually reported completion — I then violated again on worker/spec-004-residuals, pruning on the merge signal alone while its agent had never reported. The pushed commit survived; the in-flight edits did not.

WHY THE RULE KEPT FAILING: my prune step was driven by the MERGE SWEEP, which naturally iterates PRs, so 'PR merged' was the trigger I had in hand and 'worker reported' was a fact living somewhere else (task notifications). The check was expressed as a policy but not as a gate in the loop.

MAKE IT MECHANICAL, not remembered: before any prune, require BOTH (a) gh pr view <n> --json state,headRefName confirming MERGED from the branch read out of 'git worktree list --porcelain', AND (b) a recorded completion report from that agent. A FOURTH POST-MERGE PULL ABORT SHAPE, CAUSED BY CONCURRENT WORKERS SHARING FETCH_HEAD (2026-08-13).

MESSAGE: 'fatal: Cannot fast-forward to multiple branches.' Exit 128, HEAD unmoved.

This is NOT any of the three shapes mayor-merge.md documents. It is not 'local changes would be overwritten' (uncommitted tracker state) and it is not 'Not possible to fast-forward' (genuine divergence), and BOTH of those remedies are inert against it. Clearing .beads does nothing - the tree was clean. Rebasing does nothing - there was nothing to rebase.

CAUSE: linked worktrees SHARE the primary checkout's .git, and therefore share ONE FETCH_HEAD file. Three background workers had just been dispatched and each ran git fetch in its own worktree. Their multi-ref FETCH_HEAD was what the mayor's 'git pull --ff-only origin main' then read, and a FETCH_HEAD naming several branches cannot be fast-forwarded to. The mayor's own command was correct; a peer overwrote the file between its fetch and its merge.

DISCRIMINATOR: git rev-list --left-right --count HEAD...origin/main. It read '0 2' - zero ahead, two behind - which is a clean fast-forward, i.e. proof this is a race and not a divergence. The two documented aborts both show a non-zero LEFT number or a dirty tree.

REMEDY: bypass FETCH_HEAD entirely by merging the remote-tracking ref, which no peer can clobber:
  git fetch origin main
  git merge --ff-only origin/main
Then verify HEAD == origin/main and the divergence count reads 0 0.

EXPECT THIS TO GET MORE COMMON, NOT LESS: it scales with fleet size, and the merge loop's own advice to dispatch immediately after merging is what puts the fetches and the pull in the same seconds.

A post-merge pull that aborts is NOT always the uncommitted .beads/issues.jsonl — that diagnosis was wrong twice in one session (2026-08-07), and the documented remedy would have found nothing both times.

THE LOOP DOCS STATE IT AS THE CAUSE: bootstrap.md and mayor-merge both say 'If the pull aborts, an uncommitted .beads/issues.jsonl is the cause: run beads-checkpoint.sh, THEN git checkout HEAD -- .beads, THEN pull.' Treat that as ONE cause of three, not the cause.

FAILURE 1 — GENUINE DIVERGENCE, NOT THE TRACKER. 'git pull --ff-only' aborted with 'Not possible to fast-forward' on a CLEAN working tree. git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD showed 2/1: the repo's post-merge hook had committed 'chore(beads): audit merged PR NNNN' locally while the rebase-merge rewrote main remotely. The remedy is 'git pull --rebase' (or fetch + rebase origin/main). Running the checkpoint dance here finds nothing to fix and leaves the pull still aborting.

FAILURE 2 — STAGED, NOT MERELY UNCOMMITTED, AND THE DOCUMENTED CHECKOUT DOES NOT CLEAR IT. A later pull failed with 'cannot pull with rebase: Your index contains uncommitted changes'. .beads/issues.jsonl was STAGED with 3 insertions/2 deletions: bd auto-stages, and it had re-staged the file BETWEEN my 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' and the pull. 'git checkout HEAD -- .beads' does not reliably leave the index clean when bd is re-staging behind you.

THE SEQUENCE THAT ACTUALLY WORKS, and it must stay in this order (checkpoint FIRST so the Dolt re-export is committed before anything reverts the working file):
  sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh
  git reset -q HEAD -- .beads
  git checkout -- .beads
  git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main

DIAGNOSE BEFORE APPLYING ANY OF IT: 'git status --short' plus 'git rev-list --left-right --count origin/main...HEAD' distinguishes all three cases in one look — clean tree + divergence means rebase; staged .beads means reset-then-checkout; unstaged .beads means the documented remedy. NEVER git stash in any of them: stashes are repo-global and contaminate every worktree in flight.

`python -O` strips every `assert` statement. A self-test written as a run of asserts therefore executes zero checks under -O, falls through, and prints `self-test OK`. Exit 0. Nothing warns you.

WHERE IT WAS FOUND, WHICH IS THE POINT. The worker was dispatched to fix a fence checker that counted inert macro forms as live claims — a control that could not catch its own case. It then asked the generalising question of the file it was fixing and found the SAME defect class sitting in `--self-test`, i.e. in the control that was supposed to prove the fix. The instrument and the bug were the same shape.

It is family-wide here: all five hicasso sibling scripts exit 0 under -O. Filed as rf2-uyhh (P3, and the bead explicitly licenses a refusal — copying five lines into ~40 scripts may not be worth it) and rf2-df9b (P2, a related false-green in check_optional_module_reachability where `ns_of` takes the FIRST `(ns …)`, so a discarded `#_(ns …)` above the real form makes the scanner exempt the file).

THE FIX IS FIVE LINES: have `--self-test` REFUSE when assertions are disabled. Detect with `if not __debug__:` — it is False exactly when -O is in effect — and exit non-zero naming the cause. Do not try to re-enable assertions.

THE TRANSFERABLE RULE: ask of every control whether it is constructed so that it avoids the case it exists to catch. And when you fix one control, ask that question of its NEIGHBOURS in the same file before you leave — this worker found three live instances that way, and the sharpest one was in the file it had already opened.

Related: the hollow-gate test (delete the signal, keep the fault — if it stays green it was proving nothing). This is that test applied to the test harness itself.

PYTHON'S TEXT-MODE STDOUT ON WINDOWS IS A CARRIAGE-RETURN PRODUCER, exactly like jq is in
CLAUDE.md instrument item (e) — same seam, different producer, and the guard is the same.

MEASURED 2026-09-11 by worker ssrgate-a building the SSR prop-drop drift gate (rf2-7ntc, PR #9662).
A Python step derived a list of 49 checker commands out of .github/workflows/test.yml and redirected
them to a file. Python opened stdout in TEXT MODE, so every newline was written as CRLF. A bash
`while read -r cmd` loop then carried the trailing \r into each command's LAST ARGUMENT.

Result: ALL 49 invocations reported `unrecognized arguments` — with the flag plainly visible in the
usage line printed beside the error. 49/49 RED. Stripped, the true answer was 49/49 GREEN.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ONE RUN: it failed LOUDLY here only because the corrupted token happened
to be a FLAG NAME, which argparse validates. A command list whose trailing \r landed on a tolerant
argument — a path that still resolves, a value that still parses, a needle that simply matches
nothing — would have run SILENTLY WRONG and returned a plausible number.

THE CLASS, which is what generalises: wherever ONE SIDE TRAVELLED A PYTHON TEXT-MODE WRITE AND THE
OTHER DID NOT, the two sides may carry different line endings, and any comparison or argument
handoff across that seam can be defeated by the carriage return. CLAUDE.md item (e) states this
class for jq and says to carry the CLASS rather than the producer list; this is a second confirmed
producer.

THE GUARD, both halves:
  * Write with newline='' plus explicit '\n', or open the file in BINARY mode, so Python cannot
    translate. Or strip with `tr -d '\r'` on the consuming side before the value is used.
  * Take the control FROM THE TARGET: run one known-good command through the same pipeline and
    require it to succeed. A uniform failure across every item is the tell — 49/49 red is not a
    codebase in ruins, it is one broken instrument.

RELATED AND DISTINCT, do not merge them: CLAUDE.md item (n) is Python-on-Windows disagreeing with
MSYS about /tmp (a PATH divergence). This is a LINE-ENDING divergence. Same runtime, different axis.

The mayor read both as fleet-wide deaths, keep-listed two worktrees as holding unrecoverable only-copies, and told the operator no dispatch was possible for four hours.

(1) A peer session's review agent filed bead rf2-pk4i6.8 at 01:16Z = 11:16 AUSEST -- SIX MINUTES INSIDE the window the banner declared closed. Agents were being dispatched and completing throughout.
(2) The mayor's own turns never stopped landing, at 11:23 and after.
(3) The worker written off at 10:31 had NOT died: its transcript runs to 10:41 and ends "Done. PR #9879 is ready for review; both trees clean, branch in sync" -- it finished, opened a PR that merged at 10:52, and the keep row calling its tree an unrecoverable only-copy was false when written.
