It reads as a global fact because it is phrased as one, and the natural response -- stand the fleet down until the stated time -- costs hours and is unfalsifiable while you wait, because not dispatching produces no evidence either way.

THE GUARD, and it is this project's standing rule arriving through a new door: TAKE THE CONTROL FROM THE TARGET. Before believing a fleet is down, ask whether anything else succeeded inside the window -- a bead filed, a transcript that kept growing, your own turns. Before keep-listing a tree as holding a dead worker's only copy, read the agent's transcript tail by the id the dispatch ledger records (see the memory agentless-tree-report-is-on-disk-by-agent-id) rather than inferring death from a 429 you saw. A cheap re-test beats a long wait: one dispatch either dies in seconds, costing nothing, or is the work resuming.

AND THE CORRECTION HAS A SECOND HALF THAT OUTLIVES THE QUOTA: a keep-list row or a bead note written from a wrong premise is a durable false record. Both rows here said "HOLDS THE ONLY COPY ... NOTHING is recoverable from git" of trees that were, or shortly became, clean and pushed. Re-check a retained-record row's premise at each hygiene tick instead of trusting the row, which is the opposite of what such a file is for -- so state the row's RELEASE CONDITION in terms a later sweep can evaluate mechanically (is there a remote branch? is the tree clean?), never in terms of an event you believe happened.

A SESSION RATE LIMIT KILLS EVERY BACKGROUND WORKER AT ONCE, AND THEIR WORK IS RECOVERABLE — DO NOT REDISPATCH, PUSH THEN RESUME (measured 2026-09-06).

WHAT HAPPENED. Four workers died within seconds of each other on HTTP 429 'session limit'. Each notification carried a partial last line ('Now smoke_test.clj', 'Now fix the double-deref in the seeding test', 'Now the doc gates and CLJS'), which is the tell that they were mid-task rather than finishing.

FIRST MEASURE, DO NOT REDISPATCH. Redispatching would have thrown away 14 commits and three files of finished edits. The state per worktree, taken from the WORKTREE list per loops.md S4:
  attrgate-a   clean tree, 2 substantive commits, 6 UNPUSHED
  ssrdel-a     clean tree, 5 substantive commits, 8 UNPUSHED
  machtest-a   3 files modified, ZERO commits  <- most at risk
  xraydrain-a  clean, 1 commit, nothing unpushed, junction left in place
So the loop's own remedy applies: 'push existing commits, reopen with a note, redispatch' — and the push is the urgent half, because a second kill loses uncommitted and unpushed work alike.

THE PUSH FAILS NON-FAST-FORWARD, AND THAT IS EXPECTED. A worker that rebased before dying leaves its branch DIVERGED from its own remote (local ahead N, remote ahead M). A plain push is refused.

TWO TRAPS IN THE RECOVERY, both of which I hit:
(1) I ran `git push ... 2>&1 | tail -2` and read 'push exit: 0'. THAT WAS TAIL'S EXIT STATUS. The push had been REJECTED. Piping a mutating git command through a filter reports the filter's status — the identical hazard CLAUDE.md records for the beads durability sequence, reached through a different door. Never pipe a push, a merge, a rebase or a checkpoint.
(2) The reflex on a rejected push is --force. Prove it is safe FIRST:
      git -C <worktree> cherry HEAD origin/worker/<name>
    Lines prefixed '+' are commits on the REMOTE that are NOT patch-present locally — i.e. work that a force-push would destroy. A count of 0 means the local branch is a rebased superset and forcing loses nothing. Both branches read 0 here; only then did I push, with --force-with-lease, unpiped, and read the real exit code.

WHAT NOT TO DO: never force-push main, and never force a worker branch on which the cherry check shows '+'. In that case the remote carries something local does not, and the right move is to hand it back to the worker.

THEN RESUME RATHER THAN RESPAWN. SendMessage to the same agentId restores its full context — a fresh dispatch starts from nothing and re-does the work. Resume in value order and CHECK THE FIRST ONE LIVES before sending the rest: if the limit is still in force the agent dies immediately and you learn it for the cost of one message instead of four. Tell each worker exactly what you did to its branch, quote the verification, and quote its own last words back so it knows where it stopped.

MY PROVENANCE FIX WAS UNSOUND: RE-PINNING RESTORES THE PATCH, NOT THE TREE (2026-08-06, rf2-owq6p, PR #7616).

WHAT I RULED, one pass earlier: "pin to a commit already on main — the measurement happened upstream of the documenting edit, so no merge can move it." I recorded it as a memory and put it in a brief.

WHY IT IS WRONG AS A GENERAL RULE: it holds for the SSR spike, where the run was taken on an UNMODIFIED MAIN TREE. But MOST of this evidence corpus measures the workers OWN INSTRUMENT CHANGES — so the measured tree was never on main, and NO COMMIT CARRIES IT. The landed commit sits on a LATER BASE. Re-pinning therefore restores the PATCH, not the TREE that was measured.

THE FAILURE IT CAUSES IS WORSE THAN THE DEFECT: an unresolvable pin is VISIBLY broken. A re-pinned wrong one is RESOLVABLE AND WRONG — it fails silently, which is precisely what the bead exists to prevent. Measured: for 9 of 11 pins the rebase preserved every contributed blob and re-pinning was safe; for TWO it did not (one rebase resolved conflicts in three files on the measured path, another moved the file its decomposition turns on) and those were ANNOTATED rather than re-pinned.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, which belongs in the convention rather than in judgement: RE-PIN ONLY WHERE THE REBASE PRESERVED EVERY BLOB THE COMMIT CONTRIBUTED. Otherwise the page says so.

AND THE ENFORCEABLE RULE IS NOT MINE EITHER: not "no authored heads" and not "every SHA must be on main", because several pages deliberately RETAIN the authored head alongside a blob-table fallback and a must-be-on-main gate would red them for being careful. It is "EVERY CITED AUTHORED HEAD MUST BE ACCOMPANIED BY A RESOLVABLE LANDED SHA".

SCALE, so the shape is not mistaken for an edge case: 319 unique hex tokens under docs/design/hicasso/**, of which only 77 are commits — 188 are content digests and FNV hashes that must not be treated as pins at all. 44 stranded, 79 occurrences, 24 pages, ALL reachable from no remote ref.

TWO METHOD NOTES WORTH MORE THAN THE FIX. (1) The recovery was VALIDATED BEFORE BEING TRUSTED, against three pages that already document authored->landed mappings as ground truth: stable patch-id is invariant across this repos rebase-merge, and 43/44 mapped exactly. (2) The worker caught its OWN first blob check comparing WHOLE TREES — which differ for every rebased pair, so it would have condemned everything; the correct check is the commits OWN CONTRIBUTED BLOBS.

THE PATTERN IN MY OWN ERROR, for the seventh time today: I generalised a cure that was correct for ONE case into a rule for a corpus I had not measured. Same shape as generalising the CRLF override from one file to a tree, and the git-grep hazard from one ref to all refs. A CURE THAT WORKED ONCE IS A DATA POINT, NOT A CONVENTION.

REACT CAN SWALLOW A DOM EXCEPTION SO THAT NOTHING REACHES THE CALLER — a refusal is not optional there, it is the only signal (2026-08-14, rf2-h6qm7 worker).

WHAT WAS MEASURED. A :value on a file input throws InvalidStateError inside React's setInitialProperties during commit. The obvious assumption is that the author can catch it. THEY CANNOT: React caught it inside its own commit and re-reported it via reportError, so a thrown-by probe around the flushSync returned NIL — the probe printed four nils. The author had neither an error id nor an exception to catch, only a console entry naming React internals.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND ONE BUG. When judging whether a source-located refusal is worth minting, the usual test is "does the platform already tell the author?" Here the platform DOES throw and the author still learns nothing, because the framework intercepts it. So "React throws" is not evidence that attribution exists. CHECK WHETHER THE THROW REACHES THE CALLER, not merely whether something throws.

THE PROBE THAT SETTLES IT: wrap the mount in flushSync and assert on what thrown-by returns. Nil means the exception was intercepted and the author is blind.

AND THE SAME PASS PROVED A NEGATIVE PROPERLY, which is the reusable technique. I asserted that a sibling code path shared the defect. The worker showed it did not — by MOUNTING A REAL INPUT with setAttribute type FILE and measuring the asymmetry: attribute FILE, IDL property file, .files present, refusal fires. That row passed in BOTH the red and green states, which is what makes it evidence rather than assertion. A test that passes only after the fix cannot prove a path was already immune.

REACT SWALLOWS A RENDER-PHASE THROW, SO A `try/catch` AROUND THE MOUNT NEVER FIRES AND A DOM TEST
ASSERTING "IT RAISES" PASSES VACUOUSLY OR FAILS FOR THE WRONG REASON. ONLY A WINDOW `error` LISTENER
NAMES THE REFUSAL.

Measured 2026-09-11 by a worker writing a DOM suite against Xray's shell chrome.

THE OBSERVABLE. An error thrown during render -- `:rf.error/no-frame-context` was the case in hand --
does not propagate out of `flushSync`. A `try/catch` wrapped around the mount call NEVER FIRES.
React reports the error through its own error-handling path, which surfaces in the browser as a
window `error` event. So the only instrument that can see it is a window `error` listener installed
before the mount.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY AWKWARD, AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS:

  * A test that asserts a refusal by wrapping the mount in `try/catch` and expecting a catch will
    see NOTHING and report that the refusal did not happen -- when it did. That is a FALSE
    ACQUITTAL of a real fault, and the natural next move is to conclude the mechanism does not hold
    and stop looking.
  * A test that mounts and simply carries on, without a listener, sees a rendered-nothing tree and
    whatever cascade follows. The failure it eventually reports is downstream and names something
    else.

THE SECOND HALF, WHICH IS WHERE THE TIME ACTUALLY GOES: MOUNTING BARE IS ITSELF A FAULT INJECTION.
The same worker's first DOM suite mounted the shell view BARE and took 10
`:rf.error/no-frame-context` failures -- caused by its own test's mount, not by the code under test,
because `mount.cljs:396` wraps the real shell in an OUTER `[rf/frame-provider {:frame ...}]`. Any
suite against provider-wrapped chrome must mount through the real chrome, or it manufactures exactly
the error it is hunting and then cannot tell the two apart.

THE GUARD, BOTH HALVES:
  * To observe a render-phase refusal, install a window `error` listener before mounting and assert
    on what it receives. Do not use `try/catch`.
  * Before believing any `no-frame-context` result, check whether the test's OWN mount supplied a
    provider. Mount through the production mount path rather than the view directly.

AND THE GENERAL FORM, WHICH IS THE REUSABLE PART: an absence observed through the WRONG INSTRUMENT is
not evidence of absence, and a `try/catch` that never fires is indistinguishable on screen from a
`try/catch` around code that did not throw. Exercise the listener once against a throw you planted,
so a silent run means "did not raise" rather than "was not watching".

Related: [[inline-plain-defn-helpers-into-boundaries-heading-is-the-footgun]].

A THROW INSIDE A REACT EVENT HANDLER DOES NOT FAIL cljs.test — THE ROW READS GREEN OVER A LIVE EXCEPTION (2026-08-03, rf2-fki5d).

React does not let an exception escape dispatchEvent; it routes it to reportError. So a cljs.test deftest that dispatches a real DOM event and asserts 'nothing threw' sees 0 failures / 0 errors EVEN WHEN THE HANDLER THREW. The rf2-fki5d worker wrote exactly such a row first, and it passed while the code under test was raising InvalidStateError on every run.

WHAT CAUGHT IT: the runner's separate uncaught-pageerror gate (rf2-mwx08) failed the build FROM OUTSIDE the test. So the signal existed, but it was not attached to the assertion that claimed to cover the behaviour — the row itself was fail-open.

THE FIX, and it generalises: any row asserting 'this did not throw' inside a React event must install a window 'error' listener (and assert on it) so the row REDS BY NAME. Otherwise the only coverage of that case is a build-level gate that names no test.

DISPATCH RULE: when briefing browser/DOM work whose claim is 'no exception', require the listener explicitly and require a MUTATION PROOF — delete the fix, confirm the suite exits 1 with exactly one named failure. rf2-fki5d did this and it is what makes the row trustworthy.

RELATED CLASS (same shape, different mask): piping a gate through tail/grep returns the pipe's exit status, not the runner's. Both are fail-open instruments that report success while the thing under test is broken. Distrust any green whose failure path you have not personally mutated.

READ A STATUS FROM THE STATUS FIELD, NEVER BY PATTERN-MATCHING A RENDERED HEADER — and
establish a history's ORDERING before walking it. Two instrument failures, measured together
2026-09-02, where the second appeared to CONFIRM the first.

WHAT HAPPENED. A closure sweep over twenty beads used
`bd show <id> | head -1 | grep -oE 'OPEN|CLOSED' | head -1`. It reported rf2-9stk0 as OPEN. It
was not: status field 'closed', closed_at set, absent from `bd list --status open` throughout.
THE BEAD'S OWN TITLE CONTAINS THE WORD — "...the inverse ... fails OPEN" — and the title
precedes the status field on that line, so the probe returned the title's word. Of the twenty
swept, it was the ONLY one whose title could poison its own status read, and it was the one
that flagged.

THE CORROBORATION FAILED TOO, WHICH IS WHAT MADE IT CONVINCING. The confirming check was a
status-transition walk over `bd history --json`, which reported "closed -> open" at the newest
index. The history is NEWEST-FIRST, so walking indices upward walks BACKWARDS IN TIME: a pair
reading closed-then-open by index is open-then-closed by TIME. The detector printed every
transition reversed, and would report a reopen on ANY bead that has ever been closed.

COST: a no-op re-close, plus a false "reverted close, third this session" finding written onto
the bead and then corrected there.

THE TWO HABITS.
  - Parse the JSON (`bd show <id> --json` -> `status`, `closed_at`), never grep the rendered
    header. An item's own text can contain the words a status probe looks for, and prose is
    where that collision lives.
  - Before trusting any walk over a history, read the timestamps at both ends and establish
    which is newest. Ordering is a property of the tool, not something to assume, and an
    ordering error inverts every answer while producing perfectly well-formed output.

A BEAD CAN BE 'READY' AND STILL BE UNDISPATCHABLE, BECAUSE 'ready' MEANS 'NO OPEN BLOCKERS', NOT 'A WORKER CAN ADVANCE IT' (2026-08-13).

WHAT HAPPENED: rf2-hic-016 sat at the top of 'bd ready --limit 0' as the highest-priority non-epic bead (P1). Its one dependency, rf2-hic-001, was closed. Every signal the ready list exposes said dispatch me. The mayor dispatched a worker.

IT WAS BLOCKED ON AN OPERATOR-ONLY PHYSICAL ACTION. The bead's newest note carried a FINAL close rule (2026-08-12 13:11 AUSEST): the bead closes when the manual native-IME session for Firefox and WebKit is recorded in dispositions.md 2.3 with date and engine builds. PR #7992 had already landed the entire automatable deliverable. Three armed runs had established the OS will not grant a native IME session to an automated session. No worker could advance it — not a hard bead, a bead whose remainder is a human at a physical keyboard.

THE READY LIST CANNOT SEE THIS AND NEVER WILL. A dependency graph models bead-on-bead blocking. It does not model bead-on-operator blocking, so an operator hold recorded as a NOTE is invisible to every query the dispatch loop runs. The hold was on the bead, correctly, in the right place — and the dispatch loop still could not see it, because the loop reads ids, priorities and titles.

TWO THINGS SAVED IT, AND ONLY ONE IS A PROCESS. The worker read the bead bottom-up as its brief required, found the hold, made zero commits and stood down. That safeguard is real and it worked — read-the-bead-bottom-up is load-bearing, not ceremony. But it is a LAST line, paid for at ~83k tokens and one worker slot, and it only fires after dispatch.

THE FIX IS TO MAKE THE LIST TELL THE TRUTH: 'bd update <id> --defer <date>' removes an operator-held bead from 'bd ready'. Pair it with a note saying what clears the defer, or the defer becomes an unexplained disappearance — worse than the trap it closed.

THE GENERAL RULE: before dispatching the top of the ready list, read the newest NOTE on the bead, not just its title and priority. Ready is a claim about the dependency graph. Dispatchable is a claim about the world.

A BEAD CAN BE READY AND NOT DISPATCHABLE. `bd ready` answers "is this bead unblocked?" — it does not and
cannot answer "is this bead a unit of work a worker can be sent at?", and on a review wave the two come
apart for a whole tranche of beads at once.

MEASURED 2026-09-17. A peer session ran a senior-developer review wave over Xray, twelve slices, and filed
an epic (rf2-y8doi) plus children rf2-y8doi.1 .. .6. Every child was open, every child depended only on
the epic, and `bd ready --limit 0 --json` duly listed all of them. The mayor's ready set jumped from 2 to
7 in one tick, then to 9, and every new entry looked like fresh dispatchable work.

They were REPORTS, not work. Each child's description is the reviewer's own output — "Findings, ranked",
20,000 to 33,000 characters, ten numbered findings apiece, each with Where / What / Evidence / Action.
The epic states the pipeline in terms: "A read-only triage under the stance then merges, dedups and ranks
the findings; every finding judged worth a worker is filed as its own dispatchable child bead" and
"Report beads are closed once triaged, with a close reason naming the beads filed from them."

So the dispatchable beads DID NOT EXIST YET. Dispatching at a report bead sends a worker at a ranked list
of ten claims rather than at one bounded item — it hands over the triage, which the filing party had
explicitly reserved, and it does it at the moment the set is still being written.

THE TELL, AND IT IS CHEAP: read the TITLE and the SIZE before dispatching. A title of the form
`review(<area>): senior-developer findings, N ranked` is a report. A description in the tens of thousands
of characters enumerating N findings is a report. A dispatchable bead names ONE change.

THE SECOND TELL: the set was still moving. Four children at the top of the tick, six twenty minutes later,
and the epic's own wave log said twelve slices at concurrency six — so half the reports were still to come.
A ready list that GROWS WHILE YOU READ IT is a filing party mid-write, not a backlog.

THE GUARD: when a peer or a wave is filing, treat `bd ready` as "unblocked", never as "dispatch this", and
take dispatchability from the epic's own stated pipeline. "Filing is not dispatching" already covers the
one-worker-per-item case; this is the same rule where the ITEM ITSELF is not yet an item.

It fails in the productive-looking direction, which is what makes it expensive: the ready list is longer
than it has been in days, every entry is real, and acting on it looks like keeping the work flowing.

=== SECOND CAUSE OF THE SAME SYMPTOM, AND THIS ONE HAS A MECHANICAL FIX (2026-09-17, later) ===

A bead is also READY-BUT-NOT-DISPATCHABLE while a worker is ALREADY WORKING ON IT. `bd ready` answers
"unblocked", and a bead left `open` during its own dispatch is unblocked by definition -- so every
in-flight item sits in the ready pool looking like fresh work.

MEASURED on one posture tick: SEVEN in-flight items all read READY at once -- four with a live agent
holding the worktree, three already reported with an open PR. The pool read 36; the truly free set was
29. The mayor had been subtracting the live set BY HAND each tick, from its own context and a gitignored
TSV. That works exactly as long as the context holds, and a coordinating session's context is the thing
most likely to be compacted.

THIS IS THE FAILURE loops.md §3 NAMES IN TERMS: "a dead worker's items read open, look dispatchable, and
the next tick sends a SECOND worker to the same branch." A hand-maintained exclusion list is not a guard,
it is a memory, and it fails silently and all at once.

THE FIX IS MECHANICAL AND THE TOOL ALREADY HAD IT: `bd update <id> --claim` sets assignee and status to
`in_progress` atomically, is idempotent, and `bd ready` then excludes it. Measured: claiming one item
took the pool 36 -> 35; claiming all seven took it to 29, with all seven reading in_progress and none
dispatchable. The status tally had been 63 open / 0 in_progress -- the affordance existed and had NEVER
been used in this workflow, which is why the exclusion had to live in somebody's head.

THE RULE: CLAIM AT DISPATCH, in the same tick you spawn the worker, and let the close at merge clear it.
The worker cannot do this itself -- a `bd` WRITE from a worker worktree is forbidden here, so claiming is
the MAYOR's act and belongs beside the ledger row.

Claim the PR-OPEN items too, not just the ones with a live agent: a reported item whose PR has not merged
is still in flight, and redispatching it is the same error one step later.

WHY THIS BELONGS BESIDE THE ORIGINAL ABOVE: same symptom, opposite cause. Above, the bead was not yet a
unit of work; here it is a unit of work that is already being done. Both present as a LONGER ready list
full of real entries, and in both the productive-looking move is the wrong one. Related:
[[a-file-basename-is-not-a-dispatch-fence]].

I DISPATCHED FROM `bd ready` OUTPUT WITHOUT RUNNING `bd show` — AND `bd ready` IS A TITLE LIST (2026-08-06).

WHAT HAPPENED. Dispatching four workers, I ran `bd show` and read bottom-up for three of them and briefed the fourth (rf2-6ckzl) from its line in `bd ready --limit 0`. That line is the TITLE. The title said "cljs_prod / bundle_isolation are not armed by examples/*". THAT WORK HAD LANDED THE PREVIOUS DAY, in c1e833bb4c. The bead was open because its NEWEST NOTE carried a completely different charge - an audit follow-up on PR #7542 about check_gate_scheduling.py reading reachability off raw YAML. The worker verified rather than re-doing, found the arm already present, and did the real work instead.

WHY THIS EVADES THE RULE I ALREADY HAVE. I have a memory that says brief from the newest note, not the title - and I APPLIED IT to the other three beads in the same dispatch pass. The failure was not forgetting the rule; it was that `bd ready` PRESENTS A TITLE and a title is the oldest text on a bead. A bead reopened by an audit keeps its original title forever, so THE READY LIST SYSTEMATICALLY SHOWS THE STALEST DESCRIPTION OF EVERY REOPENED BEAD. On a board where a merged-PR audit reopens roughly one bead per merge, that is most of the reopened pool.

THE MECHANICAL RULE: `bd ready` IS FOR SELECTION, NEVER FOR BRIEFING. Every dispatch needs its own `bd show <id>` read bottom-up, without exception - including the "obvious" small one you are adding to fill a slot. The slot-filler is exactly where the shortcut gets taken.

AND THE INSTRUCTION THAT SAVED IT, again: the brief carried "THE BEAD OUTRANKS THIS BRIEF - read it bottom-up, newest note first, description LAST. Tell me where I am wrong." The worker opened with exactly that correction. That sentence has now caught five wrong briefs of mine. It is a MECHANISM, not a courtesy, and must never be trimmed for brevity.

COROLLARY WORTH KEEPING: also tell the worker WHY the title may be stale (an audit reopen keeps the original title), so it knows to look for the divergence rather than assuming the brief and bead simply disagree.

REAGENT 2.0.1 SWALLOWS :on-recoverable-error — hydration error-capture harnesses built on reagent.dom.client/hydrate-root are VACUOUS. Found by the rf2-53lsj worker (#6407) on 2026-07-19, in its OWN test harness, before shipping. Reagent destructures :on-recoverable-error and NEVER PASSES IT to React hydrateRoot, so the callback fires for nothing: the harness captured NOTHING on either input and passed identically on broken and fixed HTML. Driving React hydrateRoot DIRECTLY, React 19 correctly reports the mismatch ("Hydration failed... + revenue / - :revenue").
RULE: to assert on hydration mismatches, call React hydrateRoot directly. Do not route through Reagent for error capture. And whatever harness you use, PROVE IT CAPTURES: feed it known-bad input and confirm it reports, before trusting a green on good input.
SECOND FINDING FROM THE SAME PR, easy to get backwards: Reagent renders a keyword/symbol child via (name x), which DROPS THE NAMESPACE — :a/b renders as "b", not "a/b". A JVM emitter fix that merely strips the leading colon would emit "a/b" and leave the hosts FURTHER apart while appearing closer. Namespaced symbols diverge identically. Always diff the actual BYTES against the client, never reason about the shape.

GRADING A META-VERSUS-ATTRS REACT KEY NEEDS TWO DOORS AND THEY MUST BE ASYMMETRIC. '(.-key (r/as-element node))' is HOLLOW; '(.-key (codec/as-element node))' on a WHOLE node THROWS on an unmigrated subtree.

PART 1 - REAGENT IS HOLLOW FOR THIS QUESTION. Reagent reads a React key from Clojure METADATA and from the props map and returns the SAME key either way, so the assertion passes before and after the fix, on the exact defect it was reached for. Measured by worker restable-a 2026-09-10 on views/resizable_table.cljs: with the fix REVERTED the Reagent assertion PASSED while Fresco on the next line failed with [nil nil nil].

PART 2 - AND THE OBVIOUS REPLACEMENT THROWS. Measured by worker epochkeys-a 2026-09-11 on panels/epoch/view.cljs: 'codec/as-element' on the whole node raises HD-016 :rf.error/fresco-bad-head, because the codec LOWERS CHILDREN EAGERLY and any subtree still holding a plain 'defn' in head position is :invalid. That is unmigrated tree, not a bug in the change under test, and a worker who does not know this goes hunting for a fault that is not theirs.

THE WORKING PAIR, AND THE ASYMMETRY IS THE WHOLE POINT:
  Fresco door:  (.-key (rf.fresco.impl.codec/as-element (subvec node 0 2)))   head + attrs only
  Reagent door: (.-key (r/as-element node))                                    the WHOLE node

SUBVEC DROPS VECTOR METADATA. So subvec'ing BOTH sides deletes the metadata key before Reagent ever sees it and yields nil on both doors - still red, but red without saying WHICH fault it is, which destroys the diagnostic the pair exists to give. Subvec both ONLY when comparing attrs-map keys with no metadata in play. Both spellings are in this tree, four lines apart and for different questions: machine_inspector_view_cljs_test.cljs:1283 (Reagent, subvec'd) and :1289 (Fresco, subvec'd) grade attrs keys; the meta-vs-attrs question needs the asymmetric form.

IT IS FILE-DEPENDENT, WHICH IS WHY IT READS AS A TRAP RATHER THAN A RULE. static/machines/sim_cljs_test.cljs:816 calls codec/as-element on a WHOLE node and is fine, because that subtree carries no plain-defn heads. A working example elsewhere in the tree is not evidence it works on yours. A 2026-09-11 census put the plain-defn hiccup-head population at 93 sites in tools/xray/src, concentrated in panels/epoch/view (21), shell.cljs (20), views/edn_inspector (13), panels/fresco (8).

HOW TO APPLY: 'assert at the renderer, never at (meta ...)' is right but underspecified, and so is 'use codec/as-element' - that was this memory's own previous advice and it is the half that throws. Name the door AND the slice: whole node for Reagent, head+attrs for Fresco. This binds every remaining slice of the Fresco key migration.

Related: [[mayor-judgement-good-counts-bad-label-the-unverified]].

Reagent's get-react-key (reagent2.impl.template L407) only reads :key meta from VECTORS. ^{:key k} attached to a function-call list form (e.g. ^{:key g} (group-section g …)) is lost on evaluation — the meta lives on the source list at READ time, not on the returned value. Two fixes: (a) put ^{:key k} on the vector literal returned by the function, or (b) wrap the result in (with-meta result {:key k}). Found in views_view.cljs PR #1471 fixing rf2-gphsi; same anti-pattern exists across several other panels (audit bead rf2-?? filed). Tell future test authors: a test that asserts :key meta on the rendered child reproduces the bug.

REAPING ON 'PR MERGED + AGENT REPORTED' STILL CATCHES LIVE AGENTS — twice now, and the guard saved it both times (2026-08-02).

WHAT HAPPENS: an agent sends its final report, the mayor merges its PR and reaps the worktree — and the agent is STILL RUNNING. It keeps working after reporting: extra confirmatory reruns, a last gate, tidying. The worktree vanishes under its cwd and its background process dies.

INCIDENTS: the heap worker (reaped on PR-merge while alive; recorded then as 'reap only when merged AND reported'), and now proc-6tags-7uxkt — which HAD reported done, then set up a node_modules junction and started an extra test:cljs run. It found its worktree gone mid-run.

WHY IT HAS BEEN HARMLESS BOTH TIMES, and this is the load-bearing part: scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh disarms the node_modules junction BEFORE removing, so the junction-following hazard (which has emptied the mayor's real node_modules twice historically) did NOT fire. Canary held at 101 entries across both incidents. The worker's commits were pushed before reporting, so nothing was lost either time.

THE REFINEMENT, since 'reported done' is evidently not the same as 'finished': the cheap check before reaping a just-merged worktree is whether its agent is still live (a task notification arriving after the report is the tell; so is a recent mtime under the worktree). It costs one look. But the honest weighting is that the GUARD is the real protection and it works — this is a courtesy to the worker's last few minutes, not a safety issue. Do not build ceremony around it; do not skip the guard.

DO NOT force removal or bypass the guard when a reap refuses — a refusal means something still holds the tree, which is exactly when following a junction would be catastrophic.

SUPERSEDED 2026-08-11 (rf2-j689 ruling) — REAP-FIRST IS NO LONGER A REASON FOR ANYTHING. THE ORPHANED BRANCH IS SOLVED AT THE SERVER, NOT BY ORDERING.

WHAT THIS MEMORY USED TO SAY, and it was measured, not guessed: `gh pr merge --rebase --delete-branch` lands the merge but cannot delete a branch that a worktree still holds, and gh abandons the REMOTE deletion along with the local one — so roughly twenty merges in one session each left an orphaned origin branch. Reaping the worktree first made the flag work completely, four for four (#7842, #7843, #7845, #7848), because the worktree pins the branch and nothing else does. The mechanism was real and the measurement stands.

WHY IT IS SUPERSEDED ANYWAY. The ordering only ever worked when the worker had already reported done — the three merges in that same session whose workers had NOT reported were correctly merged without a reap and orphaned their branches 3/3. So reap-first solved the orphan for the easy half of the cases and left the hard half untouched, while placing the reap immediately beside a merge: the exact structural condition of the catalogrows-vkle violation, where I reaped mid-gate holding the worker's own message saying it was not done. An efficiency that re-creates the shape of the worst mistake in the session is not a bargain.

THE FIX THAT REPLACED IT: `delete_branch_on_merge` is now ENABLED on day8/re-frame2, so GitHub deletes the head branch server-side the moment a merge lands, and the server does not care what a worktree is holding. Merge with `gh pr merge --rebase` — NO `--delete-branch`. Zero orphans by construction, for reported and unreported workers alike, with nothing to remember afterwards.

SO THE ORDERING IS MOOT, WHICH IS STRONGER THAN "DISCOURAGED". There is no orphan left to avoid, so reap-before-merge buys nothing and is not a reason to reap, to hurry, or to sequence anything. The never-pair rule in mayor-hygiene.md stands VERBATIM: never pair a merge with a reap, never put the reap in the merge loop. Reaping is a separate deliberate hygiene step.

THE AUTHORISATION IS UNCHANGED AND NON-NEGOTIABLE — only the agent's own report that it has FINISHED authorises a reap. Not merge state, not PR state, not elapsed time, not mtime, not cleanliness. The test is still: can I quote the sentence where this agent says it is done? See reap-requires-a-finished-report-not-just-a-message, which cost a destroyed gate run to learn.

THE ONE REMAINING MANUAL DELETE: `git push origin --delete <branch>` is now ONLY the post-MERGED fallback for a remote ref that survives the merge — head-ref branch protection, or a cross-repo PR whose head lives in a fork the server will not touch. Verify MERGED, delete that ref, and nothing else. A surviving remote ref is never grounds to reap a worktree early.

THE REAP-ONLY-ON-A-REPORT RULE NEEDS A DISCHARGE PATH FOR AGENTLESS TREES, or residue accumulates
forever. Recorded 2026-09-07 18:56 AUSEST after two worktrees sat unreapable for nine hours.

THE RULE AND WHY IT IS RIGHT: loops.md §5 says reap a worktree ONLY on its agent's own completion
report, and names the discredited proxies explicitly — merged PR, clean tree, elapsed time, mtime,
directory age. That rule is correct and has already paid for itself this session: it stopped four
worktrees being reaped on merge evidence alone while their workers were still verifying, and an hour
earlier the same instinct (closing a bead on a PR-body mention) buried a live P2 defect.

THE GAP: a worker whose agent is long gone will NEVER produce a report. Its tree therefore fails the
only reap test forever, so every crashed, stopped or timed-out worker leaves a permanent directory.
Two here (pathspec-a, views-b) had sat nine hours across many hygiene ticks, reported each time as
"no report, so not reapable", which is true and useless.

THE DISCHARGE CRITERION, and it is a CONJUNCTION verified at source rather than any single proxy:
  1. No live agent — dispatched hours ago, agent gone, and no live task in the running-agent list.
  2. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` is 0, OR every commit reads `git cherry -`
     (patch-equivalent on main). NOT `-d` ancestry, which fails on rebase-merges.
  3. `git status --porcelain` is empty — no uncommitted work.
  4. No branch on the remote (`git ls-remote --heads origin worker/<name>`), so nothing was pushed
     that is not accounted for.
  5. EVERY bead the ledger row names is either closed, or open with its state correctly recorded
     (a dependency, a fence, a note) so nothing is lost by the tree going away.

Measured on the two: pathspec-a — 1 commit, cherry `-`, clean, no remote, bead rf2-uwvv CLOSED.
views-b — 0 commits, clean, no remote, beads .56 and .60 closed and .58 open with its rf2-kuky.57
dependency already recorded. Reaped at exit 0 with the node_modules canary 103 before and after,
measured with `ls -A` on both sides.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE RULE FAILING: clause 3 alone IS the discredited "clean tree" proxy, and clause 2
alone is the discredited "merged PR". The conjunction is different in kind — it establishes that
there is provably NOTHING TO LOSE, rather than guessing that the worker is finished. The rule
protects WORK; where no work exists, it has nothing to protect. State the evidence when you invoke
this, and never invoke it on a tree whose agent could still be alive — for that case the rule is
unchanged: message first, and stillness proves nothing.

MY INLINE REAP DELETED A WORKTREE WHILE ITS WORKER WAS STILL GATING, AND THE GATE FAILED FALSELY (2026-08-04).

WHAT HAPPENED. Earlier in the session I twice merged a PR and forgot to reap its worktree, so I folded the reap INTO the merge loop to make it unskippable. That fixed the leak and introduced a worse failure: a worker was still running the fast-PR spine in the worktree I deleted. PR #7469 merged at 02:24:42 UTC; the branch and worktree were removed; the worker's spine finished at 02:24:53, eleven seconds later, reading a directory that no longer existed. It reported FAIL implementation JS harness helpers with 11 reagent-slim policy failures, all of the form "Cannot find module", "missing workflow: .github/workflows/test.yml", "missing changed-surfaces script" -- files that are tracked in git and were present. The worker correctly discarded the result under the killed-gate rule and confirmed the CI counterpart was SUCCESS on main.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS BEYOND THE WASTED RUN. The failure LOOKS like a real policy regression naming real files. A worker with less discipline would have "fixed" the missing modules, or reported a red that does not exist. It is the mirror of the backgrounded-gate bug we fixed today, where a relative invocation graded ANOTHER worktree: same class, opposite direction -- the gate reads a tree that is not the one it thinks it is reading.

THE RULE: A MERGE DOES NOT MEAN THE WORKER HAS EXITED. The PR opening is the worker's LAST reported act, not its last act -- it may still be running gates, updating the PR body, or answering a message. Before reaping a worktree, confirm the worker is actually done: no live agent for that bead, or the worktree quiescent across a tick. When in doubt, leave the worktree; a stale directory costs disk, a deleted one costs a false red and possibly a spurious "fix".

THE CORRECTED SHAPE: keep the reap adjacent to the merge so it cannot be forgotten, but gate it on the worker being finished rather than on the PR being merged. Reaping on the NEXT tick after the merge is the cheap approximation and is what I should do by default.

RELATED, SAME SESSION: the same worker corrected two claims of mine. Local clj-kondo here is 2025.10.23 while CI pins 2026.04.15; the local build reports 0 errors on the line CI fails and 10 different errors CI does not, so a local clj-kondo pass proves nothing about the gate -- fetch the pinned binary. NO HARM THIS TIME, BY LUCK: the harness reported exactly two running agents, both named and neither an audit worktree. THAT REPORT WAS AVAILABLE AND I DID NOT CONSULT IT FOR THE REAP DECISION - which is the actual lesson, because it is the discriminator the stranded-sweep rules already put first.

THE RULE I AM RESTORING: reap on the owning agent's completion report. When none exists and never will (a prior session's leftover), the fallback is the HARNESS RUNNING-AGENT REPORT showing no live agent - not merge state, not cleanliness, not ancestry. If that is unavailable too, leave the worktree; it costs disk and a line in a listing.

REAP A WORKER WORKTREE ONLY WHEN ITS AGENT REPORTS DONE — NOT WHEN ITS PR MERGES (2026-08-01, my error).

WHAT I DID: after merging PR #7337 I ran scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh against worker/heapaxis-2rtt6-34. The removal FAILED on a Windows file lock, but the guard had already done its first job and DISARMED THE node_modules JUNCTION. The agent was still alive. Its next shadow-cljs call failed with 'shadow-cljs not found' and it spent a tool round diagnosing before reporting 'my worktree junction has vanished... Recreating it'. It self-recovered and the mayor's real node_modules stayed intact at 101, so no damage — but I cost a live worker a pointless detour.

THE MISTAKE IS THE TRIGGER, NOT THE SCRIPT. A merged PR means the WORK landed; it does NOT mean the AGENT finished. Agents legitimately keep working after opening a PR: updating the PR body, re-running a gate, hardening a mutation proof, answering a resume message.

THE RULE: reap only when BOTH hold — (1) the PR is merged, AND (2) the agent has reported done or is confirmed dead. A reap that fails on a file lock is often a SIGNAL the tree is still in use: check whether the agent is alive before retrying, and never retry in a loop.

STILL TRUE AND UNCHANGED: the guard is right to unlink the junction BEFORE removing (that is what stops git worktree remove following it into the mayor's real node_modules), and right to refuse rather than force when removal cannot complete. The defect was entirely in WHEN I invoked it.

TWO WAYS THE SEARCH FOR A WORKER'S COMPLETION REPORT READS ZERO ON A REPORT THAT EXISTS — both silent, both measured 2026-09-21, and between them they declared 8 of 8 reapable worktrees unreapable in one hygiene pass. This does NOT contradict `agentless-tree-report-is-on-disk-by-agent-id`, which is correct and names the working route; it records the two ways of failing to reach it.

FIRST: THE `tasks/<agentId>.output` FILE IS 0 BYTES FOR EVERY AGENT ON THIS BOX, INCLUDING ONE DEMONSTRABLY RUNNING. Measured across 8 ledger-resolved agents plus a live worker whose build was compiling at that moment: every one read 0 bytes. It is the file the task notification itself names, so it is the first place a reader looks, and an empty file reads as "this agent produced nothing." It is a fact about THAT LOCATION and nothing else. The reports were all present in `<claude-projects>/<project>/<session-uuid>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl` — 2396 such transcripts on disk across 39 sessions, sizes 1.5-3 MB. Take the LIVE WORKER as the control both ways: its `.output` was 0 bytes like all the others, while its subagent transcript was 1.6 MB and its final assistant block read "Now the append-only comment, and the walk itself:" — plainly mid-work, which is the instrument correctly declining to call an unfinished worker done.

SECOND, AND THE MORE DANGEROUS: THE WORKTREE PATH IS SPELLED TWO WAYS IN THE CORPUS AND A SEARCH FOR ONE MATCHES NONE OF THE OTHER. `scripts/assert-worker-worktree.sh` runs under Git Bash, so `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` prints the MSYS form and the guard emits `WORKTREE_ROOT=/c/Users/...`. The dispatch ledger's field 1 holds the WINDOWS form, `C:/Users/...`. A worker may ALSO transcribe the Windows form into its own prose report. Measured: searching the ledger spelling for an emitted `WORKTREE_ROOT=` read 0 for all 9 candidates; re-run on the MSYS spelling it read 3/2/3/2/3 for five of them; and two more (xrwidth-re7dn, xrseq2-jh12f) were found only by agent id, xrwidth-re7dn's report carrying the WINDOWS spelling. So neither spelling alone is a census — search BOTH.

WHAT MAKES IT EXPENSIVE RATHER THAN UNTIDY: it fails in the direction that LOOKS LIKE DISCIPLINE. A zero reads as "no report, so the tree stays", which is the conservative-sounding answer, so nothing on screen argues with it and the residue pile grows by trees that were reapable all along. One tree, `xrwidth-re7dn`, was recorded EARLIER IN THE SAME SESSION as permanently unreapable on exactly this zero; its report begins "Done. PR #10123 is ready for review." and it was reaped the same day.

THE GUARD, and the second half is the one that actually bit: (1) never conclude from `tasks/*.output` — go to `subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl`; (2) take the control FROM THE CORPUS rather than guessing a spelling — read the 70 characters that actually follow `WORKTREE_ROOT=` in the transcripts and let the file say how the path is written, which is what exposed this; (3) keep a LIVE worker in every such sweep as a positive control, because a live worker must read "no report", and an instrument that says that about everything is broken rather than strict.

AND ONE CONTAMINATION TO EXPECT when searching your own session's transcript: the script you are writing to do the searching is itself recorded in that transcript, so its needles match themselves. A nonsense control read 2 and a `<result>` probe read 2 purely on the text of the probe. Count self-reference before reading a small non-zero as a hit.

I REAPED A WORKTREE MID-GATE, AND I HAD THE WORKER'S OWN WORDS SAYING IT WAS NOT DONE (2026-08-11, catalogrows-vkle / PR #7813).

WHAT HAPPENED. The worker sent two interim messages. The second said, verbatim: "Holding for the spine — not done yet, and I won't report a colour I don't have." Minutes later I merged #7813 and reaped its worktree in the same breath. Its spine was in the JVM tier. git worktree list stopped showing the tree, .git went, gate.log was deleted mid-write, and the run died. The worker found gate.exit = 1 afterwards and CORRECTLY REFUSED TO REPORT IT AS A FAILURE — that 1 was written by a script whose own checkout had been deleted underneath it. My cleanup manufactured a red.

WHY I DID IT, because the mechanism matters more than the apology: I batched the reap into the merge pass. The hygiene procedure forbids exactly this — "Never pair a merge with a reap in the same breath, and never put the reap in the merge loop." A merged PR is the moment a tree LOOKS finished, which is precisely why the pull is dangerous. I had also, without noticing, promoted "the agent sent me a message" to "the agent reported done". Those are not the same thing and the difference was written in the message I was reading.

SO THE REAP CONDITION IS NARROWER THAN I HAD IT: not "the agent has spoken", but "the agent has reported that it has FINISHED". An interim status, a progress note, a partial hand-off, a PR-opened announcement — none of these are completion. A BACKGROUND GATE STILL RUNNING IS THE WORKER STILL RUNNING, even though nothing in the branch, the tree or the PR shows it.

WHY IT LOOKED SAFE, and this is the trap for next time: every proxy agreed. PR merged, branch clean, commits pushed, no junction, worker had messaged recently. All six of the forbidden proxies pointed at "done" simultaneously. That is not evidence; that is what a disciplined worker mid-gate looks like BY DESIGN, since commit-and-push-as-you-go is what every brief demands.

WHAT SAVED IT: the work was committed and pushed incrementally, so only the RUN was lost, not the diff. And CI's 90/90 on the merged PR is strictly better evidence than a local spine anyway — which is worth remembering when tempted to wait on a local gate at all.

THE RULE I AM ADDING TO MY OWN LOOP: before any reap, re-read the LAST message from that agent and find the sentence where it says it is finished. If I cannot quote that sentence, the worktree does not get reaped. Cost of waiting: one stale directory.

REBASE conflict resolution: --ours/--theirs INVERT vs merge. In a rebase, --ours = the branch you are replaying ONTO (e.g. origin/main), --theirs = the commit being replayed (the worker's own branch). So to take MAIN's version of a generated file (e.g. docs/cljs/playground-rf2.js) during a rebase, use 'git checkout --ours <file>', NOT --theirs. My earlier dispatch instructions said --theirs for this and were WRONG (caught by the rf2-ywwpx worker on #6284, 2026-07-18, which verified empirically: stage2/--ours == origin/main, stage3/--theirs == its own stale commit). Harmless for a generated file that gets regenerated afterwards, but on a NON-generated conflict the same wording silently takes the wrong side and can revert main's work. ALWAYS instruct workers to verify which stage matches origin/main (git show :2:<file> / :3:<file> and compare digests) rather than trusting the label.

Rebase-merge makes a worker branch look UNMERGED to an ancestry check. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` returns N>0 and `git merge-base --is-ancestor` fails for a branch whose PR was merged with --rebase, because the rebase rewrote the SHAs. Judging 'abandoned, holds unmerged work' from that heuristic mislabelled 7 of 9 branches in one hygiene pass (their PRs #7096-#7107 were all merged). The authoritative test is PATCH-ID containment: `git cherry origin/main origin/<branch>` counting '^+' lines == 0 means fully merged. Confirm with `gh pr view --json state` == MERGED as the second signal.

A MERGE TIMESTAMP EARLIER THAN A RUN'S START DOES NOT MEAN THE RUN'S TREE CONTAINED THAT CHANGE — this repo rebase-merges (found 2026-08-07, rf2-jv36i).

WHAT HAPPENED. A bead assumed 'the codec change is on main by then' because PR #7390 merged at 18:06:11Z and the measurement windows ran 18:14:02Z-18:21:10Z. Eight minutes clear, in wall clock. But the run was taken from a worker branch based at b4144427ec, authored BEFORE the change landed and rebase-merged AFTER. The landed history orders the commits correctly; the measured tree never contained them.

WHY IT IS EASY TO GET WRONG. Under rebase-merge the branch tip that produced a measurement is not an ancestor of main at all, and its base can predate several landings that appear, in main's log, to sit before the run. Reading merge times off main and comparing them to a run's clock is exactly the wrong instrument.

HOW TO CHECK PROPERLY — any one of these settles it, and they should agree:
  - BLOB: the evidence page stamps the blob of the file under test; compare it to the change's before/after blobs. This is the strongest check because it names what was actually loaded.
  - ANCESTRY: 'git merge-base --is-ancestor <change-commit> <producing-commit>' — NO means the tree lacked it.
  - BASE: what commit the producing branch was cut from, and what that tree's relevant blob was.

RELATED, same root cause: a stranded authored head's patch-id may differ from its landed counterpart because the rebase resolved conflicts — so 'the patch landed' and 'this tree was measured' are separate questions, and provenance prose must not conflate them.

A --rebase MERGE LEAVES NO MERGE COMMIT, SO mergeCommit.oid IS THE REBASED TIP — stop calling it "the merge commit". Measured 2026-09-07 after a worker corrected a dispatch brief.

WHAT I HAD BEEN WRITING. Every close reason this session says "Merged as PR #NNNN (merge <oid>)", taking <oid> from gh pr view --json mergeCommit. A worker pointed out that the oid I had cited for PR #9327 names a commit whose subject is about something else entirely.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY IS, verified: git log -1 --format='%h %p %s' on that oid shows ONE parent. A merge commit has two. The PR brought EIGHT commits, and the oid is the last of them after rebasing onto main — the tip, not a merge. Re-tested on a second recorded oid from a different PR: also one parent. So this is how gh reports every --rebase merge here, not a one-off.

WHY IT MATTERS ENOUGH TO RECORD, given the oid is still a correct citation. The oid does identify where the PR landed and git log <oid> is a valid way to find it, so nothing recorded is unusable. But calling it "the merge commit" tells the next reader two false things: that the PR landed as a single commit (it landed as eight), and that its subject line describes the PR (it describes only the last commit, which on #9327 was a spec/009 row edit while the PR's subject was the :inputs metadata slot). A reader chasing provenance by that subject line looks for the wrong change.

THE ACCURATE PHRASING, and it costs nothing: "merged as PR #NNNN, rebased tip <oid>, N commits". Where the whole range matters, cite <first>..<tip> or just the PR number, which is stable and unambiguous.

AND ONE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE FOR ANCESTRY TESTS: git merge-base --is-ancestor <tip-oid> origin/main still answers correctly, because the tip IS on main. But a check that assumes two parents, or that tries to read a PR's whole diff from <oid>^..<oid>, sees only the last commit of the stack. Use the PR's own file list, or the merge base, rather than the tip's single-parent diff.

A PROVENANCE PIN NAMING AN AUTHORED SHA IS STRANDED BY REBASE-MERGE — THE PAGE LOOKS PINNED AND IS NOT (2026-08-06, rf2-zn7pj / PR #7610; scope filed as rf2-owq6p).

THE FINDING: the SSR spike witness pinned its evidence to 952a3f2024. That commit IS NOT AN ANCESTOR OF MAIN, and neither is its sibling 6f40304011. This repo REBASE-MERGES, which rewrites SHAs, so the authored head a page names is stranded the moment its PR merges. Verified with `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> origin/main` returning non-zero.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE STALE FIGURES IT WAS FILED FOR: stale figures under a RESOLVABLE pin are checkable and wrong, which is a normal defect. Figures under an UNRESOLVABLE pin are NOT CHECKABLE AT ALL — a reader cannot obtain the tree the measurement was taken on. The pages central verifiability claim fails SILENTLY, and it fails while looking rigorous. This is the evidence-corpus form of the fail-open class.

THE FIX THAT DISSOLVES IT: PIN TO A COMMIT ALREADY ON MAIN. The measurement happens upstream of the documenting edit, so no merge of the documenting PR can move it — main advanced eight commits during that pass and the pin never had to change. Do not pin to your own branch head.

AND THE REASONING THAT DECLINED A BLOB TABLE, which is the better half: a blob table pins the INSTRUMENT when the anchor cannot be pinned. Here the anchor CAN be pinned, and a resolvable whole-tree SHA pins strictly more. It would also PIN LESS THAN IT LOOKS — the clock pages magnitudes are a function of three driver files, whereas these figures are a SHA-256 over a whole document plus a boundary census, a function of corpus, entry, substrate, adapter and the pinned react-dom. A short blob table would ADVERTISE A CLOSURE IT DOES NOT HAVE. Ask what the artefact is actually a function of before choosing what to pin.

RELATED, ALREADY KNOWN: `git merge-base --is-ancestor` and `git cherry` disagree for the same reason — rebase-merge rewrites SHAs, so ancestry says "unmerged" for branches that are fully merged. Same mechanism, two different wrong conclusions: there it under-reports merge status, here it strands a citation.

TWO NON-MANUFACTURES FROM THE SAME PASS WORTH COPYING. (1) X1(b)s +16 bytes was LEFT UNDECOMPOSED: the ruler moved AND the document drifted, and only X1(a) can separate its share because rf2-2rtt6.114 measured independently — no second instrument exists for the canonical DOM. The worker checked whether em dashes explained it, found the dogfood titles are ASCII, and STATED THE SUM rather than guessing. (2) The X3 refusal control turned out NOT DETERMINISTIC under load — one take refused at phase 2, another qualified throughout. It published what it got, said the 0.3 ms knob sits inside the boxs noise, and noted the 2 ms production ceiling is far from that regime, rather than re-running until the expected shape returned. Re-running until a control behaves is how a control stops being one.

AND A GATE BLIND SPOT IT CAUGHT ON ITSELF: an edit DROPPED A `## X1(b)` HEADING and `check_doc_slugs.py` passed it, because nothing links to that anchor. A heading with no inbound link can vanish silently. Diff headings against HEAD when editing a structured evidence page.

A GATE CONFLATED "THE TEST FAILED" WITH "THE TEST NEVER RAN", AND THE DISCRIMINATOR IS WHETHER THE RUNNER PRINTED ITS OWN COUNT (2026-08-06, rf2-v8561, PR #7608).

THE REPORTED DEFECT: three CLJS namespaces failing per-namespace isolation. It did NOT reproduce — clean worktree, fresh npm ci, fresh compile, the beads own repro command twice, exit 0 both times, and all 17 roster namespaces green alone (196 tests / 731 assertions).

THE TELL THAT CRACKED IT, and it is the kind of thing only a fresh reading finds: THE THREE REPORTED NAMESPACES ARE THE LAST THREE ROSTER ENTRIES, CONSECUTIVELY. That is not three independent fixture defects — it is a CONTIGUOUS TAIL, the signature of something collapsing partway through a sweep that spawns one node process per namespace over 276 measured seconds.

THE CAUSE: compile-node-test.cjs UNLINKS out/node-test.js before every compile, deliberately, so a failed compile leaves nothing stale (rf2-6t03c). A compile starting mid-sweep pulls the bundle out from under every run still to come. Injecting exactly that at t=225s of a 276s sweep reds EXACTLY THOSE THREE NAMESPACES, namespace for namespace. Both recorded sightings were worktrees with other builds running.

THE STRUCTURAL DISCRIMINATOR, which is the reusable part: --test=<ns> is a RUNTIME selector over a bundle that links EVERY test namespace, so A MODULE-LOAD CRASH CANNOT SINGLE A NAMESPACE OUT. Therefore: A RED CARRYING "Ran N tests containing M assertions." IS A VERDICT ABOUT THAT NAMESPACE; A RED WITHOUT ONE NEVER WAS. Three causes reach a non-zero standalone exit and the gate was reporting all three as the first — ISOLATION (real leak, fixture remedy), ROSTER (stale curated list; 9dd9633d0b and d3969eb67b are both commits fixing that AFTER the gate blamed fixtures), ENVIRONMENT (bundle vanished; the sweep is INDETERMINATE, exit 2, and ITS GREENS ARE WORTH NO MORE THAN ITS REDS).

TWO RULES TO CARRY:
1. When a gate accuses several namespaces at once, CHECK WHETHER THEY ARE CONTIGUOUS IN ITS ROSTER. Adjacency is evidence of one external event, not of N independent defects. The old gate under an unlink at t=6s accused SIXTEEN namespaces of leaking, every one MODULE_NOT_FOUND.
2. A GREEN MUST ALSO CARRY A NON-ZERO TEST COUNT. This is the same floor as the long-standing "Ran 0 tests reads as green" family, arriving from the opposite direction: there the count was zero because nothing was selected, here because nothing could load.

SIBLING TO CHECK, filed as rf2-1wyyb: check-ui-adapter-isolation.cjs has the same --self-test shape and plausibly the same conflation. Not verified — a shared filename pattern is not evidence of a shared defect.

Redaction/privacy threat model for re-frame2 dev tools (Story/Xray/MCP/share): a local programmer can ALWAYS reach secrets programmatically (eval, direct app-db), so redacting sensitive values from the human USING the tool is futile and NOT the goal. Only two concerns: (1) maybe handing them to an AI/LLM (MCP/agent payloads) — a soft 'maybe', and largely already handled by the MCP servers' --allow-sensitive-reads gate (OFF by default, forces :rf/redacted elision); (2) firmer: stopping them being written to logs. Implication: human-facing egress (share URLs, static export, copied EDN, screenshots of the dev's own app) is NOT privacy-blocked — unblock it. Scope rf2-qarwq narrowly to the AI boundary + logs; do not gold-plate. StoryUI packet's 'BLOCKED until common egress seam' framing (02 sec15, 04, story S11) is over-cautious against this model. -- Mike, 2026-05-30

REFINEMENT OF MY OWN FINDING FROM EARLIER TODAY — WELL-EVIDENCED CLOSES ALSO GET REOPENED, AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT PHENOMENON (2026-07-26).

EARLIER I MEASURED that gate/fixture beads closed on ARMING rather than on CATCHING are the largest category the merged-PR audit reopens, and concluded that a meaningful share of the reopen rate is my own close quality. That is true and the remediation stands.

BUT IT IS INCOMPLETE. Checking again a few hours later: FIVE beads I closed TODAY WITH FULL MUTATION EVIDENCE are open again — rf2-5o52l, rf2-12g5z, rf2-4hc9p, rf2-isp3i, rf2-lnecd — and every one carries NEW-RESIDUAL language rather than a restatement of the original defect. rf2-5o52l is the clearest: the emit-site privacy direction was accepted as correct, and the reopen names a DIFFERENT thing the SSR widening changed in the hydrate and restore :skews accumulators.

SO THERE ARE TWO DISTINCT REOPEN CLASSES AND THEY NEED DIFFERENT RESPONSES:
  (A) WEAK-CLOSE REOPENS — the close said the job was added / the roster widened / the suite is green, giving the audit nothing to verify against. The audit then does the verification I should have done. FIX: mutation proof in the close reason. Mine to prevent.
  (B) NEW-RESIDUAL REOPENS — the close was fully evidenced and ACCEPTED, and the audit found something ELSE by examining the merged code. This is the audit working as designed and is NOT a defect in my closing. Treating it as one would push me toward defensive over-closing, which is worse.

HOW TO TELL THEM APART IN ONE READ: does the reopen note ENGAGE WITH the close evidence and then name something new ("the emit-site direction is correct, BUT the SSR widening changed..."), or does it re-assert the original defect? The former is (B) and is fresh work. The latter is (A) and is my failure.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR THE BACKLOG NUMBER: I have been treating roughly one reopen per merged PR as partly my fault. Half of it is; the other half is the audit finding genuinely new defects in freshly merged code, which is exactly what it is for and which no improvement in my close reasons will reduce. So the open count will NOT converge to zero while the audit runs, and that is a property of the system rather than a throughput failure. Report it that way.

THE GENERAL LESSON, and it is one I keep relearning: a measured finding is usually true of the subset I measured, not of the whole. My first pass looked only at gate beads and generalised. Checking a wider sample a few hours later split the finding in two. BEFORE ACTING ON A MEASURED PATTERN, ASK WHICH POPULATION IT WAS MEASURED OVER.
Refinements added to an IN_PROGRESS bead rarely reach the worker (they have already read the spec and are coding). File a NEW follow-up bead instead of noting the in-progress one. (Mike, 2026-05-31)

"Stripping string literals from Clojure with the obvious regex mispairs quotes across docstrings — it claimed 39% of one file and ate two real reg-view registrations, failing in the reassuring direction for a retirement census."

**Do not regex-strip string literals from Clojure before counting forms.** The obvious pattern —
`"(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*"` — pairs the CLOSING quote of one docstring with the OPENING quote of the next,
blanking every form in between.

**MEASURED 2026-09-10** on `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/shell.cljs` (149,527 chars): the
stripper claimed **39% of the file** as string literal and the count of `(rf/reg-view` fell from
**9 to 7**. `grep -n` shows all nine at column 0, every one live code, none in prose. The two lost
were real registrations.

**It fails in the REASSURING direction for a retirement census** — fewer surviving call sites reads
as "more migrated" — which is the same shape as the bracket-expression trap in CLAUDE.md item (j),
reached through a different door. I reported 7 against a worker's 9 and the worker was right.

**How to apply:** anchor to FORM POSITION instead of stripping — `^\s*\(rf/reg-view\b` — and take
an unanchored count as the control so the gap is visible and explainable (measured on
`tools/xray/src`: anchored 30, unanchored 31, the difference being a single prose mention). Then
READ THE HITS: nine lines is a listing you can eyeball, whereas a stripper is machinery that can
lie. Reserve real stripping for cases where a parser is available.

**A cross-check that does work:** two censuses taken at different tips should reconcile through the
change between them. Worker at its base read 34 reg-view / 16 defview; mayor at trunk read 30 / 20;
the intervening PR converted exactly four regions, so the delta is 4 in each direction. That
reconciliation is stronger evidence than either number alone.

Related: [[verification-instrument-measured-symptom-not-invariant]], [[mayor-judgement-good-counts-bad-label-the-unverified]].

WHEN A WORKER REPORTS FIXING SOMETHING IN PASSING, CHECK WHETHER A LIVE WORKER OWNS THE SAME CODE — AND RELAY IT. Cost duplicate work on 2026-07-24.

WHAT HAPPENED: the F5h virtual-table pilot hit a cross-mode bug while building its pilot — node/classify-event asked fn? and a roster callback is a RECORD, so an interpreted [:div {:on-scroll (v/event ...)}] was unrenderable on the structural host. It fixed that in passing (one spec-cited clause) and reported it as its finding 1. SEPARATELY, the emitter silent-drop worker was mid-flight on rf2-berc2, whose fix REQUIRES the same function to stop refusing a Callback — so it fixed it too, independently, with a different marker.

I HAD THE PILOT REPORT IN HAND AND DID NOT RELAY IT. The overlap only surfaced at rebase time as a conflict in node.cljc and in the pilot_overlay witness test.

⚠️ THE OUTCOME WAS ACTUALLY GOOD, and the reason is worth keeping: main version had RULED THE QUESTION DIFFERENTLY — it records the mode-neutral {:rf.ui/opaque :fn} member, with a docstring citing 004B as the authority, where the second worker had a per-role marker (:v/event / :v/handler). Two independent attempts surfaced a design choice neither brief had posed. The second worker resolved correctly: took main version explicitly with `git checkout origin/main -- <file>` rather than an --ours/--theirs label, then PROVED nothing was lost (`git diff origin/main -- <files>` empty, plus `git show <old-sha> -- <files>` confirming its contribution was the same repair and therefore subsumed), and fixed two of its own test docstrings that still described the superseded marker.

THE MAYOR RULE: when a worker report says "I also fixed X" or "I had to repair Y to proceed", immediately check the in-flight set for anyone whose bead touches X or Y, and SEND THEM A MESSAGE. It costs one tool call. The alternative is a rebase conflict discovered late, in a file where one side may carry a WITNESS TEST the other side flipped differently — and witness collisions are how the trunk goes red.

RELATED, ALREADY RECORDED: two workers must never share a surface. The reported defect was that the script "reached CANARY_AFTER but printed no REMOVED= or OK:" for a bare name - which reads like a path that did real work and then declined. It was nothing of the kind. REOPENING A BEAD ERASES ITS CLOSE REASON, SILENTLY AND TOTALLY (measured 2026-09-09). When `bd` moves an issue from closed back to open, `close_reason` becomes the empty string and `closed_at` becomes null. Nothing is printed, nothing errors, and the text is NOT copied into `notes`. Measured on rf2-dokz and rf2-z5lv, both closed and then reopened by the merged-PR audit within the hour: `close_reason_len=0`, `closed_at=null`, and a grep for a distinctive phrase from each close reason read 0 in `notes`. Control: a still-closed bead read `close_reason_len=5159`.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY: this project treats close reasons as NORMATIVE RECORDS — a ruling is often the close reason of a closed dependency, which is why `bd gc`'s decay phase is banned and why the backlog-reread loop tells you to look there. An audit reopening is the SYSTEM WORKING, and every audit reopening destroys the record of what the reopened change actually did. So the loss lands precisely on the beads that are being worked twice.

DETECTION IS NOT AVAILABLE THE OBVIOUS WAY: you cannot find reverted closures by looking for non-terminal beads that still carry a close_reason. That probe reads 0 across the whole backlog even when reopenings have happened, because the field is cleared rather than retained — the reopen removes its own evidence.

RECOVERY IS COMPLETE AND CHEAP, BY TWO INDEPENDENT ROUTES. (1) `.beads/issues.jsonl` in git history: `scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` exports the full record, so any checkpoint commit made while the bead was closed carries the text. Walk recent checkpoints and read the length: `git show <commit>:.beads/issues.jsonl | jq -r --arg i <id> 'select(._type=="issue" and .id==$i) | (.close_reason // "" | length)'`. The window can be narrow — for rf2-dokz exactly ONE of the last twelve checkpoints carried it. (2) `bd history <id> --json` — the nested `.Issue` snapshots carry it (4 entries did for rf2-dokz). Route 1 is easier to verify because you can print the length per commit.

THE FIX WHEN YOU FIND IT: append the recovered text back with `bd update <id> --append-notes` (NEVER `--notes`, which replaces), under a heading saying it is a RESTORED CLOSE REASON and naming the commit it came from, so nobody reads it as newer than the audit note that follows it.

AND TELL ANY LIVE WORKER YOU BRIEFED. A brief that says "read the bead's close reason" is unsatisfiable on a reopened bead, and the worker will read the absence as its own failure rather than the tool's.

`report-changed-surfaces.sh` TAKES PATHS AS ARGUMENTS, NOT ON STDIN. Piping them is not an
error — it silently falls back to HEAD^ semantics and classifies the PREVIOUS COMMIT'S diff,
returning a well-formed and entirely plausible surface list for the wrong tree.

MEASURED 2026-09-10 on `.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh`, same single path
(`tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/panels.cljs`), both invocation forms, exit 0 both times:

    as ARGUMENT:  cljs_node_test=true   story_xray_browser=true
    PIPED stdin:  cljs_node_test=false  story_xray_browser=false

The mechanism is in the script: line 15 reads `for arg in "$@"`, and with no arguments line 112
falls back to `git diff --no-renames --name-only HEAD^ HEAD`. The script's OWN comment at line
100 says it "silently returns to HEAD^ semantics without saying so" — so this is documented where
only someone already reading the source would find it.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY WRONG. The output is a well-formed `key=value` surface
list either way. Nothing is empty, nothing errors, and the answer is plausible — it is a REAL
classification, just of a different diff. A worker using it to decide which gates its change arms
will run the wrong set and report a green that inspected the wrong surfaces. On a single-commit
branch HEAD^ may even be the merge base, so the two forms sometimes AGREE, which makes the
failure intermittent and the habit of piping look safe.

HOW IT WAS CAUGHT, and this is the reusable half: a worker noticed `story_xray_browser=false`
CONTRADICTED the script's own predicate `is_story_xray_runtime_path`, which plainly returns 0 for
`tools/xray/src/**.cljs`. Two parts of the same tool disagreeing is what exposed it — not the
output, which looked fine.

THE GUARD: pass paths as ARGUMENTS (`sh .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh <path> ...`),
and sanity-check one result against the script's own predicates before trusting a surface list.
If a surface reads false for a path you can see a predicate matching, you are classifying the
wrong tree.

SAME FAMILY as the other silent-wrong-answer instruments catalogued in CLAUDE.md: the answer is
confident, well-formed and about something other than what you asked. Distinct from the pipeline
exit-status traps — here the pipe does not hide a failure, it CHANGES THE QUESTION.

WHAT I DID. rf2-hic-009's worker reported done. Later it turned out to have stalled waiting for a nonexistent notification, so I SendMessage-resumed it to finish its spine run. The worker was live, with sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh running inside that tree, and I deleted the tree underneath it. It saw FAST_PR_EXIT=1 - its own checkout vanishing, not a defect in the diff.

THE RULE THE HYGIENE DOC IS MISSING. A completion report authorises a reap only until the agent is resumed. After a SendMessage resume, the earlier report is spent: the agent is live again and owes a NEW report. Treat resume as un-completing the worker.

WHY THIS IS EASY TO GET WRONG. Every other reap signal I distrust is a proxy - PR merged, elapsed time, mtime, clean tree. The completion report is the one signal the method says to trust, so it does not feel like a proxy. But it is a point-in-time statement, and resuming moves the point. The tell is simple: if I sent the agent a message after its report, the report is stale.

WHAT IT COST HERE, AND WHAT IT COULD HAVE COST. Nothing was lost: the PR had already merged, and the worker re-ran the spine against origin/main WITH the change in it - a stronger check than the pre-merge run, exit 0. But had the reap happened before the push, three commits would have gone with the directory. A sibling worker the same night held three unpushed commits for over an hour.

THE PRACTICAL CHECK BEFORE ANY REAP: (1) has this agent been resumed since its last report? (2) is there a process live in that tree? Neither is answered by the PR state. If in doubt, leave it - a stale directory is the entire cost of waiting, and the removal script's own husk path exists precisely because directories are cheap to leave and expensive to delete wrongly.

WORKTREE HYGIENE: `git rev-list --count origin/main..worker/<x>` REPORTS EVERY REBASE-MERGED
WORKER BRANCH AS CARRYING UNMERGED WORK. Use `git cherry origin/main worker/<x>` instead, which
compares PATCH-IDs and so survives the rebase.

MECHANISM. PRs here merge with `gh pr merge --rebase`, which REWRITES the commits onto main with
new SHAs. The original branch commits therefore never appear in origin/main BY SHA, no matter how
completely their content landed, so a SHA-reachability question can only ever answer "not merged".
`git cherry` compares patch-ids: it prints `-` for a commit whose content IS upstream and `+` for
one whose content is not.

MEASURED 2026-09-10 over 16 stale worker worktrees in one sweep. The SHA form read 1 to 4
"unmerged" commits for EVERY SINGLE TREE, 16 of 16. The patch-id form read `+`=0 for all 16 —
every commit's content already upstream, nothing stranded.

THE TELL WAS UNIFORMITY, NOT AN ERROR MESSAGE. Both forms exit 0 and both return plausible small
integers; nothing on screen says which is answering the question you asked. What betrayed it was
that the answer was the SAME for every tree — a uniform verdict across a heterogeneous population
is the signature of an instrument answering its own question rather than yours.

AND IT FAILS IN THE EXPENSIVE DIRECTION FOR THE ONLY QUESTION HYGIENE ASKS. The question is "is
there work here I would destroy?", and the SHA form answers "yes" for every spent tree — so a
coordinator who trusts it concludes the entire backlog of stale worktrees is holding stranded work
and never clears any of it, while the trees accumulate. It manufactures a blocker rather than
hiding one.

CONTROL BOTH WAYS, and take it from the same population: two worktrees whose PRs were genuinely
OPEN and unmerged at that moment read `+`=2 under `git cherry` while the 16 spent ones read 0. A
census that reads 0 for everything is not evidence until something in the same sweep reads
non-zero.

THIS ANSWERS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM THE REAP TEST AND DOES NOT RELAX IT. `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md`
§Reaping is explicit that ONLY a worker's own completion report authorises reaping a worktree —
"Not a merged change. Not a clean tree. Not elapsed time. Not directory age" — and it lists
"change state" and "clean AND merged together" among six proxies adopted and found wrong. A
patch-id census is a more rigorous spelling of the "merged" proxy and is REFUSED BY THAT RULE for
reaping purposes. What it is good for is the separate question of whether a tree that must stay is
holding anything valuable, which is worth knowing when deciding what to surface to the operator.
