THE STRANDED SWEEP'S ACTIVITY TEST IS BLIND FOR A WORKTREE YOUNGER THAN ITS OWN WINDOW, AND IT FAILS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS. Measured 2026-08-21.

THE TEST: `find <worktree> -newermt '20 minutes ago' -type f | grep -v '/\.git/' | wc -l`, where near-zero is the strand signature.

WHAT I MEASURED. Four worktrees dispatched roughly 10 minutes earlier read 4945, 4946, 4945 and 4945 touched files — near-identical across four independent workers, which is the tell. Reading the NEWEST FILENAMES, as the loop instructs, settled it: the newest files in every tree were alphabetically-adjacent `docs/design/hicasso/studio/*.md` pages that no worker had any business touching. They are CHECKOUT artefacts. `git worktree add` writes the whole tree, so a window wider than the worktree's age swallows the checkout and returns a large number for a tree where nothing has happened.

IT FAILS OPEN: a genuinely dead worker in a fresh worktree reads thousands of touched files and looks alive.

NARROWING THE WINDOW DOES NOT FIX IT — it just moves the failure. The same four read 1 file at 3 minutes, which is the strand signature, while one of that same cohort reported DONE with a merged-quality PR minutes later. A worker that is READING touches nothing, which is `mayor-hygiene.md`'s write-clock problem: the metric observes writes, and reading is most of the early work.

SO FOR A WORKTREE YOUNGER THAN ABOUT 20 MINUTES, NEITHER READING IS EVIDENCE. Do not report a fresh cohort as swept on this test. What discriminates instead, in order: the harness's own running-agent report, which observes the AGENT rather than its output; a cohort sibling that has already reported done, which is direct evidence the fleet is healthy; and only then SendMessage, which costs a live worker a turn (rf2-y7tu4 measured three such costs in one day).

THE FILENAME READ IS THE LOAD-BEARING HALF, not the count. The loop already says to read the newest filenames and that instruction is what caught this; a count alone would have been believed.

THE STRANDED SWEEP IS STRUCTURALLY BLIND HERE, BECAUSE WORKERS HOLD BEADS THAT ARE STILL MARKED open (2026-08-15 22:14 AUSEST).

WHAT I OBSERVED. `bd list --status in_progress --limit 0` returned NOTHING — zero in-progress beads — at a moment when worker/retire-final was demonstrably alive: 80 files touched in 15 minutes and a fresh JVM gate started 3 seconds before I looked. That worker holds rf2-0yp7w.4, rf2-0yp7w.6 and rf2-0yp7w.10, and ALL THREE READ open.

SO THE SWEEP'S PRIMARY INPUT IS EMPTY BY CONSTRUCTION, NOT BY HEALTH. The loop is written as "look for in-progress beads; if no live worker holds one, it may be stranded". Here the set is empty whether or not anything is stranded, so the loop cannot fire in either direction. A clean sweep means nothing when nothing is ever in the set.

*** THIS RE-READS A STATISTIC IN THE HANDOFF. *** It records "In progress: 0 — 15 CONSECUTIVE CLEAN STRANDED SWEEPS" as evidence of health. Some or all of that streak may be this blindness rather than an absence of strands: 15 consecutive reads of an empty set. Do not quote that streak as assurance.

WHY IT MATTERS CONCRETELY. If retire-final dies mid-gate, the sweep finds no in-progress bead to recover. Its 3 beads sit open, look dispatchable, and the NEXT DISPATCH TICK IS FREE TO SEND A SECOND WORKER AT THEM — which is the two-workers-on-one-branch failure the method spends a section forbidding. The blindness converts a strand into a collision.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT DOES WORK, and it is the one this session has been using all along: the worktree activity sweep. Count non-node_modules, non-.git files touched in each worker worktree in the last N minutes and read the NEWEST filenames — .cpcache / .scratch / implementation/out mean a gate is running, a tracked source or doc file means the worker is editing, near-zero means a strand. Cross-check with a process listing filtered to recent start times. That test is keyed to the WORKTREE, which is where the truth is, rather than to a bead field nobody is setting.

TWO POSSIBLE FIXES, neither taken yet because it is the operator's call which:
  (a) dispatches set `bd update <id> --claim` (or --status in_progress) as part of the brief, so the field carries the fact; or
  (b) the sweep stops reading the field and reads worktrees, and mayor-posture.md is rewritten to say so.
(b) is the smaller change and matches what actually works. (a) is more honest to the tracker but relies on every future brief remembering, which is the kind of rule that decays.

UNTIL THEN: never report "0 in progress, sweep clean" as a health signal without the worktree sweep beside it. The first number is not evidence.

THE STRANDED SWEEP HAS A FIFTH DISCRIMINATOR AND IT IS THE CHEAPEST ONE: the harness's own live progress line for the agent (2026-09-01).

loops.md section 4 lists four tests for long-running-vs-stranded: tip revision, write clock, fetch-head clock, message-first. All four are INDIRECT - they read artefacts the worker happens to touch. Twice this session I ran all four, got frozen readings on every one, and concluded dormancy. Both times the worker was alive.

The reason the four fail together is structural rather than coincidental. A worker in FINAL HYGIENE - deleting gate logs, unlinking a node_modules junction, tidying a scratchpad - writes only outside the worktree and only outside .git. So the tip does not move, the fetch clock does not move, the worktree write clock does not move, and it is too busy to answer a ping. Every indirect signal reads exactly as it reads for a dead agent. The frozen-across-three-readings pattern that feels most damning is in fact the SIGNATURE of a worker at the very end of its run, not of one that stopped.

The direct signal was on screen the whole time: the background-task notification carries a live one-line progress string. For textfix3 it read Cleaning up gate artefacts in scratchpad, which named the phase outright. Read that FIRST; the four clocks are for when it is unavailable.

AND NOTE THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES WAITING RIGHT: acting on a false dormancy costs a duplicate executor racing a live worktree; waiting on a true dormancy costs one tick. Declare a window and re-read rather than salvaging.

STRANDED SWEEP: the tracker CLAIM is a liveness signal the write clock cannot see, and it is the only positive evidence available during a worker's reading phase. The method's sweep says to corroborate an unchanged tip with worktree activity, and warns that the corroboration is a WRITE clock so a worker that is only READING touches nothing. That leaves the first several minutes of every dispatch blind: the brief's own first instruction is to read the item, walk its history and check every premise at source, all of which writes nothing. Measured 2026-08-22 on worker notesrepl at 6m27s old: 0 files written in 6 minutes (a span starting just after the checkout finished, so a genuine zero rather than the checkout), tip unmoved, worktree clean -- every write-clock signature of a dead worker. But 'bd list --status=in_progress' showed its bead claimed, which only a running agent could have done, and the claim lands in the Dolt database rather than the worktree so no find-based clock can ever see it. RULE: before calling a young worker stranded on a zero write clock, check whether it has claimed its bead. A claim after dispatch time is positive proof of execution. Its ABSENCE is not proof of death, though -- dispatches here do not always claim, which is why the sweep starts from the worktrees in the first place.

STRIPPING STRING LITERALS TO PROVE A CLOJURE CHANGE IS "PROSE-ONLY" FAILS OPEN IN THIS TREE — CSS, hex tokens, UI labels and regex sources live in strings. Found by the mayor's method-reread loop, 2026-09-18.

The tempting proof: strip every comment AND every string literal from base and head, compare what remains, and call IDENTICAL "prose-only / code untouched". A `;;` filter alone cannot do this job (docstrings and `testing` descriptions are string literals, so it reports them as code — one change of this shape read 71 "non-comment" lines while altering no code), so stripping strings too is the natural next step. It was built, briefed to workers as "PROVE IT IS PROSE-ONLY", and used at three merges.

MEASURED FALSE: PR #10053 changed the RENDERED focus-ring colour inside a CSS string in `tools/xray/src/day8/re_frame2_xray/theme/global_styles.cljs` (`outline: 2px solid #FBBF24` -> `outline: 2px solid var(--rf-xray-accent)`), and the string-stripping comparison read IDENTICAL. `theme/tokens.cljc` holds hex colours in strings the same way. It fails OPEN: a behaviour change is admitted as prose.

THE REPAIR: keep the skeleton comparison, but also LIST every string literal that differs between the versions and classify each by the code immediately before it — a string after `(ns NAME` / `(def* NAME` (metadata such as `^:private` allowed between) is a docstring; after `(testing` / `(is` it is a test description; ANYTHING ELSE must be READ before calling the change prose-only. Exit non-zero on the third bucket so it cannot pass silently. Proven three ways on real commits: #10053's CSS change flagged (the two `outline:` strings surfaced), #10047's `;;`-only change passed, #10041's code rewire caught.

DELIBERATELY NOT whitelisted: registration docstrings — `(rf/reg-view id "doc" ...)`, `reg-event`, `reg-sub`. A registration's docstring is DATA that tooling may display, so changing one can change what a user sees; "read it" is the right verdict, not "prose".

Retro-check at the time: every PR merged on the flawed rule (#10049, #10052) was re-run under the repair and was genuinely prose-only (all changed strings docstrings or test descriptions), so no bad merge resulted — the flaw was in the proof, not yet in the tree.

Distinct from `a-clj-ratchet-strips-comments-so-a-comment-only-diff-is-vacuously-green`, which is the MIRROR case: there stripping comments makes a gate vacuous on a comment-only diff; here stripping strings makes a proof admit a behaviour change.

TEST HAZARD: stubbing a process GLOBAL (globalThis.fetch and friends) inside a shared shadow-cljs :node-test build leaks across namespaces, and the leak PASSES.

Mechanism, measured 2026-09-01 in tools/testbed-support (rf2-1i1ec, PR #8880): a suite ran its multi-case client tests concurrently through js/Promise.all, each case saving the current globalThis.fetch and restoring it afterwards. Concurrency nests those save/restore pairs — the second case saves the FIRST CASE STUB as the "original" it later reinstates — so the suite finished with a stub still answering fetch for every namespace after it in the same build. It went green regardless, because nothing later in that lane happens to call fetch. A future namespace that does would fail for reasons with no visible connection to the suite that broke it.

TWO RULES. (1) Run cases that stub a global ONE AT A TIME, never through Promise.all or any concurrent combinator — the save/restore pair is not reentrant and concurrency is what breaks it, not the stubbing. (2) Have each test ASSERT the global is the platform value again at the end, and make that assertion one of your planted-fault controls, so the guard is proven to bite rather than assumed.

This generalises past fetch to any shared mutable global in a build where namespaces share one runtime: the blast radius is every namespace ordered AFTER yours, the failure is silent in the suite that causes it, and it surfaces somewhere unrelated.

RELATED, same report: scripts/check_readme_links.py --ci is SILENT on success — it prints nothing and names no file, so its exit 0 is unfalsifiable without a planted fault. Nominate it only alongside a plant.

A SUBSTRATE FIX APPLIED IN ONE CONSUMER MUST BE SWEPT ACROSS EVERY CONSUMER OF THAT SUBSTRATE — rf2-8cnxg shipped in the observation port and was hit again, unfixed, in arm1's runtime (found 2026-08-07).

THE SHAPE. re-frame's observation port learned that a Reagent-hosted subscription must be ACTIVATED before it is watched — observation.cljc:1959-1982, 'ACTIVATE, then watch, then observe — and the order is the whole fix for rf2-8cnxg ... every ViewCell over a Reagent-hosted subscription rendered ONCE and never again.' Months later, arm1's Hicasso runtime attached to the same substrate with subscribe -> deref -> add-watch and NO activation, and reproduced the identical symptom. Nothing connected the two: the fix lived in the port, the bug lived in a second consumer, and no gate spanned both.

WHY IT HID SO LONG. The candidate's own bench segment installs the UIx adapter, every p0-heap row is mount-hold-release with no write, and the write-driving arms were floor/reagent/uix only. The defect needed a WRITE driven at that arm with the RATOM adapter installed — a combination the programme had never run until an allocation row demanded it. A defect that requires an untried combination of axes is invisible to every suite that varies one axis at a time.

THE RULE. When a substrate-level fix lands, grep for every OTHER site performing the same attachment sequence and check each. Under the ratom family a subscription is a bare reagent.ratom/Reaction built WITHOUT :auto-run, and a Reaction learns its sources only through deref-capture — so a plain deref outside *ratom-context* leaves 'watching' nil and the node is in nobody's watcher set. Any code that does subscribe -> deref -> add-watch without activate-derived-value! has this bug, silently, and looks like it works because it paints correctly at mount.

THE TELL, for diagnosis: stale by EVERY write since mount, not stale by one. A drain/flush fault reads stale-by-1 invariably; a never-activated reaction is deaf from birth. That arithmetic separated the two hypotheses here without running anything.

THE SUBSTRING-PREFIX TRAP IS SYSTEMIC, AND MY OWN MEASUREMENT OF IT WAS UNDERSTATED THREEFOLD (2026-08-14).

THE TRAP: `day8/re-frame2-ui` is the RETIRING donor; `day8/re-frame2-uix` is the UIx adapter, FIRST-CLASS AND STAYING. The first is a substring of the second.

I MEASURED 6 UNANCHORED VERSUS 4 ANCHORED and reported it as the blast radius. That count was scoped to `tools/` and I stated it as if general. A worker re-measured REPO-WIDE over tracked files: **REPO-WIDE the two of us measured 72/54 and 87/70 — different filters, and I have not reconciled them. Both agree on the finding that matters: ROUGHLY SEVENTEEN TO EIGHTEEN FILES MATCH ONLY VIA THE ADAPTER NAME.** Either way it is about three times the exposure I briefed. Quote the RANGE, or re-measure and state your filter.

That is the trap's own shape applied to my report of it: a number measured in one scope, quoted in another. Same family as everything else that went wrong today — the query was fine, the claim about it was not.

TWO INDEPENDENT INSTANCES IN DIFFERENT DOMAINS, both the same evening. The second was a build id: `freehand-release` is a prefix of FOUR other real build ids, found by a worker auditing its OWN draft before review. In a repository that composes names systematically — coordinates, build ids, namespaces, lane names — shorter names are routinely prefixes of longer ones. EXPECT IT.

THE RULE: before any operation keyed on a name — grep, count, sweep, sed, roster match — list every OTHER name containing it as a substring. If that list is non-empty, anchor the pattern or read every hit. AND STATE THE SCOPE OF ANY COUNT YOU QUOTE.

WHY IT IS THE MOST DANGEROUS MEMBER OF THE FAMILY: the others produce wrong NUMBERS, caught by the next person who measures. This one produces wrong EDITS that SURVIVE REVIEW — the deleted line really does contain the searched string, so a reviewer checking the diff against the query finds them consistent.

Supersede/amend an existing bead ONLY if it is OPEN and NOT in-progress and NOT closed. A dedupe/supersede match that is IN_PROGRESS (worker is mid-flight and will not see the change) or CLOSED (work is done and will not be re-actioned) must get a NEW bead instead — otherwise the new intent/work is lost. Always verify the candidate status before amending. (Mike, 2026-05-31). Generalises the rule that refinements to an in-progress bead rarely reach the worker.

A SURFACE-ARMED CI JOB IS SKIPPED ON MOST MAIN PUSHES, SO MAIN'S GREEN SAYS NOTHING ABOUT IT (2026-08-13).

MEASURED: 'Story/Xray browser gates (PR-smoke)' had conclusion SKIPPED on main runs 31675735554 and 31678098717. The first of those IS commit fcf866ea1d, the commit that broke it. Main's rollup read success on the push that introduced the regression and on every push after.

The regression (rf2-8yyd) surfaced only because PR #8118 happened to touch .github/workflows/*, which arms that job. Nothing else would have.

THE TRAP FOR A MAYOR: when a PR reds a gate that main is green on, the reflex is 'this PR broke it'. Check whether that job actually RAN on main before believing that. Two commands:

  gh run list --branch main --workflow test.yml --limit 6 --json databaseId,conclusion,headSha
  gh run view <id> --json jobs --jq '.jobs[]|select(.name|test("<job name>"))|.conclusion'

If it reads 'skipped', main's green is not evidence and the PR may be innocent. Here #8118's diff was workflow header COMMENTS and TESTING.md prose - it could not have caused a browser failure, and the arming is the whole explanation for why it was the one to reveal it.

THE SECOND HALF, WHICH IS WHY THE MISDIAGNOSIS IS EXPENSIVE: the correct response is NOT a Shape-5 fix-worker onto the red PR's branch. That shape is for a PR whose own diff broke a gate. Here the defect is on main, so the fix belongs on a NEW branch off main, and the red PR just rebases afterwards. Sending a fix-worker at the innocent branch would have produced a workaround living on the wrong branch.

RELATED AND DELIBERATE: the merge criterion counts SKIPPED as acceptable (clause 2). That is correct for a PR - a legitimately inapplicable job must not block. It is NOT a claim about main. Policy question filed as rf2-2uy8, held for the operator.

SUSTAINED API 529 OUTAGE — THE MAYOR PLAYBOOK, learned 2026-07-26 when six workers were killed inside about twenty minutes.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE: task-notifications with status=failed and "API Error: 529 Overloaded", each carrying the worker last sentence — which is usually mid-diagnosis and genuinely valuable. Not stopped for cause, nothing wrong with the work.

THE MISTAKE I MADE FIRST: resuming them. SendMessage-resume during a live outage burns a worker turn and dies on contact — I resumed three and all three died again immediately, one of them twice. Resuming is correct AFTER the window, useless during it. The tell that you are still inside the window is a resumed agent failing within a minute with the same 529.

THE CORRECT POSTURE, in priority order:
1. STOP RESUMING. Each attempt costs a turn and returns nothing. The cron loop will retry; let it.
2. DO NOT DISPATCH NEW WORK. A bigger in-flight bubble is a proportionally bigger crash surface, and every new worker is another thing to recover.
3. SWITCH TO DURABILITY. Sweep every worktree: for each, compare local HEAD against git ls-remote for its branch, and count uncommitted files excluding .beads. Classify pushed / UNPUSHED / NO-REMOTE. Pushed commits survive anything; uncommitted files survive only as long as nobody reaps the worktree.
4. PROTECT THE AT-RISK ONE ON ITS BEAD. The mayor must NOT commit another worker uncommitted WIP (only that worker knows whether it forms a coherent change). But the mayor DOES control reaping — so the mitigation is to record on the bead that the worktree holds N uncommitted files, name the path and branch, and mark it EXEMPT from the hygiene loop zero-commit/clean/no-PR reap rule. That converts an invisible risk into a written one.
5. Message the still-live workers to commit and push immediately, WITH the reason — a live worker can still act even while resumes of dead ones fail.

FRESHNESS-CHECK TRAP HIT DURING THE SAME PASS, worth its own line: a find over a worktree for recently-touched files reports .beads/* churn, because bd re-exports into EVERY worktree from any worktree. Exclude .beads, .git, node_modules, .shadow-cljs and .cpcache or a cold worktree reads as warm. And even then, a count of ~4500 touched files is an npm ci or an mkdocs build, not liveness — the file COUNT is a proxy for a recent build, not for a running agent. The only reliable liveness signal remains the SendMessage response shape ("queued for delivery" = alive; "had no active task, resumed from transcript" = was idle).

AND THE THING THAT MADE THIS SURVIVABLE: push-as-you-go was already in every brief. Four of seven workers had their commits on origin and lost nothing. The one that was genuinely at risk was the one that had not committed yet. That single instruction is worth more than the entire recovery procedure.

CORRECTING A STALE CLAIM IN ONE CARRIER GUARANTEES THE NEXT AUDIT FINDS CARRIER N+1 — SWEEP THE WHOLE TREE IN THE SAME PASS (2026-08-11, rf2-2l17).

THE EVIDENCE. The claim "the repair arrives a macrotask later" was corrected FOUR times across THREE PRs, and each correction was found by the NEXT merged-PR audit rather than by the repair before it:
  1. invariants.md L126 — the first residual.
  2. invariants.md L110's present-tense paragraph, PLUS a second stale sentence in the same paragraph that the worker judged inseparable (PR #7910). It was right to widen: repairing only the trailing clause would have swapped a page-level contradiction for a paragraph-level one.
  3. implementation/hicasso/test/.../reincarnation_seams_cljs_test.cljs:39-40 — a test docstring.
Every individual repair was bounded and correct. The PROCESS was wrong: three round-trips of mayor, worker and CI for what one `git grep` would have closed.

THE PRACTICE: when a bead corrects a stale factual claim, the brief says SWEEP EVERY CARRIER. `git grep` the exact wording over TRACKED files, read every hit, dispose of each in the one PR, and list in the PR body what was changed and what was left correct. "Bounded repair" should bound the CHANGE, not the SEARCH.

TWO CAUTIONS THAT MAKE THE SWEEP HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, both earned here:
  - THE PHRASE IS OFTEN CORRECT ELSEWHERE. invariants.md L150's timer-callback row says "one macrotask later" and is RIGHT, because a timer callback is a macrotask. The React-controlled deferral under rf2-hic-014 is also correctly a macrotask, and its repair is unreachable by this one. `git grep "macrotask later"` also hits core/substrate/spine.cljs, the react_shared_suite and two arm1 bench tests. Reading every hit is the work; the grep is only the index.
  - NAME THE DISCRIMINATOR IN THE BRIEF, or the worker cannot tell the stale hits from the correct ones. Here it is WHO SCHEDULES THE DEFERRAL: the runtime's own collector (repaired to a microtask) versus React or a timer (still a macrotask). Without that sentence a sweep either under-corrects or breaks correct prose.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS AS THE CENSUS'S THIRD SPECIES — text that matches the search and is not about the subject — and as the "confident sentence outliving its behaviour" shape the Checkpoint 1 review named. All three are one thing: a claim and its carriers drift apart, and only an exhaustive read reunites them.

A SWEEP'S GENERATOR DEFINES WHICH FAILURE DIRECTIONS IT CAN EVER FIND (2026-08-11, rf2-skpf worker, PR #7811).

THE CASE. PR #7803 swept 1,728 quoted-fence prefix triples against the real MkDocs renderer to characterise a docs-gate defect, and its numbers held up. But EVERY shape that generator emits has BALANCED backtick runs on lines 1 and 3. So the inline-masking defect could only ever manifest there as pairing that should not happen — a FALSE POSITIVE. The false-negative half needs an ODD backtick-run count either side of a boundary, a shape the fence-triple generator CANNOT EMIT BY CONSTRUCTION.

Result: in that domain the defect was 188/188 false positives and its expensive half was invisible. Not because 1,728 was too few — because the generator excluded the direction. Running 17,280 would have found nothing more.

THE LESSON, in the worker's words: 'a sweep generator defines its reachable failure directions, and the direction it excludes is invisible no matter how many shapes you run.' A sweep's SIZE is not its coverage; its GENERATOR is. So a big clean sweep is not evidence of absence outside the directions its generator can express — and the false-negative direction is usually the expensive one, because it is the one where a checker stays silent.

THE COUNTERMEASURE THAT WORKED: two probes over the same boundary, each mapping the disagreement onto the OPPOSITE error direction (a mask probe and a wrap probe over the same middle line), so neither direction can hide. When commissioning or reading a sweep, ask: what shapes can this generator NOT produce, and which error direction does that make unreachable? Put the answer in the report.

MAYOR APPLICATION: when a worker reports 'N shapes swept, zero disagreements', that is a claim about the generator, not about the surface. Ask for the generator's excluded shapes before treating it as clearance.

AFTER A CONTEXT CLEAR, PRIOR-SESSION AGENTS STAY ALIVE BUT GO INVISIBLE TO TaskList — AND I USED TaskList AS THE LIVENESS SOURCE (2026-08-10).

WHAT I DID WRONG. Recovering from a /clear, the handoff said the rf2-vsgq worker on worker/hmrbrowser-vsgq was "live and resumed". I called TaskList; it returned "No tasks found". I trusted the tool over the handoff, concluded the agent was dead, and dispatched a fresh fix-worker into that SAME worktree on that SAME branch. Two executors then ran on one branch — the exact thing "no concurrent workers same branch" forbids.

HOW IT SURFACED. Not from any check of mine. The original agent's own completion report flagged it: "A commit I did not author appeared on my branch at 15:50 — 13e9750dc9 ... it may be a second executor in this worktree." It was mine.

NO HARM, BUT ONLY BY LUCK. Both agents happened to fix different halves of the same red gate (one renamespaced the :dev-http build id, the other added the README build->port row), the commits did not conflict, and PR #7768 merged green. Nothing about that outcome was guaranteed.

THE ROOT CAUSE IS A TOOL BOUNDARY, NOT A JUDGEMENT CALL. TaskList reports the CURRENT session's task registry. A /clear starts a new registry. Agents spawned before the clear keep running and keep pushing commits, but they are absent from it. An empty TaskList after a clear therefore means "this session has spawned nothing yet", NEVER "no workers are running". It also returned empty immediately after I spawned six agents, so it is not a reliable liveness source in this harness at all.

WHAT TO USE INSTEAD, in order:
  1. The worktree list under the re-frame2-worktrees sibling — a live worker owns a worktree, and a finished one removes its own.
  2. Whether the branch's commit count has MOVED since the last tick. bootstrap.md already names this as the cheap reliable discriminator; a moved count says alive. A still count says nothing and never authorises a reap.
  3. Whether SendMessage finds a live task to deliver to.

A HANDOFF DOCUMENT OUTRANKS AN EMPTY TaskList. The handoff was written by the session that spawned those agents and it was right; the tool was answering a narrower question than the one I asked it.

AND THE SAFE MOVE WAS AVAILABLE AND CHEAP: SendMessage to resume the existing worker keeps its full context and cannot create a second executor. Never re-dispatch a fresh worker over one that may still be live — resume it.

TENTH FALSE-GREEN VARIANT: report-changed-surfaces.sh TAKES PATHS, NOT REFS, AND SILENTLY REPORTS NOTHING CHANGED (2026-07-26, hit by the scaffold-floor worker on itself).

Invoking scripts/.../report-changed-surfaces.sh origin/main treats "origin/main" as a literal FILE PATH. No such path changed, so it prints every surface false and exits successfully — i.e. "your diff touches nothing, no gate needs to run." Re-run on the real changed paths, it correctly armed examples_compile=true. There is no error, no usage message, and no hint that the argument was misread.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE INVOCATION: this is the classifier that decides which CI jobs arm. A caller who passes a ref gets a confident all-false answer, which is exactly the answer that means "skip everything". It is the same failure direction as check-beads-pr-boundary.sh exiting 0 with no base ref — a gate-adjacent script that cannot understand its input and reports the benign case rather than refusing.

DIRECTLY RELEVANT RIGHT NOW: the ci-arming worker is editing this very script to add JVM arms for tools/machines-viz and tools/testbed-support. It must pass real paths when testing its own arms, or it will see all-false and conclude its arm does not work — or worse, conclude the arm works when it has not exercised it.

GENERAL RULE, now with two instances: a script in the gate path that accepts an argument should refuse an argument it cannot interpret, not fall through to the empty result. When touching either of these, prefer making the misuse loud over documenting the correct usage.

TENTH INSTRUMENT FAULT CLASS: A LARGE-OBJECT ARM INFLATES ITS SUCCESSOR BY 2x, REPRODUCIBLY. Measuring narrow-write allocation (rf2-jr76s), an SMI control read 16.1052 B/slot in FORWARD order and 8.0027 B/slot (+0.03% against prediction) in REVERSED order — the only difference being whether an 87 KB arm ran immediately before it. No V8-level diagnosis; filed as rf2-88pie. IT WAS CAUGHT ONLY BY RUNNING BOTH ARM ORDERS, which is now standard practice on this surface and has paid for itself twice. `npm run test:cljs` DOES NOT CATCH `:infer-warning`s, AND THOSE BREAK SILENTLY UNDER `:advanced`. The adapter smoke's RELEASE compile is what catches them. Measured 2026-09-04 on the reagent-adapter teardown fix (rf2-ss8x, PR #9201).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker's first cut attached secondary teardown errors to a rethrown primary via a property access ClojureScript could not infer a type for. `test:cljs` — 11,180 tests, 55,782 assertions — passed with **zero compile warnings reported**. `npm run test:adapter-smokes`, which does a RELEASE compile, raised **six `:infer-warning`s**. Under `:advanced`, the Closure compiler renames an un-inferrable property access, so the attachment would have compiled, shipped, and silently lost the very data it existed to carry — in production only.

WHY THIS IS THE DANGEROUS SHAPE. The failure is invisible in dev, invisible in the main test lane, and only appears in optimised output where nobody is watching. A green `test:cljs` is genuinely meaningless about it. The worker fixed it by rebuilding on two `volatile!`s plus `unchecked-set` on a string key, which needs no inference.

THE RULE: ANY CHANGE THAT TOUCHES JS INTEROP — property access on a foreign object, `js-obj`, `aset`/`goog.object`, attaching fields to an Error — MUST be compiled in a RELEASE/`:advanced` configuration before it is believed. `npm run test:adapter-smokes` is the cheap one that does this. Nominate it in the brief for any interop-touching bead; do not accept `test:cljs` alone as coverage.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, worth pairing with it: THE PRE-EXISTING "POISON" TEARDOWN PROOFS WERE VACUOUS. They passed a bare `(js-obj "not" "a reaction")` expecting the disposer to throw, but that object satisfies NEITHER disposal protocol, so the ratom disposer's `:else nil` branch skipped it silently — nothing ever threw and the per-entry catch those tests were written to pin was never reached. True in the Reagent proofs, the reagent-slim proofs, and by a different route in the shared suite. A real witness must reify Reagent's actual `IDisposable`, whose methods are `dispose!`/`add-on-dispose!` — NOT `-dispose`. The reagent-slim half is filed as rf2-vy0a.

Both findings are the same underlying lesson in different clothes: a green that inspected nothing is not evidence. RELATED: [[never-put-an-uncontrolled-extraction-in-a-brief]], [[any-new-file-under-a-zero-or-low-floor-surface-reds-the-ratchet]].

A TEST THAT LOOPS OVER AN EMPTY COLLECTION PASSES WHILE ASSERTING NOTHING, AND NO RED EVER APPEARS. The only instrument that sees it is the ASSERTION COUNT, reconciled against what the change should have added or removed.

MEASURED 2026-09-16 under rf2-79fvm (PR #9889). The suite `real-vector-params-reply-to-read-leaks-nothing-into-fx-carriers` looped over a collection that had become empty: TWELVE assertions silently stopped executing while the suite stayed green. Two further assertions in the same area compared `nil` to `nil`, which is a pass that establishes nothing. None of it was caught by a failing run -- it was caught by a worker reconciling the assertion total (7378 - 7352 = the 26 assertions the change added) and finding the arithmetic would not close.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY WRONG. It fails in the REASSURING direction for the exact question a test suite is asked: the suite NAMES the property, it RUNS, it PASSES, and the property is unguarded. It is worse than a missing test, because a missing test is visible in a coverage census while this one answers "is this covered?" with yes. And it DECAYS SILENTLY: the suite was presumably real when written and emptied later, when whatever populated the collection moved or was renamed -- so the moment of breakage leaves no trace anywhere.

THE GUARD, and it is cheap: RECONCILE ASSERTION COUNTS ACROSS A CHANGE rather than reading only the pass/fail verdict. A change that adds N assertions should move the total by N. If it moves by less, something stopped executing; if it moves by more, something is running twice. This project's briefs already require quoting the captured exit code and the test/assertion counts for every gate run -- the counts are there precisely so the arithmetic can be done, and doing it is what separates a green that means something from a green that means nothing.

THE SAME SHAPE RECURS WHEREVER A TEST ITERATES RATHER THAN ASSERTS DIRECTLY: `doseq`/`for` over a computed collection, a parameterised table built by a helper, a loop over namespaces or files discovered at runtime. Where the collection is derived, ADD A POSITIVE CONTROL ASSERTING THE COLLECTION IS NON-EMPTY, so the suite reds when its own input vanishes rather than passing vacuously. That is the same rule this project applies to censuses -- take the control from the target, and a zero must mean absence rather than a broken instrument -- arriving through a test suite instead of a grep.

A TEST CAN PASS WHILE EXERCISING NOTHING, AND NO RED EVER APPEARS. Two independent mechanisms measured on 2026-09-16, hours apart, in different artefacts — which is why this is a class and not an anecdote.

MECHANISM 1 — THE LOOP OVER AN EMPTY COLLECTION (rf2-79fvm, PR #9889). The suite `real-vector-params-reply-to-read-leaks-nothing-into-fx-carriers` iterated a collection that had become empty: TWELVE assertions silently stopped executing while the suite stayed green, and two more compared nil to nil. Caught ONLY by reconciling the assertion total across the change (7378 - 7352 = the 26 assertions added) and finding the arithmetic would not close.

MECHANISM 2 — THE STRANDED SETUP, WHICH ONLY MISBEHAVES IN A FULL-LANE RUN (rf2-0hi3x, PR #9891). New pins registered their patch driver at namespace top level; the lane's reset fixture folds its baseline back before each test, stranding the registration. The dispatch became a SILENT NO-OP. The FOCUSED run passed honestly; only the full lane was empty. Both pins would have gone green in CI while exercising nothing. Caught solely because each pin asserts a PRECONDITION — "the patch landed" — before testing its real property.

WHY THIS CLASS IS WORSE THAN A MISSING TEST. It fails in the REASSURING direction for the exact question a suite is asked: the test NAMES the property, RUNS, and PASSES, so a coverage census answers "is this covered?" with yes. A missing test is at least visible as an absence. And mechanism 1 DECAYS SILENTLY — the suite was real when written and emptied later, when whatever populated the collection moved or was renamed, leaving no trace of when it stopped meaning anything.

MECHANISM 2 ADDS A SECOND LESSON THE FIRST DOES NOT CARRY: A FOCUSED RUN AND A FULL-LANE RUN CAN DISAGREE, AND THE FOCUSED ONE IS THE LIAR. Fixtures, shared registries and reset hooks only bite when siblings run. So a green focused run is not evidence about the lane, and "I ran just my test and it passed" is the shape of report to distrust.

THE GUARDS, and each catches a different mechanism, so keep both:
  * RECONCILE ASSERTION COUNTS ACROSS THE CHANGE. A change adding N assertions should move the total by N; less means something stopped executing, more means something runs twice. This project's briefs already require quoting test and assertion counts for every gate run — the counts exist so the arithmetic can be done, and doing it is what separates a green that means something from a green that means nothing.
  * ASSERT A PRECONDITION INSIDE THE TEST, before the property. "The patch landed", "the collection is non-empty", "the registry holds the handler I just registered". Where a suite iterates a DERIVED collection or depends on setup a fixture could strand, the precondition is the only thing that reds when the test's own input vanishes.
  * AND RUN THE FULL LANE, not the focused subset, before believing a new pin.

THIS IS THE PROJECT'S OWN CENSUS RULE ARRIVING THROUGH A TEST SUITE: take the control FROM THE TARGET, so a zero means absence rather than a broken instrument. A test with no precondition is a census with no control.

TEST-RUNNER FALSE GREEN: from implementation/, 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' WITHOUT '-d <dir>' makes the Cognitect runner default to a non-existent ./test and silently report 'Ran 0 tests, 0 assertions' — which READS AS GREEN. Correct form is 'clojure -M:test -d core/test -n <ns>' (adjust the -d dir per artefact). Found by the rf2-8sc64 worker on #6308, 2026-07-18. THIS AFFECTS MAYOR BRIEFS: I have repeatedly written focused-ns gate commands as 'clojure -M:test -n <ns>' — any worker that ran exactly that and reported a small/zero test count may have proven nothing. When a worker reports a focused-ns run, CHECK THE TEST COUNT IS NON-ZERO and plausible for the ns; 'Ran 0 tests' or an implausibly small count is a red flag, not a pass. Prefer instructing the FULL artefact suite (clojure -M:test from the artefact dir) over a focused -n, or require the -d flag explicitly.

THE `:advanced`/RELEASE COMPILE GATE IS SURFACE-SPECIFIC — THERE IS NO ONE SCRIPT TO NAME IN A BRIEF. Verified at source 2026-09-05 in `implementation/package.json` after a worker corrected the mayor.

WHY IT MATTERS: `npm run test:cljs` does NOT report `:infer-warning`s, and `:advanced` renames an un-inferrable property access — so an interop bug is invisible in dev and breaks only in optimised output, in production, silently. A worker measured exactly that today (six infer-warnings, zero reported by test:cljs). So an interop-touching bead MUST run a release compile. The mistake is naming the WRONG one and getting a green that compiled nothing relevant.

MEASURED FACTS:
  * `test:reagent-slim:bundle-isolation` = `shadow-cljs RELEASE examples/counter examples/counter-slim-and-fast && node scripts/check-reagent-slim-bundle-isolation.cjs`. This IS the release gate for reagent-slim. (Its companion runtime smoke is `test:reagent-slim:smoke`, a separate script.)
  * `test:adapter-smokes` = `node adapters/scripts/serve-and-run-adapter-smokes.cjs`. A worker measured it running `shadow-cljs compile` — NOT release — and covering only Reagent and UIx. Do not nominate it as the release gate, and never for reagent-slim.
  * The per-adapter smoke file is NOT uniformly named: Reagent has `implementation/adapters/reagent/testbed/spec.cjs`; reagent-slim has `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/testbed/smoke.cjs`. A brief that copies one adapter's path to another cites a file that does not exist — the mayor did exactly this.

THE RULE FOR BRIEFS: say WHAT the gate must do — "run a RELEASE/`:advanced` compile for this surface and quote its captured exit" — and tell the worker to FIND the script, rather than naming one. Where you do name it, validate it first: `grep '"test:' implementation/package.json` and confirm the recipe contains `release`, and `git ls-files` the smoke path. Naming an unvalidated script is the same class as citing an unvalidated file path, and it costs the worker a detour either way.

AND THE PATTERN THIS IS THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF: the mayor generalising ONE worker's report into a rule for every brief. It happened with `git hash-object --no-filters` (two workers corrected it), with "the ratchet is two-sided" (two workers corrected it), with the acceptance-criteria misreading from `bd show`'s concatenated fields, and now with the release-gate script name. A single worker's measurement is evidence ABOUT ITS OWN SURFACE. Before it becomes a line in every brief, check it at source — which costs one grep.

THE ALIAS RATCHET HAS TWO KEYS THAT MOVE IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, AND A SURFACE FLOOR DOES **NOT** FAIL FROM BELOW. Verified at source 2026-09-05 in `scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py`, whose own comment block names this as the trap.

  * A SURFACE FLOOR (`scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn`) is an ALLOWANCE, checked `found > floor -> fail`. Raising it LOOSENS the gate, so it may only FALL. **A surface BELOW its floor PASSES** — it is merely REPORTED (marked `under`) so the floor can be lowered, and `--write-baseline` regenerates the file.
  * `:min-edges` IS NOT A RATCHET FLOOR. It is the anti-blindness guard on the TOTAL edge count, checked `total < min_edges -> fail`. Lowering it loosens the gate, so it may only RISE — the inverse.

The script's comment states it plainly: "THE TWO KEYS RATCHET IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, AND THIS IS THE TRAP. It reads as one rule — 'floors may only fall' — and that rule is exactly WRONG for half the file."

CORRECTING WHAT I PREVIOUSLY RECORDED AND BRIEFED. I wrote that "the ratchet is TWO-SIDED — it exits 1 on a surface below its floor as well as above" and put that in FOUR fix-worker briefs. It is wrong: it conflates the surface floor with `:min-edges`. Two independent fix workers measured the truth and both cited line 825 and lines 121-122; I then read the source myself and confirmed. The original claim came from one early fix report and I generalised it without checking — the same mistake I made with `git hash-object --no-filters`, which two other workers had to correct.

WHAT THE CORRECTION CHANGES IN PRACTICE — LESS THAN IT SOUNDS, WHICH IS WHY IT SURVIVED FOUR BRIEFS. Fixing a new file's aliases and landing exactly at the floor is still correct, and staying minimal is still right ON SCOPE grounds: a fix worker's job is the delta its branch added, not a campaign slice nobody dispatched. What changes is the REASON. "Canonicalising more would redden the gate" is false; "canonicalising more is scope creep into rf2-7sx1's campaign, and the floor should then be lowered in the same commit" is true. Tell workers the true reason, because a worker that discovers the stated reason is false may distrust the instruction with it.

AND THE CAMPAIGN RULE THAT IS REAL: rf2-7sx1's notes require every partial cleanup to LOWER ITS OWN FLOOR in the same commit. That is what keeps the ratchet monotonic. A branch that canonicalises extra aliases without lowering the floor leaves the baseline overstating the debt — not a red, but a lie in the ledger.

The 'already landed' grep has a BLIND SPOT: work fixed under a SIBLING bead's id. `git log --grep=<bead-id> origin/main` catches 'this bead was fixed and left open', but NOT 'another bead's PR captured this bead's substance'. rf2-xu6rx (interpreter memo caches -> js/Map) returned nothing for its own id, yet the swap had already merged ~12h earlier in PR #7077 under rf2-lnecd. SECOND CHECK for any bead whose body cites a finding from ANOTHER bead's report: grep the SOURCE for the change itself, not the bead id — here `grep 'js/Map' conversion.cljc` on main would have shown `#?(:cljs (js/Map.) :clj (atom {}))` already present. THE BASH TOOL SILENTLY STRIPS BACKSLASHES FROM HEREDOC STRINGS ON THIS WINDOWS SETUP (2026-07-26).

Found by the checker-residuals worker while probing a char-literal guard: a heredoc probe string lost its backslashes, so the probe read as a FALSE NEGATIVE — the guard looked broken when the input had been mangled before it arrived. It rewrote every probe as a FILE under its own worktree and the results reversed.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS THE KNOWN git worktree add BACKSLASH STRIPPING, which is already recorded, but the surface is different and more insidious: a worktree path failing is loud, whereas a mangled PROBE STRING silently changes what you are testing. Any probe involving backslashes, char literals, regex escapes or line continuations must be written to a FILE, not passed through a heredoc.

AND IT COST A REAL VERDICT IN THE SAME SESSION, in a second form: that worker plant C did not apply because of a LINE-CONTINUATION BACKSLASH in the anchor, and the self-test returned rc=0 — INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A GATE THAT MISSED THE DEFECT. Only the mandated "confirm the diff applied before reading the verdict" protocol caught it. That is the twelfth false-signal class firing in the wild and being caught by the exact rule written for it.

SO THE RULE COMPOUNDS: for any mutation or probe whose payload contains a backslash, (1) write it to a file rather than a heredoc, and (2) confirm it applied by git diff --stat AND by grepping the token back out. Either check alone would have missed one of the two failures above.

A THIRD FINDING FROM THE SAME WORKER, unrelated but worth the same memory: a PRIME-SUFFIXED SYMBOL (db-prime, tags-prime) reads as a QUOTE to the bijection walker regex — 352 occurrences in the tree, the same class the existing backslash-quote lookbehind was written for, and a FALSE-GREEN direction. Latent rather than live because all 352 sit inside binding vectors the walk cannot reach. Closed with one lookbehind. The lesson: when a regex already has a lookbehind for one lookalike, ASK WHAT ELSE LOOKS LIKE THAT — the second instance is usually already in the tree.

THE CHEAP BAND CONFIRMATION -- "read the rollup TOTAL of a PR merged AFTER the suspect commit" -- HAS A
MEASURED FALSE NEGATIVE: IF THAT PR'S FILES DO NOT MATCH THE TRIGGER'S `paths:` FILTER, IT HANDS BACK THE
PRE-CHANGE NUMBER ON THE POST-CHANGE MATRIX.

Measured 2026-09-18 on re-frame2 against `b853f9d57db5`, which added a PATH-FILTERED `pull_request` trigger
to `docs.yml` while adding zero job definitions:
  * PR #245 (spec/-only, matches the filter, merge commit HAS the change as an ancestor): 20 rollup rows,
    2 of them `docs`
  * PR #243 (0 of 1 files match the filter): 18 rows -- EXACTLY the pre-trigger number -- on the same
    post-trigger matrix, ELEVEN MINUTES after #242
  * PR #242 (3 of 7 files match): 20 rows
  * PR #238 (spec/-only, merge commit does NOT have the change as an ancestor): 18 rows, 0 docs
Controls: the `tests` workflow contributed 18 on both sides of the boundary, and exactly ONE commit touched
.github/workflows/ between the two merge commits, against 7 commits in range. Ancestry throughout, never
clocks.

So the true reading is +2 band rows from ZERO job definitions, and the prescribed confirmation returns the
old number roughly whenever you pick the wrong PR.

WHY IT MATTERS: the cheap confirmation exists precisely to settle "did the band move?" without pattern
work, and it is the step a careful reader trusts most because it needs no regex. Its false negative lands
on the side that says NOTHING CHANGED -- so a real band move reads as a phantom, and every subsequent PR
then appears to be short of coverage against a band that is genuinely two rows higher.

THE GUARD, two parts:
  1. **Choose the confirming PR for what its FILES ARE, not for when it merged.** It must touch files that
     MATCH the trigger's `paths:` list. A PR that merged after the change but matches nothing is evidence
     about nothing.
  2. **Read the workflow's rows, not only the total.** Counting how many rows a given workflow contributes
     (e.g. `docs`) discriminates directly and survives an unlucky PR choice.

AND THE DEEPER POINT, which is why this is worth a memory rather than a footnote: A TRIGGER-ONLY CHANGE
MOVES THE CHECK SET WITH ZERO JOBS ADDED. Filtering an `on:`-block match away as "not a job key" does not
discharge the question -- it REPOINTS it. Ask what the new `on:` block SCHEDULES that the old one did not.
The job-key discriminator and the `runs-on:` structural tell are both correct and both answer a NARROWER
question than the one the merge criterion actually asks.

A second measured fact in the same family, worth keeping beside it: AN `if:`-GATED-OFF JOB STILL
CONTRIBUTES A ROLLUP ROW, as SKIPPED. Gating a job to `push` does not remove it from a PR's band. Confirmed
on the 2026-05 case and again at tip.

The core JVM suite (implementation/core clojure -M:test) runs ~10min under concurrent worker/mayor JVM load — right at the 600s foreground tool limit. This is the ROOT of the 'workers strand on backgrounded gates' pattern: a worker can't reliably foreground it when the machine is contended, so it backgrounds the gate + ends its turn with work uncommitted + no PR. Mitigation: briefs must say 'run gates FOREGROUND, do not background; if the core JVM suite risks the 600s limit run a FOCUSED namespace subset (clojure -M:test :only <ns>) not the whole suite'; recover a stranded worker by SendMessage-resume telling it to finish foreground in one turn.

THE CROSS-BASE CHECK: TWO PRs EACH GREEN AGAINST A BASE LACKING THE OTHER CAN STILL BREAK IN COMBINATION (2026-07-26).

A worker did this unprompted and it is the practice I most want to adopt. Its work and PR #7081 were EACH GREEN against a base that did not contain the other. Rather than assume the combination was fine, it built a THROWAWAY WORKTREE AT origin/main WITH BOTH MERGED and ran the suite: freehand JVM 1156/7707, 0F 0E. Then removed the worktree.

WHY THIS MATTERS AT SATURATION: I run up to six workers, each rebasing onto a moving main, and I merge on green. Every green I act on was measured against a base THAT NO LONGER EXISTS by the time I merge. Nineteen PRs today merged a state older than the worker tip; several pairs touched adjacent surfaces. THE MERGE LOOP HAS NO CROSS-BASE SIGNAL AT ALL — CI re-runs on the merge commit, but I do not wait for it.

WHEN TO REQUIRE IT: when two live PRs touch the SAME artefact or adjacent seams — for example one editing implementation/freehand/src and another editing implementation/freehand/test, or two both moving spec/009 rows. It is cheap: one throwaway worktree at origin/main, both branches merged, the ONE suite that spans both surfaces. Not the whole spine.

WHEN NOT TO: disjoint surfaces. Most of the time the fence system already guarantees it, and this would be ceremony.

A blockquote, bolded "Amended", the ISO date, the bead id in parentheses, then the former wording quoted. That is the shape to follow and to cite.

WHAT I GOT WRONG, AND IT IS WORSE THAN A TYPO. I told worker after worker — roughly eight briefs across one session — that "docs/design/hicasso/product/design-laws.md law 1 is the established precedent, and peers have followed it all session." Every clause of that was false:

A claim that travels in boilerplate is the LEAST likely to be re-checked and the MOST expensive when wrong, because it is repeated verbatim into every dispatch. **Boilerplate needs validating once, hard, and then it is trustworthy; an unvalidated boilerplate claim is a lie told at scale.**

THE RULE: BEFORE A CITATION ENTERS A REUSABLE BLOCK, RESOLVE IT. `git ls-files <path>` for the file, and grep for the heading or phrase you are attributing to it. Do it once, at the moment the sentence is first written, and record the verified form here so no future mayor re-derives it. Cost: one command. Cost of not doing it: eight workers sent to a nonexistent file, each of whom had to either ignore the instruction or spend context discovering it was wrong. One of them did exactly that and reported it; the others may simply have worked around it silently, which is worse because the error survives.

THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS the other mayor-side generalisation failures this session — `git hash-object --no-filters`, "the ratchet is two-sided", the release-gate script name, the acceptance-criteria misreading. THE "git grep <ref> -- <dir>/ RETURNS FALSE-EMPTY" HAZARD IS NOT REAL, AND I HAVE BEEN PUTTING IT IN EVERY BRIEF (2026-07-26).

TESTED TODAY, three ways, same answer: git grep -l defhost HEAD -- implementation/freehand/src/ returns 7; without the ref, 7; plain recursive grep on the worktree, 7. NO DISCREPANCY.

AND THE ORIGINAL OBSERVATION WAS ALMOST CERTAINLY A CORRECT EMPTY MISREAD AS A FALSE ONE. At an older ref c6f3c3b8ed the directory implementation/freehand/src EXISTS, and git grep for defhost there returns 0 — BECAUSE v/defhost DID NOT EXIST YET AT THAT COMMIT. That is the right answer. Confirmed again on a path that genuinely moved: tools/xray/src for re-frame.ui gives 6 at the old ref, 1 at HEAD, 1 on the worktree — all three correct and all three different for real reasons.

SO THE FAILURE MODE WAS MINE: searching an old ref for something that had not landed yet, and concluding the tool was broken rather than that the code was absent. A ref-scoped search answers a question about THAT COMMIT, and the answer is often legitimately different from the worktree.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A WRONG NUMBER: the instruction did not merely mislead, IT DEGRADED THE WORK. I told workers to use `git show <ref>:<file> | grep` INSTEAD — which is per-file, has no directory recursion, and requires knowing every filename in advance. Workers have been doing by-hand file enumeration for a whole session to route around a hazard that does not exist. At least one reported a "targeted grep" workaround because of it.

THIS IS THE THIRD STANDING INSTRUCTION OF MINE PROVEN WRONG TODAY, all three boilerplate I repeated without re-testing: (1) "sample coverage unchanged at 113 of 136 proves an edit fell outside a digest fence" — the census is insensitive to block text BY CONSTRUCTION; (2) "simulate a deletion by moving the tree aside" — blind for git-reading gates, and a sibling then showed moving it aside WITHIN the search space is not a deletion either; (3) this one.

THE RULE FOR MYSELF: BOILERPLATE IS THE LEAST-AUDITED TEXT I PRODUCE, BECAUSE IT IS COPIED RATHER THAN COMPOSED. Every standing instruction is a claim, and a claim repeated forty times without re-testing is forty chances to be wrong at scale. RE-TEST ONE BOILERPLATE CLAIM PER RETROSPECTIVE, cheaply, against the actual repo — today that took two commands and killed a hazard that had been costing real worker time all session.

THE MERGED-PR AUDIT CAN DESTRUCTIVELY OVERWRITE A BEAD'S ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (2026-07-25, found by EP-0037 review gate 2). This is a process defect in a process I do not control, and it silently destroys the only record of what a slice promised.

WHAT HAPPENED: R1's and R2's slice acceptance criteria were REWRITTEN — both the title AND the description — into the audit's follow-through text. PRs #6875/#6877 name rf2-kqxe6.5/.6 as the slice owners; their original criteria no longer exist anywhere. By contrast the audits of .3 and .7 APPENDED their findings, leaving the criteria intact. That difference is exactly why an independent completeness review could verify .3 and .7 and could NOT verify .5 and .6. Named casualty: the R2 tooling clause ended up with no bead at all.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND ONE EPIC: acceptance criteria are the only durable record of what was promised. A merged-PR audit's job is to record what it found, and it is very good at that — it caught a keyword-as-Var false green, a load-order privacy defect, a declared-:on-* classification defect and a census extent bug. But an audit that overwrites the promise it is auditing removes the ability to check completeness later, and the loss is invisible: the bead still reads coherently, just as the audit's narrative rather than as the slice's contract.

MAYOR ACTIONS: (1) treat audit notes as APPEND-ONLY when I write them myself, and say so in briefs — findings go in notes, never over a description; (2) when a bead's description reads as audit narrative rather than as acceptance criteria, suspect this and check git history of .beads for the original; (3) rf2-twpp6 tracks the append-only repair for the two affected beads; (4) when commissioning a completeness review, tell it that a bead whose criteria were overwritten is UNVERIFIABLE and should be reported as such rather than passed — gate 2 worked this out unprompted and it is the reason its verdict is trustworthy.

GENERALISABLE FORM: any automated process that writes into the tracker can destroy the state a later reviewer needs. Prefer append. If a tool overwrites, the tracker's git history is the only recovery path — which is another reason the .beads export must keep being committed on the heartbeat.

The skill↔MCP drift gate has TWO distinct failure modes — do NOT assume flake (learned 2026-07-18, rf2-92dlh). (1) The TRANSIENT flake: 'Verify skill ↔ MCP allowed-tools drift' fails under concurrent-PR load; structurally impossible when the diff has 0 skills/MCP files → --admin-justifiable. (2) A REAL main-red drift: when a PR adds/changes MCP server tools WITHOUT reconciling the consumer skills' allowed-tools + the retro drift-set, check_skill_mcp_drift.py --ci reports real findings and the gate is RED ON MAIN — every subsequent PR inherits that red. I conflated the two: rf2-vxgfnd.95.8 added 5 re-frame2-pair MCP tools (explain-render/read-view-*) without updating skills/re-frame2-pair/SKILL.md allowed-tools + scripts/check_skill_mcp_drift.py's re-frame2-pair-retro intentional_server_only set, so main's drift gate went REAL-red — and I kept --admin-ing PRs past it as 'the flake' for many merges until .95.10's spine run surfaced it (rf2-92dlh). FIX GOING FORWARD: when the drift gate is red, VERIFY main's own drift state — run/check  (or check main's gate run). If it exits non-zero (real findings), it is NOT a flake — file/dispatch a fix (allow-list the new tools in SKILL.md + the retro drift-set) instead of --admin-ing PRs past it. Only --admin when main's drift gate is GREEN and the PR's red is the load flake (0 skills/MCP diff).

THE SPEC 009 CO-EDIT INVARIANT HAS A THIRD ARM: the core JVM error-catalogue conformance test exercise literal. A new ALWAYS-ON :rf.error/* id needs THREE co-edits in the same PR, not two: (1) the spec/009-Instrumentation.md catalogue row; (2) the Spec-Schemas.md row; (3) an entry in implementation/core/test/re_frame/error_catalogue_channel_conformance_test.clj exercise literal (~line 590) AND something that actually exercises/emits it (a register-error-listener! drive or equivalent). The test asserts parsed-always-on-set-equals-the-exercise-literal — a catalogue always-on row with no matching literal entry fails with only-in-catalogue: (:the-new-id).
DISCOVERED 2026-07-19 when #6440 (rf2-vxgfnd.143 custom-element conflict law) added :rf.error/custom-element-conflict always-on and its JVM core gate went red. The ui-artefact worker ran check_keyword_catalogue_drift.py (Python) + the ui suite, but NOT cd implementation/core && clojure -M:test, so it never saw the conformance failure. ADD to every brief that mints an always-on error id: run implementation/core clojure -M:test AND update the exercise literal, even for a ui/ssr/machines change — the catalogue is core-consumed.

⚠️ AND A CORRECTION TO MY OWN FLAKE HEURISTIC: I diagnosed this as a CI flake because "the diff touches 0 files under implementation/core/ and JVM core is green on main." THAT REASONING IS WRONG for cross-artefact conformance tests. The real touched surface was spec/009-Instrumentation.md (the catalogue), which the PR DID touch; a CORE test parses that shared spec file and compares it to a literal. So "diff has no core SOURCE files" does NOT imply "core gate cannot be affected" — a gate in artefact A can read a shared artefact-agnostic file (spec/009, Spec-Schemas, Conventions) that the diff edited. The flake signature must be: diff cannot affect the failing gate THROUGH ANY PATH INCLUDING SHARED SPEC FILES A GATE PARSES — not merely "no source files of that artefact in the diff." I nearly --admin-merged past a genuine touched-surface gate. The rule holds: a failing touched-surface gate is NEVER an --admin candidate; when unsure whether it is touched, READ THE FAILURE (it named the test, the file, the exact only-in-catalogue id) before concluding flake.

THE ui JVM ASSERTION COUNT IS NONDETERMINISTIC; THE TEST COUNT IS NOT. Proved by the rf2-ymfix/rf2-4vm19 worker (#6450) on 2026-07-19 by RE-RUNNING identical code rather than assuming: implementation/ui clojure -M:test reported 18723 assertions on one run and 18718 on the next, same tree, same commit. Cause: race-dependent assertions in the concurrency suites (assertion counts vary with interleaving). The TEST count was stable across both runs, so a delta in TEST count is exact and trustworthy.
⚠️ CONSEQUENCE FOR EVERY BRIEF I WRITE: I have been telling workers "counts must be non-zero AND PLAUSIBLE" and quoting expected assertion totals (~18660, ~18744, etc). For implementation/ui those assertion numbers CANNOT be used as a precise expectation — only as an order-of-magnitude sanity check. Pin expectations to TEST counts, not assertion counts, for any suite containing concurrency tests. A worker who sees an assertion count differ by a handful from my quoted figure should NOT treat that as a finding; a worker who sees the TEST count differ should.
This also retro-explains earlier session confusion where assertion totals drifted run-to-run (16136/16141/16143 on an identical tree) — same cause, and the right response then and now is: use test counts as the stable signal.

⚠️ RELATED, SAME REPORT: a `npm run test:elision` invocation died mid-compile with EXIT 127 (command-not-found shape), transient; the re-run was clean exit 0. Do not treat a single 127 from a compile-driven gate as a gate failure — re-run once and report both outcomes. But do NOT generalise this to real non-zero exits from the test body itself.

THE LOAD-BEARING TYPE MUTANT IS THE ONE THAT IS VALID IN A SIBLING CATEGORY (2026-08-06, rf2-am6qs, PR #7605).

Tightening three `:where` slots from `:any` to `:symbol`, the worker mutated four types at each slot — string, number, map, and a BARE KEYWORD. It named the keyword as the load-bearing one, and the reason is the generalisable part: OTHER CATEGORIES IN THE SAME CORPUS GENUINELY CARRY `:where :event`, `:where :flow-eval`, `:where :reactive`. So `:any` was not admitting arbitrary garbage — IT WAS ADMITTING A SPELLING THAT IS CORRECT ONE ROW OVER.

WHY THAT MATTERS FOR HOW YOU CHOOSE MUTANTS: a string/number/map mutant proves the slot rejects nonsense, which nobody was going to write. The keyword mutant proves it rejects THE MISTAKE SOMEONE WILL ACTUALLY MAKE — copying a neighbouring row. When picking negative cases for a schema slot, look for a value that is VALID IN AN ADJACENT DECLARATION and use that; the plainly-absurd mutants are the cheap ones and prove the least.

CONTROL SHAPE WORTH COPYING: each mutant had to be REJECTED by the shipped `:symbol` AND ACCEPTED by an `:any` control rebuilt from that slots OWN shipped schema, with a minimal base so only the `:where` type can be under test. Without the acceptance half you have not shown the TIGHTENING is what did the work rather than something else in the base.

AND THE CENSUS DID NOT TRANSFER, which is why it had to be redone per slot: the brief told the worker not to assume the previous slots answer carried, and the beads own call-site list was INCOMPLETE. Beyond the four sites it named there were five more through `require-frame-provider-target!` — `re-frame.freehand.substrate/frame-provider`, `v/->react`, `re-frame.ui/frame-provider` (twice, once via `require-scope-frame!`) and `re-frame.ui/->react`. A bead enumerating call sites is a starting point, never the population.

RESULT: all three tightened, no `:where` slot in Spec-Schemas.md is `:any` any more, and spec/009 needed NO edit because no row disagreed.

`git diff origin/main...<branch>` IS NOT A CONTAINMENT TEST, and it is tempting precisely
because it looks like a stronger one than `git cherry` (measured 2026-09-02, hygiene loop).

WHAT IT ACTUALLY ANSWERS: three-dot diffs from the MERGE BASE to the branch, so it reports
"what this branch changed since it forked" - not "does the trunk already have it". Under a
rebase-merge workflow those are entirely different questions, because the branch's commits land
on the trunk under NEW shas while the branch's own merge base stays where it was.

MEASURED, same eight branches, two instruments:
  - `git cherry origin/main <b>` read unmerged=0 (fully contained) for adapterswitch-oz7wr,
    twosmall-uuqek, http-issuance-rsv2n, wsreply-tb442 and xrayseam-7htk7 - all five with
    MERGED PRs.
  - `git diff origin/main...<b> --stat` returned large non-empty diffs for every one of those
    five: 242, 28, 253, 317 and 475 insertions respectively, xrayseam also showing 4717
    deletions.
A non-empty answer for a branch that is provably contained. Nothing errors; the numbers are
real; they are about the wrong question.

WHY IT MATTERS: the failure is fail-DANGEROUS in the useful direction. It never says "contained"
when a branch is not, so it cannot cause a wrong delete - but it says "not contained" for
branches that are, which keeps merged branches forever and, worse, makes a reader distrust the
cherry result that was right. I reached for it as a "secondary check that could clear a branch
honestly" and it would have done the opposite.

THE RULE STANDS UNCHANGED: patch-equivalence via `git cherry` is the containment test.
`-` is proof of containment; `+` is only the ABSENCE of proof, because patch identity is computed
over the diff INCLUDING context lines, so a sibling landing in neighbouring lines changes your
commit's identity. Keeping a `+` branch costs nothing; deleting a genuinely unmerged one costs
work. docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md section 5 "Branches" already states all of this correctly -
this memory is about the WRONG instrument I reached for, which that section does not name and
does not need to.

GENERAL SHAPE: an instrument can be right and answer a different question from the one you asked,
and the well-formed plausible number is what stops you noticing. Exercise a containment probe
against a branch you KNOW is merged before believing what it says about one you do not.

THE THREE BLOCKS THAT TRAVEL VERBATIM INTO A DISPATCH HAVE THREE DIFFERENT SHAPES, AND ONLY ONE OPENS WITH A SELF-NAMING FRAME (2026-08-23, PR #8726).

Measured in docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md:

- The worktree boundary block: payload is a FENCED text block (52 lines / 2,930 chars incl. fences). Mayor-facing rationale sits BEFORE the fence; a note about the mayor-side commit guard sits AFTER it.
- The common preamble: payload is a FENCED text block (61 lines / 3,990 chars incl. fences), opening immediately under the heading. Its mayor-facing paragraph sits AFTER the closing fence, at the TAIL.
- Gate mechanics: NO fence. Heading down to the rule before '## Reviewing what comes back'. It alone opens with '**This section is the gate-mechanics block.**' naming itself, where it stops, and the neighbouring section it is not.

SO THE OPERATIVE RULE IS: where the payload is FENCED, take the FENCE and everything outside it is yours. The frame-dropping instruction applies only to the unfenced block.

WHY IT MATTERS: PR #8723 (mine, merged 90 minutes earlier) asserted 'Each block opens by naming itself and saying where it stops' — true of ONE of three. The cost is directional: a mayor taught that mayor-facing prose lives at the OPEN checks the open of the common preamble, finds a fence, pastes the heading-to-heading range, and ships the tail paragraph ('A pass that concludes only in the ignored tree...') into a worker brief. That is the exact failure the paragraph exists to prevent, reintroduced at the other end of the same block.

A HABIT ABOUT WHICH END THE MAYOR-FACING PROSE LIVES AT IS WRONG HALF THE TIME. The two fenced blocks put it on opposite sides.

THE THREE-POINT CONTROL'S REFUSAL IS A DENOMINATOR-CLASS FAULT, NOT A ROW-CLASS ONE — diagnosed 2026-08-07 from 42 refused runs across two ensembles (rf2-8a746).

TWO INDEPENDENTLY FATAL HALVES.
(1) THE PREDICTION IS WRONG. 2.0101x is the statistic's expectation only if T is AFFINE in the dirty set over [1,200]. On the published TaskDuration clock it is not: marginal cost is 12.6 us/cell over [1,100] and 6.8 over [100,200]. True centre is 1.55x, which sits 2.6% above the band's own rejection edge of 1.5076 — so half of every run's blocks fall out the bottom ON A PERFECTLY QUIET BOX.
(2) THE STATISTIC IS ILL-CONDITIONED. Differencing away the constant also throws away the PEDESTAL that made relative noise look small, leaving a denominator of 1.25 ms carrying 0.60 ms of dispersion — 2.09 sigma from zero. Even with the centre corrected only ~60% of blocks land in band, and a strict every-one-of-18 rule turns that into P(pass) ~ 1e-4.

THE DECISIVE CONTROL EXPERIMENT: ctl3Layout — the SAME statistic on LayoutDuration over the IDENTICAL blocks and samples — reads 1.9681 / 1.9801 with marginals affine to 5% and no sign-gate firing in 756 blocks. So the arithmetic, door, tare and aggregation are all sound; the PAGE is not affine on the counter the row is published on. The non-layout half carries it: 7.13 -> 1.83 us/cell, a 3.9x collapse.

WHY ctl-2x SURVIVES AND ctl3 DOES NOT — this is the transferable lesson: ctl-2x's denominator is a LEVEL (the floor's whole tared reading, ~4.5 ms) carrying the same ~0.4 ms of estimator error, so 9% relative against ctl3's 48%; and its centre sits 20% above the edge against ctl3's 4%. Distance-above-edge and per-block scatter, raised to the strict-rule exponent, reproduce every pass rate in the programme. A DIFFERENCE-OF-DIFFERENCES DENOMINATOR IS THE FAULT. The invariance argument ('an additive constant cancels in each difference') is true of the LEVEL and is not the problem; what destroys it is the error in each arm's ESTIMATE of that level, which is independent between arms and ADDS. Measured corr(T(1),T(100)) = 0.43, so differencing removes only 40% of the denominator's variance where the argument assumes nearly all.

THE DEGENERATES ARE THE SAME FAULT, NOT A SECOND ONE: den=+0.019 ms -> 86x, den=+0.026 ms -> 114x, and in 9 of the 10 worst blocks T(1) is elevated — it enters BOTH differences, so it drives the smaller one to zero first.

RE-SITING THE POINTS DOES NOT RESCUE IT. Re-adjudicating the same committed blocks at 100/200/300 (above the knee) gives 1.9975 / 2.0777 against a prediction of 2.0000 — the affine premise holds there — but den halves to 0.70 ms while its IQR does not, and in-band blocks FALL from 47% to 33%. Span the knee and the centre is wrong; avoid it and the denominator is gone.

THE ONLY CONSTRUCTION THE EVIDENCE SUPPORTS has a denominator that is a LEVEL rather than a difference. That is a decision about what the lane measures and belongs to the operator.

THE HARNESS DOES NOT SIGNAL A CAPPED TOOL CALL — IT BACKGROUNDS IT, AND THE GATE KEEPS RUNNING (measured 2026-08-07 on rf2-ketqy, PR #7642). CORRECTED: an earlier version of this memory said the harness kills the parent and orphans the child. That model was wrong and the fix built on it would not have worked.

MEASURED, not inferred. Capped at 90s, a backgrounded 'sh scripts/test-fast-pr.sh' kept running after the tool returned — its log grew 41822 to 49220 bytes and two more stages completed. TaskStop behaves identically: reports success, kills nothing, fires no trap. So there is no signal, and a signal handler alone can never see this case.

TWO FURTHER MEASUREMENTS THAT KILL THE OBVIOUS FIXES:
- 'kill the child PROCESS GROUP' would kill the CALLER. Every child shares the caller's PGID under Git Bash.
- bash DEFERS a trapped signal until the foreground child returns — measured at 22 seconds (SIGTERM at t+3s to a script running 'sleep 25'; handler ran at t+25s). So even when a signal IS delivered, a trap is late.
- 'taskkill /F /T' is silently mangled by Git Bash into 'taskkill F:/ ...'. Behind the customary '|| true' it is a NO-OP that looks like it worked. Needs MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 and MSYS2_ARG_CONV_EXCL='*'; Cygwin ignores both.

THE DAMAGE the orphan does: it keeps writing to the SAME log as the relaunch (two writers, NUL-riddled output), and its 'npm run test:cljs' unlinks out/node-test.js underneath the next run's per-namespace isolation sweep, which then reds with 'the bundle changed on disk during the sweep' and MODULE_NOT_FOUND. That red is the sweep working correctly and is indistinguishable from an isolation regression in the worker's own diff. The culprit java.exe is invisible to 'ps -ef' entirely.

THE SHIPPED REMEDY (PR #7642): a trap for the genuinely-signalled cases PLUS the same reap invoked at the START of the next run — the only moment it can act, because the path that actually bites delivers no signal. Not a lock: the second run never waits or refuses.

DISCRIMINATORS, unchanged and still the useful part: LAUNCH failure ('Command failed:') = spawn contention. 'changed on disk during the sweep' = a live orphan; kill it and re-run quiet. ASSERTION mismatch = real.

/tmp ON THIS BOX IS THE SHARED WINDOWS TEMP DIRECTORY — every agent, worker and codex process writes there, so a generic filename WILL be clobbered (2026-09-03).

MEASURED: '/tmp' resolves to C:\Users\miket\AppData\Local\Temp. It holds hundreds of foreign '<uuid>.tmp' files from unrelated Windows processes, and '/tmp/open.json' appeared there written by something other than the mayor. A worker reported the concrete failure: it read '/tmp/open.json' twice seconds apart and got BEADS DATA back from a file it had written with something else — another process had overwritten it in between.

WHY IT IS DANGEROUS RATHER THAN MERELY UNTIDY: the mayor and its workers all reach for the same obvious names — /tmp/open.json, /tmp/files.txt, /tmp/out.log, /tmp/nred.json. A clobbered intermediate does not error; it yields a WRONG ANSWER that looks well-formed, and it is read as fact. That is the same failure class as a census with no control.

USE THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD instead — the per-session directory named in the environment preamble (C:/Users/miket/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/<project>/<session-id>/scratchpad). It is session-scoped and isolated. If /tmp must be used, embed a session-unique prefix in every filename and re-verify content after writing.

A worker caught this only because it applied a control — reading the same file twice and comparing. Intermediates are exactly where an unverified assumption hides.

GATE LOGS MUST NOT GO TO /tmp UNDER MULTI-AGENT LOAD — /tmp is SHARED across concurrently running worker agents on this box, so one worker gate log silently OVERWRITES another. Found 2026-07-24 by the rf2-drpa3.112 SSR worker, which nearly shipped a false green.

THE MECHANISM: worker A runs "npm run test:browser > /tmp/gate-browser.log 2>&1". Worker B, running concurrently in a DIFFERENT worktree, writes the same path. A then reads a log that is really B run. In the observed case the log EXIT=0 and reported "0 failures" — every number looked right. The ONLY tell was the shadow-cljs banner naming the WRONG worktree (pilot-react-interop-46 instead of the reader own).

WHY THIS IS NASTY: it defeats the standard exit-code discipline. The capture-to-a-file-and-echo-the-exit-code rule was adopted precisely because piping into tail/grep discards the runner exit status. But if the FILE ITSELF belongs to another agent, the captured exit code is ALSO another agent — a correct technique reading the wrong evidence. Both the summary AND the exit code agree, and both are about someone else run.

THE FIX, now standard in every dispatch brief: write gate logs to the SESSION SCRATCHPAD or a worktree-local path, never a bare /tmp name. e.g.
  <gate> > "$WT/gate-<name>.log" 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; tail -30 "$WT/gate-<name>.log"
And VERIFY OWNERSHIP: the shadow-cljs "config:" banner line names the worktree whose build ran. Grep it and confirm it is YOURS before believing any number in that file. That is the cheap proof.

MAYOR NOTE: my own standing gate-discipline boilerplate said "> /tmp/gate.log". That instruction is now known-unsafe whenever more than one worker runs at a time, which is the normal case at saturation. Update the boilerplate; do not keep handing workers a colliding path.

GENERAL FORM: this joins the roster of ways green has meant nothing-was-measured here. The others are about a check that could not fail; this one is about a check that MEASURED SOMEBODY ELSE. When an assertion rests on an artefact OUTSIDE your process (a shared temp file, a shared port, a shared cache), ask WHO ELSE CAN WRITE IT before trusting what you read.

tools/xray's *_cljs_test.cljs files run under `npm run test:cljs`, NOT the artefact's own `clojure -M:test`, which is a JVM run that cannot load them and goes green having inspected nothing.

**The covering gate for a `tools/xray` CLJS change is `npm run test:cljs`.** `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn`'s `:node-test` build lists `../tools/xray/src` and `../tools/xray/test` on its classpath, under a comment saying it exists so the build picks up `tools/xray/test/**/*_cljs_test.cljs`.

**`cd tools/xray && clojure -M:test` is NOT that gate and fails OPEN.** It is a JVM run and cannot load a `.cljs` test: measured 2026-09-10 by worker `restable-a`, it returned 1276 tests / 6118 assertions / 0 failures with **ZERO mentions of the new test namespace** — green having inspected nothing. It is not useless (`frame_singleton_guard_test.clj` text-scans the source), it simply does not run CLJS tests.

**Why this is worth a memory: I nominated the wrong one in a dispatch brief, in the fail-open direction.** I checked `:node-test`'s source paths with a window bounded at the first `:node-test-xray` string I found, read ~35 quoted paths, got an empty result for `tools|xray`, and wrote it into the brief as fact. The section is **41,387 characters with 107 quoted paths** — my window never reached the answer, and `[]` is a plausible-looking result, so nothing on screen said so. The worker caught it.

**How to apply:** nominate `npm run test:cljs` for `tools/xray` CLJS work. And when reading a build section out of an EDN file, bound the window on the next TOP-LEVEL key, then sanity-check the count of paths you extracted against the section's size before concluding anything from an empty result.

Related: [[mayor-briefs-ran-three-times-too-long]], [[mayor-judgement-good-counts-bad-label-the-unverified]].
