I CHOSE BETWEEN TWO DUPLICATE PRs ON WHETHER EACH TOUCHED THE FILE A BEAD NAMED. THAT TEST ANSWERED A DIFFERENT QUESTION THAN THE BEAD ASKED, AND I GOT IT BACKWARDS (2026-08-18).

WHAT HAPPENED: PRs #8440 and #8450 duplicated three beads. I preferred #8440 partly because it touched tools/xray/spec/017-Test-Coverage-Matrix.md, the file rf2-91dfb names, and #8450 did not. I reported that as a checked fact.

IT WAS BACKWARDS. rf2-91dfb's ORIGINAL headline - 017:105 teaching digit tab-jump keys - had already been fixed by PR #8435 before either worker started. The bead was reopened by a merged-PR audit whose finding lives in DIFFERENT FILES: five present-tense sites still teaching that bare letters dispatch tabs, in 007, 018, static/shell.cljs and panel_registry.cljc. #8450 repaired all five. #8440 repaired none of them; its 017 edit at :153 is a stale six-tab roster, which is rf2-gui26's class, not rf2-91dfb's.

SO THE FILE-TOUCH TEST IS A PROXY AND IT BREAKS EXACTLY WHEN A BEAD HAS BEEN REOPENED. A reopening audit routinely moves the live finding off the file in the title. The title is the historical document; the newest text is the finding. I had that rule for BRIEFING and did not apply it to ADJUDICATING between two branches.

THE TEST THAT ACTUALLY WORKS: take the bead's NEWEST text, extract the concrete sites it names, and probe BOTH branches for those sites. That is what the losing worker did when I asked it, and it produced a five-row table settling the question in one pass.

AND ASK THE LOSER BEFORE CLOSING. I nearly closed #8450 on my own reasoning. Asking it for its delta cost one message and surfaced: the five-site repair, a fourth six-tab roster in tokens_cljs_test.cljc that BOTH censuses had missed, and an honest warning that its own CLJS changes had no green run behind them because I stopped it mid-gate. It recommended merging the OTHER PR. A worker asked for its delta will argue against itself accurately.

THIRD INSTANCE THAT DAY OF ONE ROOT CAUSE: the hygiene loop also REAPED THAT WORKER'S WORKTREE WHILE IT WAS LIVE, about 20 minutes in. Nothing was lost only because it had pushed immediately after its cherry-pick. Branch deleted on a stale survey, finisher dispatched on inferred death, worktree reaped on inferred death - all the mayor acting on an inference about a worker's state instead of evidence from the worker.

THE TRACKER CONTENDS WITH THE FLEET, AND THE MAYOR IS ONE OF THE CONTENDERS (2026-09-01, mayor session 9a).

WHAT HAPPENED: at six concurrent workers, three of the mayors own tracker commands hit the two-minute harness ceiling in one tick -- a beads-checkpoint export, a combined ready-plus-JSON listing, and a plain bd ready. The same commands take seconds when the fleet is idle. Nothing was broken; the Dolt database was simply serving six workers running bd show, bd history --json and bd close while the mayor asked for a full listing.

WHY IT MISLEADS: a timeout on a tracker read presents exactly like a tracker fault. The temptation is to re-run harder, or to conclude the export is stuck and reach for a recovery that rewrites state. Both are wrong and the second is dangerous. The checkpoint that appeared to hang had in fact COMPLETED -- exit 0, confirmed later -- and the state was already consistent.

THE CHEAP VERIFICATION THAT DOES NOT TOUCH THE DATABASE: compare row counts. git show HEAD:.beads/issues.jsonl piped to wc -l against wc -l on the working file. Equal counts plus a clean git status means the export is consistent and no checkpoint is owed, and neither read costs the database anything. That answered in one second what a re-run could not answer in three minutes.

PRACTICAL RULES: (1) at saturation, ask the tracker for ONE thing per command -- a combined listing plus a JSON dump in one shell is two queries and times out where each alone succeeds. (2) Treat a tracker timeout as CONTENTION until proven otherwise, never as corruption. (3) Never respond to an apparently-hung checkpoint by restoring an older export from git history: the Dolt database is the source of truth and that would time-travel the tracker.

GENERAL FORM: this is the gate-mechanics wedge rule -- a gate heavy enough that two cannot coexist wedges rather than fails -- applied to the TRACKER rather than to a build, and with the mayor as one of the competing processes rather than an observer of them. Saturating the fleet slows the instrument the mayor uses to decide what to dispatch next.

A WRAPPED LINE IN THE TRACKER'S DISPLAY IS NOT A WRAPPED LINE IN THE FILE — and predicting one search pass from another is not running it. My error, 2026-09-07, caught by a worker.

WHAT I ASSERTED, in a bead note AND in the dispatch brief built from it: "a line-oriented grep for `install-* is not in the closed roster` returns ZERO, because the clause wraps across lines; flattened it returns 1. That false zero reads exactly like 'already fixed'."

WHAT IS TRUE: the line-oriented grep returns 1. The clause sits entirely on ONE line of spec/api-manifest-metadata.edn (line 1193). Flattened also returns 1. There is no false zero and never was.

HOW I GOT IT WRONG, and this is the transferable part. I ran ONLY the flattened pass, saw 1, and asserted what the line-oriented pass would have returned. The three-pass rule exists precisely BECAUSE the passes disagree unpredictably — so it instructs you to RUN all three, and I used it to PREDICT two from one. A rule about instrument disagreement cannot be satisfied by reasoning about what the other instrument would say.

AND THE THING THAT MADE THE WRONG ANSWER FEEL OBSERVED: I had seen the phrase broken across lines — in `bd show`'s rendered output of my own note. The tracker hard-wraps long text for display. That wrapping is a property of the RENDERER, not of any file, and it is invisible as such because the output looks like content. So I mistook a display artefact for a file property and wrote it down as measured.

WHY A FALSE HAZARD COSTS MORE THAN NO HAZARD. A worker handed "the line-oriented pass reads zero here" spends real effort confirming a trap that does not exist, and — worse — may conclude the file has changed shape when its own measurement disagrees with the brief. This one was caught and reported. The general shape is that an over-warning is not free just because it errs toward caution.

THE RULE: never characterise a file's line structure from tracker output, editor rendering, or a report's quotation of it. Ask the FILE — grep -c on the path, or awk on the specific line number. And when a brief is about to claim that one search pass differs from another, run both; the claim IS the measurement, and one pass plus an inference is not it.

THE TRACKER SILENTLY REVERTS CLOSURES TO OPEN, REPEATEDLY, AND ONLY A PER-TICK AUDIT CATCHES IT (observed twice on 2026-08-07: 2 beads, then 5).

WHAT HAPPENS. Beads closed with a verified reason read OPEN again a few ticks later, with no action of mine in between. First occurrence reverted rf2-2rtt6.56 and rf2-2rtt6.62. Second reverted rf2-kqac1, rf2-drpa3.182.12, rf2-2rtt6.103, rf2-ketqy and rf2-cvvb7 — every one of which had a PR I could verify MERGED at the moment of re-closing.

WHY VERIFYING AT CLOSE TIME IS NOT ENOUGH. I verified each of these CLOSED immediately after closing. They reverted anyway. So the audit has to run EVERY tick against the full list of everything closed this session, not just the recent ones — the second wave included beads closed many ticks earlier.

HOW TO AUDIT SO THE AUDIT ITSELF DOES NOT LIE: key on the STABLE BEAD ID, never an internal row UUID (a re-import regenerates UUIDs and a UUID-keyed diff reports phantom losses), and read the STATUS FIELD rather than grepping the whole record (the word 'open' appears inside titles). 'bd show <id> | head -1 | grep -oE CLOSED|OPEN|DEFERRED' is enough.

WHAT MAKES RE-CLOSING CHEAP: the close REASON is the durable artefact. If it names the PR number and the concrete evidence, re-closing is a thirty-second job of verifying 'gh pr view <n> --json state' still reads MERGED and pasting the reason back. If the original close said only 'done', a revert costs a full re-investigation. Write close reasons for the revert you have not had yet.

THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE PROJECT KEEPS FINDING IN ITS OWN INSTRUMENTS: a state that reports success while the underlying fact has moved. Treat the tracker as untrusted for closure state, exactly as you treat a statusCheckRollup.

CHECKING WHETHER A WORKER COMMITTED .beads: a TREE diff manufactures a false positive. Ask the commit, not the trees. Measured 2026-08-22.

WHAT HAPPENED. Worker sliceclock's branch read "git diff --stat origin/main f77316d601" -> ".beads/issues.jsonl | 7 +----". My first reading was a durability violation: the one thing a worker must never commit, with a whole CLAUDE.md section and two recorded incidents behind it.

IT WAS BASE DRIFT. The worker branched at cc563fd8fb and origin/main had moved 2 commits ahead -- my own bead checkpoints. "git diff A B" compares TREES, so it reports the worker's older .beads snapshot as a difference the worker introduced. The commit touched ONE file, a 329-line pre-registration doc.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, run both directions on the same sha:
    git diff --stat origin/main SHA -- .beads/   -> 7 lines (3+/4-)   WRONG QUESTION
    git show --stat SHA -- .beads/               -> empty             RIGHT QUESTION

WHY THIS IS MORE THAN ORDINARY GIT LITERACY: the false positive fires on EVERY worker branch once the mayor has checkpointed twice, which is every branch older than about twenty minutes. So the natural check is not merely imprecise, it is reliably wrong IN THE ACCUSING DIRECTION -- and repeated false accusations train you to stop reading the one signal that catches the real thing.

SAME FAMILY AS the ahead-count trap the hygiene loop names: this repo rebases, so ancestry and ahead-count are both wrong, and patch-equivalence via git cherry is the fix. Both are TREE-COMPARISON answers to a question about AUTHORSHIP. When the question is "what did this commit do", ask the commit.

TRUE-CONCLUSION-DEAD-REASONING — a documented defect class, seen twice on 2026-07-19 and subtler than plain drift.

DEFINITION: a document states a correct conclusion resting on an inference that has since been invalidated. Nothing looks wrong — the conclusion checks out — so a reviewer confirms the conclusion and moves on. But the NEXT reader follows the stated reason, finds it false, and "corrects" the conclusion in the wrong direction. The rot is in the justification, not the claim.

INSTANCE 1 (rf2-0qsp5, #6386): spec/005-StateMachines.md derived :rf.machine/join-dispatch target protection FROM its REJECT-tier membership. Worker verdict: "The conclusion is true; the inference is precisely what the split invalidated." Preserving the reasoning would have re-merged the two fx policies the next time anyone extended it.

INSTANCE 2 (rf2-vxgfnd.188, #6391, worse): the canonical W1 rule table declared SEVEN verbs unavailable — ui/adapter, local, effect, ui/event, ui/handler, ui/render-fn, ui/dispatch-fn. ALL SEVEN SHIP, exported from ui.cljc. MIG-16/17/18 "this gates" conclusions stayed TRUE, but the reason inverted: from "the verb has not shipped yet" to "the decision belongs to the human". Retiering alone would have let the next reader check whether S3 shipped, find it had, and UNGATE RULES THAT MUST STAY GATED. The worker rewrote the reasons and left the tiers.

HOW TO CATCH IT: when reconciling a document against code, verify the DERIVATION, not just the conclusion. Ask "if the stated reason were false, would the conclusion change?" If yes and the reason IS false, the conclusion is correct by luck and the next edit will break it.
HOW TO FIX IT: rewrite the reason, keep the conclusion. Do NOT retier/restate/delete the conclusion just because its stated basis collapsed.

RELATED, SAME FAMILY: a bead PREDICTION can be wrong too. rf2-vxgfnd.188 own preliminary map predicted six rule retirements; ALL SIX were refuted against shipped code (one, R-X7, had NO DETECTOR AT ALL and became a new rule; R-S3 was missing the cursor WRITE side). A worker trusting the bead analysis would have deleted six live rules. The bead is authoritative about WHAT TO DO, never about WHAT IS TRUE — always re-verify its factual claims against the code.

ALSO: my brief framed 36-vs-34 rules as "one book has two rules the other lacks". Wrong — the books cut the same work at different GRANULARITIES (one by construct area, one by detector), many-to-many both ways, so the deliverable was a crosswalk not a diff. When two artefacts disagree on a COUNT, check whether they share a unit before assuming they disagree on content.

THE "IS THIS BEAD ALREADY DONE?" TRUNK SWEEP MUST READ COMMIT BODIES, NOT JUST SUBJECTS (measured 2026-09-07).

WHAT HAPPENED. The mayor's bulk done-check ran `git log origin/main --format='%h%x09%s'` and grepped
the result for every open bead id. rf2-kuky.5 returned ZERO hits, so the tick concluded the work had
not landed and dispatched a worker at it. The work HAD landed: PR #9346, commit f18aa19c7b, an
ancestor of origin/main. The commit SUBJECT is "refactor(egress): explicit :frame nil is sayable and
fails closed; rf/sensitive? fails closed" and names no bead at all — the id "rf2-kuky.5" appears only
in the commit BODY. `%s` cannot see a body, so the sweep was blind to it.

THIS FAILS OPEN AND IS SILENT. A zero reads as "the work is outstanding", which is the answer that
causes a dispatch, and nothing on screen distinguishes it from a correct zero. Re-running the sweep
with `%b` included immediately surfaced FOUR more open beads named on the trunk that the subject-only
form had missed, one of them (rf2-kuky.56) verified done at source minutes later.

THE FIX: `git log origin/main --since='<window>' --format='%H%x01%s%x01%b%x02'`, then flatten the
record separator so one commit is one line before grepping — a body is multi-line, so a naive
line-oriented grep over `%b` splits records and mis-attributes ids to neighbouring commits.

TWO SECOND-ORDER TRAPS MEASURED IN THE SAME PASS.
1. BEAD IDS PREFIX-MATCH EACH OTHER. A plain `grep -F rf2-kuky.2` also matches rf2-kuky.20, .21,
   .23 — the first run of this sweep reported "10 hits" for rf2-kuky.2 on that basis. Anchor with a
   trailing non-digit class, e.g. `rf2-kuky\.2[^0-9]`.
2. jq WRITES CRLF ON THIS BOX, so an id list piped from `bd list --json | jq -r '.[].id'` into a
   pattern file carries carriage returns that ride into the pattern. `tr -d '\r'` before building
   any pattern file. (Already recorded separately as item (e) of CLAUDE.md's instrument list; this
   is where it bites next.)

AND THE POINTER IS STILL NOT A CLOSURE. A body hit means the id was MENTIONED, which includes
cross-references, "discovered-from" notes and the very change the bead was filed against. Confirm in
the SOURCE that the symbol is gone or the text now reads correctly before closing anything. In this
same pass three of five new hits were mentions rather than deliveries.

TRUTHFUL-BUT-LATE vs FABRICATED — the discriminator for unfenced async writes. Established by the rf2-2amkm worker (#6410) when it RE-VERIFIED rather than inherited a judgement rf2-6pfpt (#6405) had left.

THE TEST: when a callback settles after its subject is gone, ask whether the value it writes is TRUE-BUT-STALE or FABRICATED-ABOUT-NOTHING.
  - TRUTHFUL-BUT-LATE: runner-events/run-step! emits an unfenced emit-trace! for an abandoned stepper session. The step REALLY RAN and REALLY produced that result; only the timing is wrong. #6410 checked every trace listener under tools/story/src and none consumes :rf.story.play/step. Verdict: LEAVE UNFENCED. Fencing it would mean inventing session identity for a public one-shot executor whose recorded verdict is already fenced caller-side.
  - FABRICATED: the a11y sites. (swap! run-state assoc frame-id :done) over a map the frame was dissoc-d from RESURRECTS the entry — measured 10/10 RED with 19 failures and ZERO ERRORS, so nothing throws. The phantom slot reads :done and the resurrected violations-by-frame entry beside it is exactly what browser/register-a11y-reader! serves to :rf.assert/a11y — A TORN-DOWN FRAME REPORTING A CLEAN VERDICT. Verdict: FENCE IT.
Same defect shape, opposite correct action. Do not blanket-fence every unfenced .then; ask what the write ASSERTS.

MECHANISM REFINEMENT worth copying: #6410 stamped the run token INTO the slot rather than beside it, so "existence and identity are one question with one answer, and every present and future clearing path revokes the claim with no side atom to keep in step". Strictly better than a parallel token map, which a new clearing path can silently fail to update.

⚠️ (inc nil) IS 1 ON CLJS. That is why this class never throws — it silently rebuilds state instead. Never test for it by expecting an exception; assert the slot is ABSENT and the status is the terminal value.

TWO PROSE SOURCES THAT AGREE WITH EACH OTHER ARE NOT EVIDENCE (2026-08-14, rf2-7cuns worker, self-caught).

WHAT IT CAUGHT IN ITS OWN DIFF. It wrote "188 digest-pinned fenced blocks" into a new declaration, having copied the figure from a workflow comment AND a script docstring. Its own words: "two prose sources that agree with each other, which is not evidence." IT THEN RAN THE CHECKER — 188 blocks across 25 pages, 177 Clojure, 34 verb sites — and only then kept the number.

AND THE NEAR-MISS PROVES THE POINT: the same script's docstring says "23 CHAPTERS" where the live run reports 25 PAGES. That tree already carries a stale count. Had it cited that one instead, two agreeing prose sources would have propagated a wrong figure into a third place.

WHY AGREEMENT IS WEAK EVIDENCE HERE: prose figures are COPIED, not derived. Two documents agreeing usually means one was copied from the other, or both from a third — so agreement measures propagation, not truth. THE ONLY EVIDENCE IS RUNNING THE THING.

THE COMPANION FAILURE, from the same evening: a worker's description of ANOTHER worker's diff was wrong, and I relayed it as fact. It reported deletions at specific lines; the PR's author measured its own diff as 20 added, 0 removed, 540 lines away. A WORKER'S ACCOUNT OF A THIRD PARTY'S WORK IS A CLAIM AT TWO REMOVES — weaker than its account of its own, which is already a claim.

THE RULE: never quote a count you did not derive, and never relay one worker's description of another's diff without saying whose reading it is. If it matters, read the diff.

TWO BRIEFING PREMISES OF MINE THAT WERE WRONG, found by the pre-alpha docs audit (2026-07-25):

1. 'spec/api-manifest.edn is the authority on what is public' — NOT TRUE for every artefact. re-frame.resources is MISSING from the generator's roster (implementation/scripts/api-manifest/.../gen.clj:140-148), so the manifest carries ZERO resources rows, and doc_api_check.clj:257-259 therefore gives docs/api/re-frame.resources.md (25 headings) NO COVERAGE AT ALL. DC-09 TWO-CLOCK ENVELOPE, MEASURED (rf2-drpa3.182.12, PR #7179, HeadlessChrome 147, dev build :optimizations :none goog.DEBUG true). Sustained semantic rate ~190/s at 0 dirty siblings, ~49/s at 200. 60 Hz crossing is comfortable to 50 siblings and breaks between 50 and 200; 120 Hz never clears p95 in a dev build; 240 Hz is unreachable because the BROWSER stops offering first, not because the framework refuses.

THREE STRUCTURAL FACTS worth reusing before re-measuring anything on this surface:
1. PEAK BACKLOG IS 1, at every offered rate and both sibling loads, with rf/dispatch (async). The setInterval callback IS the main thread, so overload manifests as OFFER LOSS at the host, never as a growing queue; latency stays bounded at one crossing and the settlement tail stayed <=5.4 ms even at 240 Hz requested against a 20 ms crossing. This is why no throttle/debounce/coalesce verb is warranted — the browser already back-pressures. CAVEAT: measured with a TIMER. Coalesced pointermove / pointerrawupdate bursts can deliver several events to one task and are the only shape that could exceed backlog 1; do not quote this for raw-pointer bursts without re-measuring.
2. THE EVENT HALF IS FLAT, THE COMMIT HALF SCALES. Splitting the window at the instant dispatch-sync returns: :event-ms (router, interceptors, reducer, app-db install, 300 subscription notifications) is 3-4 ms whether 1 or 201 cells moved; :commit-ms goes 0.4 -> 17.5 ms at ~0.085 ms per dirtied cell. An expensive crossing is expensive in React, not in re-frame — attribute before optimising.
3. WHERE YOU READ THE SUB COSTS MORE THAN HOW MUCH CHANGED. Reading a high-rate value in a view that ALSO builds a collection costs a CONSTANT 40-44 ms more than reading it one boundary down — independent of payload size (Vega 96 leaves 45.6->5.0 ms, Spread 900 leaves 63->18.8 ms) — while moving THREE FEWER DOM nodes. Same 'one leaf of app-db changed', 8-19x apart. Guidance: if a high-rate value must cross into app-db, read its subscription at the boundary that USES it.

EQUALITY IS FREE AND FREEHAND ALREADY ELIDES. Fresh-but-rf=-equal is indistinguishable from stable-reference (0.2-0.3 ms at 96 leaves, 0.4-0.6 at 900) and repaints nothing; a full structural walk of a 900-leaf map is under a millisecond. Behavior :update ran exactly 52 times for 52 changed crossings and ZERO times for stable or fresh-equal ones — elision is VALUE-based (rf=), not identity-based. Proved by counting, not by reading the runtime. No equality hook is warranted.

INSTRUMENT NOTES for the next perf bead in a browser:
* A COMPUTED-DURATION POSITIVE CONTROL DOUBLES AS A CONTENTION METER. A busy-wait of exactly 4.00 ms riding in every cell read p50 4.0 with overshoot never above 0.3 ms — which is what let the numbers be published without the usual 'other agents were running' caveat. On a loaded box it would have said so in every table simultaneously. Cheap, and it retires the standing wall-clock-is-unreliable worry per-run instead of per-repo.
* A COMPUTED-SIZE CONTROL CATCHES A KNOB THAT DOES NOT TURN. Predicted DOM mutation counts (host-only 1, fresh-equal 0, one-leaf k+1) matched measured at all 15 mode x rung combinations, and the driven arm independently reproduced exactly 201.0 per crossing. MutationObserver.takeRecords() answers SYNCHRONOUSLY, which is the only reason it can be read inside a flushSync-bracketed window.
* AN ARM WHOSE POINT IS THAT NOTHING CHANGES CANNOT BE VERIFIED BY NOTHING CHANGING. The fresh-equal arm is verified at the STORE (reference moved AND value equal), because an arm that silently did nothing would otherwise be the fastest arm in the table.
* ROTATING ARM ORDER FOUND A REAL FAULT: the first equality arm built its config from a FIXED generation, so a fresh-equal crossing following a one-leaf one was equal to nothing and failed its own read-back in 7 of every 10 samples. Build the comparison value from WHATEVER IS CURRENTLY IN THE STORE, and build it OUTSIDE the timed window.
* BOTH LADDER ORDERS: the only non-overlapping range tracked a monotonic round-1-to-4 warm-up present at EVERY rung in BOTH orders — drift, not order. Three warm-up samples per cell did not fully absorb first-round JIT.

actually graded. When nominating gates for a markdown edit, say WHICH HALF of the file each one
inspected, and whether the lines you changed were in that half.

If the read universe is unbounded, the filter is not incomplete — it is WRONG IN KIND, and every future addition to it is a false sense of coverage. Run alone: 13918 tests / 70176 assertions / 0 failures, PASS fast PR spine, captured exit 0.

ITS OWN WORDS, and this is the correction to my briefing: 'The two heavy gates cannot coexist rule applies to the spine itself, not just to peer workers — I'd been applying it only to other people's runs.' I brief that rule as a fence against PEERS. It is really a fence against CONCURRENCY, whoever owns it. A worker running two of its own gates in parallel to save wall-clock produces exactly the same corruption, and the failure is a bare crash with no summary — indistinguishable from a real regression until you re-run serially.

SO THE BRIEFED RULE SHOULD READ: run heavy gates ONE AT A TIME, including your own. If a run dies with no summary line, suspect cache contention before suspecting the change. This composes with the already-recorded rule that a killed shadow-cljs run leaves a CORRUPT .shadow-cljs producing phantom ReferenceErrors in unrelated namespaces — same cache, two ways to poison it.

TWO MAYOR ERRORS THE rf2-n4by4 WORKER CAUGHT, BOTH ABOUT MY BRIEFS (2026-07-26).

ERROR 1 — I SILENTLY RESOLVED A RULING THE BEAD HAD EXPLICITLY RESERVED. rf2-n4by4 said in as many words: "ENFORCEMENT NEEDS A RULING — do not pick one silently", and listed (a) mark-and-refuse versus (b) leave it to the spec. My brief supplied (a) as though it were settled. The worker followed the brief and FLAGGED THE DIVERGENCE, noting that per my own standing instruction the bead is authoritative over the brief.

That is the sharpest form of a mistake I make often: I put "the bead is authoritative over this brief, and tell me if they disagree" into every dispatch, which is right — and then write briefs that quietly overwrite the bead. The instruction only works if I read the bead for RESERVED QUESTIONS before writing the brief, not just for facts. A bead that says "needs a ruling" is addressed TO ME, and the honest brief either states the ruling AS a ruling ("I am ruling (a), here is why") or asks the worker to return the options. Silently picking one means the tracker never records that a decision was made, and the next reader cannot tell a considered choice from an oversight.

THE RULING ITSELF STANDS, and the reason is worth keeping: the failure is SILENT — :className arriving as :class is a DIFFERENT React prop, so the component gets no class and nothing reports it. But I could not have known the cost when I ruled, which is exactly why the ruling should have been visible.

The mutually-invalidating-test rule is real and has reddened the trunk before — but a bare token grep is not evidence FOR it. Before warning about a witness collision, check whether the match is the CONSTRUCT or merely the SUBSTRING, and whether the assertion pins the old behaviour or the new. Sixteenth instance this session of the same underlying error: a cheap proxy standing in for the real question.

AND THE FINDING MY BRIEF SHOULD HAVE CARRIED, which the worker found instead: THE REFUSAL MUST RUN BEFORE THE EXACTNESS LAW. A spread canonicalises "class" into the keyword :class, so inexact-host-prop-names sees a CLEAN call — exactness would PASS and the corruption would be the answer. Ordering, not presence, is what makes that guard work. Generalise: when adding a check to a pipeline of checks, ask what the earlier checks NORMALISE, because a normaliser upstream can launder exactly the defect you are trying to catch.

THE TWO:

AND THE WORKER'S ACTUAL FINDING IS BETTER THAN EITHER NUMBER. My brief asserted "adding a job takes the gap N to N+1". THAT IS FALSE AS A RULE. A job whose checker the SPINE ALREADY RUNS through an npm chain adds NO new gap — the gap counts what the spine cannot decide, and the spine already decides it. So the figure holds at 96 across the addition.

BUT IT HOLDS ONLY IF THE SPINE_LANES ENTRY LANDS WITH THE JOB. The worker proved that entry load-bearing by rebuilding the map with the lane removed in memory: WITH the lane 96, WITHOUT it 98 — because the job has TWO steps, not one. The same is true of the three sibling jobs, which is why none of them moved the figure either.

SO THE RULE TO BRIEF IS: adding a CI job changes the fast-spine gap only if the spine cannot already decide its checker. If it can, add the SPINE_LANES entry in the same PR and the figure is unchanged — and if you omit that entry the figure rises by the job's STEP COUNT, not by one.

TWO VACUOUS-PASS TRAPS WHEN MOVING TESTS UNDER A PRODUCTION GATE (rf2-d2841, PR #7142). Both make a suite report GREEN while proving nothing, and neither is visible in a passing run. (1) A NEGATIVE trace assertion — `empty?` / `not-any?` over a trace ring — passes automatically under `-Dre-frame.debug=false` because the ring is empty BY DESIGN. It must move INSIDE the dev-only guard with the positive assertions, not be left outside as 'posture-independent'. Same for any 'no :rf.error/... was emitted' read. (2) A namespace that is 100% dev instrumentation (trace-listener-*, trace-test, db-pending-trace-test, sub-dispose-trace-test) has NO semantic residue: guarding it wholesale and removing its exclusion-roster line makes the lane report green for a namespace that EXECUTED NOTHING. GENERAL RULE: when a gate's whole point is that instrumentation is absent, any assertion whose subject is that same absence is worthless in that posture — check what each assertion would do if its subject simply never existed.

A TWO-VALUED PROBE CONFLATES 'REJECTED' WITH 'CRASHED', SO TWO VALIDATORS THAT BOTH EXPLODE AGREE (rf2-dhl4d, 2026-08-03).

THE MECHANISM, and it is the best fail-open diagnosis this project has produced. A viz<->engine parity ratchet compared two validators by asking each "do you accept this definition?" — a BOOLEAN. On CLJS, engine-accepts? wrapped the call in (catch :default ... false). So when the engine raised a host ClassCastException on a non-Named key, the probe recorded FALSE — indistinguishable from a clean, documented rejection. The viz side crashed the same way. TWO VALIDATORS THAT BOTH EXPLODE AGREE, and the ratchet stayed green over a live crash in a security gate.

THE FIX IS THE SHAPE, NOT THE CASE: make the probe THREE-VALUED — :accept / :reject / :host-throw — plus a definition-validation-is-total assertion. Proof it now sees the divergence: (engine :reject, viz :host-throw).

GENERALISE IT. Any comparison harness that reduces its subjects to a boolean, or that catches broadly and maps the catch onto one of the two legitimate outcomes, is fail-open BY CONSTRUCTION — parity ratchets, differential tests, golden-file comparators, A/B benchmark agreement checks. Ask of every such harness: WHAT DOES IT RECORD WHEN THE SUBJECT CRASHES? If the answer is "the same thing as one of the normal outcomes", it cannot see the failure class it exists to catch.

ALSO FROM THE SAME BEAD, a distinct defect class worth naming separately: THE ERROR PATH ITSELF THREW. A (pr-str offending) in the diagnostic message reached an arbitrary object's toString, so a throwing-toString key DESTROYED THE FAILURE BEING DESCRIBED. A validator that rejects correctly but explodes while explaining why is still broken on hostile input. Exercise the diagnostic path with the same forged corpus as the validation path.

AND: the bead named ONE defect site; there were TWO (an inline copy elsewhere in the same file). A worker fixing only the cited line would have shipped a half-fix that passed its own new test. Grep for the PATTERN, not the line number.

Untracking a gitignored-but-force-added path via 'git rm --cached' in a SEPARATE worker worktree then merging to main DELETES the files from the mayor checkout's disk on pull — because the resulting commit is a plain file-deletion, and 'git pull' removes working-tree copies of files a commit deletes (the --cached keep-on-disk only protected the worker's tree, which didn't have the files). Recovery: 'git show <pre-untrack-sha>:<path> > <path>' to restore each file as untracked local content (they're gitignored so git ignores them). "I specified a verification that measured the DEFECT'S SYMPTOM rather than the document invariant, so it went green on a repair that corrupted code blocks — and my second check reddened correct repairs."

**MEASURED 2026-09-10 on rf2-tdlg.** I filed a bead and wrote a dispatch brief that prescribed both
the repair and how to verify it. Both instructions were wrong, in opposite directions, and a worker
caught both.

**The repair I prescribed corrupts the artefact.** For an under-indented fence inside a list item I
said "add columns to the opening AND the closing fence, both lines". `pymdownx.superfences` dedents
a fenced block by the FENCE's indent, and the content sat at the same indent as the fence — so
moving only the fences leaves the body relatively dedented and the info string leaks into it
(measured: `[rf/frame-provider …]` became `clojure` on one line then the form on the next). The
correct repair shifts the WHOLE BLOCK, preserving relative indent.

**And my verification could not see it, because it measured the SYMPTOM.** I told the worker to
check that the `<ol>`+`<ul>` count DROPS by the stated amount. It does — under the broken repair
too. The list rejoins either way; what differs is the code block. A worker following my own
instrument would have watched the number confirm a corrupted document.

**My second check failed the other way — it reds a CORRECT repair.** I said the `<li>` multiset
must be UNCHANGED and called a moving set "a red flag". But each repaired item legitimately GAINS
the code block it should always have owned, so the worker's first run read `False` on all ten
files. The working instrument is `<li>` text with `<pre>` content EXCLUDED.

**Why:** I designed the check around the thing the defect SHOWS (a split list) instead of around
what must stay TRUE across the edit (every document unchanged except the intended move). A symptom
recovers under a wrong repair; an invariant does not.

**How to apply:** when specifying verification for a mechanical repair, write down what must be
INVARIANT, not just what must CHANGE. For a whitespace-only doc repair the working set is four
properties, not two: list-element count drops; `<li>` count unchanged; `<li>` text excluding
`<pre>` unchanged; `<pre>` count and code text unchanged. And prefer `git diff -w` empty as the
outer guard for a reindent — it is the one check that sees a corrupted body.

Related: [[mayor-judgement-good-counts-bad-label-the-unverified]], [[mayor-briefs-ran-three-times-too-long]].

VERIFY A CONFLICT RESOLUTION STRUCTURALLY, NOT BY EYE — prove the prefix relationship (2026-08-14, rf2-guidepin worker).

THE SITUATION. Two branches both appended a checker to the same npm chain in implementation/package.json. Either wholesale resolution shipped a real defect: --theirs silently un-gates the incoming worker's whole deliverable, --ours drops a gate that now has a required CI job and reds main. Both changes were correct and independent.

THE TECHNIQUE THAT MADE THE MERGE PROVABLE rather than plausible:

  main chain: 12 commands   resolved: 14 commands
  resolved.startswith(main) == True
  delta == the two commands I added, and nothing else

That is a PROOF that nothing of main's was dropped. On a fourteen-command single line, "looks right" is not evidence — the eye cannot reliably diff a long shell chain, and that is exactly the shape where a wholesale resolution hides.

GENERALISE IT: after resolving any conflict in a LIST — an npm chain, a needs: array, a roster, a require block, a nav section — assert the relationship rather than reading it. Either side's content must appear in the result; compute the set difference and check it is exactly what you intended to add. A resolution you can state as an equation is one you can defend.

TWO COMPANION CHECKS FROM THE SAME PASS, both cheap and both catching real risk:
  - `git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD | grep ^.github/` returning EMPTY proved the branch never touched workflows, which made a whole class of suspected conflict structurally impossible. Establish what your branch CANNOT have conflicted on before hunting for what it did.
  - It confirmed main had NOT touched the guide tree, so its 188 digest rows were still valid. A guide edit on main would have staled every one of them silently. After a rebase, re-check the inputs your gate pins, not just that your gate passes.

AND RE-RUN GATES AFTER RESOLVING, INCLUDING THE DISCRIMINATION. A green taken on a tree that no longer exists is not evidence. That worker re-proved its digest gate by inserting one character and taking a red naming the block, then hash-verifying the restore.

VERIFY A SABOTAGE RESTORE WITH git hash-object, NOT sha256sum - CRLF TRANSLATION MAKES A CORRECT RESTORE LOOK FAILED (2026-08-13, found by the navfence-cluster worker).

The method's rule is right: verify a restore by hashing the bytes, never by reading git diff, because 'unchanged' and 'never applied' produce the same diff. But the INSTRUMENT matters and sha256sum is the wrong one on this checkout.

WHAT HAPPENED: a worker planted a fault, ran the gate red, restored, and 'sha256sum -c' FAILED on a restore that was actually correct. Git's LF->CRLF conversion rewrote the working file during a rebase checkout AFTER the baseline hash was taken. The bytes on disk genuinely differed; the CONTENT did not.

USE git hash-object against the committed blob instead. It normalises line endings the same way git does, so it compares what git compares. Both reads agreed at c37e900... where sha256sum had disagreed.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: a false 'restore failed' is not merely noise. The worker's next move is to re-apply the restore, or to doubt the whole sabotage result - and the sabotage result is the deliverable. An instrument that misreports is the same defect class as the hollow gate it was being used to prove.

Pair it with the other half already recorded: a hash proves the SOURCE changed, not that the RUNTIME saw it. A fault outside the build's module graph compiles into nothing and the sabotage run comes back green for an unrelated reason.

A STATUS AUDIT KEYED ON A BARE ID STRING READS ANOTHER RECORD'S STATUS (2026-08-13, my own tool misreporting).

WHAT HAPPENED: verifying that five beads had really been deferred, I grepped the committed export for the bead id in quotes:

  grep '"rf2-hic-092"' .beads/issues.jsonl | grep -o '"status":"[a-z]*"' | head -1

It reported rf2-hic-092 as CLOSED. The bead was in fact DEFERRED - bd show said so, with the deferral date. The grep had matched the FIRST LINE CONTAINING that id string, which was a DIFFERENT bead whose dependency list or note text mentions rf2-hic-092. I then read that other record's status as this bead's.

Four of the five happened to be right, which is worse than all five being wrong: a spot-check would have passed.

THE FIX IS ONE CHARACTER OF PRECISION - key on the id FIELD:

  grep '"id":"rf2-hic-092"'

WHY THIS IS THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THE METHOD ALREADY NAMES. mayor-hygiene.md warns that gh pr list --search 'head:<branch>' substring-matches and returns a SIBLING branch's PR, so you must ask for headRefName and compare equality yourself. This is that rule in a second place. The general form: AN ID IS NOT A SEARCH TERM. Any tracker, VCS or CI query that accepts a bare string will substring-match it, and the record it returns will look entirely plausible because it is a real record - just not yours.

AND NOTE WHICH DIRECTION IT FAILED. It reported a live bead as closed, i.e. it manufactured a false alarm rather than hiding a real one. Reversed - reporting a closed bead as open - it would have sent a worker at finished work. Both are available from the same bug.

THE DISCIPLINE: a verification tool that misreports is the same defect class as the bug it was written to catch. Cross-check the export against the database (bd show) rather than trusting either alone; here the disagreement between the two is what exposed the grep.

A ruling on B can retire A's entire reason for existing, and nothing on A will say so — dependency edges carry no news. The direction that bites is downstream-to-upstream, which is the direction nobody reads.

WHAT THE MERGED-PR AUDIT REOPENS, MEASURED — AND IT IS A DEFECT IN MY CLOSE REASONS, NOT IN THE AUDIT (2026-07-26).

THE MEASUREMENT. Of the open beads carrying audit-reopen language, the largest cluster by type is TEST / FIXTURE / GATE beads — 7 of 16, ahead of donor (4), spec-prose (3) and privacy (3). All 16 name an explicit residual.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is clean. Gate beads I closed today WITH a mutation proof written into the close reason have stayed closed: rf2-4hc9p (3 mutation references), rf2-wns8d (8), rf2-xwa4n (3), rf2-kqxe6.25 (4). Gate beads that got REOPENED carry ZERO mutation references in their notes: rf2-wq17m (0), rf2-as6bg (0). Small n, but the mechanism is obvious once seen.

WHY IT HAPPENS. A gate bead asks "arm this check". The audit asks "does the check CATCH the thing". A close reason that says the job was added, the roster was widened, or the suite is green gives the audit NOTHING TO VERIFY AGAINST — so it reopens and writes the residual itself. A close reason carrying the planted defect, the gate reddening, the restore and the green gives it the verification already done, and it stays closed.

THE RULE: when closing a gate, fixture, census, lane or CI-arming bead, the close reason MUST carry the mutation proof — the specific defect planted, the observed red with counts, the restore, the green. "The job runs" is not "the job catches". If a worker did not supply one, that is a reason to ask for it BEFORE closing, not to close and let the audit find it.

CORROBORATING EVIDENCE FROM TODAY, all of it the same shape: rf2-wns8d proved a shipped deftest was a TAUTOLOGY by mutating the production wrapper and watching the deftest stay GREEN. rf2-4hc9p proved the pre-repair bijection gate was green on all seven planted defects and red on the one prose fixture — exactly inverted. The ci-arming worker found engine_grammar_parity_test.cljc armed on two lanes and matching NEITHER build ns-regexp, so it ran nowhere. In every case the arming was real and the catching was absent, which is precisely the distinction a close reason must record.

SECOND-ORDER POINT WORTH KEEPING: this means the audit reopen rate is partly MY OUTPUT, not just its diligence. Roughly one reopen per merged PR looked like an immovable property of running an audit; a meaningful share of it is gate beads closed on arming rather than on catching. That is fixable from my side.

WHEN A GUARD IS WARRANTED UNDER "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" — the principle that reconciles three decisions I made today (2026-07-26).

The three look contradictory on their face:
  1. rf2-bk7z5 — CLOSED, refusing to validate :role against its documented closed set.
  2. rf2-8o66x — DEFERRED, refusing a performance regression gate.
  3. The empty-export finding — FILED, asking for a row floor in the pre-commit hook.

Two refusals and one request, all under the same posture. The distinguishing principle is not size, cost or priority. It is:

  A GUARD IS WARRANTED WHEN THE FAILURE IS SILENT AND HAS ALREADY HAPPENED. IT IS NOT WARRANTED WHEN THE PROGRAMMER CAN SEE THE FAILURE, OR WHEN THE FAILURE CANNOT OCCUR.

Applied:
  1. :role validation — the failure CANNOT OCCUR. Every producer is in-namespace; no caller can pass an invalid role. Enforcing it adds a failure mode, a message to maintain and a test to keep green, and catches nothing. That is a nag-diagnostic.
  2. The perf gate — the failure would be NOISE, not signal. The no-substrate floor drifted 37% across rounds, larger than most effects being measured, so the gate would red on nothing. And a false red is expensive here precisely because the standing rule is that a failing test on a touched surface is never a flake.
  3. The row floor — the failure IS SILENT AND HAS HAPPENED TWICE, six weeks apart, by the same mechanism. An empty tracker with a CLEAN git status is exactly what a programmer cannot see. That is not distrust; it is the only way the fact becomes visible at all.

SO "TRUST THE PROGRAMMER" IS NOT "ASSUME NOTHING GOES WRONG". It is: DO NOT GUARD AGAINST WHAT THE PROGRAMMER CAN ALREADY SEE. A loud crash needs no guard — it is already a signal. A wrong value that renders visibly needs no guard. What needs a guard is the state that looks correct: an empty file with a clean status, a gate green on a defect it was built to catch, a test armed on two lanes and selected by neither.

THE COROLLARY IS THE ONE I HAVE BEEN UNDER-USING: this principle is also a REJECTION criterion with teeth. Most proposed guards fail it, because most proposed failures are either impossible or loud. Ask which of the three cases a proposal is in before pricing it, and the answer usually decides the bead without further analysis.

AND IT EXPLAINS WHY THE ERGONOMICS CLAUSE IS A DETECTOR RATHER THAN A BRAKE: a bad diagnostic is the same defect class inverted. The failure IS visible, but it points somewhere useless — an author told to add a key the source already has, or handed a JSON encoding error naming a reified malli class. That is a signal that lies rather than a signal that is missing, and both are worth fixing where a merely-absent convenience is not.

WHEN A PREDICATE HAS TWO OPERANDS, VARY BOTH - a mayor's own error, recorded against himself on rf2-uo5f (2026-09-07) and preserved here because that bead is decay-eligible.

WHAT HAPPENED. The attribution guard's rule 3 decides whether a PR-body line is an attribution marker. It has TWO operands: the SENTENCE shape and the URL at the end of it. The mayor measured ELEVEN shapes, concluded the behaviour was already correct and that only a regression test was missing, and briefed accordingly. The blind spot was systematic: every one of the eleven shapes VARIED THE SENTENCE AND USED THE TOOL'S OWN HOST IN THE URL. The next worker pinned exactly what had been measured, then constructed the case that had never been built - a citation URL whose PATH carried the word but whose HOST did not, including a link to CLAUDE.md itself - and it was a live false positive.

WHY ELEVEN CASES FELT LIKE ENOUGH: they were eleven cases along ONE axis. Coverage counted by the number of examples looks thorough; coverage counted by the number of operands exercised was 1 of 2. A count of cases is not a measure of coverage when the cases are collinear.

THE RULE. Before concluding a predicate is correct, enumerate its OPERANDS and confirm each has been varied at least once with the others held. This is the same family as the standing "a control proves your instrument works, not that it is the right instrument", and as "a control must share every feature of the target, at once, because a control that matches on the axis it shares says nothing about the axis it does not" - but it is stated over the SUBJECT rather than over the instrument, which is the reading that was missing.

THE COST WHEN IT IS MISSED: a whole extra repair round. rf2-uo5f took FOUR rounds on one detector, and its close reason records that every round after the first was caused by a brief that was right about the mechanism and silent about a qualifier. The same shape recurs on rf2-z5lv, four rounds on one gate for the same reason.

WHERE A FINDING BELONGS WHEN ITS PREMISE IS AN OPEN RULING (2026-07-25, articulated by the R6 worker and worth adopting): a finding whose premise depends on how an OPEN P1 gets ruled belongs on the PR, NOT in the tracker, until that ruling lands.

Concrete case: R6's guide audit found seven canonical recipes omitting an explicit {:sensitive ...} map and recorded the roster on its PR rather than filing beads. rf2-kqxe6.20 then shipped option A — the framework retains its own carrier classification — and the finding DISSOLVED COMPLETELY: those seven recipes had been describing the correct spelling all along; the framework was what needed fixing. Had the roster been beaded, the tracker would now hold a bead instructing people to add boilerplate that spec/012 and the auth how-to explicitly FORBID.

So the test is not 'is this finding real?' but 'is this finding real under every live ruling?'. If the answer depends on a pending decision, park it on the PR where it dies quietly if the ruling moots it, instead of in the tracker where it becomes durable instruction. check_thrown_error_messages.py: `#?@` IS A READER ERROR ONLY AT THE TOP LEVEL, AND THE WALKER MUST NOT CONSUME IT ANYWHERE ELSE. Preserved from rf2-z5lv's close reason (PR #9518, 2026-09-08, the FOURTH round on this one gate), which is decay-eligible. This is the invariant a fifth round is most likely to break.

THE INVARIANT. Reader-conditional SPLICING (`#?@`) is illegal only where the reader is not part-way through a collection - i.e. at the TOP level. Inside a collection it is legal. The gate's form-walker RE-ENTERS ITSELF on `do` bodies and on reader-conditional arms, so a consume-`#?@` branch written without a position flag fires where it must not. The repair is `_top_level_forms(masked, *, at_reader_top_level=True)`, read by `#?@` alone, with BOTH recursive entries HARDCODING `False` - a `do` body and a `(:clj ... :cljs ...)` arm list are each a list the reader is part-way through, which is exactly where splicing is legal. Three lines of behaviour change.

THE CASE THAT JUSTIFIES THE WHOLE ROUND, AND WHICH A JVM-ONLY ORACLE CALLS DEAD: `(do #?@(:cljs [...]))` was a live false red, and that shape is how this tree ships `#?(:cljs (def frame-root ...))`. EDITING THIS TREE WITH A PYTHON HEREDOC CORRUPTS ANY NEWLY-INTRODUCED NON-ASCII CHARACTER, SILENTLY (2026-09-03, measured by worker vocabname-a).

Python's default encoding on Mike's Windows box is cp1252, not UTF-8. A heredoc edit that WRITES an em-dash emits a lone 0x97 byte — invalid UTF-8 — into a file whose existing em-dashes are correct UTF-8. It renders as a replacement character and nothing catches it: 'git diff --check' exits 0, the linters pass, the suite passes.

THE ASYMMETRY IS WHY IT HIDES: text mode ROUND-TRIPS pre-existing non-ASCII harmlessly, so a worker that edits a file full of em-dashes sees them survive and concludes encoding is fine. Only NEWLY INTRODUCED characters corrupt. So the bug appears exactly when you add prose, never when you edit around it.

REMEDY: write the file in BINARY mode with explicit UTF-8 byte sequences (an em-dash is \xe2\x80\x94), or stick to ASCII in generated prose. VERIFY with 'od -c' on the changed region — not by reading the diff, which renders the corruption as a plausible-looking glyph. Restore from the committed blob and verify by 'git hash-object' if you find one.

SAME FAMILY AS THE CRLF NO-OP, AND BOTH BITE THE SAME EDIT PATH: this tree is CRLF, so a prose edit anchored on LF silently matches nothing and the edit reports success having changed nothing. Both failures are invisible in tool output and both are caught only by re-reading the file's BYTES afterwards. Treat 'edit prose in this repo' as requiring a byte-level re-read every time.

A WITNESS DERIVED FROM THE FIX INHERITS THE FIX'S BLIND SPOTS — five instances in one session (2026-08-10/11, hicasso).

THE SHAPE: a test or table whose STATED SCOPE EXCEEDS THE CASES IT ACTUALLY DRIVES. Each was green, each was honest, each claimed more than it checked.

1. rf2-hic-020 — a runtime/kit parity table claiming both arms of the raw escape, driving only the VALID raw component.
2. rf2-hic-007 — a completeness test claiming all six constructor fields unforgeable, running only where declaring! had already supplied real values; outside every extent the guarantee did not hold.
3. rf2-hic-012 — a comment recording the EXPECTED result as though it were the measured one, contradicted by the very row it annotated.
4. rf2-hic-021 — a round-trip check whose both directions ranged over ids THAT EXIST, so thirteen taught refusals with no id at all satisfied it VACUOUSLY (fail-open).
5. rf2-hic-022 — a shadow-detection walker whose letfn arm reads [nm params] and collects params only when the second node is a VECTOR; in multi-arity letfn it is a LIST, so every arity is missed. PR body and README both claimed letfn was covered.

WHY IT RECURS, and it is not carelessness: the witness is written FROM the fix, so it drives the shapes the author had in mind while fixing. The shapes that break it are exactly the ones the author did not think of — the same set. Test-after-fix is structurally biased toward passing.

THE COUNTERMEASURE, now standing in briefs: DERIVE THE WITNESS FROM THE GRAMMAR OF THE THING, NOT FROM THE FIX. Enumerate the legal shapes of the construct (for letfn: single-arity vector, multi-arity lists, docstring/prepost variants) and drive each. Require the PR body to state which shapes of the grammar were driven AND which were not — the second list is the valuable one, and writing it is what surfaces the gap.

SISTER RULE: see sweep-generator-defines-reachable-failure-directions — a generator's excluded shapes make a whole error DIRECTION invisible. Same disease at a different scale: coverage is defined by what the instrument can express, not by how much of it you ran.

A DEFECT-WITNESS TEST AND ITS FIX ARE MUTUALLY INVALIDATING — merging both without flipping the witness REDS MAIN, in either order. Cost a P0 red-on-main on 2026-07-24.

THE MECHANISM: a validation pilot reproduces a known hazard and writes it down as a LIVE TEST asserting the CURRENT (broken) behaviour. A separate slice FIXES that hazard. Each PR is green against a main lacking the other. Merge both and the witness test fails, because the defect it documents no longer exists.

THE CONCRETE CASE: the dropdown pilot independently reproduced the ref-composition hazard and shipped `a-behavior-and-a-top-layer-state-on-one-element-lose-a-ref` — a test that PASSES ONLY WHILE THE BUG IS PRESENT. I merged the pilot, then merged the ref-composition fix, and main went red with 2 failures. Every other gate stayed green, so it read like a mystery regression in a slice that had been CLEAN as a PR.

⚠️ WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH A MEMORY IS THAT I HAD ALREADY IDENTIFIED THE PATTERN AND FAILED TO APPLY IT. Days earlier I wrote into a different brief: "both pilots assert the current REFUSAL in a test, so the blocked cell re-opens loudly. THOSE ASSERTIONS WILL START FAILING WHEN YOU SUCCEED — update them deliberately as part of this slice." I understood it for the compiled-browser refusal and did not carry it to the very next fix I merged. Recognising a hazard in one place does not transfer it to another unless it becomes a CHECK.

THE CHECK, now standing — BEFORE MERGING ANY FIX, ASK: does a merged test currently ASSERT THE DEFECT THIS FIXES? If yes, the flip belongs in the SAME PR as the fix, or main goes red the moment both are in.
  git grep -l "<hazard keyword>" implementation/**/test/
Pilot and validation suites are the usual home, because documenting current-state honestly is exactly what they are FOR.

THE REPAIR IS A FLIP, NOT A DELETE, and it has three parts:
  1. Assert the FIXED behaviour positively (both participants ran), never loosen to tolerate either outcome — that discards the only coverage of the combination.
  2. RENAME the test. A name asserting the opposite of its body is a trap for the next reader.
  3. Sweep for SIBLING witnesses in the same suite rather than discovering them one merge at a time.

⚠️ AND THE DIAGNOSTIC LESSON: the failure looked like a regression in the fix. The worker got it right by READING CI OWN LOG for the failing test NAME and MESSAGE — the name said "lose-a-ref" and the message said "one of the two refs was lost", which is the test DOCUMENTING a defect, not detecting one. A test name that describes a BUG rather than a PROPERTY is the tell. My own grep for the failure lines used a pattern chosen before I knew what the output looked like and returned only the namespace roster — capture the log to a file and read it.

GENERAL FORM: this WILL recur wherever validation pilots run alongside active development, which is the whole point of running them. It is a property of the arrangement, not a mistake by either author.

READ A WORKER'S LIVENESS CLOCK IN ITS OWN METADATA DIRECTORY, NOT AT <worktree>/.git -- AND ALWAYS PRINT THE DATE (2026-08-23, two sweeps wrong on the first, one on the second).

TRAP 1 -- THE PATH. In a LINKED git worktree, .git is a FILE containing "gitdir: <path>", not a directory. So "find <worktree>/.git -maxdepth 1 -type f -printf %T@" measures the mtime of that one-line pointer and reports it as the worker's metadata clock. It fails quiet: a plausible timestamp comes back, no error. MEASURED: on worktree pr-audit-8445 the wrong form read 2026-08-23 03:13:05 while the real gitdir clock was 21:14:02 -- an 18-hour error, in the direction that reads as DEATH. I nearly recorded a live, actively-fetching worker as quiescent.

RESOLUTION: gd=$(git -C "$wt" rev-parse --git-dir); find "$gd" -type f -printf '%TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS %f\n' | sort -r | head. For a linked worktree that resolves to <main>/.git/worktrees/<name>/, holding that worktree's OWN FETCH_HEAD, HEAD, index and ORIG_HEAD.

TRAP 2 -- THE FORMAT. Printing %TH:%TM without %TY-%Tm-%Td makes a four-week-old file read as tonight. MEASURED: three frozen husks printed "20:45" beside a live worker's "22:07" in the same table, and the 20:45 was 2026-07-25. The conclusion survived only because the number contradicted an earlier reading and I re-measured with dates. In a liveness table -- where the whole question is how old something is -- a bare time is not a timestamp. ALWAYS carry the date.

WHICH FILE ANSWERS WHAT, measured on pr-audit-8445:
* FETCH_HEAD -- moves on every fetch, so it is the POLLING clock. Movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration; stillness proves nothing. Read it twice 30-60s apart.
* index -- moves when the worker actually stages work. Its index wrote at 11:41:02 and the commit "chore(beads): audit PR #8721" landed at 11:43:26, two minutes later. That gap VALIDATES index-mtime as the "is it producing?" clock, distinct from the fetch clock.

THE METHOD TREE ALREADY SAYS THE FIRST HALF, better than I was practising it: the fetch-head file lives in "that item's OWN metadata directory, which each linked worktree gets its own copy of", and "movement is proof of life and needs no corroboration". Both failures were mine, not the document's, so the repair is this memory rather than more text in the tree.

DO NOT confuse the mayor's .git/FETCH_HEAD with the worker's. Both move; only the worker's proves the WORKER is alive. Check the path you actually measured.

MEASURING WHETHER A WORKER IS ALIVE: compare the TIP REVISION ID, never a commit count (2026-08-13, corrected same day by an audit).

BE PRECISE ABOUT WHICH COUNT — the first version of this memory was wrong and the error reached main:
  git rev-list --count <branch>              counts EVERY reachable commit. Measured 21677.
                                             REBASING ONTO AN ADVANCED TRUNK MAKES THIS GROW. Not invariant.
  git rev-list --count origin/main..<branch> the AHEAD count. Measured 3.
                                             INVARIANT under rebase — the same commits are replayed.

The ahead count is the one a mayor naturally reads, and it is the one that misleads.

WHAT MOVES AND WHAT DOES NOT, under rebase:
  ahead count        NO
  %ar author date    NO
  %cr committer date YES
  tip revision id    YES

So record the tip id each tick and compare ids. Committer date is a usable second signal.

AN UNCHANGED TIP AUTHORISES NOTHING ON ITS OWN. That half is load-bearing: it is what stopped a healthy worker being called stranded across two ticks. The next step after an unchanged tip is to MESSAGE, and the reply shape is the real read — 'queued for delivery' means alive, 'had no active task; resumed from transcript' means idle.

SECOND TRAP IN THE SAME MEASUREMENT: do NOT read FETCH_HEAD after a fetch whose exit code you suppressed. Linked worktrees share one .git and therefore one FETCH_HEAD, so a raced or failed fetch leaves a stale value that reads as fresh. Prefer 'git ls-remote --heads origin refs/heads/worker/*' — one command, no shared state, no exit code to check.

WHEN TWO AGENTS DISAGREE ABOUT A COMMIT'S AGE, suspect two clocks before suspecting an error. One reported 75 seconds where another read 43 minutes; one read committer date, the other author date. Neither misread.

WORKER LIVENESS (Windows mayor loop): TaskList can return 'No tasks found' for background agents launched in a PRIOR turn even while they are actively running, AND their output-file mtime does NOT advance during a run (transcript flush is buffered). Both gave false 'dead' signals — a realm worker that TaskList showed as absent + mtime static for 9min actually completed a 624s run. NEVER infer a worker is dead from TaskList/mtime; NEVER recycle/--force-remove a worker's worktree on that basis (it clobbers live workers mid-edit). The ONLY reliable liveness signal is the completion/kill <task-notification>. To recycle, wait for that notification or confirm via a pushed branch with the expected commits.
