That works for the build, and then post-merge hygiene ran git worktree remove, which FOLLOWED the junction and emptied the mayor's REAL implementation/node_modules to 0 entries - breaking every local build in the repo. Repair is cheap and deterministic: cd <mayor>/implementation && npm ci (exit 0, restores the canary 101 entries; verify react + shadow-cljs are present). TWO fixes, both needed: (1) the WORKER should cmd /c rmdir the junction as its last act before reporting done, not leave it for hygiene; (2) HYGIENE must cmd /c rmdir <wt>/implementation/node_modules BEFORE git worktree remove, and re-check the mayor canary (~101) after each removal batch. This is the second recorded instance of the same class.

Worker path-leak mechanism (CONFIRMED 2026-07-17, rf2-r09qj + flagged by rf2-klyw5): a subagent that Reads MAYOR-checkout absolute paths during exploration can have its SUBSEQUENT Edit tool-calls carry that mayor path — so edits land in the mayor checkout, NOT the worktree. Invisible in the worker's OWN git status (the worktree looks clean); visible only from the mayor side. MITIGATION that works: the boundary-block's post-write BOTH-TREES check catches it — the worker self-recovers (git checkout-restore the mayor file, copy completed work into the worktree, verify mayor clean). HARDEN BRIEFS: instruct workers to Read AND Edit only worktree-absolute paths (never the mayor checkout, even for exploration reads), re-verify rev-parse per edit, and run the both-trees check after the first edit + any new file. Mayor-side detection: 'git status --short | grep -v .beads' in the mayor checkout should be empty; a stray modified file there = a live leak (capture the diff, don't blind-revert if the worker may be mid-recovery). This is a REAL Agent-subagent mechanism, distinct from the Workflow args-undefined misdiagnosis.

Worker PR-creation hang gotcha (2026-06-09): a worker (B6/vzld77) completed + committed + pushed its work, then hung ~1h LOOPING on 'gh pr create' with a heredoc body containing backticks/parens (bash kept mis-parsing). Mayor salvaged by opening the PR from the pushed branch. LESSON: in worker briefs, tell workers to create the PR with a SIMPLE body or '--body-file', avoid backticks/parens/heredocs in the inline body; and if a worker is committed+pushed but PR-less + idle, the mayor can open the PR for it (git -C <wt> push; gh pr create --head <branch>) rather than killing the work.

worker/receipts-hic081 IS NOT STRANDED -- do not delete it, and do not re-file it as hygiene residue (rf2-fuuqd, triaged 2026-08-15).

It is a DELIBERATELY RETAINED spike record. rf2-hic-081 ('Spike: capability receipts') closed with the verdict SPLIT and its close reason ends: 'Spike commits are pushed on worker/receipts-hic081 and retained as the experiment's record; nothing from them lands on main.' The 3 commits are pushed, have no PR and never will -- that is the design, not an oversight.

The conclusions are fully promoted and verified on main: the capability-receipt DESIGN is in docs/design/hicasso/product/specification.md, decision-brief.md and lanes/left-field-ideas.md (rf2-eoo9, PR #7898); the erasure-gate reachability rule is in check_production_erasure.cjs and siblings (rf2-nkr3, PR #7878); impl/receipt.cljs is correctly ABSENT from main.

THE GENERAL LESSON for the hygiene loop: 'pushed + unlanded + no PR' is a heuristic, not a verdict. Before filing a branch as stranded, check whether a CLOSED bead retained it on purpose -- spike branches are the class where the finding lands on main and the diff deliberately never does.

Worker recovery hazard (learned 2026-06-22, the #4910/#4913 xray-testbeds incident): (1) A worker coming to rest is NOT proof it finished. The xray-testbeds worker came to rest waiting on a gate it launched; the mayor misjudged it as done, committed its UNCOMMITTED partial work as a recovery PR (#4910) — but it had not yet written standard_epochs/core.cljs, so #4910 merged an incomplete state that crashed the two-frame surface on load and left a red gate on main. RULE: only recover/commit a worker's work after a genuine final report with a PR URL; an idle worktree mid-task is not a completion signal. (2) NEVER git worktree remove --force a worktree whose worker may still be live — it destroyed the live worker's workspace AND emptied the mayor implementation/node_modules via the node_modules junction cascade (the worker had to npm install to restore the mayor tree). RULE: only remove a worktree for a worker that has genuinely completed (final report received); the junction-rmdir-before-remove step does not protect against removing a still-active worktree.

"WORKTREE-LOCAL" IS ONLY HALF THE RULE FOR WORKER SCRATCH FILES — IT MUST ALSO BE GITIGNORED (2026-08-09).

THE SEQUENCE. Earlier in the day two concurrent workers overwrote each other's helper files and PR-body drafts in the SHARED scratchpad, and one nearly published another bead's PR body. The fix put into later briefs was "write every file you create inside your own worktree". Both workers complied exactly. Both worktrees then REFUSED to reap: REMOVE_REFUSED_DIRTY, each holding one untracked pr-body-<bead>.md that the disposability classifier will not accept as build output.

SO THE TWO HAZARDS TRADE OFF AND THE BRIEF MUST CLOSE BOTH. dispatch-prompt-template.md already says it: put EVERY gate artefact where git ignores it, and warns that one leftover is enough to make a tree unreapable (nine accumulated that way once). The ignored extensions are *.log, *.exit and *-exit.txt. A file named pr-body-something.md is worktree-local, safe from collision, and still blocks the reap.

THE COMPLETE INSTRUCTION FOR A DISPATCH BRIEF: write every file you create inside your own worktree AND give it an ignored name (*.log / *.exit), or delete it before you report done. Never a shared temp directory; never an unignored leftover.

RESOLVING IT WHEN IT HAPPENS IS CHEAP BUT MUST NOT BE BLIND. --dry-run prints each offending path tagged [KEEP] or [build output]; a PR-body draft whose content is already published on the merged PR is genuinely disposable, so --force is correct AFTER looking. Do not reach for --force-disposable (it refuses anything not recognised as build output) and never spray a blanket --force across a sweep list: when that guard was written, one worktree held four analysis files for an OPEN bead and three others carried uncommitted source and doc edits.

A WORKTREE YOU DID NOT EXPLICITLY DISPATCH MAY BE YOUR OWN WORKER SPAWNING A SECOND WORKTREE — not a concurrent session. Misdiagnosed 2026-07-24. I dispatched a 4-bead cluster to ONE worker; it did 3 beads in worktree A (PR one) then created worktree B for the 4th bead (PR two). My hygiene scan found worktree B, had no record of creating it, and I concluded a concurrent session was also dispatching workers. WRONG — it was my own worker branching per bead. THE COST: the false belief made me over-cautious about that surface being externally contested. THE DISCRIMINATOR before concluding concurrent-session: a branch named worker/<desc>-<beadid> whose bead you assigned to a live worker IS that worker, even as a second worktree. Check worker completion reports and open PRs first — a worker report names every worktree and PR it created. Track by BEAD ownership (who did I give this bead to), never by worktree count: one worker is NOT necessarily one worktree or one PR. The genuinely-separate process here (the pr-audit loop) FILES beads, it does not dispatch code-editing workers, so it never contests a code surface. No harm done — I correctly did not touch the worktree or re-dispatch the bead.

A WORKER STRANDS BY ENDING ITS TURN ON A BACKGROUNDED GATE, AND IT WILL DO IT REPEATEDLY UNLESS THE BRIEF SAYS HOW TO WAIT. Observed again 2026-08-08 on rf2-2rtt6.142, twice in a row after a resume.

THE SHAPE. A gate exceeds the tool's foreground time ceiling. The worker detaches it — correctly — and then ENDS ITS TURN "waiting" for a completion notification. Nothing is guaranteed to wake it. It reports "still progressing, continuing to wait", the turn ends, and the same thing happens on the next nudge. The work is usually fine; only the waiting is broken.

WHAT DOES NOT FIX IT: telling the worker again that gates must be foreground. It already believes that, which is exactly why it detached and then waited politely. The instruction it is missing is what to do INSTEAD of waiting.

WHAT FIXES IT — put this in every brief, not just the ones with long gates:
  "If a gate exceeds the tool's time ceiling, run it detached and BLOCK ON IT INSIDE THE SAME TURN by polling its exit file in a loop. Never end a turn with a gate outstanding."
and give the literal shape:
  for i in $(seq 1 240); do [ -f gate-<id>.exit ] && break; sleep 15; done; cat gate-<id>.exit

TWO RIDERS THAT MATTER AS MUCH AS THE LOOP:
- The detached invocation must use an ABSOLUTE path to the gate script. These scripts derive their repo root from BASH_SOURCE, and a relative invocation that gets detached adopts whatever cwd the shell really has — one did that inside ANOTHER live worker's checkout and produced a complete, internally consistent verdict about somebody else's diff. Check the run's "gate root:" first line names your own worktree.
- If the invocation writes no exit file at all, that is the real defect, not the waiting. Re-run as: sh <ABS>/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > g.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > g.exit

MAYOR-SIDE RECOVERY, cheap and reliable: check the ground truth yourself rather than nudging twice. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` and a remote-vs-local sha comparison in the worktree tell you whether the work is durable; `ls *.log *.exit` plus the log's mtime tell you whether the gate is genuinely still running or dead. On this occasion the work was already committed AND pushed, so nothing was at risk — the only outstanding step was reading an exit code.

DO NOT MISREAD THE SPINE LOG WHILE CHECKING. test-fast-pr.sh prints lines like "ok  unexpected extra dependency -> FAILED" from a negative-test harness confirming its own mutations fail correctly. Those are PASSES. The verdict is the echoed exit code, never a line in the log.

THE DISPATCH LEDGER'S ROUTE BACK TO A WORKER'S COMPLETION REPORT IS UNRELIABLE ON THIS BOX: MOST SUBAGENT TRANSCRIPTS ARE ZERO BYTES. The reap rule needs a quotable report, so the durable evidence has to be written into the TRACKER, not left in a transcript the id merely points at.

MEASURED 2026-09-16 on the mayor session. Of the five most recent worker transcripts, FOUR were zero bytes at the only location holding that agent id; twenty-two zero-byte `.output` files stood in that tasks directory overall. Three older transcripts DID persist (1.7 MB, 2.5 MB, 0.9 MB), so the behaviour is not uniform. The one live worker that had been RESUMED via SendMessage was among the survivors, which is suggestive but not established. THE MECHANISM IS DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN -- what is measured is the observable and the consequence.

WHY IT MATTERS. `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md` Section 4 makes the completion report the SOLE authorisation for reaping a worktree, and says the ledger's agent id is "the route back to the sentence" once the mayor's context is cleared. That method statement is right as written and needs no edit -- it simply assumes transcripts persist, which on this box they mostly do not. So on a long session that will be compacted, an agent id can lead to an empty file, and the reap test then correctly refuses forever: the tree stays, not because it should, but because the evidence evaporated.

THE FAILURE IS SAFE, WHICH IS WHY IT GOES UNNOTICED. Losing the report costs a stale directory, never a destroyed run -- the asymmetry Section 4 relies on. So nothing ever complains, and the coordinator discovers it only when it goes looking for a report it can no longer quote.

THE GUARD, AND IT IS ALREADY MOSTLY HAPPENING BY ACCIDENT: WRITE THE WORKER'S REPORT INTO THE BEAD. A close reason that transcribes the done-sentence and the evidence makes the tracker the durable route back -- it is committed, pushed, and survives compaction, machine restarts and transcript cleanup. Make it deliberate rather than incidental, and note the ONE GAP that pattern leaves: a worker that has reported while its PR is still in CI has no close reason yet, so during that window the report exists ONLY in the coordinator's live context and the empty transcript. Append the done-sentence to the bead AS SOON AS THE REPORT ARRIVES, not when the PR merges.

DO NOT EDIT loops.md FOR THIS. It is the OS-neutral method; this is a property of one machine's harness. The project instruction sheet and this memory are the right homes.

WORKER TRAP — git mv then edit (2026-07-25, found by the misc-cluster-a worker on PR #6946): after 'git mv old.cljc new_cljs_test.cljc', a subsequent 'git add <path>' does NOT pick up content edits made after the mv. The worker's first pushed commit therefore carried the RENAMED file with the OLD ns name still inside it — a commit that would not compile. It was caught only by noticing a stray 'M' in git status, then fixed by rebuilding both commits from the base and force-pushing with --force-with-lease. This is the exact shape of the rf2-dn6v7 / rf2-lgozq lane-suffix work (rename file + edit ns in one change), so it will recur. Put in briefs for any rename-plus-edit bead: after a git mv, re-run 'git add' on the path AFTER the content edit, and verify with 'git diff --cached' that BOTH the rename and the content change are staged before committing; a rename-only commit of a .cljc test file is a non-compiling commit.

A WORKER WORKTREE NEEDS A node_modules JUNCTION TO RUN THE SPINE. Briefs that nominate the fast-PR spine: if the node tier fails on module resolution, create the implementation/node_modules junction, re-run, and REMOVE THE LINK as your last act before reporting done, so hygiene never meets one.

CORRECTED 2026-09-08: this memory previously said to create and remove that link with 'cmd /c mklink /J' and 'cmd /c rmdir'. BOTH ARE SILENT NO-OPS FROM GIT BASH — they print the Windows banner, EXIT 0, and do nothing. A brief carrying that recipe reports success and leaves the junction live, which is exactly what the next 'git worktree remove' follows into the mayor's real node_modules. See cmd-slash-c-from-bash-is-a-silent-noop.

USE POWERSHELL FOR BOTH:
  create: New-Item -ItemType Junction -Path <wt>/implementation/node_modules -Target <mayor>/implementation/node_modules
  remove: [System.IO.Directory]::Delete('<wt>/implementation/node_modules', $false)
Or let scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh do it — it unlinks first, removes second, and snapshots the mayor's counts either side.

VERIFY THE EFFECT, NEVER THE EXIT CODE: after creating, list the link; after removing, confirm the link is gone AND the mayor's node_modules still counts what it did. Never a recursive delete — it follows the junction and empties the mayor's real tree, which has happened twice.

A FRESH WORKER WORKTREE HAS NO `implementation/node_modules`, AND THE SPINE FAILS ENVIRONMENTALLY THERE — the harness then misreports it (2026-08-11, rf2-gxry).

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker ran `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh` in a newly-created worktree. It captured exit **1** on `CLJS node integration`, with `Cannot find module 'shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'` — nothing compiled, because the worktree had no `node_modules`. **The harness announced "completed (exit code 0)" against that captured 1.** The worker junctioned `node_modules` at the mayor's real one, deleted the stale `.exit` and `.log`, re-ran the gate whole, and captured **0** with `[:node-test] Build completed. (2307 files, 2306 compiled, 0 warnings)`.

THE HAZARD IS NOT THE FAILURE, IT IS THE SHAPE OF IT. A missing-module error is not a test failure, but it PRESENTS as a red gate, and if a worker reads the harness's number instead of the captured one it presents as a GREEN gate over a build that never ran. Both readings are wrong in opposite directions, and the second is the dangerous one: a green that compiled nothing.

WHAT TO PUT IN A BRIEF for any worker that will run a compiling gate:
  - A fresh worktree has NO `implementation/node_modules`. If a gate needs one, create the junction to the mayor's real tree, and REMOVE THE LINK (never its target) as your last act — a later `git worktree remove` follows it and empties the shared tree. Canary the mayor's count before and after.
  - `Cannot find module` or `command not found` from a gate is ENVIRONMENTAL, not a verdict. Fix the environment and RE-RUN THE GATE WHOLE. Do not report the first number, and do not report it as a failure of the diff.
  - DELETE the stale `.exit` and `.log` before the re-run. A stale `.exit` survives the next run's `>` on its log, so the pair can disagree and the older verdict is the one you quote.

TWELFTH SIGHTING TODAY of the harness reporting a captured 1 as exit 0. The rule stands and is now in the method: THE NUMBER YOU QUOTE IS THE ONE YOU CAPTURED.

Worker worktrees have NO node_modules, so browser/shadow-cljs gates cannot run there by default. Do NOT junction into the mayor checkout's node_modules to fix it — that is the configuration that destroyed the mayor's real node_modules once and nearly again. THE SAFE ANSWER IS `npm ci` INSIDE THE WORKTREE (one worker did exactly this today, exit 0, no junction created, canary unmoved). Cost is a few minutes; the alternative is deferring every browser gate to CI. Put this in any brief whose gate menu includes `npm run test:browser`, a shadow-cljs build, or an adapter testbed spec.cjs — otherwise the worker hits 'shadow-cljs is not recognized', concludes the gate is unrunnable, and defers coverage that actually matters (the real-DOM gate catches repaint bugs test:cljs structurally cannot see). Related: [[windows-junction-detection-two-wrong-answers-before-the]].

Workers can get stuck in a monitor-wait loop on slow test suites (rul3ov burned ~770K tokens over 3 segments re-arming a Monitor for the full CLJS conformance run before committing). Recovery: SendMessage the agentId with a firm 'do NOT arm another Monitor — commit FIRST, push, gh pr create NOW; CI runs the full suite so CI is the gate, not your local terminal.' Over-cautious 'won't PR until local green' is the anti-pattern; the PR's CI is the real gate.

CONCURRENT WORKERS SHARE THE SESSION SCRATCHPAD AND OVERWRITE EACH OTHER'S FILES — including PR bodies (2026-08-09).

WHAT HAPPENED. Six workers ran in parallel on the hic-* Wave A set. The rf2-hic-004 worker reported that its verify.py and pr-body.md were BOTH overwritten mid-run by the rf2-hic-005 worker. Same filenames, same shared scratchpad directory. Its PR body survived only because gh had already read the file before the overwrite landed. A slower run would have published another bead's PR body under its own PR number.

WHY THE EXISTING RULE DID NOT COVER IT. The brief said 'use worktree-local log paths', and every worker complied FOR GATE LOGS — they all wrote gate-slugs.log inside their own worktree. The collision was in the HELPER FILES nobody thought to fence: scratch scripts, PR-body drafts, temp verification output. The known hazard was written narrowly as a gate-log hazard; it is really a shared-temp-directory hazard and applies to every file a worker writes outside its worktree.

THE FIX FOR FUTURE BRIEFS. Say: write EVERY file you create - gate logs, helper scripts, PR-body drafts, scratch output - inside your own worktree, never in a shared temp or scratchpad directory. If you must use a shared directory, prefix every filename with your bead id.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN A WRONG GATE LOG. A clobbered gate log yields a plausible-but-wrong exit code, which the echo-the-exit-code rule catches. A clobbered PR body is published verbatim to GitHub under the wrong PR and nothing checks it.

THREE WORKERS IN ONE NIGHT STALLED WAITING FOR A "COMPLETION NOTIFICATION" THAT DOES NOT EXIST (2026-08-10).

WHAT THEY EACH DID. rf2-8a6s: "Still running. I'll stop here and resume when the watcher fires - no more polling." rf2-hic-009: "The spine is still running ... I have a waiter armed on its exit code and will report the moment it lands." rf2-hic-016: "The fast-PR spine is still running; I'll wait for its completion notification rather than end the turn" - and then the turn ended. All three had briefs that said, in terms, run gates in the foreground to completion and never background one.

THE BELIEF IS SPECIFIC AND WRONG, WHICH IS WHY THE EXISTING WORDING DOES NOT PREVENT IT. They do not think they are abandoning the task. They think a watcher/notification will wake them. Nothing does. A stopped subagent resumes ONLY when the mayor sends it a message, and the mayor only knows to because the completion report reads oddly. "Run gates in the foreground" does not contradict the belief - a worker can believe it ran the gate in the foreground AND that something will tell it the answer later.

THE WORDING THAT ADDRESSES THE BELIEF, not the behaviour: "There is no completion notification. No watcher wakes a stopped worker. If you end your turn waiting for a gate, the task stops until a human notices. Run the gate in the foreground, block on it, read its exit code yourself. A long foreground gate is fine; an unfinished turn is not."

THE REAL COST IS UNPUSHED WORK, AND IT VARIES. rf2-8a6s had committed AND pushed - fully durable, only the PR was missing. rf2-hic-009 had pushed and opened a PR - only the spine result and PR body were missing. rf2-hic-016 had THREE COMMITS AND HAD NOT PUSHED - one lost worktree from losing an entire three-engine browser suite. So the recovery order is: check `git log origin/main..HEAD` and `git ls-remote` FIRST, and if it is unpushed, make PUSH step 1 of the resume message before anything else.

RECOVERY IS CHEAP AND RELIABLE: SendMessage to the agent id resumes it from its transcript with full context. All three resumed and continued correctly. Do not re-dispatch a fresh worker - it would redo work that is already committed.

DETECTION: a completion report that says "still running", "I'll report when", "waiting for", or "watcher armed" is a stall, not a status. Treat it as a resume trigger immediately, and check push state before replying.

Workers strand because the long gate outlives their TURN budget, not because they disobeyed 'run foreground'. Three workers in one session (dispatch-sync, ci-test-lanes, tags-ratchet) ended their turn mid-gate with 'Waiting on the spine/watcher' — commits pushed, NO PR, nothing mergeable. A brief that says 'run test-fast-pr.sh foreground to completion, THEN open the PR' makes stranding likely on a loaded box, because the spine can exceed the budget. BETTER BRIEF ORDER: commit -> run only the FOCUSED, fast, arm-specific gates (plus any non-vacuity/mutation proof, which is cheap and is the evidence that actually matters) -> OPEN THE PR -> name the slow gates as 'deferred to CI' in the ## Quality gates section. CI runs the same surface and IS the merge gate; the local spine never was. Recovery is SendMessage-resume, which works and keeps the worker's context.

Workflow rule (Mike, 2026-06-10): beads marked in_progress are LOCKED - never update their title/description/notes/scope (a worker is executing against them). To add findings or scope to in-progress work, CREATE A FOLLOW-UP BEAD (dep on the in-progress one if sequenced). Check status with bd show before any bd update.

`git worktree add` CAN BE KILLED BY THE HARNESS FOREGROUND TIMEOUT MID-CHECKOUT, LEAVING A STALE LOCK (2026-08-11; hit by two workers in one tick).

This repo's checkout is ~5308 files, and a fresh `git worktree add` can exceed the harness's 2-minute foreground limit. When it is killed partway (~25% in one observed case) it leaves BOTH a stale `.git/worktrees/<name>/index.lock` AND a `locked` marker reading `initializing`. The worktree exists, is registered, and is unusable; the guard script fails.

RECOVERY, in this order:
1. remove `.git/worktrees/<name>/index.lock`
2. `git reset --hard HEAD` from inside the worktree, BACKGROUNDED - it re-runs the full checkout and took ~9 minutes on this box
3. `git worktree unlock <path>`
Then the worker guard passes normally.

PUT THE MITIGATION IN THE DISPATCH BRIEF: every brief I write opens with `git worktree add`, so this is a first-command failure that costs a worker ten minutes before it has done anything. Tell workers to run the create BACKGROUNDED by absolute path and poll, exactly as they are already told to do for the 25-minute test spine - the same 10-minute ceiling applies to it and nobody expects it to.

Two workers hit this in a single tick (thirdsite-fbi4 and presence-5gka), so it is not rare. Both recovered without data loss, and both reported it rather than silently retrying - which is what made it diagnosable.

Worktree cleanup: a directory can be REUSED and re-pointed at a different branch mid-session, so a name-based safe-list goes stale while you are acting on it. Observed live: a hygiene agent was handed 'ci-test-lanes-cluster - safe to remove, PR #7116 merged', but between the list being written and the removal, a worker reused that same directory on a NEW branch (worker/xray-fuzzy-regression-pin) carrying an open PR #7119. Removing by name would have destroyed an in-flight PR worktree. Re-read `git worktree list --porcelain` IMMEDIATELY BEFORE each removal and re-verify the branch AND its PR state at that moment; never trust a safe-list compiled minutes earlier. Corollary: 'PR merged' is a fact about a BRANCH, not about a DIRECTORY. Related: [[rebase-merge-makes-a-worker-branch-look-unmerged]].

Worktree hygiene: `git status` ALONE IS NOT ENOUGH to decide whether a worktree holds work. The `/ai/` tree is GITIGNORED, so findings docs, gate logs, PR-body drafts and ad-hoc probes are INVISIBLE to git status — a worktree that looks pristine can hold real content. Sweep `ai/` (and any `.worker-logs/`, `.wt-logs/`) separately and READ any non-log file before discarding. Observed: three worktrees held hidden content (20 gate logs, a pr-body.md draft, an ad-hoc probe .clj) — all correctly judged residue, but only because they were looked at. Corollary for the other direction: a hygiene brief that says 'clean tree = safe to remove' is wrong on this repo.

A WORKTREE'S INDEX CLOCK MEASURES THAT WORKTREE, NOT THE FUNCTION IT WAS DISPATCHED FOR (2026-08-24, correcting my own reading across ~six sweeps).

WHAT I HAD BEEN SAYING. Every stranded sweep reported the pr-audit worktree as "alive, polling on a ~40s cadence, index still 11:41, so nothing audited since 11:43". The first half is right. The second half quietly asserted that the AUDIT FUNCTION had produced nothing, and that does not follow.

WHAT THE PARENT CHAIN SHOWS.
* 10ade546c4 "audit PR #8721", 11:43:26, parent ebc7e737bd -- which IS that worktree's HEAD and its branch tip. So that commit was made from that revision, and the index write at 11:41:02, two minutes earlier, is genuine evidence of it staging. That inference was sound.
* d1c824098d "audit PR #8730", 01:22 the next morning, parent 3c9e358a0f -- a revision that worktree has NEVER been at (its branch reflog has exactly two entries: created, then one fast-forward to ebc7e737bd, and `git cherry` reads 0 ahead).

SO AUDITS KEPT HAPPENING WHILE THAT WORKTREE DID NOTHING BUT FETCH. Tonight's audit filed a bead against my own merge and pushed a commit, from a checkout at main's tip, not from there. At least two things perform this role, and the worktree I was watching is not the one that has been working.

THE CORRECTION, and it is about the shape of the claim rather than the number: an index mtime is evidence about ONE CHECKOUT. Reading it as a health signal for the capability that checkout was dispatched to provide is a category error, and it fails in the reassuring direction -- "nothing has been audited" was false every time I said it, while the audit was in fact catching my own defects.

THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE PARENT CHAIN, not the clock: take a commit the function produced and ask whether its PARENT is a revision that checkout has actually been at. Its branch reflog answers that in one command and cannot be faked by a fetch.

STILL TRUE, and worth keeping: FETCH_HEAD movement proves that worktree is alive (measured twice, 40 seconds apart, against a mayor clock that stayed still), and it remains unreapable and unmessageable because no dispatch row records an agent id for it.

THE 'NEVER WRITE THE WORKTREE PATH INTO A COMMITTED FILE' RULE IS NARROWER THAN THE RISK, AND THE CI GATE DOES NOT CLOSE THE GAP (2026-08-18).

Adopted into mayor dispatch practice on the report of the worker on rf2-f5cma, which was fixing that very rule and is the best-placed reader of it.

THE GAP: a PR body and a bead close reason are both DURABLE and PUBLIC, and neither is a committed file. The 'No hardcoded personal/home paths' CI gate does not see either. So a worker that obeys the rule as written can still publish an absolute home path where it persists. That worker kept paths out of both only by extending the rule on its own initiative.

ADOPTED WORDING for every dispatch: report the printed WORKTREE_ROOT to the mayor in your completion message, and never write it, or any absolute home path, into any COMMITTED FILE, PR BODY OR TRACKER TEXT.

AND CARRY THE POSITIVE FORM, which the template now has and my briefs lagged a revision behind: if the deliverable is itself a written record, what makes the guard evidence is that it RAN and exited 0, not the machine-specific path it printed. A worker told only what not to write still has evidence to produce and will improvise something.

SEPARATE OBSERVATION FROM THE SAME REPORT, not yet actioned: the guard prints an MSYS-style root (/c/Users/...) while the boundary block in every brief states the worktree as C:/Users/.... A worker comparing the two LITERALLY sees a mismatch, on the one rule where a directory-level error is expensive. Every worker so far has resolved it from context. If it ever bites, the fix is to state both forms in the boundary block rather than to change either producer.

GENERAL SHAPE: the worker fixing a rule is the best reviewer of the brief that carries it. Ask. Two of the three improvements here came from asking one worker whether its own setup instruction was well worded.

WRITE EVERY DISPATCH BRIEF TO A FILE BEFORE SENDING IT, BECAUSE THE POSTURE LOOP'S FIDELITY CHECK IS OTHERWISE TESTIMONIAL RATHER THAN MECHANICAL (2026-09-03).

THE PROBLEM. loops.md section 4 asks the mayor to confirm that every dispatch since the last posture tick pasted the stance VERBATIM and carried the boundary and gate-mechanics blocks. If the brief was assembled inline in the Agent call and never written down, there is nothing left to check against afterwards — the mayor's own recollection is the only witness, and a mayor that had summarised the stance would recall having pasted it. That is precisely the failure mode the loop exists to catch, so the check silently degrades to self-report at exactly the moment it matters.

THE FIX IS ONE EXTRA STEP AND IT COSTS NOTHING. Build the brief mechanically into a scratchpad file — stance header, then the extracted preamble / boundary / gates blocks appended, then the task body — and dispatch by telling the worker to read that file as its FIRST action. Then the posture check is three greps with counts, run against bytes that still exist: grep -c on a distinctive line of each block. Anything other than 1 is a defect you can name.

TWO SECOND-ORDER WINS, BOTH REAL. (1) Telling the worker to cat the file is MORE faithful than pasting, because the bytes it reads are the extractor's output rather than anything that passed through the mayor's hands again. (2) The file survives compaction. Measured this session: four dispatches made before a compaction could not be re-verified at all, because their briefs had only ever existed inside the Agent call, and the only surviving evidence was one worker's report happening to describe gate-block-specific behaviour (planted-fault runs, git blob-hash restore). That is corroboration, not verification, and it was luck.

THE ANCHOR-DUPLICATION DETAIL. Repeat the worktree path, branch, base oid, bead ids and the premises-are-claims sentence INLINE in the Agent prompt as well. A worker that fails to read the file then contradicts an anchor visibly instead of improvising a task silently — the failed read becomes detectable rather than silent.

DO NOT read this as licence to skip the extractor. The file is where the extractor's output lands; it is not a substitute for extracting. See never-retype-a-verbatim-block.

WRITE THE DISPATCH LEDGER ROW IN THE SAME TOOL CALL THAT SPAWNS THE AGENT — never in "the next step". Measured twice on 2026-09-05, same cause both times, by the mayor.

THE MECHANISM, and it is structural rather than forgetfulness: the Agent spawn returns, and a background task-notification for a DIFFERENT worker arrives in the same turn. The notification is substantive — a completion report worth acting on — so attention moves to it, the turn ends on that thread, and the ledger write is never made. Both misses (`exserve-a`, then `httpcancel-a` + `exsubstr-a`) happened exactly that way. A worker was live, working, with NO row in `ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv`.

WHY IT MATTERS: the ledger is the only route from a worktree back to its agentId, and the reap test requires the agent's own report. A worktree with no row cannot be routed to, so at reap time it looks like a tree with no owner — which is the state that invites reaping on a refused proxy (a merged PR, a clean tree, elapsed time).

THE FIX, in order:
  * **Write the row in the same call as the spawn**, or immediately after in the SAME turn, before reading any notification.
  * **Then verify by name-keyed read** — `rows=1 fields=5` per live worktree. That read is what caught both misses; without it the omission is invisible until reap time.
  * A `rows=0` on a worktree you know you dispatched is a MISSING ROW, not a wrong key — but check the key form first, because `/c/Users/…` against a stored `C:/Users/…` also reads 0 for every row, uniformly, which looks exactly like an answer. Keep a control: query one key you know is present.

**AND DO NOT ADDRESS FIELDS BY INDEX.** Read by name. CLAUDE.md's ledger contract records that a positional parse is right about one row in eight and wrong with a well-formed answer on the rest.

RELATED: [[the-ledger-key-is-the-stored-path-form]], [[a-uniform-zero-reads-exactly-like-an-answer]].

WSL bash.exe DOUBLE-EXPANDS a -c command string. Found by rf2-sefx0 (#6357, 2026-07-18) with a decisive probe: bash -lc with FOO=hello then printf of the escaped dollar-FOO prints the literal dollar-FOO under Git Bash (single pass) but prints hello under WSL bash (an outer pass already substituted it). CONSEQUENCE: any -c string that READS BACK a variable the SAME string assigns is broken under WSL — the outer pass substitutes the not-yet-assigned name to empty. That is how a PATH= assignment referencing a FIXTURE_DIR assigned immediately to its left silently produced /bin:<real PATH>, so stub executables were never found and 15 of 15 cases failed before reaching the code under test. Pre-existing vars (PWD, PATH) survive both passes, which is why the bug looks selective. FIX SHAPE: build one env-prefixed command whose every dollar-NAME already exists in the parent environment; let the child script read the rest from its own environment rather than from the command string. DISPROVED on the way: the semicolon separator is fine, and double-quoting is fine — do not chase those. TESTING LESSON (the important half): a BEHAVIOURAL test for this cannot protect you, because Git Bash and the Ubuntu CI runner both expand ONCE — a reintroduced self-reference stays green on CI while breaking only for Windows contributors. sefx0 pinned the STRUCTURE instead (assert the command references only pre-existing variables) with a non-vacuity guard. Generalise: when a defect is invisible on the platform your CI runs, a structural pin beats a behavioural one.

(last=null)'. The naive change ships a tab that renders nothing and BOTH gates I briefed are green on it.

A RULING DETAIL WAS EMPIRICALLY WRONG: notifications CAN arrive before dispatch returns on the stock-Reagent adapter (found 2026-08-07, rf2-ynved).

THE RULING SAID (item 8) that notifications never arrive before dispatch returns. FALSE on this adapter: :flush-render! is (fn [f] (f) (r/flush)), so dispatch-sync DRAINS THE QUEUE ITSELF. A test written to assert the ruling literally went red.

HOW IT WAS HANDLED, and this is the part to copy: the worker did not quietly conform the test to observed behaviour, and did not quietly conform the docs to the ruling. It reported the ruling was wrong, and changed the DOCS to say the re-feed rides a Reagent flush rather than an inline callback inside the app-db write — while telling the author to code as though it lands on the FOLLOWING commit. That last clause is the useful part: teach the WEAKER guarantee even when the stronger one currently holds, because the stronger one is an implementation detail of one adapter.

SECOND FINDING from the same run: a sibling unmount COMMIT re-runs a surviving tracker against an unchanged value, so the survivor takes one idempotent re-feed. The DOM-free counterpart drives the identical release with NO React commit and sees no duplicate. So it is a property of the commit cycle, not of the recipe — and the assertion was rewritten property-based with the reason recorded.

GENERAL RULE: when a test contradicts a recorded ruling, the ruling is a hypothesis like anything else. Report the contradiction, establish which is true FROM THE ADAPTER SOURCE, and fix whichever is actually wrong. Do not assume the ruling wins; do not assume the observation wins.

CLAUDE.md's "Ways the INSTRUMENTS misreport" bullet exhausted its letters at (z) on 2026-09-18. RULED 2026-09-21 under rf2-z0pma (delegated by Mike): the label after (z) is (aa), then (ab), (ac) ... in spreadsheet-column order (bijective base-26), NOT (aa), (bb). AND before consuming a label ask whether the finding is an INSTRUMENT misreport at all: a lane reporting truthfully on what it compiled while the READER inferred more is a lane-coverage finding and goes as an UNLETTERED paragraph under Build & Test beside the rf2-uwa9r / rf2-d3l8g paragraph, which is where rf2-z0pma's own finding (a JVM lane READS a #?(:cljs ...) branch but never COMPILES it) was ruled to go. THE VACUITY TEST ASKS WHETHER A GATE *INSPECTS* WHAT YOU CHANGED, NEVER WHETHER IT *COMPILES* IT — and reasoning from the compiler to the gate discards real evidence, failing OPEN.

Measured 2026-09-21 at trunk `3eca0fa928`, on rf2-y8doi.60. The mayor briefed a worker: "`clojure -M:test` from `tools/xray` is VACUOUS for this diff and I am telling you so rather than letting you bank it: every file you touch is `.cljs` or `.md`, and no JVM artefact compiles `.cljs`." The PREMISE is true. The CONCLUSION is false.

`tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/frame_singleton_guard_test.clj` is a JVM `.clj` test that resolves `src/day8/re_frame2_xray/` on disk (anchoring via `(io/resource "day8/re_frame2_xray/defaults.cljs")`), walks it with `file-seq`, filters names ending `.cljs`, and `slurp`s each one as TEXT. It never compiles a line of ClojureScript and it grades every `.cljs` file in the tree.

The worker refuted the claim by PLANT rather than by argument: `{:frame :rf/xray}` planted in a `.cljs` file took that JVM lane to exit 1 with the guard naming the file and the line. Independent corroboration from a second instrument: the repo's own surface classifier arms `tools_jvm=true` for those paths. So the worker ran the lane, and its green was real evidence about the change — a gate it had been told to discount turned out to be the one gate it could take while fenced off the contended shadow-cljs lane.

WHY IT FAILS OPEN. The reasoning discards a gate, so the cost is a fault class left ungraded while the report reads more rigorous for having "correctly" declined a vacuous gate. It is the mirror of the ordinary vacuity error (banking a green from a gate that inspected nothing): here a REAL green is thrown away, and the worker is left with fewer instruments exactly when the contended one is unavailable.

THE DISCRIMINATOR, and it is cheap: ask what the gate READS, not what language it targets. A test that slurps, file-seqs, regexes or globs source files inspects files no compiler in its language ever touches — text-reading guards, path ratchets, spelling censuses, catalogue drift checks and manifest cross-checks are all this shape, and this repo is full of them. Where the answer is not obvious, PLANT a fault of the kind your diff could introduce and confirm the gate reddens; a gate that cannot be made to fail on your diff is the vacuous one, and that is a measurement rather than an inference from file extensions.

GENERALISES PAST THE JVM/CLJS PAIR. The same error shape is "the linter is for `.clj`, my change is `.md`", "the test suite is Python, my change is YAML". The question is always the same: does anything this gate runs OPEN my file?

Related: `bd recall` the entries on clj-kondo's `--fail-level error` blindness and on CI-log namespace greps — all three are cases where an instrument's reach is narrower or wider than its name suggests.

ALL THREE SIGNALS THE STRANDED SWEEP READS — NO LEDGER ROW, CLEAN `git status`, DETACHED HEAD AT AN OLD COMMIT — READ EXACTLY THE SAME ON A LIVE OUT-OF-REPO AUDIT MONITOR AS ON AN ABANDONED WORKTREE, BECAUSE THAT MONITOR'S ENTIRE WORKING SURFACE IS THE GITIGNORED `ai/` TREE.

Measured 2026-09-21 at trunk `40c4c8794d`. The mayor had reported six worktrees as residue for many consecutive ticks, in these words: *no ledger row, hence no agentId, hence no route to a report — unsatisfiable rather than pending.* Two of the six were working at that moment.

`audit-sep20-monitor` had `ai/queue.json` modified ONE MINUTE before the sweep, with `10132-remote-verified.json` and `10132-pushed.json` beside it — it was auditing PR #10132, merged twenty minutes earlier. `audit-sep17-monitor` had written into `ai/audit-remote/.dolt/git-remote-cache/` the same minute. The other four were genuinely cold at 113, 130, 134 and 157 hours.

WHY EVERY SWEEP SIGNAL FAILED, and each for its own honest reason:

- **`ledger=0` is CORRECT and means nothing here.** The dispatch ledger records the mayor's own dispatches. An out-of-repo harness never appears in it, so its absence is not evidence of abandonment — it is evidence the mayor did not start it.
- **`dirty=0` is STRUCTURALLY BLIND.** `/ai/` is in `.gitignore`, and `ai/` is per-worktree rather than shared, so a monitor whose whole output lands there shows zero porcelain lines however hard it is working. `git status` cannot see this class of work at all.
- **A detached HEAD at a week-old commit is the CORRECT state for a monitor.** It reads the tree and files beads; it does not commit. Tip movement, which the sweep treats as positive evidence of life, is something this worker will never produce.

THE INSTRUMENT THAT DOES SEE IT, and it is cheap: the newest modification time of any file inside the worktree, **including gitignored paths**, walked with a plain filesystem walk. Live trees read minutes; cold ones read days. It separated 0.16h and 0.17h from 113h, 130h, 134h and 157h with no ambiguity at all.

A SECOND TRAP IN THE SAME EPISODE. The bead that exposed this cited `ai/gate-audit-timer-audit-sep20-monitor-1.log`, and that path does NOT resolve in the mayor checkout — which reads as the familiar dangling-citation problem. It is not. `ai/` is per-worktree, so the log exists, 772 bytes, inside `audit-sep20-monitor`'s own `ai/`. **Before calling an `ai/` citation dangling, ask which worktree's `ai/` it meant.**

THE RULE THAT SAVED IT was the reap test, unchanged: only a worker's own completion report authorises reaping, and a tree with no quotable report stays. The mayor's REASONING called these trees dead for many ticks and the RULE refused to act on it, which is the asymmetry the method states — mistaking a record for residue destroys it; mistaking residue for a record costs a stale directory. **So this is not an argument for a new reaping proxy.** It is an argument for not describing a held tree as dead when the only thing established is that it cannot satisfy the reap test.

WHAT TO SAY INSTEAD. "No report, so it stays" is the whole of the justified claim. "Abandoned", "unsatisfiable", "can never report" are inferences the evidence does not carry, and stating them invites an operator to authorise a clearance that would destroy a live run — which is precisely the outcome the reap test exists to prevent, reached through the coordinator's own summary rather than through its actions.

THE STANDARD IDIOM FOR READING A BEAD'S FIELDS — `bd show <id> --json | jq -r '.[0].notes'` — IS ITSELF A `jq` PIPELINE, SO IT INJECTS A CARRIAGE RETURN ON EVERY LINE. It escapes `bd show`'s word-wrap trap and lands in the CLAUDE.md item (e) trap, and both produce the same symptom: a fixed-string probe that silently under-matches.

Measured 2026-09-21 on `rf2-z0pma`, whose notes are large enough for the effect to be unmissable:

| extraction | size | carriage returns |
|---|---|---|
| `bd show --json \| jq -r '.[0].notes'` | 54,318 bytes | **315** |
| Python's `json` module on the raw `--json` output | 53,794 chars | **0** |

Found by a worker that had been instructed, in its own dispatch brief, to use the jq form — so the coordinator prescribing the guard was prescribing the defect.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY ITEM (e) INSTANCE. The instruction exists to escape a REAL trap: `bd show`'s renderer hard-wraps to its own width and strips backticks, so probing the RENDERING reads 0 on text that landed perfectly. The remedy — probe the FIELD, not the rendering — is right. But the prescribed spelling of that remedy swaps one silent under-match for another, and it does so in the exact act a careful reader performs BECAUSE they were warned. A probe spanning a line boundary now fails on the `\r` instead of on the wrap.

THE FIX, and it costs nothing: redirect the raw JSON to a file and read it with a JSON parser rather than piping through `jq`.

    bd show <id> --json > <file>.json
    # then, in Python:  json.load(open(path, encoding='utf-8'))[0]['notes']

**Pass `encoding='utf-8'` explicitly.** Native Python on Windows defaults to cp1252 and dies `UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x9d` on any bead carrying a curly quote or an em dash — which is nearly all of them here. Measured the same day, twice.

Where a shell pipeline is genuinely wanted, `tr -d '\r'` after the `jq` restores it — but prefer the parser, because it also removes the second failure mode in the same act: a `jq` filter carrying nested quotes is easy to get wrong, and a malformed filter exits non-zero with a compile error rather than answering.

DO NOT READ THIS AS "STOP PROBING THE FIELD". Probing the field rather than the rendering is still correct and is still the rule. What changes is only how the field is extracted.

Related: the CR count is a property of the `jq` build on this machine, so a reader who cannot reproduce 315 has learned nothing about whether their own pipeline is clean — take the control from the data, not from this number.

A RETYPED COPY OF AN INSTRUMENT IS NOT THE INSTRUMENT, AND IT FAILS BY RETURNING A PLAUSIBLE NUMBER RATHER THAN AN ERROR. Where a script exports a function precisely so that ONE copy of an extraction rule exists, re-typing that rule inline to "check it myself" creates a second copy, and the two disagree immediately.

MEASURED 2026-09-21 (mayor, method-reread loop), on `ai/assemble-brief.sh`'s `gate_block()` over `docs/the-mayor-method/dispatch-prompt-template.md`:

  * the real `gate_block()`                                    -> 14,037 bytes
  * an inline retyping I LABELLED "the script's OWN gate_block,
    verbatim", which silently dropped its `!started {...}` rule -> 14,482 bytes
  * a naive two-anchor extraction including the heading         -> 14,521 bytes

The dropped `!started` block is what strips the mayor-facing frame paragraph; that paragraph is exactly the 445-byte gap. All three numbers are plausible four-figure byte counts, and nothing on screen says which one is the block anybody ships.

THE FILE ALREADY WARNED ABOUT THIS AND THE WARNING DID NOT PREVENT IT. `assemble-brief.sh` carries a comment recording that on 2026-09-16 the size check held its own INLINE copy of the extraction rule, read 14,521, and FAILED OPEN — its own words: "two copies of the rule disagree within days, and a guard reading its own copy grades a block nobody shipped". I made a third copy within minutes of reading that comment. So the guard against this is not a stronger warning; it is calling the function.

WHY IT NEARLY COST A CORRECTION TO A CORRECT CONSTANT. Carrying 14,037 as a standing figure and measuring 14,482, the natural conclusion is that the constant went stale and the document should be edited. It had not; the instrument had. `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md` section 5 names both halves of this — "a measured constant that has gone stale" as the gotcha to hunt, and "a correction tends to overshoot into the INVERSE of the claim it replaces" as the way the hunt goes wrong.

WHAT ACTUALLY CAUGHT IT, and it is the section 5 discharging question rather than suspicion: ask what you would expect to SEE that is different if the new claim were true. The candidate explanation was CRLF-versus-LF basis (a real defect in this tree, and one that had bitten a different measurement the same morning), which predicts a gap of exactly ONE BYTE PER LINE. The block is 171 lines and the gap was 445. That mismatch is what sent me to compare the two extractions instead of editing the file. A control confirmed the method rather than the hypothesis: `CLAUDE.md`, working file minus blob, gap 163 on 163 lines.

AND THE BASIS QUESTION TURNED OUT NOT TO ARISE HERE, which is worth stating so nobody adds a needless ritual: awk strips the line terminator on read, so `gate_block()` returns byte-identical output from the CRLF working file and the LF blob — 14,037 and 0 carriage returns from both, `cmp` clean. A CHARACTER OFFSET INTO A FILE is basis-dependent and must say which side it was taken on; a LINE-ORIENTED EXTRACTION piped through `wc -c` is not.

THE RULE: re-run the real function. Where an instrument exists as code, invoke it; never retype it into your shell to verify it, and never call a retyping "verbatim" — the word is what stops the reader checking. If the function must be reproduced, diff its output against the original's before trusting either.

PROMOTING A GITIGNORED CORPUS INTO THE TRACKED TREE MAKES IT MEET FOUR POLICIES THE GITIGNORED ORIGINAL NEVER MET, AND THE `findings` EXEMPTION COVERS NONE OF THEM. A findings folder IS exempt from the link gates — `check_doc_slugs.py` skips every directory named `findings` via `EXCLUDE_DIR_NAMES`, and `check_readme_links.py --ci` excludes the docs-gate roots — and that exemption is the whole of what it buys. Budget three pushes, not one.

MEASURED 2026-09-21 on rf2-nup2n / PR #10137, promoting `ai/findings/Resources` to `spec/findings/resources-parity-2026-09/` (316 files). The four went red in sequence, each only after the previous was fixed:

  1. MAINTAINER-USERNAME PORTABILITY (`scripts/check-no-hardcoded-paths.sh`). Raw run logs carry
     absolute home paths BY CONSTRUCTION. 222 violations across `.log`, `.json`, `.cjs`, `.cljs`.
     58 files scrubbed. It enumerates with `git grep`, so it sees TRACKED files only.
  2. NAVIGATION-CEILING (`implementation/scripts/_navigation-ceiling-policy.test.cjs`). Refuses a
     `page.goto` with no `timeout:` of its own, and it sweeps EVERY `.cjs`/`.mjs` ON THE FILESYSTEM
     — walk-tree, not `git ls-files`, `PRUNED_DIRS` only. So it reaches files no git-based gate does.
  3. ESLINT over every tracked JS. 37 errors. One was a 62 KB shadow-cljs node bundle
     (`shadow$provide`, `CLOSURE_DEFINES`) sitting beside hand-written evidence under a plain `.js`
     name, which the copy script's exclusions did not catch. The rest needed a first-line
     `/* global ... */` naming EXACTLY the globals each file uses — a UNION header still fails,
     because `no-unused-vars` refuses an unused name in a global comment too.
  4. REQUIRE-ALIAS DIALECT RATCHET, exit 2 with "this run CANNOT be believed". Adding `.clj`/`.cljs`
     probes under `spec/` made `spec` a NEW SURFACE carrying re-frame require edges, and
     `scripts/require-alias-baseline.edn` must name EVERY surface or the run refuses. Regenerate
     with `python scripts/check_require_alias_dialect.py --write-baseline`.

THE TRAP INSIDE (2), WHICH MANUFACTURES A FALSE RED THAT SURVIVES THE REAL FIX: the same walk-tree sweep reads the GITIGNORED `docs/spec/` staging copy that a local `mkdocs build` leaves behind, so the local re-run goes on failing on `docs/spec/findings/...` after the tracked files are corrected — evidence that contradicts the worker's own visible fix, which is the expensive direction. `rm -rf docs/spec docs/migration site` (all gitignored, confirm with `git check-ignore`) clears it. A local mkdocs build before a JS-harness run is what plants it.

AND THE CONTROL FOR (1) IS EASY TO TAKE VACUOUSLY. Verifying the merged tree, an UNTRACKED plant file reads 0 violations exactly as a clean tree does, because `git grep` cannot see an untracked path at all — a clean-looking corroboration of a clean-looking result. Plant inside a TRACKED file in the corpus: measured, that turns the gate red at exit 1 naming file and line on both its rules, and restoring returns `git hash-object` to the committed blob with `git diff --quiet HEAD` at exit 0. Only then does the zero mean absence.

GENERAL SHAPE: a directory-name exemption is an exemption from ONE FAMILY of gates, never from tracked-file status. Before promoting a corpus, ask which gates enumerate by `git ls-files`, which by `git grep`, and which by walking the FILESYSTEM — the third kind reaches gitignored build residue and is the one nobody predicts.

A BRIEF THAT ASSERTS A FILE'S EOL CLASS ON THE WORKER'S BEHALF CAN INVERT THE HEALTH CHECK INTO A DAMAGE REPORT ON A PERFECTLY HEALTHY FILE — and the "repair" it then invites is the real damage. CLAUDE.md item (u) already says to ask `git ls-files --eol <path>` BEFORE you edit; what this records is that a DISPATCH BRIEF moves that question upstream, so the coordinator must ask it too, per file, rather than generalising from the tree's overwhelming majority.

MEASURED 2026-09-21 on rf2-ystsc / PR #10139. The brief told the worker that BOTH its files were `w/crlf` and prescribed item (e)'s three-number check verbatim — require `CR == CRLF` AND `bare LF == 0`. Measured:

  implementation/scripts/_changed-surfaces.test.cjs   i/lf w/crlf   CR 7157  CRLF 7157  bare LF 0     -> PASSES
  .github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh          i/lf w/lf     CR 0     CRLF 0     bare LF 2739  -> demands 2739 == 0

So on the shell script the prescribed check DEMANDS DAMAGE BE REPORTED on a file that is exactly as it should be. The cause is `.gitattributes` line 1, `*.sh text eol=lf`, which pins every shell script in the tree to LF regardless of `core.autocrlf` — visible in `git ls-files --eol` as `attr/text eol=lf`, the third column nobody reads.

WHY THE COORDINATOR GETS IT WRONG: the tree is overwhelmingly `w/crlf` (measured elsewhere, 5103 of 5253 tracked files), so "this repo is CRLF" is true as a generalisation and false per file — and `.gitattributes` creates whole CLASSES of exceptions by extension, not the one-off outliers item (r) records. A brief naming two files from different classes in one sentence is exactly where it bites.

THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION IS THE SECOND MOVE, NOT THE FIRST. A worker meeting `2739 != 0` sees its own edit blamed, and the obvious remediation is to make the file satisfy the check — i.e. CRLF-ify a file `.gitattributes` forces to LF, which git then re-normalises on commit while the working tree disagrees. The first move is merely a false alarm; the second corrupts.

THE GUARD, and it is one command: in any brief that prescribes the three-number check, run `git ls-files --eol` on EVERY file named and paste its output into the brief, rather than asserting a class. Where the answer is `w/lf`, say that the file is LF by attribute and that bare LF is its CORRECT reading — the check becomes `CR == 0 and CRLF == 0`. Item (r)'s hash guidance is UNAFFECTED and stays as written: both files here are `i/lf`, so the DEFAULT `git hash-object` form is right for both, and the worker confirmed the `w/lf` file matches BOTH forms exactly as item (r) predicts for `i/lf w/lf`.

GENERAL SHAPE: a coordinator who states a measurable property in a brief has performed a measurement on the worker's behalf, and the worker cannot tell an asserted class from a measured one. State the command and its output, not the conclusion.

A `bd` DEPENDENCY EDGE IS SHAPED DIFFERENTLY ON EVERY SURFACE THAT RETURNS ONE, AND THE KIND KEY IS NOT THE SAME WORD ON BOTH. `bd show --json` spells it `dependency_type`; `bd list --json` spells it `type`. Measured 2026-09-12 on ONE bead (rf2-fo4ng) through both surfaces in one sitting: through `bd show`, `dependency_type` reads `blocks` and `type` is ABSENT; through `bd list`, `type` reads `blocks` and `dependency_type` is ABSENT.

THIS MEMORY PREVIOUSLY SAID THE KEY IS `dependency_type` "NOT `type`", FULL STOP. That was measured on `bd show` and is true there. As a universal it is WRONG, and wrong in the direction this memory exists to warn about: a reader who takes it to `bd list` writes `select(.dependency_type=="blocks")`, the guard conjunct is never true, and the whole backlog reads as unblocked.

THEY ARE NOT A KEY RENAME — THE TWO RECORDS CARRY DIFFERENT INFORMATION, so a filter is not the only thing that has to change.
  * `bd show`'s edge EMBEDS THE DEPENDED-ON ISSUE: its keys are id, title, status, priority, notes, description, owner, assignee, issue_type, created_at, created_by, updated_at, dependency_type. So `.dependencies[].id` is the OTHER bead's id, and its `.status` is free — no second lookup needed.
  * `bd list`'s edge is a RELATION ROW: issue_id, depends_on_id, type, created_at, created_by, metadata. Nothing about the other bead is present, so liveness needs a join against the same document.

THREE KINDS SHARE THE ARRAY on both surfaces: `blocks`, `discovered-from`, `parent-child`. Measured over a 21-bead board: 20 blocks, 7 discovered-from, 1 parent-child.

BOTH FAILURE DIRECTIONS, measured:
  * Reading the array WITHOUT filtering on kind counts `parent-child` and `discovered-from` as blockers. It reported rf2-k97c.7 blocked by its own parent epic — a circular, plausible-looking gate that does not exist. OVER-reports; the board reads more fenced than it is.
  * Filtering on the WRONG SPELLING for the surface matches nothing, so every bead reads "no live blocker" — including ones with real, live gates. UNDER-reports to a uniform, entirely plausible zero, which is the dangerous direction: it authorises dispatching into a fenced surface.

Neither announces itself. What caught it both times was a DISAGREEMENT WITH A FACT ALREADY KNOWN — rf2-fo4ng is certainly gated on rf2-uelji — two instruments, two answers, the disagreement the only thing on screen.

THE GUARD, and it is a CONTROL rather than a key to memorise, because the key is per-surface and this memory was itself wrong about it once: TALLY THE DISTINCT KIND VALUES IN THE SAME RUN THAT USES THEM. A tally coming back empty or all-ABSENT means you are reading the wrong key for the surface in front of you, not that the board has no edges. Cheaper still, print the edge's KEY SET once before writing any filter.

Same family as CLAUDE.md item (q)'s lowercase-over-the-rollup case: a filter whose guard can never be true returns a clean, uniform, reassuring answer about nothing. And the same lesson as CLAUDE.md's note that an ERROR OBJECT on stdout is a fourth `bd` JSON shape beside the three in `bd-json-shapes-differ-list-show-history` — `bd`'s surfaces do not share a schema, and nothing in the output says which one you are holding.
CORRECTION 2026-09-21 — THE KINDS ARE FOUR, NOT THREE, AND THIS MEMORY'S OWN ENUMERATION WAS SHORT WITHIN NINE DAYS. Measured on the re-frame2 mayor session over the 15 non-terminal beads through `bd list --limit 0 --json`: `blocks` 22, `discovered-from` 2, and `relates-to` 1 — the edge `rf2-pv7p` -> `rf2-1bkoc`, confirmed on a second surface by `bd dep list rf2-pv7p`, which prints it `via relates-to`. The three-kind sentence above was measured over a 21-bead board and was true of that board; it is not a closed set.

WHY THE SHORTFALL MATTERS IS THE OVER-REPORT DIRECTION THIS MEMORY ALREADY NAMES, REACHED THROUGH THE ENUMERATION RATHER THAN THROUGH THE KEY. A three-item list invites a DENYLIST filter — `select(.type != "discovered-from" and .type != "parent-child")` — and a denylist counts every kind nobody listed as a blocker, so `relates-to` fences a bead that nothing fences. Write it as an ALLOWLIST (`.type == "blocks"`), which fails CLOSED into "not a blocker" when a new kind appears, instead of OPEN into "blocker".

DO NOT NOW READ FOUR AS THE CLOSED SET — that is the identical mistake one turn later, and this correction would then go stale exactly as the sentence it repairs did. The TALLY is the instrument and the enumeration is only ever a snapshot of the board in front of you, which is what the guard above already says: the tally printed a value the list did not predict, and that disagreement is the whole detection.

THE SUBAGENT `.output` FILE IS A DECOY FOR THE REAP TEST — IT IS USUALLY EMPTY, AND THE REPORT LIVES IN A DIFFERENT DIRECTORY.

Measured 2026-09-21 on this box. Under the session scratch path `<temp>/claude/<project>/<session-uuid>/tasks/`, the `.output` files split by id family and a census that does not split reads healthy and hides the defect:

  * `a`-prefixed (SUBAGENTS): 305 files, only 42 non-empty — 263 ZERO BYTES, 86%.
  * `b`-prefixed (background Bash tasks): 671 files, 668 non-empty — 99.6%.
  * Ungrouped that is 710 of 976 non-empty, 73%, which reads as a working location.

THE CONTROL THAT SETTLES IT: a worker that was LIVE and mid-gate had a zero-byte `.output` too, alongside four workers that had demonstrably completed and reported. So emptiness there is a property of the LOCATION, never evidence about an agent — it cannot separate a worker that never reported from one that did, nor either from one still running.

THE REPORTS ARE AT `<claude-projects>/<project>/<session-uuid>/subagents/agent-<agentId>.jsonl`, exactly as `agentless-tree-report-is-on-disk-by-agent-id` already records. 2424 such transcripts stood across 39 sessions. All four completion reports were found there in full and quoted: "Done. PR #10139 is open and ready.", "PR #10140 is ready. Done.", "Done.", "Work complete." — each also stating its own WORKTREE_ROOT, which is the decisive match.

TWO READING NOTES THAT COST TIME:

  1. Reports state the root in MSYS form (`/c/Users/...`), not Windows form (`C:/Users/...`), so a matcher written in the Windows spelling reads FALSE on a report that does state its root. Check both spellings.
  2. The live worker's final assistant text was a bash poll loop waiting on a gate `.exit` file. That discriminates WORKING from DONE at a glance and is the in-turn polling pattern the dispatch template prescribes — do not misread it as a truncated report.

WHY THE MAIN SESSION TRANSCRIPT IS NOT THE FALLBACK: searching it for a worktree path returns the DISPATCH BRIEFS, which are long, imperative and full of the same tokens ("report the printed WORKTREE_ROOT in your completion message"). Four separate extraction attempts returned only briefs. That is the many-to-one hazard loops.md §4 names, and the brief outweighs the report on every keyword a naive search picks.

COST WHEN MISSED: a full hygiene loop concluded "the reap route is broken", reaped nothing, and reported the residue to the operator as needing explicit authority — while four worktrees' reports sat quotable in the other directory. Re-run correctly the same tick, all four reaped clean (NO_LINKS, REMOVED, canary 103/2933 unchanged) and their four patch-contained branches deleted by identity.

THE GUARD, AND IT IS THE ONE THIS PROJECT KEEPS RELEARNING: run `bd memories` BEFORE building a census, not after it fails. The correct path was already recorded and one search would have found it. Never conclude from an empty `.output` that a worker did not report.

THE FAST-PR SPINE TAKES THE SHADOW-CLJS LANE ON PATHS CI CLASSIFIES AS ARMING NOTHING — its "unknown surface" fallback is CONSERVATIVE in the direction that grabs a machine-wide exclusive, and CI has no such fallback, so the two disagree exactly where a brief is least likely to warn anybody.

Measured 2026-09-21 (rf2-xbig3, PR #10143) on a change confined to `scripts/report_ungraded_gates.py`. Root `scripts/**` arms no CI surface and is not a doc surface, so `.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh` handed those PATHS reads **0 of 29** armed (control: `tools/story/src/re_frame/story/ui/assertion_strip.cljs` arms **6**, so the instrument bites). But `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh` run with NO FLAGS falls to its own "conservative fallback (unknown surface)" branch and sets `jvm=true node=true` — and the node lane enters the shadow-cljs build runtime, which is the machine-wide exclusive that WEDGES SILENTLY when two runs coexist: no error, no exit file, no output, presenting to each worker as a hang on its own gate.

**So the failure is not that the spine runs too much. It is that a worker whose item cannot possibly need the lane takes it anyway, silently, while another worker holds it.** The brief for such an item will usually say "you do not need the shadow-cljs lane and must not take it" — which the worker obeys, and then runs the fast spine because that is the ordinary pre-checkin habit, and takes the lane through a door the brief never named.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE POINT: `scripts/**` is the case where CI grades least and the local spine grades most. A worker reasoning "CI arms nothing here, so my local gates are cheap" reaches the opposite of the truth.

THE GUARD, for both roles:

  * **Worker**: on a change whose classifier output is 0 of 29, run `scripts/test-fast-pr.sh --plan` and READ what it intends before executing. `--plan` exits before running anything (verified). If the plan shows `node=true` or `jvm=true` and you were told not to take the lane, do not run the bare form.
  * **Coordinator**: for any item on root `scripts/**`, either grant the lane or forbid the bare spine explicitly. "You do not need the lane" is not sufficient — it names the resource, not the command that takes it.

DO NOT REPAIR THIS BY NARROWING THE SPINE'S FALLBACK. Running more than necessary is the correct default for a local pre-checkin gate; the defect is entirely that nobody expects a `scripts/**` change to enter the shadow-cljs runtime. What is needed is the expectation, which is what this memory is.

RELATED, and the reason a census alone will not find this: the classifier must be handed PATHS, never revisions (CLAUDE.md item (v)) — handed revisions it reports every surface unaffected at exit 0, which is indistinguishable from the genuinely-unaffected reading that this trap depends on. A worker who misuses the classifier gets 0 of 29 for the wrong reason and draws the same false comfort.

A SKIPPED CHECK ROW IS THE JOB'S OWN `if:` GUARD, NEVER THE WORKFLOW'S TRIGGER FILTER — because a trigger filter suppresses the WHOLE RUN, so if it had fired there would be no run and therefore no row to read. Attributing a skip to `paths-ignore` is a confident wrong mechanism that supports a correct instruction, which is what lets it survive.

Measured 2026-09-21 at trunk 3b8ad76173, both halves, on `test.yml`'s `story-xray-browser` job (display name "Story/Xray browser gates (PR-smoke)"):

  1. The job carries a JOB-LEVEL `if:` that is a DISJUNCTION over three surfaces —
     story_xray_browser == 'true' || story_full_gate == 'true' || story_static_gate == 'true'
     (rf2-65ajl + rf2-9n2cv: three tiers, three conditions, any one alone opens the job).
  2. The sampled trunk run was built on 6682c437d0, whose ONLY file is
     `implementation/http/test/re_frame/http_privacy_test.clj` — NOT in `test.yml`'s
     `paths-ignore` list, which is why the run fired at all. Handing the classifier that
     path returns all three of those surfaces FALSE, so the disjunction was false and the
     job skipped.

So the run existing is itself the proof that the trigger filter did not fire. That is the free discriminator: READ WHETHER A RUN EXISTS BEFORE ATTRIBUTING A SKIP. A suppressed run leaves no rows; a guarded job leaves a SKIPPED row inside a run that happened.

WHY IT MATTERS RATHER THAN BEING PEDANTRY, and it cuts in the dangerous direction: from the trigger-filter mechanism a reader infers "on a commit whose paths are NOT ignored, the trunk run would grade my change" — and that is false, because the job-level surface guard applies on trunk exactly as on a PR. The wrong mechanism thus licenses treating a trunk run as confirmation, which is precisely the reading the correct mechanism forbids. Both mechanisms support the same instruction ("a skipped row is not a verdict"), so the error is invisible at the point of use and only bites one inference later.

`test.yml`'s `paths-ignore` is real and is push-only (`.beads/**`, `docs/**`, `spec/**`, `skills/**/*.md`, `tools/**/*.md`, `mkdocs.yml`, `mkdocs_hooks.py`, `TESTING.md`, `requirements.txt`), with `pull_request` deliberately unfiltered so required checks cannot hang pending. So on a PR the trigger filter can NEVER be the explanation for anything, and every PR-side skip is a job guard by construction.

THIS IS THE "A SURFACE IS NOT A JOB" RULE REACHED FROM THE OTHER END. That rule says a job's `if:` may be a disjunction over several surfaces, so "surface X is false" does not license "the job named X did not run". The same disjunction is what makes a skip a job-level fact: to conclude the job was skipped you need ALL the disjuncts false, not the one whose name matches. Keep both directions.

THE GUARD: to explain a skipped row, read the job's `if:` in the workflow YAML and classify the commit's PATHS against it. Do not reason from the trigger block — and never from a display name, which names one surface while the guard may test three.

Found by a method-reread loop rather than by the failure biting: the wrong mechanism had already been written into a live dispatch brief, and the instruction it supported was correct, so nothing downstream had gone wrong yet. The "naming the right authority is not applying it" shape — the same session had put A SURFACE IS NOT A JOB into another worker's brief and then failed to apply it here.

THE MATRIX-CHANGE DETECTOR WATCHES `.github/workflows/` AND THE CLASSIFIER LIVES IN `.github/scripts/`, SO EVERY SURFACE-GLOB CHANGE IS INVISIBLE TO IT — and the band cannot betray one either, because a SKIPPED job still posts a rollup row, so widening a surface flips a row from SKIPPED to executed under an unchanged name with the row COUNT unmoved.

Measured 2026-09-21 at trunk 4a062b91dc. `LAST=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- .github/workflows/)` returns `b9220b6dc2` (2026-09-16), while the last change to `.github/scripts/` is `6a6e31b039` (2026-09-21) — five days newer and completely outside the detector's pathspec. Over the last 300 commits touching each tree, **111 of 186** `.github/scripts/` commits touched NO workflow file at all. Control both ways: both commit sets are non-empty, and the workflows-side derivation reproduces its own rf2-vwst8 control at 1/0.

**SCOPE THIS PRECISELY — IT IS NOT A HOLE IN THE FIVE CLAUSES, AND SAYING SO WOULD BE THE OVERSHOOT.** A classifier change alters WHICH jobs execute, never which ROWS appear. So the band is unchanged (clause 1 holds), clause 2 accepts `skipped` exactly as it accepts `success`, and the check SET really was computed against the trunk matrix (clause 5 holds). Run the overshoot test on this very claim: if "there is a blind spot" were false, a surface widening would have to move the band or add a row — it does neither, so the blind spot is real, and it is confined to COVERAGE DEPTH rather than to the criterion.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY AT RISK: a PR graded BEFORE a surface widens ran fewer real jobs than trunk would run on it now, and nothing in the rollup says so — same total, same names, same colours, with skips where executions would now be. The merge is still correct on the criterion as written; what you cannot see is that the change was graded less deeply than the current trunk would grade it.

WHY THIS IS LIVE RATHER THAN THEORETICAL: rf2-xurxw's measured recommendation is exactly such a widening (arm `story_static_gate` wherever the Story/Xray browser job already opens, reusing `is_story_xray_runtime_path`). Its own numbers show the shape — 283 newly-armed commits and **0 new jobs** — which is this entry's mechanism stated in the language of a cost/benefit. If that widening lands, every PR in flight at that moment was graded under the narrower roster.

THE CHEAP DISCHARGE, when it matters: alongside the workflows-side control, ask whether `.github/scripts/` moved in the same range — `git log --format=%H <merge-base>..origin/main -- .github/scripts/` — and on a hit, re-run the PR's checks rather than reasoning about the band, which cannot answer. This is a SUPPLEMENT to the rf2-vwst8 control, never a replacement: that control is about whether the workflow matrix moved and is correct for what it asks.

DO NOT SILENTLY WIDEN THE `LAST` DERIVATION TO COVER BOTH TREES. It would change what "the matrix changed" MEANS in the merge criterion — from "the set of checks moved" to "the set or its execution conditions moved" — and that redefinition needs a ruling, not a patch. Whoever rules on rf2-xurxw is the natural place to settle it, since that ruling creates the first instance.

RELATED, from the same family: the memory `clause5-zero-is-necessary-not-sufficient` records that a surface widening adds no job key and moves no band, and prescribes a second grep over the workflow diff for `detect_changed_surfaces|strategy:|matrix:|paths:|paths-ignore:`. That second command CANNOT see this case either, for the same reason as the first — it greps the `.github/workflows/` diff, and the classifier is not in it. So the two entries are one mechanism reached through two procedures, and neither procedure's pathspec reaches the file that decides the answer.

CAPTURING `bd … --json > file 2>&1` CORRUPTS THE JSON INTERMITTENTLY, because the Dolt engine writes INFO LOG LINES to stderr at unpredictable moments and the `2>&1` splices them into the document — valid JSON followed by log text, which every parser rejects as trailing data.

Measured live 2026-09-21 at trunk 8bbdfa4f66. `bd list --limit 0 --json > board.json 2>&1` produced 667,929 bytes over 493 lines: the array closed correctly with `]` on line 490, and line 491 began

    time="2026-09-21T18:23:21+10:00" level=info msg="beginning conjoin of database" generation=new pkg=store.noms upstream_len=257

Python's `json.load` refused it with `JSONDecodeError: Extra data: line 491 column 1 (char 664178)`. The IDENTICAL command moments later, written as `> board4.json 2> board4.err`, parsed clean with **0 bytes** on stderr.

THE INTERMITTENCY IS THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY, and it is why the broken form survives use: the conjoin is a storage-maintenance event the engine schedules on its own, so the same command works dozens of times and then does not. Several earlier calls in that same session used the `2>&1` form and parsed fine. A failure to reproduce is therefore not evidence against this, and a success is not evidence that the form is safe.

IT FAILS LOUDLY WHERE A PARSER READS THE FILE — which is the good case, and the reason this is NOT one of CLAUDE.md's lettered instrument items, whose defining property is handing back a clean-looking answer. THE QUIET FAILURES ARE DOWNSTREAM OF THAT, and they are the reason to record it:

  * anything that GREPS or line-counts the captured file instead of parsing it silently includes
    log lines in its census — the counts move, nothing errors;
  * a tolerant reader that takes only the first document sees correct data and never reports the
    tail, so the corruption is invisible until a stricter reader meets the same file;
  * the log line carries a TIMESTAMP and the token `generation=`, both of which look enough like
    data to survive a careless eye in a diff or a log tail.

THE GUARD, and it is one character of discipline: REDIRECT STDOUT ONLY when the output is a document you intend to parse — `> file.json` with stderr left alone, or `2> file.err` when you want to keep it. Then READ the stderr file's byte count rather than assuming it is empty; 0 bytes is the ordinary reading and a non-zero one is the engine talking, not an error. `2>&1` remains correct for capturing a GATE's combined human-readable output, where interleaving is the point — the rule is about documents, not about redirection.

THIS GENERALISES PAST `bd`: any tool that emits a structured document on stdout AND diagnostics on stderr is defeated by `2>&1`, and a storage engine, a JVM, a package manager or a linter can all decide to say something on stderr at a moment of its own choosing. The project already records the inverse hazard for `gh` (item (k): read the FIELD with a JSON parser rather than the rendering); this is the capture-side companion — getting the parser right cannot save a document that was corrupted on the way into the file.

RELATED: CLAUDE.md's checkpoint sequence forbids piping any of its steps because a pipeline's exit status is its last command's. That rule is about the STATUS; this one is about the CONTENT, and the two are independent — a `2>&1` capture preserves the exit code perfectly while destroying the document.

REFINEMENT, measured 2026-09-21 the same day, on `gh` — TWO SHAPES, AND ONLY ONE IS QUIET.

  * DOCUMENT-THEN-NOISE (the `bd` case above): a COMPLETE valid document, then diagnostics appended.
    A strict parser refuses; a tolerant reader, a grep or a line count silently accepts the first
    document and never reports the tail. This is the quiet one and the reason this entry exists.
  * NOISE-INSTEAD-OF-DOCUMENT (the `gh` case): measured, `gh pr view <n> --json state` on SUCCESS
    writes 19 bytes to stdout and **0 bytes to stderr**, so `2>&1` is harmless there; on FAILURE it
    writes **0 bytes to stdout** and 96 bytes to stderr (`GraphQL: Could not resolve to a
    PullRequest...`) at exit 1. Under `2>&1` the file then holds no JSON at all, and every reader
    refuses loudly. Unpleasant, never silent.

So the class generalises exactly as stated, but the DANGER does not distribute evenly across it:
worry about a tool that finishes its document and keeps talking, which is a storage or build engine
far more often than a REST client.

AND THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS IS TO THE OBVIOUS REMEDY, because reaching for `2>/dev/null` trades
this hazard for CLAUDE.md item (h)'s — the natural probe suppressing the only evidence. A discarded
stderr means a failing call's explanation is gone and an empty stdout reads like an honest empty
