answer. **Capture stderr to its OWN file and READ ITS BYTE COUNT** — `> out.json 2> out.err`, then
`wc -c < out.err`. Zero is the ordinary reading; non-zero is the engine or the tool talking, and it
costs one line to see rather than to assume.

A SUBTRACTIVE PLANT AGAINST A UNION OF PROJECTIONS IS A SILENT NO-OP — remove a name from ONE source and the union is unchanged, so the gate stays GREEN while the blob hash truthfully proves the source changed. This is the documented "a hash proves the SOURCE changed, not that the runtime ever saw it" trap, reached through a mechanism the planter can compute in advance instead of discovering from a green sabotage run.

Measured 2026-09-21 under rf2-gf2of. `tools/xray/test/day8/re_frame2_xray/panel_enum_guard_cljs_test.cljs` reconciles the panel enum against `mount-<panel>!` names parsed out of `007-UX-IA.md` **and** `008-Embedding-Contract.md`, and the macro **UNIONS** the two projections. Every name in 008 also appears in 007. So deleting one from 008 leaves the reconciled set identical and the lane green — and the worker, following a brief that said "break a rostered name in the spec", would have reported a guard that fired when nothing was ever broken.

**THE MAYOR'S BRIEF PRESCRIBED EXACTLY THE WRONG DIRECTION**, and the worker caught it by reading the macro before running anything rather than by being fooled by a green. That is the whole reason this is worth recording: the trap is ordinarily discovered by spending a run and misreading its result.

**THE RULE: CHOOSE THE PLANT'S DIRECTION FROM THE GUARD'S RECONCILIATION SHAPE, never from what intuitively counts as "breaking" the file.**

  * reconciles against a UNION of sources  -> ADD to one source (removal is absorbed by the others)
  * reconciles against an INTERSECTION     -> REMOVE from one source (an addition is absorbed)
  * BIDIRECTIONAL reconciliation           -> either direction works, but only against the side that
                                              is authoritative for that direction; adding is the
                                              safer default because an extra name with no code
                                              counterpart has nothing to absorb it

The measured repair here was to ADD: planting `mount-ghost-probe!` into one projection took the node lane to captured exit **1** with two failures naming it exactly, against clean and sabotage runs reporting IDENTICAL counts, so the blast radius was provably scoped. Restored and verified by default-form `git hash-object` against the committed blob, with plant count 0 afterwards.

**READ THE MATCH COUNT BEFORE THE RUN, AND IT DOES NOT SAVE YOU HERE.** The count read 1 — the anchor genuinely matched, the edit genuinely applied. A match count answers "did my edit land", and this trap lives entirely downstream of that, in whether the landed edit can change what the guard COMPUTES. So the free pre-run check is necessary and is not sufficient, and the sufficient one is reading the macro's combining operation.

**THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC AND FAVOURS THINKING FIRST.** A no-op plant costs a full gate run and then yields a green that reads as "my restore worked and the guard is fine" — the most reassuring possible wrong answer, arriving at the end of the verification step that exists to catch exactly this. Computing the combining operation costs one read of the macro.

GENERALISES past this guard to any gate that derives a set from several documents: a spec roster unioned across pages, a manifest merged from sidecars, a lint allowlist assembled from multiple config files, a ratchet floor summed over surfaces. Ask what the consumer COMBINES before you decide which way to break it.

A WORKER'S DRIVER SCRIPT THAT FINISHES ITS WORK BUT NEVER EXITS WEDGES ITS AGENT OPEN FOR DAYS, AND EVERY SYMPTOM IT PRODUCES POINTS AWAY FROM THE CAUSE. Measured end to end 2026-09-18 to 2026-09-21 on rf2-st7j0 / rf2-azxt5: cost was 70.6 hours of a held-open agent, a husk worktree, repeated spurious notifications into the coordinator's context, and a coordinator who asserted the opposite diagnosis out loud.

THE CAUSE, in the worker's own words: "it never called `System/exit`, so the JVM stayed alive on the test HTTP server's non-daemon threads after writing a complete log. The harness capped the shell, which is why that run and the one before it both got backgrounded despite finishing their work quickly." A JVM exits when its last NON-DAEMON thread ends; a test HTTP server, an agent pool or a scheduler started inside a driver script is exactly such a thread. THE SCRIPT COMPLETED AND WROTE ITS WHOLE LOG — only the process lingered.

THE GUARD, one line, and it belongs in any brief that has a worker drive a JVM from a script: END THE SCRIPT WITH `(shutdown-agents)` AND `(System/exit 0)`. Nothing else in the run needs to change.

THE SYMPTOM CHAIN, because no single link names the cause and each is attributed elsewhere by default:
(1) the harness holds an agent open while it has LIVE BACKGROUND CHILDREN — its notification text says so in terms, "fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own" — so the agent cannot deliver its completion report, and its worktree therefore fails the section-4 reap test FOREVER while being perfectly reapable;
(2) the lingering JVM holds FILE HANDLES inside the worktree, so `remove-worker-worktree.sh` cannot complete and leaves a HUSK — loops.md's "Locked" refusal mode, which the method says is transient and to be retried, and which here would never clear on its own;
(3) the same agent RE-NOTIFIES on a cadence, each firing costing the coordinator a turn;
(4) any re-attempt artefacts look like FAILURES (here `EXIT=127` and a `sed` error on a log the worker had already deleted) while the underlying work was sound.

THE TELL THAT ACTUALLY DISCRIMINATES, and it is cheap: a CPU DUTY CYCLE near zero over a long wall time. Measured 115.0s and 117.3s of CPU across 70.4 HOURS = 0.045%. A process that is wedged, hung, or looping does not look like that; a process held open by an idle non-daemon thread does. Read it with `Get-Process` (`.CPU` against `StartTime`), not from a task list.

A SECOND TELL, for a coordinator reading its own roster: `ListAgents` showing exactly ONE subagent for a session that dispatched dozens, and that one the OLDEST. Any recency-retention explanation predicts the opposite. The inversion is the live children.

TWO WRONG INFERENCES THIS PRODUCED, both of which read as careful:
* "The transcript has not moved in three days, so the agent is dead." The transcript reading was CORRECT and the inference WRONG — AN AGENT'S REASONING AND AN AGENT'S PROCESSES DIE SEPARATELY, and a transcript can only see the first. The coordinator said "a gravestone, nothing is running" while four of its processes were live.
* "`clojure.main -i <script>` is sitting at a REPL prompt waiting on stdin." Inferred from the `-i` FLAG rather than measured, and it prescribes the wrong remedy (launch it differently) instead of the right one (exit cleanly). Both accounts predict the same 0.045% observable, which is why the flag-shaped guess survives inspection.

ATTRIBUTION TRAP FOR THE COORDINATOR: such processes present in a machine-wide lane census as unexplained "strays" and get written off as furniture tick after tick. ASK WHOSE THEY ARE — identify by ANCESTRY plus the script name and classpath roots on their own command line, which name the owning worktree outright. Here the parent chain ran to the coordinator's own `claude.exe`, and the ledger dispatched that worker seven minutes before the processes started.

KILLING THEM IS SAFE ONCE THE WORK HAS LANDED, AND THE KILL'S EXIT CODES LIE IN THE REASSURING-LOOKING DIRECTION: children-first from PowerShell, `Stop-Process` reported "Cannot find a process" for BOTH `clojure.exe` launchers, which was SUCCESS — a launcher exits the moment its JVM child dies. Grade the kill by a fresh census (here ROWS 8 -> 5, rows naming the worktree 4 -> 0), never by the status lines. The six `bash.exe` ancestors exited unaided.

AND THE PAYOFF CONFIRMS THE DIAGNOSIS WITHIN SECONDS: killing the children let the agent stop with no live background children, and it immediately delivered the completion report it had been holding for three days — "the work is complete and pushed ... Both worktrees are clean". Its own `duration_ms` read 254323068 (70.6h), matching the JVM wall time. So the reap test was satisfiable the whole time, and the thing blocking the report was the same thing blocking the removal.

REFINEMENT 2026-09-21, from a SECOND instance through a different door — orphaned `sh.exe` gate shells rather than a lingering JVM, and it corrects this entry's remedy.

Measured on the `simafter2-kmr2i` husk, whose item `rf2-kmr2i` was CLOSED (6308-char reason), whose branch was gone (0 refs) and whose directory held 0 entries: two `sh.exe` running `runchecks-simafter2-kmr2i.sh` from the coordinator's own scratchpad, 672 minutes old, parent dead so the elder was an ORPHAN. This entry's discriminating tell reproduced exactly — duty cycles of **0.0006%** and **0%** over 11.2 hours, i.e. idle-held rather than wedged or looping.

Killing them children-first from PowerShell worked and was graded by a fresh census, 2 rows naming the worktree -> 0, with the three Codex/MCP `node.exe` rows untouched.

**AND THE DIRECTORY WAS STILL `Device or resource busy` AFTERWARDS.** So the remedy above is NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT, and this is the correction: killing every holder you can SEE does not establish that you have killed every holder.

**THE INSTRUMENT IS THE DEFECT.** A census matching on COMMAND LINE finds only processes that NAME the path, which is a SUBSET — the same defect CLAUDE.md already records for the shadow-cljs lane census ("a worktree-path filter over command lines sees only a SUBSET of one build, so 'zero remain' can read true while the build lives"). A process holding a handle through its WORKING DIRECTORY, or through an inherited descriptor, names the path nowhere and is invisible to it. So `rows naming the worktree = 0` is not `holders = 0`, and reading it as such is how a kill gets graded as a success that did not clear the lock.

**WHAT THIS DOES AND DOES NOT CHANGE.** Killing the visible orphans is still right on its own terms — they were leaked, idle and belonged to a closed item, so they were pure cost. What changes is the INFERENCE afterwards: do not conclude the husk is now removable, and do not escalate to a recursive delete or a force flag on the strength of a clean process census. Retry the removal, and if it still refuses, the refusal is the authority — loops.md's "note it and retry" stands, and the entry above is right that such a lock "would never clear on its own" only once EVERY holder is gone.

A COMMAND-LINE CENSUS IS TRIAGE. To conclude, you need an instrument that enumerates HANDLES rather than command lines; absent one, the removal's own refusal is the only honest verdict.

A PROCESS CENSUS COUNTS ITSELF WHEN THE PATTERN APPEARS IN ITS OWN COMMAND LINE — AND THE SHADOW-CLJS LANE CHECK IS EXACTLY THAT PROBE (mayor, 2026-09-18).

MEASURED, both directions, on this box. Asking whether the machine-wide shadow-cljs exclusive was held:

  Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.CommandLine -match 'shadow-cljs|shadow.cljs' }

read 5 PROCESSES against a control of 9 java/node — a completely plausible "five workers are all building" answer at the exact moment five workers had just been dispatched and told not to build. Printing their command lines is what refuted it: the matches were MY OWN powershell probe plus the Git-Bash wrappers that spawned it, every one of them matching because the pattern STRING sits inside the command line being searched. Re-measured with the executable constrained and the pattern assembled so it cannot match itself:

  $pat = 'shadow' + '-cljs'
  Get-CimInstance Win32_Process | Where-Object { $_.Name -match '^(node|java)\.exe$' -and $_.CommandLine -match $pat }

read 0, against a live control of 8 node.exe/java.exe on the box — so the instrument can see processes and the zero is absence rather than a broken probe. THE LANE WAS FREE THE WHOLE TIME.

WHY IT EARNS A MEMORY RATHER THAN BEING TIDINESS: CLAUDE.md's shadow-cljs bullet instructs, in terms, to verify lane state BY EFFECT — "find the spawned process, filter on its OWN worktree path so it cannot touch a peer's, confirm zero remain". So this is the probe the protocol sends every worker and the coordinator to run, and the naive spelling of it is self-matching. The worktree-path filter that bullet prescribes is what accidentally immunises a worker's own version; the COORDINATOR's machine-wide variant has no such filter and is the exposed one.

THE DIRECTION IT FAILS IN, and it is the expensive one for a coordinator rather than the merely noisy one: it reports the exclusive as HELD when it is FREE. That does not wedge a build — it manufactures a disciplinary event. I was one step from messaging five workers to accuse them of starting builds they had been told to ask for, and from killing five healthy runs to "clear" a lane nobody held. A false positive here costs the fleet, not the lane.

THE GUARD, two parts, both needed:
  1. CONSTRAIN THE EXECUTABLE, not just the command line — a real shadow-cljs build is node.exe or java.exe, never powershell.exe or bash.exe.
  2. Keep the pattern out of its own command line where you can (assemble it, as above), and ALWAYS print the matches before acting on a non-zero count. A count alone cannot tell you it counted itself.
And take the control both ways, as ever: a zero means absence only beside a live count of processes the instrument CAN see.

GENERALISES PAST THIS LANE: any `ps`/`Win32_Process`/`pgrep` census for a token, run from a shell whose command line carries that token, counts its own pipeline. The classic `pgrep -f foo` self-match is the same defect on POSIX. Whenever a process census returns a small non-zero where you expected zero, suspect the probe before suspecting the fleet.

THE TRAP IS INVOCATION-DEPENDENT, measured both ways 2026-09-21 — which decides WHEN the guard above is needed, and explains a coordinator seeing honest zeros for a whole session and one false five in the middle of it.

  * A census run DIRECTLY through the PowerShell tool CANNOT self-count. Probed with a sentinel token
    unique to the running script: rows whose command line contained it read **0**, against positive
    controls of 3 rows naming 'codex' and 15 naming 'node' and a negative control of 0. So that tool
    does not expose the script text in any process command line, and a `-like '*shadow-cljs*'` filter
    written there does not match itself.
  * A census NESTED THROUGH BASH DOES self-count, because the pattern lands in the spawned
    `powershell -Command "..."` argument. Measured the same day hunting a husk's holder: the nested
    form read **5** rows naming the target where the non-self answer was **0** — the two real holders
    had already been killed, and all five hits were the probe and its shells.

So the same logical query is trustworthy in one invocation and self-matching in the other, with nothing
in the output saying which you ran. **Assume self-matching whenever the pattern travels through an
argument** — a nested shell, a `-Command`, a `-c`, an `--exec` — and assume nothing when it does not.

A SECOND, INDEPENDENT REASON FOR GUARD 1 (constrain the executable): **a command-line census is blind
to a large minority of processes outright.** Measured on this box, **199 of 522 rows (38%) have NO
readable CommandLine** — svchost.exe x92, csrss.exe, WUDFHost.exe and friends, i.e. SYSTEM-owned
service processes. That blindness cannot hide a build here (**0 node.exe and 0 java.exe** sit in the
opaque set), and the NAME-keyed leg is immune to it by construction, which is why "constrain the
executable" is the load-bearing half of the probe and the command-line match is only the refinement.
Read the name count as the answer and the command line as the attribution.

PYTHON IS A CRLF PRODUCER ON WINDOWS AND `encoding='utf-8'` DOES NOT STOP IT — so a Python step that writes a file a SHELL loop reads hands every line back with a trailing carriage return, and `read -r` then fails a string comparison silently. CLAUDE.md item (e) names `jq` as the producer of this class; Python is a second one, and the idiom this project already teaches for the READ side does not cover the WRITE side.

Measured 2026-09-21 at trunk 5c32a6c482, three writers, same shell, `cat -A` on the output:

  * `print(...)` bare                                                    -> alpha^M$
  * `sys.stdout = io.TextIOWrapper(sys.stdout.buffer, encoding='utf-8')` -> alpha^M$
  * `... TextIOWrapper(..., encoding='utf-8', newline='')`               -> alpha$

THE MIDDLE ROW IS THE WHOLE POINT. That wrapper is the exact line CLAUDE.md item (k) prescribes — correctly, for READING a `bd` JSON field without a cp1252 UnicodeDecodeError and for PRINTING U+2192 to a cp1252 console. It fixes the codec and says nothing about newline translation: `TextIOWrapper` with the default `newline=None` translates every `\n` written into `os.linesep`, which is `\r\n` here. So the reader who applied item (k) most carefully is the one who believes this is already handled.

The shell consequence, measured both ways: a file holding `x\r\n` read through `while read -r v` compares UNEQUAL to `x`, while `x\n` compares equal. No error, no exit code, nothing on stderr.

IT FIRED LIVE ON THE CHECK-COUNT BAND, which is the worst place available, and in the DANGEROUS direction. A `§5` band re-measurement built the PR list with a Python heredoc redirected to a file, then looped `git merge-base --is-ancestor "$LAST" "$oid"` over it. Every oid carried `\r`, so `--is-ancestor` refused all twelve and the tick read "0 of 12 PRs qualify". That is indistinguishable from the honest case CLAUDE.md already prices — too few qualifying PRs to measure the band — whose prescribed next move is to WIDEN THE WINDOW, which reaches back past the matrix change and measures the OLD band, inventing exactly the phantom band the file warns about. The tell was not the zero; it was that TWO of the excluded PRs had been merged BY THIS SESSION weeks after the matrix commit, which is impossible. Re-run directly with no pipeline, both read AFTER; with `tr -d '\r'`, ten of ten qualified and the band measured 88, the figure being carried.

THE GUARD, and the first half is the cheap one:

  * When a Python step writes a file another tool will PARSE, pass `newline=''` to the wrapper, or write bytes (`open(p,'wb')`), or `tr -d '\r'` on the consuming side. Deciding which side is authoritative first is item (e)'s rule and still applies.
  * Prefer not producing the seam at all: `gh ... --jq` piped straight into the loop with `tr -d '\r'` needed no Python step here.
  * TAKE THE CONTROL FROM A CASE WHOSE ANSWER YOU ALREADY KNOW. A uniform answer over a list is the tell — twelve exclusions in a row is not data, it is a broken predicate — and the discriminator was a row whose truth was independently certain (a PR this session merged itself). A control drawn from the same broken pipeline would have agreed with the failure.

GENERALISES past ancestry tests to anything where a Python step hands identifiers to a shell: branch names into `git update-ref`, ids into `bd show`, paths into a `for` loop, shas into `gh`. CLAUDE.md item (e) already records that `bd show` answers a CR-suffixed id with an ERROR OBJECT on stdout rather than the expected array, so the same carriage return produces a different confusing failure at each callee.

RELATED AND NOT THE SAME: item (o), backslash halving in the Bash tool's command text, fired in the SAME command — an inline `.replace('/','\\\\')` arrived halved and died at `SyntaxError`. That one is loud and this one is silent, which is why they are worth keeping apart.

A POST-MERGE NAME CENSUS CANNOT TELL A FIX FROM THE FAULT IT NAMES — because a correct repair very often KEEPS OR ADDS the offending token, in the routing line, the parenthetical or the explicit denial that the repair had to write. So "the bad name is still there" is the EXPECTED reading of a good change, and the mayor's after-each-merge drill — verify that what you routed into the change landed in the diff — misfires in the direction that manufactures a defect hunt against work that is correct.

Measured 2026-09-21/22 across two merges in one session, three instances, every one a false alarm:

  * `reg-event-db` predicted 0, read 1. The fix REPLACED it as a trigger and added the routing
    line "a v1 name in the prompt is that skill's trigger, not this one's — `reg-event-db`,
    `reg-event-fx` … route them to re-frame-migration", which must name the forms to route them.
  * `npm install -g` predicted 0, read 2. Both survivors were the "(Once published: …)"
    parenthetical the brief itself had required be kept.
  * `machine-meta` predicted 0, read 8 files. It is the MCP TOOL's own legitimate name; what the
    finding removed was the claim that it routes through a VAR of that name, and the repaired
    descriptor says in terms "there is no machine-meta accessor".

THE SHAPE IS NOT "the probe was sloppy" — it is that the QUESTION CHANGED and the probe did not. A finding says a token is used in the wrong ROLE (a trigger, a route target, an accessor). The repair changes the role and usually must still mention the token to explain what it is no longer. A presence probe answers "is the string here", which was never the question, and it answers it correctly.

THE GUARD: probe the ROLE, not the token, and the spelling that carries the role is usually longer and qualified.

  * not `machine-meta` but `re-frame.machines/machine-meta` — the qualified var — and better still
    ask whether a DEFINITION exists (`\(def(n)? <name>` read 0 anywhere in the tree).
  * not `rf/` but `form: "(rf/` — the token in the published position that the finding was about.
    That probe read 0 files at trunk while 33 files still carried prose `rf/`, which is the
    expected and correct outcome.
  * where the role cannot be expressed as a pattern, READ THE LINE. Three lines were read here and
    each settled its case in seconds.

AND TAKE THE CONTROL FROM THE SURVIVORS RATHER THAN FROM THE ABSENCE. The useful control is not "does the instrument work" — it plainly does — but "what are the remaining occurrences, and is each one a citation, a denial or a genuine leftover?" Listing them is cheap (8 files here) and is the only step that discriminates. A count cannot.

THE COST IS ASYMMETRIC AND IS WHY THIS EARNS A MEMORY. The false alarm arrives at the END of a merge, after the change is already on trunk, when the reflex is to suspect the merge. It invites reopening a correctly closed item, or dispatching a worker to "finish" a fix that is complete — which is the defect-manufacturing register CLAUDE.md prices for item (p) and item (x), reached through the verification step rather than through a gate.

RELATED: CLAUDE.md item (g) records the same family from the other end — a census treating PROSE as evidence, contaminated in both directions, where `\b` matched across a hyphen and a domain term answered for a mutation call. Item (f) records a grep matching a record that MENTIONS an id rather than the one that IS it, with the remedy "select on the identity field". This is that remedy applied to a verification rather than to a lookup: select on the ROLE, never on the name.

NOT a reason to skip the drill. Verifying that routed work landed caught real things this session; what is wrong is only the inference from a non-zero count.

A SURFACE CLASSIFIER ANSWERS "WHICH CI JOBS WILL RUN", NOT "WHICH GATES GRADE MY CHANGE'S BEHAVIOUR" — and for a tree that is on another lane's SOURCE-PATHS the two answers differ, so a gate nomination derived from the classifier can UNDERSTATE coverage and send a worker to verify compilability when the real grading is behavioural.

Measured 2026-09-22 at trunk b0d5419609, found by the worker on rf2-fn0kx.7 against a brief of mine that was wrong.

THE CASE. A mayor brief for an `examples/real-apps/realworld_http` change nominated `implementation/scripts/check-examples-compile.cjs` (the derived compile sweep, 58 builds) because the classifier arms `examples_compile` for that path. That nomination is not wrong, it is SHORT:

  * `../examples/real-apps` is on `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn`'s top-level `:source-paths`
    (its own comment at the :examples/realworld-resources build says "already on :source-paths").
  * Therefore example production source is on the `:node-test` classpath, and test namespaces
    REQUIRE it: 26 tracked test files under implementation/ reference realworld, and
    `re-frame.realworld-cljs-test` says so in its own docstring.
  * Two of that namespace's cases sit DIRECTLY on the change's deliverable — "a save that replies
    after logout does not restore the session" and the account-switch twin — which was a
    cross-account settings-draft leak, the most serious finding on that board.

So `npm run test:cljs` graded the change BEHAVIOURALLY while the nominated gate graded only that it compiles. A worker running exactly what it was told would have reported a green that could not have failed on the defect it was fixing. Corroboration the worker noted: CI's last two pending checks for that diff were precisely the two gates it had run locally.

WHY THE CLASSIFIER CANNOT ANSWER THIS. It maps changed PATHS to CI surfaces — which jobs get scheduled. It knows nothing about classpaths, so it cannot tell you that a job scheduled for a DIFFERENT reason (the node test lane, armed here as `cljs_node_test`) will compile and exercise your files. Both facts were on screen: the classifier armed five surfaces including `cljs_node_test`, and the brief still nominated one. THE SURFACE LIST WAS RIGHT AND THE NOMINATION DERIVED FROM IT WAS WRONG.

THE GUARD, and it is one question asked of the build config rather than of the classifier: IS THE TREE I AM EDITING ON ANY OTHER LANE'S SOURCE-PATHS OR CLASSPATH? Read `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn`'s `:source-paths` and the relevant `deps.edn` aliases, and ask whether any test namespace requires what you are changing. If yes, nominate that lane TOO and say which of the two grades behaviour.

  * cheap positive check: `git grep -l <example-ns-or-dir-token> -- 'implementation/**/*test*'`
  * the classifier remains right for what it answers; keep using it for WHICH JOBS RUN, and per
    CLAUDE.md item (v) keep handing it PATHS rather than revisions.

THIS IS THE MIRROR OF THE COVERAGE GAPS CLAUDE.md ALREADY CATALOGUES, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS. The rf2-uwa9r and rf2-z0pma paragraphs warn that a green lane is NOT evidence about something it never compiled — two green columns with a live red in the gap. This is the same seam read from the other side: a lane you did not nominate IS compiling your files, so the coverage you have is BETTER than the brief claims, and the cost is not a false green but a worker verifying the wrong property and a mayor believing a thinner gate set than exists. Both errors come from reasoning about coverage by FILE LOCATION instead of by what each lane actually compiles.

GENERALISES to any repo where one artefact's sources are added to another's build for fixtures or examples: testbeds, sample apps, docs-site demos, shared fixtures. The question is never "where does this file live" but "whose build reads it".

ROSTERING A CHANGE'S GATES BY NAME-GREPPING A GLOB OF GATE FILES IS WRONG IN BOTH DIRECTIONS AT ONCE — it OVER-reports gates that merely mention your surface in prose, and UNDER-reports every gate that lives outside the glob you chose. Measured twice in one session, on two different dispatches, by two different workers.

The method under indictment is the obvious one, and it looks careful because it takes a control:

    grep -l '<skill-or-surface>' scripts/check_skill_*.py     # and a nonsense control reading 0

CASE 1 (rf2-ikbgk.7, xray). The roster read THREE gates and a broader name-grep returns FOUR: `check_gate_scheduling.py` matches on an incidental comment about the preload bundle. Over-report; the three named were right.

CASE 2 (rf2-ikbgk.3, re-frame-migration). Wrong BOTH ways in one roster:
  * OVER — `check_skill_implementor_partition_drift.py` matched and does NOT cover this surface.
    Its single hit is the ENGLISH WORD at line 59, in prose about `:reply-to` addressing.
  * UNDER — two ratchets that DO grade the diff were missed entirely, because they do not live
    under `check_skill_*.py`: `scripts/check_retired_spellings.py` (retired-vocabulary scan,
    permitted count zero) and `scripts/check_inject_cofx_residue.py`. The worker found and ran
    both; both exit 0.

WHY THE TWO ERRORS HAVE DIFFERENT COSTS, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH REMEMBERING. The over-report is cheap and self-correcting: a worker runs a gate that turns out not to care, reads 0, and loses a minute. **The under-report is the dangerous half** — it is the "gates nobody nominated" class, and it hands a worker a brief whose gate list is short in exactly the direction that lets a real regression through. Both dispatches were saved by workers who went looking beyond the list they were given, which is behaviour to keep asking for rather than a reason to trust the list.

THE GUARD, and it is two questions rather than one pattern:
  * WHICH FILES does the gate ENUMERATE? Read the gate's own roster/glob, not the gate's prose. A
    gate that enumerates by glob (`*/SKILL.md`, `rglob *.md`) covers you whether or not it names
    you; a gate with a hardcoded list covers you only if you are IN the list.
  * WHAT ELSE grades this path? Do not scope the search to one directory or one filename shape.
    `scripts/check_*.py` is wider than `scripts/check_skill_*.py`, and the ratchets, the
    workflow-level source-scans and the lane tests are all outside both.

And keep the standing rule from the dispatch template rather than replacing it with a better list: the worker is obliged to FIND the gates its diff arms, and a brief must not hand it an enumeration as though the enumeration were complete. Say which gates you believe apply AND that the list is not exhaustive — a brief that reads as complete is what stops a worker looking.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: the memory `a-surface-classifier-names-jobs-not-the-gates-that-grade-behaviour` records a different way the same nomination goes short — a lane compiling your files because they sit on its `:source-paths`, which no name-grep of any gate file could reveal. Together: the classifier tells you which JOBS run, a gate-file grep tells you which gates MENTION you, and neither tells you which gates GRADE you.

SHARPEST INSTANCE OF THE UNDER-REPORT, because it defeated the file that teaches the discipline: CLAUDE.md states that both link gates skip absolute `http(s)` targets, resting on a census of `github.com` over `check_doc_slugs.py` that correctly reads ZERO — while that script carries `_github_slugs()` and `_in_repo_github_url_problems()` and validates in-repo GitHub anchors, as proved by it going red on one. A zero from a name search is the absence of a SPELLING, never the absence of a CAPABILITY.

FINDING A ROSTER ERROR IN ONE BRIEF DOES NOT FIX IT IN THE BRIEFS ALREADY IN FLIGHT, AND NOTHING BRINGS IT ROUND. Measured twice in one session, on the SAME gate file, by the same coordinator, minutes apart — caught the second time, shipped the first.

THE INSTANCE. Two dispatches, about forty minutes apart, both asking "which gates grade this skill?" and both reaching for `grep -rl <skill> scripts/`:

  * Dispatch A (rf2-ikbgk.5, re-frame2-improver). The grep returned `check_skill_eval_docs.py`, and
    the brief told the worker that gate "names your skill in a HARDCODED TARGETS registry" and
    grades it on three axes — making finding 1(c) look like a five-place change and inviting the
    worker to hold it.
  * Dispatch B (rf2-ikbgk.8, re-frame2-pair-retro). The same grep returned `check_skill_mcp_drift.py`
    and the coordinator, this time, OPENED THE FILE: both hits were NOTE comments recording that the
    skill is deliberately absent from that gate's rosters. The brief said so and told the worker not
    to nominate or plant into it.

The identical defect sat in dispatch A's brief while dispatch B's was being written. `TARGETS` in
`check_skill_eval_docs.py` reads `(_REFRAME2, _XRAY)`, and lines 209-215 carry
`NOTE: re-frame2-improver is deliberately absent from TARGETS (rf2-hpq96d)` — so the grep hit was a
comment about non-coverage, exactly as in dispatch B. The worker refuted the brief, found the axis
that DOES grade it (A4 identity-uniqueness, which globs every `skills/*/evals/evals.json`), planted
there instead, and landed the fixture as the one-file change its own `evals/README.md` documents.

WHY THE CLASS IS DIFFERENT FROM THE ONE ALREADY RECORDED. The memory
`gate-rostering-by-name-grep-over-a-glob-is-wrong-in-both-directions` covers the ERROR. This covers
the PROPAGATION: a coordinator who learns the lesson mid-flight fixes only the brief in front of it,
because a dispatched brief is a file already read by an agent and is not on any list the coordinator
rereads. `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md` §5 says the fix is "bounded in change, not in search —
a defect in one place usually has siblings", and the sibling here was not in the tree, it was in a
worker's hands.

THE GUARD, and it is a coordinator action rather than a better pattern:
  * When a roster claim in a brief turns out wrong, IMMEDIATELY ask which other briefs dispatched in
    this session made a claim of the same shape, and message those workers. A live worker can be
    messaged; a consumed brief cannot be edited.
  * A brief's gate roster should say which claims were verified BY READING THE GATE'S OWN ROSTER and
    which were taken from a name search, so the worker knows which to distrust. "Treat this list as
    incomplete" is not enough — it warns of omissions, not of confident wrong entries.
  * Prefer asking the gate to ENUMERATE (run it, read its `TARGETS`/glob) over asking whether it
    MENTIONS. A gate that prints a row for your skill is grading it; a gate that merely contains its
    name may be recording that it does not.

COST ASYMMETRY, which is why this is worth a memory rather than a shrug. The over-report is not
free here: it did not merely waste a gate run, it carried a false SIZE estimate ("this is a
five-place change") that was an argument for HOLDING a finding. A worker that trusted it would have
shipped less work and recorded a reason that read as careful. The under-report remains the more
dangerous half in general; this is the over-report doing real damage by a second route.

WHAT THE WORKER DID RIGHT, worth asking for explicitly in briefs: it treated the ITEM as governing
over the brief where the two disagreed, said so plainly, and proved it at source. Three workers in
this wave have now corrected a gate roster the coordinator handed them.

A NEGATIVE CENSUS INHERITS THE SCOPE IT WAS RUN AT, AND RELAYING ONE YOU DID NOT RUN LAUNDERS THAT SCOPE INTO A UNIVERSAL. Measured on this project 2026-09-22, at the cost of a false statement to the operator.

THE INSTANCE. A worker measured "no gate enforces the 16 KB leaf ceiling" by searching `scripts/` for `16384`, `16 KB` and `leaf size`, against a live control (`def main` matching 48 files). For that scope the result was CORRECT. The coordinator relayed it — into a tracker note, into a close reason, and into a report to the operator — as the unqualified claim that nothing enforces the ceiling.

It is false. `skills/re-frame2-setup/tests/setup_drift_test.clj` carries the deftest `every-leaf-meets-the-family-byte-ceiling`, asserting `(<= (committed-byte-size f) 16384)` over every reference leaf, citing `skills/README.md` and the closed P1 `rf2-rc0yh` AC2 as its authority, and running under `bb` in CI's `skills-structural` job. A second and different ceiling lives in `scripts/check_skill_migration_o1617_router_drift.py` as `MAX_LEAF_LINES = 60`.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY WRONG ANSWER, and this is the part worth carrying:

  * A POSITIVE claim carries its own evidence — "this gate greps that file" can be checked by opening
    the file. A NEGATIVE claim carries only the absence, and absence is a fact about the SEARCH, never
    about the tree. The scope is the entire content of the claim, and it is exactly what does not
    travel when the claim is quoted.
  * Relaying is worse than running a narrow search yourself. Run your own and you at least know where
    you looked; relay someone else's and you inherit a boundary you never saw. The coordinator could
    not have said, when challenged, which directories the claim covered.
  * It fails in the REASSURING direction for the question it usually answers. "Nothing enforces this"
    licenses treating a convention as unpoliced and asking the operator to rule on something the tree
    had already decided — here, the byte convention, which `committed-byte-size`'s own docstring
    settles as LF-normalised while naming the exact CRLF error the coordinator had made.

THE SHARPEST PART: THE HIDING PLACE HAD BEEN FOUND ONE TICK EARLIER, IN THE SAME SESSION, AND WAS RECORDED AS AN ANECDOTE INSTEAD OF BEING ADDED TO THE SEARCH. A worker on a different item had just discovered that the gate with real teeth on its diff was a `bb` test inside a skill's own `tests/` directory, invisible to any search of the gate folder. The coordinator wrote that into a close reason — and then, one tick later, relayed a negative census scoped to exactly the folder that discovery had just shown to be incomplete.

THE GUARD, two halves:

  * BEFORE RELAYING A NEGATIVE CLAIM, ask what scope produced it, say that scope out loud in the
    relay, and widen at least one axis yourself. "No gate in `scripts/` enforces X" is a publishable
    sentence; "no gate enforces X" is a different and much stronger one, and the gap between them is
    where this defect lives.
  * WHEN A HIDING PLACE IS DISCOVERED, ADD IT TO THE SEARCH RATHER THAN TO THE STORY. A newly found
    location for gates, tests or enforcement belongs in the next census's pattern, not only in the
    write-up of the item that found it. Known hiding places in this tree so far: a skill's own
    `tests/` tree (`bb` suites looped by `skills-structural`), a gate's `--self-test` fixtures, and
    a `MAPPINGS`/`TARGETS` roster that names a surface only to record that it is deliberately
    EXCLUDED.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: `gate-rostering-by-name-grep-over-a-glob-is-wrong-in-both-directions` is about building a roster for one item; `a-roster-error-found-in-one-brief-is-not-fixed-in-briefs-already-in-flight` is about propagating a correction to live workers. This one is about the coordinator's own speech act — quoting somebody else's measurement as if it were its own, and stripping the scope on the way through.

ENUMERATING A SUBTREE AND REPORTING IT AS THE PARENT'S TAXONOMY MANUFACTURES A CONFIDENT NONEXISTENCE CLAIM — and the refutation was inside the very document I was correcting. Mayor error, measured 2026-09-22, caught by the worker I had briefed.

THE INSTANCE. Correcting `skills/re-frame2/spec/inputs.md:73`, whose sentence excludes "the fundamentals or pattern leaves" from consuming `tools/**`, I censused `skills/re-frame2/references/*`, found four subdirectories — `cross-cutting`, `fundamentals`, `state-machines`, `tooling` — and wrote into the dispatch brief, in bold:

  "pattern leaves" names a directory that does not exist.

It exists. `skills/re-frame2/patterns/` holds FOURTEEN leaves and is a SIBLING of `references/`, not a child of it. My enumeration root was one level too deep, so the directory was not missing — it was outside the walk. 0 of the 14 cite `tools/`, so that half of the sentence was true, and the word needed no decision at all. I had told the worker to "decide what it meant before you rewrite it; do not simply delete the word" — advice that was only harmless by luck.

THE PART WORTH CARRYING, because it is what makes this different from an ordinary scoping slip:

  * A ZERO FROM A SEARCH IS A FACT ABOUT THE SEARCH. Converting it to "X does not exist" is a
    POSITIVE assertion about the tree, and it is strictly stronger than the evidence. `find` under
    `references/` can never see a sibling of `references/`, so no amount of care INSIDE that walk
    could have corrected it. The defect is the choice of root, which is invisible to every control
    run within it.
  * THE DOCUMENT UNDER REPAIR CONTAINED THE REFUTATION. `inputs.md` §6 refers to `patterns/` twice.
    I was editing that file, quoting line 73 of it, and the disproof sat a few sections below in the
    same document. When correcting a document, READ IT WHOLE before asserting that something it
    mentions does not exist — the text you are fixing is a primary source about its own subject
    matter, and it is the cheapest control available.
  * IT FAILS IN THE AUTHORITATIVE DIRECTION. A brief that says "this names a nonexistent directory"
    reads as the most rigorous line in the document. It invites the worker to delete the word, which
    would have shipped a NEW false claim in place of the old one, in a file whose whole purpose is
    to say accurately what the skill consumes.

SECOND, INDEPENDENT ERROR IN THE SAME CENSUS, and it is CLAUDE.md item (g) exactly: I counted the literal `tools/` per leaf and reported `references/state-machines` as having one leaf that cites it. The single match is the substring inside the ENGLISH PHRASE `humans/tools/AIs` at `reg-machine.md:145`. Not an incidental reference to the tree — not a reference to the tree at all. I had even flagged that row to the worker as "a judgment call I am handing you", which dressed a measurement error up as a question of taste, so the worker had to do the work to dissolve it. Same class at `evals/README.md:29`, where `agents-and-tools/` sits inside a URL.

THE GUARD, two halves:
  * NAME YOUR ENUMERATION ROOT OUT LOUD when you report a census, and state the claim at that scope:
    "0 of the leaves under `references/`" is publishable; "the directory does not exist" is a
    different and much stronger sentence. If the conclusion is about a PARENT, walk the parent.
  * BEFORE ASSERTING SOMETHING DOES NOT EXIST, grep for the name itself across the tree rather than
    inferring absence from a structural walk — one `git ls-files | grep patterns` would have cost
    nothing and settled it.

"THE FILE CONTAINS WHAT THE GATE INSPECTS" MUST BE READ AT THE GRANULARITY OF THE THING'S KIND, NOT ITS CATEGORY — a page can carry a link, and both link gates still inspect nothing. Mayor error, measured 2026-09-22, refuted by the worker's plant.

THE INSTANCE. Briefing a one-sentence fix to `docs/core/25-from-re-frame-v1.md:21`, I wrote: "Your paragraph carries a relative link into `skills/`, so both are live for you" — meaning `check_doc_slugs.py` and `mkdocs build --strict`. I reasoned from CATEGORY: the file is under `docs/`, the gates' root includes `docs/`, the paragraph has a link, therefore graded.

The worker did not believe it. It broke that link deliberately (predicted match 1, measured 1) and **BOTH GATES STAYED GREEN** on a plant that had genuinely applied — `check_doc_slugs.py` exit 0 with empty output, mkdocs exit 0. Two independent, deliberate blindnesses, each documented in its own source:

  * `mkdocs_hooks.py` rewrites `](../../skills/<anything>)` to a GitHub blob URL BEFORE MkDocs
    resolves links, so there is nothing left for the build to resolve.
  * `check_doc_slugs.py` skips any destination that is not a `.md` FILE — this link names a
    DIRECTORY. Its own comment block is headed "THE DECLARED GAPS, all measured against the
    renderer", so the skip is declared, not accidental.

It then ran two further plants to separate mechanism from blindness, which is the part worth copying: a broken ANCHOR elsewhere took the slug gate to exit 1 naming file/line/anchor (so the gate does read this file), and a broken `.md` TARGET took it to exit 1 with BROKEN TARGET (so it does grade targets of the right kind). Only with those two reds is the first green attributable to the link's KIND rather than to the gate not seeing the file.

WHY THIS IS A REFINEMENT AND NOT A NEW RULE. CLAUDE.md § Build & Test already says: before nominating a gate, check the file CONTAINS what that gate inspects, and where it does not, say so and verify by hand (rf2-9h0f9). That rule is right and it is the one I broke. What this instance adds is the GRANULARITY at which "contains" has to be read:

  * NOT "does the file have links?" — mine did.
  * BUT "does the file have a link OF THE KIND this gate resolves?" — an in-repo `.md` target, an
    anchor, an external URL and a bare directory are four different kinds, and a gate may grade some
    and skip others by design.

The same sharpening applies past links: "has tests" vs "has tests this runner selects" (a namespace suffix decides that here), "has Clojure" vs "has Clojure in the branch this lane compiles" (a reader conditional decides that).

IT FAILS IN THE REASSURING DIRECTION AND IT FAILS IN A BRIEF. A coordinator asserting "both gates are live for you" tells the worker its change is covered, which is exactly the claim that stops it verifying by hand. Here the worker verified anyway; the cost was zero only because of that.

THE GUARD: never assert that a gate grades a worker's specific change — state it as a claim to verify BY EFFECT, and prefer the instrumentation that settles it (instrument `open`/`read_text`, run the gate's `main()`, count how many of the changed files it opens; or plant at the exact construct and watch the colour). A plant that comes back GREEN is a result worth reporting, not a failed plant.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: `gate-rostering-by-name-grep-over-a-glob-is-wrong-in-both-directions` is about WHICH GATES exist for a surface; this is about whether a gate you correctly identified actually inspects the construct you changed. `enumerating-a-subtree-and-calling-it-the-parents-taxonomy` is the same family of error — claiming more than the measurement supports — reached through a census rather than a gate nomination.

LANE NEED IS A PROPERTY OF WHAT THE WORKER WILL RUN, NOT OF WHAT CI ARMS — and a surface classifier answers the second question, so using it to decide the first serialises work that could have run in parallel. Mayor drift, found by §5 axis 2 on 2026-09-22, after several ticks of enforcement.

THE RULE I WAS ENFORCING. "An examples slice needs the shadow-cljs lane, because examples changes arm `examples_compile`, which enters the shadow-cljs runtime." On that basis every slice of a seven-slice wave was queued behind a machine-wide exclusive, one at a time.

WHAT THE TREE ACTUALLY DOES. Measured with `.github/scripts/report-changed-surfaces.sh` handed PATHS: a leaf `.cljs` source arms `implementation_jvm`, `cljs_node_test`, `cljs_browser`, `examples_compile`, `cljs_prod`, `bundle_isolation` — and **a leaf `README.md` arms five of those same six**, as does a leaf `index.html`. The classifier keys on the path prefix, not the extension. So the premise is true: CI really does run the compile sweep for a markdown-only examples change.

AND THE CONCLUSION STILL DOES NOT FOLLOW. CI runs that sweep OFF THIS MACHINE. The lane is a MACHINE-WIDE exclusive, so what it protects is a LOCAL run. A worker needs it only when it intends to run such a gate itself — and it only has reason to do that when its diff could change the gate's COLOUR. A markdown-only diff cannot, so the honest move is to say which gate cannot move and why, and rely on CI.

A worker demonstrated exactly this unprompted and was right: holding the lane 20+ minutes against a queue, for a sweep whose colour its three-markdown-plus-comment-only-`.cjs` diff could not alter, would have been pure cost. It declared CI reliance in the PR body instead.

WHY THE CLASSIFIER IS THE WRONG INSTRUMENT HERE, AND THE METHOD ALREADY SAYS SO. `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md` §2 states it in one line — **"Quiet is a property of the whole set of gates an item arms — no single classifier describes that set"** — and pairs it with "hold the fleet thin on purpose and keep dispatching work whose gates leave the machine quiet". The document was right; I was misapplying it, and I reached for the classifier precisely because it LOOKS like the authority on what an item arms.

THE COST IS INVISIBLE, WHICH IS WHY IT RAN FOR SEVERAL TICKS. Over-serialising produces no error and no wrong answer — every merge stays correct. It shows up only as throughput: slices sitting in a queue behind a lane none of them needed. Nothing on screen ever says "this worker did not need the thing it waited for", so the rule never gets tested by its own failures.

THE CORRECTED RULE, decided per item at dispatch:
  * Read the slice's FINDINGS and ask what the repair will actually change.
  * Findings that land in compilable sources (`.cljs`/`.cljc`/`.clj`/`.edn`) -> the worker should run
    the lane gate locally -> grant the lane, serialise.
  * Findings that land in markdown, host pages or comments -> the local gate cannot change colour ->
    NO LANE, dispatch in parallel, and require the worker to SAY which gate it is relying on CI for
    and why that gate could not have moved.
  * Mixed -> decide on the compilable half; when genuinely unsure, grant the lane. The asymmetric
    cost favours granting: two holders wedge SILENTLY, while an unnecessary grant only costs queue
    time.

RELATED AND DISTINCT: the shadow-cljs bullet in CLAUDE.md § Workflow is about WHICH COMMANDS enter the runtime and how to tell (ask what a command ENTERS, not what it mentions) — that half is right and unchanged. This memory is one level up: even for a command that genuinely enters the runtime, whether a given ITEM needs to run it locally is a separate question, and the dispatch filter must ask it.

A BRIEF MUST NEVER STATE A GATE ROSTER AS COMPLETE — say what you found and require derivation, because the gates that do not carry your subject's NAME are invisible to the search that built the list. Mayor error, fourth of the same family in one session, measured 2026-09-22.

THE INSTANCE, and it is a clean double failure. Briefing the core-large examples slice (7GUIs + TodoMVC), I wrote in bold: "**Five PINNED WRAPPER TESTS grade these examples**", and listed five files under `implementation/core/test/re_frame/` whose names carry an example's name (`crud`, `flight_booker`, `todomvc`, `circle_drawer_undo`, `seven_guis_cells_parser`).

There are EIGHT. The worker found the three I missed, and they covered exactly what it changed:

  * `implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_generation_guard_cljs_test.cljs` — IN THE DIRECTORY I
    SEARCHED, invisible because its filename carries no example name. It is the real pin on the
    timer finding.
  * `implementation/core/test/re_frame/example_frame_scoping_cljs_test.cljs` — same directory, same
    reason; it pins all six seven_guis app-schemas.
  * `implementation/adapters/reagent/test/re_frame/todomvc_cljs_test.cljs` — A SECOND TREE. There are
    TWO files named `todomvc_cljs_test.cljs`; I found the `core` one and stopped.

So one roster violated both halves of the guard at once: wrong FILENAME SHAPE (generic names beat a name-keyed search) and wrong DIRECTORY SCOPE (a second tree). The population is large enough that this is not bad luck — 354 `_cljs_test.cljs` files live under `implementation/*/test/**`.

WHAT IT WOULD HAVE COST. The worker's own words: "a worker trusting the five would have believed the timer and adapter changes ungraded." It fails in the reassuring direction twice over — a short roster looks like a complete one, and the gates it omits are the ones whose subject is not in their name, which correlates with them being cross-cutting and therefore load-bearing.

CONCRETE REPO FACTS WORTH KEEPING, since they are what a name search cannot give you:

  * Example-pinning tests live in AT LEAST TWO TREES: `implementation/core/test/re_frame/` and
    `implementation/adapters/<substrate>/test/re_frame/`. The same basename can exist in both.
  * Some pins are named for the PROPERTY they enforce, not the example they cover —
    `example_generation_guard`, `example_frame_scoping`. These are exactly the cross-cutting ones.
  * Examples are test-free by lock (rf2-8cevm), which is WHY the pins live outside `examples/` and
    why a search rooted at the thing being changed can never find them.

THE REPAIR IS TO THE BRIEF'S GRAMMAR, NOT TO THE SEARCH. I keep getting the search a little better and the list stays short, because no search finds what is not named. So stop asserting rosters:

  * NEVER write "these N gates grade your change". Write "these are the ones I found; the list is
    NOT complete; derive your own and report the count you ran."
  * Prefer an instruction that cannot be short: "run every `scripts/check_*.py` and
    `scripts/check-*.sh`" beats any roster, and workers who did it reported 46/46 and 50/50 for
    trivial cost.
  * For test pins specifically, tell the worker to RUN the candidate suites BEFORE editing as well as
    after — a before reading both makes the after meaningful and surfaces pins the roster missed,
    because an unexpected red names the file for you.

RELATED AND ALREADY RECORDED: `gate-rostering-by-name-grep-over-a-glob-is-wrong-in-both-directions` states this class correctly and I violated it anyway — reading the rule is not applying it. This entry is the CONCRETION for this repo's example pins plus the briefing-grammar repair, which is the part that actually changes behaviour. Same family as `a-gate-may-grade-the-file-and-skip-your-construct` (a gate you correctly identified that skips your construct) and `enumerating-a-subtree-and-calling-it-the-parents-taxonomy` (a census narrower than the claim built on it).

A SETTLED ROLLUP CAN BE SHORT RATHER THAN STILL-BUILDING, AND THE MISSING CHECKS ARE ONES THE RUN NEVER CREATED — not skipped ones. Measured 2026-09-22 on PR #10169 at band 88.

THE READING. #10169 reported total 83, pending 0, failed 0. Every instinct trained on this repo says "0 pending, 0 failed" is the green shape, and the only thing refusing it is clause 1's requirement that the rollup be non-empty AT BAND. 83 is not 88.

WHAT THE FIVE WERE. Diffed by NAME against #10168, a PR merged minutes earlier at a settled 88, the absent checks were all in the `tests` workflow: the Reagent Slim bundle-isolation + client-runtime smoke, JVM tools/machines-viz, JVM tools/testbed-support, the tenant-switcher testbed browser smoke, and the re-frame2-pair shipped-preload pure-core node-test.

ABSENT IS NOT SKIPPED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. On #10168 all five read COMPLETED/SKIPPED — present in the rollup, counted toward 88, and accepted by clause 2, which takes skipped. On #10169 they were not in the rollup at all. At the RUN level the same gap: 66 jobs against #10168's 71, those exact five missing and nothing extra. So a rollup total can fall below band without a single check failing or pending, purely by jobs not being created.

CONFOUNDERS ELIMINATED, so the observation is not mistaken for something already catalogued:
  * NOT a partial re-run — both runs are `run_attempt` 1 with a null previous-attempt URL.
  * NOT a matrix sized from detected surfaces — `test.yml` contains ZERO `fromJSON` matrices; all five
    are statically defined jobs with `needs: detect_changed_surfaces` and a boolean `if:`.
  * NOT a workflow-file difference — `git diff --name-only <merge-base> origin/main -- .github/workflows/`
    reads 0 files, and the job names are present in both revisions of `test.yml`.
  * NOT the branch being stale in the matrix sense — the last workflow commit is an ancestor of that
    PR's merge base.

THE MECHANISM IS NOT ESTABLISHED AND THIS MEMORY DELIBERATELY DOES NOT GUESS ONE. A statically defined job with a false `if:` is supposed to yield a skipped check, and these yielded none. Recording a plausible-sounding cause would be worse than recording none, because the next reader would stop looking.

THE INSTRUMENT TRAP MET ON THE WAY, and it fired in the reassuring direction. Checking whether trunk's `test.yml` still contained the five job names, `git show origin/main:.github/workflows/test.yml | grep -c` read **0** for all five — which reads as "these jobs were deleted from trunk", a complete and plausible explanation. It was CLAUDE.md instrument item (d): a slashed ref plus a dot-leading path, mangled by MSYS. The tell is in the error text, which echoes the argument back rewritten as `origin\main;.github\workflows\test.yml`. With `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` the same greps read 31 / 1 / 2. A false zero here would have inverted the diagnosis entirely.

WHAT TO DO. Refuse on clause 1 — a short settled set is indistinguishable from a change that genuinely lost gates, and that is the fail-open direction. Then get a FRESH run rather than re-reading the old one: rebase onto current trunk and push, which computes a new `pull_request` run against the current base, and re-run the ordinary gates on that final base. A sabotage/plant result taken at the pre-rebase base does not need re-earning if the rebase does not touch the planted file — say which base it was taken at.

THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT SETTLED IT, and it is cheap: diff the rollup's check NAMES against a PR merged at band under the same matrix, then confirm at the run level with the jobs API (`total_count`, and the job-name set). Comparing TOTALS alone tells you a number is wrong; comparing NAMES tells you which gates are gone, which is the only form that supports a decision.

RELATED: [[never-state-a-gate-roster-as-complete-in-a-brief]] is the same family one level up — there a roster short by name-shaped search, here a check SET short by a mechanism nobody can see from the total.

THE HARNESS REPORTED "exit code 0" FOR A RUN THAT DIED IN ITS FIRST SECOND — so the fallback "the harness is roughly right on long healthy runs" is REFUTED, and there is no regime in which its number can be trusted (2026-09-22).

NO COUNT IS GIVEN HERE ON PURPOSE, and this sentence is itself a correction. The first version of this memory was headed "third instance in one session"; within the hour the worker that reported it filed its own two as instances THREE AND FOUR, so the number was stale before the memory was a day old. That is the add-don't-recount failure [[harness-exit-census-recount-owed]] describes, reproduced by the very note recording it. The SHAPE below is what generalises; the tally does not.

THE INSTANCE. The rf2-ktkhn P1 worker (worktree rwown-ktkhn, draft PR #10169) ran the node lane in a freshly created worktree. The run failed immediately — `compile-node-test: could not resolve shadow-cljs: Cannot find module 'shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js'` — because that worktree had no `implementation/node_modules` yet. Captured exit file read 1. The harness's completion notice read `completed (exit code 0)`.

WHY THIS ADDS SOMETHING TO THE THREE MEMORIES ALREADY IN THIS CLASS. They establish the disagreement, its direction (always toward green), and the capture-and-quote procedure. None of them bounds it by RUN SHAPE, and a reader who has met it only on long multi-minute gate runs quietly forms the fallback that the harness is approximately right when a run is healthy and long, and that the `.exit` file is a belt-and-braces check for suspicious runs. This instance kills that: the run did not get as far as loading its runner. The worker who hit it said so explicitly and was right to — the shape is the finding, not the count.

THE WORST PROPERTY, and it is worse than a missed failure. A run that compiled NOTHING was reported as a pass. So the harness number is least reliable exactly where it is cheapest to be fooled: an environment fault produces no output to look wrong, no failing test names, no red banner — just a short run and a green number. A worker who trusts it reports a passing gate for a gate that never executed.

THE CONSEQUENCE FOR READING BUILD OUTPUT, which is the operational half. Once an environment fault is possible, `0 compiled` or a MISSING build line are TWO different things — a genuinely stale incremental build, or a runner that never started. Read the captured exit AND the build line together; if the exit is non-zero the build line is meaningless rather than evidence of staleness. The same worker's run 1 was precisely this: exit 1 with no build line at all, which is the runner-never-started case.

DO NOT INCREMENT THE CENSUS WITH THIS. [[harness-exit-census-recount-owed]] forbids carrying the counted figure forward by appending newly seen instances, which is how it came to be understated by two thirds. This is an input to a recount and a statement about SHAPE, not a tally mark.

RELATED: [[harness-reported-exit-code-disagrees-with-the-captured-one]] is the primary account and its procedure is unchanged and sufficient — capture `$?` to a `.exit` file on one command line in one shell, name the artefacts for the worktree AND the attempt, and treat an absent exit file as NO VERDICT rather than a pass. [[harness-completion-notice-can-report-a-false-exit-0]] records the same `shadow-cljs/cli/runner.js` error from a fresh worktree in 2026-08, so the environmental cause is itself a known repeat: see [[worker-worktree-without-node-modules-fails-the-spine-environmentally]]. Prefer `npm ci` inside the worker's own worktree over junctioning the mayor's.

THE REAP TEST HAS ONE CONDITION, NOT TWO, AND I HAVE BEEN ENFORCING IT AS A CONJUNCTION — "the worker's own quotable completion report AND after its change merges". `loops.md` §4 forbids exactly that in terms. Found by §5 axis 2 on 2026-09-22, after a whole session of repeating it.

WHAT THE DOCUMENT ACTUALLY SAYS, at `docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md:390` and :409:
  * "**Only a worker's own completion report authorises reaping its worktree.** Not a merged change, not
    a clean tree, not elapsed time, not directory age, not 'no commits and no open change', not clean and
    merged together — all six were adopted in one session and all six were wrong."
  * "**Deferring the reap until the change merges is free insurance** — a worker can need its tree after
    reporting, when its change hits a conflict. **Do not make that a second condition on a rule whose
    strength is having one.**"
  * And :406: "**Never pair a merge with a reap, or put the reap in the merge loop.** A merged change is
    the moment a tree *looks* finished, which is exactly the pull, and a rule encoded in a loop condition
    is delegated to a predicate that cannot see what you know."
  * :200 says it a third time from the dispatch side: "That is not a second condition on the reap rule,
    whose strength is having one."

So merging is a PRACTICE (free insurance, and a good one), never a CONDITION. The one condition is the
operational test at :393 — **can you quote the sentence where this agent says it is done?**

WHY THIS MATTERS EVEN THOUGH IT IS STRICTER AND FAILS CLOSED. No worktree was wrongly reaped by it; every reap this session had a quotable report. The damage is to the SHAPE of the rule, in three ways:
  1. It makes MERGE load-bearing, and "not clean and merged together" is named at :391 as one of the six
     proxies that were adopted and were WRONG. Promoting it to half the test re-admits the proxy the
     sentence exists to exclude.
  2. It licenses the pairing :406 forbids. Holding "report AND merged" makes the merge the moment the
     conjunction completes, so the reap naturally lands in the same tick as the merge — which I did,
     reaping a worktree minutes after merging its PR. The document calls that moment "exactly the pull".
  3. A two-condition rule is weaker than a one-condition rule under pressure, because a reader who has
     one of the two feels partly justified. The document says the strength IS the singularity, twice.

THE CORRECT FORMULATION, to be used verbatim in reports and briefs: **the reap test is the worker's own quotable completion report, full stop. Waiting for the merge as well is optional insurance against a conflict sending the worker back to its tree — do it, but never call it a condition and never let a merge be the thing that triggers the reap.**

HOW IT WENT UNNOTICED FOR A WHOLE SESSION. The conjunction is stricter, so it never produced a wrong outcome — no error, no bad reap, nothing on screen. It was corroborated every tick by the fact that its reaps were all correct, which is what a stricter-than-necessary rule always does. Only reading the source sentence caught it, which is precisely what §5 axis 2 is for: check the rules you have been ENFORCING against what the tree actually says, rather than re-reading the tree for novelty.

RELATED: [[trunk-is-disjoint-from-me-is-a-decision-that-expires]] is the same species of drift in a worker's reasoning rather than the coordinator's — a rule that keeps giving right answers for a while and so never gets tested by its own failures.

A DECISION RESTING ON "TRUNK IS DISJOINT FROM MY FILES" HAS AN EXPIRY DATE, AND THE THING THAT READS THE EXPIRY IS THE CHECK COUNT, NOT THE FILE LIST. Measured 2026-09-22 on PR #10169.

THE DECISION, AND IT WAS CORRECT WHEN MADE. A P1 worker deliberately did not rebase past its base. Its reasoning: trunk's moved files were disjoint from its three, `origin/main...HEAD` confirmed the push reverted nothing, and rebasing would have retired locally captured plant evidence for no gain. Every clause of that was true and well evidenced.

WHAT IT MISSED. The file-level question ("does trunk collide with me?") and the gate-level question ("will CI compute a COMPLETE check set against my base?") are different questions, and only the first one is answered by a disjointness check. The branch's rollup came in at 83 against a band of 88, with 0 pending and 0 failed — the shape that reads as green. Five `tests` checks were ABSENT, not skipped, and at run level the run had 66 jobs against a comparable PR's 71. After rebasing onto current trunk and pushing, the fresh run climbed past 83 with checks still settling, which is what confirmed the stale base as the cause.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MAKES THIS WORTH A RULE. Disjointness protects against a CONFLICT, which is loud — git refuses, or the diff shows it. Staleness of the check set is SILENT and reads as a pass: nothing fails, nothing pends, the total is merely lower, and a lower total is only visible to someone who knows the band. So the evidence that the decision has expired never appears in the place the decision was made.

THE READING INSTRUMENT IS THE TOTAL, AND THAT IS THE PART PEOPLE MISS. The worker's own summary was that it "had no mechanism that would have told me the ground had moved." It did — the rollup total — but it was reading that number as a PASS/FAIL signal rather than as a STALENESS signal. Nothing about "83 total, 0 failed" says "your base is old" unless you already compare the total against a band derived from PRs merged under the current matrix. So the repair is not a new mechanism; it is reading an existing number for a second thing.

THE RULE:
  * A "trunk is disjoint, so I need not rebase" decision is valid only until the next merge to trunk.
    Re-ask it whenever trunk moves, and especially whenever a sibling PR in the same wave lands.
  * The cheap re-ask is the rollup TOTAL against the band, not another disjointness check.
  * A short-but-settled rollup is the signature. See
    [[a-settled-rollup-can-be-short-by-jobs-never-created]] for the measurement and the confounders
    that were eliminated.

WHAT SURVIVES A REBASE WITHOUT BEING RE-EARNED, because the fear of losing evidence is what motivates skipping one: a plant/sabotage result survives if the planted FILE is byte-identical across the rebase, and that is provable rather than arguable — compare the blob id at the old head and the new one. Here `settings.cljs` hashed to the same blob both sides, the same blob the restore had verified, so the sabotage result remained a statement about the tree that is there now. Say which base the plant was taken at and show the blob identity; re-run the ORDINARY gates on the final base, not the sabotage.

COORDINATOR'S HALF: say plainly whose fault it was. The decision was right when made and what changed was a sibling landing, so a worker told to rebase should be told that too — otherwise a correct piece of judgement gets filed as a mistake and the instinct not to churn a branch for nothing, which is a good instinct, gets trained out.

I WROTE "RE-VERIFIED AT TRUNK IMMEDIATELY BEFORE THIS DISPATCH" ABOUT PATHS I HAD NOT CHECKED, AND TWO OF THEM DID NOT EXIST. Asserting a verification you did not perform is a different and worse error than under-measuring, because it tells the reader where NOT to spend their scepticism. Mayor, 2026-09-22, on rf2-v9qqk.

WHAT HAPPENED. A worker's report (rf2-bc17l, PR #10170) listed remaining defect sites including `spec/API.md:46`, `spec/011-Launch-Modes.md:397` and `spec/018-Event-Spine.md:307`/`:1385`. I copied those strings verbatim into a new bead and a dispatch brief, and wrote in the bead: "Re-verified by the mayor at trunk 1feb11e612 immediately before this dispatch." I had not re-verified them.

Measured afterwards at trunk 14f9bac9fd: `spec/011-Launch-Modes.md` and `spec/018-Event-Spine.md` DO NOT EXIST; `spec/API.md:46` exists and is a tier-table row about "front-porch" carrying no keybinding at all. The real files are all under `tools/xray/spec/`. Control both ways so this is not a search artefact: repo-level `spec/` matches `j/k/L/G` in 0 files and "snap to LIVE" in 0, while `tools/xray/` matches 1 and 2.

THE MECHANISM, AND IT WILL RECUR. A worker working inside a subtree writes paths relative to ITS OWN working context. This one was in `tools/xray` and wrote `spec/API.md` meaning `tools/xray/spec/API.md`. That shorthand is natural, correct in context, and indistinguishable from a repo-relative path once lifted out of the report. **A path quoted in a worker's report is a CLAIM about a location, not a location.** Resolve it against the filesystem before it enters a bead or a brief — one `ls` per path.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN THE SESSION'S OTHER ROSTER ERRORS. The recurring pattern had been under-measurement: five pinned tests that were eight, two L sites that were ten, eight that were nineteen. Those understate and a sceptical worker can find the rest. This one does something else: a brief saying "re-verified at trunk immediately before this dispatch" INVITES the worker to treat those paths as settled and spend its scepticism elsewhere. I converted my own unchecked assumption into the reader's licence to stop checking.

IT ALSO FABRICATED A HAZARD, WHICH HAS ITS OWN COST. On the strength of the wrong path I declared `spec/API.md` a HOT-ZONE file, explained the api-manifest one-holding rule, and instructed the worker to run the manifest gate and to STOP and report if it disagreed. None of that applies to `tools/xray/spec/API.md`. An instruction to STOP on a gate that was never relevant is an invitation to halt real work, and fabricated hazards spend attention exactly like real ones.

THE GUARDS, and the first is the only one that is not already written down somewhere:
  * **Never write "verified", "re-verified" or "measured at trunk" unless the check ran in the same act
    as the sentence.** If the claim is inherited, attribute it: "the rf2-bc17l worker reported these;
    I have not resolved them."
  * **Resolve every path before it enters a bead or brief.** `ls` or `git ls-files` per path, and note
    that a NONEXISTENT path is the cheap case — the expensive one is a path that exists and is about
    something else, which `spec/API.md:46` was.
  * **Suspect subtree shorthand whenever a report comes from a worker fenced into one tree**, and
    especially when a repo-level file of the same basename also exists. `spec/API.md` and
    `tools/xray/spec/API.md` both exist, which is what made the wrong one look right.

WHAT MADE IT SURVIVABLE. The brief also said "treat this list as a floor and not a roster" — language added because the PREVIOUS worker had found sites my census missed. The new worker resolved the paths to the real files rather than stopping, found 11 more sites (19 total), and dissolved the fabricated hot-zone concern by measurement: porcelain 0 on `spec/API.md` and both sidecars, with `gen --check`, `xray-spec-check` and `api-md-check` all exit 0. **The floor language, not my paths, is why the item completed** — which is an argument for the briefing grammar in [[never-state-a-gate-roster-as-complete-in-a-brief]] rather than for better copying.
