TWO MAYOR DISPOSITIONS I HAD BEEN RESTATING WITHOUT RE-TESTING, PLUS THE STANDING §5 INSTRUCTION I HAD BEEN VIOLATING THAT EXPLAINS BOTH. Found 2026-09-22 by running loops.md §5 against the section's own gotcha: *a conclusion you keep restating is a rule you are enforcing, and the discharging question is whether you can state the check you made THIS pass*.

## THE INSTRUCTION I WAS VIOLATING, WHICH IS THE ROOT CAUSE

`loops.md` §5 says, as a standing rule rather than a cadence: **"Read a loop's page when you are about to do that loop's work, whatever this loop's cadence says. A destructive step performed hours before its page comes round is a step taken without it, and the reread that follows finds nothing wrong because the damage is already done."**

I had been running §1, §2 and §4 from memory and reading a page only when that loop was explicitly invoked. That is exactly what the sentence forbids, and it is the mechanism behind every method drift found this session: the reap rule enforced as a two-condition conjunction (see [[the-reap-test-has-one-condition-not-two]]), §3 run from a remembered shape that started from the wrong list and ignored the live-agent status. Each was caught only when its page happened to come round.

**THE REPAIR IS BEHAVIOURAL AND CHEAP: read the section before doing the work, every time, especially before anything destructive.** Reading §3 corrected two practices on the spot; reading §4's Reaping corrected one; reading §5 produced this note. Three for three.

## DISPOSITION 1 — "the audit worktrees are the out-of-repo harness's, not mine to reap"

Restated in four reports. What I could actually quote was my own earlier report, never a check.

**What re-testing established, and it is narrower than what I had been saying.** Measured over the six (`audit-sep15-b`, `audit-sep16/17/20/21-monitor`, `merged-pr-audit-a`):
  * **NOT MINE — solid.** Exact-path match against `ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv` reads **0 rows each**,
    against a control of **1** for a worktree that is mine.
  * **SOMETHING IS ACTIVELY MAINTAINING THEM — solid, and this is the part the name never gave me.**
    `audit-sep21-monitor` was **0.3 days old** sitting exactly on `1feb11e612`, the merge commit of a PR
    I had merged hours earlier. A worktree appearing per merge is a behavioural signature.
  * **REAPING WOULD LOSE NOTHING — solid.** All six read **0 porcelain lines** and all six HEADs are
    literal ancestors of `origin/main` (they are checkouts of trunk commits, not feature branches).
  * **THAT THEY ARE SPECIFICALLY THE `codex-pr-audit` HARNESS'S — NOT ESTABLISHED.** 161
    `.git/codex-pr-audit-*` directories exist, so that harness is demonstrably real and active here, but
    the worktrees carry **0** `checkpoint.py` between them — the harness's per-PR scripts live under
    `.git/`, not in those trees. My attribution rested on the prefix "audit-" in their names, which is
    the same name-shaped reasoning that under-counted a gate roster, a defect census and a path list
    this session.

**The ACTION is unchanged — do not reap them — but it now rests on "not mine, and one is demonstrably active" rather than on a name.** State it that way; and since reaping would cost nothing and they accumulate, it is worth surfacing to the operator rather than carrying "not mine" indefinitely.

## DISPOSITION 2 — the `.claude/commands/` claim, carried across a context compaction

I had been reporting "`.claude/commands/`: 0 tracked AND absent on disk" from a summary, never re-run — while §5 explicitly names "your loop command files" as a thing this loop checks. Re-tested: `.claude/commands/` is absent and 0 tracked, so the conclusion HOLDS; but `.claude/` itself exists and has one tracked file, `settings.json`, which is a permissions file and never a loop command file. **So the "check your command files" step is VACUOUSLY satisfied — there are none — and saying "checked, clean" would report a pass from a check that could not fail.** Say vacuous when it is vacuous.

## THE NEAR-MISS WORTH KEEPING: TWO HONEST INSTRUMENTS, ONE WRONG QUESTION

In the same pass, `git merge-base --is-ancestor` reported `restoregc-9nlg1` NOT contained, appearing to contradict an earlier "containment proven" from `git cherry` (which had read `-`, proof of containment). **Both readings are correct and they answer different questions.** `git cherry` tests PATCH equivalence; `--is-ancestor` tests literal ancestry. Under rebase-merge a merged branch is patch-equivalent to trunk but is NOT an ancestor of it, so `-` together with `NO` is the EXPECTED pair for a branch that has landed. §4 and CLAUDE.md both prescribe `git cherry` for the reaping question, and ancestry is simply the wrong instrument there.

**The trap is that the wrong instrument produces a clean, confident refutation of a correct earlier finding** — the register of a false "restore failed". Had I acted on it I would have gone looking for lost work that had merged days ago. Before believing that a new reading refutes an old one, check that both were asking the same question.

THE MAYOR IS ONE OF THE CONCURRENT WRITERS, AND I HAD EXEMPTED MYSELF FROM THE ARTEFACT-NAMING RULE I PUT IN EVERY DISPATCH. Measured 2026-09-22.

`loops.md` §2 "Two standing conditions" states the general case and predicted this precisely: **"A rule scoped to a ROLE exempts whoever does not identify with the role"** — one mayor enforced the naming rule on eight dispatches and then lost its own change body to a peer under exactly the bare name it forbids. I read that sentence for the first time today, having spent the session pasting the worker half of it into brief after brief.

THE MEASUREMENT, which is what this note adds to the document. The session scratch directory held **5,100 files, of which 5,023 carry no worktree or owner in the name** — 77 were worktree-disciplined. Among the bare ones: `F.txt`, `N.txt`, `O.txt`, single letters, plus `CLAUDE-edited.md` and `CLAUDE.md.repaired`. My own contributions that tick were all bare: `triage.py`, `diffrollup.py`, `mapwt.py`, `probe5.py`, `runs10172.json`, `close_*.md`, `mem_*.txt`, `note_*.md`.

WHY THE EXEMPTION FELT REASONABLE, AND THIS IS THE GENERALISABLE PART. The rule as I was writing it named the ROLE — "name every gate artefact for YOUR WORKTREE and the attempt" — and I have no worktree. A coordinator reading that hears an instruction addressed to workers, so the rule's own phrasing granted me the exemption. **The scope is not "workers"; it is every directory you do not exclusively own**, and a session-keyed temp directory is the reverse of private however much it feels otherwise.

THE COST IS THE ONE THE DOCUMENT NAMES, AND IT FAILS QUIETLY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: nothing errors on a clobber, so the loser can READ the survivor and take a plausible-looking artefact with the wrong subject for its own — a change body, a census, or a gate exit code belonging to somebody else's run, which reads as a clean pass and fails a merge decision open.

THE FIX I HAVE ADOPTED: prefix every file the mayor writes to a shared scratch area with `mayor-`, and add an attempt or tick discriminator where the same name recurs across ticks (`mayor-runs-10172-1.json`, not `runs10172.json`). Cheap, and it makes the mayor's files identifiable as the mayor's to anyone else reading that directory.

A FLEET-WIDE 529 KILLED ALL THREE WORKERS IN ONE INSTANT, AND THE SALVAGE TRIAGE RAN OPPOSITE TO ELAPSED TIME. Measured 2026-09-22, trunk c57907e130.

THE EVENT. Three background workers died simultaneously with `API Error: 529 Overloaded` (three distinct request ids, one model). This is the shape `loops.md` §2 predicts for a SHARED ALLOWANCE — "N workers are not N independent bets: they fail TOGETHER, mid-run, on a limit none approached alone" — reached through server capacity rather than a quota. All three resumed successfully minutes later, so the remedy was resumption, not redispatch, exactly as §3 says.

THE FINDING, AND IT REFINES A SENTENCE IN §3 RATHER THAN CONTRADICTING IT. §3 says to spend one resume message on "the worker with most context to lose", which reads naturally as the longest-running one. **Measured here, elapsed time was INVERSELY related to work at risk:**

  * substrates worker, ~43 min, closest to done: working tree CLEAN, **0 unpushed commits**, 15 files
    already in a draft PR. Nothing at risk.
  * patterns worker, ~35 min: **0 unpushed commits**, draft PR open, 1 uncommitted file.
  * CORS worker, ~17 min, YOUNGEST: branch still at its base revision, **ZERO commits**, no PR, all of
    its work existing only as uncommitted files in the worktree. **Everything at risk.**

So the youngest worker held the only irrecoverable work, because the older two had pushed continuously and it had not yet reached its first commit. **A coordinator triaging by "who has most context" would have resumed exactly the wrong one first.**

THE OPERATIONAL RULE: **triage a fleet-wide kill by UNPUSHED WORK, not by elapsed time or context size.** Per worktree, read the tip against its published ref and the porcelain count. The worker with commits on the remote has lost reasoning, which resumption recovers cheaply; the worker with none has lost the work itself, which nothing but resumption can recover at all — and `loops.md` §4 forbids the obvious alternative, because **you must never build a commit from someone else's uncommitted work**.

THE SECOND-ORDER REASON THIS IS COUNTERINTUITIVE: the brief instruction that produces safety — push continuously — takes EFFECT only after the first commit, so every worker passes through an early window in which it is maximally exposed. The window closes with the first push, not with elapsed time, and it is invisible to any clock.

WHAT I CHANGED IN THE RESUME MESSAGE, and it is the actionable half: I told the at-risk worker to **commit and push before resuming its analysis**, so a second outage could not cost it the same work twice. Tell a resumed worker its measured state (tip, unpushed count, porcelain, whether a PR exists) rather than asking it to rediscover it — it cannot see its own death.

A DISTINCTION WORTH KEEPING: a 529 is NOT an exhausted allowance, and §3's warning that "a remedy drawing on the resource whose exhaustion caused the failure is not a remedy" does not apply. The discriminator is liveness after resume — an agent under a genuinely exhausted allowance dies within seconds, so a resumed agent still running after a minute is positive evidence the cause was transient. I resumed ONE first and read its liveness before resuming the other two.

A GUARD WHOSE PRESCRIBED REMEDY NAMES A SESSION-SCOPED PATH IS UNSATISFIABLE IN ALMOST EVERY SESSION THAT READS IT, AND THE FAILURE IS INVISIBLE BECAUSE "NO ENTRY" AND "NO RECORD AT ALL" PRESENT IDENTICALLY. Measured 2026-09-22 at trunk be35565ae1 by a mayor method reread (loops.md section 5).

THE INSTANCE. ai/assemble-brief.sh emits an advisory NOTE when a brief offers session history as a credential ("five workers have matched their predictions exactly this session"). Its remedy read: "Re-derive each against the merge-note record (scratchpad m_*.md) before shipping, or drop the number." The record is one file per merge, m_<bead-suffix>.md.

THE MEASUREMENT. Of 56 session scratchpad directories for this project, exactly ONE held any m_*.md — 59 files, all written by that one session — and the other 55 held ZERO. ai/ held none. So a remedy addressed to every session that runs the assembler was reachable in 1 session in 56, while reading in all 56 as a standing authority. Controls both ways: the directory census counted all 56 siblings rather than sampling, and the sibling-defect sweep over ai/ tooling returned exactly 1 file (the assembler itself), so the defect is not a class here.

WHY IT SURVIVED. The scratchpad is where correct practice puts disposable scratch — this repo's own findings docs cite it a dozen times, always to say a probe script lived OUTSIDE the repo, which is the legitimate use. What makes the guard's citation different is that it names the path as a THING TO CHECK A FIGURE AGAINST, i.e. as evidence, and evidence has to outlive the session that produced it. The two uses are one character apart in the prose and opposite in kind.

THE DISCHARGING TEST THE GUARD LACKED, and this is the generalising half: an empty result is TWO answers wearing one face. Test the CONTAINER before the CONTENTS. A missing directory means you are not looking at the record at all — stop trusting the check; an empty glob inside a present directory means the entries genuinely were never written — go and measure. Under a session-scoped path both present as the same empty listing, and the reader takes the reassuring reading, because "nothing to check against" reads as "nothing to correct".

THE REPAIR, and note WHICH artefact changed. Not more prose in the brief, and not a refusal added to the guard — the record was moved to ai/merge-notes/ (local-only and gitignored, but it survives session boundaries, which is the whole of what a record needs), the guard's citation repointed there, and the discharging test written into the guard beside it with a do-not-tidy-it-back note, because the next reader's instinct is to put scratch back in the scratchpad. Verified by effect: 59 copied with 0 differing, credential guard still fires on "Five workers" and still stays silent on "P1 worker" (the \b false-positive fix intact), sh -n clean, file still pure LF, ai/ still 0 tracked files so the check-ai-tracking-ratchet is untouched.

THE COORDINATOR-SIDE LESSON: loops.md section 5 says to fix the document rather than note it, and this defect had been FOUND by the previous reread and left noted. A finding recorded but not repaired is re-found at full cost every pass, and the second finding reads as new. If a reread produces a note instead of an edit, that note is the finding's failure, not its record.

PIPING `bd show --json` INTO PYTHON'S STDIN INFLATES EVERY LENGTH PROBE BY THE FIELD'S NON-ASCII BYTE COUNT, AND THIS REPO'S BEADS ARE FULL OF EM DASHES. Measured 2026-09-22 at trunk be35565ae1.

THE OBSERVABLE. One close_reason read two ways, minutes apart, no write between them:
  * `bd show <id> --json | python -c "...len(r['close_reason'])..."`  ->  8057
  * `bd show <id> --json > f.json` then `json.load(open(f, encoding='utf-8'))`  ->  8018

PREDICTED AND CONFIRMED EXACTLY. The source text carries 20 non-ASCII characters (19 em dashes plus one other), contributing 39 extra bytes under UTF-8. 8018 + 39 = 8057, predicted before the count was taken and matched to the character.

THE MECHANISM: reading through a pipe gives Python no encoding declaration, so the JSON arrives decoded by the platform default rather than as UTF-8 and each multi-byte character is counted as its byte length. The file form with an explicit `encoding='utf-8'` is correct.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN AN OFF-BY-39. It fails in the direction that MANUFACTURES REASSURANCE for the commonest use of a length probe. Every close and every append in this project is verified by asking whether a field is the expected size — an inflated length reads as "at least as much content as I wrote", so it would MASK A TRUNCATION, and a field that lost its tail could still read long enough to pass. It also manufactures false alarms: here an unchanged field appeared to have grown by 39 characters between two reads, which reads exactly like another process having written to a closed bead.

THE GUARD IS ALREADY IN CLAUDE.md ITEM (k) AND I DID NOT FOLLOW IT. That item prescribes redirecting the raw JSON to a file and reading it with `json.load(open(path, encoding='utf-8'))`. **Its stated reason is jq's CRLF, so a reader who has switched from jq to Python feels the hazard is discharged and pipes into Python instead — which is a DIFFERENT fault reached through the same shortcut.** The rule to carry is the FORM, not the reason: redirect to a file, open with an explicit encoding, every time. Keep the `encoding='utf-8'` on stdout too — native Python on Windows defaults to cp1252 and dies on these same em dashes while printing.

THE CHEAP CONTROL, and it is what separated an instrument fault from a real tracker write: compare the stored field against the SOURCE FILE you wrote it from. Equal lengths (modulo a trailing newline) mean the field is intact and any disagreement is in the reader. Do that before concluding that a closed bead changed under you.

A COORDINATOR REPLICATES A FACT ACROSS THE ITEMS IT CONCERNS AND IT GOES INCONSISTENT WITHIN TWO TICKS — THE SAME DEFECT THE COORDINATOR IS SIMULTANEOUSLY SENDING WORKERS TO REPAIR IN THE TREE. And the repair for a marker problem is itself liable to be a marker problem. Measured 2026-09-22 by a mayor method reread (loops.md section 5) at trunk 58a2ea983f.

THE INSTANCE. Three items were fenced behind one machine-wide exclusive (the shadow-cljs build lane). I recorded, on each item's notes, both its own fence AND its position in the queue. Two ticks later a reread found three inconsistencies at once: the item holding the lane still advertised itself as FENCED and QUEUE POSITION: FIRST, having been dispatched without the hold being struck; the second item's governing note said SECOND when it had become first; and the third item recorded itself as SECOND while the first item's note recorded it as THIRD. Nothing downstream noticed, because nothing reads these notes except the next tick's coordinator, who is scanning rather than reading.

WHY IT IS WORTH A MEMORY RATHER THAN A FIX AND FORGET. In the same session I dispatched two workers to repair this exact class in the tree: a port diagnostic that TRANSCRIBED a band list from the build config (PR #10180 — the worker refused to re-transcribe it and REMOVED the enumeration, citing an existing in-repo ruling that "a transcribed band list goes stale in silence"), and a skill whose file inventory was maintained in THREE hand-written copies (PR #10181 — reduced to one authority plus a pointer where packaging allowed). So the rule was being enforced outward and violated inward in the same hours. A replicated fact with ONE COPY PER HOLDER is the shape; the holder's own copy always looks locally correct, which is why no single read catches it.

THE REPAIR IS NOT MORE NOTES. Make the ordering DERIVABLE and record none of it: the lane goes to the fenced item with the highest priority, ties broken by tracker creation time, re-derived at the tick that grants it. Each item records only its own fence and its own release condition. A derived order cannot drift because there is nothing to keep in step.

THE SECOND FINDING, AND IT IS THE MORE GENERAL ONE: THE STRIKE DEFEATED ITS OWN SCAN. To say what it was discharging, the strike note QUOTED the hold marker and the position line verbatim. A text scan then finds those strings INSIDE the strike, at a LATER position in the field than the original, so a newest-governs reader lands on the quotation and reads the hold as live again — on the one item that was already running. This is documented twice in this project and I met it anyway, from inside a repair for the same class: loops.md says a marker scan over-reports items that QUOTE a marker and that a second scan built to discriminate fails the same way, because marker text instructs whoever rules to strike it; and CLAUDE.md's commit-attribution guard records the same distinction, that what must be refused is a line that IS the attribution and never a line that MENTIONS one.

THE DISCRIMINATOR THAT CANNOT DRIFT is not a marker at all: A HOLD IS DISCHARGED WHENEVER THE ITEM IS NOT IN A WAITING STATE. An item reading in_progress has been dispatched, which is what every such hold releases on. Ask the STATUS FIELD keyed on the item id and treat any hold marker on a non-open item as spent. The status field is maintained by the dispatch act itself, so it cannot fall out of step with the dispatch the way a hand-written note can — which is the same property that makes a derived ordering safe. Prefer a field the act itself maintains over prose the actor must remember to update.

DO NOT REWRITE THE STALE NOTES. They are the record of what was believed when, and loops.md is explicit that where you cannot edit the original you append the negation in the same words so a scan returns every occurrence and the newest governs. What changes is which instrument you read first.

A BRIEF'S SUPPORTING DETAIL IS A CLAIM AND MUST BE LABELLED AS ONE, OR MEASURED EXACTLY — TWO FALSE DETAILS SHIPPED IN ONE SESSION, EACH IN THE PART THAT MADE THE BRIEF READ AS RIGOROUS (2026-09-20, mayor).

Briefs in this project already label COUNTS as claims to re-derive ("a count in a brief is a claim, not a
measurement you inherit"). That convention works. What shipped wrong twice in one session is the class of
detail NOT covered by it: POSITIONAL and ATTRIBUTIONAL detail, asserted in the FENCE and in the CENSUS
METHOD, where it reads as established fact.

A GATE WHOSE PUSH TRIGGER IS PATH-FILTERED CANNOT BE ARMED BY A CHANGE TO THE VERY SURFACE IT GRADES, SO TRUNK CAN HOLD A VERDICT WHOSE CAUSE WAS FIXED SEVERAL COMMITS AGO -- AND THE PR-TIME GREENS BESIDE IT ARE NOT EVIDENCE, BECAUSE THE JOB IN QUESTION NEVER RUNS ON pull_request.

Measured 2026-09-23 on re-frame2 at trunk 75596b6043.

THE INSTANCE. lint.yml's `provenance-pins-corpus` job carries `if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'`, so it runs only on push, schedule and workflow_dispatch. lint.yml's push trigger is path-filtered, and `docs/design/fresco/**` is NOT among its paths -- yet that tree is exactly what the corpus job grades. PR #10251 (a fail-open repair to the checker itself) made the job stop failing open and surface 2 real pre-existing findings, so main went red. #10253 decided and fixed those two findings. But #10253 and the two commits after it were fresco-docs-only, so none of them could arm lint.yml at all, and the four lint runs in between were all `pull_request` events whose check set excludes the corpus job by its own `if:`. Main therefore read FAILURE for three commits after the failure's cause was gone, with the nightly cron (`30 3 * * *` UTC) still about 7 hours out.

WHY THE GREENS BESIDE IT MISLEAD, and this is the half that fools a careful reader. "The last four lint runs are green" is TRUE and worthless: all four were PR runs, and the one job at issue cannot appear in a PR run. Reading workflow-level conclusions hides this completely, because the workflow name is the same on both kinds of run. THE DISCRIMINATOR IS THE EVENT: list runs by event and read only the non-`pull_request` ones when asking what trunk actually says.

THE CHEAP SETTLEMENT, and the order matters. (1) Run the gate LOCALLY at trunk FIRST -- here `python scripts/check_provenance_pins.py`, the bare invocation (there is no `--all`; passing one exits 2 on an argparse error). It read exit 0, 0 findings, 913 pins / 785 landed / 1 stranded / 124 unresolvable / 3 foreign, so the dispatch below was a confirmation rather than a gamble. (2) `gh workflow run lint.yml --ref main`, because `workflow_dispatch` is a non-`pull_request` event and therefore DOES schedule the job. It settled success, 8 of 8 jobs, corpus included, and trunk's newest non-PR verdict became green at the current head.

COVERAGE WAS NEVER LOST, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A READING TRAP AND NOT A HOLE TO PLUG. Changed fresco pages are graded per-PR by docs.yml's own `provenance-pins` job; a change to the checker's rules touches `scripts/**`, which IS in lint.yml's push paths; and the nightly sweeps the whole corpus. What is exposed is a REPORTING window of up to a day. So do NOT "fix" it by adding `docs/design/fresco/**` to lint.yml's push paths: that would run clj-kondo, Splint, ESLint and the API-manifest drift check on every docs commit to buy back a few hours of freshness, which is exactly the gold-plating the project stance forbids.

GENERALISES BEYOND THIS GATE: wherever a job's `if:` narrows it to a subset of the events its workflow accepts, that job's freshness is bounded by which of those events actually fire -- and a path filter on one of them can exclude the job's own subject matter, which is the self-defeating shape here. Ask of any trunk verdict: which EVENT produced it, and could the commits since have triggered that event at all? Same family as this project's vacuity rules under Build and Test -- a gate cannot fail on what it never inspected -- reached through the TRIGGER rather than through the file contents.

TWO 100-CAPS ON LARGE PRs, measured 2026-09-25 on PR #10375 (111 commits, 104 files).

1. gh pr view <n> --json files RETURNS AT MOST 100 FILES, silently. On #10375 it listed 100 while the change touched 104. So a "files outside the fence" check, or a per-file diff built from that list, covered 100 of 104 and read clean. It fails in the reassuring direction, because the four unlisted files are exactly the ones nobody inspected.
   Guard: take the file list from git, not from gh. Use git diff --name-only <merge-base> <head> before merging, or git show --name-only --format= <merge-commit> after. Compare the count against the change's own stat line.

2. gh pr merge --rebase REFUSED with "GraphQL: This branch can't be rebased (mergePullRequest)". The same PR was mergeStateStatus CLEAN, merge-tree clean, had no merge commits and no empty commits, and git replay --onto origin/main of all 111 commits exited 0 locally. So nothing conflicted. The likely cause is GitHub declining a rebase-merge above 100 commits. That is INFERRED from the count, not confirmed: earlier sweeps at 32-64 commits rebase-merged fine.
   What was done: squash-merged with --match-head-commit pinned to the graded head. There is precedent (#5142), and the repo allows squash. Afterwards, git diff --quiet <head> <squash-commit> over the squash commit's FULL file list read 0, i.e. the landed tree equals the graded head.
   Prevention: a sweep worker told to commit one file per commit should cap its branch below ~90 commits, e.g. by grouping small files per directory, or expect the squash path.

THE WRITE AND EDIT TOOLS DECODE A LITERAL \uXXXX IN THEIR CONTENT INTO THE REAL CHARACTER, SILENTLY. Measured 2026-09-25 in the session scratchpad, reading the bytes back with Python.
- Content "\u00e9" written with the Write tool landed as the UTF-8 bytes of the real character (c3 a9), with no backslash.
- The same "\u00e9" given to the Edit tool as new_string landed the same way.
- A DOUBLED "\\u00e9" did NOT decode to one backslash: it landed as TWO literal backslashes followed by u00e9. So no spelling typed into Write or Edit produces a single-backslash unicode escape.
- Reported first by worker ptssr-tv5ac (PR #10390), which found two unicode-escape examples in implementation/ssr already damaged this way and restored them by writing the bytes with Python.

Why it matters: the tool reports success and the file looks right in a viewer, so nothing announces the change.
- A Clojure string "\u00e9" and a literal é are the same value, so many hits are harmless.
- It changes meaning in docs and comments that SHOW an escape, in JSON fixtures, in a regex source meant to read as an escape, and in .cjs where a literal U+2028/U+2029 can break older parsers.

Guard: to write a literal single-backslash \uXXXX, write the bytes with Python, building the backslash as chr(92) so no tool layer can touch it. Then verify by reading the bytes back: count b'\\u' and the decoded character, never judge from a viewer.
Related: CLAUDE.md instrument item (o) (the Bash tool halving backslash runs). Write preserves plain backslash runs; it is the \u sequence specifically that is decoded.

Merged-PR audit policy: Never change existing Bead status, title, description, criteria, closure metadata or existing notes. Every new actionable finding gets its own NEW open Bead, including findings against already open or closed source work. Only deduplicate an ID created for the SAME finding during recovery of this unfinished PR checkpoint. Link with bd dep add <new> <source> --type discovered-from and append only the required forward pointer with bd update <source> --append-notes; never --notes. Do not append routine review receipts to existing Beads: record independent completeness/correctness/implementation-quality conclusions in the Dolt commit message. Update only the rolling audit cursor memory, push after EACH PR and verify remote cursor, new records, dependencies and pointers before reviewing the next PR.

On this Windows box, a bare python / python3 / py resolves FIRST to the WindowsApps app-execution alias of the Python Install Manager package, and each launch triggers an AppX update check that leaks committed memory inside AppXSvc (svchost; ~96-99 GB on 2026-09-26).

Symptoms of the leak: JVM runs and bd/dolt calls failing with "cannot allocate memory", errno=1455 or 0xc000012d, and git failing with "packfile cannot be mapped: File too large".

Evidence:
- Measured by the mayor, 2026-09-26: `Get-Command python -All` lists `...\Microsoft\WindowsApps\python.exe` before `...\AppData\Local\Python\bin\python.exe`, and likewise for python3. py resolves ONLY to WindowsApps.
- Measured by a peer session the same day, not re-measured by the mayor: the AppX event log showed 3,916 UpdateUsingAppInstallerOperation events for that package in about 20 hours (336 in one hour), and installs failing 0x8007000E (out of memory).

Guard: in briefs and scripts, call the interpreter directly, C:/Users/miket/AppData/Local/Python/pythoncore-3.14-64/python.exe (same runtime, same site-packages). The durable fix is operator-side: restart AppXSvc or reboot, and turn off the python/python3/py app-execution aliases in Windows settings.

Mayor working rule (operator, 2026-09-27): do not issue shell commands that stop for the operator's approval; the prompts kill fleet throughput. Avoid heredocs, command substitution, for-loops, inline python -c and long compound chains in the Bash tool. Write any logic as a script file in the session scratchpad with the Write tool, then run it as ONE plain command (python FILE or sh FILE). Keep bd, gh and git invocations single and simple. Long bead text goes into a file written with the Write tool and is passed via --reason-file or a script.

bd READ from outside the repo silently answers from a DIFFERENT database. Run from outside a checkout (e.g. the session scratch directory), bd uses a home-level ~/.beads database carrying the same rf2 prefix and OLDER contents. So bd show <id> can answer "no issue found" and bd history <id> can return null, both at exit 0, for a bead that exists; an older bead may come back normally, which makes the instrument look healthy. Measured 2026-09-29 by a worker (rf2-by74t.3): rf2-by74t.3 read as missing from the scratch dir while rf2-uelji came back fine from the same place. It is the READ-side sibling of bd-write-from-wrong-cwd-silently-discarded. A null history is NOT only the trailing-carriage-return case the dispatch preamble names. Guard: run bd from the repo root (or pass -C <repo>), and run bd where when an answer surprises you.

FLEET CEILING (Mike, 2026-09-29): a worker that is ONLY waiting on its PR's CI does not count toward the 6-worker ceiling. It loads nothing locally, and keeping it alive preserves its context to fix a CI red itself. Count a worker as active while it edits, runs local gates, holds or waits for the shadow-cljs lane, or is fixing a CI red. Signal: the worker reports CI-WAIT <PR> (briefs ask it to), or its PR is open, its lane window is released, and its report says only CI remains. A CI-waiting worker that goes red becomes active again, so the active count can briefly exceed 6; do not stop it to make room.

## Docs Gates — What Covers `docs/design/**`

`mkdocs build --strict` does **not** cover `docs/design/**`. `mkdocs.yml`'s
`exclude_docs` block deliberately keeps the design trees out of the site, so
never nominate it as the gate for an edit confined to that tree — it will exit 0
having verified nothing. That block is the authority on what else the build
cannot see, and it holds more than the design trees: read `exclude_docs` in
`mkdocs.yml` before nominating `mkdocs build` for any path, rather than trusting
a list in prose. A prose list drifts, and this one already had, naming two of
the six trees the block excluded (rf2-yxuta).

`scripts/check_doc_slugs.py` does cover the design trees: markdown link targets
and heading anchors, in the fast-PR spine and — since rf2-v7fui —
unconditionally in `test.yml`'s `verify-readme-links` job, so on every PR rather
than only a docs-classified one. Its `--verbose` banner
prints the per-root file counts it walked, which is the thing to read when you
need to know what a green actually inspected. That banner counts FILES, and the
second bound on a green is inside them: fenced code blocks are stripped before
links are extracted, so a broken target or anchor written inside a fence is not
checked by this gate or by `scripts/check_readme_links.py` — they share the one
extractor — and the exit 0 is silent about it (rf2-sodfq). The skip is
deliberate and documented at the top of the script; what it means for you is
that an edit confined to a fenced block is ungated, so verify those links by
hand and say so. `docs/design/fresco/` and `docs/the-mayor-method/` are the
exception, and they invert the rule rather than relaxing it: in those two trees
a documentation link inside a fence is itself reported as a defect.
So does `scripts/check_provenance_pins.py`, on changed pages under
`docs/design/fresco/`, as its own `docs.yml` job. It prints one line on every
run naming the pages it opened and the pins it classified, so read that before
believing a green: `--changed-since` reads the working tree, so an uncommitted
edit to a tracked page IS checked, but a page git has never been told about is
invisible until you `git add` it (a commit is not needed). A `0 pages inspected`
line is the gate saying it checked nothing. Under `--verbose` it also lists the
pins that are not landed but were rescued by an anchor in the same block — the
line to read when a planted SHA does not redden the gate, because a plant beside
an existing citation is absorbed by its neighbour rather than missed.
Nothing checks tables, rendering, or nav, so verify anchors and table column
counts by hand and say so in the PR body.

AGENTS.md now carries a compressed form of this rule; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood at trunk bba75d0f5b before rf2-bidyt trimmed the file. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:AGENTS.md

## A Backgrounded Gate Runs by Absolute Path — or in Someone Else's Worktree

The shell gates — every `scripts/test-*.sh` — derive their repo root from
`${BASH_SOURCE[0]}`, which is relative when the invocation is, and a
`cd <worktree> && sh scripts/…` does not reliably keep that `cd` once
backgrounded, so the run adopts whatever cwd the shell really has. One did
exactly that inside *another live worker's* checkout: it took that tree as its
spine root, its diff root and its classifier input, then reported the resulting
verdict as its own. A complete, internally consistent run about somebody else's
work is far harder to catch than a broken one, so those same gates print
`gate root: <path>` as their first line, and some node runners emit it too —
check that line against your worktree before believing any colour. That check,
not any naming rule, is what has actually caught this class: both 2026-08-12
scratchpad collisions (next section) were caught by a worker reading
`gate root:` and finding a sibling's worktree name there.

**Every other gate prints no banner at all** — not one of the
`scripts/check_*.py` gates, nor their `check-*.sh` siblings, and several print
nothing whatever on success. They do pin themselves to the script's own
location, and harder than `${BASH_SOURCE[0]}` manages — their repo root
defaults to `Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent`, absolute by
construction — which makes the absolute path matter MORE here rather than
less: `python scripts/check_….py` resolves that RELATIVE script path against
the cwd first, so a leaked cwd hands the interpreter the SIBLING'S copy, and
the script then pins faithfully to the sibling's tree and returns a verdict
about somebody else's work. Given the absolute path it scans YOUR checkout
from any cwd at all — measured 2026-08-13 by running `check_doc_slugs.py`
from a directory outside every checkout and watching it name a fault planted
only in one worktree. There the proof is the same shape
drawn from a different source — **plant a fault at a line you are already
editing and run the gate red.** Do not expect the failure to name your
worktree; `check_doc_slugs.py` reports repo-relative paths, which cannot tell
two checkouts apart. The discrimination is the red itself: the fault exists
only in your tree, so a run that had wandered into a sibling's comes back
**green**, and a green sabotage run is a reason to stop rather than a pass.
This half is written down because the section used to claim that every gate
under `scripts/` did both, which is an instruction a worker on a Python gate
cannot satisfy — two hit it in one day, and one improvised its way to the
negative control unprompted. So the check is mandatory on every gate run, by
whichever of the two routes that gate affords.

## Gate Artefacts Go Where Git Ignores Them

Never pipe a gate through `tail`, `head` or `grep` — a pipeline's exit status is
its *last* command's, so a red runner reads green. Redirect to a file, capture
the runner's own exit code, and quote that number in the PR body. **Every**
artefact that produces — the log *and* the exit-code file — must land on an
ignored path (`*.log`, `*.exit` and `*-exit.txt` all are) and carry **your
worktree's name AND the number of the attempt that wrote it**:

```bash
sh <WORKTREE_ROOT>/scripts/test-fast-pr.sh > gate-fastpr-<worktree>-1.log 2>&1; echo "$?" > gate-fastpr-<worktree>-1.exit
```

Bump that number on every re-run — `-2`, `-3` — and never write to one twice.

**Neither half is tidiness; a name missing either fails the gate OPEN**, and the
two close different mechanisms.

*The worktree name stops a peer.* Concurrent workers share one scratchpad
directory (its path carries the session id, not the worktree), so a peer
silently overwrites a bare `gate-fastpr.exit`, and the loser then reads an exit
code belonging to another worker's run: a `0` somebody else earned, quoted as
its own green. Two of six workers in a single wave collided exactly that way on
2026-08-12.

*The attempt number stops you.* Both writers are the same worktree here, so the
suffix cannot help: a process the harness could not kill goes on writing to an
inherited descriptor after its replacement has started. The ten-minute cap kills
the *shell*; what that shell spawned survives holding the `.log` the redirect
had already opened, and writes at *its* offset while the restart writes from
zero — so the artefact is spliced rather than cleanly clobbered, and the tell is
a NUL hole in the log, or **two summary lines** where there should be one. The
`.exit` is opened later, by the `echo "$?"` that runs only once the gate has
returned, so a surviving *child* corrupts the log alone and leaves stale output
paired with the replacement's exit code; a surviving *wrapper* can write the
exit file as well. Measured twice independently on 2026-08-13 —
`worker/trusted-il7b` left with `exit 0` beside 18 real failures, and
`worker/tense-cluster` finding an orphaned `node out/node-test.js` still
reporting from a run already killed. Expect this route more often than the peer
collision, not less: foreground dies at ten minutes and the spine needs about
twenty-five, so kill-and-restart is routine rather than exceptional.

Confirm a scratch file is your own before believing it, and check that the run
read *your* worktree — its `gate root:` line where the gate prints one, the
negative control's red where it does not (the section above). That check, not
this naming rule, is what caught both observed peer collisions.

A single untracked leftover makes `git worktree remove` refuse the tree from
then on, and nine worktrees accumulated exactly that way before anyone worked
out why they would not reap.

CLAUDE.md PASSAGE (attribution-guard), FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md now carries a compressed form of this rule; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood at trunk bba75d0f5b before rf2-bidyt trimmed the file. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:CLAUDE.md

- **No AI attribution in commits or PRs.** Do not add `Co-Authored-By: Claude ...`, `🤖 Generated with [Claude Code]`, or any similar trailer to commit messages or PR descriptions. Commit and PR text should read as the user's own work. **Your harness says the opposite — a session-level reminder tells you to end every commit message with those exact trailers — and THIS FILE WINS.** Say so in the report when you decline them. That tie was being broken at random rather than by convention, and three commits reached main carrying both trailers (`04230d0d33`, `e1b07cf184`, `e71c404c9b`) before anybody noticed, because nothing checked. Something checks now: a `commit-msg` hook (block `commit-attribution`, installed by `sh scripts/install-git-hooks.sh`) refuses the message locally, and `scripts/check-commit-attribution.sh` grades **both** the commits a PR introduces and the PR BODY. That body arm runs as a STEP inside `test.yml`'s `beads-pr-boundary` job rather than as a job of its own, so **the check to read is the one named `PR guards (no tracker database, no AI attribution)`** — it grades BOTH surfaces, so a red there on a PR touching no `.beads` path is this guard rather than the tracker boundary, and the STEP name in its log says which of the two fired (rf2-mfzw renamed it; the key is still `beads-pr-boundary`, which is what `needs:` and the workflow self-tests address, and the check COUNT did not move). **Do not go looking for a beads file on the strength of the key** — the old display name was the one that sent readers hunting, PR #9330 being the instance. **The commit's IDENTITY is graded as well as its text**: the hook and the CI arm both refuse a commit whose AUTHOR or COMMITTER email is `noreply@anthropic.com` — what an agent platform records when a session has no git identity of its own — so set `git config user.name` / `user.email` in such a session, and rebuild a branch already carrying one with `git rebase --exec 'git commit --amend --no-edit --reset-author' <base>`. **WHAT IS REFUSED IS A LINE THAT *IS* THE ATTRIBUTION, NEVER A LINE THAT MENTIONS ONE.** Prose naming the trailers passes at column 0 — a marker with words around it attributes nothing to anybody, and `git interpret-trailers` would not read it as a trailer either — so only a whole-line `Co-Authored-By:` carrying the assistant's address, a whole-line `Claude-Session:`, a marker line with nothing but decoration in front and its own link at the end, or a bare session URL alone on its line is refused. **That repair (rf2-uo5f) is why no brief needs an “indent your compliance sentence” workaround any more.** Before it, rule 3 was a bare substring test: PR #9330 went red on the sentence in which its author stated they had DECLINED the trailers, and could not be cleared by editing the body, because the workflow reads the body from the FROZEN EVENT PAYLOAD — a re-run re-reads the old text for ever and only a new event clears it. **This very bullet was one of the false positives** (measured: 1 offending line under the old detector, 0 under the new), so the guard refused the text of the rule it enforces. **A trailer-shaped line at column 0 still offends** — indent it by one space to quote one on purpose, which is what a commit documenting this rule has to do, and the layer-10 tests in `scripts/git-hooks/test-pre-commit.sh` pin both directions so a future widening cannot quietly disarm it. **The three existing commits are ACCEPTED and trunk history is NOT rewritten** — ruled 2026-09-06 under rf2-2e8f (option C: accept history, close the source at the harness, enforce with hook + CI, no sixth merge clause). That call is made; do not reopen it.

CLAUDE.md PASSAGE (check-band-clock), FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md now carries a compressed form of this rule; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood at trunk bba75d0f5b before rf2-bidyt trimmed the file. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:CLAUDE.md

- **Measuring the check-count band compares a `git` time against a `gh` time, and nothing AT THE POINT OF COMPARISON says the two use different conventions.** `git log --date=iso` prints LOCAL (`2026-09-16 15:18:39 +1000`); `gh`'s `mergedAt` prints UTC (`2026-09-16T15:22:46Z`) — as wall-clock digits those look four minutes apart while the instants are ten hours apart. Measured 2026-09-17 on the live case, matrix change `b9220b6dc2`: compared naively **1** of five candidate PRs qualified, and naively against that commit's committed time **0**; with both sides in UTC, **all five** do. **The zone is only half of it, because a change carries two clocks** — `b9220b6dc2` is authored `05:18:39Z` and committed `06:00:43Z`, 42 minutes apart, which under rebase-merge is the ordinary case. **Take the COMMITTED time, because it is what entered trunk history** — corroborated to the second here by the matrix change's own PR #9888 reporting `mergedAt` `06:00:44Z`. And the gap between the clocks is not hypothetical: **#9886 merged at `05:32:23Z`, inside it**, so the authored clock admits a PR whose checks were computed against the OLD matrix (the band read 88 either side of that boundary, so the seam is the finding and not a damaged band). **It fails CLOSED, and the danger is the next move** — a short qualifying set presents as "not enough PRs to measure the band", and widening the window to get more samples reaches back past the matrix change and measures the OLD band, which is the phantom the bullet above already prices. **The guard: put both instants in one zone before comparing (`TZ=UTC git log -1 --date=iso-local --format=%cd <sha>`), or drop the clocks altogether and ask ANCESTRY, which is what "did this land before that merged" actually is** — `git merge-base --is-ancestor <matrix-commit> <pr-merge-commit>`, measured agreeing with the committed clock on all five qualifying PRs and correctly reading #9886 and #9887 as BEFORE. **When confirming the matrix has not moved, take the positive control FROM THE TARGET rather than from a fixed offset (rf2-vwst8)**: `LAST=$(git log -1 --format=%H -- .github/workflows/)`, then `git diff --name-only "$LAST^" origin/main -- .github/workflows/` must list at least **1** file and `git diff --name-only "$LAST" origin/main -- .github/workflows/` must list **0** — and a `$LAST` other than the commit you have been treating as the matrix change means the band's qualifying set must be re-derived. A fixed offset such as `origin/main~40` EXPIRES SILENTLY as the trunk advances: measured 2026-09-18, it read **0** at every trunk point of a session some 450 commits past the last workflow change, while the self-derived pair read **1** and **0** — so the control could not bite, leaving the clause-5 zero beside it unverified rather than wrong. **Both tools report their own times honestly, so this is a reading defect rather than an instrument misreport, and nothing mechanical separates a correct comparison from a naive one — do not add a gate for it.**

CLAUDE.md PASSAGE (close-reason-inline-measurement), FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md now carries a compressed form of this rule; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood at trunk bba75d0f5b before rf2-bidyt trimmed the file. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:CLAUDE.md

- **A close reason or a ruling must carry its DECISIVE MEASUREMENT INLINE, and may cite a path under `ai/` only as supporting detail** — so the path stays a convenience that can rot without taking the finding with it. The disposability stated above is correct and is NOT what changes; what is wrong is citing a disposable tree as though it were durable. `.beads/issues.jsonl` is a full database export living in git history, which is why [Beads durability](#beads-durability) can promise complete recovery for an erased `close_reason` or a replaced `notes` field — and there is no such promise for a findings doc that has been tidied up, which is simply gone, from every checkout, for ever. **Measured 2026-09-16 over all 1,674 issue records in the export, counting distinct `findings/` paths that carry a FILE EXTENSION so that prose fragments cannot inflate the count: 93 citations, 67 resolve, 26 DANGLING (28%), and the most-cited dangling doc is referenced by 12 separate beads** — 69 / 51 / 18 restricted to `ai/findings/` alone, while the deliberately looser pattern over every `findings/` token reads 138 / 97 / 41 and IS inflated by prose, `ai/findings/exit` and `ai/findings/X` being the tell, so control the pattern if you widen it. **It fails in the REASSURING direction, which is what makes it expensive rather than untidy**: a bead citing a path looks BETTER sourced than one that does not, so the beads carrying dangling paths read as the most rigorous ones on the board. The failure they produce is the one the reopen bullet's dispatch clause describes — a worker briefed to read something that is not there reads the absence as its own failure rather than as the record's — reached by a different cause, and that clause's remedy has NO ANALOGUE here, because there is nothing to restore. **Do not delete or "fix" the existing dangling citations** — they are gone, mostly deliberately, and hunting them is the expensive half of a cheap problem — **and this is deliberately NOT a gate**: nothing is mechanically checkable that would not also flag every legitimate supporting reference.

CLAUDE.md PASSAGE (dispatch-ledger-contract), FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md now carries a compressed form of this rule; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood at trunk bba75d0f5b before rf2-bidyt trimmed the file. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:CLAUDE.md

- **The dispatch ledger is `ai/worktree-agent-ids.tsv`, and THIS BULLET is its contract — the file is local-only and untracked, so its own header is not an authority and has already drifted from its rows.** One tab-separated line per dispatch, five fields, in this order: **`worktree`** (the absolute path, never the bare directory name), **`agentId`**, **`dispatched`** (timestamp), **`branch`**, **`beads`**. Per *Reaping* in [`docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md`](docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md#reaping) the reap test reads the **report**, never a field of this line; `agentId` is the route to it, and **there is no done-sentence field**, because whether to hold report text locally at all is still an unmade operator call. Both recorded drifts came from reading the header instead of this contract: taking the last field for a done-sentence returns a bead id — well-formed, reassuring, wrong, and it would have authorised reaping 17 of 30 worktrees on no report at all — and keying column 1 by bare name made a name-keyed grep return 0 rows for 28 worktrees that had rows (rf2-83z0). The header also cites `.claude/commands/mayor-hygiene.md`, under a directory that no longer exists. **The contract binds the NEXT line, and does not describe the file — when this was written, 34 of 261 rows matched it, 13%.** Measured at that same point: 44 rows did not carry five fields at all and 127 began with something other than an absolute path, because this shape only settled on 2026-08-21 and every conforming row postdates that. **Every figure here is a snapshot of a file that grows each tick, so re-measure rather than quoting them.** And binding the next line is not automatic: of the first TEN rows written after this contract merged, four conformed and **six did not, all six by the author of the contract** — because the shape has no spelling for a worktree the MAYOR occupies, which has neither an agent id nor beads, so the writer improvises, and that improvisation put the record's own timestamp in field 1 and shifted every field by one, which is the positional failure this bullet exists to stop. **A mayor-occupied row uses the same five fields**: the absolute path, `(mayor)`, the timestamp, the branch, `--`. **And a dispatch with NO worktree — a zero-edit research or verification bead — uses them too**: `(none)`, the agentId, the timestamp, `(none)`, the beads, so a path-keyed sweep skips it on an exact match rather than trying to parse prose (the same improvisation recurred in this new position on 2026-09-09, one row in eight reading `(no-worktree: zero-edit research bead)` in field 1 while already carrying `(none)` in field 4). **So read a row's fields; never address them by index.** A positional parse is right about one row in eight and wrong with a well-formed answer on the rest, which is the failure this bullet exists to stop, one level up. Normalising the history is explicitly NOT wanted: the contract is here so the next line is right, not so the old ones are.

CLAUDE.md PASSAGE (examples-and-testbed-coverage), FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md now carries a compressed form of this rule; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood at trunk bba75d0f5b before rf2-bidyt trimmed the file. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:CLAUDE.md

**Examples are test-free (locked 2026-05-19, rf2-8cevm).** No `*.spec.cjs` may live under `examples/`. Browser smoke coverage is one adapter-level smoke per shipped adapter — each mount + dispatch + assert — but it lives at TWO filenames under TWO runners, so **a census keyed on `spec.cjs` under-counts it by construction** (rf2-kdaw): Reagent and UIx sit at `implementation/adapters/<name>/testbed/spec.cjs`, rostered as `ADAPTERS` in `implementation/adapters/scripts/adapter-smoke-filter.cjs` and run by `npm run test:adapter-smokes`, while reagent-slim's is `implementation/adapters/reagent-slim/testbed/smoke.cjs`, run by its own `npm run test:reagent-slim:smoke`. Both runners are wired into `test.yml` and the nightly `expensive-tests.yml`. **(e) A pattern JOINED from `jq` output matches nothing but its LAST alternative, because `jq` writes CRLF here and the carriage return rides into the interior of the join.** Measured 2026-09-05 over 1500 trunk commits in one shell: `grep -F -f ids.txt` read **22**, a `paste -sd'|'` alternation built from that same 99-id file read **1**, and `tr -d ''` before the join restored it to **22**. It is NOT a size limit, which is the natural guess: a 10-id, 99-character alternation already read `0` where `-F -f` read `3`. The producer is `jq` (jq-1.8.1), not `bd` and not the shell — `bd list --json` ends its lines `
`, `echo '[{"id":"aaa"}]' | jq -r '.[].id'` ends them `
`, and a single-value `$(… | jq -r …)` capture comes back clean — so it bites wherever those lines are JOINED, read as patterns, **or handed back to a command as an ARGUMENT** — that third case was written here as "and nowhere else", and it is not. Measured 2026-09-09: piping `bd list --json` through `jq -r '.[].id'` into `while read -r id` leaves a trailing CARRIAGE RETURN on `id`, and `bd show` then refuses that id **in the shape callers least expect — exit 1, the human-readable refusal on STDERR, and a JSON ERROR OBJECT on STDOUT** where every caller expects the ARRAY a good id returns (measured both ways: `type=object` on the CR-suffixed id against `type=array` on the clean one). So `.[0].dependencies[]?` dies with `Cannot index object with number`, the near-universal `2>/dev/null` discards the one human-readable clue, and a `$(...)` capture of the filter yields empty — so the caller's else-branch fires UNIFORMLY. It read `(unblocked)` for **all 23** non-terminal beads in one sweep, a uniform and entirely plausible answer that would have authorised dispatching workers into fenced surfaces. **Treat an ERROR OBJECT on stdout as a FOURTH `bd` JSON shape** beside the three in the memory `bd-json-shapes-differ-list-show-history`, and check that the document is an array before indexing it. **And note which control actually exercises this, because the obvious one does not**: a `$(...)` capture of the very same pipeline comes back CLEAN, so a control built that way passes while the sweep is broken — only an id that arrived through `read -r` reproduces it. **One trap specific to editing THIS file**: writing this entry inserted four REAL carriage returns where the escape was meant literally, git reclassified `CLAUDE.md` from `w/crlf` to `w/-text`, stopped normalising it, and staged **156 changed lines** for a one-clause edit. After editing here, check that the total CR count equals the CRLF count — **and take both of those numbers with PYTHON reading the bytes, never with a bare `grep -c`, which reads 0 on this very file and so makes this check pass vacuously as `0 == 0`; see (s)**. **COUNT BARE LINE FEEDS TOO — the CR-equals-CRLF test CANNOT SEE THEM, and they are the likelier damage when a tool writes the file for you.** In a CRLF file an inserted LF-only line leaves the CR total and the CRLF total both unchanged and therefore still EQUAL, so the prescribed check passes on a file that has gone mixed — the same vacuous-pass shape as the `grep -c` trap beside it, arrived at from the opposite direction. The three-number check read `cr=158 crlf=157 bare_lf=1` and refused it; the old two-number form would have caught the CR and been blind to the line feed. So take the three numbers with Python — total CR, total CRLF, and bare LF as the count of line feeds minus the count of CRLF pairs — and require BOTH that CR equals CRLF and that bare LF is zero, for any file git reports as `w/crlf`. **And per item (o), build the replacement text with the Write tool rather than a heredoc whenever it carries backslashes at all**, which a sample of this check inevitably does. **Use `grep -F -f <file>` for any multi-needle search** (a fixed-string pattern FILE, not the aborting `-iF` flag pair of (a) — there is no `-i` — and measured immune: `1`, correct, on a deliberately CRLF pattern file). **And take the control FROM the file rather than splicing it into the pattern.** A known-present id appended to the alternation read `1` and passed — which is how the original sweep's control passed while the sweep reported zero — and splicing that same id into the MIDDLE also read `1` and also passed, because a shell literal carries no `` wherever it sits. Not every mixed comparison fails — the single-value `$(… | jq -r …)` capture this bullet already records as coming back CLEAN is one that does not — so the seam is a thing to CHECK, never a thing to assume in either direction. **FOURTH DOOR — a DUPLICATION PROBE built from two `jq` outputs taken from DIFFERENT invocations.** Restoring an erased field, the probe asked whether the payload was already present in `notes` and read **0**: the notes lines carried a trailing carriage return (length **453**) while the probe, drawn through a second `jq` invocation, did not (**452**), so the fixed-string match could not land. ` alone) where the regex means to match them. Decide which side is authoritative before reaching for `tr`. **Second, and this half IS universal: take the control FROM THE TARGET, so a zero means absence rather than a broken instrument** — it is what detects the failed regex recipe above, so getting the pattern right never makes it redundant. Every RUN is halved, while a lone backslash before an ordinary character (`\t`, `\d`, `\"`, `\$`) is untouched — and that selectivity is what hides it, because nearly every backslash in an ordinary script survives and only the doubled ones move, which are exactly the ones that mean *a literal backslash*. **IT FAILS IN BOTH REGISTERS FROM THE SAME CONSTRUCT IN THE SAME LANGUAGE, so meeting the loud form teaches you nothing about the quiet one.** LOUD: Python `sep = '\\'` arrives as `sep = '\'` and dies at parse time (`SyntaxError: unterminated string literal`, exit 1); JavaScript `p.replace(/\\/g, "/")` arrives as `p.replace(/\/g, "/")` and node refuses it (`SyntaxError: missing ) after argument list`, exit 1), because the surviving `\/` escapes the regex's own closing delimiter and swallows it. SILENT: move that same literal-backslash pattern off the delimiter and the damaged form is still a valid pattern with a different meaning — `/a\\b/` becomes `/a\b/`, a WORD BOUNDARY, and `/\\d/` becomes `/\d/`, a DIGIT — while in a string `"C:\\Users\\dev"` becomes `"C:\Users\dev"`, which evaluates to `C:Usersdev` with the separators simply gone. So whether this announces itself turns on where in the token the surviving backslash happens to land, which is incidental to what the author meant. **The guard: write anything carrying a backslash with the Write tool rather than through the Bash tool's command text — heredoc and single-quoted argument alike — and verify by EFFECT — read a distinctive backslash-bearing line back out of the written file — because the writer's exit code is 0 either way.** Measured on one identical three-line file: through the heredoc it carries **8** backslashes and prints `C:Usersdev`; written directly it carries **16** and prints `C:\Users\dev`. Measured in both directions 2026-09-12 against four real call-site shapes — `(skip! off-browser)`, `(skip!` then a newline, `(skip! ":node-test: no DOM")` and the zero-arity `(skip!)` — `\(skip!\b` missed all four, `\(skip!` matched all four, `\(skip!\s` matched the first three and missed the zero-arity, and `\(skip![\s)]` matched all four; probing the assertion directly, `skip!\b` reads *no boundary* before a space, a `)` and a newline, and MATCHES before `a`, `1` and `_`. **It bites HERE specifically because this project's symbols end in punctuation by convention** — `skip!`, `assoc!`, `conj!`, `persistent!`, `volatile!`, `browser?`, `some?`, `fn?` — measured over 3004 tracked Clojure files, **4265 of 19415 distinct `def*` names, 22%, end in `!` or `?`**, so a census over this tree reaches for `\b` around a bang or question-mark symbol constantly. **And it fails in the DEFECT-MANUFACTURING direction, which is what makes it expensive rather than merely wrong**: in the instance that found it a DOM-test census read **399 MARKED / 183 UNMARKED** where the true reading was **579 / 3** — 183 is a plausible worklist naming real files, so nothing on screen says it is wrong, and an auditor who trusted it would have filed against 180 correct rows. The gap was **exactly 180**, the identical number an earlier pass had produced by omitting the `skip!` spelling altogether: **two passes failing in the same place by different mechanisms**, which is the detail worth the space — getting the spelling into the pattern is not the same as getting it to match. Surrounding context: git show bba75d0f5b:CLAUDE.md

**(y) `gh run view --log --job <id>` REFUSES WHILE ANY OTHER JOB IN THE RUN IS UNFINISHED — for a job that has COMPLETED, and whose log the server is already serving — because `--job` is a FILTER over a RUN-WIDE fetch rather than a selector that narrows what is fetched.** The refusal reads *"run <run-id> is still in progress; logs will be available when it is complete"*, and every word of it is true about the RUN; what is false is the reader's inference that the log they asked for does not exist yet. **The tell is that the message names the RUN id nobody typed rather than the JOB id that was typed** — and the same CLI will, in the same breath, report that job as finished. Measured 2026-09-18 at `df3523ec77` against one live run of this repo's `tests` workflow while 68 of its 70 jobs were complete and both stragglers were shadow-cljs lanes, all three commands naming the SAME completed job: `gh run view --log --job <id>` exited **1** with **0** bytes on stdout; `gh run view --job <id>`, the same job without `--log`, exited **0** and printed it as a completed job with its duration; and `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/jobs/<id>/logs` exited **0** and returned **87,322** bytes of that job's log. **The mechanism is measured rather than inferred**: the run-level archive `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/runs/<run-id>/logs` answered **404** on that open run and exit **0** with **970,515** bytes of ZIP on a completed one, so `--log` is waiting on an archive the server does not cut until the whole run ends, while the per-job endpoint is served as soon as the job itself finishes. **Control the other way, so the refusal is known to be about RUN STATE rather than about the job, the id or auth**: the identical `gh run view --log --job <id>` form against a job in a COMPLETED run exited **0** and returned **42,686** bytes. **It fails CLOSED and LOUDLY, and earns its place for a COST that is structural here rather than incidental** — the jobs holding a run open longest on this matrix are the shadow-cljs lanes, so the lane whose log is wanted most often is the one whose slowest sibling is withholding it. You ask for a job's log precisely BECAUSE it has finished, usually finished RED, and the refusal reads as *the evidence is not written yet*, so the move it invites is to wait for something already in hand; the item behind this entry records two readers concluding exactly that independently. **The guard: when the CLI refuses with an in-progress message and the JOB named is complete, ask the per-job API endpoint, and settle that job's own state with `gh run view --job <id>`, which answers about the job while the run is still open.** **Nearest to (x)** — an instrument not misreporting about itself, the false step being the reader's — and distinct from (p) and (q), which are `gh` misreads of a field's VALUE where this is a misread of which OBJECT the precondition is asked of.

**(z) GREPPING A CI JOB LOG FOR A TEST NAMESPACE ASKS "DID IT FAIL?" RATHER THAN "DID IT RUN" — this tree's quiet reporter prints the `Testing <ns>` banner ONLY on that namespace's first failure, so a namespace that PASSED is absent BY DESIGN and a HIT is bad news rather than the confirmation being sought.** Having got a green lane, the natural corroboration is *did my new namespace actually run?* and the natural probe is to grep the job log for its name. **The zero it returns is true and carries no information** — and the probe is not uniformly dead either, which is what lets it survive use: it is LIVE in exactly two situations, and each of them answers a different question from the one asked. Measured 2026-09-18 over two green `CLJS (shadow-cljs :node-test)` job logs from this repo's `tests` workflow: `Testing ` appears **0** times in a job whose suite reported **12,237 tests containing 61,248 assertions**, and **0** times again in a second reporting **12,227 / 61,135**. **The only namespace names a green log carries come from a LATER STEP OF THE SAME JOB** — `implementation/scripts/check-per-ns-isolation.cjs`, which re-runs a hardcoded roster of namespaces standalone and prints `isolating <ns> ... ok` for each — so those names answer *is this namespace on the standalone-isolation roster?*, and the log's own line puts them at **197 tests, 735 assertions** against that same run's 12,237. **The control both ways, taken on ONE log**: `re-frame.projection-cljs-test`, a roster entry, reads **1**; `re-frame.test-quiet-shadow-node-cljs-test` — which `implementation/shadow-cljs.edn`'s own comment says is placed on the `:node-test` classpath so that `npm run test:cljs` runs it — reads **0**; and `re-frame.no-such-namespace-cljs-test`, which does not exist, reads **0** as well. **A namespace that RAN and a namespace that DOES NOT EXIST are indistinguishable through this probe**, and that is the whole defect in one line. On a RED job log from the same lane, `Testing ` appears exactly once and names the namespace that failed. **The mechanism is this repository's rather than `cljs.test`'s, which is the attribution most likely to be got backwards**: `implementation/test-quiet/src/re_frame/test_quiet.cljc` defmethods `[:cljs.test/default :begin-test-ns]` to suppress the default `Testing <ns>` line — its own comment says exactly that — and defers it to `print-namespace-banner!`, which the `:fail` and `:error` methods call on the first failure inside a namespace. So the banner is a FAILURE BANNER by construction, and the library being wrapped prints the line unconditionally. **Nor is it a node-lane quirk to be dodged by reading a JVM artefact's log instead**: the same file installs the same suppression for `clojure.test`, and measured 2026-09-18, **31 of the 37** `deps.edn` files carrying a `:test` alias run `re-frame.test-quiet.runner`. **It fails in the REASSURING direction twice over** — the zero reads as *my tests did not run* to one reader and gets written up as corroboration by a tireder one — and what makes the probe feel trustworthy is that a log is usually opened when something FAILED, which is precisely the case in which the name IS there; the lesson learned on red runs is then carried to a green one, where it is inverted. **The guard: predict the COUNT DELTA from the diff before any log is opened, and compare it against a baseline taken at YOUR OWN merge base** — recorded on the item behind this entry, the prediction was +10 tests / +40 assertions and the run matched exactly, which is evidence that CI compiled that branch, where the namespace grep would have been silent whatever had happened. **And if a grep for your namespace DOES hit, read it as a failure banner or a roster line, never as attendance.** **This is the vacuity rule reaching CI logs** — the one under [Build & Test](#build--test) holding that a gate cannot fail on a file containing none of what it inspects — arriving through a SEARCH that cannot find what a successful path never prints. **NOT the family of (f), (j) or (t)**, where the query is malformed and the repair is to write it properly; here the query is correct, the tool reads the file, and the target genuinely does not contain the answer. (y) is how the log is obtained at all; this is what it will not tell you once you have it. **No gate is wanted**: what a runner chooses to print is the runner's business, and the count delta already settles the question the grep was reaching for. **The label after (z) is (aa), then (ab), (ac) … — spreadsheet-column order, ruled under rf2-z0pma on 2026-09-21; the existing letters are never renumbered, and a lane-coverage finding (a gate reporting truthfully on what it compiled while the reader inferred more) is not an instrument item at all — it goes unlettered under Build & Test beside the rf2-uwa9r paragraph, which is where rf2-z0pma's own finding went.**
