The Opus adversarial-review corpus (ai/findings/advisarial-review/opus/, 18 reports plus README.md, local-only) is a MAINTAINED document. Mike, 2026-10-11: "I want it to be kept up to date and to reflect the current status." Sol's corpus (ai/findings/advisarial-review/sol/) is Sol's own job, so do not edit it from the Opus side, and leave the README's "Cross-review with Sol" section alone.

Each report carries two header lines:
- `Pruned:` records the first pass, done at 5c27bc3057 against epic rf2-mn2ht.
- `Refreshed: <ts> at HEAD <sha> — removed N items resolved since the last pass (<ids>)`, or `— no items resolved since the last pass`. Every check stamps this line, even when nothing changed.

Filing work: when an item becomes a bead, it LEAVES its report (no tombstone), the report gets a `Filed: <ts> at HEAD <sha> — moved N items to beads (<ids>: what)` header line (the `Refreshed:` line is left alone, because it dates the merged-PR check), and the README lists the bead under "Filed, awaiting work" until it closes, when it moves to "Resolved since review". The corpus keeps only what could still be done (Mike, 2026-10-12). Only file what needs no ruling; an item that changes deliberate, specified or test-pinned behaviour is a design choice and stays as a proposal. Cross-check each item against Sol before filing.

The README carries a matching `Refreshed:` line with the corpus word total.

How to refresh:
1. Take the oldest `Refreshed:` timestamp as the cutoff. Convert AUSEST to UTC (AUSEST is UTC+11 in October).
2. List the PRs merged since the cutoff: `gh pr list --repo day8/re-frame2 --state merged --limit 200 --json number,title,mergedAt,body`, filtered by mergedAt in UTC.
3. List the beads closed since the cutoff: `bd list --status closed --limit 0 --json`, filtered by closed_at.
4. Fan out to about 3 background workers, about 6 reports each. Give each worker the stance verbatim plus these rules:
   - Remove an item only when a merged PR or a closed bead resolves it, after confirming at HEAD.
   - Remove its text, its action entry, its table row and its Sol paragraph, with no tombstones. Renumber and fix cross-references, and keep the Verdict accurate.
   - Where a proposal was partly implemented, keep the remainder with one present-tense line saying what now exists.
   - Add an open bead id beside any item that now has one.
   - Edit only the assigned reports. No bd writes, no git mutations, no builds.
5. Then have one worker update the README: word counts, headlines, the resolved list (bead → PR), themes, open questions and follow-ups. It also leaves the Sol section untouched.
6. Item-level history lives in the reports' header lines and on the beads. It does not go into a memory.

Adding notes to (or otherwise updating) a bead that is already in_progress will probably NOT reach the background agent working on it: the worker read the bead at dispatch and does not re-read it (Mike, 2026-10-12). So put everything a worker needs on the bead BEFORE it is dispatched. Once a bead is in_progress, a note on it is only a record for the reviewer or audit, not a channel to the worker. If something must reach the worker in flight, tell the mayor in one line so it can relay it, or file a follow-up bead that is sequenced after the in-progress one. Example: on 2026-10-12, Sol's duplicate detail was appended to rf2-0qiq6 and rf2-ztt72 after the mayor had dispatched them to worker/fresco-batteries, so that worker probably never saw it.

GIT --since=YYYY-MM-DD WITH NO TIME OF DAY USES THE CURRENT TIME OF DAY, NOT MIDNIGHT, so the same command answers differently depending on when you run it. Measured 2026-10-15: `git log --oneline --since='2026-10-13' origin/main -- docs/the-mayor-method/` counted 1 commit when run at 00:10 and 0 when run at 10:09, about the same commit (5d1a76dd70, committed 2026-10-13 00:30 +1100). Git's approxidate fills the missing time from the clock, so the cutoff was 10-13 00:10 on the first run (commit included) and 10-13 10:09 on the second (commit excluded). It fails in the reassuring direction for a "has anything changed since X?" probe. GUARD: give an explicit time (`--since='2026-10-13 00:00'`) or a revision range (`<last-seen-sha>..origin/main`), and take a control: `git log -1 -- <path>` with no date filter, which must show the newest commit you expect.

`bd dolt push` can fail with "fork/exec C:\Program Files\Git\ucrt64\bin\git.exe: Not enough memory resources are available to process this command" while the machine shows tens of GB free and commit far below the limit. Measured 2026-10-15 ~10:20 AUSEST: it failed twice, then succeeded on a plain retry about 25 minutes later ("Push complete.", exit 0), with no bd, dolt or git process left over between the attempts. The git push of the same checkpoint succeeded throughout, so only the Dolt remote leg was affected. The machine-level suspect at the time: AcerCentralService (PID 5156) held about 1.55 million handles and was still climbing, and kernel nonpaged pool read 1,341 MB, paged pool 1,172 MB, against committed 39 GB of a 138 GB limit. So the failure points at kernel or system resources, not RAM. Unverified: whether that handle leak caused it. What to do: read the push output TEXT, not only the exit code. Retry once later. Do not restore or force anything in the tracker. If it keeps failing, report the Acer service handle count to Mike: restarting that service, or a reboot, is his call.

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: CHECKPOINT FIRST, THEN CLEAR .beads, THEN UPDATE, FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

- **Checkpoint first, then clear `.beads`, then update — and never stash.** An uncommitted `.beads/issues.jsonl` makes the rebase step below abort (`cannot rebase: You have unstaged changes`), freezing HEAD at a stale base, so the file does have to be cleared. Rebase refuses on *any* unstaged change, not only one the incoming commits would overwrite, so this bites even when nothing upstream touches the file. But clearing it *after* a `bd close` or `bd create` reverts the export to its pre-close state, and the next checkpoint writes that revert back over the database — the close evaporates (rf2-51uz1: rf2-5e8zv was reopened exactly this way, and commit `e80786e007` records three more re-closed by hand). The order is therefore fixed, and a checkout of `.beads` must never follow a tracker mutation within a tick:

  ```bash
  sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh                   # export from the database, verify, commit
  git checkout HEAD -- .beads                      # now safe: HEAD carries the tracker
  git fetch origin main && git rebase origin/main  # explicit ref, not a pull — see below
  ```

  **Take that third step's target from `origin/main`, and don't restore the `git pull --rebase origin main` it replaced — naming the remote and branch does not make a pull equivalent.** A pull is two steps: it fetches into `FETCH_HEAD`, then rebases onto whatever `FETCH_HEAD` says by the time the rebase reads it. Naming remote and branch constrains only the fetch half, so the rebase half still takes its target from a scratch file that any concurrent git process **in the same checkout** rewrites — which is why the named form was measured aborting with `Cannot rebase onto multiple branches` on a clean, undiverged tree, exactly as the bare form had (2026-09-01 22:4x AUSEST, mayor checkout, six worker worktrees live). The reasoning is the one already written out for the merge case in the fast-forward bullet under [Workflow](#workflow) — *a ref can't be captured that way* — and this sequence was simply left behind when that case was fixed; keep the `&&` for the same reason that bullet does, so a failed fetch can't be followed by a rebase against a stale ref. Read the session-completion block above the same way: it is tool-generated — and so is the copy of it in `AGENTS.md`, which sits inside a `BEADS INTEGRATION` marker carrying the same block hash — so if a regeneration restores the pull form in **either**, correct it in both rather than following it. The generator is `bd` itself, not anything in this repository, so there is no template here to fix; the two copies have to be kept in step by hand.

  Naming remote and branch is still worth doing on the fetch, which is the half it does reach: the earlier instance recorded here was of the **bare** form, whose own fetch is unconstrained too (measured 2026-08-29 22:31 AUSEST, mid-checkpoint, one line after a `git fetch origin worker/<branch>`). The contaminating process is a concurrent one in the same checkout rather than a peer worktree — `FETCH_HEAD` is per-worktree, as `git rev-parse --git-path FETCH_HEAD` resolves inside a linked worktree's own git directory — and the mayor checkout, where several git processes run at once, is where that bites.

  **Do not pipe any step of this sequence, and do not chain past one with `&&` through a filter.** A pipeline's exit status is its *last* command's, so a step written as `… 2>&1 | tail -3 && bd dolt push && git push` reports `tail`'s success and walks straight past a fatal abort with the rebase never performed. That is how the 2026-09-01 abort above went unseen, and why it was inert only in the sense that the push behind it still landed. It is the same hazard as piping a gate through a filter, reached through git instead of a gate runner.

  `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh --pre-pull` (or `-PrePull` on the `.ps1`) answers "would clearing `.beads` throw tracker state away?" — exit 0 means the checkout is safe. **Do not `git stash`**: stashes are repo-global and contaminate every other worktree in flight.

  **This sequence answers one abort message and only that one.** The other cause — the checkpoint you just made having diverged from a racing push — surfaces as `Not possible to fast-forward`, and that is the fast-forward bullet's `git merge --ff-only origin/main` speaking, not the rebase step here, which rebases your checkpoint on top and exits 0. Clearing an already-clean `.beads` is inert against it either way. Branch on the message; both branches are set out under *After each merge* in [`docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md`](docs/the-mayor-method/loops.md#after-each-merge).

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: THE TRACKER DATABASE IS THE MAYOR'S TO COMMIT, FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

- **The tracker database is the mayor's to commit.** Worker branches carry code, spec, docs and tests — never `.beads/issues.jsonl`, `.beads/metadata.json`, or any other database-derived path. The human-authored config (`.beads/README.md`, `.beads/config.yaml`, `.beads/.gitignore`, `.beads/hooks/**`, `.beads/PRIME.md`) is fair game from anywhere. **`.beads/PRIME.md` is hand-written prose, not an export**: `bd prime` reads it and emits it INSTEAD of its own default text at SessionStart and PreCompact (both `.claude/settings.json` hooks pass `--no-memories`, because otherwise every persistent memory, megabytes of them, is appended after it), so it is the file that decides what rides in every session's opening context — edit it like any other doc, and re-sync it by hand against `bd prime --export --no-memories` after a `bd` upgrade, since the override suppresses upstream changes to that default. It is advice from a tool and **this file outranks it**; never cite it as "CLAUDE.md says". A pre-commit hook enforces this in linked worktrees **once installed** — run `sh scripts/install-git-hooks.sh` (or `scripts/install-git-hooks.ps1`) once per clone; worktrees share the primary checkout's hooks directory, so one run arms them all, and `--check` answers whether a checkout is currently guarded **through its EXIT CODE ALONE — on success it prints nothing at all** (0 installed and current, 1 otherwise; it writes only when it fails, as its own usage line says). **So never read it through a pipe.** `… --check | tail` hands back `tail`'s status, and empty output beside a 0 looks identical whether the hooks are armed or missing — which is the pipeline-status hazard this file catalogues elsewhere, arriving through a guard everyone is told to run. Measured 2026-09-08 on a checkout whose four hooks WERE installed: piped through `tail` it printed nothing and the pipeline exited 0; re-run bare it printed nothing on stdout, nothing on stderr, and exited 0 — so the piped form cannot separate that case from an unguarded one. Run it bare and read `$?`; to SEE the answer rather than infer it from silence, list the hooks directory and expect `commit-msg`, `post-merge`, `post-rewrite` and `pre-commit` (`core.hooksPath` unset means `.git/hooks`). `scripts/check-beads-pr-boundary.sh` is the CI arm. See `scripts/git-hooks/README.md`.

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: bd update --notes REPLACES THE NOTES FIELD, FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

- **`bd update --notes` REPLACES the notes field; `--append-notes` is the flag that adds to it.** The loss path here is the bead's own content rather than the export, and it is silent in the same way: `--notes`' help text reads *"Additional notes"*, which is how a reader takes it, nothing errors, `bd` prints its normal success line, and the damage stays invisible until somebody re-reads the bead — on a held bead, possibly never. Measured across five beads in one session (~72,800 characters, `rf2-9wmqd` 46569→3294 the worst), and it had happened before: `rf2-y1jkm` carries an earlier account of the same mistake, surviving only because its author restored it by hand. **Recovery is complete and cheap, so this is not an occasion to panic** — `.beads/issues.jsonl` in git history is a full database export, so the pre-damage notes sit in any checkpoint commit predating the update: `git show <rev>:.beads/issues.jsonl`, rebuild as old + newline + current, write back. One trap in that recovery is worth knowing, because it fails silently where the rest of this is merely quiet: a value past roughly 27,000 characters is rejected by the shell with a non-zero exit and **no message at all**, so split at line boundaries into ~18,000-character chunks — `--notes` for the first, `--append-notes` for the rest — and confirm by probing for known content from the start, middle and end rather than by comparing lengths, which chunking shifts by a byte or two. **A second trap in the same act, and this one DAMAGES the note rather than rejecting it: BACKTICKS inside a DOUBLE-QUOTED shell string are command substitution**, so the backticked words are deleted and whatever they print is spliced in where they stood. `bd` prints its normal success line either way, so the note lands looking healthy while the passage carrying the evidence is gone — and a note about this repo is exactly where backticks cluster, since every path, var and flag in it wants a code span. It damaged a note on `rf2-fmst` in precisely the places quoting the measurements. Measured both ways: ``"epoch anchor `echo REMOVED-BY-SUBSTITUTION` restored"`` arrives as `epoch anchor REMOVED-BY-SUBSTITUTION restored`, while the identical line through a QUOTED heredoc (`<<'EOF'`) arrives verbatim with its backticks intact. **The guard: write the note with a quoted heredoc and pass it as `"$(cat <file>)"`** — the same move the chunking above already needs, so both traps in this bullet share one remedy. If the heredoc will not parse, build the file by any other means and still pass it as `"$(cat <file>)"`: what protects the note is that the content reaches `bd` from a FILE rather than through a double-quoted shell string, and the heredoc is one way to build that file rather than the thing doing the protecting.

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: PER-PR AND PER-RUN BOOKKEEPING NEVER GOES INTO A MEMORY, FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

- **Per-PR and per-run bookkeeping goes on the bead and in the commit, never into a memory — `bd remember` is for findings that GENERALISE** (ruled under rf2-ornb). An audit of one merged PR is already recorded three times — in its `chore(beads): audit merged PR` commit, in the bead's own notes, and on the PR itself — so a memory copy adds nothing. **The rule lives here because its violator does not**: the writer is a generated `.git/codex-pr-audit-<PR>/checkpoint.py`, re-emitted per PR by an out-of-repo merge-audit harness, so no tracked file can enforce it and this bullet is the only durable artefact a future harness author reads. The legacy per-PR receipts are deleted and survive in git history — `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1 git show 4520025651:.beads/issues.jsonl | jq -r --arg k merged-pr-audit-pr-9664 'select(._type=="memory" and .key==$k)|.value'` recovers one — and "was PR N audited?" is `git log --oneline --grep='audit merged PR #N'`. **Nine `merged-pr-audit-*` keys stay; leave all nine**: the rolling `merged-pr-audit-cursor`, which is the key the harness's resume logic recalls, and eight method memories — `merged-pr-audit-cursor-correction-pr-7568-timezone-comparison` among them, a correction record that shares the cursor's prefix rather than a second cursor.

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: THE SAME FLOOR IS IN THE PRE-COMMIT HOOK, FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

- **The same floor is in the pre-commit hook, so a plain `git add` cannot route around it (rf2-or8te).** The checkpoint's guard only protects commits that go through the checkpoint, and twice an empty export reached main by a path that did not: `7aea52459` (2026-06-10, 7172 rows) and `4d8042d80d` (2026-07-26, 2573 rows), both plain `git add` from the mayor checkout, both leaving `git status` clean afterwards. The hook now refuses any staged `.beads/issues.jsonl` below 90% of HEAD, from every worktree. **An empty export is a REGENERATION event, not a data-loss one** — the Dolt database is the source of truth, `sh scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh` rebuilds it, and restoring an older export from git history would time-travel the tracker instead. For a genuine mass delete the message names the escape: inspect with `bd status`, then `git commit --no-verify`.

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: REOPENING A BEAD ERASES ITS close_reason AND closed_at, FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

- **Reopening a bead ERASES its `close_reason` and its `closed_at`, and the text is not copied into `notes` or anywhere else.** Same class as the `--notes` trap above — a silent field-level loss with a cheap git-history recovery — so read that bullet for the recovery pattern and for the chunking and backtick traps rather than looking for them restated here. Measured 2026-09-09 on a throwaway bead created and disposed of for the purpose (`rf2-i834`): closed with a 419-character reason, it read `close_reason` 419 and `closed_at` a timestamp; one `bd update <id> --status open` later it read `close_reason` **0** and `closed_at` **null**, and a probe for the reason's sentinel token across the WHOLE stringified record — not merely `notes` — read **0**. `bd` prints its ordinary success line either way, so nothing on screen says a field was emptied. The same was measured that day on `rf2-dokz` and `rf2-z5lv`, both closed by the mayor and reopened by the merged-PR audit within the hour. **It bites HERE specifically because this project treats close reasons as NORMATIVE RECORDS** — a ruling is often the close reason of a closed dependency, which is why `bd gc`'s decay phase is banned and why the backlog-reread loop sends you to read them — and because an audit reopening is the system WORKING, so the loss lands precisely on the beads being worked twice, whose account of what the first pass actually did is the one most wanted. **The obvious detection probe cannot work, and that is worth stating because it is the first one a careful reader reaches for**: you cannot find reopened closures by listing non-terminal beads that still carry a `close_reason`, because the reopen removes its own evidence. Measured over the export at HEAD: **0** of the 33 non-terminal beads carry one, against a control of **1084 of 1085** closed beads that do — the probe is live, it simply cannot see this. **Recovery is complete and cheap by two independent routes, and neither needs the tool's cooperation.** (1) `.beads/issues.jsonl` in git history is a full database export, so any checkpoint commit made while the bead was closed carries the text: `git show <commit>:.beads/issues.jsonl | jq -r --arg i <id> 'select(._type=="issue" and .id==$i) | (.close_reason // "" | length)'`. **Select on the IDENTITY field — a bare grep for the id is instrument item (f) and here it fails in the reassuring direction**: bead ids cross-reference each other in dependency lists and close-reason prose, so on checkpoint `4cbaba034c` five records MENTION `rf2-dokz` and exactly one IS it, and `grep '"rf2-dokz"' | head -1 | jq` duly reported a `close_reason` length of 0 on the very checkpoint carrying 5181 characters of it. **And the window is NARROW** — exactly one of the last fourteen checkpoints carried that text — so walk a range and never conclude from the newest. (2) `bd history <id> --json --limit N`, whose per-commit snapshots nest the fields under `.Issue`: on the throwaway bead the lengths read `[0,419,0]` newest-first with exactly one snapshot carrying the sentinel, and four carried it for `rf2-dokz`. **Take the `--limit`, and size the output before anything reads it — the unbounded form on a large bead is GIGABYTES, and it does not fail, it SUCCEEDS.** A bead keeps a full record copy per commit, so history size is record size times snapshot count: measured 2026-09-16 on `rf2-uelji`, the unbounded form returned **1,591,359,019 bytes (1.59 GB)** at exit 0 in 14 seconds with nothing on stderr, against **200,683** at `--limit 1` and **602,043** at `--limit 3` — about 200 KB per snapshot across some 7,900 of them. So the idiom this bullet used to invite, piping it straight into `jq`, is not a slow command but a dead session, and the bead most likely to need recovering is the one that takes the damage, because a record grows large by being argued over. **Redirect to a FILE and `wc -c` it first**, and raise `N` only as far as the walk needs. **The snapshot is NOT truncated**: the same `notes` came back byte-identical from `bd show` and from `--limit 1`, 193,646 bytes, 2.95x the 65,535-byte `TEXT` ceiling — so a short answer here means the field was genuinely empty at that commit, never that it was clipped. **For a large bead route (1) is simply the better route** — a checkpoint export is complete and one `git show` away, where route (2) has to be bounded and sized before it can be read at all. Restore with `bd update <id> --append-notes` (never `--notes`), under a heading naming it a RESTORED CLOSE REASON and citing the commit it came from, so nobody reads it as newer than the audit note below it. **AND A DISPATCH CLAUSE, because this one cost a real cycle**: a brief telling a worker to "read the bead's close reason" is UNSATISFIABLE on a reopened bead, and the worker reads the absence as its own failure rather than as the tool's — two live workers were briefed that way on 2026-09-09 and had to be messaged mid-flight. So either restore the reason into the notes BEFORE dispatching, or do not cite it. Record the behaviour and stop there: no wrapper around `bd`, no gate, nothing to keep in sync.

CLAUDE.md BEADS DURABILITY ITEM: THE OPENING PARAGRAPH (THE TRACKED EXPORT IS A SNAPSHOT), FULL TEXT. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability now carries this item's rules, each with its one-line why and guard; this memory is the complete account, measurements included, exactly as it stood in CLAUDE.md at trunk efa4293d55 before rf2-nho5z condensed the section. Surrounding context: git show efa4293d55:CLAUDE.md

`.beads/issues.jsonl` is a full-database export, not an ordinary source file, **and it is a SNAPSHOT SOMETHING HAS TO INSTALL rather than a mirror `bd` keeps current. An ordinary tracker write does NOT regenerate it** (rf2-xmpm8): a `bd create`, `bd update` or `bd close` lands in the Dolt database, and the tracked file does not move. Measured at trunk `7bfa3bab2e` on `bd` 1.2.2 (6c124203e), taking the write from another agent's authorised update rather than one of the reader's own — the database and a stdout `bd export` carried this very bead at `in_progress` with a 2609-character `notes`, while the tracked `.beads/issues.jsonl` in BOTH the worker worktree and the primary checkout still read `open` at 689 characters, byte-identical to each other and unchanged in SHA256, size and mtime across that export; controls both ways, a third bead reading identically in all three and a nonexistent id absent from all three. **An explicit `bd export` does not write it either, because `bd export` DEFAULTS TO STDOUT** — its help reads `-o, --output string   Output file path (default: stdout)`, so it takes a redirect or an `-o` to land anywhere at all. What installs the tracked file is `scripts/beads-checkpoint.sh`, which exports to a TEMPORARY file (`bd export --include-memories > "$TMP_EXPORT"`, lines 497-505), validates it against a row-count floor and a divergence guard, and only then copies it over the tracked path (lines 694/699). A checkout therefore receives this file the way it receives any other tracked file, so each worker worktree carries a snapshot of the tracker as it stood at the commit that worktree was created from, and that snapshot goes stale as the tracker moves on. Committing that snapshot **time-travels the tracker**: beads closed since it reopen, beads filed since it vanish. PR #6677 landed exactly that — 135 insertions / 136 deletions of pure collateral. **A `bd` READ is not how a worktree acquires tracker state, and reading your own bead is safe** (rf2-oitjw): measured 2026-09-17 on `bd` 1.2.2, five reads — `bd show --json`, `bd ready`, `bd list`, `bd recall` and a plain `bd show` — run from a FRESHLY created worktree and again from one already in use each exited 0 and left that checkout at zero porcelain lines with `.beads/issues.jsonl` byte-identical, the same blob hash, the same size, an unchanged mtime and no file added to `.beads/`; an 18-byte append to that same file moved every one of those readings, so the zeros are the instrument working rather than a probe that cannot see. **Read that as a statement about READS ALONE** — not because a write would dirty your checkout, which is precisely what the measurement above refutes, but because a write from a worktree mutates the SHARED database every other worktree is reading. **So the tracked file is the wrong instrument for noticing one: a clean `git status` after a `bd` write is the EXPECTED reading, not evidence the write did nothing**, and it fails in the reassuring direction. **None of this licenses the converse that `bd` never writes a JSONL, and the scope is the CONFIGURATION rather than the tool**: `.beads/config.yaml` documents a `no-db` mode in which `.beads/issues.jsonl` IS the source of truth and every write therefore moves it, an `events-export` that appends `.beads/events.jsonl` on each flush, and a periodic JSONL backup "Auto-enabled when a git remote exists", which this repo's `sync.remote` satisfies. Those three are read off that file's own commentary rather than measured here, and that is the point — a changed setting, a `bd` upgrade, or an `-o` pointed at the tracked path would each falsify the measurement above with nothing on screen saying so. The staleness needs no `bd` invocation at all to arise — two live worktrees created seven minutes apart held export snapshots differing by 11 insertions / 7 deletions — so every prohibition below stands as written, and none of them was ever a reason not to read the tracker from a worktree.

bd history <id> --json CAN RETURN A BARE `null` AT EXIT 0, INTERMITTENTLY. It reads exactly like "this bead has no history", and the plain-text form run beside it can still list entries. Measured 2026-10-16 (bd 1.3.1).

WHAT HAPPENED. Two independent workers, both running from linked worktrees while the tracker was busy (a Codex pruning campaign plus a merge-audit harness both writing), got `null` from `bd history <id> --json` with and without `--limit`. Each also got `null` for a control bead. One saw the plain `bd history <id>` list 9 entries in the same window. Minutes later the mayor re-ran the same commands, from the primary checkout and from one of those worktrees, and both returned full JSON arrays (`Issue` nested per snapshot, about 9-10 KB for 3 entries). It did not reproduce.

WHY IT MATTERS. CLAUDE.md § Beads durability names `bd history <id> --json --limit N` as recovery route (2) for a close reason erased by a reopen. A `null` there reads as "no snapshot carries it". That sends the recoverer to give up, or to restore from the wrong place.

GUARD. Treat a `null` (or `[]`) from `bd history --json` as UNKNOWN, not as empty.
- Re-run it, and check a control bead known to have history in the same breath.
- Compare with the plain `bd history <id>` count.
- For close-reason recovery, route (1) does not depend on bd at all: walk `.beads/issues.jsonl` across checkpoint commits with `git show <rev>:.beads/issues.jsonl | jq ... select(.id==$i)`.

NIGHTLY TRACKING ISSUES ("Nightly `expensive tests` is red") CLOSE THEMSELVES: NEVER CLOSE ONE BY HAND, AND NEVER LET A PR CLOSE ONE WITH A "Fixes/Closes #N" KEYWORD. `.github/scripts/nightly_failure_alert.py` opens, edits and closes them, and closes only after `--close-after` (default 3) CONSECUTIVE green nightlies, because a single green after a red is often an intermittent gate (its header measures this against 30 runs). Its state lives in the issue body marker `<!-- nightly-alert:v1 signature=… reds=N greens=M -->`, and it queries OPEN issues only (`issues?state=open`), so a manual close throws the streak away: a recurrence then opens a brand-new issue (a loud notification, history split across issues) instead of editing the old one. Measured 2026-10-17: the mayor closed #11459 after one green re-run of the failed job ("transient dependency-resolution failure") and Mike flagged it; it was reopened with the marker intact (reds=1 greens=1). The same day #11448 was closed by a merged fix PR's closing keyword before any green nightly on main, so the next red (a different signature) opened #11459 instead of editing #11448. HOW TO APPLY: when a nightly issue's fix merges, comment on the issue with the fix PR and any green run link, and leave it open; the script closes it after three greens. In worker briefs, tell the worker to reference the issue in the PR body without a closing keyword. To confirm a fix early, a workflow_dispatch run on main counts toward the script's green streak.

An orphaned bd process can stall the whole tracker for every session on the machine. Measured 2026-10-20 08:35-08:48 AUSEST. A worker's Bash tool call hit its 120 s timeout and was backgrounded; its `bd show <id> --json` kept running as bd.exe with no live parent shell. It held .beads/embeddeddolt.gate.lock and the store's noms data file (about 1.65 GB) for about 13 minutes while using roughly 9% of a core. Every other bd call from every worktree and session queued behind it at 0 CPU, writes included, and the store's last write froze. Diagnose with Windows' Restart Manager (rstrtmgr RmGetList on embeddeddolt.gate.lock and noms/vvvv...): the ONE process with the noms data file open is the holder, and the rest are waiters. The oldest bd process is NOT necessarily the holder; here it was another session's `bd list --all`, which was only waiting. Remedy: do not kill (it was progressing and finished on its own), and stop the pile-up by telling workers never to re-issue a queued bd call, because each retry adds an orphan waiter. Run bd under `timeout 600` in the foreground, or backgrounded with run_in_background, never under a shell call that can time out and orphan it.

A HUNG `bd dolt push` HOLDS THE EMBEDDED STORE LOCK FOR ITS WHOLE RUN, SO EVERY WORKER'S bd CALL QUEUES BEHIND IT SILENTLY (measured 2026-10-21). The mayor's `timeout 900 bd dolt push` started 21:17:06 AUSEST, printed only 'Pushing to Dolt remote...', and was killed at 21:32:12 (exit 124); earlier pushes the same day took 1-3 minutes. During those 15 minutes six worker bd processes (show, update --claim, update --append-notes) sat queued, the oldest created 21:17:06, and a mayor `bd ready --limit 1` took 20.5 s. Within a minute of the kill the queue was empty and the same read took 4.5 s. Nothing reports the stall: the workers' calls just wait. GUARD: run the push detached with a SHORT timeout (300 s, not 900), and if it times out, check for queued bd.exe rows (Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='bd.exe'") before retrying; retry at the next checkpoint rather than at once. The git checkpoint of .beads/issues.jsonl is the durable copy in the meantime, so a skipped Dolt push loses nothing. Cause of the hang itself not established (no dolt.exe child was alive; the Codex merge-audit harness also pushes this remote).

DOLT'S GIT-BACKED REMOTE RE-UPLOADS THE WHOLE DATABASE EVERY 64 PUSHES, AND THAT ONE PUSH NEEDS MORE TIME THAN THE OTHERS (measured 2026-10-23 under rf2-hwp30).

The mechanism:
- Dolt's git-remote code (dolt 796d07497741, the version bd 1.3.1 is built on) has a compiled-in `maxParentedCommits = 64`.
- Before each manifest commit it counts the remote branch's history. At 64 or more it writes the next commit with NO PARENT and force-pushes it.
- That commit shares no history with GitHub's copy, so git uploads every table file. Measured: 901,154,178 bytes (859 MiB), about 2 min 40 s at 5.6 MB/s.
- Every other push is small and takes seconds.

The symptom: `bd dolt push` prints "Pushing to Dolt remote..." and hangs while holding the store lock. Every other bd call on the machine queues behind it; see memory bd-dolt-push-holds-the-store-lock-and-a-hung-push-stalls-every-worker. A timeout that kills it leaves the remote at 64, so EVERY retry is the full upload again, and under a short timeout every retry dies identically. That is how 10-21's pushes stalled for a day.

The tell: the remote branch is at 63 or 64 commits. Count the history of the cache repo's fetched ref: `git -C .beads/embeddeddolt/rf2/.dolt/git-remote-cache/<hash>/repo.git rev-list --count FETCH_HEAD`.

GUARD:
- Run ordinary pushes detached under `timeout 300`.
- When one times out, do not retry under the same budget. Run ONE push under `timeout 900`, detached, while the fleet is quiet.

Not a fault:
- The local staging refs under that cache repo are leftovers of killed full uploads. They are harmless.
- The remote itself holds only refs/dolt/data, heads/main, heads/__dolt_remote_info__ and HEAD.

Growth matters: about 30% more data, or a slower link, pushes the full upload past 300 s.

Operator rule (Mike, 2026-10-29): never create a shell-script file and then run it, and never run anything that stops to ask for a yes or a confirmation. Every prompt blocks the run until Mike answers it, so it kills fleet throughput. Mike said so explicitly: "Don't create shell scripts which require me to press yes to continue" and "It kills throughput".

How to apply: run commands inline rather than from ad-hoc .sh files, and the mayor's own merge-check counts as one of those. Use non-interactive forms throughout: -y / --yes, npx --yes, -Confirm:$false in PowerShell, -o BatchMode=yes. Never use read -p, rm -i, cmd /c from Git Bash, or an interactive git flag. Every dispatch brief should carry this line, because workers write probe and gate wrappers by reflex. If a step seems to need a confirmation, use its non-interactive form, or stop and report.

Tool hazard (measured 2026-10-29, hit twice in one session): the agent harness's file-editing path DECODES a JSON-style escape in the text it writes, so `<` typed into a Write/Edit payload, or into a `bd --reason` / `--append-notes` string, lands as a bare `<`. The edit reports success, and the line reads plausibly afterwards ("escape `<` as `<`"), so nothing flags it.

It struck the SSR fix (PR #11722, caught before merge) and the security fix (PR #11737, which merged a wrong row into implementation/SECURITY.md; repaired by #11739). The security bead's close reason lost the escape the same way.

Guard: after any edit whose intended text contains a backslash-u escape, search the written file for the literal `u003c` (`git grep -F 'u003c' -- <file>`) and confirm it is present. To write one, edit the bytes with Python (`open(p,'rb')` / `replace(b'...', b'\u003c')`) rather than through the editing tools. Related: CLAUDE.md instrument hazard (o), where the Bash tool halves backslash runs.

NEVER WRAP scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh IN A SHORT `timeout` — A KILL MID-REMOVAL LEAVES A GUTTED TREE THAT GIT STILL REGISTERS (2026-10-30).

WHAT HAPPENED. The mayor ran `timeout 280 sh scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh <tree>` on a finished worker's tree. That tree had its own `npm ci` node_modules (no junction), so the delete took longer than 280 s. The timeout killed the script, and with it `git worktree remove`, partway through deleting the tree. The log stopped at `NO_LINKS=`, with `rm=124`.

THE STATE IT LEFT. This is not the script's documented husk. The worktree was STILL in `git worktree list`, but its `.git` file was gone, so `git -C <tree>` failed with "not a git repository". Most source files were still on disk, and `git branch -D` refused ("used by worktree").

RECOVERY THAT WORKED:
1. `git worktree prune --dry-run -v`. It named only that entry ("gitdir file points to non-existent location").
2. `git worktree prune -v`.
3. `sh scripts/remove-worker-worktree.sh --husk <abs path>`. It established HUSK_PROVENANCE (210 KB of blobs git knows), printed NO_LINKS, then exited 3 with REMOVE_PARTIAL and recommended `rm -rf`.
4. `rm -rf <abs path>`, run detached.
5. `git branch -D`.
6. The mayor's node_modules count was unchanged.

HOW TO APPLY. Run the removal script detached (`run_in_background`) with no `timeout` wrapper, and read its own exit code. A tree with a real `npm ci` install can take many minutes to delete on Windows. The same hazard on `git worktree add` is in [[worktree-add-killed-by-2min-timeout]].
